Server randomly gets desynced. You play 80% of the game desync'd. If you don't know what that means, it means the server is at one point, and the client is at another. This can cause rubberbanding. There isn't rubberbanding per say, but as soon as you look at the combat system you'll notice something is messed up. Hitting players while "lagging" or being desynced is beyond stupid. You cannot hit ever. You can only hit if they stand still for a second, which nevner happens. You can test it yourself by joining any server with a decent amount of players, play for a few minutes, then strafe back and forth and try to hit someone who has ping higher than 100 (which is most of the game.) It might seem like a small thing but the whole game is combat. You protect yourself with it, and you gain advantages with it. Hell, even the bunnies running around get desyned more than often.
Game is very fun beyond this, but infuriating when you can't even fight fairly. Unplayable to an extent with this. Once it's fixed then you can think about buying it. Until then, I'd wait.

Slime Rancher is one of *those* games - you know the kind. You don't think it'll interest you because it looks repetitive and limited. And it's early access, so why would you invest if you don't know for sure where it'll go? But then you watch someone close to you play it. And he seems to enjoy it quite a lot, too. Then he asks you to come check out his cute new slime. Or the statue he just added to his ranch. And then he'll let you try it once - just vacuum up those carrots and throw them at the slimes. Vacuum up their little drops. Put them in the machine in exchange for gold. This is actually kind of fun! So you buy the game and start playing. It's only €20, worst case scenario, you decide you don't like it as much as you thought, after a couple of hours. So you start playing, suck up some cute pink slimes, build them a nice house, figure out what the big slimes are, explore the lands, collect treasures, buy upgrades - and before you know it, you are 75 hours into the game and are asking yourself if the game was really worth it... and the answer is "Yes".

Creating something unique is becoming a more and more difficult task in the world of smartphone gaming. There are so many games out there, and so many other people making new ones, that your brilliant idea has probably already been built and released.
Equally, the huge swathe of clones and copycats that bloat the App Store make it even more refreshing when something does come along that's that little bit different. Muffin Knight, from Angry Mob Games, is one such breath of fresh air.
As original as it is in the context of the App Store, however, it's important to note that Muffin Knight borrows heavily from Vlambeer's excellent Super Crate Box, which is also coming to iOS this month.
Knights currant
You play a young boy who accidentally scatters a basket of magic muffins to the four corners of a cartoon-style fairytale world. Incensed by your actions, the fairy whose muffins they were turns you into a knight and sends you off on a quest to retrieve the arcane cakes.
This takes the form of jumping around enclosed levels, killing scuttling pigs and other beasts and grabbing the deliciously enhanced buns. The twist is that every time you pick up a muffin you change class. You'll start as the eponymous Knight, but for the first few play throughs you'll swap between a mage, an archer, and a goblin as well.
The characters all have different strengths and weaknesses, and as you play through the game you'll unlock new classes as well.
While the original four are all quite similar ranged fighters, later in the game you'll have rainbow mine-pooping unicorns, fire-breathing dragons, and claw swiping bears at your disposal too.
Confectionery crisis
You unlock new classes when you've picked up enough muffins, but you also gain XP for slaying enemies and gathering the small cakes. You can spend this XP on levelling up your characters, making them quicker and their attacks more potent.
Of course, you're never sure which characters you're going to be in the game, so it's entirely possible to swap straight from a super-powered Knight to a one-starred kitten ninja in one muffin-fuelled swoop.
All in all there are six levels to play through, all of which can be attacked multiple times, and 15 characters to unlock and upgrade. There's a multiplayer mode as well, which lets you connect with other iPhones over a local wi-fi network, to duke it out over who's the muffin-collecting monarch.
Buns of zeal
Muffin Knight looks good, sounds good, and has a great, original idea at its core, but it's not all sweetness and light. The control system isn't perfect, with taps of the on-screen buttons sometimes not registering.
It's pretty difficult as well, though even failure is rewarded with XP, meaning you'll be stronger the next time around. The lack of levels might put some off, but every play through is going to be different because your character changes are allocated entirely at random.
These problems are mere niggles, though, and shouldn't dissuade you from playing this hugely enjoyable action-platformer. This is a leaping, blasting, clawing slice of fun that deserves to find a home on as many iOS devices as possible.

In defense of this game, it works.  Which is really a big thing for a lot of low effort 2D platformers/shooters/whatever the indie studios churn out in shovelware by the tonne every year.
The sound and graphics really function.
The art style for a lot of the levels is thematically ripped from a strange combination of Mario and World of Warcraft.   Look, we're in Undercity! Look, we're in Zangarmarsh!
Gameplay is nothing new, the basic mechanic is present in literally over 1,000 Steam titles, you jump, you shoot, there's multiplayer jump and shoot.
totally inventive new enemies like sheep fall out of the sky and you have to kill them.
It's hard to give this the thumbs down, because the developers achieved what they set out to do.
So, why the thumbs down?   Firstly - there's not enough technical customisability.  We can't even force the resolution.  The game handles okay today, but next year, the year after, it's going to fail to remain playable on newer systems.   This is a handicap enforced by the multiplatform system (because you know, console gamers and tablet gamers and PC gamers have so much in common).
Secondly, well, what is this game contributing to anything?  I said earlier the developers achieved what they set out to do.   They succeeded in creating a game that fills no special niches, is derivative, and will certainly fail to be remembered alongside hundreds of other 2D indy platformers released every year hoping to be Super Meat Boy.  Was it a good idea to set out to do this? No, even if they succeeded.   This isn't worth the current price of $7 USD on Steam they're asking for.   Go play Super Mario Brothers on an emulator or something if you really have to do 2D platforming.

*This review was written after completing the game on beta patch 1.2*
Dishonored 2 when released did not perform well on most systems although with Beta Patch 1.2 performance has improved by a significant margin.
With a I5 4690K and a GTX 980 I was able to get 60 FPS with dips to 50 at certain times with the settings at HIGH and texture and model settings set to VERY HIGH. So by no means does this game run as well as it should but it is in my opinion more than playable.
Now onto the game itself.
DESIGN:
Dishonored 2 takes up the good aspects of Dishonored 1's design and expands on them with bigger mission areas, more variation in the contents of the missions themselves while it also has improved on the level design itself. the art direction is still very much inline with the first Dishonored but the improvement to the animations, lighting, models and texturework give the game it's modernized edge and actually helps set up an even more gripping atmosphere than Dishonored 1 did.
COMBAT:
As in Dishonored 1 the game allows you to play in a vast amount of ways, if the targets are to live or die is up to you but this time around both Emily and Corvo have a bigger variaty of tools to help them along. Many return from the first installment but fresh new additions mix up the gameplay quite a bit. Even pacifists can now punch peoples lights out while in combat meaning conflict doesn't have to end up in bloodshed. However if you want to splatter some blood you can now do that in more ways than before so it's a win-win for all.
STEALTH:
The AI has been notably improved, they now notice whenever things in the enviroment have changed and this time  whenever our protagonist is leaning in and peaking from a corner they won't ignore the head sticking out from behind the doorframe meaning getting by undetected is more of a challenge now. In addition the gaurds can actually see more than 10 feet in front of them this time around which in my book is an improvement.
STORY:
Just as in the first game the story plays out diffferently depending on how you handle situations throughout the game, playing the game differently will result in different endings. And with two different protagonists there is an abundance of ways key parts of the campaign can play out meaning multiple playthroughs will still feel fresh. The characters themselves are interesting as well with some returning from the first game but none of the characters in Dishonored 2 are there purely for fanservice they all have their purpose in the story. The game also still features a ton of books notes letters and scribbles that tell you a lot about the history, people, areas, folktales that the world of Dishonored has to offer so in short: More Lore. And it's all stilll as well written as in the first game.
CONCLUSION:
Would I recommend Dishonered in it's current state?
1)Have you played Dishonored 1? Then yes, if not I recommend playing the first title before this one so you can get a beter understanding of the story and the atmosphere of these games.
2)If you have a high(er) end pc then yes. If not I would wait for more patches untill the game runs as it should be running. But performance issues aside the game is incredibly well designed, taking everything good that made Dishonored 1 stand out and improving upon it while also ironing out flaws which the first installment had. So it's more of the good stuff and less of the bad stuff, all in all it is worth the price.

This seems to be easily the best Worms game since Worms World Party, but that is not saying very much or make me sing praises. This is getting positive reviews because it's better than the last dozen weak Worms games and because there isn't any competition in the genre. It's an alright game for casual gamers and kids, but the 30 euro price tag??? If this was 10-20 euros, I could've given a positive review. For more hardcore wormers Worms Armageddon is still the only choice.
I didn't have that much time to play the game myself, but I've watched several hours of gameplay videos. This is what I gathered:
+ Map textures are pretty cool looking and there's no noisy disruptive background.
+ UI and menus are better and more PC friendly than in the previous games, also better optimization, plays much smoother than Rev/CW for example.
+ Physics gone to the right direction as well?
- UI still really consoley, the PC version really should have slicker look and handling.
- Team17 created this purely for casual players and kids only. You won't find that much skill-based weapons or scheme customization. A lot of the weapons and utilities have been dumbed down to oblivion, for example Parachute.
- Crafting! Such crappy idea. If it was completely optional, but no: you can't include craftable weapon variations in scheme editor, which is the dumbest thing I've seen in a game in a while. The vehicles are boringly implemented as well and unbalanced.
(- I must mention the exclusive pre-order bonuses?!? What were they thinking? If the bonuses were purely cosmetic, it would've been fine, but this is not the case...)
They took a step into the right direction with this one, but it's not enough for me, I will refund. Lastly I want to bring up a couple of big problems the Worms series has had for years:
1. If Team17 created the perfect Worms game, they couldn't keep making a new ones every other year. They need to make money, so they consciously leave stuff out (for example deep customization, which would bring a lot of replayability). The solution could be f2p, but it's hard to do well. Or maybe they should just make more games that are not Worms?
2. Team17 wants to make casual games for kids, but there is a big group of old school WA wormers who want a new competitive and skill-based Worms type game with modern ELO ranking ladders etc. Who will bring them that? Obviously not T17, they clearly don't care about that or still even understand what WA is all about.

Having played and beaten both Demon Souls and the first Dark Souls multiple times, I thought this game would be somewhat of a cake walk... I've never been so wrong in my life. From Software once again does not fail to deliver in the brutality department.

What can I say about Dark Souls that hasn't already been said? Do you like games? check. Do you like RPGs? check. Then get this now!
Have you hacked and slashed your way to boredom? Then master the art of precisionly calculated strikes and actions that will have your anxiety face tingling. Gasp in regret as your ill-timed assaults lead to your immediate demise. Praise the sun in glorious satisfaction as you emoticon your way to an intensly satisfying boss kill.
Tired of the endless grinding in mmos? Why spend hours working up to the fun of endgame, when you can enjoy an experience that is tailor made to kick your♥♥♥♥♥at every single encounter you ... encounter.
All you duty callers need to get on this pvp. There is no other game in existence that lets you invade another player's game and put a direct stop to his progress and humanity. What does he think he is, making progress. None of that. You be dead, I be red.
But I like exposition!! Explanations you say?! Dark Souls takes it back to the days when abstract half directions were all you needed. You don't like the jib of that NPC? guess what? you can break his face and loot his junk. Can you really reign death upon everything in this game? yes ofcourse ... but no ... don't do that or else who will upgrade your stuff and stats.
Who needs stats, you say?! Take it easy there diablo fan and listen up. There is freedom granted to your stat deprived♥♥♥♥♥life with tons of ways of potentially gimping your character. 9 main upgradeable stats await your scrutiny as well as countless weapons, armors, magicks, pyromancy, lightning, dark, ranged all of them capable of dishing out pierce, slash, poison, cursed, fire ... and then they can scale with primary stats ... and ... there's so many ... combinations ... so much planning ... wiki help ...
The world is dark and foreboding, the atmosphere pulls you in and the gameplay demands you bring your full focus and strategizing abilities. If you feel lonely just drop a summon sign and practice in someone else's world. Need some help? Pray no one invades you as you seek out them summon signs. Do not be dismayed by the challenge it presents, because with it you will know the sweet nectar that is victory ... and then you will die ... but eventually you will overcome ... and then you will die again ... but never unfairly so, because with each death you will learn and grow a bit wiser. Every enemy is a threat, every encounter has a strategy, know your character inside and out and you will succeed.
It is among the most satisfying experiences you will ever have playing a video game.
Praise the sun.

I love smite I really do, it was my game of the year last year, and it will almost always be at the top of my lists, despite all things I hate about it. These devs also listen....and I do mean LISTEN.....to what their user-base are saying and they act on it as quickly and as much as they possibly can do.  You definitely get a sense of the devs loving this game as much, or maybe even more than, the 98 (that's NINETY-MOTHERF*CKING-EIGHT!!!) percent of users who rated this unfinished game positively, and this shows in the discussions as they're always on there, either making notes of what they might need to change or replying to users who are stuck with a certain aspect of it.  Questions like,
"I bought Broforce and it won't run on my PC.  I start it, it pops up for a second then closes again.  What's the problem?", to which the correct response is,
"Holy Sh*tting f*ckaduck!!  We didn't know there were still people running RIVA TNT2 graphics cards!!".
At this juncture, on a semi-serious note, I'd like you, yes YOU, to show me any other Early Access game with a 98% positive rating from 8,000+ reviews, seriously, try and find one.....That's right, you CAN'T!! That alone should tell you how god-damn, mamma-jamma-in', dog's-b*ll*ck's, bee's-knees, badger's-'nadgers and other funny, rhyming animal body parts chuffin' awesome this game truly is.

I do wish however that the 7zee rewards club prices were a bit lower, and maybe the lvl 3 treasure cracker cotsing 20k instead of 25k (unless the lvl 2 cracker costs 20k, which I don't think it does).

This game is a Spectacular chaos of sheer joy. You will bound to have hours and hours of fun. (Pro's and Con's down the list). Also i have heard AMD users have many troubles playing this game, but Nvidia users like me have perfect performance.
The story is you are Rico Rodriguez who goes to a Mediterranian County complete with multiple gigantic islands and vast warm environments, Rico has come here to rid the county of it's oppressive ruler by liberating towns, cities , outposts or straight up miltary bases. The culture of the people is a mix of Italian and Spanish roots. And the gameplay is just complete fun throughout.
You can access to a great amount of guns and vehicles as well as many other things. What's best about this game is the ability to use a Grappling hook (which can instantly transport Rico to places fast, even on roofs, tether two objects together and pull them together), Wingsuit which is a superb and fun way of travelling the skies, Parachuting for the slower and simpler flying and the absurdly high resistance to taking damage like crashing into cliffs and cars as well as plumeting from big heights.
Along with this you have a GIGANTIC world to explore, it's so massive and is fun to go across as well as so vast and big. Theres also so many activities and challenges you can do along the way. however you do come across repetition which is expected with open world games, alot of the cities and sights look roughly the same but there is some variety with different things in each town or city, for instance you can go to one base and find you need to get rid of the speakers, destroy fuel tanks and destroy the transformer. OR you could find you have to do a timed event of shutting off the monitors, destroying speaker vans, destroying billboards and causing ramage in the police stations.

The newest entry in the venerable Worms series includes training missions, campaign scenarios, challenges, local multiplayer skirmishes on random maps, and online ranked and unranked matches. Customizing the team comes with fewer options than before, although the game rules can be tweaked multiple ways. The same general gameplay survives, but several significant new features are present. First, weapons can be crafted, either from parts taken from crates or from existing weapons that are dismantled. This allows for new or more powerful versions of weapons to be created, and allows for some adaptation to the current game situation. Buildings can be entered, which protect and hide worms from the enemy. Vehicles are also new, with rocket cars, tanks, and helicopters able to grant fast movement and mobile attacking. Finally, stationary turrets give additional firepower to the battlefield. All of these new features can be disabled in the game rules, so they are completely optional. The AI is a capable opponent on higher difficulty levels. With meaningful additions to the game mechanics, Worms W.M.D. is the best version of the turn-based strategy series to appear in years.

Nice try, but no cigar.  This game looked really promising.  I was excited that we finally had cross-platform Worms and online multiplayer.  I was excited to see a game ready to take the mantle of Best Worms from Armageddon.  Unfortunately, it's just not ready for prime time.
First, cross-platform multiplayer is not possible.  You can't play with your friends on Linux from a Windows machine, for example.
Second, because the Steam overlay is broken for Worms in Linux, you can't invite someone to multiplayer games in Linux, making multiplayer lobbies with your friends on Linux an impossibility at this point.  I expect they'll fix this bug soon, but when I buy a game I expect to be able to play it with my friends today, not at some nebulous point in the future when the bug is fixed.
Finally, and this is a minor detail, you can't have bots in online multiplayer matches.  So, if you wanted to play multiplayer with a friend online to teach them to play, you're going to have to do it without bots for a punching bag.
Worms is a game that's all about multiplayer.  Nobody buys it for campaign.  Without cross-platform multiplayer, your community is split in three.  Without bots in online friends lobbies, you can't introduce new people to the game as easily.  Taken together, this makes it hard to grow the community.  With that in mind, I can't recommend Worms WMD.  It's a niche game to begin with, and without a single, consistent multiplayer experience and a way to introduce new players to Worms, I expect it's going to stay niche for the foreseeable future.

Worms W.M.D is the latest installment in Team 17‘s long running artillery strategy series about warring annelids. Due to popular demand, the game’s developer decided to go back to the series’ roots and make a true 2d game, though W.M.D still presents many changes over its predecessors.
The basic gameplay mechanics are the same as they’ve been for two decades. Players command a team of worms (which may be customized with different voice packs, gravestones and visual styles) and must defeat an opposing worm force using a wide variety of wacky weapons. The action still flows perfectly from turn to turn, and drowning enemy worms is as satisfying as it was a decade ago.
Worms W.M.D‘s presentation echoes Worms Armageddon, a game which most longtime fans of the franchise still consider as the best. From the detailed 2d art, to the removal of some controversial features such as classes or water physics, everything screams “your childhood favorite is back!” This doesn’t mean that W.M.D doesn’t try a few new things though. Team 17‘s new game introduces several new concepts to the strategy franchise, with varying degrees of success.
Chief among the game’s new toys is the ability to pilot vehicles and man static weapon emplacements. Worms can now get in the driving seat of tanks, mechs and helicopters, adding some interesting dynamics to the battlefield. Taking command of a helicopter and raining fire from above as the enemy team sits in an oil barrel filled zone never gets old. The static guns also offer new strategic options, as players have to choose between mobility and firepower, and the mounted weapons platforms can be destroyed, dealing damage to their operators when that happens.
The second game-changing addition is the crafting system. Worms can now collect resources (or dismantle old weapons to obtain the bits that make them work) and craft new weaponry, making an already unpredictable game even more chaotic. Enterprising players will rapidly learn that they can actually use the enemy’s turn to craft new gear, a welcome distraction when the opposing commander is laying waste to your troops.
Players can now make use of buildings to shelter themselves from enemy bombardment or prying eyes. Sadly, the execution isn’t as polished as one would desire, and sometimes it’s hard to tell which part of the environment is a building, and which is just part of the map’s decoration (a problem that was already present in Worms: Clan Wars, although that game didn’t feature buildings in the same way as W.M.D)
Worm customization, a hallmark of the series, has been given an incredible amount of detail. There is a leveling system that gradually unlocks more hats, gravestones, voice packs and music, making players feel as if there’s always something new to try out.
The game’s content is as plentiful as the customization options, with a generous amount of singleplayer missions and challenges, and an extensive multiplayer suite. Worms W.M.D also features Steam Workshop support, letting players download new maps created by other gamers with the included level editor.
Worms W.M.D is a successful reimagining of the long running artillery strategy series, mixing Armageddon‘s colorful visuals and tight gameplay with some welcome additions. Team 17 has created a new classic, easily recommended for both newcomers and longtime fans of the franchise.

Let's see, where to start with this free, but surprisingly good game?  I admit I was initially skeptical about how a game with seemingly simple graphics could receive so many positive reviews after being released so recently, but I am now a believer and I think anyone who is reading this review and has not tried this game yet?  Download it.  Download it now.  Not tomorrow.  Not next week.  Do it now.  Because it is that good.
Now, if you want to hear my thoughts, this is what I think of the game:
This game is well crafted and I have only one complaint which I will address at the end of this review.
The combat, while simple at first glace, has a surprising amount of depth in that it is not just a typical hack and slash approach to the top down format of retro games like this Eternal Senia appears to be (though that does not mean a person cannot go full berzerker in all combat if they wished to :P).  But beyond the normal sword swinging, there are the four primary skills which are gained progressively as the story unfolds where each has its own uses and none of these skills ever truly feel useless even as the enemies become more tough and varied in their own attacks.
The music is a decent mix and works to complement the story rather than jarringly remove the player from immersing in this game.  There is even one piano piece roughly two-thirds to three-quarters through the game that is an almost hauntingly beautiful expression of what is yet to come when the final confrontation occurs.   If you are a completion freak like me, you will fight to get all three possible endings and likely hear this piece again and again and again.
Even with the dialogue taking up a significant portion of the cutscenes, it never feels as though the words are coming out in a way that is overpowering the player in an information dump of sorts.  Instead, the dialogue is concise enough to not be a bore but contains enough to help establish the history of each character, the motivations behind what pushes each of them to reach their goal, and how our heroine ended up fighting her way through each location all for one of the most basic driving forces in human biology and human history: love.
Between all the fighting and all the dialogue, there are a number of puzzles encountered.  Some of them need to be solved in order progress the story while others are optional in order to gain rewards that do not affect the ending of the story.  For this little addition in how the ending is not affected, I must compliment the maker of the game as this makes the overall experience less of a grinding session and more of a fun little tease to search for ways to accomplish the side goals and gain a few more rather nice rewards along the way.
And another thing that makes this already good game better?  It is free.  Yes, you heard it right.  It is not so many percent off during certain sales periods on steam.  It is not limited time offer with in-game purchases.  It is not pay to win.  It is free.  Period.  How much better can this game get?
But, all good things must come to an end and that was and is my only complaint.  As much as I wish for more, every good story has an ending and some or even all of the endings may have you complaining that there are too many onions being cut nearby (hint: bring some tissues :P).  Still, it was a very touching set of endings and if the maker ever decides to make more games in the future, I will definitely try them out.

Alien: Isolation captures the 80's retro magic of the traditional Alien movies with the futuristic notion of space travel to bring you a stealth-based action/horror experience that you won't forget.
__________
Synopsis:
You play as the Amanda Ripley, the daughter of Ellen Ripley from the movie Alien, as she attempts to find any trace of her mother that disappeared 15 years ago. Using a plethora of hand-crafted gadgets and weapons, you must make your way around the Sevastopol, fixing critical ship mechanics and finding more information about your mother's disappearance. Be warned; there are many more dangers than you think.
_____
Story: The story is a pleasant mix of predictable, yet surprising elements, coupled with an almost overwhelming sense of dread at what comes around the next corner. It borrows many elements from Dead Space, but not all of them positive. As Issac did, you board a derelict spaceship and start finding mechanisms to repair in order to progress throughout the story. After a while, however, you feel like the game has adopted a "Murphy's Law" type of philosophy, and the game seems to drag out towards the end after fixing almost everything on the ship by yourself. The actual story is good, but suffers towards the end of the game.
Graphics: Marvelous graphics and environments really capture the essence of the traditional Alien movie. Light years from Earth, yet staring at an old Macintosh using an IBM keyboard shows a level of attention to detail that is not regularly seen. The environment really helps impose a sense of helplessness and dread as you realize the ship has gone to hell.
Functionality and Gameplay: A:I gives a sense of empowerment, yet helplessness to the player. While you may acquire new weapons and gadgets to kill your enemies, the goal at the end of the day is not to get yourself killed. Coupled with the lack of resources to blast everything with your shotgun, combat is often the last resort. Therein lies a small problem: As you acquire new equipment, you might have a desire to use it to make your life simpler. Often enough, it actually is only usable in a very particular circumstance, and sometimes makes your life harder. The name of the game is being a shadow; staying out of anyone and anything's way. At times this can be incredibly frustrating, but there lies the magic. It really gives you that sense of helplessness. There are enemies around that WILL kill you if you make yourself known, but killing them may not be feasible.
_________________________

**This review contains no spoilers**
I don’t normally review games on these portals but this is an exception and dammit it’s worth it.
It’s been a while since I last completely immersed myself into a single player game having looked forward to it  for many months after announcement. The last game was Metro Last light which was an unexpected surprise considering I played several hours of Metro 2033 and had to uninstall it as I got really bored (and continue to get bored after repeated attempts at getting back into it).
My gut told me that Alien: Isolation was something different. From the get go CA’s steady updates about the game, showing gamer reactions during play testing and easy to digest information being released felt transparent.
Among forum members fears ran wild as to whether the game would live up to the mostly user generated hype and as early reviews started to crop up close to release many people thought it was done for. IGN/Polygon and a couple others rated Isolation with average scores saying it was either too lengthy or too difficult....
Thankfully we actual gamers know what’s what and at the time of writing Isolation has hit the 2nd spot in the UK game sales ranking. Position 1 being the latest FIFA (meh).
Just goes to show professional reviewers aren’t all what they’re cracked out to be.
Let’s get the engine out of the way first. It’s outstanding. CA made a custom engine for this game and the visuals will blow you away especially once you unlock additional reflections and effects. Unlocking has zero hit on performance and even on low to mid end hardware the game runs and looks fantastic.
At an ultra wide resolution of 3440x1440 the game works really nicely and gives full immersion. If you’ve got one of these monitors then you’re in for a treat. The FOV at 55 is the equivalent  of 85 in other games, just be sure to select that.
The gameplay is sound too and the ambience reminiscent of Ridley Scott’s original film. They had access to all of the data archives from the original film so everything is authentic to the movie and it feels like you’re playing a continuation of the film.
There are a few quirks with AI but nothing major. Play on hard and you will be killed many time, the Alien is brutal as are the Working Joe androids. If their eyes glow white you’re safe but if they are red then stay well away unless you have plenty of shotgun shells
It’s nice to see a game not restricted to an aspect ratio or framerate. A game that isn’t a shoddy console port but a PC game giving our platform its all.
I’m still some 12 hours in but felt I had played and seen enough to be able to write an accurate review so far. I would easily give it a 8.5 or 9/10. No game is ever a perfect 10.

Muffin Knight is a super simple platforming game where you run around a level trying to collect muffins and fight monsters. It's a fun concept, and it works great on mobile devices, but this port just doesn't work on a computer. It's just way too simple for a computer, and gravity feels way stronger than in most platformers, which doesn't matter much on a tiny screen but on a computer screen it just feels wrong, especially if you play other platformers with better physics. The layout of the game is exactly like the mobile version, with a level select screen that feels a lot like Angry Birds, or really any other smartphone game. Also, your character changes every time you collect a muffin, which makes it a very fast paced game and it's very hard to have any kind of technique because you never know which character you'll be playing with next. Overall, it's a decent port of a mobile game that just doesn't work on a computer.

Pros and Cons first, description after.
Pros:
- New weapons. Stationary turrets, vehicles, new ways of destruction.
- Inside buildings for cover. For years have Worms introduced a "make your own map" idea and then you spent hours trying to make your map with crawl spaces that resembled buildings for more interesting map interaction.
- Multiplayer is great, adds a series of ranking systems to the game including the training or specialist missions for those who want to prove they are in the top flight of Worms die hards.
- Finally has 8 player Worms teams. No longer are the days when the company gets lazy and imports the console version onto PC with 4 Worms per team.
- Familiarity with weapons and movement makes it easy to get into. A good game for a quick no nonsense mess around.
- Male and Female voice packs available in national languages. Nice to have a little diversity to your worm ensemble.
- Able to craft items during a game and after. These items can be "Super jump rope" or advanced versions of existing known Worms weapons to make it so you can explore other destructive means through playing.
- Jump rope chain linking is possible.
- Magnets, auto turrets, barrels, crates, all things you remember from previous games are there.
Cons:
- Very limited speech packs. I remember other Worms games such as Worms World Party and Worms Armageddon had many more voice packs.
- Current level of unlocks for voice packs is small (5-6 extra). Some of the voices available aren't that different to each other.
- I feel as if the customisation of Worms teams is far less in this edition than previous versions. No doubt they will release more eventually.
- No map maker built in. There is a map generator with limited options you can randomly roll into. You are allowed to see the final product of the creation through their brief window before playing it.
This has the Worms feeling around and those who are fans of the franchise will enjoy it a lot. The individual unlocks, progression on level and crafting system give an option of more replayability than previous games. Previously you had the missions, the specialist trials/missions and multiplayer and that was it.
It's a great game for someone who just wants to sit down with a friend or two and have a laugh blowing up something. If you're reading reviews for it then you're already interested in the Worms game genre. You WILL enjoy this game and it has just about all the things you remember from previous iterations and then more ontop.
Die Hard Fans:
- Check the keyboard settings as you start the game and change as needed, some things aren't where they used to be.
- Don't expect a hilarious falling on the floor wetting yourself voice pack for your team. They are entertaining but not AWESOME.
- They changed classic Worms English voice. They CHANGED it.... Infact, they changed the way Angry Scots sound too. Even their words are different. Why would you re-release the game and then take away or remake the most iconic games voice packs.

First of all, I know what most of you people are thinking as you scroll down the reviews: this game looks ***, why the **** would I play a game where you ******* suck up slimes with a vacgun thingy? My answer: THIS GAME IS AMAZING. I know that most people are hesitant to buy early access games, as most of them have lazy*** developers who ignore their games and its super buggy, glitchy, and poorly optimized. Especially since 20$ seems like a steep price tag. This game is different. The devs have been constantly adding new updates and stuff for the game for a while now, and I got to say, yes, currently at this stage of the game you can "beat it" (I mean unlock everything and be drowning in cash) in about 10 hours. Ok, please don't be those people. Don't watch lets play videos on Youtube. This will severely ruin your experience. You want to take your time and explore. Don't forget-the devs are adding new stuff soon. Don't bore yourself of the game before its full release.
Here's the basic idea of the game(no spoilers): You are on a ranch and you have to raise slimes. There are various types, which you can find around the map with various rarities(careful, some can damage you). These slimes need food, so you need to gather food around the map. When you feed them, each slime produces a plort, which can be used to sell at the market for money. There are 3 basic types of food:Veggies, Fruit, and Meat. The most common slimes, pink slimes, eat anything you throw at them. All the other slimes have only one basic food that they like. Each slime has their own specific favorite food(You can look it up in the Slimepedia after you have sucked them up at least once), and when you feed it to them, they produce double the plorts. That means more money, but all of the slimes' favorite foods(eg stony hens, heart beets, cuberries)  are harder to obtain than regular food(pogoberries, carrots, chickens). Obviously. Using the money you make from selling plorts, you can upgrade your vacpack to hold more stuff, get more energy, health, and buy a jetpack(and etc). You can also spend the money on gardens, coops, silos, incinerators, etc. Gardens are helpful when you dont want to scavenge around for food. Insert a fruit or veggie and the plot fo land will start growing it. Sorry, I have given you too much information already. You need to learn the rest by yourself.

Having played 50 hours, beaten the game 2 times, once on hard and another on medium I can positively say that this is the best Alien game ever to be made. The Creative Assembly set out to do one thing; make the most authentic Alien game, the most horrifying and tense game in the genre and they've succeeded. You are Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, the protagonist from the movies. You find yourself on the space station Sevastopol, only to find that you are not alone and there is a killer on the loose. An 8 foot tall killing machine, a Xenomorph that found its way onto the station. The Xenomorph has an amazing A.I. suite attached to it, it's literally like playing with someone in a multiplayer match. It hunts you down, learns from its mistakes and yours and does not stop until the game manually transfers the pace, which is such a relief at times. You're armed mostly with an arsenal of tools and a trusty motion detector. With these items you can trick the Xeno or manipulate him however you see fit. On board the space station is also humans and synthetic working robots called "Working Joe's", think a dumber ash, a walking mannequin. Both inhabitants can be both helpful, or very lethal.
What makes this game shine is the aesthetic tone to the game. It is incredibly authentic to the original Alien movie, think a 70's vision of the future. Clunky CRT's, cassette tapes and shiny lenolium flooring litter the games world keeping you engrossed in atmosphere the entire (25 hours my first play through). The sound is also incredible. From the orchestral music also authentic to the original movie, to the sounds of floppy disk drives and dot matrix printers. The sounds the Xenomorph are probably the most tense, reptilian, feral and primitive. It strikes fear into you, especially when you have not saved in some time. The thought of having to go toe-to-toe again with the Xenomorph keeps you on the edge at all times. By 15 hours, my diaphram was achey, my nerves were shot and I felt the physical toll this game had taken on my body. Holding my breath for extended amounts of time and not thinking to pause the game was really what caused it. The game wants you to keep playing, YOU want to keep playing. Not just because it's a good game, but because you want to survive, you want to keep going and see Amanda Ripley through this hellish ordeal. That's what makes this game so special. I've never really felt so close to a character before, maybe because I'm such a huge fan of the first film and I can understand her pain and suffering, her sadness of never actually knowing what came of her mother. It was great that CA developed a game that somewhat closed that chapter of the story. I would absolutely love some kind of sequel, but the way it ended was pretty solid. All in all, I'm very happy with this game, I'm very happy with my purchase and I'm glad that this game exists and that I've had the priveledge to experience it.

Dark Souls II is a game about how the post apocalyptic world has to suffer from diseases and such in which you have to save the ones you love dearly by embracing this disease and wandering into the ruins of shrunken version of Brazil.
You start out choosing your attire and your stand and meet some old Brazillian ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who are known as the flame keepers. This hints towards the inevitable failure of the 2016 Summer Olympic Games in Rio De Janeiro where a large nuclear weapon would wipe out the entire South American continent. The flame remaining from the Olympic Games was treasured and spreaded around the corners of the fragmented country to help survivors seek their ways.
Your character seeks to enter Dangalang Castle, an analogy to the old Palácio do Planalto building of Brasília but to enter you require the souls of former major atheletes of Brazil. You venture through out the broken nation to find allies like Luca Tael, Walter Payton, and the Chaos Emerald Herald to help you along the way as you fight through super mutants and blood stained American invaders.
The game also features gang violence as you have the ability to enter a gang and spread their notoriety around the nation. These gangs worship ancient religions such as rodents and celestial bodies. You also venture to churches to ring bells of good fortune but get caught in an unbelievable amount of gang violence on the way there, a symbolism for drug cartels and how religion gets mixed up in such crimes.
Do I recommend this game?
Yes, it's a good foreshadowing of our near grim future and plays very well.

For any and all Half-Life fans, this is fantastic. For any newcomers to the series, this is also fantastic, and you should seriously consider making this your entry into the series if you were put off by
's age.
Black Mesa is a re-make of Half-Life, that's true, but with the effort put into its development over eight-plus years it might as well be a whole new game. And all because they were dissatisfied with Valve porting it to their then-new physics engine in 2004. Pretty much every aspect has been remastered. Worskhop support lets you modify you experience easier than ever before.
If you're not familiar with Half-Life...that's okay. You don't have to be. But if you're looking for a solid FPS that doubles as a solid
, with some brains, a lot of tension (bordering on survival horror at times) and even a little pathos up its sleeve? You could do far worse than this. Just play it on Normal or Easy, for reasons I explain below.
And hey, there's multiplayer included with good maps and decent netcode. It's quite similar to HL's deathmatch at HL2 Deathmatch speed, with a much wider range of player model choices. The actual gameplay is still old-school 'player who gets the best guns first gets to kill everyone quicker' for better or worse.
Okay, now for more technical details/notes for people who've played the mod's original release or the original Half-Life:
Maps have been streamlined from the mod's first launch and from Half-Life. The gameplay itself is different from HL in only one way: it's generally better. The previously mentioned Marines no longer quite resemble hideously overpowered Counter-Strike aimbots (which was a problem in the original release).
The only criticism that could be said of the campaign is that the devs made it noticeably harder than the original Half-Life. At times, this makes the game incredibly frustrating on Hard difficulty unless you follow an optimal strategy and know exactly what to expect for some areas. While classic HL had its difficult moments on Hard difficulty, I don't think it'd be unfair to say that some of BM's hardest moments more resemble tactical shooters like classic Rainbow Six/Ghost Recon. Although considering you're effectively playing Joe Schmoe Freeman, PhD and fighting highly trained US Marines, it might be fitting.
(Being able to land consistent crossbow headshots helps if you have ammunition for it; the energy weapons either come too late or are too weak to efficiently dispatch enemies with.)
BM's graphics, as you might know, could be described as an improvement. Every security guard no longer looks the same. There's actually women scientists now. The Marines have much better voice acting. The 'Black Mesa' tab in the options menu lets you configure a lot of the game's new graphical effects, such as sideways movement bob, revolver ironsights and houndeye tinnitus.
The music is pretty good. Not quite as iconic as the original music, but it definitely shines at times. Comprehensive Workshop mod support, map-making tools and Steamworks features are pretty alright too.
BM's most beautiful element to me, though, is the weaponry. The arsenal's feel is massively improved over the original mod's guns; every one of them is great in their own right. I'd say they even give the original game's weapons a good run for their money.
I already said the developers have put a huge amount of effort into this thing, but they aren't done, either. As of this writing, they're still working on a version of the final section of Half-Life that they said they wanted to make better than the original. There's also various physics bugs that I'm pretty sure they're working on.
Given all of this, Black Mesa is well worth paying for. And even if you didn't like Half-Life, I would recommend it.

My Honest Review of Black Mesa.
To start off, the game is actually quite good, actually better than the original mod version of the game.(I’m not talking about the source version or gold source, i’m talking about the one Crowbar Collective had originally released)
The Game is a Full remake of the First Half-Life game and feels completely different, many Veterans would see this but maybe differently. As movement is more fast paced and weapons feel slightly awkward as if it was trying to mimic Quake a lot more than it means to.
The game is smooth and voice acting is reminiscent of the original. All the graphics are top notch and perfectly fits the game perfectly how it should always be. My only complaint about the core game (The Story) is that there were a ton of loading screens (at least for me). The weapons are still great and very nice and well done. Ammo seems to be a problem, as in the original game I would have stockpiles of ammo ready for any part.
Now the multiplayer was alive, but it’s dying as there really no one playing online anymore. If you can get people to play with you the multiplayer is fast paced and always seems to keep you on your toes. But if you look past what is the base multiplayer, the mode is broken. Lag seems to be a big issue (At least during launch), the lag issue is now at least better and rarely occurred for me. Though over the time the game has been released the game has been patched so performance is no longer a big issue and multiplayer is more bearable.
Overall the game is a 9/10

The negative aspects of this game are the DLCs.  They are not overally inventive, almost all of the factions you can play as fall into several cultural groups (there is no uniqueness to many of the units or even overall look of each faction).
Overall best aspect would be the history part of the armies.  I enjoy looking over the history of my armies, makes creating them and using them far more meaningful.

is an
developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2K Games. It is the second game in the Borderlands series!
is an action role-playing game played from a first-person perspective. The gameplay revolves around the completion of missions and the collection of randomly generated "loot" (such as weapons, shields, skins, and other items) with various rarities, statistics, and elemental effects.
are available in the base game, each with their own unique abilities and skill trees:
can summon a turret to provide offensive support.
can "phaselock" enemies by trapping them in a sphere of energy for a few seconds.
can temporarily become invisible and spawn a hologram decoy to distract enemies; an attack delivered in this state provides bonus damage.
can use his titular ability to temporarily dual-wield weapons.
Five years have passed since the events of Borderlands, when the four Vault Hunters, Roland, Mordecai, Lilith, and Brick were guided by a mysterious entity known as "The Guardian Angel" on the planet of Pandora to the Vault, a mysterious alien structure that was rumored to hold ancient and exotic technology and riches. Instead, these Vault Hunters were confronted by an alien abomination known as "The Destroyer" inside the Vault. After defeating The Destroyer, a valuable mineral called "Eridium" started flourishing through Pandora's crust. Handsome Jack, the president of the Hyperion Corporation, secures this new resource and makes use of it to attempt to "bring peace" to the planet. Now, Handsome Jack rules over the inhabitants of Pandora with an iron fist from his massive satellite built in the shape of an "H", always visible in the sky in front of Pandora's moon. Meanwhile, rumors of an even larger Vault hidden on Pandora spread across the galaxy, drawing a new group of Vault Hunters to the planet in search of it.
The opening cutscene introduces the four new Vault Hunters, who are betrayed by Jack and left for dead in a frozen wasteland. The Vault Hunters are found by the last remaining Hyperion CL4P-TP ("Claptrap") unit. The Guardian Angel contacts the Vault Hunters and instructs them to accompany Claptrap to the city of Sanctuary, and to join the Crimson Raiders, an anti-Hyperion resistance movement, in order to defeat Handsome Jack.
Upon arriving at the gates of Sanctuary, the Vault Hunters are asked to rescue Roland, now leader of the Crimson Raiders, who has been captured by a bounty hunter called the Firehawk. The Vault Hunters meet the Firehawk, who turns out to be Lilith (an existing and playable character in Borderlands), whose powers as a Siren have been significantly enhanced by the new supply of eridium. Lilith informs the Vault Hunters that Roland was actually captured by a group of bandits. After fighting through the bandits' territory, the Vault Hunters rescue Roland and return to Sanctuary.
Roland and Lilith learn that the Vault Key is being transported aboard a Hyperion train, and ask the Vault Hunters to retrieve it. To accomplish the mission, the Vault Hunters enlist the aid of former Vault Hunter Mordecai, and of Tiny Tina, a psychotic explosives-obsessed thirteen-year-old. The Vault Hunters derail the train, but instead of finding the Vault Key, they encounter Wilhelm, a powerful Hyperion cyborg. After Wilhelm's defeat, the Vault Hunters recover his power core, which Roland recommends be used as the power source for Sanctuary's shields. The power core turns out to be a trap; it allows the Guardian Angel, who is actually working for Jack, to lower the city's shields and render it vulnerable to a bombardment from the Hyperion moon satellite. Lilith saves Sanctuary, which was originally a large spacecraft, by activating its engines and teleporting it away; for the rest of the game, Sanctuary exists as a flying city in the sky.
Jack's plan is to open Pandora's second Vault and unleash The Warrior, a powerful lava, eridium, and rock creature controlled by whomever releases it; he uses Angel to help him charge the Vault Key more quickly than usual. Angel communicates with the group in Sanctuary, and despite hostile treatment from Roland, divulges that the Vault Key is kept with her in a Hyperion facility. She also shares information about the formidable defenses of the facility. The Vault Hunters embark upon a series of missions in order to assemble what is needed to overcome these defenses, including obtaining an upgrade for Claptrap, visiting the Hyperion city of Opportunity, and enlisting the aid of Brick, now leader of the Slab clan of bandits. During the process, Mordecai's pet bird Bloodwing is captured and killed by Handsome Jack; an enraged Mordecai vows revenge and joins the other three former Vault Hunters at Sanctuary. Roland and the Vault Hunters assault the Hyperion compound and meet Angel, who is not only a real person, but a siren, and Handsome Jack's daughter. She requests to be killed in order to stop her father from charging the Vault Key and gaining control of The Warrior. Handsome Jack sends in waves of security forces in order to protect his daughter, but ultimately, Roland and the Vault Hunters, with the help of late arrival Lilith, successfully kill Angel. An enraged Handsome Jack teleports in, kills Roland, and captures Lilith, whom he forces to resume charging the Vault Key in Angel's stead. Lilith manages to teleport the Vault Hunters out of the facility and back to Sanctuary.
Mordecai and Brick decide to learn the location of the second Vault and confront Handsome Jack and The Warrior. While the Vault Hunters travel to the Hyperion Information Annex and obtains the Vault's location, the two steal a Hyperion ship. The Vault Hunters approach on foot, battling elite Hyperion security forces, while Brick and Mordecai are shot down but left alive. Ultimately, the Vault Hunters confront, battle, and defeat Handsome Jack himself but arrive too late to prevent him from opening the Vault. Handsome Jack summons The Warrior, a gargantuan dragon-like lava creature, and orders it to kill the Vault Hunters. After a long battle, the Vault Hunters defeat the Warrior and execute Handsome Jack in the aftermath.
Brick and Mordecai arrive just as Lilith attempts to destroy the Vault Key. However, she accidentally activates a secret information bank containing a huge map of the galaxy with several Vaults marked on it. Lilith remarks that "there ain't no rest for the wicked" before the screen cuts to black.

Here's the basic idea of the game(no spoilers): You are on a ranch and you have to raise slimes. There are various types, which you can find around the map with various rarities(careful, some can damage you). These slimes need food, so you need to gather food around the map. When you feed them, each slime produces a plort, which can be used to sell at the market for money. There are 3 basic types of food:Veggies, Fruit, and Meat. The most common slimes, pink slimes, eat anything you throw at them. All the other slimes have only one basic food that they like. Each slime has their own specific favorite food(You can look it up in the Slimepedia after you have sucked them up at least once), and when you feed it to them, they produce double the plorts. That means more money, but all of the slimes' favorite foods(eg stony hens, heart beets, cuberries)  are harder to obtain than regular food(pogoberries, carrots, chickens). Obviously. Using the money you make from selling plorts, you can upgrade your vacpack to hold more stuff, get more energy, health, and buy a jetpack(and etc). You can also spend the money on gardens, coops, silos, incinerators, etc. Gardens are helpful when you dont want to scavenge around for food. I'm writing this review disregarding the performance issues, as most of you be well aware of it by the time you read this.
The game improves upon the original Dishonored in its level design and general elements of its stealth gameplay: guards are more perceptive, light/shadow contrasts are utilised more and height factors based on the level layout also affect where and how you should be sneaking. There's more tools for non-lethal playthroughs now; stun mines, drop-attacks and sting darts. It really feels like Arkane listened to feedback on the first game and delivered a solution. The levels in this game are phenominal, real wide open areas with tons of tiny details packed into them. Even the ones that aren't spectacles visually are still made interesting with lots of events, exploration opportunities and secrets to find. I'm really glad they kept this approach to level design over going open world like every other game feels they have to do now.
Along with solutions comes compromise; Dishonored 2 is a great game, and builds upon its interesting lore with lots of audiographs, newspapers, letters and books to really make you invested in its world. Beyond all this, the writing falls short. The plot is a generic revenge plot outshadowed by Corvo's escapade 15 years earlier in the original game. Characters are dull - Erica Luttrell and Stephen Russell are fantastic voice actors that were wasted on monotone dialogue and commentary. The plot just doesn't have as much bite this time, you as a player don't feel urgency to pursue these assination targets as you did in the first game.
Nevertheless, even with the lesser points weighed in, Dishonored 2 is a great game with many options available for the player just as they were in the first. Worth playing, if not buying.

Rating: Solid 9/10
Dark souls 2 is an unforgiving and mysterious combat driven game. It's all Dark Souls 1 was and more, but slightly less. First off, the PC Port is great, it isn't the trainwreck that one was and fully playable, the summoning works too; about 5 second waits between duels in the Iron Keep and constant co-op in most areas.
Compared to one, the art style is less of itself, the hollows that would shake their broken weaponry at you at mach5 speeds are now actual hollows, dead soldiers in armor, simply succumbed to the curse instead of some tattered prisoner. It's beautiful in it's own right, yet not as charming as it once was.
I hold no doubt in this being the more accesible and enjoyable Dark Souls game. New players will quickly find their place in Drangleic and begin to piece together what they are.
Combat
---
Combat in Dark Souls 2 is truly amazing, there is 186 weapons between the 19 categories; Great swords, Katanas, Spears, Axes, Whips, Bows, Catalysts, etc. Each have their advantages and disadvantages between the many variables such as Move set (how you use it in combat), durability, special attacks, speed, power, poise break damage, reaction to shields and the like.
To go alongside this huge arsenal is 106 armor sets with their own effects and looks, as expected of any good Fashion Souls game.
A good man at arms will be handy with a wide variety of weapons as a good mage will be handy with a wide variety of magic and hexes. There is no lack of weapons to upgrade, infuse and try and as a result stays fresh even after the fourth playthrough.
PvP is a big experience, its highly accesible and truly fun against people close to your skill level and higher, it has evolved in the community to have its own generally known events and etiquette from fight-clubs to duels, all have their own kinds of players. For example, in the arena of the Brotherhood of Blood, you will find that players play to the covenants theme, cut-throat and mercilessly.
Story
---
I wish I could say a lot about this, but I'd just end up rambling and spoiling. Dark Souls chooses to not notice you as it simply sits there and lets you play it compared to other games in which they will tell you what is happening, why its happening and maybe throw in a few plot twists. This is not a souls experience.
The mysterious story telling seen here is simple, you piece together what you are and go from there and make your own story from ingame notes such as Item Descriptions, things you notice by chance and sudden realizations, example! In
Not a single person is truly right about the story and with that comes a great community effort to build whatever is true. Remember who you are, don't lose purpose and maybe you'll make it to the end without going hollow.

The main thing about this game is difficulty. I say "thing" because the difficulty is the draw for some and the put off for others. For me, it's a put off. Don't think I didn't like this game because it was difficult. I didn't like this game because of how the developers made it difficult. Let me list some ways they made it difficult and hopefully that will help you decide if you really want to pick the game up.
1) Enemy Damage: Basically put, if an enemy hits you full out, it’s going to hurt. If you block it will hurt less, and if you block with the right kind of shield it may not hurt at all. I actually have no issue with this kind of difficulty so long as it is avoidable. And for the most part, as far as I’ve seen, in Dark Souls 2 it is avoidable. Sort of. More on this later.
2) Obscurity: Here is where I start having issues with the game. It’s obscure in so many areas that often times you have no idea what you’re supposed to be doing. To break it down further…
a) Stat obscurity: Just go to any Dark Souls 2 forum and you will see huge debates on the usefulness of ADP. Some say it’s worth putting a massive number of points into, some say none, and there are all the colors of thought in between.
b) Item obscurity: This one doesn’t bother me, but may bother others or may encourage others to go ahead and pick up the game. Some of the items in this game are a pain to find. Explore every nook and cranny to make sure you’re not leaving anything behind.
c) Mob obscurity: To do well in this game you have to know what the mob is going to do. Even for regular mobs, you have to know if the down swing is coming, or if a wider swing is coming, or if he is going to add an extra swing onto the animation you already know (and trust.) You basically have to study the mobs before you can do particularly well on any fight. Some people will enjoy this. It just isn’t entertaining for me.
3) Artificial Difficulty: I’m going to have to break this one down into different sections for sure, and these are, without a doubt, the reason I’m saying not recommended and probably never finishing this game.
a) Controls: The controls for this game are intentionally difficult to use. That’s not to say impossible, and it’s not to say that people can’t and don’t get used to it, but that doesn’t make it good. Jumping is a prime example. In order to jump you MUST be sprinting with the B button and then you have to click down on the right stick to actually jump.
b) Damage avoidance: “Hey, wait! Did you say the damage was fine?” Yes, I did say that. IF it’s possible to avoid it. And in Dark Souls 2 it is, somtimes. As far as damage avoidance goes, your main option is to get out of the way. However, that doesn’t work very well in Dark Souls 2. Some people just stopped reading right there and are now scrolling to the comment section to tell me off. For those that kept reading, it’s a combination of a few other points, namely learning what the mob is going to do, and bad controls. Yes you CAN avoid the damage that mob is going to put out, IF you’ve studied the mob enough and IF the bad controls don’t get in your way. One you can get down if you’re determined enough. The other isn’t always a guarantee.
c) Camera lock on: I had to shorten this greatly to fit within the maximum characters for the review. Suffice to say, if you’re locked on to something close, you’re looking at the two of you and the floor.
d) Tricks: This is a big thing for me. The game will constantly lure you into situations you can’t possibly win without the right preparation. A fantastic example of this is right in the starter area. In this area you will see a huge mob that you’re under no requirement to fight. It doesn’t stand in your way and it doesn’t even try to trick you into the fight. Simply walk the other direction and you’ll never get killed by it. I have no issue with the game putting an optional tough mob in the starter area. In fact, I decided to try my luck and see what I could do against him. I went in, hit him while his back was turned and dodged his first attack. Pretty good. Did I dodge his second? No. He didn’t do a second attack. His buddy, another giant mob who the developer had hidden in a corner and programed to jump you when you attacked the first one, made sure of that. This is what you will find throughout the game. Situations in which you WILL die the first time simply because you didn’t know what would happen. It’s not fun for me. Maybe it will be for you.
4) Bad port: I’ve got to admit, when I first started the game and saw “Push the Start button” I chuckled a little bit. Silly game, there is no start button on a keyboard. Then I saw “Press A” in the commands. Okay, where is the option to tell the game I’m using a keyboard and mouse. There isn’t one.. huh.
Don’t get me wrong, I don’t find it that difficult to associate “Start” with “Enter.” However, the problem goes much further than that. While researching the issue online I kept finding the same answer. “Just plug in a controller.” And sadly, that’s true. If you’re still looking to pick this game up, I highly advise you have an Xbox controller. I say Xbox because many people have reported issues with other gamepads, and this port was obviously made for the Xbox.
One personal example that I have from the short amount of time I tried to use the keyboard and mouse was sitting at a bonfire. I opened the menu, took in the options, and wanted to back out. How do you back out? Esc. But no, not esc. I found that if you right click the menu a floating dialog box appears with a red Xbox “B” in it, then if you click that it will back out. Really?
It’s obvious this game was made for the consoles, and the developers made no effort to hide that in the port.
5) Punishing the player: Dark Souls 2 is a learning experience, there is no doubt to be had on that. That wouldn’t be bad if the game didn’t punish you for what it does to you (see “tricks” above.)
a) Death penalty - Souls: As I said before, when you die once, you “drop” your currently held souls at the point of your death. You must then make your way back and pick them up again to regain them. This wouldn’t be too big of an issue if souls didn’t fuel everything from levels to items to item upgrades, coupled with the issue below.
b) Limited souls: I was actually shocked to find this one out. Enemies don’t have an infinite respawn. You can not go back and fight normal mobs to recover souls. This is done to force you to continue on.
c) Death penalty - HP: When you’re human, you’re golden. You get 100% of your HP and you don’t look like moldy beef jerky. However, if you die you go hollow. Which means you lose 10% of your HP and you do look like moldy beef jerky. Die again, and you lose another 10%. Die again, and you lose another 10%. Down to 50% of your total HP. Now, if you’re having trouble with a section, how much his having 50% of your life going to help? There are people who will and do say “get gud.” This apparently means continue trying at a major disadvantage until you can overcome the obstacle. Which is possible, true. It’s just not fun.
So, let me say here that I don’t think Dark Souls 2 is a bad game. It does what it promises, kills you. And this isn’t bad. There are people who want to do that. If you don’t know if you’re one of those people, go through the points above and see how you feel about each one. Many sound negative because I didn’t like them. However, if you read a section and think “What is this guy talking about? That sounds awesome!” then put that point in the “yes” pile. If the yesses overcome the nos, give the game a shot. If your primary reaction to most of the points is “That sounds cheap.” Welcome to my world and save yourself a few bucks.

In Dark Souls 2 the level design is more like 100 peoples ideas somehow crafted into one thing and therefore not making any sense at all. It is diverse and nice to look at, but that is about it.
Lava level. How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Water level. How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Castle level. How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Some dark area. How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Some poison area. How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Okay whats missing? How about a cave? How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Still any ideas? Forest area. How to access it? Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Did I forget something? Ah yeah... flying sky-islands. How to access it? Guess what... Elevator after previous boss. Check [x]
Way to the boss? Some straight hallway, add an enemy here and there. There you go. Game complete. Check [x]
- There are a lot of weapons, but most of them are so useless and pointless, that you are being forced to use the same crap as everyone else. This applies to PVP as well as PVE. Muffin Knight is a cute and simple throwback to older arcade-style games, where the goal is to dodge enemies and rack up points by collecting muffins.  Each time a muffin is collected, your character will lose his current attack ability and randomly select another from a decently long list of possibilities.  Scoring high earns points which can be used to upgrade the effectiveness of each job class.
I found Muffin Knight pretty fun for a little while, but ultimately I cannot recommend the game.  At first, new classes and upgrades and levels come very quickly, but after a short while, it becomes a slog - each upgrade might cost three points, and you have to play the same level a dozen times just to earn one.  It seems as though the game was designed to be more addictive than fun or balanced - something that is not helped by the game's appearance, which looks and feels very much like it was a hastily done mobile port.
The nail in the coffin for my enjoyment of the game, though, are the cheap deaths incurred from a broken enemy indication system.  Enemies drop onto the board from the sky.  Usually, there's a few frames of smoke as in indicator that enemies will soon be appearing.  However, that indicator seems really buggy - sometimes it appears in the wrong place, and sometimes it doesn't appear at all.  You'll grow used to enemies popping out of thin air directly on to you quite a bit.
You might enjoy this title a bit, but unfortunately its an experience that wears thin after a while.

For any and all Half-Life fans, this is fantastic. For any newcomers to the series, this is also fantastic, and you should seriously consider making this your entry into the series if you were put off by
's age.
Black Mesa is a re-make of Half-Life, that's true, but with the effort put into its development over eight-plus years it might as well be a whole new game. And all because they were dissatisfied with Valve porting it to their then-new physics engine in 2004. Pretty much every aspect has been remastered. Worskhop support lets you modify you experience easier than ever before.
If you're not familiar with Half-Life...that's okay. You don't have to be. But if you're looking for a solid FPS that doubles as a solid
, with some brains, a lot of tension (bordering on survival horror at times) and even a little pathos up its sleeve? You could do far worse than this. Just play it on Normal or Easy, for reasons I explain below.
And hey, there's multiplayer included with good maps and decent netcode. It's quite similar to HL's deathmatch at HL2 Deathmatch speed, with a much wider range of player model choices. The actual gameplay is still old-school 'player who gets the best guns first gets to kill everyone quicker' for better or worse.
Okay, now for more technical details/notes for people who've played the mod's original release or the original Half-Life:
Maps have been streamlined from the mod's first launch and from Half-Life. The gameplay itself is different from HL in only one way: it's generally better. The previously mentioned Marines no longer quite resemble hideously overpowered Counter-Strike aimbots (which was a problem in the original release).
The only criticism that could be said of the campaign is that the devs made it noticeably harder than the original Half-Life. At times, this makes the game incredibly frustrating on Hard difficulty unless you follow an optimal strategy and know exactly what to expect for some areas. While classic HL had its difficult moments on Hard difficulty, I don't think it'd be unfair to say that some of BM's hardest moments more resemble tactical shooters like classic Rainbow Six/Ghost Recon. Although considering you're effectively playing Joe Schmoe Freeman, PhD and fighting highly trained US Marines, it might be fitting.
(Being able to land consistent crossbow headshots helps if you have ammunition for it; the energy weapons either come too late or are too weak to efficiently dispatch enemies with.)
BM's graphics, as you might know, could be described as an improvement. Every security guard no longer looks the same. There's actually women scientists now. The Marines have much better voice acting. The 'Black Mesa' tab in the options menu lets you configure a lot of the game's new graphical effects, such as sideways movement bob, revolver ironsights and houndeye tinnitus.
The music is pretty good. Not quite as iconic as the original music, but it definitely shines at times. Comprehensive Workshop mod support, map-making tools and Steamworks features are pretty alright too.
BM's most beautiful element to me, though, is the weaponry. The arsenal's feel is massively improved over the original mod's guns; every one of them is great in their own right. I'd say they even give the original game's weapons a good run for their money.
I already said the developers have put a huge amount of effort into this thing, but they aren't done, either. As of this writing, they're still working on a version of the final section of Half-Life that they said they wanted to make better than the original. There's also various physics bugs that I'm pretty sure they're working on.
Given all of this, Black Mesa is well worth paying for. And even if you didn't like Half-Life, I would recommend it.

Graphics are well done.

CONS:
AI is dumb as bricks. They walk around, aim, swap weapons, stare at the wall for 10 seconds, swap weapons, aim, move, aim and then shoots a wall. Every bloody turn.
There is no option AFAIK to speed through AI turns, and they take forever.
The vehicles are cool at first, but they're fairly gimmicky and not strategically designed. You can hop in a mech fly around a little
Commands and UX are poorly designed. You can change the key bindings, but at the first get-go, the aiming, shooting and jumping commands are clunky and unintuitive.
There's a bit of a learning curve to understand how the weapons/gadgets work (range, aiming, whether it ends your turn or not), which is weird because for a simple game, there shouldn't be anything but a shallow learning curve.
Maps are kind of cool but a little bland. Some "walls" are actually in the background which can throw you off. You'd be better off using the jetpack to move around the map, rather than the not-so-useful-anymore grappling hook, which can't get you around anywhere (which defeats the purpose).
RATING
5/10

Remy is an idealistic and ambitious young rat, gifted with highly developed senses of taste and smell. Inspired by his idol, the recently deceased chef Auguste Gusteau, Remy dreams of becoming a cook himself. When an old woman sees his clan, they are forced to abandon their home; Remy is separated from them as a result of the woman's gunshots. He ends up in the sewers of Paris and eventually finds himself at a skylight overlooking the kitchen of Gusteau's restaurant.
As Remy watches, a young man named Alfredo Linguini is hired as a garbage boy by Skinner, the restaurant's devious current owner and Gusteau's former sous-chef. When Linguini spills a pot of soup and attempts to recreate it with disastrous results, Remy falls into the kitchen and cooks the soup to perfection rather than escaping. Linguini catches Remy and is confronted by Skinner. As Skinner yells at Linguini, the soup is accidentally served and proves to be a success. Colette Tatou, the staff's only female chef, convinces Skinner to retain Linguini, who is assumed to be the soup's creator. After Skinner catches Remy in the act of escaping, he orders Linguini to kill him, but he cannot do it. Linguini then discovers Remy's intelligence and passion for food, so he keeps him.
