This will be my first and only review, ever. Writing based on all the false(misinformed) negative reviews that for some reason get a lot of "Yes" to being helpful.
First of all, and let me make this absolutely clear. This game is NOT pay to win, by ANY means. Yes, you can pay to get certain things earlier, but everything is accessable through normal gameplay. The cash shop(Armas market) offer unique weapons which are essentially reskins. The weapons that are unique(not reskins, but has it's own stats etc.) are tradeable. You can get them from the AH with ingame currency, and they are by no means more powerful than other weapons. In fact, the starter weapon (the STAR 556) is one of the best all round weapons in the game, that I use quite often, spite having mor or less every weapon available. Furthermore, the newly released weapons are underpowerd, but unique, niche.
ANY claims of p2w here is down right false. The gear you unlock, will not make your character better. All equipment have trade offs, ie increase health by a small margin, but move slower and the likes. The top review stating players are getting the "best" gear straight from devs... I don't even. False reviews like that should be flagable.
That said, here's my pro and con for this interesting game.
PROS
-Customization, from modding the myriad of weapons available, to designing your own character, clothes, cars and even music, is absolutely unmatched.
-Gameplay. What can I say? Gameplay is just fun. You lean out of cars and shoot, you stand on TOP of cars and shoot. Surfing on the car with a rocket launcher is one of my favorite things to do. The environment (The city) allows for strategic objective based mission. From sniping from atop a bridge or rooftop, to running cqc with SMGs.
-Cars. Cars are a big part of the game and they aid you in missions, not only do they get you to the objective, but they have strategic use as well. Run people down, block their paths and use your car as cover.
CONS
-matchmaking. The matchmaking isnt' exactly... fair all the time, but this is because of the game's rather low population. It does what it can, and you always get a mission quickly. And I'd prefer quick matchup, over sitting around for an hour waiting for someone exactly your "skill". This creates competition. Nothing beats the feeling from winning a match that is not in your favor.
-Hackers. People are ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and they try to cheat, it happens. But the hacker, cheater presence here is nowhere what some of these reviews are portraiting. They met one or two cheaters and gave up on life, simple as that.
-performance. I know a lot of people are having issues with the game's performance. But this is unknown to me. I have played the game on a variety of connections, the one I have now is unbelivably crappy, but I still have no issues. Makes me wonder what connection these people have. I have neither had issues with the game's performance fps wise. I've ran the game on a multitute of computers including outdated laptops and have never had issues. Again makes me wonder what kind of potatoes people are trying to run their games on.
And that's what I can think of for now. I love the game and will continue playing a lot. The once or twice in a week I face a hacker I just let them win and move on. I don't cry and write false reviews over it.

With nearly 200 hours in this game, the most of my library, I'd like to make a few points; We must first go back to Shogun 2 and Empire/Napoleon, however. All of these titles were nearly broken upon release, something Rome II bashers are quick to forget when lambasting the state of Rome II when it was released. Today Empire and Napoleon are very playable, though they do require mods to shine, while Shogun 2 Vanilla is a damn near perfect game in terms of AI and Graphics with mods only improving on these. Bearing this is mind, it is not surprising that Rome II was fairly unplayable when it was released, but since that time CA has put out a plethora of patches along with DLC that do add to the base game (Ceasar in Gaul and Hannibal at the Gates), which has done much in improving the AI as well as optomization. In its current state (June 2014) the Vanilla game is playable, but certainly not at its prime, which is where mods come in. If you truely want to have a great game you must download one of the more fleshed out mods (My preference is Divide et Imperia, arguably the most extensive and wll done mod). These mods take the stunning graphics that Rome II is capable of, improving them and fixing historical inaccuracies, and combines them with a greatly enhanced Battle and Campaign AI to create an enjoyable Total War Experience.

Review of Early Access version 0.5.1 with ~7 hours of playtime.
Slime Rancher is a very cute, fairly relaxed exploration farming game. The premise of the game is to farm cute slimes and sell their slime manure to get rich. Most slimes have a preferred food and some have certain environmental requirements (water, darkness). There is a reasonable amount of automation that stops it from being too grindy and there is a neat mechanic that allows you to create hybrids of two slimes.
It's pretty polished for an early access game (no crashes or bugs) but could really do with a map and chickens that reproduce more quickly.

I'm not the sort of person to write reviews. I'd rather be playing the game in all honesty but I need to come clean and air our my issues with Just Cause 3 so I'll stop trying to justify it over Just Cause 2.
Does it do things better? Yes. Does it do enough better? No. Not even slightly. In fact it does a lot worse.
It's poorly designed in a lot of ways (you want to grapple and instantly enter a helicopter? Push E. Push it too early, which is very easy, and you will rag-doll into the side of it and probably get #rekt by the roters on the way over.) There is no effort in the bases or towns, they are all cookie-cutter and a chore to do. In Just Cause 2 every base was so much more unique and fun to play with and taking over one was a big event to boot. It all just feels less involved than Just Cause 2.
It's less fun.
It's more difficult in all the wrong ways.
It's got less going on.
It feels emptier.
It's stepping over itself in terms of design and controls.
Just Cause 3 can summarised in it's main mechanics.
You have infinite sticky bombs but they're your last resort or the main tool of a very boring player. The tether is given a lot of focus but it's not fun to use.
You can't fast travel infinitely anymore and must use flares which can be upgraded, however you can bypass this by doing two other things.
Helicopters are♥♥♥♥♥♥weak in terms of guns, much easier to control and downed by a random number of SAMs (and it ♥♥♥♥ing is random to, I've gone down to one in a god-damn gunship and taken six in a low tier attack chopper) and SAMs respawn.
Vehicles aren't fun to control and all are slow as hell and made of tin-foil and a wish when it comes to gunfire and explosives.
There's no weapon varity or progress, you're given your meagre lot at the start and have to deal and can only unlock a number of special weapons which won't fare much better than the bog-standard RPG you've been using or the LMG in terms of sheer practicality which is the only terms Just Cause 3 understands.
Chaos serves no purpose as far as we could discern over a long weekend of gaming it non-stop.
You respawn at the base you were fighting with everything reset except the permanent stuff. No more commitment, just "LOL, died, trying again right now."
Outposts are beyond lazy. Three chaos objects at most (boring ones too, no giant radar towers here), the only thing stopping you from clearing them in seconds is the SAM sites, serious, you could reduce this game to a 3 hour speed run if you had a mod to disable SAMs on outposts.
What is going on? It feels like it's had the soul sucked of it and the fun went along for the ride. Just Cause 2 had it's flaws, yes but it did gameplay much better. Hell, it's story was kind of fun at quite a few moments too. Just Cause 3... really has no story to it.
Listen, just go buy Just Cause 2. It's more fun, got more going on, more things to do, hell of a lot more cinematic, handles a hell of a lot better, runs a lot better, can be modded with a lot of fun toys, has vehicles you actually want to get in and drive and the powerful things feel powerful because they weighed properly. It's just better. Yes you have to sit through the item drop screen for things, but the pay off is worth it.
I'm sorry Just Cause 3, I had to defend you as the good angel but I spent more time picking you apart than praising you. I tried to love you.

Rating: Solid 9/10
Dark souls 2 is an unforgiving and mysterious combat driven game. It's all Dark Souls 1 was and more, but slightly less. First off, the PC Port is great, it isn't the trainwreck that one was and fully playable, the summoning works too; about 5 second waits between duels in the Iron Keep and constant co-op in most areas.
Compared to one, the art style is less of itself, the hollows that would shake their broken weaponry at you at mach5 speeds are now actual hollows, dead soldiers in armor, simply succumbed to the curse instead of some tattered prisoner. It's beautiful in it's own right, yet not as charming as it once was.
I hold no doubt in this being the more accesible and enjoyable Dark Souls game. New players will quickly find their place in Drangleic and begin to piece together what they are.
Combat
---
Combat in Dark Souls 2 is truly amazing, there is 186 weapons between the 19 categories; Great swords, Katanas, Spears, Axes, Whips, Bows, Catalysts, etc. Each have their advantages and disadvantages between the many variables such as Move set (how you use it in combat), durability, special attacks, speed, power, poise break damage, reaction to shields and the like.
To go alongside this huge arsenal is 106 armor sets with their own effects and looks, as expected of any good Fashion Souls game.
A good man at arms will be handy with a wide variety of weapons as a good mage will be handy with a wide variety of magic and hexes. There is no lack of weapons to upgrade, infuse and try and as a result stays fresh even after the fourth playthrough.
PvP is a big experience, its highly accesible and truly fun against people close to your skill level and higher, it has evolved in the community to have its own generally known events and etiquette from fight-clubs to duels, all have their own kinds of players. For example, in the arena of the Brotherhood of Blood, you will find that players play to the covenants theme, cut-throat and mercilessly.
Story
---
I wish I could say a lot about this, but I'd just end up rambling and spoiling. Dark Souls chooses to not notice you as it simply sits there and lets you play it compared to other games in which they will tell you what is happening, why its happening and maybe throw in a few plot twists. This is not a souls experience.
The mysterious story telling seen here is simple, you piece together what you are and go from there and make your own story from ingame notes such as Item Descriptions, things you notice by chance and sudden realizations, example! In
Not a single person is truly right about the story and with that comes a great community effort to build whatever is true. Remember who you are, don't lose purpose and maybe you'll make it to the end without going hollow.

The main thing about this game is difficulty. I say "thing" because the difficulty is the draw for some and the put off for others. For me, it's a put off. Don't think I didn't like this game because it was difficult. I didn't like this game because of how the developers made it difficult. Let me list some ways they made it difficult and hopefully that will help you decide if you really want to pick the game up.
1) Enemy Damage: Basically put, if an enemy hits you full out, it’s going to hurt. If you block it will hurt less, and if you block with the right kind of shield it may not hurt at all. I actually have no issue with this kind of difficulty so long as it is avoidable. And for the most part, as far as I’ve seen, in Dark Souls 2 it is avoidable. Sort of. More on this later.
2) Obscurity: Here is where I start having issues with the game. It’s obscure in so many areas that often times you have no idea what you’re supposed to be doing. To break it down further…
a) Stat obscurity: Just go to any Dark Souls 2 forum and you will see huge debates on the usefulness of ADP. Some say it’s worth putting a massive number of points into, some say none, and there are all the colors of thought in between.
b) Item obscurity: This one doesn’t bother me, but may bother others or may encourage others to go ahead and pick up the game. Some of the items in this game are a pain to find. Explore every nook and cranny to make sure you’re not leaving anything behind.
c) Mob obscurity: To do well in this game you have to know what the mob is going to do. Even for regular mobs, you have to know if the down swing is coming, or if a wider swing is coming, or if he is going to add an extra swing onto the animation you already know (and trust.) You basically have to study the mobs before you can do particularly well on any fight. Some people will enjoy this. It just isn’t entertaining for me.
3) Artificial Difficulty: I’m going to have to break this one down into different sections for sure, and these are, without a doubt, the reason I’m saying not recommended and probably never finishing this game.
a) Controls: The controls for this game are intentionally difficult to use. That’s not to say impossible, and it’s not to say that people can’t and don’t get used to it, but that doesn’t make it good. Jumping is a prime example. In order to jump you MUST be sprinting with the B button and then you have to click down on the right stick to actually jump.
b) Damage avoidance: “Hey, wait! Did you say the damage was fine?” Yes, I did say that. IF it’s possible to avoid it. And in Dark Souls 2 it is, somtimes. As far as damage avoidance goes, your main option is to get out of the way. However, that doesn’t work very well in Dark Souls 2. Some people just stopped reading right there and are now scrolling to the comment section to tell me off. For those that kept reading, it’s a combination of a few other points, namely learning what the mob is going to do, and bad controls. Yes you CAN avoid the damage that mob is going to put out, IF you’ve studied the mob enough and IF the bad controls don’t get in your way. One you can get down if you’re determined enough. The other isn’t always a guarantee.
c) Camera lock on: I had to shorten this greatly to fit within the maximum characters for the review. Suffice to say, if you’re locked on to something close, you’re looking at the two of you and the floor.
d) Tricks: This is a big thing for me. The game will constantly lure you into situations you can’t possibly win without the right preparation. A fantastic example of this is right in the starter area. In this area you will see a huge mob that you’re under no requirement to fight. It doesn’t stand in your way and it doesn’t even try to trick you into the fight. Simply walk the other direction and you’ll never get killed by it. I have no issue with the game putting an optional tough mob in the starter area. In fact, I decided to try my luck and see what I could do against him. I went in, hit him while his back was turned and dodged his first attack. Pretty good. Did I dodge his second? No. He didn’t do a second attack. His buddy, another giant mob who the developer had hidden in a corner and programed to jump you when you attacked the first one, made sure of that. This is what you will find throughout the game. Situations in which you WILL die the first time simply because you didn’t know what would happen. It’s not fun for me. Maybe it will be for you.
4) Bad port: I’ve got to admit, when I first started the game and saw “Push the Start button” I chuckled a little bit. Silly game, there is no start button on a keyboard. Then I saw “Press A” in the commands. Okay, where is the option to tell the game I’m using a keyboard and mouse. There isn’t one.. huh.
Don’t get me wrong, I don’t find it that difficult to associate “Start” with “Enter.” However, the problem goes much further than that. While researching the issue online I kept finding the same answer. “Just plug in a controller.” And sadly, that’s true. If you’re still looking to pick this game up, I highly advise you have an Xbox controller. I say Xbox because many people have reported issues with other gamepads, and this port was obviously made for the Xbox.
One personal example that I have from the short amount of time I tried to use the keyboard and mouse was sitting at a bonfire. I opened the menu, took in the options, and wanted to back out. How do you back out? Esc. But no, not esc. I found that if you right click the menu a floating dialog box appears with a red Xbox “B” in it, then if you click that it will back out. Really?
It’s obvious this game was made for the consoles, and the developers made no effort to hide that in the port.
5) Punishing the player: Dark Souls 2 is a learning experience, there is no doubt to be had on that. That wouldn’t be bad if the game didn’t punish you for what it does to you (see “tricks” above.)
a) Death penalty - Souls: As I said before, when you die once, you “drop” your currently held souls at the point of your death. You must then make your way back and pick them up again to regain them. This wouldn’t be too big of an issue if souls didn’t fuel everything from levels to items to item upgrades, coupled with the issue below.
b) Limited souls: I was actually shocked to find this one out. Enemies don’t have an infinite respawn. You can not go back and fight normal mobs to recover souls. This is done to force you to continue on.
c) Death penalty - HP: When you’re human, you’re golden. You get 100% of your HP and you don’t look like moldy beef jerky. However, if you die you go hollow. Which means you lose 10% of your HP and you do look like moldy beef jerky. Die again, and you lose another 10%. Die again, and you lose another 10%. Down to 50% of your total HP. Now, if you’re having trouble with a section, how much his having 50% of your life going to help? There are people who will and do say “get gud.” This apparently means continue trying at a major disadvantage until you can overcome the obstacle. Which is possible, true. It’s just not fun.
So, let me say here that I don’t think Dark Souls 2 is a bad game. It does what it promises, kills you. And this isn’t bad. There are people who want to do that. If you don’t know if you’re one of those people, go through the points above and see how you feel about each one. Many sound negative because I didn’t like them. However, if you read a section and think “What is this guy talking about? That sounds awesome!” then put that point in the “yes” pile. If the yesses overcome the nos, give the game a shot. If your primary reaction to most of the points is “That sounds cheap.” Welcome to my world and save yourself a few bucks.

TL;DR: Cheap mobile port. Expect nothing.
- No resolution option.
- No resizable window in windowed mode.
- No local co-op.
- Clone of Super Crate Box.
- Can't see the entire level at once, making it a bit harder to see the enemies.
- Sometimes the enemies drop from the spot without the cloud (unfairly killing you).
- Grinding for unlocking characters and for getting points to upgrade characters.
- No Steam cloud, no easy way to backup the save.
- Navigating the menus with the joystick can be frustrating.
~ Partial joystick support.
+ Mouse works in the menus.
+ Rebindable keys.
+ Anti-aliased graphics if the "high" quality is selected.
-- Full review below --
This is mobile port. This game is also available on Android, iOS, and even Windows Phone.
There is a Chrome App version (available for free, playable inside Chrome). If you are curious about this game, play that version before spending any money on this.
When compared to the Chrome app version, this Steam version has online multiplayer support (good luck finding anyone else with this game). And anti-aliased graphics. That's all. Otherwise, it is the same game.
Talking about "same game", this is a clone of Super Crate Box. The exact same mechanics from that game are in this game. What else do we have? Grinding for unlocking new characters! Grinding for leveling up and getting points to upgrade characters! And what do you get after you beat the first "boss"? More grinding!
For a game consisting mainly of grinding, being difficult to backup the progress is a sin. People claim that the save is stored in the Windows registry, but at least one person complained it couldn't restore the save.
The options menu is a joke. At least it has rebindable keys, but there is no option to change the resolution. Alt+Enter changes to windowed mode, but the dimensions are fixed.
In a mobile game, it makes sense to keep zoomed in and scrolling the level, because the screen is small. In the PC version, the behavior is exactly the same, unfortunately. I'd prefer to have a zoomed out view, i.e. I'd prefer to see more of the level at once.
The xmas level has two spots where the enemies can spawn. Before enemies spawn, a cloud shows up. However, in that level, many times the cloud shows at one spot but the enemies spawn at the other spot (at that moment, the cloud teleports to the other spot). Unpredictable, nullifies any strategies from the player, and ends up unfairly killing the player.
Finally, I couldn't find a way to exit from the character upgrade screen, while using the joystick. I had to use the mouse or the keyboard (Esc key) to get out of it. And the digital D-Pad can't be used in the menus.

Remy is an idealistic and ambitious young rat, gifted with highly developed senses of taste and smell. Inspired by his idol, the recently deceased chef Auguste Gusteau, Remy dreams of becoming a cook himself. As Remy watches, a young man named Alfredo Linguini is hired as a garbage boy by Skinner, the restaurant's devious current owner and Gusteau's former sous-chef. When Linguini spills a pot of soup and attempts to recreate it with disastrous results, Remy falls into the kitchen and cooks the soup to perfection rather than escaping. Linguini catches Remy and is confronted by Skinner. As Skinner yells at Linguini, the soup is accidentally served and proves to be a success. Colette Tatou, the staff's only female chef, convinces Skinner to retain Linguini, who is assumed to be the soup's creator. After Skinner catches Remy in the act of escaping, he orders Linguini to kill him, but he cannot do it. Linguini then discovers Remy's intelligence and passion for food, so he keeps him.

If you have never been near a Worms before, all you need to know is that it is a single and multi-player (local + online) turn-based strategy game in which teams of funny little Worms try to murder each other with a vast arsenal of conventional and unconventional weapons, and the destructible background reflects the violence taking place on its surface while adding new layers of possibilities. And failure can be hilarious.
I have fond memories of the Worms series since 1995. There has been a peak in 1999 with Worms Armageddon, and since then it has been a bumpy road that timidly tried new things here and there but never a solid offering with all the features that are expected to be present.  The potential of the series was diluted by entries that thought they were trying some new things while constantly dropping the good stuff from the previous episodes. Strangely, overall no real progress was made and more was lost than gained.
Worms W.M.D still has some of these issues. The map specificities (fog, earthquake, gravity) from a few of the previous entries (mostly Worms Open Warfare 2) are lost. The dynamic water weapons from the 2.5D entries are missing too. The funny videos are long lost since Worms 1 and 2. The ability to draw maps did not come back (however, it is now possible to import pictures again). And finally, some details such as deeper customisation and some rope features (length) will not please die-hard Worms Armageddon fans.
Apart from those nit-picks, however, Worms W.M.D is the strongest entry in the series since Worms Armageddon. Most features are there, from the local multiplayer to classic commando missions. The 2D graphics are gorgeous, the Worms re-design is great and the overall feel is more military than goofy. It runs well (apart for the somewhat slow AI), binding new key inputs is possible, and so on. Overall, it is solid. But that’s not enough to set itself apart. So here come the novelties.
Buildings that can be entered. Good hiding places and protection, while putting tunnels back to the heart of the series. Mounted weapons that add a layer of danger. And most excitingly, vehicles! Tanks and mechas, both can jump and are easy to handle. Then helicopters, which end up being a very useful taxi for those players that dominate you and fly back to safety without burning jetpack fuel or having to master the rope. Mmmf, I have mixed feelings about that. Whatever I think of the helicopter, all those additions completely re-write the dynamic of the game. It feels a lot less static for us that are not masters of the ninja rope, and also I think the basic movements, albeit slow, are much smoother than usual since the Worms don’t get stuck just because of a small slope hindering their slimy way. And finally, crafting. I hate crafting, but thankfully it is not obnoxious here. Can be a life-saver to get a new jetpack, or eventually craft a concrete donkey if you have enough parts. Why would you craft anything else? It’s the most reliable.
To conclude, Worms W.M.D is not the perfect game. I will always miss the explosive violence of Worms 1, with its maps and bridges full of mines for chaotic chain reactions. The die-hard Worms Armageddon fans will not have every single feature that they are used to and expect to find. But then Worms W.M.D is better than everything else that the series has recently brought us, with its own novelties that are enough to justify its existence. Good, solid entry, that I hope will be expanded upon rather than dropped in favour of a quick new episode that forgets the good things once again. If it’s your first Worms or if you casually like the Worms series, or if you need to find something new to play with your friends, this new Worms is an easy recommendation, albeit a bit expensive for now.

I have not played this game for some time so some of the complaints I have may have been fixed through patches. Rome II is a good game a succeeds in a few aspects. The campaign map has more features and it is easier than ever to manage your empire. Everything has been streamlined when it comes to constructing buildings, walls, etc. The map has new features such as the ability to hide troops for an ambush or build a camp around your mobile army. The governement system is a little confusing and there is not much introduction to it. I did not explore in this area and for the most part left it alone. If I recall correctly, you no longer have to wait to spawn agents like spies, diplomats, etc. now they are just hired. There are a few new ones such as diplomats and warlords. These added some nice variety and are easy to use. For the most part things are stright forward, streamlined, and enjoyable. My major issue with the game is the AI. About half the time the AI works really well but during seiges, and there will be a lot of seiges, it fails horribly. Often the enemy AI will do nothing but stand around. This is extermely irritating when the enemy is attacking you and you do not have enough forces to leave your base and attack them. All you can do is either give up, let the AI kill all your troops, or sit and wait for the time to run out. The minimum time for a battle is something like 40 minutes so if an enemy attacks you and does not move, theres nothing you can do until the timer runs out. If you quit, you will lose the battle and your base. I had to spend a lot of time doing nothing in this game as a result. This problem only really occurs in one situation, seiges, but that is a major part of the game. It was enough that I stopped playing the game and have yet to go back. Again this may have been fixed through later patches but I would look into it before buying it.

What a relief! I've just finished my first 20-hour haul through this game, and while I thoroughly enjoyed it, I admit I am pretty psyched to be done with it. Alien: Isolation is less of a game and more of a survival simulation that spirals out of control, while you sit glued to the edge of your seat thinking you might need therapy after the experience. It is one of the scariest games I've ever played, and also one of the most addicting. I've been re-watching all of the Alien movies over the past few days, and I feel that A:I could easily have been a highlight of the series if it were a movie and not a game. It plays like a movie, with a solid plot that's thrilling to take part in, and I feel strongly that this game does justice to the Alien franchise.
I can't say enough good things about the visuals, the controls, the mechanics of the game - all are truly flawless and immersive. The soundtrack and audio are masterful and captivating. It has some of the best AI I've ever experienced in a stealth game. The crafting is fun and the weapons/tools are excellent. Most of the negative reviews I've read center on the fact that the game is very long, and not only long but grueling. While this is true, and while I did feel certain parts of the game were padded a bit much (especially towards the end) I was content to get a full 20-hour experience from this title. I certainly wouldn't have wanted it to be shorter. And perhaps most importantly, I feel that the never-ending twists, turns and terrors of the plot mirror the Alien films. Those aliens are damned resourceful, and they just don't know how to die. So I feel it's appropriate that the game made you work to reach the end of it, in the same way that Ripley struggles until the last minute of each film, only to find out in the sequel that the aliens are still alive and well. So to put it bluntly, I was not expecting a 12-hour jaunt with a quick and happy ending, and I'm glad I didn't receive one. Personally, I think it's a shame to see the game receive negative ratings for that reason.
The biggest complaint I can make here is that many of the objectives center around using switches or powering up/down generators, and while the plot keeps it interesting and the locations are all well-designed, that doesn't change the fact that the actual motions you go through to complete each objective are very similar. This may just be a matter of taste, but personally I would have liked more puzzle-oriented tasks like in Dead Space, rather than the "let's pull the switches in the right order" thing that A:I seemed so fond of. The way you use switches and other machinery is unique though, and it evokes a Resident Evil sort of feeling that your actions may have very real consequences. Using machinery is a visceral experience and leaves you vulnerable to attack, and most things you do in this game tend to attract unwanted attention. So, switch-pulling aside, it never takes long for the action to resume once again.
And action there is. I must admit I was more afraid of the androids than the alien. They have a strange way about them, and you can never be sure that they won't turn hostile on you. More than once, I thought I was safe with a particular android, only to have Ripley whip around to see those red glowing eyes strangling the life out of her, declaring "You're not supposed to be here." Really, excellent work with the design of those androids. Their nature also stays very much in keeping with the series canon, androids often being fundamentally untrustworthy and providing that extra bit of uncertainty.
Sevastopol is huge, sprawling, and often beautiful, especially during the rare moments when you can see outside. Its story is interesting, unraveled through computer documents and audio logs, and I still wish there was more of it to read. I look forward to playing this with Oculus Rift some day, even if I just find a spot and gaze out toward the massive gas giant out the window. I look forward to playing this again.
There are so many moments in this game that I could rave about, but I'll spare you the spoilers. If you're a fan of the Alien series and if you can handle some intense horror and stealth, you should play this game. 9/10

Slime Rancher is a zenlike experience of managing a farm and adventuring out in order to find new slimes to breed. The basic point of the game is that you collect slimes, feed them, collect their poop, and then sell it. Its a never ending cycle of collecting in order to increase your effeciency to collect. This is a game thats best in short bursts, because if you really sit down and play for several hours at a time, you may feel like youre not really doing anything except going in circles. Despite the games simple premise, the gameplay mechanics are actually complex. There is a market with fluxuating plort values, different slimes mix together to create different species, each of them have their own preferance of food as well. When exploring the world there are many secrets to find and as you enhance your base you will discover a lab which allows you to research new tools in order to enhance the gameplay experience. If youre looking for a relaxing game that you can play for short bursts then I would recommend Slime Rancher.

Only 4 hours into this game and I'm absolutely loving it. If you're looking to get this game, understand that it's quite repetitive at the early stages. You gather slimes, feed them, earn money to upgrade/open up the world. Here are the two things I like about the game the most so far.
Exploration: This is something I look for in many of the games I play these days. Being able to go about playing the game in your own way and not being forced down a certain path is a huge plus for me.
Upgrading: Being able to unlock new areas, upgrade existing areas, and upgrade your own player? You can't ask for anything more than that in an EARLY ACCESS game. It adds a lot of replay value in my opinion.
Only negative things I have to say about the game currently is that throwing loot boxes at walls sometimes ends with one or two pieces of food/plorts being stuck in the wall. Other than that, it's a really good time. Impressive amount of content in the game for it being Early Access. I recommend it 100%, maybe pick it up when it's on sale if you're unsure.

Every instance of connecting with other players has been streamlined tremendously. It's never been easier to summon, or be summoned to help others in their world. Finding PvP is very quick however invasions are infrequent throughout all of my New Game playrhoughs. Only when I went to NG+ or further would I start receiving invasions from red or blues but there are many other chances to PvP in NG (Bell convenant most notably).
Definitely includes more content than the first, with a huge amount of bosses to fight, including some optional bosses (32(?) total bosses). There's also a lot more choice in weaponary and previously unviable weapons classes (fist weapons, whips etc) are now perfectly viable, given you upgrade your weapon accordingly you can beat the game with any weapon you choose. Generally level design and boss design is a bit of a step down from its predecessor however, there are still areas that will continue to amaze after several visits.
Probably less re-playable in the long run than Dark Souls due to the fact that there's a (relatively rare) item to respec your stats so there's less of a need to create different characters for different playstyles. I've made a point to decide the direction of my character in terms of playstyle upon creating it and stick to it, as for example you would lose the experience of going through the game as a caster if you played as a melee character the whole game and then respecialised in casting magic (of which there are three schools) towards the end of the game.
I'm trying to keep this short so I'll wrap up here, I give this game a 9/10 and the original 10/10. The first was really one of my favourite games of all time but I still have (and am continuing to have) a lot of fun with DaSII. There are definitely issues with the game in terms of mechanics and balancing but non that seem out of reach in terms of patching, FromSoft really should've sorted these things before launch but the first Dark Souls also suffered heavily from this and wasn't regarded as 'balanced' by the community until a year had passed since launch.

As one who doesn't really like to partake in PvP, I thought I would hate this game but the only really infuriating parts were in the 2 belfries, all other PvP was minimal. Cooperation is a really big part of this game too and most of the people I've encountered have been really helpful and sometimes funny.
This game isn't for everyone, only those who PRAISE THE SUN

"Visions of reviews ahead"
This is certainly not a game for those who get angry quickly at their failures.  For this game is full of failures, especially if you don't already have some experience and undestanding of basic techinques of the series from Dark Souls.  You will have a very real chance to beat this game if you stick with it.  Don't let your ego take over.  You'll brag about how easy it was beating that one boss, only to die 15 seconds later by some unknown entity you were unprepared for.  The game can be linear, but will still give you the option of which things to do first.  I personally got a greatsoul that I wasn't supposed to get for a while, and only figured this out by looking it up on a forum.  Compared to Dark Soul's GFWL finicky online multiplayer, Dark Souls II is quite the improvement.  While I wasn't invaded very much on my first playthrough, excluding certain PvP heavy areas, I did get invaded a bit on NewGame+.  However my favorite multiplayer mechanic is currently co-op.  The co-op in Dark Souls II is certainly a mechanic you will want to try out with a friend or random player you find.  Be it helping another worldmaster with their challenges or summoning other players to your world, you'll find this can be a load of fun.  Just remember the more players you summon the harder your foes will get, gaining increased health and whatnot.  My recommendation when you do manage to beat the game and pass all the challenges your world has given you, is to not rush into NG+, and instead prepare yourself for NG+ by getting any items you may have left behind and upgarde your equipment.
Now I'll leave you hollows to collecting your souls and preparing for the real challenge ahead.

I'm not the sort of person to write reviews. I'd rather be playing the game in all honesty but I need to come clean and air our my issues with Just Cause 3 so I'll stop trying to justify it over Just Cause 2.
Does it do things better? Yes. Does it do enough better? No. Not even slightly. In fact it does a lot worse.
It's poorly designed in a lot of ways (you want to grapple and instantly enter a helicopter? Push E. Push it too early, which is very easy, and you will rag-doll into the side of it and probably get #rekt by the roters on the way over.) There is no effort in the bases or towns, they are all cookie-cutter and a chore to do. In Just Cause 2 every base was so much more unique and fun to play with and taking over one was a big event to boot. It all just feels less involved than Just Cause 2.
It's less fun.
It's more difficult in all the wrong ways.
It's got less going on.
It feels emptier.
It's stepping over itself in terms of design and controls.
Just Cause 3 can summarised in it's main mechanics.
You have infinite sticky bombs but they're your last resort or the main tool of a very boring player. The tether is given a lot of focus but it's not fun to use.
You can't fast travel infinitely anymore and must use flares which can be upgraded, however you can bypass this by doing two other things.
Helicopters are♥♥♥♥♥♥weak in terms of guns, much easier to control and downed by a random number of SAMs (and it ♥♥♥♥ing is random to, I've gone down to one in a god-damn gunship and taken six in a low tier attack chopper) and SAMs respawn.
Vehicles aren't fun to control and all are slow as hell and made of tin-foil and a wish when it comes to gunfire and explosives.
There's no weapon varity or progress, you're given your meagre lot at the start and have to deal and can only unlock a number of special weapons which won't fare much better than the bog-standard RPG you've been using or the LMG in terms of sheer practicality which is the only terms Just Cause 3 understands.
Chaos serves no purpose as far as we could discern over a long weekend of gaming it non-stop.
You respawn at the base you were fighting with everything reset except the permanent stuff. No more commitment, just "LOL, died, trying again right now."
Outposts are beyond lazy. Three chaos objects at most (boring ones too, no giant radar towers here), the only thing stopping you from clearing them in seconds is the SAM sites, serious, you could reduce this game to a 3 hour speed run if you had a mod to disable SAMs on outposts.
What is going on? It feels like it's had the soul sucked of it and the fun went along for the ride. Just Cause 2 had it's flaws, yes but it did gameplay much better. Hell, it's story was kind of fun at quite a few moments too. Just Cause 3... really has no story to it.
Listen, just go buy Just Cause 2. It's more fun, got more going on, more things to do, hell of a lot more cinematic, handles a hell of a lot better, runs a lot better, can be modded with a lot of fun toys, has vehicles you actually want to get in and drive and the powerful things feel powerful because they weighed properly. It's just better. Yes you have to sit through the item drop screen for things, but the pay off is worth it.
I'm sorry Just Cause 3, I had to defend you as the good angel but I spent more time picking you apart than praising you. I tried to love you.

Now here is a solid dose of old school thinking man's shooting, the way games should be. Firstly (admittedly because for some reason half life 2 engine doesnt like my laptop) load times are terrible. But when you get there... wow. Black mesa, not just the way you remember it, but the way you imagined it... the way it would have been.
The old fashioined puzzles that are still from the original have been augmented by puzzles thattake advantage of the newer engine. Stunning. Still nothing more delightful than doing away with the tentacles in blast pit. Or watching the rocket launch... awesome.
The new sound track is great, emotive and appropriate to the setting. The look of the aliens is entirely convincing, and you really believe that the alien slaves are just fighting because they have been ordered to, so they dont clash too much with their role in the second half life. I particularly like the Houndeyes, which i missed a little in the sequel. And seriously the bullsquid is just as horrifying as the first time round, with more convinving chemical spit, which glows and sticks to your hands and weapon most beautifully.
This is a GREAT re working of a classic. But there are at least 2 reasons why it needs work. 1; AI of army and assassins is bloody atrocious, and occasionally aliens will ignore you until you shoot at them. Head crabs appear to move towards some sort of "anchor point" before trying to attack again, rather than continuously attacking. 2: Although i love the use of the modern engine for some puzzles, i think it could have been used more. Flares being used instead of a crowbar for killing the first few zombies GREAT, why not a flare based puzzle, flammable liquids or weak ceilings supported by burnable boxes. Re-connecting electrical supplies by picking up the plug, wonderful! Why not some cable length based puzzles (like HL2E2) where you have a load of electrical points which need connecting up, but you only have wires of cirtain lengths.
Lets not forget, Freeman is a scientist. Lets see some science puzzles in there.
But regardless, these bad points are MINOR, appart from the AI which varies from Unforgivable to OK. If, like me, you love a trip down memory lane and find that Valve's HL1 redux was a bit pointless (it looked WORSE than the original if you had an openGL driver, remember them? wonderful bit of kit) then this is the bees knees. The sheer pleasure of slotting baddies with the revolver, the great achievements, the knowlege that SOMEONE cares about Dr Freeman... its great.
One question... What about Cpl Shepherd?

Muffin Knight Review
I like this game, a lot. But that's only because I love Super Crate Box. And this is literally Super Crate Box, just a rip off version of the game. Oh and this is the $6.99 version, SCB is free! And better!
Honestly, it's easier to name the differences than the similarities.
Okay where to begin. Differences:
In SCB, you start with a random weapon each round. In Muffin Knight, I always start with the knight.
In SCB, there are no popups mid game telling you you leveled up. In Muffin Knight, you have to put down your controller and click to continue.
In SCB, the controller works perfectly except for a small glitch when going to the menu from your controller. In Muffin Knight, for some reason even though I rebinded my controller, the up on the d pad goes down in game. And there is no button to click to continue when there is a popup on the screen, which is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off a lot. You have to literally set your controller down and click. What if you are sitting on a couch?
In SCB, when you shoot the grenade launcher into the fire, it falls from the top of the screen. In Muffin Knight, the fire is a stopping point. At least when I tried it.
In SCB, there is recoil. No recoil in Muffin Knight. You just shoot.
And the most obvious, the artwork is different. I like it though! That is a strong part about the game.
Similarities:
You literally get a random weapon when you pick up a muffin. The Archer is clearly the dual pistols from SCB. Since when does an Archer ever have 2 bows? I've never seen a dual bow archer ever. Then this game introduces it like it's new, clearly a copy of the dual pistol from SCB. Honestly, most of the weapons are the same from SCB.
There are 3 kinds of monsters, small, big, and ghosts. They even come out in the same pattern as Super Crate Box! 3 small ones will come out all at once! Or a single monster of any type. This is the exact same pattern from SCB!
Kills aren'r score, Muffins/Crates are.
The Forest map is literally Construction from Super Crate Box. Literally the exact same thing. Not one difference. They literally just reskinned it.
Gameplay is exactly the same. Everything about it. Random weapons from each pickup, monsters spawn at the top and follow a path to the bottom hitting walls and turning, when they hit fire they spawn faster.
This is literally a weaker version of Super Crate Box. I like the art work of this game, it's beautiful. But sometimes it's hard to tell where the edge of a platform is. I found an area where it looks like I'm jumping through the floor. It's in the Forest level, there is the second platform from the top, on the left side. I tried it on the right side but it wasn't as bad. But on the left side of Forest, it looks like you're jumping/falling through the floor. I literally don't know where the edge is, and I don't know why it's worse on the left side, it might be the artwork or something, but the right side feels more solid. That might be a visual thing, they might be the same exactly. I didn't try as much on the right side.
Things I like:
Killing monsters actually helps you because they give XP. In SCB, killing monsters does nothing other than stop them from going into the fire and going faster.
Problems:
The controller problems really need to be fixed. The controller only navigates in the settings, not the start menu. And the vertical navigation is inverted even though I rebinded. Pushing up does down, and pushing down goes up. But in game, the controls are perfect.
You can hear the spot where the music loops and wow that is annoying. The music is awesome, but hearing the spot where it loops is annoying for some reason. The Forest level specifically. Or it might have been the first level. But one of the first 2 levels, you can hear where the music loops.
No recoil. Is there a mode where there is recoil? In SCB, the machine gun has some recoil. In Muffin Knight, the mage (fully automatic shots) has no recoil.
Anyways, I like the game, but it is just a bad version of Super Crate Box. And it costs $6.99 while Super Crate Box is free. If some of the problems I listed are fixed, then I will change my review because I love Super Crate Box and I want to love this game.

While the gameplay for Muffin Knight is actually kind of fun for a little while, it quickly becomes repetitive and boring. The different levels that you unlock as you go along are pretty much all the same and don't really do much different with the gameplay. The only thing that changes between the levels is the enemies and the layout. The Layouts rarely make the game more interesting to play or change things up, and while the enemies change, the basic enemy types do not. There are the flying enemies, and the small and large enemies, both speedy and regular. I'd have liked to see them add different enemies types as the game progressed.
Another big problem that I had was the character types that you can play as. As far as I can tell, when you collect a muffin, you randomly change to a different character type, and the problem with that is that the game becomes less fun as it goes on as a result of this. The vast majority of the character types that you play as are terrible, so as the game goes on and you unlock more of the character types, you spend less time playing as the few good character types, and more on the terrible character types. The only character types that I enjoyed playing as are the Knight, the Archer, the Gnome, and the Mage, and the rest were mediocre to outright horrible.
It's can be a fun game to play for about 20-30 minutes, but it definetly is not something that I would pay money for again.

Eternal Senia was a very good surprise for me, the gameplay is very simple anyone can learn it within a few seconds, I feel like it's an essential point since a game is made to have fun.
The plot is also rather simple but is quite entertaining and you may find yourself wonder how it ends.
The length of the game, this game is rather short 6-7 hours to end it, it's a good point since it doesn't bore you with unnecessary text, battle or content.
The art is good, all mobs and monsters are nicely design, most of them are very well drawn and suit perfectly the action and the universe. The number of artworks and where they are display is also well calculated it doesn't flood you at all but they are there when they are needed.
The characters, there is no superficial and useless character, the author just introduce the perfect number of characters to have all of them developed enough. Despite the feelings of the main characters a bit naive and childish sometimes they share very strong feelings well described by the text.
The sounds are excellent, I really enjoyed each of them, they suit pefectly the mood and the universe, only the first one is a bit too rocky for the place in which we listen to it.
The gameplay, this the best advantage of this game but also it worst drawback, the gameplay being easy it's really fun to play the game but when you are doing all the sidequests and starting to think about the game it gets really really easy to beat all the mobs. Mini boss is just spell spam. Bosses remain rather challenging. Despite the spells being usefull and funs, there is some really balance issue with them some are too strong some are nearly useless. Last thing the game isn't for controller buttons by default are really poorly or not configured.
I higly recommed to give a try to Eternal Senia, but you should take the game how is it that is to say a fun game, no try hards, no theory crafting if you are able to do so you'll find a very fun and enjoyable game.

Pros
Cons
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Controls are typical of a FPS and gameplay is overall unchallenging and relaxing.
The story is revealed through letters from home back on earth and messages left from the previous owner of the slime ranch. The game is still under development, so further details will likely be revealed as content is finished and released.
There are no physical NPCs so far besides the slimes. They appear through letters and messages and a sort of job board to offer rewards in exchange for resources, and they are more for flavor than to add to the gameplay.
The art style is extremely charming, somewhat similar to a child's painting in it's simplicity. Soft colors and gentle shapes make up the world overall, and it's clear what the artists were aiming for.

Possibly my favourite game of all time and I only bought it last weekend :D
Pros
- Destruction is amazing, no other game can do destruction as well as Just Cause can
- Graphics are nice, visuals are bright and vibrant.
- Attention to detail is very good, e.g. when you run over sun flowers in their fields in a vehicle each one individually gets flattened
- Extremely fun! Finally a game that pretty much just focuses on pure fun, messing around and nothing else
- Progression is very enjoyable, upgrade your wingsuit/other gear and slowly take Medici settlement by settlement, also store every vehicle that you can find in the game to have it delivered to you in a rebel drop whenever you like (This includes F1 Cars, Sports cars, Jets, Tanks, and the huge cargo planes)
- Every limitation is removable! At the start of the game you may notice that some annoying limitations are added to stop you from immediatley getting lots of jets and other things in rebel drops and destroying everything on the island. There are of course legitimate intentions for this as it would not be very challenging if they did not have these limitations but every single one can be removed later game as you progress and unlock more things.
- Literally limitless possibilities! Drop 2 buses out from a cargo plane onto one of Di Ravello's bases, or create your own home made mortar strike using dual tethers, a ramp and random passing by cars. Anything you can think of is do-able in Just Cause 3 :)
Cons
- Some hardware issues with the game - apparently does not work on a lot of different systems which could be worrying for some.
- FPS drops are often. I run this game on high settings with some set to ultra. I have a Gigabyte GTX 970 graphics card and an AMD 8320 3.5ghz processor with 8gb of RAM. My FPS usually stays at a straight 90 but can sometimes dip as low as 17fps.
- The game crashes fairly often. It is usually when I get into helicopters or any kind of airborne vehicle the game sometimes crashes - roughly once every 2 hours
- Load screens take a long time to load
- Is perhaps a little repetative after a while, but this can all be fixed with your out of the box thinking and creativity on how to complete tasks!
NOTE: Make you sure you have manually updated your windows to service pack 1. I went through the hassle of reinstalling Windows TWICE before figuring out that all I had to press was one button to get my Just Cause to work. R.I.P :(

Edited from my answer in the comments:
It's a lot like it [Worms Armageddon] to me.
The balance is different on weapons, weapon speed, gravity, jump height, fall damage (and fall threshold), but it ultimately feels a lot like Armageddon.
Most of the iconic weapons act really close to their Armageddon counterpart, like the Super Sheep, the Ming Vase or even the worm selection thing.
It feels like a sequel, with the addition of vehicles and crafting: taking base features and expanding upon them.
Vehicles add more liberty, more movement, and specific strategies. Crafting allows for less wait time between turns and make the crates more crucial.
Even the UI feels really close, with the wind display, health bars, fonts...
And finally, singleplayer features feel a lot like Armageddon: training (Super Sheep training \o/), missions as a campaign, the team editor with its iconic voices. I miss the map painting editor though!
There are a lot of differences, obviously, but it really feels like Team 17 went back to Armageddon and expanded upon it.

If you're interested in the game because T17 claims it has the W:A feel, it doesn't. It might be an entertaining tongue-in-cheek party game in its own, though.

* Missing kamikaze, dragon ball and cows among other things. W:A had 60 vastly distinct weapons, W.M.D has 35 plus their craftable variants.

Cons

I did feel that some of the "Mission Moments" were rehashed or underwhelming but it never interfered with the high octane action. If you love shooters or are fans of CoD you will love AW, its not the best in the series but it a bast and with the new Exo-Abilities it's sure to entertain.

What a relief! I've just finished my first 20-hour haul through this game, and while I thoroughly enjoyed it, I admit I am pretty psyched to be done with it. Alien: Isolation is less of a game and more of a survival simulation that spirals out of control, while you sit glued to the edge of your seat thinking you might need therapy after the experience. It is one of the scariest games I've ever played, and also one of the most addicting. I've been re-watching all of the Alien movies over the past few days, and I feel that A:I could easily have been a highlight of the series if it were a movie and not a game. It plays like a movie, with a solid plot that's thrilling to take part in, and I feel strongly that this game does justice to the Alien franchise.
I can't say enough good things about the visuals, the controls, the mechanics of the game - all are truly flawless and immersive. The soundtrack and audio are masterful and captivating. It has some of the best AI I've ever experienced in a stealth game. The crafting is fun and the weapons/tools are excellent. Most of the negative reviews I've read center on the fact that the game is very long, and not only long but grueling. While this is true, and while I did feel certain parts of the game were padded a bit much (especially towards the end) I was content to get a full 20-hour experience from this title. I certainly wouldn't have wanted it to be shorter. And perhaps most importantly, I feel that the never-ending twists, turns and terrors of the plot mirror the Alien films. Those aliens are damned resourceful, and they just don't know how to die. So I feel it's appropriate that the game made you work to reach the end of it, in the same way that Ripley struggles until the last minute of each film, only to find out in the sequel that the aliens are still alive and well. So to put it bluntly, I was not expecting a 12-hour jaunt with a quick and happy ending, and I'm glad I didn't receive one. Personally, I think it's a shame to see the game receive negative ratings for that reason.
The biggest complaint I can make here is that many of the objectives center around using switches or powering up/down generators, and while the plot keeps it interesting and the locations are all well-designed, that doesn't change the fact that the actual motions you go through to complete each objective are very similar. This may just be a matter of taste, but personally I would have liked more puzzle-oriented tasks like in Dead Space, rather than the "let's pull the switches in the right order" thing that A:I seemed so fond of. The way you use switches and other machinery is unique though, and it evokes a Resident Evil sort of feeling that your actions may have very real consequences. Using machinery is a visceral experience and leaves you vulnerable to attack, and most things you do in this game tend to attract unwanted attention. So, switch-pulling aside, it never takes long for the action to resume once again.
And action there is. I must admit I was more afraid of the androids than the alien. They have a strange way about them, and you can never be sure that they won't turn hostile on you. More than once, I thought I was safe with a particular android, only to have Ripley whip around to see those red glowing eyes strangling the life out of her, declaring "You're not supposed to be here." Really, excellent work with the design of those androids. Their nature also stays very much in keeping with the series canon, androids often being fundamentally untrustworthy and providing that extra bit of uncertainty.
Sevastopol is huge, sprawling, and often beautiful, especially during the rare moments when you can see outside. Its story is interesting, unraveled through computer documents and audio logs, and I still wish there was more of it to read. I look forward to playing this with Oculus Rift some day, even if I just find a spot and gaze out toward the massive gas giant out the window. I look forward to playing this again.
There are so many moments in this game that I could rave about, but I'll spare you the spoilers. If you're a fan of the Alien series and if you can handle some intense horror and stealth, you should play this game. 9/10

Summary:  It's like System Shock 2 meets Amnesia.  The fact that it's set in an astoundingly realized, lovingly created depiction of the "Alien" film universe make it a dream come true.  But do NOT buy if you are expecting a shooter!
This game is a truly amazing experience, and an instant classic.  But it's certainly not for everyone, as you do not play a powerful super soldier or master assassin.  Instead you play as an engineer, Ellen Ripley's daughter, Amanda, as she works to outsmart and outlast not only the Alien (which is unkillable) but the human and android survivors who populate the ruined spacestation Sevastapol.
The most obviously outstanding part of this game is its state-of-the-art AI.  For the Alien, this means that a deadly, and frankly terrifying monster is going to be stalking you, reacting your movements and actions, trying to surprise and trap you.  For the humans/synthetics, it means that they follow unscripted patterns (instead of just marching like clockwork over the same old patrol routes like in every other stealth game) and look long and hard when trying to locate you.  No scenario plays out the same way twice, and incredible scenes result from the interplay of your actions, the Alien's actions, and the actions of the other survivors.
The second thing that impresses me is the uniqueness of the game design.  Ripley is never powerful, and on "hard" difficulty (the way everybody should play it) can die after one or two gunshots.  That means the majority of the game is spent avoiding conflict vs. plunging in.  You do find guns, but using them is often much more dangerous than stealth, as you run the risk both of getting shot and of attracting the Alien.  This does not mean guns are useless, but that you must be smart about when and where you chose to use them.  The game keeps you constantly thinking about what the best strategy is to survive in any given context.  This is not only more realistic and more true to the spirit of the 1979 film Alien, but is also fun, intense, and unique enough that it feels fresh and new.
The third most impressive part of the game is it's graphics and art style.  While I reccomend turning down the film grain a bit, the game looks gorgeous.  The designers really took 70s/80s feel of the Alien films are lovingly recreated it here in a way that feels incredibly authentic and real.  From the chunky mechanical keyboards, to big analog knobs and glowing NASA-style buttons, to the green-on-black CRT displays, the game's retro look, cribbed from the movie (which, of course, had legendary set and prop design).  The engine renders and lights these objects in such a way as to make the world incredibly beautiful, convincing, and immersive.  Although poly count may be low compared to other games, the overall beauty of the world makes such details irrelevent.  Top notch wound and fire effects add to the graphical experience.  And at ~25 hours for a completionist playthrough, you get plenty of value for your buck.
Do not buy this if you simply can't get behind the idea of a game where cowering under a desk equals winning and blasting away with your shotgun equals losing (most of the time).  But if you like the idea of a unique stealth horror game set in one of the most iconic sci-fi universes ever, then this game is a must-buy.

At this point, I've finished Dishonored 2 three separate times. Twice as Emily (High/Low Chaos) and once as Corvo (High Chaos). I just started a Low Chaos run with Corvo.'
I'm on an i5-4590 with a GTX 970. I bought the game on release day. Upon first opening the game, I ran into the same issues a lot of other people seem to be having. However, instead being like most people crying and returning the game (but not before leaving a bad review for a game they didn't play), I took 2 minutes to Google the issues I was having. All I had to do was reset the resolution to the correct one and change the playback to Borderless Full Screen. After doing those 2 simple things, I was playing on Very High/Ultra settings and never dipping below 55 fps. Now that the first of a couple performance patches is out, I'm not sure this is even an issue anymore.
The original Dishonored is one of my favorite single player games, and now Dishonored 2 is right up there with it. With that being said, the series' strong suit is not the story. I will say that Dishonored 2's story is much more compelling and less predictable than the first game's, but it still isn't anything that will blow you away. It is what it is: a way to get you into what the game is REALLY about and REALLY excels at...
I do not feel like I'm overexaggerating when I say that the gameplay in the Dishonored series is absolutely incredible. Dishonored 2 manages to take every aspect that made the first game's gameplay so rewarding and challenging and expand on almost every part of it. Doing a High Chaos (killing everyone) run with either character will make you feel more powerful than almost any other game, while managing to not also feel easy. When you're about halfway through the game, the upgrades possible for your powers are so fun to experiment with and just make you feel like a general badass. Doing Low Chaos (no/few killings, no/some detection by enemies) is about 200% more fun than in the original Dishonored. You can now choose to knock enemies unconsious with a drop-assassination move, and your powers are more viable to use for stealth gameplay than the first game, which really held a lot of the gameplay back if you were trying to complete the game without killing anyone. All in all, you will be hard-pressed to find more rewarding and fun gameplay in any other stealth action game.
Another strong suit of the Dishonored series is the intricate level design. Even being on my 4th playthrough, I'm still finding new paths to take through the levels, and alternate outcomes to situations that I hadn't seen at all in previous playthroughs. No matter what playstyle you're going for, there's always some way through the expansive level that will be perfect for you. If there's any reason at all to buy this game, it's to see this masterpiece of level design and world-building.
Dishonored 2 goes above and beyond to give veterans of the first game everything they love + more, while serving as an amazing experience for those new to the series. It makes me sad to see a "Mixed" by the reviews on Steam for this game, because I believe if people didn't have the performance issues (or were willing to try to work around them at least for a minute) this would be GOTY for a lot of people, because I know it is for me. Performance issues aside (because I never even experienced them in game, just in the menu when I first opened it) I think Dishonored 2 is the best game of the year and a master-class in world building and gameplay from Arkane.

In Rome's absence I have not been idle. I have extended the rule of God to Saracen heathens. I have subjugated India by the power of musket and moustache. I have checked the pugnacious pride of Japan's Daimyos. Yet during all these exploits, I have longed to march once more under the Aquila. "Give me back my legions!" was my cry. Creative Assembly have at last acceded to my Augustine demands.
Beginning in the early republican period, before the mediterranean azure was mired by the effusion of Punic blood, Rome II shares a similar timeline to that of its immortal, deified predecessor. The scale of the maps are largely the same, though in this latest iteration, it is possibly to extend Rome's dominion to the tip of the Arabian peninsula. The game thus offers an enormous range of climates in which to do battle. My legions have slaughtered Etruscans in the auburn glades of Italy and stained the deserts red with the lifeblood of Egypt.
The map itself is divided into provinces which are roughly consistent with contemporary cartography, containing various minor, specialised settlements dominated by a larger provincial capital. The game thus presents a hybrid of Empire's regional buildings and Shogun's unified territorial development, doing away with a lot of frustration (no more will a single unit of routed infantry lay waste to an entire region's industrial infrastructure).
The battlemaps resemble the campaign map with almost perfect accuracy. The positions of forests, coasts, roads and hills all correspond to their representations in the campaign, presenting generals with a more involved process of determining where to do battle. Pick well, for an obscure and unimportant mound of earth in the campaign map may conceal an entire army of screaming barbarians in battle mode, thanks to the news line of site feature.
Battles play out wonderfully. The AI, always the weakest point in the TW series, is now more inclined to actually try to kill you. Exposed skirmishers will be annihilated by that unit of cavalry you neglected to keep track of. You will be flanked. You will be ambushed. Your auxiliary infantry will be butchered by (screaming) Celtic Oathsworn swordsmen. Do not expect the enemy to simply sit there in potato mode as it did in other titles. (I'm looking at you MTW II).
Sieges differ in one very important aspect - they now come with enjoyment! Cities are huge and dominate the entire battlemap, sprawling over hills and towering over their besiegers. Conquer enough of them, however, and you r chosen faction may come to dominate the classical world. Whatever your choice, be it Roman civilization, Hellenic rennaissance, Persian reqonquest or barbarian screaming, Rome II has a lot to offer for fans of strategic and tactical warfare.

Muffin Knight is a game that looks catered towards toddlers, but is a perfect example of the idiom 'don't judge a book by its cover'. Despite looking very innocent and easy, 'Muffin Knight' is a surprisingly challenging game - especially if you're attempting to 5-star it.
With a fantastic single-player and multiplayer co-op, Muffin Knight is a fast-paced game full of enjoyment, challenge and charm. Whilst the plot is simple and the graphics are subpar, Muffin Knight excels in its gameplay and can become dangerously addicting. The music is catchy, the controls are fantastically responsive and the added perks and upgrades really add to the game and genuinely make a difference, saving a very repetitive formula from going stale.
My only complaints would be its lack of more settings, there isn't a lot of availability on how to customise the settings to best suit your PC, plus the menus are pretty awful if you plan to use a controller. Whilst I would highly recommend a controller for its movement flow and simplicity, I would suggest opting for a computer mouse when roaming through the menus.
The randomisation for the characters can be frustrating, especially as some of the starters are incredibly weak until you upgrade them. Whilst upgrading doesn't take too long, to go from a strong character such as Cyclops or Grizzly, to a ridiculously weak character such as Monkey or Dragon, can really be annoying. Whilst mentioning characters, it is worthy ot note that the order of the unlockables seems very odd as well - whilst only a minor nitpick, I did feel very disappointed that the final unlockable was one of the worst.
Overall, Muffin Knight is an incredibly fun and simplistic game to play. The added perks really help the game to feel different every time, and the challenge bar is at the perfect level for this type of genre. Whilst the plot is weak and some of the power-ups are far worse than others, due to the upgrades and points, you can quickly improve the weaker characters and make them some of the strongest. Muffin Knight is great fun with friends, but is also very enjoyable as a solo game - so go forth and find those muffins!

First of all: I'm not going to show mercy on this game. So if that's something you wish to avoid, then here's your warning.
TL;DR: It can be a fun experience, but that's most of it. That aside, it still remains a clone and lacks any love put into it from the developers. If you can get it for really cheap, check it out. Otherwise, stick with Super Crate Box, which is free.
-----full review-----
How to describe Muffin Knight... Well, I think saying it's Super Crate Box mixed with the graphics of Ducktales Remastered might just be the most accurate thing. But for the people who have never played Super Crate Box, allow me to ellaborate. The gameplay consists of you being put into some kind of arena, in which you have to gather enough Muffins to unlock the next stage, while being cautious of enemies who are trying to ruin your progress. Muffins also unlock new weapons when you obtained a select amount of them. And that is really all there is to it. I would say it's an innovative combat system, if they didn't straight out rip it off Super Crate Box. Some of the weapons do the EXACT same effect, but just having a dual pistol being replaced with an archer. This game is more on the child-friendly tour, so it replaced all weapons and enemies with weapons or mythological creatures.
The story is very... vague. Protagonist finds a basket of Muffins and boom, he gets turned into a guy who can switch between weapons. Don't know what his goal is, but apparently he just needs to get his muffins back from some... dragonguy. NOTHING is explained in the game, except for the first part.
At first it creates the illusion of difficult. You can't touch an enemy, or you're dead. Fortunately there are upgrades for that. You really have to make decisions about what to upgrade though. At first it might look easy to level up, but it becomes more of a grindfest at later levels. That is, if we exclude the extra modes this game has.
Oh wait, did I say extra modes? Hahaha, aaah, how funny. Where do I begin...
You start of the game in Knight Mode. Once you have beaten all the stages and defeated the final boss, you unlock a mode. And after you have finished that one, you unlock another. And another. And another. Would this be a problem? Not really, if it wasn't the EXACT same, just with increased difficulty. Why, in the name of Last Order, do this? Let us choose our dificulty, don't force it on us.
And those reasons above form my biggest complaint with the game: It lacks love from the developpers. Like I said, I won't show mercy and I definitely won't here. They literally ripped off Super Crate Box, gave it a more child-friendly and HD design, and to avoid having a short game, let us repeat the game over and over again a total of 5 times. It's not even funny.
If you can get this game for really cheap, go ahead. I definitely won't stop you. When I started this game, I did have a fun time. But over time, it just decreased. If you want to try out a game like this, get Super Crate Box.
Note that I'm not trying to advertise Super Crate Box, but it's not only the same original game, but it's free too.

I preordered Just Cause 3 around August of 2015 and after waiting for some of the major bugs to get squashed, I can definitely say that it is all that I hoped it would be and more.  First, you have a plethora of vehicles and weapons to choose from and although the game can seem like a grind sometimes, there is a practically infinite amount of ways to move through the game.  If you have a decent computer and you liked Just Cause 2, I heavily recommend this game.  Although there are still some bugs to be fixed, it is much improved since release.

I did not experience technical issues.  I did experience a somewhat bland, but somewhat hilarious, sandbox game that fills a unique niche in the sandbox universe.  To be fair, I can't even remember its prequel to compare it to, because it, too, must have had the same flaws.
This game is all about the grapple and stunts.  You can do a lot of fun, memorable stuff.  But, because of some design decisions and flaws, the gameplay doesn't feel spectacular or worthy of re-playing.
1. The controls are not polished enough.  This is something most open-world games have a problem with, but when you're gliding and grappling around it's a huge pain point.  I found myself swearing as I flew into walls or got stuck under ledges.
2. When you die, you just respawn where you left off. So you can basically liberate the whole map before doing any missions.
3. New enemies spawn behind from all sides, making battles chaotic and not strategic in any way. This negates any use of the sniper rifle.
4. Because of the lack of battle tactics, Rico is almost invincible, and so they didn't include crouching or cover because of this and the above point.
5. Upgrades (or 'mods' as they call them) are mostly optional. They help a little, but not enough to make the game easier or feel rewarding.
6. Most of the time, it was easier to glide/parachute/fast-travel rather than find a vehicle. Traveling got to be quite a shlep in the mountains.  The vehicles and attention to their detail are amazing but mostly superfluous.
These points together contributed to a loss of enjoyment in gameplay.
A typical attack on a military base involves parachuting around haphazardly and shooting missiles at targets.  This could have been much more fun if there were a stealth element, or 'level up' health/abilities before attempting, or both.
The story has a lot of interesting characters who are never fully fleshed out.  Some side-missions with them would have been fun, or at least some more back-story.  I think maybe I was supposed to remember them from a previous game?
Overall, the game is beautiful and fun, to an extent. The story isnt bad, but there's not enough of it to be fulfilling.  There is little replay value and gameplay gets repetitive quickly.  I'm left wishing I could go back into sandbox mode and have a good romp, but everything's liberated, and the battles weren't that fun to begin with.

- OST is great especially piano, love it!
