At this point, I've finished Dishonored 2 three separate times. Twice as Emily (High/Low Chaos) and once as Corvo (High Chaos). I just started a Low Chaos run with Corvo.'
I'm on an i5-4590 with a GTX 970. I bought the game on release day. Upon first opening the game, I ran into the same issues a lot of other people seem to be having. However, instead being like most people crying and returning the game (but not before leaving a bad review for a game they didn't play), I took 2 minutes to Google the issues I was having. All I had to do was reset the resolution to the correct one and change the playback to Borderless Full Screen. After doing those 2 simple things, I was playing on Very High/Ultra settings and never dipping below 55 fps. Now that the first of a couple performance patches is out, I'm not sure this is even an issue anymore.
The original Dishonored is one of my favorite single player games, and now Dishonored 2 is right up there with it. With that being said, the series' strong suit is not the story. I will say that Dishonored 2's story is much more compelling and less predictable than the first game's, but it still isn't anything that will blow you away. It is what it is: a way to get you into what the game is REALLY about and REALLY excels at...
I do not feel like I'm overexaggerating when I say that the gameplay in the Dishonored series is absolutely incredible. Dishonored 2 manages to take every aspect that made the first game's gameplay so rewarding and challenging and expand on almost every part of it. Doing a High Chaos (killing everyone) run with either character will make you feel more powerful than almost any other game, while managing to not also feel easy. When you're about halfway through the game, the upgrades possible for your powers are so fun to experiment with and just make you feel like a general badass. Doing Low Chaos (no/few killings, no/some detection by enemies) is about 200% more fun than in the original Dishonored. You can now choose to knock enemies unconsious with a drop-assassination move, and your powers are more viable to use for stealth gameplay than the first game, which really held a lot of the gameplay back if you were trying to complete the game without killing anyone. All in all, you will be hard-pressed to find more rewarding and fun gameplay in any other stealth action game.
Another strong suit of the Dishonored series is the intricate level design. Even being on my 4th playthrough, I'm still finding new paths to take through the levels, and alternate outcomes to situations that I hadn't seen at all in previous playthroughs. No matter what playstyle you're going for, there's always some way through the expansive level that will be perfect for you. If there's any reason at all to buy this game, it's to see this masterpiece of level design and world-building.
Dishonored 2 goes above and beyond to give veterans of the first game everything they love + more, while serving as an amazing experience for those new to the series. It makes me sad to see a "Mixed" by the reviews on Steam for this game, because I believe if people didn't have the performance issues (or were willing to try to work around them at least for a minute) this would be GOTY for a lot of people, because I know it is for me. Performance issues aside (because I never even experienced them in game, just in the menu when I first opened it) I think Dishonored 2 is the best game of the year and a master-class in world building and gameplay from Arkane.

Alien: Isolation is a successful throwback both to the classic 1979 film and the games that were inspired by it. Nearly everything in the game works to evoke memories of the film in a sometimes less-than-subtle way that will make fans smirk. But even if you've never seen the film, you'll still get a kick out of the great visuals of out-of-date technology and feel creeped-out by the horror cliches that weave together to create a game that stands out among other horror survival games.
You won't get cheap jump-scares like in something like Slender - at least not outside of a few of the more scripted cinematic moments. This game is built on the tension of knowing you're in danger at almost every moment. To that end, while enemies aren't always present as you make your way through the station, you'll always feel like they could be due to the game's AI allowing dangerous enemies, human, robot or alien alike, to roam to some degree. Players should expect some frustration as some areas can feel like they don't give you enough room to avoid unnecessary deaths and you'll sometimes feel like you'd rather just rush through to the next part that isn't so tough. Players will enjoy the game much more if they can savor the feeling of hiding in a locker, hoping that the alien will hunt for you somewhere else so that you can get to the save point in the next room over. It can be difficult to keep that in mind when you've made it to the same point a dozen times only to get killed in the last few steps. But for every moment of frustration, the game rewards you with some really amazingly tense or interesting moments.
The game's 20-ish hour campaign length feels perfect to me. I never felt too frustrated to continue, or wished it would just be over by now. The pacing and length justifies itself with some fantastic variety that builds tension or intrigue, adding unexpected twists in the gameplay and rewarding you with some great opportunities for exploration between high points in the tension.
One more note on Oculus Rift support: I played through the last half of the game using the unofficial Oculus Rift tweaks that were found shortly after launch. If you have a Rift, I strongly recommend trying it. It's the best VR experience available so far. It raises the immersion and scariness to a new level. While I usually get some amount of motion sickness in VR games, there was surprisingly little in this until the very end, probably because the pace of player movement is usually extremely slow. However, the game is certainly not made for Oculus as it stands. The positioning of the camera makes doing certain actions difficult or impossible. Swiveling your head around to avoid clipping through locker doors is common, and many of the in-game menus or interactive devices are unreadable, even after recalibrating. So, if you do plan on playing with a Rift, I'd suggest playing through at least the first few hours without it to learn the game, and using a controller would probably help with some of the failings of the UI.

Well... I have to say after the Aliens Colonial Marines "saga" I was not expecting much from this game at all, we have had it all before, a dev blustering on about their amazing aliens game only to discover it was a steaming pile of dog crap... yeah we know the story...
This game in a nut shell is not any of those negative things.  Creative assembly have done the series justice with this amazing game, and it is amazing, the graphics look good and the music score is second to none its  really amazing how the music and sounds thicken the atmosphere so much that it can have you nervous and your heart pounding in your chest before the alien has even appeared, you genuinely feel in danger the entire time and it can get quite unnerving at time which for an Alien game is perfect.
The Alien creature is just absurdly good... it stalks you for most of the game and even when it isn't on the same level as you, you can hear it scratching and clattering around the ducting searching and listening for its next victim, you will find yourself skulking from locker to wall to under a bed or behind a table praying that it doesn't see you for if it does?  Game over man... Game over.
A wide range of tools are available however to aid you in surviving, throwing flares and various crafted items to confuse and distract your would be killer into giving you a few more precious seconds to grab that key card or punch in that door code before it realises where you are.
I won't go into many details about the various levels however they explore a wide range of the Alien universe and you get a taste of everything with this game... it is never the same from mission to mission and it mixes it up just enough to keep you nervous and paranoid of the next calamity to be headed your way.
The game is single player only so fans of coop or other multi player games might not find what they want here, however for single player story rich fans like myself this game was fantastic, and as well as being fantastic it is BIG, I clocked in 18 hours on my first play through and to be honest I wasn't exploring as much as I wanted because I was just to paranoid the alien was going to catch me.  Lots of replay value here between the survivor modes and just the sheer fun of playing through again, or hunting for collectables missed in a previous run etc. it will keep you coming back for more.
The only thing that was a negative for me, is that I would have liked a little more interaction with some off the other characters in the game, they are not in it for much and as much as I wouldn't have wanted escort missions (it simply wouldn't have worked with that alien running around) it would have been great to at least interact with them more further than required static cut scenes.
My rating of this game is 9.5/10 I love it that much, and I hope any future DLC we get is of equal quality.  I also hope SEGA let this team create further Alien games because the love they have for the franchise is oozing from ever single bulkhead in this game.

Great palate cleanser, super addictive qualities throughout. Sure, its your standard 2D platformer affair. Not dissimilar to a Mario Bros. Single screen kill/collect top score based fun. But this game has a lot of heart. You collect muffins. That's endearing in itself. Every time you collect one, your character switches which may seem jarring at first until you become familiar with all the attacks. Then it becomes rather strategic.
One of the more surprising aspects is every second spent in game feels like you're earning something. XP is earned for collecting muffins and killing enemies that goes into a player level which awards you with skill points which can be spent on each individual creature. New levels can be unlocked either through collecting a specific number of muffins in one run or overall player level. Perks and extra lives are also available for purchase.
Respawns are super fast, controls are tight. The characters are adorable and silly (see Sumo Panda) All these features lend themselves to something familiar, easy to enter and super hard to put down.
Just one more run. Then I'll stop.

Let's face it: the game is horribily HORRIBLY optimized. Even with my quite good build, I hemorrhage ram like crazy unless I turn everything down. As of right now it wont even SLI correctally. So basically, I play on low-medium settings so that I don't experience framerate issues, but even then I get sometimes some drops, and whats the fun in having a HIGH end computer to play a game (you havto pay moneys for) to play on medium.....
Anyways:
Pros
1) The game, even if I play on low settings, looks good. It's colorful, bright, smooth, and the explosions are incredibly enjoyable
2) The sounds are ok, and the voice actors are really funny and well done.
3) I liked the music, even though they are quiet and you don't really hear them.
4) The gameplay is fun and addictive. I love the wingsuit, I enjoy moving through the mountains with my gears, the shooting is fun. Though I had to remap a bit my controls because I wanted it to feel like Just Cause 2, it plays well, and it is fun.
5) The explosions and the grappling hook... Nothing else to say, it's just well done. The game become somewhat a physics-based game with the ability to use your grappling.
6) Huge map, a lot of places to blow up.
7) The leaderboard thigie is neat (i dont care if im not as good as my friends)
Cons
1) You won't give a crap about the story/missions, as for Just Cause 2.
2) The map is too big. Yes, I said it was a pro, but my main problem is when you try to go from an island to the other. If you don't have a jet, it'll take forever to crosse the water.
3) I still don't get how the chaos work for this episode - might change this point once I figure it out.
4) As stated above,
5) the optimization,
6) IS
7) ABSOLUTLY
8) POSITIVELY
9) HORRRRRRIIIIIIIDDDDD
10) Having to log into Square Enix servers for everything, so if their down the game props you every few minutes, or every time you open the map
11) Initial Load times, the main menu--game start is dreadful, and yes i've heard of the SSD vs HDD
12) Gets repetitive quickly
Conclusion
Overall, this game is a fun experience, if you like blowing things up and killing people like there is no tomorrow (which is my case so...). If you want deep story, dark intrigue, multiplayer mode or realistic gunfight, just ignore this game. I think that if you liked Just Cause 2, you'll like this one too. It's no where near perfect, it surely isn't as good as JC2, but it's fun, and it gives you explosion, so it's nice.

This game is one of the best zombie survival games I have ever played. Not only it is the old fashioned zombie game without any weird mutating zombies, but because it has a certain feel of urgency when there are twenty four zombies walking toward you and you have only five bullets left. It also makes you think for the team, because even if it is possible to survive for a short period of time without any teammates, it isn't survivable for long. The infection and bleeding effects are also great addition to the experience. If you are infected, and in relatively safe location with your teammates, you can cause a lot of trouble, when you turn.  There is nothing more stressful than being with your friends and no meds, it makes you think how to save at least them from you, and thats when realism comes to play, what would one do in this kind of scenario? The answer was simple, the game has won my heart when i felt real fear when i pressed the button and the gun was turned toward my head.
I would recomend this game anytime and to anyone.

"Eternal Senia" has its ups and downs. The game is fairly easy as it requires little more than moving around with the arrow keys, as running into enemies is your main means of attack. Due to this and the fact that there are items you will want to grind, "Senia" can get somwewhat repetitive, and repetitiveness is not something you want in a 7.5-8 hour game. However, the plot and art are pretty good, even if the plot could stand a little more flesh. In terms of sound, "Senia" has good music, but nothing to write home about, but some of the sound effects seem a bit out of place. Considering that most of the game was made by Holy Priest and that it is his/her first game, the game is good for what it is: a first step into the scene by the creator.
Score : 7 / 10, a good time killer, lasting 7.5-8 hours for 100%. "Senia" is a nice game if you want to find something new and since it's free there's no reason to not at least check it out

I grew up in the 90s on a steady stream of the best-worst action movies. They were over the top, stupid, and loud as hell- Everything America stands for. And they were great.
BROFORCE toes the same line as many of those old action flicks.  It's a celebration of testosterone, bullets, and bombs, taken to the nth degree +1. If Stephen Colbert and Torgue Flexington developed a game, it would come out a lot like this.
And it's magnificent.
The controls are better than you'd think with a keyboard. They're tight. Responsive. It takes getting used to, and a controller would be better, but it's not bad.
The gameplay is simple and open-ended in a great way. You could go all out and dive straight in like a madman. You could take your time and pick out the best possible attack route... Or you could defeat your enemies by exploiting the environment, which is the most patriotic way.
All that aside, BROFORCE is one of the few games I've played in a while that's just plain fun. No intricate plot. No dark, brooding hero. No 'LOOK AT HOW GRIMDARK AND BROWN THE WORLD IS, BLOO BLOO BLOO'. You shoot, stab, and explode your way through everything ( including your friends ) in a colorful world, and laugh the whole time.
Awesome.

Alien: Isolation is a 20-hour romp through Sevastopol station, with palpitation-inducing tension gnawing at you through the entire voyage. The game's top-notch artistic direction can only be matched by its execution and deliberate pacing.
My only complaints are minor, with some bad lip sync during in-game dialog (cutscene dialog is excellent, with full face-tracking), and two specific sections that don't update your map with your next objective clearly enough, and as a result you have to guess a little at what to do next.
Overall, I give Alien: Isolation a highly recommended 9/10

First, I want to say, this is just a temporary rating, as it's based on the current Alpha of the game.
Do I recommend this game?  Almost, but ultimately, no.  Or at least not yet.  The game currently feels a lot like Rust...  except with more ways to die, more ways to grind, and all kinds of glitches, such as..  disappearing throwing spears, laggy weapon mode toggling, and a malfunctioning chat screen.  Throw that together with no in-game map, no explanation of necessary items (like beacons, seriously, without one you're going to get lost), and a massive amount of MMO style grinding of random spawned mining points/creature spawns,  and you end up with mixed feelings before you even make it to the pvp.  Especially if you get as unlucky as I did with my first couple hours of play, and/or have as bad of short term memory as I do.
Keeping Early Access in mind, the game does feel like something I would play, after some polishing.  I'm also sure the game is more enjoyable when things go a little more smoothely for you.  I had a series of unfortunate events, like originally spawning at night and almost freezing to death before knowing how to play, then not finding food my first hour of play (only rabbits, and I missed every time), then finally getting settled in, starting the harvest/gear grind, getting lost without a beacon while out gathering (got confused about which road I was following), and of all things, I died by sliding down an angled mountain side that looked walkable.  I built enough speed that once I touched some more level ground, I just instantly died as if I had just fallen off a cliff or something, losing some hours of mining/killing in the process.
Will that same experience happen to you?  I have no idea.  I'm hoping it was just bad luck mixed with poor sense of direction, but you never know.  It's something to keep in mind.
I'll most likely come back to this review in the future, maybe after some updates have come out, maybe sooner.  I don't feel that it's necessarily a bad game...  I just can't recommend that people purchase it yet in it's current state.  Wait a while.  It's never good to buy into hype too much.

Alright, sit your butts down, here's another essay review on a game I have very meh feelings about. Not to say that the game is bad, just that I am writing an awful lot for a game that I don't care too much about. I actually rather enjoy the game, actually. It might not look like that, since the head of this review is a lot of whining and moaning, but, I genuinely think this game is fun. And it's still in early release as of writing this, so it's possible any criticisms have already been noted by the devs. But so far, this game has lots of potential, and I do hope this game does do as much as possible as it can with its potential.
Basically, the game is about feeding slimes, and then selling the "plorts" on the market. There's quite a bit to talk about.
The corral is the main and nearly only manner of keeping slimes on your ranch reliblely. It currently has many addons, which add some functionalities to the cage. An issue I have is that you cannot rotate the cage, or a more preferable option, to move the addons independently of eachother. Although I don't care about which corner the speaker hangs from, I do care about which corner I have to put food into. The plort collector, naturally, collects plorts, via a vacuum, which also moves the slimes, toys, and food in the corral when it collects plorts. Personally, I dislike this, but there's too much to talk about to get hung up about this one thing.
I think a nice addon to add on later versions (haha) would be a "sensor" that tells you how many slimes are still angry, or gives you some insight to the slimes. I don't know about other players, but I can never tell how many slimes are hungry, since 5 or 6 largo slimes cover eachother, and its nigh impossible to tell how many are hungry, even with a longer, or closer look, which can be hard when dealing with more dangerous slimes. (Crystal and Boom slimes come to mind). Sometimes, I can tell, because the entire corral of BoomRad Largos just exploded at the same time and nearly killed me, but sometimes, when it's just a bunch of HoneyHunter Largos, not much can be seen, except one or two faces with the hunger emote.
In the vein of addons that would be a nice addition, I think there should be
slime specific addons. There's only one type of slime that benefits from the solar shield walls(phosphor), so why not have more of the same? Have, say, a teleport proof wall that's exceptionally expensive, maybe it ties into late game slime science, which would force quantum slimes even more into late game ranching. Along these lines there could be lead lined walls, to stop rad slimes from poisoning you while you're outside, and much stronger ceilings, so that phosphor, or feline slimes are less likely to escape, or for those ranchers who just really like crowded corrals.
Let's keep this short:
In one of the most recent updates, the auto-feeder has been changed to have settings to it. Now, this is great. I don't have the same amount of slimes of each type in each corral. However, I have no idea what these settings do. What setting should I set if I have 12 slimes? 10? 6? 20? What does the setting change? Timing of feeding? The amount in each? What if I put more slimes in a corral, than the highest setting could feed? And I'm fairly certain the food dispensed doesn't count how many slimes are inside, since I've had corrals' grounds covered in food, on the lowest setting.
Now, what I propose is that instead of making 5 bars, the autofeeder provides two slider options: how much food per feeding, and how often they are fed. If this solution would be adopted, it would also need to have a more "transparent", for lack of a better word, method of continuing from here on out. What I mean by this, is that the slime-a-pedia should contain more information regarding how often a slime should be fed. This also feeds into various other things that I previously brought up. This could allow for slimes to be different in their feeding habits, which would make for more varied gameplay, which is always interesting. This could also support the sensor addon. No need to set the amount of food per drop, if the corral will count it for you.
Early in the game, when there's only so much to grab, there's not much to complain about. The vacpack may be a bit small, but it's unlikely you'll want to grab 5 things, and even if you do, the ranch is right there. What's disappointingis that in the late game, as your run through various areas to get to a specific one lures you into grabbing many things: "Well, I do need another HoneyHunter, might as well grab a few more Honey slimes..." "Ooh, look at all these pink plorts, might as well suck them all up for now!" This game is realy good at distracting you, whether from real life or from itself.
There's never any real inventory upgrade- besides a water pack, which lets you get only water. Perhaps, if they still want to stick with only 4 "boxes", then perhaps you could buy "seperators", which take up 5 or so spaces when used, which allow you to pick up to 8 or 12 types of items. If you want the "second" item type in the first box, then your press 1 twice. And the controls continue from there. Or, could just buy more rows of boxes, and rotate them with the ~ key or something. Maybe the devs already thought of this, and are working on it. Maybe the devs think both these options suck and I'm an idiot. They're definitely right about one of those. I don't know what the devs' plans are, but their sight obviously overrules mine on this matter.
A map would be nice. Oddly, that's all to say about that. The treasure cracker, at least for me, was unclear in that it was multi-use. I thought it was 4500 coins a pop, and was another money sink(the other being the 7Zee club). This also is related to another thing that irked me. It should be clear if and when there are more purchasable or craftable items coming out in game. For example, I thought there was at least 3 tiers of extractors in game, but it turns out there are only 2. This could've been avoided if, say, there was some sort of "tree" for upgrades/craftables, which allowed you to look at the whole future tree. Then, there would be a 0% chance of me thinking there was a 3rd extractor tier, and that I just had to wait until the game released it for me.
There's a story in Slime Rancher, and it's... interesting. I mean that unironically. It's not bad, but it's definitely at odds with the game. The game is full of cutesy slimes and adventuring. Meanwhile, you're getting e-mails and reading notes about how your(might be someone else's) ex broke up with you back on earth. Maybe they'll flesh out the story more in future updates, but it's definitely interesting. Can't wait to see where it goes.

This game is like exploring an alien world, where you have an almanac about that world, and someone back at Earth is buying alien poop you find for five cents apiece.
A common criticism of exploration games like this is that they are often obtuse for beginners and almost require reading a wiki. This game condenses everything you need to know about a particular subject (i.e. slimes, food, and locations) into a few concise and humorous paragraphs. You spend less time wondering what to do with each new thing you find and more time learning the subtleties that make for more efficient money-making, or just enjoying yourself by watching these adorable creatures bounce around.

This is a wonderful game. It has one of the largest maps I've ever seen in a game, and that map is well populated with a diverse array of quests and objectives. It also has more explosions than all other video games combined. Not only, are there a million and one explosions, there is a vast variety of ways you can make things explode. You can even modify your equipment with upgrade points acquired at side missions. The story is, though not complex or subtle, is fun. It has some very likeable characters, and even has a sense of humor, which I value especially highly in videogames. The gunplay is fairly good for a third person shooter, and is certainly sufficient for a game mostly focused on blowing up large fuel tanks. I would have to say, that, other than blowing stuff up, the most enjoyable aspect of the game is travelling with a parachute and wingsuit. The vehicles (some of them) aren't bad either, but there's something about just floating around the world, going 70 kilometers and hour that is just amazing. I would say this is an excellent game, but would not recommend it to anyone who particularly favors stealth in their games. There is no stealth is Just Cause. Why? Just Cause.
Two things are bad about this game. 1: The multiplayer server thing that tracks and compares scores is almost always down, and it'll take you about a minute and a half to try to log in, and it's automatic when you open your menu. I find this annoying. Get it working, or have it toggled on or off. 2: Unstable framerate. This mostly seems due to the game attempting to retrieve very large amounts of data from your hard drive to your RAM. I say this because, when entering a town, I get a big framerate drop, and after about 30 seconds, it's back to normal. Beware this, and make sure to have lots of fast RAM, or you're going to have a rough time of it.

As a big fan and someone who has over 1k hours in Worms Armageddon, I can say that WMD has impressed me. The vehicles and crafting are fun to play with and fairly balanced. The art style is clean and fresh.
There is however some downsides that keep me hanging on to WA, but hopefully will be added in updates.
1.Scheme customizability:
- Can't play mole shopper, theres no mole bomb in this game.
- Can't play hysteria, you can't set turn time to 1 second.
- Can not set mine fuses to random.
- Can't set power of weapons like you can in WA, nor can you let worms spawn with the new craftable weapons if they are an upgraded version. Eg: a worm cant have a "Cluster Bomb mkII" at the start of the round because it MUST be crafted.
Overall the scheme customizer and map editor still feels incomplete, but i have hope that T17 will update them.
2.Rope knocking physics: It takes too much force to knock a worm compared to WA in my opinion.
3.MAP EDITOR: Please make a WA map to WMD map converter.. enough said. The current map maker program is not fun to use and has to be run when WMD itself is closed. It would be nice if it were integrated into the game with more features.
4.HP Bars: They disappear... WHY!? sometimes we need to see who the leader is in shopper schemes while we are moving around...
Overall I have had a lot of fun playing basic schemes like intermediate, classic mode and ranked. but for more complex schemes I go back to WA.

Muffin knight a game that emulates real life where the goal is to get the muff before the other person in order to score.
Honestly it is a game worth buying if you have a friend and some time to kill. Jumping around trying to get the other person killed by the monsters before they do the same to you is fun, especially when the muffins change you everytime you grab one. There is a basic level up progression and character unlock and you will unlock everything with just playing the game.
Fun in increments of 30 minutes or so on random occasions with a buddy.

So it's similar to Super Crate Box? That doesn't mean that it's a rip-off. I haven't played much of SCB so I won't comment more on the issue, just about Muffin Knight itself. Suffice to say; if you loved SCB you'll probably (at least) like MK.
It's colorful and fun, with a joyus soundtrack. It's the kind of game that'll put you in a good mood ... until you get frustrated from dying all the time, but hey, that's a part of the game. The goal is to collect muffins, but every time you collect a muffin you change character randomly. All characters do different things; you have the knight who shoots arrow in one direction, you have the archer who shoots arrows in both directions, you have the pumpkinhead (miserable little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) who bowls enemies with his head.
The game is fun. It's one of those "just one more round"-games that gets you hooked for hours upon hours. The co-op is the best part IMHO, but then again I haven't tried the Versus-mode yet. Playing it single player is super fun too.
The menues... are horrible. Utterly horrible. But don't let that keep you away. Also; for some reason I find the keyboard controls (cursors + Z) to be more responsive than playing with a Xbox controller (left analog + A & X). That might be a personal preference, but then again I usually enjoy a controller more when it comes to games with platforming-elements.

Every now and then you unlock a new character and when you pick up a muffin you randomly and instantly turn into it, changing your playstyle. Very faced paced.
Looks a lot like super crate box, don't know which was first but this definitely has some new features, like exp. You can improve your characters' range and damge with that.
Has multiplayer versus and coop. No couch coop, just online.

Not all stories need to have a happy conclusion. Personally, I believe the third ending was fantastic (If you haven't witnessed this ending, do it now. Seriously, it was deeply emotional and was a great way to lead into a sequel if there ever is one). This game brought out emotions that are seemingly rare nowadays — a mixture of fear, hate, depression, happiness. Deep emotions that I haven't felt since I played Gears of War 3 for the first time.
If there was anything I would change, it would have to be the combat. Excluding the bosses, it was quite simplistic in design. Offering no sense of difficulty throughout the entirety of the game. If there is a sequel in the works, I would suggest refining what you have now and make it better, while still maintaining emphasis on story; that would be ♥♥♥♥ing great.
I do have to admit, I really enjoyed the crafting system. While it lacked in complexity, it made up for me wanting to get the best gear I could before advancing to the next dungeon, simply to get that reward from the Legendary Sheep. Also, while on the subject, I loved the three NPCs located at the end of each dungeon. Yeah, the ones that had set milestones for the player to achieve, and in return for their time, granting the player items such as the components to reforge the Hydrangea Sword and Violet Crystal Armor, which broke during the first portion of the game.
Overall, I thought the game was lovely. While lacking in gameplay and length, it did give me a good five hours of enjoyment. I'd recommend this game to anyone so long as you have the time. It's an enjoyable experience. Also, it's free, so why not play it? (Play the game. Do it now.)

I just can't recommend this game. I am a fan of Souls, I even played DeS until I got three characters to 712, a third to 650, and a fourth to 475, without using an exploit. I didn't get a whole out of DaS1, but it was still a very fun game and even felt innovative with what it was doing with DeS's foundation.
DaS2 is pretty broken. it feels a lot like it's♥♥♥♥♥♥riding Demon's while not quite understanding what made Demon's good. If I had to guess, I would say that From is just obligated to make hard games. DaS2 is very easy to cheese every enemy, while if you are brave enough to play normally; you'd quickly find that (at least on the PC version), enemies can do some real
things.
On top of enemies being rather broken, this game uses frames as a timer for how things work. For example, more frames your weapon is in an enemy, the more durability damage it takes. Since DaS2 isn't moving faster in real time while at 60fps, your weapon takes twice as much durability damage potentially, when compared to 30fps. Also your rolls will have a tendancy to not work properly (Jumping can work pretty reliably though), and just simple button inputs can be buggy when at 60fps. Like.. I have a huge delay before I start sprinting, but locking to 30fps fixes that and it is really annoying.
Bad port issues aside; Is the game good on its own merits? Well... I had some fun, but spells don't feel particularly well balanced post mid-game, the +10 mundane dagger is rather overpowered for backstabs, and a lot of the gear people use seems to constantly be hit and miss.
Enviroments feel uninspired and very classic high-fantasy. They are not much different in idea in comparison to Demon and DaS1, but the issue is that the other two games were consistant with the paths. In Demon, you go to a storm temple, you finish at a storm temple (with a rather awesome air based boss). In DaS2, you start at a mountain side at night, end up at a mountain full of poison at day, then a windmill tower filled with poison, then you finish in a volcano. I suppose you can make the arguement that volcanos are toxic, but the lead-up to going into a volcano was non-existant and was really confusing.

I highly recommend this game to all souls veterans and anyone who wants a challenge.

This is the first Alien game that does everything (or almost everything) right, that gives justice to the universe seen in the original 1979 movie. It's a must-play.
You're the daughter of Ellen Ripley, fifteen years after the event of the first movie. The very basic summary of the premise is that you're trying to get assigned to jobs close to where your mother was last seen; you're looking for traces of her. The story isn't the likes of modern Hollywood movies and that's a good thing; something overly dramatic or with a big scale would have not worked at all.
The first thing you're going to notice here is the technical presentation. It's nearly flawless. It's the first movie come to life, with its imperfect retro-futuristic technology that runs on magnetic tapes and cartridges. The space station is GORGEOUS. You'll find yourself jaw agape when looking out of a window, towards the stars, the gas giant, the sun, the rest of the station. It's amazing. And it runs really well, too; I could max out the settings at 2560x1440 on a GeForce 670 and achieve nearly-constant 60fps (or more, as I am using a GSync monitor). Its only big problem is the lack of effective anti-aliasing; temporal SMAA 2x helps, but it's not doing miracles.
And while we're at it: the audio direction of this game should win many awards, and then we should invent new audio awards just so it can win them. It's really good. Get a headset.
Eventually you first come face-to-face with the Alien. And this is when the paranoïa settles in. It's wholly unpredictable; you'll often hear the creature around you, in the ceilings, in the walls. There are other ennemies around the station (creepy androids that have gone haywire and forgot about their "do no harm to human life" directive, and other humans), and you will have to work around them... and you will constantly be faced with the choice of whether to deal with them directly, at the risk of causing enough noise to attract the Alien.
One of the main tools of the game is the motion tracker. It will allow you to get a general idea of other presences around you (most notably the Alien). However, something the game doesn't explicitly tell you is that it draws attention to you, with its faint noises and beeps being enough to reveal you in a few cases. You won't want to use it if you're hiding in a locker and the Alien is looking for you in the room.
You can craft a variety of devices and tools to help you deal with opponents (noisemakers, pipe bombs, molotovs, EMP mines...) by finding blueprints and loot which are usually not too far off the main road. There are weapons in this game; you have a melee attack, you'll find two guns and, eventually, a flamethrower, which is a get-out-of-jail-free card against the Alien. Ammo is scarce for everything, and Androids are hard to deal with (they generally require half of your total ammo, and can't be melee'd unless stunned).
You have room for emergent gameplay tactics, such as drawing the attention of the Alien to other hostile humans instead of you, and slide past the whole bunch unnoticed. It's pretty fun to try and come up with solutions (the classic one being "throw a distraction the opposite way you're trying to go to"), but there are a few factors to stealth that Alien: Isolation does differently to other games of the genre. You can't just expect to hide in a dark corner and survive; you have to keep moving at the right times, out of the lines of sight of ennemies, or when they're busy with something else. This is of utmost importance with the Alien, as its senses are heightened, and it will hear you very easily.
So yeah, the game is scary. And there are very few "automatic" checkpoints, so you'll find yourself burning with desire to find a save point. This is what primarily creates tension in the game; you don't want to have to redo that scary part again. It's a bit of an "artificial" way to do it, but it works! However, I dislike how it paces the game in a way where your next goal, story-wise, is overshadowed by "oh god i have to find the next save point please please please please where is it".
I should talk about a few other things that the game, in my opinion, fails to do right.
First, the alien is actually not *that* unpredictable; it's scripted to appear in a handful of moments. Most of which are right before save points. So you'll be prepared to throw a molotov at its face on your next attempt. There are also a few other moments where it *feels* like the Alien is scripted to show up on your motion tracker, lurking around you, but not actually coming out to hunt you until the point where you have to backtrack through an area to go somewhere else and it's inconvenient for you. Overall, its presence does not feel really systemized, though.
Second, there are some puzzles where the solution is really oddly placed or designed. The prime example I have in mind is a moment where you have to escape from a fire, on a time limit (draining health). The center of the room is on fire, the back of the room isn't, and there are doors there. Your first instinct is to go back there and look for the exit, but it took me a good three minutes (and 2 medkits) before I realized the ladder to escape was actually right above the fire at the center. The game has a few other moments like that in which what you're supposed to do is weirdly placed in relation to what you just did beforehand.
Third, on a technical point, there are a few bugs, all of which have to do with other NPCs and cutscenes. I've had three cases where an in-gameplay cutscene was supposed to play with NPCs, but they just stood there motionless, and even a save reload would not fix it. These bugs, however, didn't impede my progress in any way.
The game is far longer than you will come to expect; a few times I was thinking "okay, this is the end", but it kept going. Not in a hamstrung, forced way (except for one case where you're like "oh COME ON"). Total playtime was ~16h30.
Overall, this is a game that understands the 1979 movie, its universe, its aesthetics, why it was good, and which transposes its qualities in a game in a nearly flawless way. It attempts to tune down the "video gameisms" and doesn't always succeed, but the attempt alone is enough to set it way apart your run-of-the-mile AAA title. I'm wholeheartedly recommending it.

This is when the source engine is used at its best, by the best.. Black Mesa is a fantastic remake of VALVe's world famous 'Half-Life' (1998), with updated visuals, graphics and physics gameplay updating to modern day requirements. Black Mesa still captures the excitement and isolation the Half-Life created and takes you round the old Half-Life scenes and encounters, as well as polishing them up to the best standards. The new weapon models (My favourite being the Tau cannon), the textures and new NPC models make Black Mesa seem almost like a window into reality compared to Half-Life's old graphics.
One of my personal favourites of the improvements was that the HECU Marines did not speak through Radio's, but instead spoke normally in their voices. This immedietly made me more immersed and empathetic towards them, as you could hear their emotions through their voices for the first time, ranging from determined and aggressive to terrified and nervous. They did not have the bad-guy, kill em' all tone that they had in Half-Life but are now showing a more Human side. This was so effective that I even felt sorry killing the marines!
Black Mesa has also included a multiplayer gamemode, which uses some of the old maps multiplayer maps from half life 2, such as Gasworks and re-imagines them like the rest of the game. The multiplayer itself is a fun, enjoyable experience which has sucked a lot of my time into it. The fact multiplayer has been revived and focused on in such detail shows the amount of work and consideration being put into this project.
Unfortunately, the final Xen chapter is still going under development at crowbar collective. I predict that Xen will still have a while to go until it is ready for release. But the only possible outcome is that it will be outstanding and provide an excellent conclusion the this shining game. After all, the amount of work that was made to the main bulk of the game must surely tell us what Xen will be like!
I did encounter a small jigglebone bug with the scientists' ties and the Tau cannon pipe. They spasmed manically all the time and made the game a little funny. However, this did not turn out to be a major problem, as the game is centered more on yourself and personal experience than the involvement of NPC's and the use of certain weapons.
In conclusion, I take my hat of to Crowbar Collective and the other Dev's that are taking the time and contribution to this game and the amazing improvements they have made. I wish them the best for their futures and I give them a very big Thank you!

I love this game. I played the first Dishonored about 6 months ago, quite recently relative to it's release in late 2012. I played the crap out of the game on my friends PC, about 100 hours, 15 or so playthroughs because there was so much to do, so many ways to play. Dishonored 2 was brought to my attention in June of 2016 at E3; after the E3 2015 teaser I didn't think much about it. But I got really hyped up for it, I waited and waited with my calendar marking down the days, and I spend about $1000 essentially building a new PC, minus the HDD and PSU. Dishonored 2 lived up to all the hype, and here are the reasons I think you should buy it in ranking order.
1. Gameplay: The gameplay here is expanded about 3-4 times as much as the original, they added so many more animations for lethal and non-lethal takedowns, added many more NPC's to interact with, and made the environments huge, each level with it's own unique twist on gameplay (Whether or not you play each one in it's unique way is of course up to you). More weapon and upgrade options are an added bonus too.
2. Characters: As you may already know, there are two
playable main protagonists, Corvo Attano and Emily Kaldwin. Corvo's powers have been expanded with options like freezing time during blink while stadning still on the ground or in air, and having his rat swarm(s) follow him around. With out spoiling too many new powers, Emily has her own form of a blink, and other cool powers like Domino, linking targets together so that they share the same fate, whatever that may be, and Doppleganger, summoning a "shade" of herself that can be upgraded to do thinks like assassinate nearby enemies and trade places with Emily.
3. Story: This may rank higher or lower on this list depending on what you thought of Dishonored's emergent story, but if you enjoyed the first game's way of storytelling, you will enjoy it yet again in Dishonored 2. The main story is good, there are some holes, like the events during the first 10 or so minutes, but once you get going, you will start to appreciate some of the nuances. A lot of the story and exposition (background info) is found through notes, audiographs, diaries, journals, etc.. scattered throughout the environments. If you rush through, you will miss important information, and some of the pieces you find will give you different options for finding and taking out your targets. Listening to conversations is also more important this time around, as it will sometimes reveal secrets and hidden objectives in the surroundings.
4. Environments/Graphics: As I talked about in the Story and Gameplay sections, the environments look amazing even when the don't run well (while I'll get into in the Performance section). They feel alive, there is lots of solid NPC dialogue to overhere, and there is never one "right" or "straight" path when it comes to finding and eliminating your targets. There are hidden routes just like there were in the first game, special NPCs to find and eliminate or rescue/help/ Overall it feels alive, and Karnaca includes way more colors than the sometimes dreary looking Dishonored (1) did. The graophics are stunning and breathtaking in the Void Engine, and when you crank it to the max it is hard not to look around and want to stay in Karnaca.
5. Performance/Graphics Continued: I built a brand new PC with an EVGA GTX 1070 SC and an Intel i5 6600 (non k) with 16 GB of RAM. I have had no issues at all with the mouse and keyboard controls or the framerate, but I did have to take about 90 seconds to install a 3rd party program called "Process Hacker 2" to get Dishonored 2 to stop putting itself at low CPU priority, otherwise the game would have significant input delay. Everything on ultra settings, full anti-aliasing, the particles look great, character models are much improved (as you would expect over 4 years) everything maxed except for the stupid lens flare and motion blur. People do not have camera lenses in their eyes, and I like to save motion blur for console games (no offense intended).
I will warn you that these were brand new parts, in my brand new PC and many other people have not been as lucky as I have been. There is a good chance that this game will not run satisrfactory, and if you are on what Bethesda and Arkane consider "older" hardware you might have to play on lower settings than you would expect, and even then you will probably have problems until they patch it within the coming weeks.
Personal Score: 10/10 This game is a masterpiece, easily game of the year for me.
Score: 8.5/10 This game is great for me, but I cannot give it a 10/10 reccomendation to everyone just because of the performance issues, which is a real bummer.
Conclusion: I think this game is super duper fun, but I don't think it would be fun to be having the problems others are having, and I don't think it is fun enough to just ignore the issues, especially when they ruin the moment to moment gameplay, which I think is Dishonored 2's strongest aspect. If you were already hesitant, hold off for a few weeks, maybe get it for Christmas (if you celebrate it). If you really want the game though, and aren't super worried about your hardware then I would get it. Hope that eventually everyone can have as much fun as I did! Enjoy!

All and all the game is a solid addition to the franchise, it adds just enough to make it feel new but still maintains what made call of duty one of the best selling games of all time.

I love this game. I played the first Dishonored about 6 months ago, quite recently relative to it's release in late 2012. I played the crap out of the game on my friends PC, about 100 hours, 15 or so playthroughs because there was so much to do, so many ways to play. Dishonored 2 was brought to my attention in June of 2016 at E3; after the E3 2015 teaser I didn't think much about it. But I got really hyped up for it, I waited and waited with my calendar marking down the days, and I spend about $1000 essentially building a new PC, minus the HDD and PSU. Dishonored 2 lived up to all the hype, and here are the reasons I think you should buy it in ranking order.
1. Gameplay: The gameplay here is expanded about 3-4 times as much as the original, they added so many more animations for lethal and non-lethal takedowns, added many more NPC's to interact with, and made the environments huge, each level with it's own unique twist on gameplay (Whether or not you play each one in it's unique way is of course up to you). More weapon and upgrade options are an added bonus too.
2. Characters: As you may already know, there are two
playable main protagonists, Corvo Attano and Emily Kaldwin. Corvo's powers have been expanded with options like freezing time during blink while stadning still on the ground or in air, and having his rat swarm(s) follow him around. With out spoiling too many new powers, Emily has her own form of a blink, and other cool powers like Domino, linking targets together so that they share the same fate, whatever that may be, and Doppleganger, summoning a "shade" of herself that can be upgraded to do thinks like assassinate nearby enemies and trade places with Emily.
3. Story: This may rank higher or lower on this list depending on what you thought of Dishonored's emergent story, but if you enjoyed the first game's way of storytelling, you will enjoy it yet again in Dishonored 2. The main story is good, there are some holes, like the events during the first 10 or so minutes, but once you get going, you will start to appreciate some of the nuances. A lot of the story and exposition (background info) is found through notes, audiographs, diaries, journals, etc.. scattered throughout the environments. If you rush through, you will miss important information, and some of the pieces you find will give you different options for finding and taking out your targets. Listening to conversations is also more important this time around, as it will sometimes reveal secrets and hidden objectives in the surroundings.
4. Environments/Graphics: As I talked about in the Story and Gameplay sections, the environments look amazing even when the don't run well (while I'll get into in the Performance section). They feel alive, there is lots of solid NPC dialogue to overhere, and there is never one "right" or "straight" path when it comes to finding and eliminating your targets. There are hidden routes just like there were in the first game, special NPCs to find and eliminate or rescue/help/ Overall it feels alive, and Karnaca includes way more colors than the sometimes dreary looking Dishonored (1) did. The graophics are stunning and breathtaking in the Void Engine, and when you crank it to the max it is hard not to look around and want to stay in Karnaca.
5. Performance/Graphics Continued: I built a brand new PC with an EVGA GTX 1070 SC and an Intel i5 6600 (non k) with 16 GB of RAM. I have had no issues at all with the mouse and keyboard controls or the framerate, but I did have to take about 90 seconds to install a 3rd party program called "Process Hacker 2" to get Dishonored 2 to stop putting itself at low CPU priority, otherwise the game would have significant input delay. Everything on ultra settings, full anti-aliasing, the particles look great, character models are much improved (as you would expect over 4 years) everything maxed except for the stupid lens flare and motion blur. People do not have camera lenses in their eyes, and I like to save motion blur for console games (no offense intended).
I will warn you that these were brand new parts, in my brand new PC and many other people have not been as lucky as I have been. There is a good chance that this game will not run satisrfactory, and if you are on what Bethesda and Arkane consider "older" hardware you might have to play on lower settings than you would expect, and even then you will probably have problems until they patch it within the coming weeks.
Personal Score: 10/10 This game is a masterpiece, easily game of the year for me.
Score: 8.5/10 This game is great for me, but I cannot give it a 10/10 reccomendation to everyone just because of the performance issues, which is a real bummer.
Conclusion: I think this game is super duper fun, but I don't think it would be fun to be having the problems others are having, and I don't think it is fun enough to just ignore the issues, especially when they ruin the moment to moment gameplay, which I think is Dishonored 2's strongest aspect. If you were already hesitant, hold off for a few weeks, maybe get it for Christmas (if you celebrate it). If you really want the game though, and aren't super worried about your hardware then I would get it. Hope that eventually everyone can have as much fun as I did! Enjoy!

Worms has been a favorite of mine since the mid/late 90s and I have always loved these games. Yes, even the 3D ones.. Not as much as Armageddon though. Never as much as that one.

Finally a good Worms game!
After a lot of fails and some remastered versions (which didn't add anything really new) here we have a decent Worms title. It is basically what it should have been Worms long time ago. It can be played with classic rules (for nostalgic players) and it also can be played with modern rules: new weapons, vehicles, buidings where you can hide and a new crafting system in which you have the abbility to craft weapons (even if it's not your turn).
Of course some modes remain: in single player you have training, campaign and challenge as usually. Scheme and team editor are also there. In multiplayer there is a global ranking in which you can compare your position and stats with your Steam friends. The max number of online players is 6 (up to 8 worms per team) in friendly matches or 1 vs 1 in ranked games.
Technically the game has beautiful and colorful graphics. It's very enjoyable to play it on a 2K monitor. The music fits well (with some chords of the classic Worms theme). It can be played with keyb/mouse or gamepad.
I hope the online community doesn't die so fast like in previous titles because it would be a shame. Worms has always been one of the funniest multiplayer games for me. Fortunately, the firsts user reviews are being very positive as well so this are good news.
In short, this is a must-have if you like (or you ever liked) Worms.

The biggest issue I've seen people complain about with this game is that it runs very poorly. I'm 17+ hours in, and I have not experienced any such problems with Just Cause 3.
If you've played Just Cause 2, you know what you're in store for with Just Cause 3; explosions, destruction and a blatant disregard for the laws of physics. The game is more of the same, but I must admit the story and characters are much more engaging this time around than in the previous game.
Not only does the new game engine help the game to look absolutely stunning, but the destruction is more satisfying thanks to the upgrade in environmental and destructible objects physics. Just messing around with blowing up bridges and causing train crashes is great fun.
As for game play additions, Just Cause 3 adds up to six simultaneous grapple lines that you are able to retract to cause some fantastic havoc in the game world. The other big addition is the wing suit. I have read about many players complaining that the wing suit is difficult to control, but within the first few minutes of getting the suit, I had no trouble flying between buildings and under bridges. I guess they’re just bad at video games.
Overall, if you enjoyed Just Cause 2, you will enjoy Just Cause 3 even more, for the same reasons and a few new ones.

No More Room in Hell is a zombie survival game. There are 2 modes, one called Survival and one called Objective. Survival is where you (and your teammates) have to hold down an area or multiple areas from waves of zombies until the extraction comes. If your area(s) go down to 0% HP, then you will not be able to be extracted and therefore, will have to restart. The other mode, called Objective, is where you (and your teammates) will have to do certain objectives leading to extraction. The objectives range from blowing up something to placing certain objects somewhere. There are 2 difficulties as well, one called Classic, and one called Casual.

Classic is where you spawn with nothing, and you don't spawn at all when you die unless a major objective is completed or a wave is completed. Casual is where you will always spawn with a melee weapon, and you have respawn tokens. You have 3 when you join/start, but every 10 zombie kills will earn you a token. Each token will allow you to spawn in 5 seconds near a player when you die.

There are 3 zombie types in the game. The most common is slow, walking zombies. These guys just walk very slowly and attack if you get close. Be careful though, because these are common they can swarm you if your not careful. Less common is running zombies, which don't appear too often in the game. These guys run towards you very fast and sometimes require good timing to take down. The last is child zombies, which are basically childs that are zombies. These little guys are slower then runners, but faster then slow zombies. They will attack you, and it will not do that much damage but they can attack fast and can be a pain. They have a lower hitbox therefore requires you to aim a bit down to hit them. They have less health too and will usually die by one or two hits by a melee or gun to the head.
The game, overall, is really fun, especially with friends to play it with. The game, at first, may seem really hard to play, as guns and ammo are scarce, and melee you have the risk of getting hurt while striking. However, as you get more used to it, the game will turn out to be much easier. It is good to read the players survival guide for the game by clicking where it is located at the right where it says "Players Survival Guide" when you play the game at first, or if you need to be reminded about something.
There is a good range of guns and melee weapons you can find, and even get achievements for getting certain amount of kills with them. The game's engine is the Source Engine, which means that the game might be similar to Valve games such as TF2 and CS, such as the Developer Console. There is a few glitches in the game which may seem to make the game easier or slightly break the game, however it doesn't seem like a major thing. Most games have glitches sometimes, so it's fine. The developers of the game are constantly working on adding new content and fixing glitches. The developers also interact with the community in forums, and such as get players' opinions on certain things, which is nice. It's also free to play!
(TL;DR Really fun realistic zombie survival game that has multiple modes and zombie types that requires teamwork and coordination.)
Overall, I rate this game 10/10. Keep up the great work developers! :D

There have been a large number of games based on the Alien franchise over the years.
Atari 2600 (actually a better version of Pac Man than Atari's official one)
Three versions of Aliens for the C64 and other PCs of the '80s, with only the Activision release having any real success.
Several Alien 3 games, and also several Aliens vs. Predator releases.
But back in 1984, Argus released Alien for the C64.  It wasn't a platformer.  It wasn't a first person shooter (which hadn't even been invented at the time).  It wasn't even a puzzle game really.  What it managed to do, with the most rudimentary graphics, interface, and sound, was be scary.
In the game you chose various members of the Nostromo crew and had to search the ship to either kill the alien without damaging the ship too much, blast it out the airlock, or if there are 3 or fewer crewmembers remaining, set the autodestruct, catch the cat and escape on the shuttle.  Of course the alien is moving from room to room as well, and encountering it opened an animated screen showing the monster with loud sound effects.
I've played basically every game based on the franchise, and the only one that ever got the tone of Alien was that little C64 game.  The rest of the games took their cues from Aliens and made the creatures easily killable cannon fodder.  The games might have been exciting and less fun than they should have been, but the developers seemed to think the subject matter was enough to work.  "Let's take a mediocre shooter and put aliens and predators in it!"  None of the games have been scary.
Until now.
Alien: Isolation had a lot of hype before its release.  So did Aliens: Colonial Marines, and we know how that one turned out.  Like ACM, AI had some great preview videos.  It had people who had played the demo raving about it.  But there was still the expectation from a lot of people that when the final game came out, it would fall on its face like ACM did.
It didn't.
Alien: Isolation is by far the best single player game I've played in years.  The story is well thought out and meshes well with the film.  It basically ends up being a 12-18 hour long horror movie.  However, I don't think that everything with Alien in the name requires a character named Ripley.  They could have easily written this with any generic new character and lost almost nothing except a small emotional part nearing the end.
The graphics engine is well optimized for its setting, with the gloomy corridors, harsh single point lighting, smoke and fire well represented.  The flamethrower effect is probably the best I've seen in any game.  It also runs well on fairly low end video cards, but keep in mind DirectX 11 is the minimum supported.  On the two cards I tried (GeForce GTX 680 and 980 at 1920x1080 144hz vsync on) there were no instances of stuttering or slowdown that I could see.  The art direction followed the design of Alien slavishly and it works.  Like the set of the Nostromo, the interiors of Sevestapol station look functional, lived-in, and real.
Load times were good, with levels changing in about 5-7 seconds.  The save system may drive some people nuts, but the relative rarity of the save points, coupled with the fact that it takes several seconds to save with you being vulnerable the whole time, adds even more tension to the game.
The alien itself.  It's BIG.  Like really big.  I'm not sure how they did it, but in a lot of games it's hard to get a sense of scale when you see something in the game environment, but they absolutely nailed it.  It's about 8-9 feet tall in the game, which is fairly close to the height of the original actor in the suit.  Bolaji Badejo was 7'2", and the head of the costume added another foot.  It's also smart.  If you move something, bump into things, open doors, it will notice.  If you keep hiding in an area, it will start to examine the area more closely.  If you hide in lockers a lot, it will start checking them.
Lockers.
You will see a lot of the inside of lockers.
The human and android AI isn't quite as good, with some glitches, but nothing game breaking.  If someone shoots at you, hide.  Not just from the person shooting, but what that sound inevitably attacts . . .
Now, sound.  The sound design on this game is nothing short of amazing.  I'm not sure if there are awards for sound design and editing in games, but if there is the team on this game deserve every one of them.  The creaks and groans of the damaged space station are incredibly immersive.  The movement of the alien through the vents and its footsteps when it's walking around are suitably creepy.  It also has a number of vocalizations that can clue you in on its mood.  The muted sounds in space owe a debt to Gravity.  Basically, if nothing is touching your suit, you don't hear it.  The other sounds, sirens, klaxons, doors, keyboards, welder, etc. are all spot on.  This game absolutely screams for a 5.1 or 7.1 system.
Very highly recommended.

A great game that improves on many gameplay and technical details from the first Dark Souls, but falls short in some crucial areas like story, level and map design, and player challenges.
Now don't get me wrong, I really enjoyed this game - but found myself disapointed when I found out that I had been helping kill the final boss over and over as a phantom with other players before I was anywhere close to being there myself, simply because the level design put the final boss near a mid-game area. That, coupled with some really lackluster areas, along with less than ideal level design, made this game less memorable for me than Dark Souls 1.
An example of what I mean by level design deficiency - Dragon's Aerie is a gorgeous area of the game with complex navigation from cliff to cliff - and yet the whole area is very sparsely populated with enemies and/or challenges, making what could have been a carefully tuned bit of gameplay feel like an empty jog. A number of the final areas of the game share this feeling - like the development team was running out of time and had to populate these areas in a hurry. Enemies start getting reused in areas that needed something new and fresh, so instead of carefully crafted original challenges, we get a handful of hallways and a smattering of standardized foes.
Where was the pitch black nightmare of the Tomb of the Giants from the first game and the terror inspiring beauty of scenery like the misty grey archtrees? Where was the incredible design originality of bosses like the Gaping Dragon and Sif the white wolf? The last boss, Nashandra, isn't much to look at - her textures appear low resolution even on the highest settings, and her design, while admittedly creepy, doesn't hold a candle to the terrifying Nito from the first game.
Story has always been a subtle part of this franchise, but the game lacked in that area as well by comparison. The ending and final boss were bare bones to say the least, and presented no dire choice or meaninful interaction like the first game.
In summary - the game was still a lot of fun, I would rate it an 8/10, but a tad disappointing when compared to what came before.
I haven't played any of the DLC yet, however, and I expect that the experience will be deliciously extended when I finally do.
Update - I've recently been playing through Scholar of Sin, and have found that they have strengthened the storytelling in some very positive ways.

What a journey it's been through the souls universe. Having my first taste with the Dark Souls PC port, and even purchasing a PS3 to play exclusives with Demon's Souls on the list, I was hyped for Dark Souls 2 and thought "What could go wrong?"
Well, unfortunately... Quite a bit. This isn't to say the game is a complete wash, as I still had fun and would recommend playing it to fans of the series, but I wouldn't say it's worth the full sale price. My main gripes with this game in particular mostly comes down to gameplay mechanics and level design. Levels this time around with a few exceptions felt very bland and uneventful. It felt like one place suddenly went into the next completely unrelated area. Take Earthen Peak for instance - a huge tower esque structure surrounded by poison which somehow after you take an elevator even further upward from the top, you find yourself in the Iron Keep. Iron Keep is a fortress surrounded and filled with lava. Invisible, floating lava sky fortress? I think not. A lot of parts in the game just collided with one another, no particular blending in any way. This killed a lot of the immersion for me, as you don't suddenly go from one extreme to another without some sort of buffer zone in between - unless you're playing Dark Souls 2. The art style was nice overall, and I did find myself enjoying the scenery rather frequently (enhanced moreso with an ENB shader mod and SweetFX).
Gameplay has the same general feel as the previous souls games, with noticeable improvements to AI. This would seem great, as the original in most cases required a sidestep and backstab to cheese your way through opponents, except this time around attacks track your movements while your opponent spins like some type of turret to face you, no matter where you move. Ultimately this leads to some frustrating deaths along with seeing your physical character well out of the way of an attack, but still being hit by it despite the fact it should have been impossible (Looking at you, Rat King). I found bosses to be very lackluster this time around, and in most cases I couldn't give half a♥♥♥♥♥♥about who or what I was fighting - especially when the actual fights themselves ended up being an absolute joke most of the time. Save for the Old Dragonslayer, Smelter Demon, and Nashandra - most fights in the game were a pushover. Worse so - a number of fights involve multiple enemies or bosses in order to increase the difficulty and seemingly cover up the fact that the fight was terribly designed from the start. Most enemies copy a similar tactic and instead of being a well designed and clever foe, they simply swarm you with 2 or 3 at a time to add 'difficulty' where there otherwise wouldn't be. It's okay for a while, but towards the end it just starts to feel like poor design.
All in all, I had an okay time with this game. It's fun, and for fans of the series it'll likely be a must play - but it's nothing close to what I'd hoped for. The port to PC was handled much better this time around and the options are plenty, but the overall lasting appeal of this game really pales in comparison. I've barely managed 40 hours on this game, whereas I got at least 70 on a single play through of the original. Chalk it up to me having been more experienced after playing Demon's Souls and Dark Souls perhaps, but I expected more from this game. Those of us with experience in this series expected a challenge and better design, as we had two games previously to learn from, and it wasn't really delivered.

Alright, sit your butts down, here's another essay review on a game I have very meh feelings about. Not to say that the game is bad, just that I am writing an awful lot for a game that I don't care too much about. I actually rather enjoy the game, actually. It might not look like that, since the head of this review is a lot of whining and moaning, but, I genuinely think this game is fun. And it's still in early release as of writing this, so it's possible any criticisms have already been noted by the devs. But so far, this game has lots of potential, and I do hope this game does do as much as possible as it can with its potential.
Basically, the game is about feeding slimes, and then selling the "plorts" on the market. There's quite a bit to talk about.
The corral is the main and nearly only manner of keeping slimes on your ranch reliblely. It currently has many addons, which add some functionalities to the cage. An issue I have is that you cannot rotate the cage, or a more preferable option, to move the addons independently of eachother. Although I don't care about which corner the speaker hangs from, I do care about which corner I have to put food into. The plort collector, naturally, collects plorts, via a vacuum, which also moves the slimes, toys, and food in the corral when it collects plorts. Personally, I dislike this, but there's too much to talk about to get hung up about this one thing.
I think a nice addon to add on later versions (haha) would be a "sensor" that tells you how many slimes are still angry, or gives you some insight to the slimes. I don't know about other players, but I can never tell how many slimes are hungry, since 5 or 6 largo slimes cover eachother, and its nigh impossible to tell how many are hungry, even with a longer, or closer look, which can be hard when dealing with more dangerous slimes. (Crystal and Boom slimes come to mind). Sometimes, I can tell, because the entire corral of BoomRad Largos just exploded at the same time and nearly killed me, but sometimes, when it's just a bunch of HoneyHunter Largos, not much can be seen, except one or two faces with the hunger emote.
In the vein of addons that would be a nice addition, I think there should be
slime specific addons. There's only one type of slime that benefits from the solar shield walls(phosphor), so why not have more of the same? Have, say, a teleport proof wall that's exceptionally expensive, maybe it ties into late game slime science, which would force quantum slimes even more into late game ranching. Along these lines there could be lead lined walls, to stop rad slimes from poisoning you while you're outside, and much stronger ceilings, so that phosphor, or feline slimes are less likely to escape, or for those ranchers who just really like crowded corrals.
Let's keep this short:
In one of the most recent updates, the auto-feeder has been changed to have settings to it. Now, this is great. I don't have the same amount of slimes of each type in each corral. However, I have no idea what these settings do. What setting should I set if I have 12 slimes? 10? 6? 20? What does the setting change? Timing of feeding? The amount in each? What if I put more slimes in a corral, than the highest setting could feed? And I'm fairly certain the food dispensed doesn't count how many slimes are inside, since I've had corrals' grounds covered in food, on the lowest setting.
Now, what I propose is that instead of making 5 bars, the autofeeder provides two slider options: how much food per feeding, and how often they are fed. If this solution would be adopted, it would also need to have a more "transparent", for lack of a better word, method of continuing from here on out. What I mean by this, is that the slime-a-pedia should contain more information regarding how often a slime should be fed. This also feeds into various other things that I previously brought up. This could allow for slimes to be different in their feeding habits, which would make for more varied gameplay, which is always interesting. This could also support the sensor addon. No need to set the amount of food per drop, if the corral will count it for you.
Early in the game, when there's only so much to grab, there's not much to complain about. The vacpack may be a bit small, but it's unlikely you'll want to grab 5 things, and even if you do, the ranch is right there. What's disappointingis that in the late game, as your run through various areas to get to a specific one lures you into grabbing many things: "Well, I do need another HoneyHunter, might as well grab a few more Honey slimes..." "Ooh, look at all these pink plorts, might as well suck them all up for now!" This game is realy good at distracting you, whether from real life or from itself.
There's never any real inventory upgrade- besides a water pack, which lets you get only water. Perhaps, if they still want to stick with only 4 "boxes", then perhaps you could buy "seperators", which take up 5 or so spaces when used, which allow you to pick up to 8 or 12 types of items. If you want the "second" item type in the first box, then your press 1 twice. And the controls continue from there. Or, could just buy more rows of boxes, and rotate them with the ~ key or something. Maybe the devs already thought of this, and are working on it. Maybe the devs think both these options suck and I'm an idiot. They're definitely right about one of those. I don't know what the devs' plans are, but their sight obviously overrules mine on this matter.
A map would be nice. Oddly, that's all to say about that. The treasure cracker, at least for me, was unclear in that it was multi-use. I thought it was 4500 coins a pop, and was another money sink(the other being the 7Zee club). This also is related to another thing that irked me. It should be clear if and when there are more purchasable or craftable items coming out in game. For example, I thought there was at least 3 tiers of extractors in game, but it turns out there are only 2. This could've been avoided if, say, there was some sort of "tree" for upgrades/craftables, which allowed you to look at the whole future tree. Then, there would be a 0% chance of me thinking there was a 3rd extractor tier, and that I just had to wait until the game released it for me.
There's a story in Slime Rancher, and it's... interesting. I mean that unironically. It's not bad, but it's definitely at odds with the game. The game is full of cutesy slimes and adventuring. Meanwhile, you're getting e-mails and reading notes about how your(might be someone else's) ex broke up with you back on earth. Maybe they'll flesh out the story more in future updates, but it's definitely interesting. Can't wait to see where it goes.
