If you liked Dishonored, you should really enjoy this one. Technical hurdles aside (was perfectly playable for me and is much improved with the 1.2 patch not even a week after launch), its a fantastic stealth action game. I play very methodical and enjoy trial and error type stealth. This game caters very much to that playstyle with quicksaves and a multitude of options at any given time.
Whether you enjoy rushing through and killing everything in sight, methodically eliminating everyone, or simply bypassing enemies, there is a playstyle that works for you. There is a lot of replayability here if you want it. Playing as Emily vs Corvo allows for differing powers which can greatly affect the options you have. You can also choose to play without taking any powers should you choose.
The side quests aren't quite as involved this time around from the first and seem to exist solely to help you out on the current mission but the eliminations (particularly non-lethal approaches) themselves are quite interesting and varied.
The game rewards exploration more often than not. The level design is superb with a couple real standout levels. I ended up spending over 4 hours on most of the 9 levels checking out every nook and cranny I could. There are so many different approaches to most areas that it really does feel like a proper sandbox where your creativity can pave the way.
It's truly a sad day when technical issues mar such a great game but that's how it goes these days on pc. I'd personally recommend the game to anyone that enjoys stealth games and exploring for loot. I don't know if I could recommend full price for a person that just want to shoot their way through without exploring however as the length might become an issue.

Well, I recently purchased this game since it has been released as a buy to play model. I am going to keep this short and sweet.
I followed this game for the year that it was out and decided against it. The reason's I chose to not get the game were due to the terrible reviews and supposedly they veered away from the original Elder Scrolls gameplay. (No stealing, pick pocketing, killing villagers. The stuff you play Elder Scrolls for.)
This caused me to not think about the game for a good six months.
Two major new systems have been implemented in this update: The Justice System and The Champion System. With Justice, crime has come to the once-friendly streets of Tamriel's cities. You can now become a wanted criminal, sneaking, stealing, and even murdering your way through the world. But be careful—the guards can and will seek to punish you if your crimes are witnessed.
The Champion System gives players with Veteran characters a new way to gain power. Once you have a Veteran Rank character on your account, you'll start earning Champion Points, which you can invest in a variety of new passive abilities.
That's not all Update 6 has to offer! they've completely overhauled provisioning. You'll notice new recipes and much more inventory space as a result of our updating and streamlining. There's also a new way to keep track of your mounts, pets, and costumes: the Collections Window because you can access everything you've earned through the new UI at any time.
That basically covers the biggest changes since the buy to play change. Since all the updates it genuinely feels like its single-player predecessors rather than a cookie cutter MMO, and that in itself is enough to draw me back into the game for many, many more hours!
10/10, this game is a must buy now!

Black Mesa is a precious and rare jewel for those frustrated awaiting any word on HL3. As for the BM deathmatch... You will never laugh harder at so much ensuing morbid hilarity amongst the spray of bullets, blood, guts, and dismembered limbs.
I probably played the free pre-Steam release of BM four times, and just finished the Steam release version. There is some new content added to the game  -- graphics, areas, etc. -- including new voice acting for the marines, which is a good thing since the previous voice for the marines was amateur compared to the rest of the voice acting quality. The developers really do improve on HL1 in many ways, and I would highly recommend this game to anyone who loves FPS games or the HL series. I can't wait for Xen.
However, in my latest BM experience, the Steam release version notably had more bugs than the pre-Steam version. The AI was pretty bad on a number of occasions which didn't occur during the pre-Steam version. A few glitches of dead characters miraculously standing up manifested themselves (see my screen shots). The physics also needs some tweaking; for example, instead of some items leaning on each other or moving out of the way they just passed right through each other. These bugs made my play-through less great than it could have been, and these bugs need fixing to perfect this game.
Other than bugs, one complaint is that I think BM should not have omitted some content from the original HL1. Some things may be cheesy to keep -- and I understand omitting those things. But there are scenes missing from Surface Tension, for example, where the chopper is hunting Freeman down on the desert surface amongst minefields. And I think such a scene would have been great to preserve. Maybe those will turn up on the Workshop, but I would have liked to see the BM devs do them right. And of course, we need the Xen chapter soon, too. But none of this, of course, makes BM worth overlooking!

Ignore the IGN and Game Spot reviews. Read the PC Gamer review -- it's on the money.
Alien: Isolation is an amazing game, and currently my personal choice for Game Of The Year, but it won't be everyone's cup of tea.
The game looks great, and the game design holds up very well for the duration of the game, never once becoming stale or losing its edge. You will be on edge for the entire 20+ hours of the campaign, so if you're an anxiety sufferer you should probably avoid Alien: Isolation like the plague.
I don't want to give anything plot-wise away, so suffice it to say the story is fantastic. Its themes of fear of the unknown and corporate greed are both consistent with and resonate strongly with both Alien and Aliens. I've already played through the campaign TWICE and I'm now starting a third play-through on the hardest difficulty. Given it's rare for me to finish a game even once, let alone several times, that should speak volumes as to the quality of this game.
As I mentioned, though, not every type of gamer will get everything out of this game that I did. Those who dislike or don't have the patience for a slow, methodical pace should probably skip this -- as they should skip the original Alien movie. There is combat in the game, but it's not the game's primary focus and that shows. It makes perfect sense in the context of the game, but for anyone looking for a Halo or CoD level of shooter gameplay, they should look elsewhere -- this is not the game they're looking for.
If you can give yourself to the tension and live in the moment in which Alien: Isolation wants you to live, you will have an amazing experience. If you can't or if this much tension, fear and anxiety it's too much for you, I suspect you'll hate it.

I am not an unbiased reviewer when it comes to Alien Isolation. I've been a fan of the Alien franchise since I was way too young to have been allowed to see the movies. I've forgiven the sins of David Fincher, and leapt over the plot holes of Prometheus.  When I read comic books as a kid, instead of Superman, I had Aliens; instead of Batman, I had, well, Batman versus Predator — a damn fine series, by the way. I have played all of the video games in the franchise so far released — barring some mobile games — and I've been disappointed in all but two. I know all too well the failures of the Alien franchise, and have been disappointed in a very personal way many times. I thought the concept of the Alien was only going to be fit for a certain caliber of game. This game was a revelation.
This is the best Alien gaming has ever been, and — barring a few missteps and a dash of predictability — it’s come the closest to capturing the soul of the franchise in an interactive form. The pervasive sense of dread and — wait for it — isolation along with the authenticity of the environments and the deliberate pacing combine to virtually recreate Alien as a twenty hour game instead of a two hour film.
From my first moments aboard Sevastopol, I was filled with a sense of nervous dread. You know what kind of game you're playing. You know there's a monster here. But you don't know where it is or when it will appear. Ominous noises from the environment could be the damaged Sevastopol station groaning and creaking, but could it be the beast? This game is positively stressful to play. I can't tell you how many times my own dog spooked me in real life while I was playing this game. I figure it should come with a warning like a roller coaster: people with heart issuies may be endangered by this game.
The Alien is at its very best when its menace is felt instead of seen. Alien Isolation instills that lurking menace within you from moment one, and it persists throughout the game. Even when you know that you're safe and the beast is far, far away, you feel the gut tightening anxiety of its presence. The typical power dynamics in video games have been about enabling the player to dominate the world of the game. Isolation eschews this trend by making the player almost helpless, relying on stealth and ducking into concealment at the first sign of trouble like a scared mouse. Alien: Isolation isn't about winning, it's about surviving.

Two major new systems have been implemented in this update: The Justice System and The Champion System. With Justice, crime has come to the once-friendly streets of Tamriel's cities. You can now become a wanted criminal, sneaking, stealing, and even murdering your way through the world. But be careful—the guards can and will seek to punish you if your crimes are witnessed.
The Champion System gives players with Veteran characters a new way to gain power. Once you have a Veteran Rank character on your account, you'll start earning Champion Points, which you can invest in a variety of new passive abilities.
That's not all Update 6 has to offer! they've completely overhauled provisioning. You'll notice new recipes and much more inventory space as a result of our updating and streamlining. There's also a new way to keep track of your mounts, pets, and costumes: the Collections Window because you can access everything you've earned through the new UI at any time.
That basically covers the biggest changes since the buy to play change. Since all the updates it genuinely feels like its single-player predecessors rather than a cookie cutter MMO, and that in itself is enough to draw me back into the game for many, many more hours!
10/10, this game is a must buy now!

The best part about the game is the Infamy System. Let me explain what that is. You have your basic tools, gear (cloths) and items including resources and ammo and such.  When you're starting out and get killed by another player you will lose all of your ammo and resources BUT NOT lose your tools and clothing, basically the essentials. If you've killed another player you get infamy which means for 15 minutes if you die, you have a chance of dropping your tools such as guns, pickaxes and other things. This will stack higher and higher if the player does not let his infamy disappear first.
This makes the game so much better due to the fact that not EVERYONE will KOS. You will need to be cautious.

My run in with the Truck Simulator series started as a method of reproducing my stepdad's Kenworth T680 as a birthday gift. Then I actually got in there and realized that the truck I wanted was locked at level 20. So I got in and started playing. And boy did I get addicted. I started in Dijon, the closest city to my old French teacher's hometown of Arbois and bought my first Renault. It was a neat little Renault. I took all the jobs with it's weak little engine. But then I encountered the Scanias. Huge, streamlined, powerful engines that could cut through traffic like butter. And all that additional customization with the DLC pack made my second and hands-down favorite truck the Scania.
Controller support is great. Keyboard needs to be used for some functions like cameras, airhorn, and switching the RouteMaster display, but it drives well and solidly through over 10 European countries and Great Britain. Almost every aspect of the truck is fully functional, from the headlights to the drop axle to the blinkers and hazards. Mods can be downloaded to the game to give you not only more paint, but also more trucks and even more of the map to explore.

Alright, here's what I think. After 43 hours and almost completely liberating everything in just under a week, I have to admit I like it and it's a ton of fun. It's everything I wanted from the next instalment in the franchise.
I have heard some people complain that there's not much content beyond liberating bases and completing challenges. This is true, but then I think that Just Cause 2 was exactly the same, and everyone loved that.
Next thing is complaints about stuff being locked behind challenges. Personally, I do not mind this, I already get more than what I got in vanilla Just Cause 2 (unlimited explosives, multiple tethers). So getting more is technically optional (although I do recommend it, it makes the game significantly easier). Just try to do the challenges. They may seem repetitive but each one is just about fresh enough in my humble opinion.
There is *one* thing that bothers me to no end though and that is the  always online feature. It often disconnects me from the servers, making me often have to reconnect, sometimes it won't reconnect and I have to go into offline mode where it will try to reconnect me every 5 minutes when I pause the game as well. I know you want to keep your game out of the hands of those pesky pirates and I respect that but at least make sure that the people who do purchase it are not inconvenienced by your measures.
That said, the game runs fairly well on my set-up with I7-4790K, GTX 770 and 16 GB of RAM. Running it on high and maintaining 60 FPS most of the time. FPS drops are present but rather rare.
I personally would give this game a solid 8.5/10.

Now before any of you start raging at me for my thoughts on this game, and giving it a thumbs up, take off your nestalgia goggles and look at this from a new angle, otherwhise move along, nothing for you to see here.
First off I'd love to say how amazing this game is graphically. The detailed and rich enviroments, and character models are one of the best parts of this game.
Next I will say "Let's be honest here." This is an MMO, not a normal Elder Scrolls game, we are no longer the legendary god like hero saving the world alone. Now we are part of a faction, an army, fighting for two things. 1: To get our souls back from Molog Bal, and 2: to claim Cyrodil in the name of our faction for a cause we think is right. The way the story was written and executed for this is AMAZING.
There is literally something for everyone in this game, from the Role Players, to the PvP junkies who will talk trash for killing you in the cheapest way possible. I love every part of the game. Role Playing, Exploring, playing the PvE content, and when I feel I'm ready for it, the siege PvP.
The Crafting system is awesome, and rewarding, with the ability to get hirelings who bring you crafting materials once to twice a day, helping speed up your ability to craft epic arms and armor.
In a small way, the game brings back some of our fave classes, though in a new light, such as the Nightblade for example. Though, you do not have to follow this classes skill lines, it's just there to give you something to start with. If you want to be a melee mage with a Warhammer, wearing heavy Armor focusing on combat boosting magic, then you can. Your imagination is the only limit here.
You can become a Vampire or Werewolf, and depending on the character you play, either one can be very rewarding, but at the same time, highly punishing, if you're not aware of the negative effect it has in combat against poison or fire.
With the recent addition of the Justice System, we are finally able to pickpocket and assassinate SOME NPC. Thankfully Zenimax/Bethesda had the good grace to make vendors immune to all of this.(Again take off your nestalgia goggles.)
If you're a fan of MMOs and a fan of Elder Scrolls games, I do recommend getting this game when you can.

If you like Alien, survival horror and stealth (emphasis on stealth), you'll definitely enjoy Alien: Isolation. The gameplay is almost always tense and Creative Assembly has done an excellent job of recreating the atmosphere of the original film.
The game does falter a bit in the second half, mainly because you get a bunch of guns that thoroughly undermine the threat presented by enemies. Balancing in general could have been better, as I always found myself overloaded with ammo and crafting resources. Your reaction to the Xenomorph may vary depending on your experience with stealth games and your ability to discern nuances with AI. I never felt it was cheap or unfair and when I got caught, it was always my own fault. If you don't understand how the AI works, you might get frustrated. The game lasts between 15 and 20 hours, depending on your difficulty setting, your aptitude for stealth games and your willingness to backtrack for collectibles.

I just want to say to Creative Assembly, thank you for making this game! This is the Alien game, as a fan of the Alien franchise, we have been waiting for. The attention to detail and atmosphere is incredible and all the hard work that was put in to making this a great game really shows. For anyone that is on the sidelines as  to whether or not to get this, do it! If you are a fan you will not be disappointed. If you are not a fan , but love survival horror this game will not dissappoint.The game is difficult, but rewarding if you take your time with it. Im not good at stealth games, but that does not keep me from enjoying the game. Being in that atmosphere, hiding from the Alien, It really makes you feel the terror of being hunted. The games mechanics come together so perfectly. Turn off the lights, put on your headphones, and get lost in the Alien universe. 10/10

So let's start from the beginning of everything really, pretty much every Alien game that has come out in the past was pretty bad.  They may be fun but lets be honest, the game developers werent up to the challenge of the huge universe and legacy that is the Alien series.  I can proudly say that this is completely different.  The developers cared and succeeded in making a truely incredible game.
Now on to the real meat and potatoes of what everyone really cares about and that is how fun it is and if it is actually worth your while.  For a stealth and survival game to be judged on how "fun" it is, is pretty hard and really depends on what games you're into.  If you play MOBAS or FPS or strategy games etc. exclusively, then you probably wont enjoy a stealth survival game now would you?  For fans of games like Outlast and dare I say Slenderman, then this is definitely worth your while.  The Alien that you encounter is fast, smart, and deadly just like it should be which stays true to the movies.
Like many people have said in other reviews, the AI isnt perfect because if it was the game would be impossible to complete.  Seriously, if the Alien was as cunning and insanely smart as they are in the movies you wouldnt last very long and no one would enjoy playing.  For what all the AI do (including human survivors, androids, and the Xenomorph) I think their performance is more than satisfactory and will give you a chilling and intense experience.
I would also like to mention how amazing the graphics are throughout the entire game are.  The style and design of everything holds true to the original Alien movie and is throughout the entire eperience. the actual textures and lighting effects are truely next gen and thats pretty much all I have to say because the game speaks for itself.  I cannot begin to explain how well the game devs have optimized this game, I honestly cant think of any other company who have done a better job making their game run as smoothly and insanely well as these guys have.  Just for an example, my rig can pull out about 30 frames sometimes dipping to as low as 15 to 10 on Battlefield 4 with all of the settings on low.  I can run this game on everything maxed out on ultra settings and I get a constant 60 frames (maybe higher).  I cant stress how well this game runs.
There is actually a surprising amout of playablitly I would say for this game. This installment in the Alien franchise advertises that you will essentially be running and hiding from the Xenomorph on a space station out in god knows where of space. Let me break it to you, you wont be safe there forever.  The Alien's AI may not have realistic lines of sight (because like I said the game would be impossible), but it does know how to hunt your♥♥♥♥♥down, lure you out of the vent you were hiding in to see if it left, and then crawling into the same vent that you felt ever so safe in and killing you from behind. We’re reaching that time of year where, once again, the ghosts, ghouls and vampires come out of the woodwork and begin to walk the streets in search of brains, blood and ungodly amounts of sweets. With Hallow’s Eve soon to be upon us all I was eager to find a suitably scary game in my Steam library, to get me in a spooky mood. It was slim pickings except the FEAR games, Five Nights at Freddy’s and a little-known game called “Naninights“. Having never played Naninights before, I loaded it up and boy was I terrified by what I saw.
For all intents and purposes, Naninights is Five Nights at Freddy’s. Well, it would be if Five Nights at Freddy’s was a complete piece of ♥♥♥♥ing dog♥♥♥♥♥♥
Instead of Freddy and his band of animatronic bad guys, Naninights gives us some sort of failed infant experiment, wearing a gas mask. Spooky ….(!)
The basic premise of the game is the same as Freddy: keep an eye on the other corridors and rooms in the building, and manage your energy reserves effectively so that you can make it through until morning. Failing to keep your eye on the titular “Nananight” results in the usual jump-scare and the game spits you straight back on to the menu screen. Yet, even with the barest of feature sets, Naninights’ developer still manages, somehow, to ♥♥♥♥ things up even further.
Graphically, the game looks beyond dated, sound effects are on an endless loop and there are zero options whatsoever – not even for resolution. Naninights is the kind of game you’d expect a group of executives to greenlight at a business meeting, I imagine the meeting went something along the lines of:
Corporate guy:
“I hear jump-scares are all the rage these days, can we make something quick to take advantage of that?”
Developer:
“We could, but Scott Cawthon has that market pretty much cornered. He’s published 8 Five Nights at Freddy’s games since Monday”
Corporate guy:
“Well tough ♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The market wants jump-scares and we’re getting in on that action. Make me a clone of these Five Nights at Freddy’s games you mentioned. If you could, give it a really stupid name, try to make it look much worse, be really boring to play and be a generally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ experience for everybody. Oh, and have it on Steam by the end of the day. Thanks!”
Developer:
“Uhh..”
Only, there was no corporate meeting. Naninights is the ‘effort’ of a single developer; a cynical ploy to line their pockets and to dupe unsuspecting gamers out of their hard-earned cash. That’s the scariest part of all this.
I’m not offended by Naninight‘s attempts to clone Freddy, rather I am offended by the sheer lack of effort put into it by its developer – and that the people at Black Shell Media could publish this tripe with a straight face.
This game is a product of the “me-too” generation, where no marketplace can be too overcrowded. It’s a quick cash-in farted out in a couple of days and then♥♥♥♥♥♥out on the Steam storefront. For the love of God, don’t buy it.

Basic synopsis: This seriously needs QA.  It's not horrible, but in my opinion, it's nowhere near good.
I've beaten all phases, and have beaten all phases on Hard++ mode.  I still don't get it.
{ Gameplay }
- I beat the first two parts of the game by closing the gate and lighting the cube whenever I saw the warning graphic.  I ended each of these parts with just about 100% in each category.
- I beat the third part of the game by staring at him the ENTIRE NIGHT with the mirror with the gate open and the cube off.  Hard+ and Hard++ mode, you can do the same thing if you see him up close in the hallway.  None of this is explained.
- Hard++ mode seems really random, but after beating it, you just hear the alarm go off and you are taken back to the main menu.  Absolutely nothing special for winning this due to a bug in the .ini save file.  If you transfer the info written to the wrong file to the correct file, you see a new background image...but I have no clue what it means.
{ Presentation & Bugs }
- The game has tons of spelling and grammatical errors (see 'How to Play' for the ultimate example -- e.g. "keep you Mind", "greater then", "keep your gate close", "Naninight need to make 3 steps", "for the rest levels").
- There is a flicker on the home screen that makes it look like a graphical bug, even if it's not.
- The "jumpscare" noise is more hilarious than anything else.  It sounds like a one-take random growl noise.
- The "A.L.I.F.A." mask is never explained, and the story is not drawn out to any satisfying level.
- The font on the Hard+ and Hard++ menu is all messed up...way too big, and overlaps the text you need to see.
- The About screen has a big blank text box...no content.  Just the author up top.  It's also a pop-up window, which isn't characteristic for any of the rest of the presentation.
- Instructions in-game are also incorrect.  The cube won't stop "Naninight" unless he is in the "bedroom"/crib room...but there's really no advantage in looking at the "camera" or whatever until Hard++ mode, when the alert for Naninight is disabled.
- The music also cuts out and never loops on the How to Play page, which is very odd.  Loud with no resolution, then nothing.
- Volume is deafening on some of the piano riffs on side menus, but gameplay isn't nearly as loud.
- Hard+ mode is labeled as "Standard difficulty" under the text that says "Hard+"...
- Beating Hard++ mode all the way through gets you NOTHING.  This is due to a save file error.  The main game saves to Enjoy (file), but the other modes save to Enjoy.ini.  The background is based on Enjoy, but it never gets the updated data to put the actual ending graphic.  You literally get nothing special due to that bug.
- Fun fact: You can hear the alarm noise and still die.
{ vs. FNAF }
- At least Naninights doesn't mess up your screen resolution by defaulting incorrectly in CTF application settings...but this is due to the restriction set in-game.  It's a simple fix for FNAF, but it was never actually resolved properly.  However, there is no title bar, so you can't move the Naninights window.  Even more, clicking on Fullscreen doesn't work at all in Naninights.
- Music still plays when the window isn't in focus, which is a good thing.  FNAF?  Change to another window and you don't get any audio.
- Disabling Music doesn't Disable Music.
- Story in Naninights isn't nearly as endearing as FNAF, and story frankly isn't explained in any real depth in Naninights.  Why does lighting a cube stop a kid with a mask on from...growling in your face?  Does he kill you?  Does he just make you laugh and thus, you lose since you can't laugh at your job?  It's never explained.  A.L.I.F.A. mask..what even?  Also -- what does "Naninight" mean, and why is this kid nicknamed that?  Why does the kid wear the mask?

It's entertaining.
For about 15 seconds.
Then it's confusing and pointless.  Save your money.

Alright, here's what I think. After 43 hours and almost completely liberating everything in just under a week, I have to admit I like it and it's a ton of fun. It's everything I wanted from the next instalment in the franchise.
I have heard some people complain that there's not much content beyond liberating bases and completing challenges. This is true, but then I think that Just Cause 2 was exactly the same, and everyone loved that.
Next thing is complaints about stuff being locked behind challenges. Personally, I do not mind this, I already get more than what I got in vanilla Just Cause 2 (unlimited explosives, multiple tethers). So getting more is technically optional (although I do recommend it, it makes the game significantly easier). Just try to do the challenges. They may seem repetitive but each one is just about fresh enough in my humble opinion.
There is *one* thing that bothers me to no end though and that is the  always online feature. It often disconnects me from the servers, making me often have to reconnect, sometimes it won't reconnect and I have to go into offline mode where it will try to reconnect me every 5 minutes when I pause the game as well. I know you want to keep your game out of the hands of those pesky pirates and I respect that but at least make sure that the people who do purchase it are not inconvenienced by your measures.
That said, the game runs fairly well on my set-up with I7-4790K, GTX 770 and 16 GB of RAM. Running it on high and maintaining 60 FPS most of the time. FPS drops are present but rather rare.
I personally would give this game a solid 8.5/10.

While on the surface, this game may seem like just a farming game with a visual twist, Slime Rancher has a surprising amount of depth and strategy that will keep you engaged for hours.
The basic mechanics of the game in Slime Rancher are feed slimes, collect the plorts they produce, and sell them for money (or newbucks). That’s it. Other than the tutorial, there is nothing you are required to do. This lets you play the game at your own pace, and with your own playing style.
The game looks and plays smoothly. The graphics are colorful and well-made, and locations can sometimes make you sit back in awe. The sound effects and music are all composed masterfully. Each press of a button produces a short, but satisfying sound, and the sounds of the slimes just sets the mood for the game. The music adapts to where you are and what you’re doing. Each slime in the game is like it’s alive, with facial expressions, movement, and reactions to their surroundings. Although there usually are many moving things on screen at once, the game runs smoothly with little to no lag.
There are many forms of strategy in this game, such as inventory management, where you place structures and facilities on your ranch etc. These all play a role in the overall gameplay, and these choices work. If you had in infinite inventory, collecting plorts and items would be too easy, and if you didn’t have a choice on where buildings go, you might not realize strategies you could have developed if you’d place buildings next to each other.
On top of the dozen or so slimes currently in the game (and more to come), each slime can ‘fuse’, or create a largo with any other slime. For example, if I fed a Pink Slime plort to a Rock Slime, they would form a ‘Pink-Rock Largo’, and when fed, would produce both plorts, and potentially more profit. Each slime also has specific foods it can and cannot eat. While Pink Slimes can eat all food items, a Rock Slime can only eat vegetables, and a Tabby Slime can only eat meat.
The map in this game is colorful, vibrant, and full of secrets for you to discover. Apart from the Ranch upgrades you can purchase for more land, features, and routes to explore, the world (The Far Far Range) is vast, and this game encourages exploration. By going to different areas, you may encounter a new type of slime, different fruits, vegetables, and meats, new items, upgrades and secrets. The world feels complete, and while there are distinct areas, they feel carefully stitched together, and not like they were just placed next to each other.
What I think the game does best is that sense of discovery every game depends on. When you unlock a new area, or uncover a hidden canyon, you are eager to explore, and see all the game has to offer. There is no in-game map, and I think this is a good choice. You are forced to remember to layout of the world on your own, and when you tread the same route over and over, you start to feel like part of the world. There are so many little quirks and crevices to get yourself lost in that the game keeps you engaged.
Slime Rancher also has one of the best communities I have ever seen, full of helpful people, people who discover new things, new ways to play, challenges, and tons and tons of art. Not only this, but the developers of the game, Monami Park, engage frequently with the fanbase, posting on Twitter, and socializing on Reddit. They will post new screenshots of upcoming features, answer questions, and make tons of jokes. Although the community is not technically part of the game, it helps you buy more into the world, and you want to see all those secrets others have found, leading to a more exciting experience.
The game also has controller support, and while it may need a little tweaking, and digging through settings, it’s still fluent and fun (especially with gyroscope turned on). That’s really all I have to say about controller support.
Slime Rancher provides a unique experience you can find nowhere else, and with the new updates and constant developer support, the game has never felt bigger. I hope everyone will be able to enjoy the game as much as I have.

This game should be called Advanced Lag. Sledgehammer did an awful job implementing the matchmaking and the players have absolutely no influence on the amount of lag they get. It does not matter what they say about the game, the only thing that matters is how many hours you put into it: MW2 949; Bops 260; MW3 374; Bops2 201; Ghosts 256 (you can't even play with it now cos nobody is in the playlists); AW (AL) it will be a miracle if I reach 100 hours. It is definitely not worth the 59 Eur price (I bought it for 25). It will never give back the feeling once it had with MW2.

**WAIT FOR ON SALE OR FOR SERVER SUPPORT**
Feels like a CoD game, but that's not a bad thing anymore. I feel like the franchise should be further along than it is, but this is a good start. AW feels like a natural progression. Like a real next step. It feels new, it feels unique, it has personality all its own. Mobility is a key factor, and weapons systems have been honed down into specialized categories to fit play style, not skill. However, lack of optimization on PC and no dedicated servers as of yet mean that this game is not worth a whole $60. The gameplay is tight, but until there is support to keep the multiplayer from lagging down the toilet it's just not worth the money for the campaign alone.
Worst part to me is unlocking vanity items in multiplayer that only persist for a certain amount of game time before disappearing to be unlocked again. This is a facebook-game style of money grabbing that needs to disappear. It doesn't even give you the option to pay for the items to keep them. It just infuriatingly makes them go away after a while.
In addition, survival mode is tuned badly. Classes available in survival are not balanced well for the gameplay, and weapons are unlocked anew by wave count every single game. This means that if you like the "best in range" SMG, you may have to be super good at the game to ever get to use it here.
Kevin Spacet looks great, as do the rest of the voiced actors. Graphics and lighting are great. However, non-voiced actors and set NPCs are low quality.
I won't spoil any story or gameplay for you, but one of the missions in the middle of the campaign is one of the best stealth missions I have ever played. Fast-paced, dynamic, tense. Needing to respond quickly to unexpected threats and being given free reign to use you arsenal and environment should be what video game stealth is all about. Also, guards are not as stupid as usual stealth games.
Shows definite potential, but needs more experienced support or longer deadlines to make viable for modern expectations. Design is fantastic, programming needs more help or time.

I'm not even into horror games but this is amazing.  It's more of a stealth game that will terrify you than a straight horror game.  And it is everything you could ask for in the alien franchise.  Everything is so faithful and well done.  Graphics are great, sound is great, AI is good (I advise playing on hard, which is reccommended by the game anyways), campaign is good length (I just beat it at 22 hours, I'm not a completionist but I'm a patient player), story is pretty good and the last several hours are positively gripping.
Best Alien game!  Superb graphics and sound!

I don't even know where to begin.  It will be hard to explain why I loved this game so much without including any spoilers but I'll try.
First off... if you like the 1979 film Alien just stop reading now and buy this game.
If you've never seen the movie (seriously?!) then you MUST watch it first.  It would be criminal to not have seen the movie before playing this.
The aesthetic matches the original movie so well it's like you've been thrown directly into it... complete with clunky old CRT monitors, mechanical keyboards and cables hanging haphazardly along the walls.  The attention to detail from The Creative Assembly is truly astonishing.  You can tell they have a deep respect for the franchise.  Along with the 70's aesthetic another key point brought over from the movie is that the Alien is essentially immortal.  It is to be feared and respected.  It is death and you will cower from it in lockers and under desks holding your breath.
In addition to the Alien there are other threats to contend with - other survivors and synthetics known as "Working Joes."  Human survivors can be dealt with rather easily but the Working Joes are another story.  You can shoot them point blank in the face only to be strangled by them while they calmly instruct you to "cease your outburst."  You can set them on fire and they will continue to stalk you informing you that you are "becoming hysterical."  They are creepy to the extreme and add a fantastic element to the game.
In short this is the antithesis of Alien: Colonial Marines - a comparision that shouldn't even be made (an entirely DIFFERENT developer... many people fail to realize that!).  Pair this with clever and meaningful tie-ins to the original movies including new voicework from the original actors and actresses from the 1979 movie and in my opinion you've got the first meaningful entry in the Alien franchise from the video game medium.

Now before any of you start raging at me for my thoughts on this game, and giving it a thumbs up, take off your nestalgia goggles and look at this from a new angle, otherwhise move along, nothing for you to see here.
First off I'd love to say how amazing this game is graphically. The detailed and rich enviroments, and character models are one of the best parts of this game.
Next I will say "Let's be honest here." This is an MMO, not a normal Elder Scrolls game, we are no longer the legendary god like hero saving the world alone. Now we are part of a faction, an army, fighting for two things. 1: To get our souls back from Molog Bal, and 2: to claim Cyrodil in the name of our faction for a cause we think is right. The way the story was written and executed for this is AMAZING.
There is literally something for everyone in this game, from the Role Players, to the PvP junkies who will talk trash for killing you in the cheapest way possible. I love every part of the game. Role Playing, Exploring, playing the PvE content, and when I feel I'm ready for it, the siege PvP.
The Crafting system is awesome, and rewarding, with the ability to get hirelings who bring you crafting materials once to twice a day, helping speed up your ability to craft epic arms and armor.
In a small way, the game brings back some of our fave classes, though in a new light, such as the Nightblade for example. Though, you do not have to follow this classes skill lines, it's just there to give you something to start with. If you want to be a melee mage with a Warhammer, wearing heavy Armor focusing on combat boosting magic, then you can. Your imagination is the only limit here.
You can become a Vampire or Werewolf, and depending on the character you play, either one can be very rewarding, but at the same time, highly punishing, if you're not aware of the negative effect it has in combat against poison or fire.
With the recent addition of the Justice System, we are finally able to pickpocket and assassinate SOME NPC. Thankfully Zenimax/Bethesda had the good grace to make vendors immune to all of this.(Again take off your nestalgia goggles.)
If you're a fan of MMOs and a fan of Elder Scrolls games, I do recommend getting this game when you can.

It's official. I love the game. TESO has gone through many shifts in gameplay over the last year, and with Tamriel Unlimited they have hit the mark. Between crafting, exploration, and combat there are so many mechanics that are just quintessential to Elder Scrolls. The only thing I recommend people do before purchasing is realize that this is an MMO! You cannot expect the same level of immersion, but you can feel how awesome the game is if you take the genre into account. Last, I know many people are curious whether it is pay to win at this point because of the in game cash shop. Not at all, the only slightly unfair point of the shop is that you can purchase a mount ahead of time. Something you can still purchase in the game. The shop provides no other advantages among players. Definitely recommend this purchase if you are an Elder Scrolls fan.

While on the surface, this game may seem like just a farming game with a visual twist, Slime Rancher has a surprising amount of depth and strategy that will keep you engaged for hours.
The basic mechanics of the game in Slime Rancher are feed slimes, collect the plorts they produce, and sell them for money (or newbucks). That’s it. Other than the tutorial, there is nothing you are required to do. This lets you play the game at your own pace, and with your own playing style.
The game looks and plays smoothly. The graphics are colorful and well-made, and locations can sometimes make you sit back in awe. The sound effects and music are all composed masterfully. Each press of a button produces a short, but satisfying sound, and the sounds of the slimes just sets the mood for the game. The music adapts to where you are and what you’re doing. Each slime in the game is like it’s alive, with facial expressions, movement, and reactions to their surroundings. Although there usually are many moving things on screen at once, the game runs smoothly with little to no lag.
There are many forms of strategy in this game, such as inventory management, where you place structures and facilities on your ranch etc. These all play a role in the overall gameplay, and these choices work. If you had in infinite inventory, collecting plorts and items would be too easy, and if you didn’t have a choice on where buildings go, you might not realize strategies you could have developed if you’d place buildings next to each other.
On top of the dozen or so slimes currently in the game (and more to come), each slime can ‘fuse’, or create a largo with any other slime. For example, if I fed a Pink Slime plort to a Rock Slime, they would form a ‘Pink-Rock Largo’, and when fed, would produce both plorts, and potentially more profit. Each slime also has specific foods it can and cannot eat. While Pink Slimes can eat all food items, a Rock Slime can only eat vegetables, and a Tabby Slime can only eat meat.
The map in this game is colorful, vibrant, and full of secrets for you to discover. Apart from the Ranch upgrades you can purchase for more land, features, and routes to explore, the world (The Far Far Range) is vast, and this game encourages exploration. By going to different areas, you may encounter a new type of slime, different fruits, vegetables, and meats, new items, upgrades and secrets. The world feels complete, and while there are distinct areas, they feel carefully stitched together, and not like they were just placed next to each other.
What I think the game does best is that sense of discovery every game depends on. When you unlock a new area, or uncover a hidden canyon, you are eager to explore, and see all the game has to offer. There is no in-game map, and I think this is a good choice. You are forced to remember to layout of the world on your own, and when you tread the same route over and over, you start to feel like part of the world. There are so many little quirks and crevices to get yourself lost in that the game keeps you engaged.
Slime Rancher also has one of the best communities I have ever seen, full of helpful people, people who discover new things, new ways to play, challenges, and tons and tons of art. Not only this, but the developers of the game, Monami Park, engage frequently with the fanbase, posting on Twitter, and socializing on Reddit. They will post new screenshots of upcoming features, answer questions, and make tons of jokes. Although the community is not technically part of the game, it helps you buy more into the world, and you want to see all those secrets others have found, leading to a more exciting experience.
The game also has controller support, and while it may need a little tweaking, and digging through settings, it’s still fluent and fun (especially with gyroscope turned on). That’s really all I have to say about controller support.
Slime Rancher provides a unique experience you can find nowhere else, and with the new updates and constant developer support, the game has never felt bigger. I hope everyone will be able to enjoy the game as much as I have.

While this game is definately playable (Though ideally when heavily modded), this is not the successor to the orginal Rome which Total War veterens wanted. It's more akin to Empire: Total War in its structure and yet more simplified. Its controversial released combined with the dumbed down approach to campaign management (the province system, general system and recruitment system) means that I would recommend any other Total War title (with the exception of possibly Empire) over this one. However the game has been patched to a level where a new player to the Total War franchise should at least consider it , however I would suggest you wait for a sale ($60 is not worth it for this game in my opinion).
On top of this, the game seems to have shed some of the aesthetic features which made the first Rome so immersive. The lack of a family (while not required) means that you feel little to no immersion to your generals. They're just "spawn general and give him a random name", a tool to be used worn out and thrown away. Emperor edition has not changed this other than the presence of a few historical generals in the Imperator Augustus campaign and the limited use of them as political tools to gain gravitas.
The same can be said for the politics system. While the concept is great, the exectuion leaves a player feeling likes its strapped on to the side, since there was no actual politcal positioning involved other than gathering Gravitas (The resource the game uses to increase politcal support percentage). [Edit] The Emperor edition patch has fixed this somewhat by adding a politics tab which you can use to determine your overall politcal standing in the same way the senate slider functioned in Rome 1 as well as guage the risk of a civil war. While there still isn't an organised map of senate positions (where you would be able to determine how high up your general is in the senate), it still places faction politics into a position where the player can see its benefits to the faction as well as its relevence to the game over all. In the original Rome, having a high ranking general in the senate (Consul or other high ranking positions) felt like it was of immense importance in terms of your standing with the senate. But you don't feel that connection to your generals. Its like theres supposed to be a connection to the senate but there is none to be seen apart from a rank which isn't really displayed.
The armies and recruitment system is also a step backwards. The number of armies you can field at one time has been hardcoded with a limit based on your faction's Imperium level. This severely restricts your capability to spread your forces, as they limited to working only within an army. You cannot detach a small force to bolster a garrison and you find your self forced to move an entire army in order to swap a few units between them. The recruiment is linked to these armies aswell, so you cannot have an army on the move and produce reserves at the same time. This all has a severely negative effective effect on your ability to field armies in a dynamic manner. The arguement for this change has been to stop random small ai forces jsut roaming your lands for no reason, however in my experience, the only difference is that these warbands now have a general at their head and a raiding stance icon above them.
Navies in this game are virtually useless due to uncanny strength of transport vessels. This is due to the fact that armies now automatically form a fleet of transports the moment they are ordered into the sea. Considering that a considerable portion of Roman conflict occurred around the Mediterean, this ability to magically make a transport navy appear out of thin air is a major oversight, as it renders navies pointless, as transports make equally effective fighting vessels. The ramming mechanic is messed up to the point that a light skirmisher bireme can sink a heavily loaded quintareme filled with marines in a few hits, rendering most expensive naval vessels useless.
The province system restricts your ability to build your cities by hard coding them into two presets, provincial villages and provincial capitals. Capitals can build practically any structure and have pre-built walls which cannot be improved in any manner. Villages by contrast can only build certain building types and cannot be fortified in any manner. This greatly diminshes the ability to customise your empire as it existed in the original Rome. In other Total War games, every settlement was the same preset, it could be built up, fortified and garrisioned as needed. You could created industrial or military cities where you wanted and when you wanted. This is something you simply cannot do in Rome 2. On top of this, the limited number of build slots which has haunted the last few Total War games also makes a return, limiting what you can do with the city's space.
[Edit] After 15 patches the vanilla balance of units atleast feels good enough to credit the combat in this game. Graphically stunning with only a few things to nit pick such as the inccorrect modeling of the hoplite phalanx.(use the argive grip please)[/edit]
Rome 2 has finally become a playable experience similar in many aspects to Empire. For a new comer to the Total War series, this game would be worth a look though not at $60, however from the point of a veteren of the Total War series, this entry seems far more restrictive than previous titles and I cannot recommend this game over other Total War titles. Instead you should consider other Total War titles like Shogun 2 or the original Rome.
[Edit] After 15 patches the base game has reached a state somewhat similar to Empire. It is now a decent game and newcomers to the Total War series should have no problems with this game. Regardless because of the cost of the game (60$) combined with the misgivings I've provided above, I still will not recommend this game when the other Total War titles provide a better experience at a better price at the cost of only graphical quality.
To address the questions regarding my over 300 hours of game time, yes I've continued to play Rome 2 despite my concerns (And with several mods to boot) , however I feel that my concerns mentioned above are still legitimate.[/edit]

The rebranded Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unliminted makes it seem like you buy the game and then bam you get all the access, however, Zenimax Online has cleverly decided to make you pay for mounts, costumes, and anything else you want, including an entire race in their special "Imperial Edition". The gameplay is very boring into the first few hours of playing, but it still seems to have that Elder Scrolls feel to it, but overall I would say the Elder Scrolls should stay out of the MMO world from now on and just be what it does best, a free roaming single player RPG. I was very excited to purchase the game and although it has its downsides the game really is great for fans of the Elder Scrolls Series. It felt refreshing to begin exploring new areas and lands and begin seeing some of my favorite Elder Scrolls creatures and races. The world is beautifully made and the cities large and explorable for hours. However, after about 3 hours playing it does get boring since it takes so long to travel anywhere, not to mention the fact that the game crashes just about every 30 minutes, making you have to relogin and reload the game all over again for 10 mintues just to continue what you were doing.
Overall, if you are into paying the $59.99 it costs to buy The Elder Scrolls Online Tamriel Unlimited or if you want to give Zenimax a nice contribution by paying $79.99 for the Imperial Edition, be my guest. If you are not really a fan of either the Elder Scrolls or MMOs then this game is probably not for you. Out of 5 stars, I would give Elder Scrolls Online a 3. After playing it for about a year now and seeing all of the new DLC's that have been added, I would highly recommend that fans of the Elder Scrolls series purchase the Online game and begin playing today. Adventure awaits you in Tamriel, so don't hesitate to get your journey started!

Before anything else, I've played this before years ago so I know the kind of progress they have made from then.
Let's start with the bad news first...
I don't know if there was some kind of rush to get this out or what the story is behind this game, but it is riddled with bugs. Either it's bugs or people are cheating, hoping bugs because that would be easier for the devs to deal with and fix.
The servers aren't very stable and constantly go down for me, I'm not sure how well it works on everybody else's end, but for me it can hardly hold out for a single game. I know what you're thinking, "It must be your internet connection, or perhaps you're computer can't handle it." Every time I lost my connection to the game I check my internet and each time it was working perfectly. My computer runs much larger scale games than this with ease so I know my computer is't the issue.
At first most players are quiet and just trying to learn, same as you, but when you get into higher levels you start to meet the toxic players that crowd to every MOBA. Let me tell you, these people are usavory, one misstep and they will report you for some unknown reason. Even if you had been carrying the entire team to that point, they will jump on you.
While there is a profanity filter in the game that replaces swear words with these things ****, it doesn't seem to do anything to prevent offencive names and I've noted alot of players taking advantage of this. One in particular was "HangThe(N-word's)". I hope that is enough for you to get the picture because I'd rather not bring up some of the others I've seen.
The modes are basic, but one of them really irks me in the wrong way, Assault. In this mode there is only one lane and no jungle and each player is given a random god from the pool of the ones they own or are renting. You can trade gods with other players in your team or change the god you have for another random one by paying with favor, the in-game currency. Trouble is that while trading with a teammate is free, it is pricey to change your god and that may result in you getting something worse suited for the team. That's not the worst of it though, the mode actually more often than not chooses who will win based on the gods given. You can try to fight the odds but a team of 5 assassins with nowhere to hide in this one lane only mode doesn't stand much of a chance against a well balanced team. You have my pity if you have the god pack and chose to play this mode.
Onto the good now...
Though everything else doesn't change much from the standard MOBA, the third person is a nice change from the norm. It forces you to be much more aware of your surroundings unless you want people sneaking up behind you.
The number of different mythologies and gods for each in to applauded. The devs seem to take great care in showing the proper respect to each god when they design them and give them their abilities, but they keep them all tastefully clothed.
In conclusion...
There is alot more bad than good in this game and regardless of how many times you bring these issues up, the devs only seem concerned with making more gods to throw at you instead of fixing any lingering problems. There is little if any effort put in to improve the game. I'm fairly certain at this point though that they could care less about the complaints of others and doubt they even acknowledge them.
I can't reccomend this to MOBA fans or fans of games in general. If you want to try it regardless though, I won't stop you. Good luck.

Let’s get the housekeeping out of the way first: the beta patch helped some people.  It didn’t help others.  It helped me.  Releasing a PC game in this state is unacceptable, console port or no.  I preordered the game by a few hours, knowing full well it had substantial issues. My computer meets the minimum specs and I expected to have to play with everything on low. Even doing this, the game was objectively terrible, but most of the issues are now resolved.
However, if you have an expectation of running this game perfectly on maximum settings, and you don’t have a Titan X, don’t buy this game.  You’ll be disappointed.  I have faith that Arkane and Bethesda will fix this ridiculous graphics boondoggle, and when they do they'll have made a great game for you, but for now your best bet is to wait.
That said, the /gameplay/ of Dishonored 2 is fun.  It’s a long-awaited update to an excellent concept and engine.  If you played the first one, you’ll enjoy this one.  If you haven’t played the first one, go do that first -- it’s better, and a lot less expensive -- then decide if you want to drop the bucks on the sequel.  You probably will.
Okay, “better” is a pretty subjective thing.  Plenty of things are better in DH2 than they were in the original.  A lot of the delicate mystery in the first game is trotted out as main plot here, which just feels ham-handed, but though the direction just feels off to me, the story is much deeper than that of the original, and that is very welcome.  The levels also feel larger, and the game on the whole seems longer, probably as a result of the more involved story.
The game is good, a solid four out of five stars, and in no way deserving of a thumbs down.
I still don’t like DH2 as much as the original DH.  Now, I don't mean to be overly negative; the original Dishonored is one of my favorite games of all time, and will continue to be well into the future. This game was never going to measure up, even if it were perfect, and I can recognize that.  But it is difficult to talk about how great this game is, when compared to its predecessor, it’s just not.
I’ll go down the list in the comments, but there’s one thing I need to criticize front and center: the game has many more ending variants than the original DH, with six major results and a number of possible states in which you can leave Karnaca.  This is good!  But the game gives players only three “campaign slots.”  This is bad.  That’s not even enough for a single low and high chaos run on each character.
The game didn’t need campaign slots -- the original was fine with just a pool of saved games.  I cannot even begin to understand why this decision was made.  If you want to see all the endings, you will have to delete your completed playthroughs.  How this will interact with Arkane’s plans for New Game Plus, I have no idea, but I do not expect a thoughtful solution.
Additionally, DH2 has no level select -- if you want to play it at all, you’re stuck playing it from start to finish.  If you want to be able to practice a particular part of a particular level, your only option is to leave your own saved games at the beginning of each chapter.  Arkane, I don’t care about New Game Plus, just give me a damn level select.
In conclusion, is the game perfect?  No.  Is the game worth playing?  Yes.  Is it worth $60?  It’s worth $60 in the sense that $60 is the price point for a AAA video game, but when I look at DH2 next to DH it really does make me wonder why that is.  The original Dishonored was clearly a risk, and a labor of love.  Dishonored 2 has all the hallmarks of a hotly anticipated cash cow, rushed to market by uncaring executives.
I reiterate my original recommendation: if you’ve played Dishonored you won’t be too disappointed by the sequel.  If you haven’t played Dishonored, I’d pick that up instead.

While this game is definately playable (Though ideally when heavily modded), this is not the successor to the orginal Rome which Total War veterens wanted. It's more akin to Empire: Total War in its structure and yet more simplified. Its controversial released combined with the dumbed down approach to campaign management (the province system, general system and recruitment system) means that I would recommend any other Total War title (with the exception of possibly Empire) over this one. However the game has been patched to a level where a new player to the Total War franchise should at least consider it , however I would suggest you wait for a sale ($60 is not worth it for this game in my opinion).
On top of this, the game seems to have shed some of the aesthetic features which made the first Rome so immersive. The lack of a family (while not required) means that you feel little to no immersion to your generals. They're just "spawn general and give him a random name", a tool to be used worn out and thrown away. Emperor edition has not changed this other than the presence of a few historical generals in the Imperator Augustus campaign and the limited use of them as political tools to gain gravitas.
The same can be said for the politics system. While the concept is great, the exectuion leaves a player feeling likes its strapped on to the side, since there was no actual politcal positioning involved other than gathering Gravitas (The resource the game uses to increase politcal support percentage). [Edit] The Emperor edition patch has fixed this somewhat by adding a politics tab which you can use to determine your overall politcal standing in the same way the senate slider functioned in Rome 1 as well as guage the risk of a civil war. While there still isn't an organised map of senate positions (where you would be able to determine how high up your general is in the senate), it still places faction politics into a position where the player can see its benefits to the faction as well as its relevence to the game over all. In the original Rome, having a high ranking general in the senate (Consul or other high ranking positions) felt like it was of immense importance in terms of your standing with the senate. But you don't feel that connection to your generals. Its like theres supposed to be a connection to the senate but there is none to be seen apart from a rank which isn't really displayed.
The armies and recruitment system is also a step backwards. The number of armies you can field at one time has been hardcoded with a limit based on your faction's Imperium level. This severely restricts your capability to spread your forces, as they limited to working only within an army. You cannot detach a small force to bolster a garrison and you find your self forced to move an entire army in order to swap a few units between them. The recruiment is linked to these armies aswell, so you cannot have an army on the move and produce reserves at the same time. This all has a severely negative effective effect on your ability to field armies in a dynamic manner. The arguement for this change has been to stop random small ai forces jsut roaming your lands for no reason, however in my experience, the only difference is that these warbands now have a general at their head and a raiding stance icon above them.
Navies in this game are virtually useless due to uncanny strength of transport vessels. This is due to the fact that armies now automatically form a fleet of transports the moment they are ordered into the sea. Considering that a considerable portion of Roman conflict occurred around the Mediterean, this ability to magically make a transport navy appear out of thin air is a major oversight, as it renders navies pointless, as transports make equally effective fighting vessels. The ramming mechanic is messed up to the point that a light skirmisher bireme can sink a heavily loaded quintareme filled with marines in a few hits, rendering most expensive naval vessels useless.
The province system restricts your ability to build your cities by hard coding them into two presets, provincial villages and provincial capitals. Capitals can build practically any structure and have pre-built walls which cannot be improved in any manner. Villages by contrast can only build certain building types and cannot be fortified in any manner. This greatly diminshes the ability to customise your empire as it existed in the original Rome. In other Total War games, every settlement was the same preset, it could be built up, fortified and garrisioned as needed. You could created industrial or military cities where you wanted and when you wanted. This is something you simply cannot do in Rome 2. On top of this, the limited number of build slots which has haunted the last few Total War games also makes a return, limiting what you can do with the city's space.
[Edit] After 15 patches the vanilla balance of units atleast feels good enough to credit the combat in this game. Graphically stunning with only a few things to nit pick such as the inccorrect modeling of the hoplite phalanx.(use the argive grip please)[/edit]
Rome 2 has finally become a playable experience similar in many aspects to Empire. For a new comer to the Total War series, this game would be worth a look though not at $60, however from the point of a veteren of the Total War series, this entry seems far more restrictive than previous titles and I cannot recommend this game over other Total War titles. Instead you should consider other Total War titles like Shogun 2 or the original Rome.
[Edit] After 15 patches the base game has reached a state somewhat similar to Empire. It is now a decent game and newcomers to the Total War series should have no problems with this game. Regardless because of the cost of the game (60$) combined with the misgivings I've provided above, I still will not recommend this game when the other Total War titles provide a better experience at a better price at the cost of only graphical quality.
To address the questions regarding my over 300 hours of game time, yes I've continued to play Rome 2 despite my concerns (And with several mods to boot) , however I feel that my concerns mentioned above are still legitimate.[/edit]

Despite all the flak it took online immidiatly after its release, Total War Rome II in its current state is a good game.  Im not denying that it was utter unplayable crap when it first launched; it was unacceptably to launch the game in the buggy and unoptimized state it was in.  In the last 12 patches however, CA has not only eliminated most of the bugs but optimized the game superbly and released loads of free lc including entire new factions.  The single player campaign is long but rewarding but where Rome II really shines is when it is played with friends.  The multiplayer campaigns seem to have finally been freed from the prevelent gamebreaking desync issues and conquering the Ancient World with a friends is a blast.  The online battles are also surpurb, with a plethora of units to experiment with and maps to fight strategically on.  Also excellent is Rome II's extensive modding community.  With mods that enhance graphics to completly new campaigns mods give Rome II hundreds of hours of extra replayability. The only main flaw in Rome II is its horrendous naval combat.  Having gone an played the layered and realistic approach to naval combat in Napolean, Rome II's naval aspect is a step back for the series.  I frequently enountered glitches that caused two ships to simutaniously destory each other while ramming, ships that refused to board other ships, glitchy pathfinding, and graphical bugs that left chunks missing from the ship models.  As a person whose first Total war game was Rome II (although I've played many others since then) , Rome II is a game with good mechanics and excellent multiplyer that is only dragged done in its current state by minor (but irritating) bugs and the atrocious state of naval combat.  6.5/10

Just Cause 3 was the first game of the franchise I played. It combines elements of Far Cry and GTA and adds a whole lot of explosions to this mix.
The map is incredibly huge, but with the grapple-wingsuit-parachute combination JC3 manages to fix the problem of Open World game travel. Furthermore all usual vehicles such as trains, planes, cars, bikes, helicopters and boats can be found on the beautiful islands of Medici - and are very much recommended to be used against the regime of dictator Di Ravello - as the enormous world of JC3 is filled with countless military bases, villages and cities to be liberated.

While somewhat repetitve in liberating bases and cities, the story missions are surprisingly fun. Although you may not find yourself heavily invested in the story of Rico and the other characters, the dialogues are funny and the action is delightfully exaggerated.
Furthermore there are lots of different challenges, such as wingsuit courses, boat races etc, you (unfortunately) need to complete to gain access to game internal mods.
Luckily I was one of the players for whom the game worked
good from day one, that means only a few bugs occasionaly; such as missing street textures, the vanishing of all the water in the game, crashes when closing the game and more.
Additionally I had to fight with constant fps drops and the longest of loading screens ever. It is needless to say
let's hope this gets fixed eventually.
Nevertheless I was having a ton of fun in the 70 hours I played before finishing the story, maybe because it's just the right game for me. Just Caus 3 is what you make of it. If it runs.
8/10

Let’s get the housekeeping out of the way first: the beta patch helped some people.  It didn’t help others.  It helped me.  Releasing a PC game in this state is unacceptable, console port or no.  I preordered the game by a few hours, knowing full well it had substantial issues. My computer meets the minimum specs and I expected to have to play with everything on low. Even doing this, the game was objectively terrible, but most of the issues are now resolved.
However, if you have an expectation of running this game perfectly on maximum settings, and you don’t have a Titan X, don’t buy this game.  You’ll be disappointed.  I have faith that Arkane and Bethesda will fix this ridiculous graphics boondoggle, and when they do they'll have made a great game for you, but for now your best bet is to wait.
That said, the /gameplay/ of Dishonored 2 is fun.  It’s a long-awaited update to an excellent concept and engine.  If you played the first one, you’ll enjoy this one.  If you haven’t played the first one, go do that first -- it’s better, and a lot less expensive -- then decide if you want to drop the bucks on the sequel.  You probably will.
Okay, “better” is a pretty subjective thing.  Plenty of things are better in DH2 than they were in the original.  A lot of the delicate mystery in the first game is trotted out as main plot here, which just feels ham-handed, but though the direction just feels off to me, the story is much deeper than that of the original, and that is very welcome.  The levels also feel larger, and the game on the whole seems longer, probably as a result of the more involved story.
The game is good, a solid four out of five stars, and in no way deserving of a thumbs down.
I still don’t like DH2 as much as the original DH.  Now, I don't mean to be overly negative; the original Dishonored is one of my favorite games of all time, and will continue to be well into the future. This game was never going to measure up, even if it were perfect, and I can recognize that.  But it is difficult to talk about how great this game is, when compared to its predecessor, it’s just not.
I’ll go down the list in the comments, but there’s one thing I need to criticize front and center: the game has many more ending variants than the original DH, with six major results and a number of possible states in which you can leave Karnaca.  This is good!  But the game gives players only three “campaign slots.”  This is bad.  That’s not even enough for a single low and high chaos run on each character.
The game didn’t need campaign slots -- the original was fine with just a pool of saved games.  I cannot even begin to understand why this decision was made.  If you want to see all the endings, you will have to delete your completed playthroughs.  How this will interact with Arkane’s plans for New Game Plus, I have no idea, but I do not expect a thoughtful solution.
Additionally, DH2 has no level select -- if you want to play it at all, you’re stuck playing it from start to finish.  If you want to be able to practice a particular part of a particular level, your only option is to leave your own saved games at the beginning of each chapter.  Arkane, I don’t care about New Game Plus, just give me a damn level select.
In conclusion, is the game perfect?  No.  Is the game worth playing?  Yes.  Is it worth $60?  It’s worth $60 in the sense that $60 is the price point for a AAA video game, but when I look at DH2 next to DH it really does make me wonder why that is.  The original Dishonored was clearly a risk, and a labor of love.  Dishonored 2 has all the hallmarks of a hotly anticipated cash cow, rushed to market by uncaring executives.
I reiterate my original recommendation: if you’ve played Dishonored you won’t be too disappointed by the sequel.  If you haven’t played Dishonored, I’d pick that up instead.

I got to say this game is absolutely astounding. The lighting in the game is perfect and the Alien AI lets just say it's super smart. The first time I encountered it was in a vent of all places right before I was actually supposed to see it for the first time. Knowhere is safe no matter where you hide. I've died so many times from getting pulled out of lockers and storage cabinets just when I thought it would leave. However I figured out later on that you can hold your breath and lean to the back of the cabinet or locker if it senses you. You have to be really quick though and you can't be leaning back already which is most likely the reason I died so many times.
The Alien itself looks exactly like in the movie and is very unpredictable. You can hear it crawling through the vents above you. You never know when or which one it will come down from. It will hear you running, walking, or if you bump into things so you spend the majority of the game crouching and looking where you walk. If it sees you you can either scare it away with fire which will♥♥♥♥♥♥it off or it was nice knowing ya. It can't be killed. The sound effects and music are brilliant. They play just at the right moment and keep the atmosphere of the game tense.
Aside from the Alien itself there are other dangers like Androids and other humans. The humans are not much of a problem because you only have to lure the Alien to them (you probably know what happens next), but the Androids on the other hand are a problem because the Alien is not interested in them. Also the only time you can save in the game are at "Save Stations." When you die you'll start next the last one you were at. This can be frustrating because in some parts of the game you won't run into another save station for a good while. This along with backtracking through the same areas you've already been through in the second half of the game is quite rage inducing.
For this being Creative Assembly's first take on the survival horror genre I think they nailed it. They really did the movie honor and it seems they truly cared about the content that went into the game. This is the game that Aliens Colonial Marines wishes it was.

To quote gamesradar reviewer, David Houghton:
"Many licensed games use art and sound assets from the original source, but most, at best, do a good impersonation. Alien: Isolation feels like Alien. Clean lines and dirty surfaces.
