Right now, the game is undergoing a spell of patching after a very poor PC release.  The game worked for some, but not for many, and so your mileage will vary depending on your PC (not necessarily how powerful it is either - but how balanced, how much VRAM you have and such).  As most reviews already centre around performance issues, I won't spend too much time on those because I'd rather review the game itself but please bear them in mind (they are mentioned in the 'not so good' section below)....
While you can certainly play and enjoy the 'toys' of this superb game, the story will really make zero sense.  In the first game, the graphics and gameplay haven't aged at all and so I recommend you visit that title first, otherwise it will feel like starting to read a good book half way in.  The first game is often on sale, and it's an absolute gem, still carrying an 'overwhelmingly positive' review.  This game does genuinely feel like Part 2 of the series, and you'd be doing yourself a disservice by skipping the first game (its story-based DLC is also a must-have, so buy the 'definitive' version which includes the DLC).
This second instalment manages to recreate that special Dishonored atmosphere of the first game.  I was worried that, not being set in Dunwall, the game would be altogether more sunny and cheery, but Karnaca is every bit as poor and derelict as Dunwall, with more opulence of the 'haves' rather than 'have nots' intertwined.  From the start, the game feels familiar in both setting and story; it truly IS 'more of the same' but in a great way: more of the same AND much more besides...
The game feels shorter, but when I look at the hours played, it actually isn't.  Nine missions only, but these missions are made in typically bigger maps than we saw in the original game which of course means more replayability because there are again many ways in which to infiltrate an area.  There are more runes and charms to collect than in the first game, giving the game more side-mission style playability without detracting from the main story, and all the 'fun' toys are back so you can again mercilessly rig a Wall Of Light against your foes.  More importantly, as well as two chaos levels, you now have two different characters from which to choose, with different but wide-reaching skills and power sets that will give you a different game experience.  Finally, the skills upgrading has been given a huge overhaul.  You still collect the beloved runes and bone charms, but this time you can opt to craft your own bone charms which can be made up of up to four individual charms, thereby allowing you to tailor your character with many more perks than was previously possible.  10 bone charm slots can therefore give you a maximum 40 upgrades from the many bone charms you will uncover in this game.
The plot itself is similar to the first game and the parallels are obvious, but the game does feel like an all-new title rather than a rehash, which is great.  There are plenty of nods back to the original story.  Replayability of this title is even greater because the playable characters of Emily and Corvo offer very different play-styles and approaches.  Arkane have provided a better balance of NPCs of different race and gender (one of the few poor things about the original title) which is great to see - it's clear that the developers listened.  And as if the game wasn't fun enough already, there is also a really clever level where you will manipulate time (travelling to through a map by choosing to switch between past and present as suits your route).  That is SO well done - a genius addition to the game.
In summary, everything about this game brings about all the good of the first (which was pretty much all of it) and expands on it in numerous ways without destroying that special 'feel' created in the first game.  If it wasn't for the performance problems, this game would be an absolute guaranteed 'Game Of The Year' because it is truly excellent.  I really hope Arkane have good story-based DLC planned as they did for the original game, because I want MORE of this superb experience, and I hope they can solve the issues because everyone should be able to enjoy it.
Mostly, performance issues on PC.  These range from variable or very poor framerates, to crashes and total black-screen non-starts (the negative reviews all focus on these problems rather than actual gameplay).  Please do check the discussion forums to see who experiences what (so you can compare your PC with others) and do make the most of your two-hour refund window to progress through Mission 1 to the outside (where the performance tends to manifest once outdoors).
The game FEELS short even though it really isn't.  I suspect this is because there are only 9 missions.  They are HUGE missions, but never-the-less that single digit makes the game feel much shorter than it really is.  I found myself in mission 7 of 9 in no time at all, or so it felt, yet in reality I'd been playing 25 hours or so by that point.  Being such a good game, I just wanted even more!
Finally, a really minor point, but the Outsider has been reinvented with new voice actor and I don't really like what has been done.  In the original game, it was impossible to determine the Outsider's stance (was he a force for good or evil).  He was a dark, paranormal character who seemed moderately amused at your progression through Dunwall's affairs.  In the new game, the Outsider feels much less enigmatic and also biased more against 'bad' rather than being a mysterious force.  This is no show-stopper by any means, but I did prefer the original Outsider.
Dishonored 2 is an incredible game that is an absolute 'must-buy' if you enjoyed the original title - but only IF you can play it.  Patches are being released which have already made improvements.  Hopefully, the stuttering, crashes and frame-rate issues will be stamped out fully, leaving people with a truly excellent experience in the Dishonored universe that, despite current Steam ratings, is even better than the first game (and as players of the first game already know, that was a very high goal indeed).

The game is great, and is all around a wonderful sequel to the first game. If you are thinking of buying it, though, please check other reviews and look around online to make sure you will be able to run it (even if you are above the recommended hardware). There have been a lot of performance issues, but a recent patch has apparently fixed a lot of them (not all). Personally, I have been running the game consistently around 30 fps, even before the patch, with a gtx 960m, which is actually slightly below the minimum requirements, but there are plenty of people with high-end cards that were getting as low as 15 fps.

10/10 Game of the Year material in my book. What an absolute masterpiece. The "recommended length" of the game is 12-20 hrs but it took me 36 hrs to finish my first low chaos Emily playthrough. The levels are packed with deep optional content and the envirionments are so stunning that I found myself just wandering and exploring for a lot longer than I anticipated to.
The level design in this game is second to none. They offer so many options in how to traverse the dense districts of Karnaca and allow for a variety of paths to be taken. Combat is damn fantastic as well. I missed out on all the fun killing because I never killed anyone in my first playthrough, and now I'm just going to town with High Chaos Corvo.
There's so many quality of life improvements in this game over the first one. The Heart, for one, is now re-designed to how people actually used it in the first game and will even narrate the personalitieis and character of those who you aim it at, completely changing the way you play because you now get to decide who gets to live and who gets to die. Bonecharm crafting is another welcome addition, now allowing you to sacrifice crap bonecharms that you may not need for your specific playstyle in exchange for whalebone and letting you craft more powerful versions of the bonecharms that you do want.
There's so many decisions and varities to play this. Emily or Corvo? Stealth or Assault? High Chaos or Low Chaos? Lethal or Nonlethal? Upgrade your existing powers or acquire new ones? On top of that, you get to decide how to want to navigate through the level, which offers more choices in playstyles. This is player freedom at its best.
Story is significantly improved over the first game too. I personally enjoyed it a lot more. Loved the fact that you had to have played both the DLCs to really comprehend what's going on here. A+ stuff, Arkane.

In my opinion this game is a worthy addition to the Alien Universe. The station that the game takes place at is crafted with incredible attention to detail, and tells of stories and events that will chill you to the bone.
Some tips on getting the right experience:
1. Play the game on hard difficulty.
2. Do not turn off the film grain.
3. Put the brightness all the way down to the levels the game advises.
The shadows create a big chunk of this game's terrifying world.
4. Put the volume up and use a headset.
Some random things I really liked:
1. The stealth system in the game is well made and challenging. Enemies can detect you even if you are in total darkness crouched down. You need to avoid their line of sight if you want to stay hidden.
2. Leaning at corners for more then a few short seconds also alerts enemies to your presence. Use it with care.
3. The optimization is excellent, it runs with a smooth FPS on my average PC despite all the beautiful particle effects and Ultra settings.
4. The game does it's most important job very well. It maintains the presence of the Alien at all times, and builds up as much terror as I could think possible around the character.
5. The audio is excellent and it really helps to create the atmosphere and to make everything a hell of a lot more scary.

9/10
THE GOOD:
Fantastic horror/sneaking game. Finally an Alien game that does the movie justice. The game is played from first person view. While you do find weapons, most of the time it is advised to stay hidden, as humans and androids are not to be trifled with. The Alien will kill you in seconds. The game succeeds in creating the atmosphere of the movies, where the protagonists are weak, but not helpless.
Luckily there is a convenient crafting system that allows you to build things like smoke bombs and medkits. The other important aid is the motion tracker.  Though, while using the motion tracker your vision is blurred and it emits a beep, so it can alert nearby enemies.
Graphic and sound ambience in this game are great, and they do a good job conveying the claustrophobic atmosphere on a space ship. Suprisingly even my humble Geforce 560 GTX runs this on ultra. The cohesive art style in particular is one of the best I have seen in a video game in years. Creative Assembly succeeded in transplanting the late 70s/early 80s art style of the original movies. Particularly the lighting in this game is phenomenal, and huge part why the deserted space station is so creepy. Very similar to System Shock 2 and Bioshock I in gameplay and emotional impact.
THE BAD:
Not much to say here. Apart from some glitches like floating weapons I didn't find any bugs. The save system could be annoying to some people who are spoiled by frequent auto saves in other games. This game does not hold your hand, and you need to find save terminals to save the game. Worse, it takes 3 seconds for a terminal to save, so make sure no one is around. I like the system, as it makes progress meaningful, and adds to the suspense.
THE VERDICT:
Game of the year for me so far. A game that respects the gamer and does not hold his/her hand. Your actions and decisions have real consquences, something that has become far to rare in video games. Gameplay and art style come together beautifully, just like in Bioshock I and Half Life 2. Worth the full price of admission in my mind.

Tamriel Unlimited attempts to bridge a difficult gap between the MMO experience and the Elderscrolls.  If you love the Elderscrolls world, exploring every nook, discovering ancient lore, and experiencing content that has not existed since Arena you will enjoy this game.  If you love high paced castle destroying intense PVP and combat you will enjoy this game.  If you are looking  for Skyrim the MMO you may be disappointed.  If you are expecting the most amazing MMO experience ever (because it is Elderscrolls)... you may also be disapointed.  But as it stands Tamriel Unlimited is beginning to shine as long as you reel in your expectations a bit.
My praise lies in the the fact they have managed to craft a world that looks and feels overall like an Elder Scrolls.  My ventures into Morrowind had me tingling with that old feeling of romping through the cliffs of Vvardenfell.  Finally the quest lines in ESO feel much more epic and important than any other MMO I have played.  Not to mention that nearly every quest you encounter is in someway related to the main plot line, it sometimes may not be immediately apparent but I find makes it a much more immersive experience.  Finally combat is what you would expect from an Elderscrolls MMO, The feel of Skyrim as most reliably done on a Server client system.
My complaints are simple and for the most part superficial.  Hair... why oh why can't anyone over at Bethesda or Zenimax (and many other american game companies) make decent character hair.  A few extra polygons and texture resolution on such an incredibly important part of your experience is worth any kind of performance penalty I may suffer.  TES has squeaked by this since Morrowind thanks to the modding community but you don't have that in ESO.  Also no barber or character appearance changing ability at all which means if you choose a hair style you later find god ugly you are stuck with it.  I truly hope this gets changed later.
Finally my one and only complaint.  The Character class system is amazingly limber, but in my opinion not necessary even in ESO.  You must choose one of 4 classes that imparts a set of class based skills and magic.  Your choices in constructing that character's abilities as it levels can turn them into a tank, a healer, a powerful magic damage dealer or some combination of the above.  But I can't help but feel it is unnecessary.  There are plenty of skills you acquire throughout the game world, why can't a similar system be used uniformly throughout the game.  Weather you are a Templar, Dragon Knight, Nightblade, or Sorcerer you can be any role you want to be, use any weapon and armor combination you want to use, but a Dragon Knight can never learn the Sorcerer skills.  It is the one aspect of ESO that to me still feels out of place.  What if I want to gain the Sorcerer abilities even though I am a Dragon Knight?  The original Elder Scrolls never put any kind of restriction on your ability to use or learn skills and it is the one aspect of ESO I would love to see changed.
Zenimax Online Studios (ZOS) is new to MMOs, they have definitely made mistakes.  But they have also been adequate at improving the experience of ESO in attempting to bridge that gap between the elements that make the Elderscrolls and the elements that make a great MMO.  It's not all there yet but If they continue down this road I can foresee an MMO unlike any other set in one of the most beloved settings of any game that will making it worthy of being called an Elder Scrolls game and I believe that is what all of us who are fans of the series wants to see.

Ellipsis was quite a delightful surprise for me.  I recieved it as part of a Humble Freedom Bundle (Feb 2017) and having played it I can say it is definately worth purchasing on it's own.  It's an arcade style game that has over 150ish levels where you collect five orbs while avoiding traps and enemies.  Blue good, red bad.  The universe which you play through is interesting throughout, and the difficulty slowly increases always keeping you on your toes, but never making you want to bang your head on your desk.
The game has a star based system for each level.  3 stars if you do the minimum, 4 stars if you beat it and obtain all the orbs, and 5 stars if you get all of the orbs and beat a timer.  Be prepared to die a lot to get five stars, but don't worry - it's super fun doing it.  It is not an easy game to get 100% achievements in, but once you'll do you'll get a good feeling of accomplishment - in some levels that time is super hard to beat.
The minamilist neon graphics are sharp and clear.  No studdering or lag what so ever, and no loading times.  I played on a keyboard and mouse - all you need is the mouse - and I rocked it.  It does support controllers and touch screen however.  Sound effects are also right on target.  This game really blew me away with how polished it is.
This game is excellent.  Huge congrats to the developers - Salmi Games.  I just don't think it's worth $10.  $5 yes, but not $10.  As an arcade game, it is now my favorite, however once you beat the levels at five stars I'm not confident it is going to have replayability like Pac Man or other arcade games.  That being said, it does have Steam Workshop support where you can make and upload your own levels, as well as download others (please check out my Workshop creations!).
10 out of 10. Highly Recommended.  Be prepared to always want to play one more level with this one.

Singleplayer
Story
Gameplay
Multiplayer
Gameplay
Singleplayer: The story is a masterpiece. Simply put. The music, the cinematics, the voice acting, the general theme is expertly put together. I havent enjoyed a single player game this much since the first Modern Warfare and Halo games came out.
Gameplay: This almost feels like a whole new game; There are so many details put into the game mechanics (for example: When climbing icy cliffs on a snowy mountain, your character will grab for the nearest ledge if you fall - i tested this by jumping intentionally, as long as you are close enough he'll attempt to grab a ledge and climb back up. In the prison, the guard hits you IF you turn around to look behind you - extremely cinematic. The plot is very deep and philosophical (you might need a bit of a brain to understand some of it) and though filled with clichés to the point of being predictable, it is still a very fun and memorable experience. Sledgehammer shows their experience with vehicles when you get to drive a tank and fly a jet in near-open world gameplay. As long as you stick to the right difficulty setting, you WILL enjoy this campaign.
Multiplayer: The multiplayer can be a bit buggy (especially considering loading maps and synchronizing to other players), since the game does not use dedicated servers (or so i've heard). Other than that i find it extremely fun and definitely the most fun gameplay since MW2, which i consider the best game in the CoD franchise. I'd pick this thing over Battlefield 4 any day - luckily i have both.
Conclusion; If you enjoy a cinematic, action-movie like experience, this is the game for you. Wether you play alone or with other players you'll experience several epic moments. Yes, the game is buggy. No, it's not broken - think back to CoD 4, add grappling hooks and jetpacks, and you know what you're getting. It even features a very Assassins creed-esque mission!
I love this game, it recaptures the glory of HL1. Deathmatch is as hilariously chaotic as I remember it. Somebody will hopefully remake bfield.

Hurtworld is a pretty MMO that is very DEEP in Early Access.
Incase your in a hurry, TLDR:
It's a fun game, but like all Early Acess games it has flaws, however this game has quite a few more flaws than most Early Acess games I have played in a while. Only buy if you plan on dealing with a bad community like Rust's for example or if you want to play SP, which means you gotta set up servers and stuff.
POSITIVES:
*Cute graphics.
*Difficulty
*Map is cool
*Cool creatures to face.
*Cool creature system. You start off seeing bunnies and such, but the deeper inland you go the bigger they get.
*Community can be fun at times.
NEGITIVES:
*Problems here and there with FPS. A lot of people talk about how fps can suck at times.
*Server wipes. Although, this being an early access game, it's kinda expected. Just really hard to get stuff in the first place.
*Glitchy. The creatures will sometimes just sit there and let you kill them, or run in place. I have really good internet, so it can't be because of my connection.

Overall I reccomend for people looking for SP or people who enjoyed Rust despite the toxic community. This game, at the time being, is a 6/10 from me. Although, i'll probably not play it for a while. I'll wait for some more patches and stuff.

This game, especially for where it is at the time of my review, is pretty great.
It has vehicles, a decent building system, the combat feels good, and the animations look great!
My only complaints are that this game does not have sleepers. Some will like that it doesn't, but I for one don't like it. There's no "risk" when you log out which really is what makes these games fun. When you die, you don't lose your tools, you just lose your resources. The only way for you to lose your tools is to be "infamous." This game is attempting to solve the KOS issue in most survival games by incorporating this infamous system. If you kill someone ( even in self defense, which is an issue) you become infamous and can then lose ALL of your gear. So, you have to think twice before you kill someone if you've spent a lot of time upgrading your tools. BUT, it still doesn't stop the person that killed you from just logging off... which is more annoying than anything since there are no sleepers.
Regardless though, I love being able to spawn with all of my tools so you can get right back in the mix, but at the same time, the consequences for dying aren't near as dire, which can hurt the immersion.
It also needs some ambient sound!!!!!

Creative Assembly absolutely nailed it with Alien: Isolation. The atmosphere and sound design are unparalled and the attention to detail displays a level of understanding and polish that is rarely seen in the genre. This is the best game based on the Alien franchise to date and one of the finest survival horror games I have ever played. This is one of those rare times when a game has completely lived up to my expectations.
The core gameplay revolves around using stealth and redirection to avoid dangerous encounters. You will often travel through ventilation shafts and air ducts, and may find yourself hiding under tables or inside lockers and containers to avoid detection. You will need to remember to lean back and hold your breath if you don't want to be snatched out of your hiding spot! Being hunted by an unrelenting and dangerous alien isn't the only source of terror in Alien: Isolation; you will encounter hostile androids and humans that can be equally as frightening. To assist in your survival on Sevastopol, you can scavenge for resources to craft items like flares, flash bangs, smoke bombs, noise makers, EMP mines and other tools, which are useful for creating distractions or to disable your enemies. While revolvers, blunt objects and other weapons are available, these should be used as a last resort. The enemies are no push-over.
The story primarily unfolds through cinematic cutscenes and character interactions, but is supplemented with information and lore from audio recordings and computer terminals that are scattered throughout Sevastopol. Alien: Isolation does a fantastic job of building tension and fear with direction and design that pays great homage and rivals Ridely Scott's original 1979 film, "Alien". For fans of the Alien franchise, this is a no brainer, and for everyone else, it is an experience that rivals the best the genre has to offer.

Euro Truck Simulator 2  is a vehicle simulation game developed and published by SCS Software for Microsoft Windows, Linux and OS X and was initially released as open development on 19 October 2012. The game is a direct sequel to the 2008 game Euro Truck Simulator and it is the second video game in the Truck Simulator series. The player can drive one of a choice of articulated trucks across a depiction of Europe, picking up cargo from various locations and delivering it. As the game progresses, it is possible for the player to buy more vehicles, depots, and hire other drivers to work for them.
Gameplay
Players choose their HQ's location in any of the game map's cities. At first, the player can only take what are known as Quick jobs—these jobs involve making hired driver deliveries while employed by a delivery company, with a provided truck and all expenses (fuel, road tolls, ferry crossings) covered. As the player earns money or takes bank loans, they can eventually afford to buy themselves a truck, acquire a home garage, and start making more money by delivering cargo using their own truck instead of just being a driver for hire. Money earned in the game can be spent on upgrading or purchasing new trucks, hiring NPC drivers to take on deliveries, buying more garages and expanding the home garage to accommodate more trucks and drivers.
The player gains experience points after each delivery. A skill point is awarded after each level-up. 10/10 Game of the Year material in my book. What an absolute masterpiece. The "recommended length" of the game is 12-20 hrs but it took me 36 hrs to finish my first low chaos Emily playthrough. The levels are packed with deep optional content and the envirionments are so stunning that I found myself just wandering and exploring for a lot longer than I anticipated to.
The level design in this game is second to none. They offer so many options in how to traverse the dense districts of Karnaca and allow for a variety of paths to be taken. Combat is damn fantastic as well. I missed out on all the fun killing because I never killed anyone in my first playthrough, and now I'm just going to town with High Chaos Corvo.
There's so many quality of life improvements in this game over the first one. The Heart, for one, is now re-designed to how people actually used it in the first game and will even narrate the personalitieis and character of those who you aim it at, completely changing the way you play because you now get to decide who gets to live and who gets to die. Bonecharm crafting is another welcome addition, now allowing you to sacrifice crap bonecharms that you may not need for your specific playstyle in exchange for whalebone and letting you craft more powerful versions of the bonecharms that you do want.
There's so many decisions and varities to play this. Emily or Corvo? Stealth or Assault? High Chaos or Low Chaos? Lethal or Nonlethal? Upgrade your existing powers or acquire new ones? On top of that, you get to decide how to want to navigate through the level, which offers more choices in playstyles. This is player freedom at its best.
Story is significantly improved over the first game too. I personally enjoyed it a lot more. Loved the fact that you had to have played both the DLCs to really comprehend what's going on here. A+ stuff, Arkane.

The first Dishonored is definitely one of my most cherished game (right beneath Bioshock 1&2). The balance of story, gameplay, and choice guaranteed an immersive experience that had to be relived multiple times. So of course I decided to preorder Dishonored 2 Collector's Edition. I have no regrets in this regard as the game is almost as great as the first.
It is true that this game can be intensive, I have a i5 6500 and gtx 960 in my rig and can run at 60fps on medium graphics. I don't find this any issue because the game is stunning regardless. I really do hope however that a fix will come in for all those who are experiencing issues or wish to buy this game. Hopefully this is not a pattern within future games by these companies because PC Games Matter.
Gameplay: Giving the choice between Corvo and Emily was a beautiful addition. The new playstyle that Emily supplies requires that you play the game repeated times. The gameplay, especially the combat and AI, is a lot more involved and flexible. I would say that the gameplay in this Dishonored is better than that of the first.
Story: The story is pretty straightforward, I don't find it as motivating and inclusive as the story of the first, but it is logical. I didn't feel the same sense of closure that I felt at the end of the first, and really wish they would have tied up more lose ends. Overall, the story is solid, there is so much lore within the world that (if you like to read) you will find lots of tie-ins to your situation and world. I do wish they would have included some more audio journals however like in the first, but I suppose books are more practical(?).
Overall, I love this game, not as much as I love the first, but it's such a great time that I still experience now. I am hoping that they fix optimization for those that are experiencing issues, but the game is otherwise worth a try.
(IF you haven't played the first Dishonored, DO NOT play this one first, do yourself a favor and play the first one)

Tamriel Unlimited attempts to bridge a difficult gap between the MMO experience and the Elderscrolls.  If you love the Elderscrolls world, exploring every nook, discovering ancient lore, and experiencing content that has not existed since Arena you will enjoy this game.  If you love high paced castle destroying intense PVP and combat you will enjoy this game.  If you are looking  for Skyrim the MMO you may be disappointed.  If you are expecting the most amazing MMO experience ever (because it is Elderscrolls)... you may also be disapointed.  But as it stands Tamriel Unlimited is beginning to shine as long as you reel in your expectations a bit.
My praise lies in the the fact they have managed to craft a world that looks and feels overall like an Elder Scrolls.  My ventures into Morrowind had me tingling with that old feeling of romping through the cliffs of Vvardenfell.  Finally the quest lines in ESO feel much more epic and important than any other MMO I have played.  Not to mention that nearly every quest you encounter is in someway related to the main plot line, it sometimes may not be immediately apparent but I find makes it a much more immersive experience.  Finally combat is what you would expect from an Elderscrolls MMO, The feel of Skyrim as most reliably done on a Server client system.
My complaints are simple and for the most part superficial.  Hair... why oh why can't anyone over at Bethesda or Zenimax (and many other american game companies) make decent character hair.  A few extra polygons and texture resolution on such an incredibly important part of your experience is worth any kind of performance penalty I may suffer.  TES has squeaked by this since Morrowind thanks to the modding community but you don't have that in ESO.  Also no barber or character appearance changing ability at all which means if you choose a hair style you later find god ugly you are stuck with it.  I truly hope this gets changed later.
Finally my one and only complaint.  The Character class system is amazingly limber, but in my opinion not necessary even in ESO.  You must choose one of 4 classes that imparts a set of class based skills and magic.  Your choices in constructing that character's abilities as it levels can turn them into a tank, a healer, a powerful magic damage dealer or some combination of the above.  But I can't help but feel it is unnecessary.  There are plenty of skills you acquire throughout the game world, why can't a similar system be used uniformly throughout the game.  Weather you are a Templar, Dragon Knight, Nightblade, or Sorcerer you can be any role you want to be, use any weapon and armor combination you want to use, but a Dragon Knight can never learn the Sorcerer skills.  It is the one aspect of ESO that to me still feels out of place.  What if I want to gain the Sorcerer abilities even though I am a Dragon Knight?  The original Elder Scrolls never put any kind of restriction on your ability to use or learn skills and it is the one aspect of ESO I would love to see changed.
Zenimax Online Studios (ZOS) is new to MMOs, they have definitely made mistakes.  But they have also been adequate at improving the experience of ESO in attempting to bridge that gap between the elements that make the Elderscrolls and the elements that make a great MMO.  It's not all there yet but If they continue down this road I can foresee an MMO unlike any other set in one of the most beloved settings of any game that will making it worthy of being called an Elder Scrolls game and I believe that is what all of us who are fans of the series wants to see.

Ellipsis is a game where you collect 5 bubbles before flying through a goal at the end. Enemies try to kill you before that happens.
Do I recommend this game? Yes! After getting 100% on the game, I think you can overlook the issues I list down below and have a great time! It's worth the price and even more so on sale!
The levels are well-made and you want to keep trying them over and over to get those ellusive 5 stars. The controls are tight (mostly) and the enemies are really diverse, so it doesn't get boring. I love the aesthetic (many have said it reminds them of Geometry Wars, which I like as well). Also as you complete levels, it creates a giant picture made up of the lines from level to level and little representations of the enemies. I love this idea and I enjoy zooming out and seeing all the progress you've made!
The game does have issues that make me want to rage and slam my desk in frustration. It sadly takes away some of the enjoyment.
The first issue is probably just my own opinion, but sometimes is seems like your circle avatar is too big. I'll be speedrunning through the level but a tight turn that feels like it should work somehow clips the side of an enemy, killing me. Again this is probably just my opinion, but the problem still stands.
The second thing is how the bubbles are collected. In the bubbles are little orbs that you have to collect in order to get stars for that level. The problem arises when you are going quickly, popping the bubble can make the orbs scatter everywhere. It adds an element of randomness that is not fun to play against and makes getting 5 stars on tough levels seem impossible. I can see where the devs were going with this because it looks really cool and all. But the design seems to point to a more serious audience (finishing levels quickly) and those really clash in this case.
The last issue occurs when hitting walls and gravity patches. In a game like this, you want to be very precise in your movements and be able to do them quickly. But when something causes your character to move in a different way from your mouse, it feels like the game is fighting you or that your mouse is unresponsive.
Overall, Ellipsis shines in a lot of ways and its cool to see an indie developer release a good game like this. But just keep in mind of these issues and if you want to buy, probably get it on sale first!
(Edits: Rewrote parts to show opinions after I finished the game)

I'm thinking this could work with a more developed, intricate art style. Thing is, the game lends itself perfectly to the basic lines and curves. You wouldn't be wrong by thinking it looks simple. It is, on the surface. But it's immediately clear that the developer knew exactly what would make it fun. The levels.
If someone gave me a dollar for every video game that could've been better with more competent, nuanced level design, I would be somewhere north of 7 or 8 dollars richer.
And I could put that money towards another copy of Ellipsis, because the levels are fantastic. After you've seen a handful of twists on a familiar conceit, you're then promptly handed a fresh take. Though never wiping the palette entirely clean, it's introducing shades and hues at a brisk, comforting pace.
To achieve 5 stars on any given level, you're encouraged to carve a path through chaos. Occasionally it's fully reactive, but just as often I had to attack with intent and strategy. Blazing through a level can mean you've made twelve discrete moves in 3 seconds, which, for what is essentially a cursor flying around a screen, actually feels kinda rad.
And despite what I said at the top: in motion, the game can be genuinely striking. The colors are pleasingly vibrant and shifting, with the sound offering the necessary punctuation. The screenshots tell a meager story by comparison.

Heres what i think. It all adds up to a game that's utterly lacking in urgency or momentum. Yes, the woefully inefficient pace of Rome II after every single turn is the biggest culprit. But there aren't enough fair battles to break up the normal pacing, and those that happen aren't compelling. Developing provinces and economics feels more like tossing a dart at a board than counting down the turns until your shiny new building. The enemy artificial intelligence is practically pacifist, which is extremely odd for a game called “Total War.” Perhaps what's most dismaying about Total War: Rome II is that it doesn't seem salvageable—its problems are as much conceptual as they are pragmatic. I can't imagine a patch or expansion with a smaller map, even though that would be the biggest possible help the game could get. In most grand strategy games, the motivation to play “just one more turn” is the most appealing part. In Total War: Rome II, “just one more turn” is a threat.

Just to start off this review this years call of duty game advanced warfare was created by sledgehammer games and i
do recommend it. Some quick background of sledgehammer, they were the co creators of MW3 (Yea... not much
bakcground). Now by looking at a lot of the reviews for advanced warfare your probably tempted not to get it but im
honestly really enjoy playing the multiplayer apart from most other cod games. First thing to talk about is campaign then
exo survival and finally multiplayer (Saving Best For Last) Campaign was actually pretty fun i understood the story
pretty well and the missions were nicely done with good variation. Now of course this is call of duty were talking about
so the campaign isnt exactly 5 star worthy but compared to other call of duty campaigns this one was designed well. Not
much too say about exo survival except that its pretty much mw3 survival with exoskeletons (ill talk about exoskeletons
soon). Now ive saved the best for last call of duty advanced warfares multiplayer which to me one of the best call of
duty multiplayers ive ever played. Keep in mind im into faced paced games so considering the exoskeletons which give
the game that speed boost that ive been waiting for call of duty to implement however if you prefer more of a slower
pace kinda game well advanced warfare still has you covered with gamemodes like TDM, domination, and search and
destroy without exoskeletons. Real quick lets talk about what exoskeletons or exos as they call them allow you to do,
exos give you a legit way to double jump dash forward, backward, left, and right. Exos also give you access to exo
abilites, exo launcher and an exo powered punch rather than call of duty's standard knife. The exo launcher is basically
your grenade however you dont throw it you shoot it out of a small machine located on your wrist (Like in black ops 2's
campaign). Exo abilites are special abilites for exo's some are exo shield, exo ping, and exo trophy. Advanced warfares
loadout system is almost identical to black ops 2's (which i dont have an complaints about) however instead of 10 points
you get 13 points to spend on various weapons, equipment and gear as well as wild cards. Anyways the point is this
was actually a change of pace to normal call of duty's and i recommend it to fans of sci fi games, fast paced games, and
call of duty (obviously). I hope this helped give you a clear overview of advanced warfare's game changing system.

Very cute game. But the gameplay is repetitive. It comprises of collecting various different slimes, each with different diets. You feed them and they drop plorts. These are what you sell for in game currency and later you can use plorts to make things. I think it could be developed further. At the moment when it comes to night time you get 1 different type of slime. You can cross breed sort of, if a pink slime for example eats a tabby plort it will become giant and grow ears. This then drops a plort from each species it was made from. You use these to expand and buy powerups. Currently 2 areas can be unlocked and a workstation which lets you make drills and such to get items to make transporters or turrets to defend your ranch. Each area has some different slimes and also largos, which are hidden giant slimes which drop keys to unlock areas within the area, or they will make a transporter activate.
But if it eats a different plort it'll turn into tarr and eat all your slimes.
DO NOT MAKE THAT MISTAKE. I didn't realise and did it 5 times in a row over 3 days. They quickly split so when you have no way of killing them other than flinging them into the sea you quickly lose everything.
It's also quite buggy. I have gone through the floor and died in about 5 different places. It was fine until I changed the resolution. Weirdly happens in different places depending on game mode. With the five day rush it happens on the first slope you encounter. Fine going down but getting back up you go straight through and drown.
Might be better once it's complete but I'm not sure I would recommend it until then.

Warning, these are my personal opinions on the game. And in this case they are very negative opinions. If you read this and love the game, keep loving the game. I do not hold that against you. It is an Alien game most will love.
I had high hopes for it, and maybe thats why im left here with more negative things to say about it than i have positive.
The beginning of the game is very slow, the first hour is basically a slow build up learning you the controls and the mechanics of the game, of which there aren’t very many. The control mappings are fine on both keyboard and controller. However the feel of motion is sluggish, sort of like you are moving through molasses, even your run feels kind of awkward and too slow.
You will be represented with a space station to walk around, where you will carry out many tedious tasks. Which often revolve around the same things, like powering up sub-systems, finding a keycard, finding a new tool that will let you open a new set of doors, and a ton of backtracking. In Between those segments, you pretty much play a hide and seek game, combined with a walking simulator.
You will come across other humans in that time, but it usually always ends in a gunfight if they spot you. As it seems no one are interested in working together or just letting you walk by with no hassle. You do have the option to bypass or let the Alien sort them out.
Then there are the androids, which are equally as hostile and are best bypassed altogether if possible, as it takes a metric snot ton of bullets to take them out. And don't even try to wrench them they will grab you each time, unless you manage to sneak up on them and get some good shots in. Again androids best avoided.
And finally there is the Alien(s), the center piece or at least it should have been.  I thought it would have a big impact on the game. I was kind of wrong about that one. It doesn't really add any tension to the game, at least it didn’t for me. Maybe because it showed up so much, seeing it over and over makes you accustomed to it and unafraid of it. Plus you will know what to expect and what to do each time.
It really added an annoyance in the fact that it would make me have to wait to carry out my mission to an extent it actually added a comical value too, the AI on it is kind of stupid. Sometimes it would actually see me, but it will be stuck in its hide in vent animation, and wouldn’t be able to break that cycle.
Then there is the issue of even though you will be crouching most of this game, the Alien oddly have the ability to just keep on you at all times, even though you left it in another room like 2 meters back, it will and can emerge just as you enter a new room like all the way in the back of the next room. This even happen when you transit from one part of the station to another. Like it has its own personal teleportation device, or maybe its just psychic?
The save system is just like the one found in say Dead Space. Though in Dead Space it actually worked without any issues. Here it seems to only serve the purpose of adding additional down time for more opportunities to get attacked and to interrupt your save. You can literally die before you manage to save, as there is no backing out of the save animation.
To save you need to find a save station, wait for the terminal to light up 3 lights, which takes around 5 seconds. And then you can hit the save button. It feels very archaic, and i get why some people are frustrated with it. Especially if they have lost 30 minutes of play time and have to backtrack. While in the meantime the Alien AI can completely hump you over again. I know that the game would lose difficulty if you could just quick save, but it's kind of appalling that you can get a cut scene and you would think that the game automatically would save your game after the cut scene ends. But it doesn’t. I’m actually still not sure when the game saves by it self.
This is a game you either love or loathe. I count myself as a big Alien fan, love the movies and i have watched them so many times. That doesn't mean that i have to give this game a pass though. It has flaws, and for me it has a lot of them.
On a positive note, the graphics are really awesome. They nailed the look of the movies, down to the smallest details. Sound design is for the most part really good aswell. There is a few minor things like not all voice actors are very good, and that the motion tracker is not using the iconic sound from the movies. But overall in the sound and graphics department its pretty damn solid. It is a bit of a shame though that really good set pieces only happen when you are over halfway through the game. There are some really striking locations near the end of the game.
I would only recommend this if you wouldn’t mind any of the negative things i have listed above and a few random deaths on top of that.
Self proclaimed Alien elitists will be happy with anything, i mean those people love Alien: Colonial Marines and find no faults with it. So if you are one of those go for it, nothing will change your view on it in the first place.
Bottom line for me, i regret buying it. And i regret writing all this nonsense.

So i just finished playing Alien Isolation's main story mode after 15 hours on medium difficulty. In this review i will cover some basics about the game, things i enjoyed, things that i didn't like so much, my final statement and a score out of 100.
So to start with, there are many aspects of this game that make it great, and these in my opinion outweigh the bad points completely. We've seen many game titles under the Alien and Predator franchises such as the action based AVP and the James Cameron take on Colonial Marines, where we had big guns, trained marine allies and a bad attitude. Alien Isolation however, attempts to re-install the original terror and fear we had of the Ridley Scott's monster. It does this by stripping you, the player, down to the extreme basics. You don't have any prior survival or combat training, you're simply just a human stuck on a very large broken spaceship with no way off.
The game is a survival horror, meaning you basically have to make the best of a very bad situation and do whatever it takes to survive. So let's talk about your options:
As Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, you are trained in mechanics to some extent, and you can use this to your advantage by picking up world items and combining them to create devices or medical supplies. You can create smoke bombs to escape sticky situations, noisemakers to distract enemies while you slip by unnoticed and EMP mines to deal with the on board crazy synthetic androids and many more. You will find guns as you progress through the story line, but you will quickly realize that they are only a final resort. Ammo is very scarce for anything other than the Flamethrower and they are almost entirely useless against the Alien and the tough Androids. They are however, suitable methods of dealing with the crazed population of humans quickly.
The Alien: The Alien is the star of this game, it's the big bad boss which you cannot fight, all you can do is hide from it and prey that it doesn't find you. You can use crafted devices to lure it out of your way, but if you choose to do this too often, the alien will wise up and stop playing ball. For example, you could throw a flare across the room, and the Alien would follow it and become mesmerized by it for a short while. The next flare you throw, the Alien may see it and already know what it is, so there is no need for it to examine it or walk over to it. The next time, you may find that the alien instead of looking at the flare, it turns and tries to find the source of where it came from, so if you don't move, then you're basically screwed.
Stealth and Sneaking: The game is largely based of sneaking around and hiding. In the world there are many places the player can choose to hide, such as lockers, under beds and under desks. These are all a temporary solution, because if the Alien catches a glimpse of you, or hears a noise in your area, it is going to stay around allot longer, giving you less time and opportunity to move away.
Pros:
The Fear: My favorite thing about this game, was the constant feel of dread. The Alien is progressively hunting Amanda throughout the game after a certain point, meaning you're never truly sure if you're safe or not. There are points in which the alien is scripted to appear, but it doesn't entirely keep to just scripted events. On your motion tracker, you occasionally see movement quickly dart over your head through the vents system. This is not a world ambiance mechanic at all, because if you make enough noise, no matter where you are, the Alien will appear to punish you. Death in this game from the Alien is 80% of the time instant. Once it's seen you, if you don't have a flame thrower, or some kind of explosive, then you are going to die straight away. Once it's got hold of you, you're dead.
The Clever AI: The Aliens AI is by far the most advanced artificial intelligence I've ever seen. It responds to sound, sight and maybe even possibly smell. However, it mainly works off sound. The Alien doesn't let up either, because if it hears you in a certain area, it will refuse to move away until it's caught you, leaving you with few choices such as: Duck, cover, crawl, progress or distracting it.
The Length: For a 60$ game, you would expect a double figure in the amount of playtime. For me it took 15 hours, for others I've heard it take upward of 20 hours. It all depends on how you play and the difficulty. I played through on medium because i suck at stealth games, but i did surprisingly well and made progress very fast as i refused to stick around in areas where the alien was.
Survival mode: This mode is great for scaring your friends. It throws you into a small area with a couple of missions to beat and a roaming Alien. There's also a timer, putting pressure on you to get the best time. You're given some basic supplies and craftables, and a Flamethrower with a few good shots. It's a great competitive mode to play with friends, and it is the first mode you should show to anyone new.
Cons:
The Story itself: While the length of the game in my opinion was perfect, it could have benefited from a better story line. Although another survival horror title "Dead Space 1" borrowed heavily off the concepts in the original film, this game felt like it then heavily borrowed off Dead Space's actual plot. You're an engineer, you get stranded on the ship, and then you're apparently the only person left out of hundreds of still alive people that have probably been on the station for years of their working life, that knows how to fix the station. And fixing the ship basically consists of walking to different areas, pulling leavers and pressing buttons. Is there seriously no one else who knows how to do this on the station?
Humans: Some of the humans on board the ship are friendly, and they will pose no threat to you at all. Some of them are scared, and will make you back off at all costs. Some are just plain stupid and will shoot at you at first sight. I didn't like this so much, as i was hoping human encounters would have been much more diverse and unscripted. You can however, hide nearby and listen to their conversations to gauge what kind of people they are, and whether you should approach or not. But the most common outcome is they just shoot on sight, which can be stressful. With most human encounters, it's better to usually just summon the alien through noise and let him deal with them. A nice touch was though that you can actually play the game without killing a single human. You can sneak past them, avoid them or just get the Alien to deal with them.
Overall, Alien Isolation has become one of my favorite games, I've already began replaying the story to see what else i can find, and I've also yet to play and finish both DLC's "Crew Expendable" and "Last survivor". While i think the Story itself is a bit of a let down, it makes up for it with it's insanely awesome gameplay mechanics. I didn't feel bored at any point of it.
I give Alien Isolation a 92/100. Great gameplay, great concept and execution, however, the story and human encounters are a let down.

Im a huge fan of the alien films (First 3 only) so this was a definite purchase for me and luckily, I wasnt disappointed.  The game looks wonderful and is really well optimised for PC.  I was getting over 200fps at 1080p with full graphical settings.  The anti-aliasing options are.... disappointing.  You will be better off forcing some proper AA through your graphics card driver because the ingame options leaved jagged edges everywhere.
The atmosphere is great.  The bumps, hisses, screeches and creaks that the Sevastopol makes, all sound similar enough to the Alien that you live in a constant state of fear and paranoia.  The music is lifted straight from the first film and sounds wonderful.  The lighting is dark enough to leave you wondering if that shape in the distance is a threat, or just an inanimate object, yet light enough for you to find your way around easily.  The shadows and light shafts thrown around the space station also look great as an added bonus.
The Alien is suitably terrifying, although not without its issues.  When its crawling through the air vents, hunting you out of sight, but constantly alerting you to its presence with the sound of its talons scraping against metal and sheet metal bulging under its weight.  The motion tracker adds to the terror, bleeping frantically as it senses the Alien rapidly closing on your location.  Its a different story when the Alien is out in the open though.  It stomps around the narrow corridoors of the Sevastopol, blocking your path and sniffing out your hiding spots.  When its out in the open, the Alien is more of an annoyance than an object of fear, certainly in the early stages of the game.  Later on when you have the tools to make the Alien retreat, this is less of an issue.
There are other threats to contend with as well.  Human survivors protecting their territory, or defending their supplies from looters.  Wonderfully, there are also some humans who dont know why people are dying and assume that there is a serial killer on the station and that you could be the threat.  Unfortunately you cant always tell if the humans you encounter are friendly or hostile until you are right on top of them, at which point they have shot you in the face.  You cant pre-emptively take them out either because killing a civilian is an automatic fail state.
The androids are also fantastically designed.  The look like crash test dummies with glowing red eyes and can be absolutely horrifying as they walk towards you in a darkened corridoor.  Unlike the humans, the androids have no ranged attack, and unlike the alien they lack the speed to close the distance should you run away.   They will try to overwhelm you through sheer numbers though and if they manage to corner you, a horrific bludgeoning and/or choking death awaits.
Overall I was really pleased with how this game turned out.  The pacing of the story can be a little bit strange at times, going from "abject terror" to "leisurely stroll down a hallway" with only a loading screen separating the two.  The content of the story is great though.  The story of the Sevastopol and Seegson is brilliantly realised and is, in many ways, the true star of the game.  Until you actually play the game, it can be difficult to believe that the space station and the company that runs it is the most compelling part of the game, but it really is.  I cared about Seegson and the people that worked for them far more than I cared about Amanda Ripley
Overall I found it well worth the purchase and a worthy addition to the Alien franchise.  Frankly, if Aliens: Colonial Marines is now part of the official Aliens canon, then this should be too.  Its the best Alien story Ive seen since the original 2 films.

In Ellipsis, you move a circle around to collect a series of 5 other circles while avoiding various obstacles. From that simple mechanic, the developers have done a good job of crafting over 100 engaging and varied levels. Some of the levels evoke other genres (stealth, puzzle, etc.) without deviating from the core mechanic and aesthetic.
For the most part, the levels are relatively easy to complete. But each level is timed and achieving the best possible score requires beating the level-specific par time. That additional challenge could add a few extra hours onto the 3.4 I put into simply beating ever level. A level creator just came out recently, so if the community puts in some work, there could be loads more content added on as well.

It's very hard to describe Ellipsis, but one pretty accurate way is "action puzzle game" - the game is about finding the optimal way around a small level so that you can collect all the objectives without running into an obstacle, but still quickly enough that you can reach the goal before time runs out. Each level takes just a few seconds to beat, but getting the highest ranking requires finding a solution where you spend no time idling or dodging, dashing through cascades of bullets and lasers with several enemies on your tail. Each time you fail, you know exactly why you failed, and through quick iterations of trial and error you figure out what works and what doesn't work on your way towards that elusive 5-star ranking. The game has several worlds with unique gimmicks, which keeps the game fresh throughout, and it comes with a level editor with Workshop support that promises an infinite supply of levels once you've gone through the well over 100 levels in the base game.
Ellipsis is also a very capable art game - there is no text at all in the game, and the way everything is explained by symbolism and actions is executed in a clear and consise way that makes you learn about a new mechanic in every level. Gorgeous particle and light effects, as well as adaptive music made from melodic sound effects caused by all your actions, lead to a game that is hypnotic to play.
Ellipsis is easy to pick up and play. It is also a game you'll easily lose an hour in without even realizing time has passed. If you're looking for an addictive timesink which you can pick up and play in just a couple of seconds whenever you have some time to kill, it's just the thing for you.

"A bit Osu-like, but with bullet hell instead of the rhythm. Something I'd give a to a relative who's new to computers and wants to practice mouse control, I guess."
...or would I?
I've been called out (by the developer himself, no less!) to be a bit more specific about my initial, lazy (10 minutes of playtime, no kidding) review. Is the game actually bad? Have I misjudged it? Is it just not for me? Nope, kind of, perhaps. Let's dig in.
I'd summarize the game as a mouse-only, bullet-hell-ish platformer. We traverse an Osmos-like galaxy of levels, completing each one for a 1-to-5 star rating, one that we typically see in mobile games. Each level requires a combination of mechanical prowess and a bit of a brain to solve a puzzle: mostly the former, sure, but it has its moments of giving a player a satisaction of find the best way out by clever timing or whatnot. Some levels frustrated me, some made me curse the designer, some made me giggle at the enemies or layouts – as they should. Each takes few minutes at most to complete, though I wouldn't say the devs chose quantity over quality: they don't seem lazy or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in any way, some are pretty great, and I'd say that all are pretty decent overall.
One thing that I didn't initially spot but really appreciated when I did is how good of a job the game does by leading you through the game without using a single word: even numbers are only there for the sake of stats and point-keeping. Throughout the galaxy of levels Ellipsis is really good job at relaying the rules out of the game and teaching you things empirically. There are a few mechanics that I still don't quite get (except "it's a field where the movement is wonky"), but all in all, huge props for visual design.
Overall, the game is quite simple mechanically but manages to get quite a bit out of it. It initially reminded me of Osu or those millions of Japanese rhythm games, mostly consisting of precise mechanical movements with music as a background (or "plot"), which were never really my kind of thing. Taking a second look revealed a neat puzzle platformer, which I think I may come back to when I'll feel like killing some time and chilling out a bit. I got it from the Humble Freedom Bundle: would I buy it if I didn't? Probably not. Am I glad to have it? I'd say so, yeah. Would I recommend it to others? Actually I would: it may not be my kind of game, but it's pretty solid overall, and does have some interesting and memorable elements. Give it a shot, it's not bad at all.
Thanks a lot Christopher for calling me out and making me try the game again :)

Pros:
- Huge open ended levels with multiple points of entry to nearly every building
- Fantastic voice acting

- Choices you make do leave an impact in the game
- Enemy AI is really good
- Mini city hubs before each main mission are a blast to go through, the ingame shops are a very nice touch too
- Very beautiful artwork and stunning visuals
- Clockwork soldiers are freakin' awesome from the voice work to the design of them. Very cool.
- The ability to play lethally or non-lethally and offering up very creative ways to get rid of a target.
Cons
- Performance issues, I have a high end rig but even ran into the occasional lagging points myself. I imagine on even a moderately built PC there to be performance issues too
- The story, I am keeping this spoiler free but lets just say the chances are quite high that you will enjoy the little stories told as you go along rather than the main over arching story.
- Bugs bugs bugs! If you're trying to go for a shadow achievement or a no kill achievement be careful where you rest bodies and be sure to regulary check the menu that the game hasn't accidentally ticked you off for something you weren't aware of. Very frustrating
- The game really tends to teach you that killing is bad, I feel that it really caters towards the non-lethal stealth approach but of course you can be a killer too.
Overall
I recommend this game as it is a big improvement over the first Dishonored, the feeling I walked away with was that I got to enjoy a good experience and remember more of the side missions and explorative parts then I did the main storyline.
This game gets compared to Thief a lot however I don't think that's accurate as this game really focuses on assassinating targets (either lethally or non-lethally) and you play as a bold and almost heroic player, saving this person or seeking revenge on that person whereas Thief was more about stealing valueable items to pay rent, score a favor with a fence or to keep some faction off your back and most importantly trying to stay out of the spotlight. Garrett and Corvo are very different characters, both enjoyable in their own way but I wouldn't call the games these characters are from all that similar just because D2 has Stephen Russell and you can stealth.

Dark Souls 2 follows the same as Dark Souls 1. It tries to tell you it's a hard game that will test the most hardcore of players. This is not the case with either of these, but this is about 2, not 1. I'll do the best to explain the issues with the game.
Pve issues: This game, just as before, has horrible hit detection problems. Adding in the additional ability for the AI to instantly turn towards your character both comes off as lazy and cheap. Why not just make more wide range of moves instead of using such methods? Guess you needed to use that time to ignore good ideas in the beta to cancel that out. Clipping is once again a issue, but the enemies are not put into positions that exploit it, which I commend in this case, but still gets in the way a majority of times, such as the dragons. Invisible walls still exist to either prevent lockon or block arrows. Lock on is still awful, even when turned off the lock on will still do whatever it wants when something dies and when activated if there's more then 1 enemy the game usually (90%) will go for the one a million miles away from you. Camera is still god awful in close quarters, either causing you to be completely blinded or going at a slow crawl while you try to force it into position. The Durability is complete failure due to the aspect of hitting a dead body, which causes massive damage to your weapon. This is an issue due to many weapons having multiple hits or the drastic differences in damage and animations of said weapon.
Complete Imbalance in spells/weapon types: This game has a really nasty habit of making certain things unviable in this game, which was a strong point for Dark Souls 1.
Lets start with Sorcery first. If you choose to do such a thing as sorcery, good luck to you. Even with full knowledge of the game, all the spells and items you can run into are pretty much garbage until near the end of the game. You'll pretty much be casting really weak spells of the same varient multiple times. I'd consider the spells at the end of this game kinda like Skyrims, you think they're cool, then you try them and it's just disappointing. You'll pretty much be using the same spells you've been using since the beginning, beyond maybe having a few extra soul spears. Also, most enemies are naturally resistant to magic who matter. The reason it's an issue is hex spells exist. All you gotta do is kill one boss and you'll be able to get an awesome item for hex casting and youll get alot of the awesome spells. It has a soul cost? I'd hope so for something that casts as fast as a Soul arrow but does 3 times as much damage. And thats the weak one. The biggest issues would probably be the low damage output of sorcery spells, even with a Crystal Soul Spear youll only be doing like 1k at best on a player and maybe around that to an enemy with the best gear for sorcery, which is at the end of the game >.> This game has a nasty habit of doing that with pretty much everything. They cast extremely slow as well even with full increase to spell cast. You could be doing a hex spell that could one shot about twice as fast with the same setup. This one is a huge issue considering they were going to fix this in their beta test. Being able to manual aim. Instead you have two block buttons when you 2 hand it and have to use binoculars. What's wrong with that? if you lose all of your stamina the game freaks out about it and wastes your spell, throwing it no where from where you were looking. The bow doesn't have this issue, crossbow doesn't so wth.
Next unbalanced for Pve, pretty much anything that doesn't state it goes through armor or doesn't do strike damage:
The mace and rapier are kings of this game, being able to easily topple everything. The game stuffs armored enemies for like 80% of the game, which is a huge issue since pretty much all armor in the game goes Slash/Thrust/Strike where strike has the lowest defense position at anytime. Why is there no diverisity here, it just makes doing any other weapon a pain in comparison for no real reason. Axes don't do anything significantly special and have lower poise break plus leave you open longer and all of the good axes are at the end of the game. They also pretty much have the really ineffective duel stance of maces, which is pretty bad. Swords can be ok in this regard with a wider swing but lack actual damage or poise break. Maces on the other hand as far as finding decent ones is extremely quick, hell, all you have to do is get past the tutorial to get a good one or just start with it. If ya don't do that you can just buy an awesome one, or find the giant club versions early on after fighting 3 bosses or going down a the well, but that's more if ya know where that one is. Whips are really bad, for one particular reason. It's fineish in pvp, but the reason that is dumb is if you use the advantage of the whip, it cuts the damage about 33%. Unless you are right in someone's face with it, it will not do full damage. Kinda defeats the purpose for something that is hindered by characters wearing armor. Pretty much all weapons go into this kinda thing, they just lack general damage in comparison and don't stand out to be used by someone wanting to use them in a purposeful manner. They just turn into challenge runs with those items, and no wonder, since they're so pathetic in comparison.
Covenants: There's only a few issues here. Lets start with the Rat Covenant: These are the only two issues this has. The time restraint needs to be cut down, I've had to seriously wait 5-10 min for someone to invade me, and the second is this. If I don't try to bumrush my target in any area, they can crystal out, then I have to wait to be invaded again. You're taking the risk by being in this covenant by being able to die, don't put unnecessary punishment that isn't needed. Either remove the ability to just leave for the invader or reduce the timer to like a min. It completely defeats the purpose of the entire area if they don't even have to attempt to go through it.
Blood Covenant: This one is just a mess, primarally on ranking part. So invades cost a million dollars and can only be done on ng+ if you dont wanna farm them off enemies, ok. So do they count towards the ranking? No. Fine, I got this duel marker, seems good, put it down, you win. Does it count? No. Well the basic premise doesn't work, so what does? Well, in a covenant that is known for bloodletting, only duels count, and there's a +/- system involved where if you lose you get -1 point. Well, for such a odd system that has a penalty to it, the ranks for wins can't be too high right? 500 wins :P gud luck. If for some reason this isn't the case, well, then the game has a bug that doesn't allow this covenant to work properly then, which is about a 100 times worse.
Online/Pvp: Coop in this game seems pretty good. Some times has some lag to it, but was rare. Pvp on the other hand. Due to the Peer to Peer, you're pretty much at the mercy of latency. Possible exciting combat turns into people swinging at ghosts that completely ruins the experience. Just an overall bad system to use, expecially when you force people to pvp in your game. This is a huge negative due to this. Go offline? Use some of that money and get a real service so this doesn't happen. No one should have to get top of the line, most expensive service, so they can get to play only your game in a reliable manner. Also, just remove poise. You didn't put the effort to make it work, so why have it.
Last thing I can think of is just scaling. Reason I bring this up is I've done a whip only run and noticed it there. I had a B rating on a Whip +7 and a A on a Whip +10. 30 dex to duel wield the old whip if I wanted to. Both give +61 damage. Why have letter scaling? This game could have been so much more, but they just didn't put in the effort. If the company cares about improvements, they'll pay attention to these and try to improve.

Score: 4/10
Not Recommended.
[Opinions follow]
This review is for my friends who might consider spending money to purchase this game. Especially since Black Mesa is in a Beta state I recommend NOT making this purchase unless certain circumstances apply.
Those circumstances would be: 1. You are a big Half-Life 1 fan and want to play the game in an updated form. 2. You want to play a modern looking shooter with old school mechanics and level design.
What is it?: Half-Life 1 remake with modern graphics and sound. The story is you are scientist who must escape a top-secret research facility where a catastrophe has occurred and is now being invaded by inter-dimensional aliens and counter attacked by the military. The finale is a showdown with a powerful alien entity in its own dimension. This is a puzzle and combat based first-person shooter (FPS). Your character “Gordon Freeman” never speaks and you never see a reflection of the character.
Pros: Technically flawless art and model design throughout the entire available game. Great sound design and implementation. Runs smoothly on my system. No noticed bugs. Some variety of game levels. Great atmosphere for the most part. If you are into this design style of games this game combines shooting (run & gun, duck and cover) with FPS first-person puzzle game play (some implementation of the physics engine to solve puzzles).
Cons:
If you like shooters the puzzles will frustrate you or just slow you down. If you like puzzles the combat bits will frustrate you or slow you down. The puzzles and levels in this game all read like they were designed by programmers instead of story-writers or level designers. The issue is that the levels only have one solution or one path to get through them. There are other locked doors or seemingly moveable objects or seemingly climbable exterior surfaces to which you are denied access. This game would be more fun as an open world sand-box game. As it is the level design seems uneven. Game design and my expectations have changed a lot since Half-Life 1 was released. This game doesn’t hold up past one or two play-throughs for me. There are too many map specific triggers for me. That means that events in the map won’t progress or let me progress until certain conditions are met. The maps and levels of this game are too linear. There are many cool ideas that seem underutilized. The shooter sections are too short and the puzzles too long. It plays like a designer trying to show off how smart they are by the specificity or complexity of the puzzles rather than level design with fun or empowerment in mind. This could be seen as a narrative tool but the narrative is too shallow overall to justify that. Generally the whole thing is too linear. I would get the same enjoyment out of watching the YouTube play-through videos. There are long stretches of silence which don’t really build any anticipation for me but just seem empty and boring. There is an uneven pace between long empty abandoned sections and the fast paced crowed shooter sections. On most of the YouTube walk-throughs I’ve seen players wander around in a maze of rooms or the available space bumping into walls until they find the unlocked door or hidden passage or the trigger to allow them to move on to the next map or section. Players who have been through the game and are familiar with maps and puzzles breeze through it in an almost intuitive fashion. The puzzles are not intuitive though because if you see an object on the ground that logically could be used to solve the puzzle odds are it isn’t interactive. I got stuck in the section of the original Half-Life because I put myself in the role of the protagonist and didn’t know that jumping the span of an open elevator shaft was the solution to move on to the next section. Thinking as the character in the game isn’t rewarded. Instead there are contrived puzzles without evident solutions that are unintuitive. I’m sure many other gamers would have no problem with any of the puzzles and that is fine. If you are like me though you will go into this expecting fully interactive environments and finding that the opposite is the case.  In the levels of the game where I was in an outdoor canyon I just wanted to climb the cliff or float down the river and find my own way to civilization as a solution. There were many interior sections where I wanted to blast or pry open a hanger door and walk away.
Instead of a faithful remake this game deserves a new version using modern level design and more intuitive open world game play with more choices of solving the puzzles or avoiding them altogether. I wish I could be offered the option to take one path and shoot my way out or another and avoid the shooting through logic and puzzle solving with multiple branches for either path. One day that Half-Life game might be made but for now I can enjoy this limited execution of a grand concept and story or avoid it altogether. Half-Life could learn a lot from “The Stanley Parable” and perhaps the converse is true as well.
My recommendation is that if you like FPS puzzle games then play “Portal 2” and if you like single-player shooter games play “Borderlands 2” or something from the “Far Cry” series or something from the “Unreal Tournament” series or any military shooter.
I will play through this and re-review the game once it is released in its finished state.
