To anyone interested, Dark Souls II is a game that I would recommend for anyone to try. I recommend this installment far more widely than I would any of its predecessors simply because it is much easier to get into. Fans of the Souls games, such as myself, picked this game up in a heartbeat for more of what we love from the Souls series, but that is not all we got. Changes in the gameplay, direction and ease of play has made this game fantastic for newcomers to this series. If you've been tempted by Dark Souls or Demon's Souls before, but hesitated because of its tough-as-nails and unforgiving gameplay, you will be pleased to know that this installment is the perfect place to start. It's not any easier, oh no, but you will certainly find yourself enjoying what From Software has to offer easier and quicker than their previous games.
It is, of course, important to note that this game is certainly not all about how hard it is. It is no walk in the park, certainly, but it is also one of the most precise, skill-based action-rpg's that exists. With a multitude of weapons and spells, you may find yourself playing through entirely different experiences than your fellow undead. You have your pick of 25 different, unique weapon types, 3 types of shield, 4 classes of spells with over 20 spells for each class; your playthrough will be unique to your preference. Do you want to be an agile rogue, adept at the dark magic of hexes? What about a hulking, heavily armored paladin, verse in sacred miracles? Well, you can, and much, much more!
If the combat isn't enough for you, you can immerse yourself in the breathtaking vistas of Drangleic. The best part of 'Absent' is the puzzles. Some solutions are hinted at while conversing with other characters and interacting with objects, but they are never fully revealed. This provides just enough direction to keep the gameplay from becoming stagnant, while still demanding you use your brain. The art is all original, which is pretty cool as well.
But. I couldn't get into the cartoony graphics or silly dialogue. I found myself hurriedly reading and clicking through scenes and dialogue; not experiencing or enjoying it. It's a shame because the voice acting was great. I also felt a little lost when it comes to the story, especially towards the end. I get what happened... but why? Things feel unresolved.

Also, as it's a point-and-click game with the good old mechanics of the cursor cycling through the actions, you may have an hard time by moments. I remember that for one achievement, you had to click on the door of the teacher's room. You think that the discussion will let you an option to show something. In reality, you have to use the item first, else, well, no cheevos for you. Also, don't forget to speak with everyone so that you can learn more about the school, the students, the town or to simply find the solution to go forwards.
Absent has also correct graphics: it has a nice retro touch. You're not staying in the school during all the game, but you visit the town, forests and even another world. The soundtrack is correct too.
For a free game, I must say that it's doing great. The game isn't short at all, can provide a good challenge, though sometimes, you wish that the clues were more obvious and the achievements aren't too hard. However, keep in mind that maybe, the game isn't for you if you're not into adventure gaming. It's not the best way to get to know the genre, especially with these mechanics, for that, you have better series like Blackwell or A Golden Wake or even other free gems that aren't on Steam.
Anyway, it will not hurt you to install it.

In our daily lives, we are rather vexed by everything around us, given that reality is always stressful, but every time I open up this game, I am met with a wonderfully calming and even therapeutic experience. I got this game thanks to my older sister's Steam Sharing, but then I was somehow separated from that. Later on, I had decided to buy it myself, and it is well worth the price.
This game is about the happy ranching life of Beatrix LeBeau, who now lives on a faraway planet full of these adorable slimes with happy faces. They bounce around without a care in the world and your job is to take them in and feed them in order to produce plorts, which apparently, according to the SlimePedia, are wonderful for any purpose one could think of, usually depending on the type of slime there is. Then you sell these plorts on the market to make money, which you can use to expand your ranch or get upgrades for your equipment and such.
Slimes come in a variety of types, with their own defining color and special little quirk that makes them special. And aside from the common pink slime, each slime has their own diet and favorite food in the fruits, veggies, and meats category, so on your ranch, you can also cultivate crops, fruit trees, and chickens in their own coops while your slimes stay in a corral.
If a slime eats a plort of another type of slime, they become a largo combination of the two, eating foods from both slimes' diets and producing plorts from both types as well, but be careful not to let slimes eat other slime types' plorts too much, or else they will become a corrupt Tarr, which will attack you and eat other slimes to reproduce.
As you explore the Far Far Range, you'll unlock new areas and find neat new things, like new slime types or some beautiful scenery. Monomi Park, the developer of the game, does a very good job of making all this scenery wonderful, even while it's in Early Access, and the huge world is simply something you will love to get lost in time and time again.
I highly suggest this game for any occasion really, whether you need to relax a little after work, calm down after some stressful event, or simply to enjoy looking at the beautiful world of slimes while hanging out with these cheery little guys that always have a smiling face! It is always a good way to wind down, especially with the great soundtrack that plays throughout the world.
If you're looking for a lovely, calming, and interesting adventure, this is definitely the game for you. <3

Warning, these are my personal opinions on the game. And in this case they are very negative opinions. If you read this and love the game, keep loving the game. I do not hold that against you. It is an Alien game most will love.
I had high hopes for it, and maybe thats why im left here with more negative things to say about it than i have positive.
The beginning of the game is very slow, the first hour is basically a slow build up learning you the controls and the mechanics of the game, of which there aren’t very many. The control mappings are fine on both keyboard and controller. However the feel of motion is sluggish, sort of like you are moving through molasses, even your run feels kind of awkward and too slow.
You will be represented with a space station to walk around, where you will carry out many tedious tasks. Which often revolve around the same things, like powering up sub-systems, finding a keycard, finding a new tool that will let you open a new set of doors, and a ton of backtracking. In Between those segments, you pretty much play a hide and seek game, combined with a walking simulator.
You will come across other humans in that time, but it usually always ends in a gunfight if they spot you. As it seems no one are interested in working together or just letting you walk by with no hassle. You do have the option to bypass or let the Alien sort them out.
Then there are the androids, which are equally as hostile and are best bypassed altogether if possible, as it takes a metric snot ton of bullets to take them out. And don't even try to wrench them they will grab you each time, unless you manage to sneak up on them and get some good shots in. Again androids best avoided.
And finally there is the Alien(s), the center piece or at least it should have been.  I thought it would have a big impact on the game. I was kind of wrong about that one. It doesn't really add any tension to the game, at least it didn’t for me. Maybe because it showed up so much, seeing it over and over makes you accustomed to it and unafraid of it. Plus you will know what to expect and what to do each time.
It really added an annoyance in the fact that it would make me have to wait to carry out my mission to an extent it actually added a comical value too, the AI on it is kind of stupid. Sometimes it would actually see me, but it will be stuck in its hide in vent animation, and wouldn’t be able to break that cycle.
Then there is the issue of even though you will be crouching most of this game, the Alien oddly have the ability to just keep on you at all times, even though you left it in another room like 2 meters back, it will and can emerge just as you enter a new room like all the way in the back of the next room. This even happen when you transit from one part of the station to another. Like it has its own personal teleportation device, or maybe its just psychic?
The save system is just like the one found in say Dead Space. Though in Dead Space it actually worked without any issues. Here it seems to only serve the purpose of adding additional down time for more opportunities to get attacked and to interrupt your save. You can literally die before you manage to save, as there is no backing out of the save animation.
To save you need to find a save station, wait for the terminal to light up 3 lights, which takes around 5 seconds. And then you can hit the save button. It feels very archaic, and i get why some people are frustrated with it. Especially if they have lost 30 minutes of play time and have to backtrack. While in the meantime the Alien AI can completely hump you over again. I know that the game would lose difficulty if you could just quick save, but it's kind of appalling that you can get a cut scene and you would think that the game automatically would save your game after the cut scene ends. But it doesn’t. I’m actually still not sure when the game saves by it self.
This is a game you either love or loathe. I count myself as a big Alien fan, love the movies and i have watched them so many times. That doesn't mean that i have to give this game a pass though. It has flaws, and for me it has a lot of them.
On a positive note, the graphics are really awesome. They nailed the look of the movies, down to the smallest details. Sound design is for the most part really good aswell. There is a few minor things like not all voice actors are very good, and that the motion tracker is not using the iconic sound from the movies. But overall in the sound and graphics department its pretty damn solid. It is a bit of a shame though that really good set pieces only happen when you are over halfway through the game. There are some really striking locations near the end of the game.
I would only recommend this if you wouldn’t mind any of the negative things i have listed above and a few random deaths on top of that.
Self proclaimed Alien elitists will be happy with anything, i mean those people love Alien: Colonial Marines and find no faults with it. So if you are one of those go for it, nothing will change your view on it in the first place.
Bottom line for me, i regret buying it. And i regret writing all this nonsense.

The Elder Scrolls Online is a surprisingly great game filled past the brim with grade A quests, characters, mechanics and more. The game constsntly makes me smile and I play it almost every day. This game has done a lot of things right and has even done a lot of things better than Skyrim. Here are the pros and cons of the game,
--PROS
-Massive game world full of adventure and culture
-Meaningful and mostly exciting quests
-Hundreds of memorable characters
-Simple yet powerful character creation
-Detailed crafting systems involivng styles, levelled crafting, traits, etc . . .
-Engaging combat consisting of a combination of skyrim's "Hack n' Slash" combat, WoW's hotbar ability styled combat, and a little bit of rolling to dodge attacks
-Massive player made guilds with banks, guild merchants, and more
-Player based economy for trading and guild merchants
-Intelligent AI that can detect when they are outnumbered, cooperate with other NPCs, etc . . .
-Skyrim style skill-based levelling
-Armor dyes that can be gained as rewards for completing achievements
-Intricate PvP based in Cyrodil with forts, seige weapons, missions, etc . . .
-Players can become the Emperor based on the war in Cyrodil
-Free-form classes that can use any kind of weapon or armor (For example, a sorcerer using a battleaxe)
-The world basically levels with you, as to alleviate the ned for grinding
-Hundreds of lore books scattered throughout the world to be added to your "Lore Library"
-Great dungeons filled with powerful enemies and unique loot
-Many teamwork based possabilities in the form of "synergies"
-Great voice acting
-Player emotes and animations
-Mounts and pets
-Dynamic weather and time cycle
-Decent graphics
-Polished UI and menus
-Hours upon hours of content including lots of late-game content
-Incredible framerate (compared to Skyrim)
-World events like "Daedric Anchors"
-One of the best final boss battles in modern video games
-A "phasing"  system that changes certain areas of the world for certain players after they do certain quests in those areas to provide the feeling that you are actually making a difference
-Epic backround music along with bards that play their own songs
-Continous flow of new content and patches
-"Crown Store" filled with asthetic and conveniance items (Nothing overpowered)
--CONS
-Slightly buggy (mostly hilarious visual bugs)
-Short "MMO Style" agro ranges for enemies (Kinda needed in most areas)
-Very few mounts and pets you can get normally in game
-No way to easily communicate during combat
-Player-made guilds are account-based, not character-based
-People can easily (and accidentally) steal your kills, and in doing so, steal your loot and experience
-People aren't honorable in PvP, causing the fun and challenging character builds to be useless, stupid, and suicidal in PvP. Prepare for a painful amount of ganking in Cyrodil.
-Lack of sweetrolls (Couldn't think of anything else)
--Things that I would like to see (MY OPINION)
-1v1 dueling between members of the same faction (They added it!)
-Player housing where players can either purchase upgrades or build it themselves (possibly using racial styles?) (They added it!)
-The ability to lock your guild to certain factions (For example, a guild is locked to the Ebonheart Pact, so a charcter in the Aldmeri Dominion doesn't have access to that guild)
-More mounts and pets that can be aquired normally through questing
-The function to go through a certain instance ALONE
-Some sort of "Voice to Text" system
-More sweetrolls (MORE OF THEM)
This game is great, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone. It's completely worth the sixty dollors its normally on sale for.

This is a fun game on two levels- both the game play itself, and in trying to figure out what to do or how to play. As you go, you figure out more about how it works, and it gets more fun. It reminds me of Myst in this way. In the game you collect various "points" while trying to avoid the bad guys that kill on contact. Quick reflexes with your mouse or finger on a touchscreen device are needed. Game physics is used for collisions, which enhances the feeling that you are manipulating real objects (and makes the "bull in a china shop" approach to just crash around in the game not very effective; it requires some finesse). There are lots of levels of increasing difficulty to work through, and a level editor to make your own. The graphics are nice, simple geometric figures in neon colors on a black background. I sometimes even let myself get "killed" because the resulting explosion of color is fun to watch!
It's a sign of good game design when the game doesn't need a single line of text to explain itself. It even conveys a story wordlessly as well.

Pros:
- Huge open ended levels with multiple points of entry to nearly every building
- Fantastic voice acting
- Very immersive, makes you really feel like you're apart of the world through readables and witty quips
- Choices you make do leave an impact in the game
- Enemy AI is really good
- Mini city hubs before each main mission are a blast to go through, the ingame shops are a very nice touch too
- Very beautiful artwork and stunning visuals
- Clockwork soldiers are freakin' awesome from the voice work to the design of them. Very cool.
- The ability to play lethally or non-lethally and offering up very creative ways to get rid of a target.
Cons
- Performance issues, I have a high end rig but even ran into the occasional lagging points myself. I imagine on even a moderately built PC there to be performance issues too
- The story, I am keeping this spoiler free but lets just say the chances are quite high that you will enjoy the little stories told as you go along rather than the main over arching story.
- Bugs bugs bugs! If you're trying to go for a shadow achievement or a no kill achievement be careful where you rest bodies and be sure to regulary check the menu that the game hasn't accidentally ticked you off for something you weren't aware of. Very frustrating
- The game really tends to teach you that killing is bad, I feel that it really caters towards the non-lethal stealth approach but of course you can be a killer too.
Overall
I recommend this game as it is a big improvement over the first Dishonored, the feeling I walked away with was that I got to enjoy a good experience and remember more of the side missions and explorative parts then I did the main storyline.
This game gets compared to Thief a lot however I don't think that's accurate as this game really focuses on assassinating targets (either lethally or non-lethally) and you play as a bold and almost heroic player, saving this person or seeking revenge on that person whereas Thief was more about stealing valueable items to pay rent, score a favor with a fence or to keep some faction off your back and most importantly trying to stay out of the spotlight. Garrett and Corvo are very different characters, both enjoyable in their own way but I wouldn't call the games these characters are from all that similar just because D2 has Stephen Russell and you can stealth.

Heres what i think. It all adds up to a game that's utterly lacking in urgency or momentum. Yes, the woefully inefficient pace of Rome II after every single turn is the biggest culprit. But there aren't enough fair battles to break up the normal pacing, and those that happen aren't compelling. Developing provinces and economics feels more like tossing a dart at a board than counting down the turns until your shiny new building. The enemy artificial intelligence is practically pacifist, which is extremely odd for a game called “Total War.” Perhaps what's most dismaying about Total War: Rome II is that it doesn't seem salvageable—its problems are as much conceptual as they are pragmatic. I can't imagine a patch or expansion with a smaller map, even though that would be the biggest possible help the game could get. In most grand strategy games, the motivation to play “just one more turn” is the most appealing part. In Total War: Rome II, “just one more turn” is a threat.

Absent recounts the events surrounding a small college town when a mysterious disappearance throws several students into a conflict that's much more than it initially seems. It delivers much more of a game than I expected for free, but isn't without some minor problems.
On the plus side, the game area is fairly compact, the voice acting is pleasant, and the story is compact and coherent, if a bit deus-ex-machina-laden toward the end. The animation style may be a bit off-putting at first, but it has enough charm that it grew on me before the game was over, and I appreciate the dedication put into animating everything by hand. There were only a few puzzles I had any real difficulty with, and most of those were in the last phase of the game. Absolutely EPIC. From start to finish this game is a wild ride, especially for an avid Ridley Scott fan. The games enviroments match the film to such a degree that I doubt a single bolt, or rivet is out of place.
Sound design is some of the best I've seen in my many years of gaming. Subtle noises like the ventilation fans, or computers chirring away. To our friendly neighborhood Xenomorph clanging in the crawlspaces. I've found myelf more than once just taking pause for a moment to enjoy the sounds of each different area of the game. The high tech medical facilities to the deep underbelly of Sevastapol's Engineering sections. Good sound design can make or break a game like this. Creative Assembly frickin' nailed it.
The AI is brutally unforgiving on the hardest difficulty setting. Human enemies react to the slightest sound, spot you across the room when just peeking over a crate,  Patroling randomly while searching for you making it a hair pulling experience in some areas.
Speaking of hair pulling... The Xenomorph is ruthless and terrifying! The sound of it dropping from a vent anywhere near you is enough to make you dash for the nearest hole to hide in until it leaves the area. Anything from sprinting to a accidently knocking somethign over can ruin your day.
A fantastic story breathing new life into our beloved world of Alien. One that was suprisingly long and more challenging as it progresses.

Alien Isolation is the best Alien game since 2001's AVP2, and is arguably better. This is the first time I've really enjoyed a survival game.
If there's only one word to describe it, it would be Atmosphere. The game's atmosphere comes at you right when you launch the game, as the intro movies play. It even builds tension at the main menu. When you begin the story, it immediately presents you with the feel of the Alien movies, with detailed level design, sounds, and quality lighting making you feel involved. Playing as Ripley's daughter, you have to think your way out of trouble, because you're not a machinegun-weilding Colonial Marine, you're just a regular person. With some tech skills, you can push the odds of survival in your favor via wall consoles, buildable items, and stealth. The 1970's retro-future tech environment fits very well, is a nod to the movies, and is one of my favorite features. If you like Science Fiction, you'll see they've done an excellent job here.
The game starts out strong, and makes you feel the tension as Ripley would experience it. As it progesses it gets better and better, by introducing new mechanics, environments, and enemies. It is not predictable, and will suprise. Some tips: don't run, keep aware of your surroundings, look for ways to make the situation easier, conserve ammo, and save often.
Have a good time in Sevastopol.

After SEGA purchasing the rights to make games based off of Alien back in 2006 it has been quite a rocky start for them. There was 2010's adaptation of AVP which was supposed to be an appetizer for Gearbox's Aliens Colonial Marines...but we all knew how that one turned out last year. I thought I lost hope with Alien games after that disaster because I was just convinced a good quality Alien game couldn't happen..but now we got this. After investing 20 hours into the first playthrough I am more then convinced that yes a good Alien game can be made. I'm actually very surprised how this game turned out.
From the amazing graphics to the awesome lighting effects  and the "1970's vision of the future" feel this game has left me more then convinced I was playing a sequel to 1979's Alien. Now we all know graphics don't really make a game which is why Creative Assembly created great AI for the xenomorph as well as a good sound engine. After a good 45 or so minutes into the game you're treated to an alien that can't be killed in any shape or form and is pretty much unpredictable. Depending how you go through the sections of the station it can simply roam the air ducts above you waiting for an opportunity to descend and go on it's hunt.
When it does hunt you it relies on sight,sound and smell. For example if you accidentally leave a door or air lock open that wasn't opened before it will look for who did so. You can build devices like sound makers to throw it off your scent, but do it too much it will catch on and know you're playing it.The sound engine the developers created helped bring that tension even more. If you're hiding and the xeno approaches you, the engine will recognize that and suspenseful music will play in the background as it tries hunting you down. It's very neat because it really does bring the tension.
You get weapons throughout the game that can assist in your encounters with the threats aboard the station like a pistol,shotgun and even a flamethrower just to name a few, but only thing that can affect the alien is either a flamethrower or molotov cocktail.Using either on it can make it retreat, just buying you seconds before it resumes it's hunt again to try and kill you.
I could go on about how awesome this game is, but I should just say that please do yourself the favor and download this game. If you're an Alien fan like me or appreciate a good science fiction/horror game with a rather good story then look no further because this is THE Alien experience by far.

I've played this game 3.6 hours.  I've beaten every level though I still have to perfect about half of them.
So clearly I enjoyed this game.  When a game says "minmalist" I prepare myself because most developers don't understand minimalism.  However Ellipsis seems to get minimalism right.  Almost every enemy is a relatively primitive form.  There's only a few graphical tricks in the game, and while there's a car or two, everything is pretty reduced.   Is it true minimalism?  probably not, but it's a good effort.
The entire game play loop is avoid the red, touch the blue (especially the five circles) and survive, and pretty much from the first level of the game to the last, that's the rules.  There's quite a few VERY interesting mechanics in the game, there's a lot of variety in the levels, though some concepts might go stay for one level longer than they could, overall it's a solid game.
The entire game also has a gorgeous map.  Every time you beat a level a new level is added.  There's about 100 levels I think (maybe give or take a few) and there is eventually multiple paths.  However the player is free to explore the levels as he wants with the exception of the final level which requires four specific levels to be completed, around it).   When you zoom out though the map is beautiful and each level is surrounded by imagery that reminds you of the features of that level for the most part.
Honestly this game is EXTREMELY well done.  The only question I'd have is the price.  I'd recommend the game, but 10 bucks is hefty.  However I really enjoyed the game and I'm sure we'll see some price drop over time if 10 bucks isn't the right price for you.
It was recently in the Humble Bundle Freedom pack which is where I bought it, and while that meant I paid around 1 dollar for it (less as the bundle grew). Though its Early Access price might seem a little steep, Black Mesa offers some pretty great value: you've got the near-complete Half-Life experience, minus Xen levels to be added at a later date (as they're being significantly redesigned and improved from their lackluster 1998 incarnation), which is a solid 10+ hours. As Early Access adds new features to the game, expect to give it a few more playthroughs along the way (also, try to get the hidden hat achievement). Then you've also got the multiplayer, which is a great and very well constructed throwback to classic 1990s deathmatch. It's a lot of fun and though the map selection right now isn't too good, more levels are on the way.
As for the singleplayer: well, you've got a remake/reimagining of one of the greatest and most innovative games ever made. For one, it looks, feels and for all intents and purposes, plays better than the original, which sometimes suffered from issues inherent to games made in the late 90s. You've got a few clever surprises on the way that subvert player expectations in really cool ways, although they're few and far between. Overall, the story has been improved and in some ways expanded, a lot of new dialogue has been added, the environmental "mise en scene" storytelling has been conserved if not improved. In a lot of respects it's simply a better experience - with all the amenities, details and mechanics of HL2 but the satisfying difficulty, diversity, setting, atmosphere and engagement of HL1.
However, significant parts of the game have been removed almost brutally, without any attempts at improving or streamlining them (the We've Got Hostiles vent crawl, almost half of On A Rail and a good third of Surface Tension). It just doesn't add anything to the experience and it stands out like a sore thumb on an experience that is otherwise light-years beyond anything AAA-supported studios put together these days (that includes Valve until they finally get around to making another singleplayer game).

Now that the Early Access release of it is here - I'm glad to say they are pretty damn close to it. Originally picking up the free release back in 2012, I was certainly impressed - grinning from ear to ear like a moron from I started playing, until it was over. But while the graphics were nothing short of spectacular (and are even more so in the Steam release), there were a few things that irked me about it;
The gunplay was quite a ways short of satisfactory - the MP5 was essentially useless, among other things, and the AI had the odd moment of spectacular stupidity at certain points as well. Not to mention that parts of certain maps just aren't up to par (Xen, On a Rail, I'm looking at you.)
I am happy to report, that for the most part, my issues with the 2012 release has been resolved. The gunplay has improved tremendously, to the point where the weapons have the most satisfying feeling I've seen in a game for years, only the weaponry of Wolfenstein: The New Order comes close to feeling as good. They have even greatly improved the MP5, making it a viable medium-long range weapon - something the entire Half-Life franchise has been lacking completely ever since 1998. The Glock 17 could stand to have it's rate of fire increased slightly, but other than that I genuinely find little more to be desired.
As for the AI, it has improved immensely since the 2012 release, and I'm fairly confident in claiming it's the best AI we've seen in anything attached to the Half-Life universe yet. That said - I did have a few encounters during the course of the game where certain NPCs' AI simply failed to initialize until after they were attacked - that goes in the bug category though, and is certainly not a design choice reflecting upon the future finished product.
Some people have also been quite vocal about their dislike of the change to the Vortigaunt's attack speed - I myself, on the other hand find it quite refreshing. You still have enough time to get out of the way of their attacks, but it requires more of you, and as such makes it feel much more rewarding when you manage to take out a pack of them without getting hit.
On the subject of level design, I genuinely can't think of a missing piece of the (currently released) maps that I feel are missing, even though I fully know where they were in the original game. There are also quite a few interesting additions made to the level design of the game - most just for flavor and realism - but some of them are actually completely new routes through which to traverse parts of the levels, which is refreshing for someone like me who has played through the original game several dozen times by now, and know Black Mesa like my own house. The long and short of the level design is plainly speaking that anything they took out genuinely isn't missed, and anything they added either makes no impact to the flow of the game, or are genuine improvements upon the original.
I can't wait to see what these people have in store for us with the eventual release of their reenvisioned Xen borderworld - but even as it stands now without Xen, this game is a complete self-contained gameplay experience on it's own.
With regards to general bugs (aside from the aforementioned AI initialization issue), I am quite frankly astounded with regards to how well polished both the 2012- and the Steam release are. These guys are putting Triple-A developers and publishers to shame, and do so on a volunteer part-time basis. I only encountered one bug that was so jarring that it stuck in my mind after completing the game, and it was a hilarious wardrobe malfunction affecting a scientist's necktie, caused by the physics engine, in the armoury of the Lambda teleportation labs.

I know its ALPHA so things will change, but currently my thoughts are:
[Pros]
-Great atmosphere and crafting
-Graphic style is great and helps performance on lower end systems
-Plenty of different resources to gather and use
-Animations are great and don't feel left out
-Huge world to explore with dangers in every area.
-Vehicles (and you can build a garage for it in your base)
[Cons]
-Grindy type resource gathering. If you hit a node, you should get more than 2 rocks from it.
-Cold/hot timers seem to come too soon
-Some areas are devoid of valuable resources to survive (no felled trees for wood in some places you might need to survive the night)
-Trees are everywhere but you can't cut them down for wood
-Base building lacks stairways and windows and is generally weak. Walls for example should be double their width to cover more area.
Overall I think this game is great. Coming from a survival game type person (played them all) I approve this so you can purchase it and enjoy yourself alot.

I was skeptical on purchasing this game because I never was really a bit MMO fan. I really did like Skyrim, and heard this wasn't exactly the same, but similar.
I am pleasently suprised. Great combat system. You got the whole hack and slash like Skyrim then hot keys for your spells. Makes you feel like a battle mage. I always hated how much you had to switch your equoment around in Skyrim and this game fixes that issue I had.
You still get the same feel of doing what you want and leveling up for it instead of just spending points on skills for leveling. Really gives you an option to try new things. For each class there is a few routes you can take for it, and you can use whatever weapon you want for it. Basically you get to play the character you want to play instead of feeling stuck into a role. You also get rewarded for playing your hand to hand combat skills which I like. It's not just a bunch of clicking on hot keys.
The quests are nice and comparable to Skyrim as well. There is stories that fit into the lore, and avoid doing the whole collect this many or kill this many creatures.
Graphics are pretty nice as well. You'll notice it is a lot less "cluteered" than Skymin, but I kind of expected that from a MMO.
Can't wait to play more.

Now that the Early Access release of it is here - I'm glad to say they are pretty damn close to it. Originally picking up the free release back in 2012, I was certainly impressed - grinning from ear to ear like a moron from I started playing, until it was over. But while the graphics were nothing short of spectacular (and are even more so in the Steam release), there were a few things that irked me about it;
The gunplay was quite a ways short of satisfactory - the MP5 was essentially useless, among other things, and the AI had the odd moment of spectacular stupidity at certain points as well. Not to mention that parts of certain maps just aren't up to par (Xen, On a Rail, I'm looking at you.)
I am happy to report, that for the most part, my issues with the 2012 release has been resolved. The gunplay has improved tremendously, to the point where the weapons have the most satisfying feeling I've seen in a game for years, only the weaponry of Wolfenstein: The New Order comes close to feeling as good. They have even greatly improved the MP5, making it a viable medium-long range weapon - something the entire Half-Life franchise has been lacking completely ever since 1998. The Glock 17 could stand to have it's rate of fire increased slightly, but other than that I genuinely find little more to be desired.
As for the AI, it has improved immensely since the 2012 release, and I'm fairly confident in claiming it's the best AI we've seen in anything attached to the Half-Life universe yet. That said - I did have a few encounters during the course of the game where certain NPCs' AI simply failed to initialize until after they were attacked - that goes in the bug category though, and is certainly not a design choice reflecting upon the future finished product.
Some people have also been quite vocal about their dislike of the change to the Vortigaunt's attack speed - I myself, on the other hand find it quite refreshing. You still have enough time to get out of the way of their attacks, but it requires more of you, and as such makes it feel much more rewarding when you manage to take out a pack of them without getting hit.
On the subject of level design, I genuinely can't think of a missing piece of the (currently released) maps that I feel are missing, even though I fully know where they were in the original game. There are also quite a few interesting additions made to the level design of the game - most just for flavor and realism - but some of them are actually completely new routes through which to traverse parts of the levels, which is refreshing for someone like me who has played through the original game several dozen times by now, and know Black Mesa like my own house. The long and short of the level design is plainly speaking that anything they took out genuinely isn't missed, and anything they added either makes no impact to the flow of the game, or are genuine improvements upon the original.
I can't wait to see what these people have in store for us with the eventual release of their reenvisioned Xen borderworld - but even as it stands now without Xen, this game is a complete self-contained gameplay experience on it's own.
With regards to general bugs (aside from the aforementioned AI initialization issue), I am quite frankly astounded with regards to how well polished both the 2012- and the Steam release are. These guys are putting Triple-A developers and publishers to shame, and do so on a volunteer part-time basis. I only encountered one bug that was so jarring that it stuck in my mind after completing the game, and it was a hilarious wardrobe malfunction affecting a scientist's necktie, caused by the physics engine, in the armoury of the Lambda teleportation labs.

The paid Steam release is the free release from a couple of years back with a number of jaw-dropping improvements to visual fidelity.... and a number of bugs the old free release didn't have, mostly relating to NPC meshes and quickloading so if you're one of those 1377d3wdz who plays on hard and hasn't died in an FPS since 1998 you'll never have most of the problems I experienced with the game.  The reflection mapping is cute but the fact that the player character does not reflect gave me a headache at first, as my art-brain was strenuously offended by such a glaring omission - though the PC does not "exist" in most FPS in any meaningful way and that's entirely consistent with the original Half-Life.  As of May 2015 the developers seem to be focused on multiplayer so if you want the final act of the story you'll still need to play Half-Life: Source or the original Half-Life.
Feature-wise, the game would benefit enormously from some very un-Half-Life FPS luxuries such as leaning, a melee function that is detached from weapon select (see: the Metro games, Bioshock: Infinite, Borderlands), and maybe a shorter grenade chucking distance.  It feels like the shotgun is way off from the previous release, the Source version, HL2, etc - damage is light and the spread is tight.  In point of fact the shotgun handles less like a shotgun and more like a weaker, slower, range-limited revolver with a spread that feels about as wide as the MP5.  Marines are hyper-vigilant and very aggressive, with long sight lines and instant reflexes - the crossbow is only useful at range if the target is completely oblivious; otherwise they dodge the bolt long before it can strike.  Other reviews critical of Marine AI (and AI in general) provide more and more accurate information about NPC behavior - it's changed from the previous release and in my opinion not for the better.  I found sniping by selecting the .357, sighting with the Z key then releasing Z and pressing fire at the same time to be much more effective than the crossbow - everything can and does duck bolts but I have yet to encounter an NPC that can duck a properly aimed bullet.  I did not find single player combat satisfying but I'm used to different games and I'm mentally comparing the experience to Half-Life 2, Half-Life: Source, and the previous Black Mesa release - all of which seem a bit more forgiving by comparison.
I bought this game for two reasons - to give the devs some money in exchange for the enjoyment I gleaned from the free release, and to rack up a bunch of achievements in a game world I was already familiar with.  I have not played multiplayer and do not plan to; I consider the fact that the current release does not have multiplayer achievements to be a feature and wish more story-centric games would structure their achievements similarly.
Recommended if you like the Half-Life games and haven't played it yet.  If you didn't like Half-Life this game isn't going to change your mind, though the modern visuals might make a convincing argument.
I'll try for the "Rare Specimen" achievement in the final release.

Ellipsis is a neon-themed minimalistic action puzzler where you have to dodge obstacles and enemies. No shooting involved but plenty of being shot at!
The concept of the game requires no tutorial, it's immediately obvious what to do. You control a blue circle and you have to collect the 'beads' from other circles which appear one after another, while avoiding all kinds of moving spikes, barriers, lasers, enemies chasing you, cannons firing at you etc. Each target circle contains one more bead than the last, and sometimes when you hit a circle at the wrong angle it can send some of the beads flying around the place, so you can either chase after them or accept a lower rated score. After you hit the 4th circle the exit appears but you can optionally go for the 5th for a better score, which is always in a more difficult area.
There is full controller support but I found it much better with the mouse as it allows for faster, more accurate movement, which is often necessary, especially if you're going for a 5-star rating (see difficulty section below).
Level overview is a sprawling network with the same neon design, very slick and intuitive, and shows all the necessary information at a glance. You can zoom in and out and drag it around to visit whichever sections you like.
Built-in level editor allows you to create your own fiendish challenges and share them with others via the Steam Workshop.
I'm running Linux and 20% of the time starting the game crashes my DE (Gnome) and dumps me unceremoniously at the login screen. All is forgiven though, as I'm happy that Linux is supported and it doesn't affect the gameplay, which is otherwise smooth and glitch-free.
A more concerning problem is with the trash bin function. It's confusing, and makes it far too easy to accidentally delete the wrong save file. I say this from bitter personal experience, having wiped my progress after 80% completion of the game :(
Use of bright neon colours is not only gorgeous to look at but also coordinates the different types of enemies and such. There is a rainbow-themed enemy in the early levels that is particularly stunning.
As well as being easy to control, the level overview shows the various enemy factions moving around, patrolling their areas. Super cool.
There is no background music. Instead you can hear the enemies making their individual sounds and you can tell a lot of thought has been put into this because the noises are perfectly suited.
The game has a 5 star rating system. If you exit after only 4 circles you can only get a maximum of 3 stars - less if you don't collect all the beads. To get 4 stars you have to collect all the beads from all 5 circles. For 5 stars you have to do this under a strict time limit and for this you will definitely need to use the mouse. You have to dash around the screen with pinpoint accuracy and it always deserves a Freddie Mercury fist pump when you nail it.
So in other words, the difficulty is of your own choosing and has a wide range, making it a good game for all ages. The fact that all you have to do is move your mouse around makes it suitable for even the very young age group.
It has everything: cards, achievements, cloud, leaderboards, level editor, cross-platform.
150 levels and plenty of replay value, along with extra levels from the community. It's a fair price but, personally, for this type of game I would probably wait for at least a small discount.
This game can be either relaxing or challenging, it's up to you. It looks great, feels satisfying to play and the level designs are diverse and fresh throughout. Just beware of the trash bin.

I was excited to discover that after you first tackle a stage, wherein you can earn four stars at most, you can revisit previous puzzles and attempt to earn a fifth star by perfecting the stage in points and against an added timer. While the comparison to Geometry Wars' pacifist achievement stands out, I'd actually compare Ellipsis more closely to games like Flywrench or N++ where the challenge shines in hitting that clean and perfect run through each stage.
All aspects of this game, from the art to the audio, is sharp, stylish, and smart; and the gameplay is, quite simply, fun!

Spoilers: I gave it a perfect score!

The most addictive games come in the most simple seeming of packages. And simple is only what Ellipsis appears to be on the surface. A geometrical avoid 'em up of abstract neon vectors. Mazes of lazer-light obstacle courses and seas of deadly shapes unfold through stages on a flourishing map of abstract trails for you to blaze. No shooting and no attacking, this is an absolute test of reflex and accuracy as you wind through the neon corridors and avoid the complex contraptions in your path.
People who remember the Iraira Bou (Irritating Maze) style of games from Japan will see similarities in the addictive and punishingly pinpoint obstacle navigating gameplay. The movement of your small blue orb through these psychedelic fields of aggressive obstacles and enemies is incredibly precise. It's so precise it made me realize I need a better mouse, as every sudden motion and flinch of your wrist is responded to with such accurate sensitivity. The game is also playable with a gamepad but I found the needed precision to be best with a mouse as many of the later stages require such accuracy and speed that a stick just won't cut it.
The stages are quick, incredibly fast paced and to the point. Each one contains five orbs to collect, and each orb appears in progressively precarious positions. Collecting each orb isn't as easy as it seems, as the points they contain spill out once touched. Collecting four consecutively appearing orbs creates a gate, and the fifth orb that appears is optional and usually incredibly hard to reach in comparison.
A seriously sweet slice of bright and beautiful arcade chaos. The simple and minimal but enticingly colorful visual style starts with a retro elegance then quickly spirals into a chaotic neon ballet along with the growing complexity of each level. Glowing red triangles that group like a psychedelic school of fish chase you down, rotating orange turrets track your movements down with a hail of bullets, and spike-y blue bombs explode in a large radius when you get close enough. The variety of obstacles and colorful geometrical enemies is incredibly broad, I was blown away by the amount of new and inventive threats I was being killed by even far into the chaotically large and vibrant stage map.
As you complete each lightning quick stage the map expands. As it expands a living world of retro lighting and visuals opens up. Alternate paths branch and turn through a busy overworld and bright lights travel across lines like the circuits of some colorful motherboard. The completion of stages and the building of this impressive overworld map is a accompanied by an ambient droning, soft enough to lull into into a false sense of comfort before your assured demise.
Ellipsis is a formula of purely distilled arcade mechanics, the best of the best that have stood the test of time. The core of what makes shoot'emups and action games so fun to begin with, the dodging and avoiding of walls of bullets that lets the player feel like a badass. It's something I keep coming back to over and over again, because it scratches a purely reflex based itch that most games these days can't scratch. The sounds and visuals draw you into it's addictive world, and top off an already complete package for something that is a treat to all of your senses.

Having been riding shotgun on this rocky slope since the engine first breathed life, I've bared witness to the rise and fall of many events both majestic and miniscule. From the very beginning, connecting across the ocean to the Real Time Worlds European server to participate in the closed beta program through one scheduled hour a week, I felt that there was something metaphysical at work. Something without form, without function, sleeping beneath the silver sheen of this seemingly genre changing cops and robbers MMO.
There was something there behind the flying bullets, the untapped expression of creativity driven forth from every player, the static walls of San Paro and it's fleeing citizens. Like a father watching his infant son strike his first fluke homerun well out of the confines of the park, I remember excitedly tossing and considering the possibilities of a game like APB. It was destined for many things, much of which can only be described as allegory in light of the failed future this game was given by fate.
The son that knocked the ball out of the park, he could have been in the Major Leagues. He could have been so much more. Instead, somewhere between that first fluke shot and college, he found drugs and greed and turned that bat into a tool of violence for the dealer that provided him with his fix. The story of APB, sadly, is not that much different.
I stand now with a precious handful of survivors that took the train and never got off, and it is from this seat that I can humbly nominate APB Reloaded for the "Monument To What Could Have Been" award.
Nothing further, your honor.

It's clear and quick, unlike most point and click games, but the substance is both dull and the characters are unbelievable so you're forcibly disengaged from the shoddy narrative as often as possible. I will spoil a bit here because you shouldn't play it anyway.
'School Student' elects to stop drinking school beer and leave his girfriend at the school bar to catch the last bus home because despite being apparently really in love with her, he doesn't want to sleep at school with her. I'm assuming they're talking about university, but it's never made clear afaik.
As he's walking out, 'Guy on the Football Team' 1 and 2 come in. Girlfriend freaks out a bit, says to SS that GotFT1 is a jerk to her and proceeds to make a snide remark within earshot of him, which he acknowledges that he heard. SS *continues to leave* despite obvious tension in the room involving GF, and soothes her nerves with a parting comment that makes you wonder if the developer is one of those people who actually doesn't know how regular humans talk, like the Tommy Wiseau, or Birdemic writer/director James Nguyen.
Literally two minutes later he gets a call from her; she's just left the bar because GotFT1 threatened to kill her, and has stumbled into a cheesy b-grade horror forrest. A pile of leaves freaks her out, then she's abducted by a ghost for some reason, leaving the phone on the ground. USG1 acknowledges that the call ended with weird noises, and once again exercises his impeccable decision making skills by:
1) Not doing anything about it
2) Calling her house later that night, finding out she's stil not home
3) Still doing nothing about it
4) Waiting three days
5) Telling his friends, who react with, "That's weird. Come on, we're going to be late for school!"
6) Conceeding to tell *a teacher* about it only after they find her phone
Where are her parents? How did she go missing for three days and nobody else noticed? Why aren't police involved?
I'm assuming at this point I should be asking different questions, wondering where she is or what the ghost is up to, but it's impossible to care about the characters or the story.
I feel justified attacking these elements, as I believe a good point and click relies strongly on immersion in the game reality, however I should also take a moment to attack the gameplay.
I had about fifteen options. There's the clearly obvious way to go, which one of the characters has already suggested in exposition, six speech options that didn't make sense ("We're gonna be late, let's go!" "How was your weekend?" "Oh not bad you know, I...") and eight, "I don't think that's a good idea," clicks.
LISTEN HERE, ****FACE, I'M THE IDEAS MAN HERE, AND I SAY GO USE THAT MAN.
Seriously though, without interesting alternatives, the rails get very confining.
In summary, I'm considered a very creative and resourceful man and I see nothing redeemable about this game.

If you found people who knows actually what to do, this game could be amazingly entertaining.
Just a few tipps for the newbies:
- The most important thing to learn how to kill with melee weapon. Don't forget the power attack.
- PUSH!! Countless time i saw people don't know what to do when a zombie catch them. If i am right it's the key V.
- Don't be greedy. The most common issues, people try to pick up all the ammos and guns. Your inventory has limited capacity so its a bit pointless picking up everything you see. Use one gun and ( to see what kind of ammunition you need, hold R) and one melee.
- Shooting: Aim. Some people just shoot the whole clip into the air, and if they have luck, maybe one bullet reach the target. So aim ( Left mouse button if i remember well) to the heads. Also, don't shoot every zombies, spare the bullets for the runners, and in survival games, for the last wave.
- Molotov, grenade, tnt. Its a good idea spare them for the last wave ( on survival of course). You can find some red gasolnie cans, they are also explosive. And the traps, don't forget activating them if there is a need.
- Lockers: You can find locked dors, mostly on survival maps. to open them find the key, the welder or the code for the dor. ( One example: On Silence there is a body lying somewhere around the church, in the cemetery, you can find next to some of the lanterns, they are also on the ground. Next to the body is the key for the basement lockers. There, you can find a welder, and with the welder you are able to open the sheds). Open them in the first two wave, or when just a few zombies walking around. They contains ammos, weapons or health crates.
- Injuries: If you are infected, use pills. If you are bleeding, use bandages. If you barely have life use a medkit or a health crate. These are the most rarely items so use them wisely.
- Barricades: Unfortunately just very few people can keep in mind. On survival maps they can extend the time what you spend alive. Pick up a simple hammer, some planks, choose the hammer for weapon, right click and now you are able to build barricades. But don't block all the entrances fully. Only one plank can hold up zombies, but you can go in or out.
- Surviving points: On Survival map there are points ( A, B or C), choose one base, and protect that point. If All points condition reach zero, game over. To raise their condition use fema bags. Also, it's good idea escort all the staff you don't need ( another type off ammos, etc.) to your base.
I think that's all, i hope it will help some of you.

Broforce is a very fun shooter game that mimics the stereotypical American culture and patriotism. You play as a "Bro", who is named and shaped after a popular character from a movie or TV series. "Half Life" was practically the soundtrack to my wasted youth. This game is like the ultimate relapse into a great addiction, complete with the shakes and shivers experienced back in 1998. This is like the DeLorean time machine of flashback games...
We all know what "Half Life" is about and what made it great. This here is an incredibly faithful recreation of the classic game, complete with new graphics, new voicework, and an all-round perfect blend of modern day fun and the classic elements we know and love. I played through the original so many times over the years, it was nice to see how it translated to the new engine. There were no disappointments in the general delivery. The graphics were crisp and clean, the locations were very familiar and took me back to simpler time, and the sound design was good.
The characters of "Half Life 2" were added into this game so they could be more readily identified than in the original and I enjoyed that touch. The weapons were all there, the joy of exploding someone's microwave casserole was there, it was all there and made better than in the original.
But, with praise, there are also some minor quips I have with the game. First and foremost is the hit detection. Many times, if an enemy does not see you and you shoot at them, the hit will not register. I had it at one point in the chapter "Unforeseen Consequences" where a headcrap zombie was coming out of the water and standing at a door near a hatch and I unloaded a clip into it point blank without any of the hits registering. Also, as much as I disliked the Xen chapter in the original game, it would have been nice to have it in "Black Mesa" because jumping to "Half Life 2" after this ends just feels like its missing something without fighting the final boss. Other then that, I was very pleased with this game and sunk more time than I wanted to into it...and you know what? I don't regret a second of it!

Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare is the next entry in the ever-so popular FPS Action Franchise. This time around, it's focused on futuristic warfare, where PMCs (Private Military Companies) are taking the lead in the world, one in particular trying to do away with government and politics all together. Also, the Exo-Suit.
Story:
The story is played in the eyes of Pvt. Mitchell, a United States troop working for the Marines. After the loss of his best friend Will in a fight against North Korea (Along with an arm), he is confronted by Will's father, Johnathon Irons (Played by Kevin Spacey) at Will's funeral to work for Atlas, a PMC that works for any country that pays them. Wanting to avenge Will's death, Mitchell agrees to work for Atlas and gains a prostetic arm for his missing one. Mitchell makes some friends along the way, including the likes of the rough and tough Gideon, and the sharpshooter Illona. Their mission is to kill Hades, a man that has been responsible for Nuclear attacks that killed innocents for 4 years. Things aren't what they seem, however.
The story is good, I'll say that. It's nothing groundbreaking or connecting like Black Ops or MW1-MW3. It does have lots of action packed scenes and beautiful scenery thanks to the breathtaking look of the game, however. Sadly, I think much more potential could of been put into the actual gameplay here, as most of it is your standard "Follow the Leader" and "Cover/Shoot" fare. With the new Exo-Suit and double jump, there should be much more freedom. There is fun and rather exotic locations, though, and some scenes in the story to take advantage of the Exo-Suit's abilites, allowing for some creative flow. I never really felt that connected to the characters because they didn't have much... Well, character. The only one I actually liked at all was Gideon, because he's with you through just about the entire story, and you really see him and Mitchell grow a bond together. The others are rather forgettable. Irons isn't that bad, though. You'll see why. (No, not because it's Kevin Spacey.)
Overall the story is a good one, it definitely isn't bad. Good length as well, about 6-7 hours. It's one to play, that's for sure.
Multiplayer:
Multiplayer is the main focus, is it not? Well, I must say I was thankfully impressed by how this was pulled out. Thanks to the addition of the Exo-Suit, this spices up gameplay a ton, and then some. Every player has a double jump, and a boost. These may seem like minor additions, but in reality, they completely change up the game. There's tons of verticality, evasive manuvers, and faster paced action than ever before, it's very exhilirating. This is the kind of change that the series needed to be fresh, and this is a much welcomed addition. Creating a class is just like Black Ops II, 13 spaces, and you can fill it up however you like. One neat change is that scorestreaks you earn can now be upgraded, at the cost of needing a higher score to achieve. You can upgrade the UAV to last longer, show enemy direction, stuff like that. It makes for lots of creative combos.
You can customize your character just like you can in Ghosts, but it's more expansive. This time your soldier can range from helmets, tops, and pants, to gloves, shoes, and your Exo. You earn supply drops now, which contain variants of existing items and even new cosmetics, each with their own rarity. This is a nice way to earn new guns and clothes, so you always have something to win after a game, if you do recieve one.
Anyway, multiplayer is amazing because of the Exo-Suits implimentation. It brings fresh variety into the series, and I garuntee it's more heart-pumping than ever before.
So overall, Advanced Warfare is one of the best CoD games to be released, in my opinion. It's worth it to buy whenever you get the chance, so I hope you enjoy it!

Call of Duty Advanced Warfare is an exceptional game – in theory.  The Campaign is well written, spectacularly visualized, and challenging to complete.  Following the story of a young Marine fallen on hard times, the player comes into their own through extensive practice opportunities built into the campaign storyline.  Call of Duty Advanced Warfare sports new weapons and armaments that allow a more vertical player experience that redefines the Call of Duty brand.  Strong character development and stunning visuals allows the player to control a game on par with a summer action blockbuster – in theory.
However, the game has drawbacks.
Due to the graphics intensity of this next-gen title, the Campaign load screens for a computer like mine that just meets the recommended specs are anywhere from 45 seconds to 5 minutes longer than the cut-scenes placed between chapters.  The game lacks a way to interrupt a cut scene to save and quit, leaving the player trapped at a loading screen waiting to safely exit the game.
The Multiplayer experience is expansive and very fun to play – if you can gain access to “Online Services.”  Overall, the connectivity experience falls well short of my expectations.  With a PC setup, I would have expected much better connectivity to online matchmaking in Exo-Survival and normal Multiplayer formats.  A shortage or outright lack of dedicated servers cripples the number of available matches in obscure game types and opens up lobbies to be unfairly dominated by the P2P host.  I tried to play Exo-Survival tonight after today’s recent patch and gave up after 54 minutes of receiving “System unavailable” messages.  Perhaps recent attempts to remedy the matchmaking system’s poor performance have instead exacerbated the initial problem.
All in all, Call of Duty Advanced Warfare is somewhat fun in Campaign mode but unattractive as an online Multiplayer FPS.  I hope that the developers of the franchise will fix the multiplayer issues that have plagued Call of Duty games since Modern Warfare 2 and earlier.

I had heard horror stories about the difficulty of the souls games so I d never picked one of these dark fantasy hack and slash before;
I am glad I finally did, t is an excellent game.

Do not let the stories about the difficulty turn you away from this game. It is well worth a try if you like medieval action RPGs. It is tough but not impossible.

First let me say that I am never one to board the hype train.  Additionally, I don't take time to write reviews unless I have something to say.  Alien: Isolation deserves that time so here's what I have to say:
A:I has some incredible things going for it.  Right when you load up the game and the 20th Century Fox logo flashes like the pre-dated days of the past you know you are in for a treat.  I immediately selected Hard mode as it was the recommended mode - which is another indication as to how this game is going to be.  The first things I noticed were the amazing details given to the environment.  10 minutes in and I found myself freaked out simply by the environment.  It wasn't until the first hour or so was I in actual danger and running for my life.  From that moment on (and to this one) my character has been in a constant state of despair and struggle.  I've died a total of 6 times today and all of which were completely different.  It wasn't at different times either, I'm stuck on the same mission and that stupid Xenomorph is ALWAYS THERE!  This isn't a game where you can wait for the AI script to run and there are noticable "dark" times for you to run from cover to cover.  You are Amanda Ripley, you are weak, you are running, and you are scared... prepare yourself....

[Written 11 hours into the game]
Before Gone Home was found to be nothing more than a propaganda walking simulator, I had this vain belief that it was going to be a stealth/haunted house deal wherein a monster is constantly lurking around and will drop you in a second. I got a taste of this when I first heard of Outlast but again it did not live up to the stadard.
Upon First Loading Alien: Isolation, I knew I was going to get what I wanted. The main menu screen is almost completely mute, with only the slightest hint of sound in thew background, indicating the original Alien tagline "In space, noone can hear you scream." I immediately picked the hardest difficulty as the game reccomends, unbenkownst to the sheer struggle that it would bring me. At time of writing I am 11 hours into the game, which should put me just over the halfway mark. (Spoilers ahead). At this point it seems the Alien has gone away for now: Throwing myself out of an airlock as the alien is launched into space from a detached station section.(Spoilers end) I know am a bit of a lul in the game where very little new is taking place and I am instead thrown against the wall against multiple human and synthetic enemies which seem to exist only to drain my ammo and item supply so that they devs can set something else up later on.
If you are a fan of the Alien franchise and want a horror game that actually feels scary again, play this.

I would highly recommend this game to others, especially if you've seen the original Alien movie when it came out. The level of nostalgia this game brings is through the roof, and the sheer horror of surviving versus an unpredictable AI foe is something that I've been missing in games. There are one or 2 points in the game where it does drag, but otherwise it's a nonstop thrill ride.
My first playthrough was on Normal, and despite watch some others stream this on Twitch, I was caught by surprise many times by the Alien. I'd recommend this difficulty for most players on their first time; then either Easy on a following playthrough to get more of the story experience, or Hard if you're an outright masochist.
I haven't played the Crew Expendable DLC yet as of this review, but as the base game by itself, it is more than worth the money.
Ratings:
------------
Graphics: 10/10
- Looks Beautiful, incredibly well-optimized for PC. The detail they put in to remake the 1970's version of future spaceships/stations in the Alien movie is phenomenal.
Sound: 9/10
- The mood of the game couldn't have been much more
Controls: 8/10
- Sometimes I ended up fighting with the inventory to get the right sub-weapon, which did get me killed a few times. The controls to activate some doors/items did seem awkward. Weapon combat was very straightforward thankfully
Story: 9/10
- Fit perfectly as a gap between Alien and Aliens, although the Working Joe androids became rather tedious the longer the game went on.
Overall: 9/10
- Very solid game, one of the most enjoyable games I've played after accounting for all the deaths I had.

Alright, so I know that I haven't put in a million hours to maybe give a super rounded review, but I have played enough to get a feel for the Campaign as well as the multiplayer.
Call of Duty automatically has reputation going against it that is turbulant to say the least.. but for the most part it has deserved it. With its repetitive and unimagined rehashings of the previous entries.. Which i'm probably wasting my time getting into, cause anyone who plays games knows about Call of Duty.
Now, I can honestly say with a bit of optimism that Advanced Warfare breaks the mold.. or at least pushes as far from it as it can without losing that signature COD feel..
With the Exo suits now in play in the Campaign and MP, it opens up a whole lot more as far as options in how you play the game.. Making the gameplay a lot more vertical and frantic..
If you figure out your Exo suit controls you can really move around ridiculously quickly, as well as evade oncoming attacks with style.
They also emphasize on personalization of basically everything about your avatar, which again isn't something all too new to the franchise, but it is always nice being able to make something completely your own.
Some of it's obvious downfalls is the fact that they have no support for dedicated servers, which I know drove quite a few people away.. As well as there being perodic ping issues.
Aside from those issues (which one can only hope get addressed in the near future) I would say that there is a lot of good aspects of the game that can be pulled out of it, for some one who enjoys a fast, competitive shooter.
And with those new Exo-suits coming into play, especially in multiplayer, your own creative mind is really one of the best tools you can use for winning matches.
7.5/10 (not perfect by any means, but fun, none-the-less)

Early Access Review:
Black Mesa, for those of you that don't know, is a complete remake of Half Life 1 by a small team of folks. When it comes down to remaking one of the best games of all time, it's a very high bar to set for yourself to even be acceptable in the gaming community, but I'll tell you, it was definitely accomplished. Triple A multimillion dollar games fall flat on their faces compared to this game. If you followed the developement of this game, you'll know there was several snags, and several delays with such a small team that was changing constantly over the past 8 or so years. When the free version released in 2012, it was a ton of fun, lacking the Xen levels, but it gave you a taste of what you were going to be getting when the finished product was here. So here's the steam release. If you played the free version, the first thing you'll notice is how much smoother and cleaner the game feels. The visuals have all been bumped up to probably being the prettiest source GAME let alone the prettiest source mod. When you got lost in half life for the first time, you experienced action, tension, and entertaining puzzles and sometimes fierce battles. Black Mesa succeeded completely in being able to bring this feeling out again. While feeling very familiar, every environment was brand new and designed brilliantly. I'd find myself normally know where to go thanks to playing the original so much, but there were also more than a couple moments where I'd get lost and have some minor issues progressing, but that's a good thing in my mind, taking an old game and making it challenging again. Certain aspects of Half life that got annoying or tedious have more or less been altered to make it quicker, more managable, and less hassle. For example, during the "Power up" level, you may remember the useless guard laying on the floor that does nothing while you go and turn on the generator, get the train going, and then you have to run all the way back up to where the guard is to turn the train to continue forward. Now, that same useless guard will turn the train for you so the gameplay doesn't get interrupted and stopped for the moment. It may be a small thing to some, but many improvements like that will come up having you say, "Oh I remember having to do it like this, but this is a lot more useful". Being in Early access still, Xen is incomplete yet, but even without it, there's a solid 6-8 hours of gameplay depending on how often you get lost. Overall, if you were looking to relive a game from your past in a new and improved, and dare I say BETTER way than you remember it? Don't be stingy, $20 is practically a robbery for this game, and you would be letting yourself down to not pick this up.
Pros:
-The best looking source game you'll find
-A classic remade into a modern, new, but familiar experience
-Good challenge
-Vintage multiplayer (if you're interested in it)
Cons:
-Missing Xen (Early access, acceptable as it will come)
-Sometimes enemy AI gets a little brain dead (soldiers walking right past you even if you're in front of them, Vorts stop and just stand in front of you; rare and minor issues)

Dark Souls II takes the beautiful, no mercy formula of its predecessor and improves on it. Although an initially accessible bonfire fast-travel system has been added, you can use Bonfire Ascetics to increase the difficulty around any of these bonfires. You'll die often, but you'll feel more powerful as your skill and your character grow. The graphics are amazing this time round, and it doesn't feel like a PC port. You'll curse at your screen over and over, just like before, don't worry. By the way, that's the point of this game. It's supposed to be hard and frustrating, so if difficulty in a game turns you off, this isn't the game for you.

Dark Souls 2 is a good game, but it's the weaker entry to the series (having not played Demon Souls).
It's significantly weaker in overall story, level (including world) and audio design, however it has iterated and improved on the combat and the story told through action making both feel more tense and immediate. While FROM has taken steps to reduce newbie bullying through character and gear twinking, it also mostly negates those improvements through inept game design, mainly through the interaction of the mechanics of a specific covanent and some items.
Multiplayer interactions are generally improved, however the abysmal netcode found in Dark Souls, while improved (most likely because of using Steamworks as opposed to GFWL) is still to be found. Cooping with specific people can intrinsically be done almost as easily as modded Dark Souls, an addition that's has pros and cons. A lack of invasion tools early in the game (read: most, if not all of NG), puts a serious dent in ~30% of the covenant interactions, however it does ease newcomer's to the series, something that also has it's pros and cons. Not to be mistaken, many of the balance exploits regularly done in Dark Souls are absent in Dark Souls 2, at least for the moment. I would unquestioningly recommend Dark Souls 2 multiplayer over Dark Souls, regardless of current balance issues.
Overall, it really feels like an extended expansion for Dark Souls done by a third party, both with good and bad changes. If this is your first entry to the Souls series, it should prove a memorable and challenging experience. If not, then it may feel like a bland repaint of Dark Souls. Filling and familiar, but not something lasting.
