After playing the game for a long period and fighting both Major and Minor wars, I think I'm ready to give my final verdict on Rome 2.
Essential Rome 2 mods that you MUST own to play Rome 2:
Rome: Total War Music (fixes the music)
Hegemonia - Large Empires standalone 4TPY (Makes the empires as strong as they should be)
Graphic Enhancement Mod (removes the ugly blue lighting that the game suffers from)
Pikemen start battles with pikes (Something CA should already have patched into the game)
Better City Names (City names that weren't named by Neanderthals)
Rome 2 has a variety of problems, there's no denying that. The game is poorly optimised with certain features and at certain points. It can lag when you look at the campaign map and it can lag when you look at grass with the soft foliage feature. The UI can sometimes become an AI and order your troops in ways that you did not give it permission to do. A precise cavalry charge for example can be sent instead into a spearman unit when you specifically ordered it to avoid that unit, something that previous total wars have all managed to avoid. The HDR still doesn't have an option in the Graphics Options menu, meaning that you will have to look at black/blue battles instead of the colourful HD ones you've come to expect from Shogun. Some of the city names are not the ones you grew up knowing, like the legionary city of Arretium, in Rome 1. The music rarely has any flair and is often forgettable. You wont find the music you were expecting or teased with
in the trailers by the fantastic Jeff Van♥♥♥♥♥♥(He did the music for Rome, Medieval 2 & Shogun 2).
These are problems, obviously, but none of them are crippling to the game itself. If I cast off the nostalgia of Rome 1 and look to what this game actually has, it's a pretty good game. My previous gripes with transport fleets and undead armies has been squashed, conquest is less of a grind than it used to be. When you destroy a nation, their various military assets still roam about looking to raid your settlements and pose a general resistance, but isn't this what would really happen? Perhaps they might just disband, but if it's a loyal army (Not mercenary's), wouldn't they try to fight using guerilla tactics? If there is a grind, it is mostly justified and removes the gamey tactic of taking the last enemy settlement before they capture your town in the hopes that they will turn to dust. A good thing, in my mind.
So what about the Army=Transport fleet thing? Well, fleets are now delicate little flowers, and their existence makes it so that you MUST have a navy. This is good, and I would not remove it. Naval battles have went from being simple zig-zags when the game first came out to what are practically land battles on the sea. I have major problems with the AI of your ships in sea battles, they can't decide to attack on their own, you must tell each individual one what it is to do every time it is to do something, but if you can keep on top of that they can be quite fun. It's a different world though, you should expect to lose several ships if facing a naval force. Ships burn, men die, rams smash. They are high maintenance, but without them you will be missing half of your military power and opening yourself up to Guerilla pirates.
The game implements many new features like food and emphasises squalor and public happiness so that you can't simply build a barracks in every city. You must make Arrentium your legionary city, make Ariminum your fishing and farming city and  Neopolis your trading port, maybe make Brundisium your shipyard or as I had it, Karalis. Careful though, all those new high tech buildings require food, perhaps you should turn your new Carthaginian conquests into masses of farms? Don't forget to honour the gods or the people might remember that you aren't the Carthage they know and love. It adds a new layer of complexity to the game and I like it.
The diplomacy is some of the best I've seen, especially in a total war game. It's not necessarily the options that are great, they're pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥poor to be honest, but it's the way the AI behaves. They are much more willing not to hate you, in fact they often love you and fear you and show proper respect to their Roman masters by offering to become vassals. The AI knows when it's out gunned and it's best option is to surrender half to keep the rest, lest they become my newest visitors to Mediolanium's slave market. The existence of city states is refreshing to say the least, it's quite nice to have Massila be an ally of Rome in hostile Gaul. It's something you couldn't have in the original with the Rebels being the minor factions. Beware of them though, in my game Athens took Macedon proceeded to vassalise Sparta and conquer Turkey. As far as I'm aware they are fighting a long and bitter war with Egypt against Parthia, who destroyed the Seleucid's (even with the Hegemonia mod). All of this occurred while I was fighting the Carthaginians, which since Rome is united, I was guided into going to Spain before Gaul as happened in history. No Roman balloon expansion here.
The politics is sadly reduced. The lack of a family tree makes the family's seem a bit abstract and the assassinations seem irrelevant, but the events that crop up can be interesting and securing promotions and general/admiral positions for your house could be called intrigue I guess. It's not really a massive downer; it could have been better but it's hardly game breaking.
On the land battles, my nostalgia is hurting my opinion of them. In my opinion, you can't have a melee battle without archers and skirmishers are a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor substitute, let alone slingers. Who wants those eh, they are for the kinds of people who use war dogs and explosive pigs. Not for the serious general, am I right?
Apparently not, Rome never used archers until it had conquered Syria according to forum based sources that I read, so you'll have to use those lousy skirmishers and their throwing sticks and wolf pelt hats. In all fairness they can be quite useful, but their range is so short that I rarely actually use them, they sit at the back with no actual part in the battle apart from inflicting friendly fire. That's what I see anyway.
Cavalry feels a bit weak as well, but it might be because everyone and their mother has a spear and they don’t trample ground units like they used to. Every little thing seems to bog them down and the anvil seems to break the enemy without needing a hammer anyway. They can be useful, but most of my battles are sieges rather than open field, so perhaps that has something to do with it. I've never had the AI siege my city, but I hear that they can use fire on iron doors, so keep that in mind when deciding whether to purchase or not, it seems to snap some people's minds in half. Not that it's right, but again it's not a game breaker.
Overall I feel that Rome 2 has the qualities of a good total war game, now that it's properly developed and patched. On my rankings, It's better than Empire and Napoleon, but probably equal to or less than vanilla Shogun but it still is not the greatness of Fall of the Samurai.

[Written 11 hours into the game]
Before Gone Home was found to be nothing more than a propaganda walking simulator, I had this vain belief that it was going to be a stealth/haunted house deal wherein a monster is constantly lurking around and will drop you in a second. I got a taste of this when I first heard of Outlast but again it did not live up to the stadard.
Upon First Loading Alien: Isolation, I knew I was going to get what I wanted. The main menu screen is almost completely mute, with only the slightest hint of sound in thew background, indicating the original Alien tagline "In space, noone can hear you scream." I immediately picked the hardest difficulty as the game reccomends, unbenkownst to the sheer struggle that it would bring me. At time of writing I am 11 hours into the game, which should put me just over the halfway mark. (Spoilers ahead). At this point it seems the Alien has gone away for now: Throwing myself out of an airlock as the alien is launched into space from a detached station section.(Spoilers end) I know am a bit of a lul in the game where very little new is taking place and I am instead thrown against the wall against multiple human and synthetic enemies which seem to exist only to drain my ammo and item supply so that they devs can set something else up later on.
If you are a fan of the Alien franchise and want a horror game that actually feels scary again, play this.

I would highly recommend this game to others, especially if you've seen the original Alien movie when it came out. The level of nostalgia this game brings is through the roof, and the sheer horror of surviving versus an unpredictable AI foe is something that I've been missing in games. There are one or 2 points in the game where it does drag, but otherwise it's a nonstop thrill ride.
My first playthrough was on Normal, and despite watch some others stream this on Twitch, I was caught by surprise many times by the Alien. I'd recommend this difficulty for most players on their first time; then either Easy on a following playthrough to get more of the story experience, or Hard if you're an outright masochist.
I haven't played the Crew Expendable DLC yet as of this review, but as the base game by itself, it is more than worth the money.

I played through the game in about 4 hours, yesterday, I think?
I will try and avoid spoilers for this.
So, anyway, I liked the story, even if I didn't quite understand it around the end (though that might be a problem with me and not the storytelling). I did feel Murray wasn't particularly interesting as a protagonist, but he did have some funny lines, and thought that the other playable character later could have had more time devoted to her.
I did feel the tone needed work, though. I felt it was rather inconsistent, like making fun of traditional Point & Click Adventure game tropes and other conventions (like a dialogue option has Murray and Mrs. Fish commenting on the latter's Leitmotif), but had a rather serious and creepy plot. It just kind of felt unbalanced, particularly when the moments of the former leaked into the latter (like Murray asking a Reaper why they didn't phase through the door, and the Reaper gives an adequate answer, and Murray says "Plot hole averted!"). I don't mind what you were trying, but it could have been done better.
As for the artstyle, it grew on me, but I did think it could have been better (like Crystal and Murray have very silly walks). There were definitely some proportion and scale issues I can recall, like arms not the right length. I definitely hope that the artstyle gets a slight overhaul for the sequel.
I thought the gameplay was solid, though at least one or two puzzles felt a bit obtuse. It's pretty standard Point & Click Adventure game fare (take that how you will).
I'd recommend it, it's a bit unpolished in a number of places, but it's kind of an interesting experience.

But where the game really shines.... and frustrates is its business model.
Unlocking gods with favor is fairly easy,  64(soon to be 65) unlockable gods,  and just with dailys and login rewards you can unlock 5 or 6 a month.  Or for 30 bucks you can unlock them all.

Some of the really rare skins will end up costing you 50+$, such as during the odyssey event (but you get a pile of random stuff to go with it)
The only real problem I have with it are the 200gem voice packs for each god, which provide an in game benefit of knowing whos saying what with out needing to be distracted and look at your chat window.  Overall though,  this isnt enough to detract too much from the game.

Now my time on here says one thing, but my ingame level says another (Level 30) This is one of the best MOBAs out there, and it has broken a lot of boundries.

The one complaint I always had with existing MOBAs was, that there is no point in having a strategic simulator view of the characters and indirectly clicking their walking path and attacks. SMITE solves the issue flawlessly, bringing real direct action into the MOBA genre.
The problem with SMITE for me is the matchmaking. I thought I felt, that they have a separate matching for the really low levels, but once I reached level 5 or so, which happened fast, I was matched against pre-mades of 5 with 5 solo queuers, or matched against players with hundreds of games played, as someone who plays his 20th round. This can't work. I also did have an amount of fairly balanced matches though.
Looking at past matchmaking on smite.guru makes me think, that the only matchmaking criteria is ELO. It is a huge mistake not to consider, that someone with 1000 games played and an ELO-1800 is at an entirely different level of playing than a player with 20 games played and an ELO-1800.
Maybe that would mean that the concept of ELO is flawed, or SMITEs determination process of ELO, but I just don't see it working that well. Obviously matching parties of 2 against parties of 5 can't work either.
If you can handle a hand full of frustration due to the slightly flawed matchmaking and a very beginner-unfriendly community, give SMITE a try. I would highly recommend reading up about the laning roles though, before you ever queue into "Conquest" mode.

Dark Souls is a hard game. If you don't already know that, you probably don't travel in PC Gaming Circles. Either that or your circles are so highly specialized that nobody in them plays this particular blend of Action-RPG.
So, let's get the obvious out of your way. This game is hard. You will die a lot. It's the understudy of every first-party title made for the Nintendo Entertainment System. This game is unforgiving... however it's also very fair with how unforgiving it is.
Every enemy is designed to telegraph its moves to a degree. If you learn the enemy, you can defeat it very easily. If you don't learn to read your enemies, you'll be seeing you "You Died" banner a lot more than you should. Every death you experience will be your own fault. That's just how the game works.
You'll try to slip in one extra attack and get finished off by a enemy twice your mass, carrying a weapon that no human being should be able to so much as lift. You'll dodge-roll off the side of a cliff because you weren't paying attention. You will walk right onto a pressure plate and get perforated with arrows. That's just the highlight reel. There are many, many deaths waiting for you in Dark Souls.
But that doesn't make it a bad game. Quite to the contrary really, it makes it a
game. Dark Souls is a solid piece of Game Design. Nothing supurfluous has been added, and nothing essential has been removed. Everything can be defeated, in theory, by a level one character if the player is skilled enough. Every attack can be evaded, if you know how to time your dodge. Every attack can be blocked, if you can time your shielding right. Every enemy can be slain, if you have the patience to learn from your excrutiating deaths.
Of course... that's just Dark Souls being Dark Souls. You'll also have to get used to the fact that this game is "Single Player with Benefits." The Multiplayer features are about half-optional. You can play offline easily. However you'll be losing a lot of information by doing so. If you're playing offline, you won't be able to see messages or bloodstains. Both of them will warn you of danger, and tell you of secrets you might want to poke your head in at.
The tradeoff for that information is the ability to be invaded by other players, but invasions are realtively uncommon in my experience. If you're worried about them, join the Apostles of Blue Covenant and wear the ring. That will give you good odds of having a Sentinel of Blue Covenant member "counter-invade" your game to help you fight off the other invader.
That's all I've got for you guys. Good luck, and Praise the Sun.

I believe that I owe this game a review, though I feel that it won't be quite justified for me to write a review till I've clocked a certain ammount of time in this game. Alright, here goes.
Yes, you die. You always die, and that's the first thing you will know. You die more than taking a sip of water from your cup. You will die from stepping into some unknown hole which sucks you in like a vortex. You will die when some idiot pokes you at the back with a sword too big for him. You will die when something rolls towards you and you touches it. You will die from poison, bleeding, curses, idiot teammates ...
Dying is the everyday life of Dark Souls™ II, like breathing or, more importantly, searching for usable wifi. Of course, no one wants to die, because after dying, you will become a hollow when you respawn.
Staying alive in Dark Souls™ II is more important than it seems. The main reason is that you can summon other players into your world only when you are human, and this is extremely important. There are other reasons as well, such as you will turn into an ugly old hag when you are hollowfied, and your skin will start to turn saggy, your hair will start to fall ... ... ...
Everyone dies. No one who ever played this game will not die once in a while. So, how do you turn back into human? There are two ways. One is to use an item known as Human Effigy. There are't many of those, so don't burn them up. Another is to help another player by allowing them to summon you to their world and help them with tasks (mostly boss fighting). This is a great way to maintain a supply of "people waiting to be summoned" for boss fights.
Multiplayer is a big aspect of the game. There are two types: coop or versus. In coop, you can summon up to two dudes or dudettes to help you in your quest of staying alive. These players will help you to fight a boss, and once the boss is down, they will be gone and turn back into humans again (if they aren't already are). In versus, some random scoundrel will come into your world to kick you in the nuts so that you will turn into a hollow. Meaning, they will invade your world and try and kill you. Sucks, right?
The first thing you will learn from playing this game is that solo-ing can be quite difficult. It is always good to have a friend or two to fight along side you. It took me more than 30 tries to kill one of the first few bosses when i try and solo him. Well, I did manage to kill him, but that's not really worth the effort and time in my honest opinion. Having a friend, especially when he or she is of an other class, will be extremely critical and helpful. I, a sorcerer, would really like some meat shields to tank bosses' dammages while I nuke them with whatsoever I have. Also, if someone scoundrel invades your world while you have 2 friends with you, he he he ... muahahahahahaha~
Oh and there's an in game item which allows you to filter friends to invite to your world, so, unlike Dark Souls 1, you can actually invite a friend with great ease.
So, do try Dark Souls™ II, and I sincerely hope that you won't start invading my world.

The loot system is a configuration setting on the server, it has 4 modes including full loot. Its a fair statement that our official servers shouldn't all be set to infamy mode, I will spin up some full loot servers and see if the playerbase is there for them.

Edit: After 18 Hours of Playtime.
What can I say about this new gem that has been brought upon us? Hurtworld is going to stay true to its name, this game will hurt you. After playing roughly 18 hours in one session I feel I am capable enough of giving a fair review after what I have experienced.
PROS:
The "Progression System" feels authentic. There's no fast tracking way to reaching the maximum potential right now. Everyone is capable of obtaining the same items no matter if you're a solo player or a group player, but obviously groups are superior on this.
Crafting: The crafting system is easy to learn and with the items you receive/upgrade the benefits are shown easily.
Vehicles: Having vehicles are a luxury and are not in any means easy to come across. The driving inputs are a little awkward and your car may get jammed randomly in objects but they are possible to unbudge and continue.
Combat is fair and brutal: If someone gets the jump on you first, chances are you may go down unless your skills can suffice.
Tools/Essentials kept on death: This is the only Non-Hardcore part I've found about hurtworld. Tools such as Hatchets/Bows/Guns/Pickaxes etc are kept upon death as long as they're binded to your toolbar.
One last thing before we get to the Cons. SLEEPERS AREN'T IN THIS GAME! I've been stressing it since Rust about this issue. Having sleepers in a survival game kills the Solo/Duo community. People have lives, jobs, children and families, There is no way you as a Solo player are going to be able to establish yourself if there's no way of guaranting progress after you log off because some naked with a spear finds your body out in the wild. Thank you for removing this toxic mechanic.
CONS:
Hunger meter: Food is hard to come by even while hunting it seems like you're always hungry and need a bulk of food at all times.
Day/Night cycles: Day and Night together run by too fast when playing, feels like you are getting prepared to go on a journey and right when you are about to leave it's nightfall.
You will not build a base quick, It's difficult to especially as a solo player to establish yourself within your first session (2-4 hours) Luckily whatever's in your posession on logout will be retained due to having no Sleepers.
Population Cap: Personally I believe it's still too low and should be increased to 100/200 per server, but this game's still new and chances will continue to be made.
At the end of all of this, Do I recommend this game? Personally if you're a fan of survival titles and are sick of looking for your perfect match this is the perfect survival title in my opinion. It has every gritty aspect of grinding about in hopes of surviving every day. It's easy to catch on at the start and will keep beating you into the ground every minute you're playing. Even once you are comfortable with your living, you can go outside and get speared down by several players for your loot within seconds.
9.5/10

Hands down the best surviral horror game I've played in a long time. Alien: Isolation had me absolutely terrified at all times, to the point where I'd just insta-quit when I'd get caught by the Alien, only to come back a couple of hours later. Three times did the game broke my morale, whenever I was about to get a jolt of hope, it sent it crashing down moments afterwards. I seriously considered quitting and never touching it again. But I went back, and I conquered my fear.
Alien: Isolation is the first horror game that trolled me and made me feel utterly powerless, even when I found some cool-looking new weaponry. The Alien made me feel like I was hunted and worst, like it litteraly just wanted to toy with me, blocking the correct path and forcing me to stare at it for longer than I'd ever wanted. It's unpredictability became me worst fear and one of the highest merit of the game.
You never know where its going to come from, if it's going to come, and for how long. It may even decide to leave right away, or stay still in order to fool your motion detector. It will come and sniff you through the locker you're hiding in and come back numerous times to your hiding spot, only to disappear, making you believe you could be safe. The alien will end up terrifying you, until you develop this very odd relationship with it, where you'll come to learn the dialog of its hisses, snarls and growls. But this knowledge, you'll learn it the hard way. And you will be terrified.
And yet, this experience made me grow some balls up. Even though my hands were cold and my fingers barely responding, I pressed on. And I did it. As the kind of guy who plays almost everything on the market, I don't recall when I was that satisfied to reach the ending of a game. Not because how the game ended, but just because I had done it. It was exhausting, terrifying and reminded me how the human spirit can get through almost anything under intense pressure.
Props to you, Creative Assembly.
Hope we'll get another ride with you sometimes in the future.

Absent is a largely one-man adventure game project by James Fenton. It's also completely free.
Some obtuse triggers aside that necessitate the average adventure game method of inventory and dialogue spam, Absent doesn't feature any annoying puzzle, they're for the most part straightforward and not unpleasant.
These are all the positive things I have to say about Absent. It's free and not annoying. When it comes to largely one-man indie projects, the compulsion is there to give it more leniency than a game with a larger team, but having been released on Steam it is directly next to the greats of the genre in shelf space and suffers from no dearth of competition.
Absent is an incredibly uninteresting game. There's not much to say about it that isn't a litany of criticisms.
The gameplay isn't even worth mentioning. Made with Adventure Game studio, you can expect nothing but item combinations and rubbing different items on different surfaces. None of the puzzles are noteworthy or interesting.
The art, it has a charming style to it, in a Bob's Burgers kind of way. Characters compete to have their chins recede into their necks and everybody is a winner. It's also incredibly amateur. Character's proportions will nightmarishly shift as they turn, heads warping shape and limbs cracking. Aliased binary pixel art melds anti-aliased smudging like nails on a chalkboard.
Clear inexperience with animation shows as vertical walk cycles turn legs into indecisive jello, and horizontal walk cycles turn into chin high marches. The composition is raggedy, several scenes placing objects in awkward positions, characters general stand with the stiffness of boards (the Reapers in particular may as well be t-posing) and the colour palette looks right out of MS Paint's default selection.
Story is there, but never in danger of being interesting or engrossing. The amount of contrivances, nervously laughing lampshade attempts and incredibly ill-paced exposition immediately nips that in the bud. It feels incredibly "safe", and suffers immensely as a result, terrified of being misinterpreted.
None of the characters are remotely interesting, least of all the Reapers, the central driving force of the game. The murder mystery is resolved "safely", the Reapers are resolved "safely", the entire games ends in a scene so neutered that it looks straight out of a family-friendly cartoon.
If I didn't know any better, I'd say the creator was acutely aware that their parents were going to play the game.
As a side note, the voice-acting wasn't horrible, but delivery was hampered by an awkward script and the microphone quality differences between actors were so palpable I could taste the tinniness.
For an enthusiastic amateur attempt at a videogame, Absent is an admirable attempt. A sentence that would not be said if it were being offered for money. While I'm sure it did amazingly well on enthusiast forums, Absent does not offer anything of value to a consumer-driven market - not to adventure game fans, not to horror/thriller fans, not even to freeware fans.
While it does not ask for your money, Absent isn't particularly worth your time. I don't recommend this title.

I found this game to be an enjoyable experience reminiscent of classic point-and-click adventure games like Monkey Island. This is a game for people that like puzzles and thinking about things from different angles. This kind of game can be frustrating to some as sometimes a very small detail is not obvious and overlooked which will halt your progress.
A few tips when you get stuck would be to make sure you pay close attention to everything the characters say and to the environment around you. Keep a mental map of where you see certain cutscenes happen. If the most obvious path to a goal is not available start by thinking what do I have in my inventory, can I go around, over, under or through this obstacle? Sometimes you have to combine items. One particular puzzle was hard for me to figure out because the logical thing to do in real life would not fit the solution in the game. All I will mention there is the atm card.You really have to think of a different solution on many of these problems. In the end if you really get stuck there are some hints available online.
The voices were done well, the animations look a bit funny but they are not completely out of place for this style of games from the ‘90s. The story imho was well done and it all comes together nicely in the end. I downloaded this game from the free-to-play section here on Steam and to be honest I wasn’t expecting much. In fact I had planned just to play for about 20-30 minutes and then move on to another game. I ended up liking it and kept playing. It starts a bit slow but if you like puzzles and winding story arcs give this game a try. The developer could have charged for it in my opinion.

This game is lots of fun and very addicting! Sank 13h into it in my first 2 days!
Herd slimes, build corrals or ponds for them, build gardens and coops for veggies, fruits or hens to feed your slimes. Slimes when fed drop valuable plorts that can be sold or traded with other Ranchers. Slimes can be fed plorts to make larger hybrid slimes called largos that drop both source plorts. Also slimes have favorite foods, which eaten cause them to drop twice the plorts. Hint, largos can have 2 favorites, but be wary Rancher: not feeding a coral slime long enough will make it feral and cause it to bite you! Fend of the Tarr, monster slimes, that form when a largo eats a second plort! (The Tarr hate fresh water, so once you upgrade your gun with a water tank, keep it loaded from springs or ponds!)
Upgrade your gear and buildings, buy new land for the ranch, including a cave, a small plain and a small lab. SCIENCE! Buy bluebrints, pump and drill the land or extort bees for precious resources! Use these to build teleporters for ease of travel or decorations for your ranch.
Explore the land, find resources out in the wild if a Rancher's work is too hard for ya. Locate and feed gordo slimes, HUGE slimes which have merged from many smaller ones. Once fed enough they will fall apart back to the dozens of small slimes that formed it and possibly reveal a hidden key inside the gordo slime. These can be used to open up new areas for exploration!

Altho it was still great fun like I said earlier so if they release a new patch I'll most likely do another playthrough!

Dishonoured 2 is a cut above Dishonoured and an enjoyable experience with great gameplay.
I decided to play as Corvo at the start, and it feels familiar straight away. Blinking and knocking guards out is heaps of fun.
The environments are more than an art choice, they each have their own characteristics which change the way you play. Furthermore, they feel bigger and more open than in Dishonoured 1. Levels such as 'The Clockwork Mansion' or 'A Crack in the Slab' are so influential that the environments themselves feel like characters. All the levels are stunning too.
I decided to go non-lethal in my first playthrough. While the options have improved, such as dropping down and punching guards, the non-lethal options haven't increased on the scale as say, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided.
Playing as Emily lethal is also very enjoyable. Exploring new powers such as 'domino' makes for a great way to do crowd control, be it through mass assassination or using 1 sleeping dart on 4 guards. The different chaos levels, play styles and characters make for great replayability, and the up-coming 'New Game Plus' while only increase the replayability.
The only real areas for improvement are the story and voice acting.
If you're a fan of Dishonoured, this is a must buy.

If you liked Dishonored, you'll very likely enjoy Dishonored 2. It has the same excellent level design and world building as its predecessor, with improved AI and expanded abilities. Stealth and combat are equally compelling, though the silly morality system remains intact and still punishes you for killing people. There were some performance issues at launch but they've mostly been resolved as of this review. The only part of the game I found disappointing was the story and supporting cast. The story feels predictable and routine whereas the first game had a pretty major twist that turned everything on its head. The first game also had a large and diverse cast of supporting characters with whom you had meaningful interactions and were a large part of why the twist was so effective. As I am writing this I have somewhere around 586 hours of gameplay for this title through Steam.  I would like to point out that all of this gameplay time has been spent on one character; ONE!

We don't even play alts - nope, we play our main characters, every time we get on here; we've sunken all of this gameplay time into a total of two characters: her main and my main... and we STILL have not done everything there is to do.
The DLC's that they have released for ESO are huge, with new crafting motifs, recipies, etc. to learn, as well as different forms of PvP, PLENTY of dugneons, pets, you name it.

I will admit, on initial release ESO was a let down.  As a title to follow Skyrim, this game had a lot to live up to, especially for something which is online.
You have to understand, from a programming and game design perspective, Online and Offline (singleplayer) games are made differently.  Single Player games often have more features than online ones do, mostly because of the constant battle with Polygons which artists must face, and the other constant battle of Server-Client issues which programmers contest through development.
In order to make an online game EXACTLY like Skyrim, it wouldn't be impossibe, but it would be heavily demanding on the users computers, etc.
I go off track though...
This is no longer anything, in my opinion, like it was on its initial release.  This is as close to Skyrim as an MMO could possibly get with balanced gameplay for all, in my opinion, and I love it.  Slowly, one piece at a time, they will have the entirity of Tamriel completed and you'll be able to walk the island of Morrowind, and so on...
If you are an original player from the initial release, come back and give it a try now that SO much has changed.
If you like your Elder Scrolls titles and you have been hesitant to try this because of what you may have heard, IGNORE THE ILL REVIEWS and give it a try for yourself.
What do you have to lose?  There's no monthly subscription.  If you don't like it, add it to the pile of your other steam games which you've purchased and played only once.
I promise you though - You'll become addicted.

I have mixed feeling for Dark Souls 2, but if asked, I would NOT recommend getting Dark Souls 2, sale or no. It eats away at your time, and soul, but no one benefits from that except the Time Played meter.
TL;DR: The game feels as if it is in an unreleasable state. Game mechanics appear broken, effects of high latency on PvP are game-breaking, and it is inconsistent with its own rules and behavior, at the player's expense. The one thing that may save this game is online co-operative play, which is fun and makes the game's virtual unplayability just a bit easier to experience.
Read on to know why this is.
I'll begin with the good, rather than the bad, to avoid going into a rant early:
Online co-operative play is one of two favorable features of Dark Souls 2, the other being the [empty] sense of accomplishment when progressing.
When connected online, you are able to summon other players to your adventure, or to be summoned. While temporary, this lets you go through a particularly difficult area with up to two other players watching your back, or complimenting your character's loadout. The summoning feature is the best and most enjoyable thing the game gives you. Gestures to interact with one another and the ability to fight alongside friends and allies provides camaraderie that should be experienced whenever possible.
The game also has the unique feature of creating a sense that you are not alone in your troubles. Dark Souls does this through the ghostly outlines of fellow players while adventuring. This allows you to see what other players are doing, and may give hints to what new threat is ahead or show you where a secret door is located.
Now to the things that just grind my gears and may very well have pushed me to stop playing:
The game thrives on masochistic behavior, whether you are prone to it or not. You play and continue forging on to beat the game, and when you fail, you must try again. And again. And again.
Death in this game is meant to have you learn from your mistakes, your successes, and to learn how the game works.
But just when you've learned something, that knowledge then becomes useless.
This game praises itself for being difficult, but how is it difficult? Is it hard because the AI is dynamic and advanced? Or maybe damage output is favored towards your enemies? This, unfortunately, is not the case.
The game is difficult because it is inconsistent and, strangely enough, breaks its own rules with no warning or explanation.
It is a shame when you die in this game. All to often you lose a fight because the very things given to you to survive are rendered ineffective. Sometimes at random, sometimes shamelessly floundered about.
As an example, at a certain point, enemies start tracking your character with their attacks, which makes dodging pointless. Their weapons also begin bypassing armor, resistances, and utilized shields, making those virtually useless. Using bows and magic offensively also comes with slow to zero movement while casting, allowing swift (and ambushing) enemies to finish you off in a moment.
And wow. PvP, especially the surprise 'invasion' feature, is a joke. Usually one-sided on the get-go (too often in the invader's favor), the problems mentioned above are worsened threefold. And that's without high latency. It also comes with its own, unique problems, like weapons hitting twice their distance away, and other things that make PvP, which could have been one of the highlights of the game, into something that makes you want to intentionally play offline.
And that, folks, is that. Unless things change, I doubt I will enjoy what could have been a great game, but truly may be the worst.

Fairly well executed spiritual successor of Alien 1 movie. It is dark, terrifying, slow-paced. The lighting and environments are some of the finest computer generated game graphics I've seen to date. All the visuals serve to keep immersion sky-high. The alien is also gorgeous, and in this game you will see and hear plenty of it.
The immersion is great enough that after a gaming session, all stomping noises in the neighborhood are going to cause you to immediately evaluate your neighborhood for hiding places and figure out where the vents are so you know which places are especially dangerous to be in.
Playstyle is almost completely stealth based. It mostly runs with a few tropes, like being locked in a mazelike environment with the alien with the goal to push various buttons and pull various switches while evading it. There are also stealth sections where the Alien hunts the player but usually doesn't make an appearance unless the player first makes some msitake. Overall, the game is ideal for the patient people who like exclusively stealth-based gamestyle, and have cold, calculating nerves to gauge the risks in a dynamically changing situation, and know how to react. The game is forced into stealth mode because the alien can not be harmed by weapons provided. Nevertheless, there are some fire-based weapons that cause the alien to run away and hide if the player chooses to attack it with them.
I in particular enjoy the hiding-in-the-cabinet mechanic, where it's not enough to just go inside a cabinet to be undetectable. The alien will still hear your breathing unless you choose to hold it (but you can't do it for very long) and may see you if it chooses to peer inside, unless you immediately move further away from the door. These simple devices enhance the stealth experience enormously and keep you at your toes, where other games have erred in making cabinet hiding 100% safe.
The game, unfortunately, suffers from its second half that feel grafted on, on top of almost impeccable beginning. At halfway point, the game starts to get FPS-like elements such as plenty of ammo and enemies you need to shoot with standard gallery of weapons such as pistols and shotguns. Even more worryingly, there is a severe problem with the Alien eggs in this game, which any Aliens fan is sure to notice. There is also no satisfying conclusion, so the narrative just breaks in an obvious DLC/sequel bait. These mistakes significantly degrade the experience. In this reviewer's head-cannon, the game simply ends at its peak on the first half. The rest was simply unnecessary crap piled on top of well thought out and executed sequel/reinvigoration of the alien of the first movie.

The one complaint I always had with existing MOBAs was, that there is no point in having a strategic simulator view of the characters and indirectly clicking their walking path and attacks. SMITE solves the issue flawlessly, bringing real direct action into the MOBA genre.
The problem with SMITE for me is the matchmaking. I thought I felt, that they have a separate matching for the really low levels, but once I reached level 5 or so, which happened fast, I was matched against pre-mades of 5 with 5 solo queuers, or matched against players with hundreds of games played, as someone who plays his 20th round. This can't work. I also did have an amount of fairly balanced matches though.

This game is lots of fun and very addicting! Sank 13h into it in my first 2 days!
Herd slimes, build corrals or ponds for them, build gardens and coops for veggies, fruits or hens to feed your slimes. Slimes when fed drop valuable plorts that can be sold or traded with other Ranchers. Slimes can be fed plorts to make larger hybrid slimes called largos that drop both source plorts. Also slimes have favorite foods, which eaten cause them to drop twice the plorts. Hint, largos can have 2 favorites, but be wary Rancher: not feeding a coral slime long enough will make it feral and cause it to bite you! Fend of the Tarr, monster slimes, that form when a largo eats a second plort! (The Tarr hate fresh water, so once you upgrade your gun with a water tank, keep it loaded from springs or ponds!)
Upgrade your gear and buildings, buy new land for the ranch, including a cave, a small plain and a small lab. SCIENCE! Buy bluebrints, pump and drill the land or extort bees for precious resources! Use these to build teleporters for ease of travel or decorations for your ranch.
Explore the land, find resources out in the wild if a Rancher's work is too hard for ya. Locate and feed gordo slimes, HUGE slimes which have merged from many smaller ones. Once fed enough they will fall apart back to the dozens of small slimes that formed it and possibly reveal a hidden key inside the gordo slime. These can be used to open up new areas for exploration!

Quick wikia read showed there isn't anything more in the treasure pods that peaked my interest and customizing my ranch and slimes appearence wasn't making me excited.
Altho it was still great fun like I said earlier so if they release a new patch I'll most likely do another playthrough!

No More Room in Hell is a great game that is both enjoyed and hated by many and I am here to tell you why.
Basically, this game is about surviving in a zombie apocalypse. The game is made to be creepy and when you start to play, you could understand that it is one of those play in the dark games. This is a great game to play with friends concidering that many aspects of the game revolves around teamwork. Trust me, it is close to impossible to survive for long without a friend or two. It's pretty easy to host a server if you know how to port forward and servers can fit up to 16 people, so this makes thisgame a great co-op experience.
There are a lot of things I need to get through in this review so I will try to summarize it as best as possible. Let's start with zombies. There are 2 types of zombies. There are the normal slow walking zombies. These guys have a decent amount of health but can be killed easily with a good enough weapon. The other type of zombie is referred to as a runner. These are the most annoying pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥that you will ever meet. Although they have low health, they run faster than you and when in groups, they can be deadly. There are also child zombies which is a rare spawn. I think these are the most annoying since they are all runners but their hitbox is smaller. As usual, the head is the most sensitive spot on a zombie's body. Zombie bites are what make this game classified as "hardcore". Basically, if you get bit, there is nothing you can do. You can never be cured and eventually turn into a zombie. The only thing that can help you is a special pill you can find in the map. The pill doesn't actually cure you, but it prolongs your life before you turn. If you are bit and die (from something else) you will turn into a zombie anyway. When you turn, you go into spectate mode. All players who turn become runners (this can be annoying, but a good prank too). Gun choices are fairly limited and you do not start with them. Ammo is limited. Your character is a preset and nobody is unique. There are 2 main types of game modes. Survival and objective. Survival is basically just waves of zombies and you need to defend yourself but keep your bases health up too. Objective is when there are no bases, zombies keep spawning, and the gaem gives you random objectives to follow and eventually you can win.
If you already read this far, congratulations! Now I will talk about the pros and cons.
- Small download
- Little to no lag even on low-end computers
- Can play on Mac
- Teamwork oriented
- Different roles (stay in base, go on runs for supplies, etc.)
- Up to 16 people can play at once
- Great game to play with friends
- Decent graphics (same engine as TF2)
- Few to no advertisements and micro-transactions (depends on server)
- Many maps to choose from (lots of community made ones)
- Suicide option
- Optional friendly-fire (for deathmatch style)
- Overall friendly community
- No tutorial, just plops you into the game
- You will die a lot when you are a noob
- Bites can be annoying if you can not find pills
- Too hard when played solo
- Can get repetitive if no gameplay changes are made
- Learning curve
- Bugs (as every game, but only few)
- No info on what icons mean
- Can be creepy (some can argue this is a good thing)
Overall, this is a great game to play with friends. It can get boring after a while but during the time I played it, I was always having a great time. My favourite thing to do was purposely get bit and follow my friend around. Then when I turn  into a zombie, he doesn't see it coming and dies. Many things you can do in this game if you just be creative. I would rate this game a 7/10.

This is a remake done right, it respects it's source material and improves upon it greatly.
I'm a big fan of the original Half-Life, as are most if not all people interested in this remake I guess, my expectations were high.. and pretty much all of them were met or even exceeded.
This isn't just Half-Life with HD textures slapped onto it, this is a total remake that has been in the making since 2005, you have to respect the developers for passionately working on the mod for that long, that alone deserves supporting them by buying this game in my opinion.
If you've played original, the levels will feel familiar but fresh thanks to the heavily upgraded visuals, additions of some new areas and even a new soundtrack which is outstanding too.
Some areas have been tweaked to improve gameplay, the most apparent example of this would be the chapter 'on a rail' which no longer has you going in circles several times, though the old version is downloadable from the workshop.
Another thing that felt is worth noting as a huge improvement is the fact that the scientists and guards no longer feel like robots, but more like actual people stuck in the same mess as you with more dialogue and emotions.
However, the game is still in early access, the final chapters of the game which are set in the Xen borderworld are still missing, but I trust the developers to finish those too, I doubt they'd call it quits after all this time and having come so far.
So, is Black Mesa worth your money? absolutely, I had a blast revisiting Black Mesa, and I'm absolutely pumped for Xen!

I'm going to start this with a statement that Half Life was never among my favourite games. That is not to say it isn't a milestone in game design - far from it, HL 1 was actually one of the DEFINING games of the late 90's. Probably the first game that tells a story without cutting any corners, Half Life to me is like a diamond waiting to be cut, it's what kickstarted the genre. Duke Nukem and Quake were there before it, but not a single one of those was as immersive, as "alive", as content-filled and believable.
Now, the undisputed king of all 3D FPS games to me is Unreal. But that comparison wouldn't be overly fair. There is infinitely more sexiness in alien vistas where no man has trodden before (or so you think when you (crash-)land in Na Pali for the first time, than in decaying concrete buildings and scrapped experiments where man has already done plenty enough. Still, both games by any standard, especially when compared to what we are used to having today, are MASSIVE. There is so much "terrain" to cross, so many places to visit, and all that was done with high enough fidelity to let players feel what Mr. Freeman felt (perhaps, except for the sticky tongue of a barnacle, but those things still give me the creeps).
Now both these games have aged, and would hardly elicit the smile in a modern player like they did back then. Half Life got lucky, however, in this remastering. I am glad indeed that more and more "classic" games are being remastered, re-released today for new folks to enjoy them, but what always worries me is the "quality" of those remakes. Often the publisher thinks perfection can be "improved" by integrating some new mechanics... ugh!
This particular release is as true to the original as any could ever be. In fact, I do remember a few differences between the old game, and the new one. But it is not something that bothers me too much, far from it. It IS Half-Life 1 where it counts. And it's gorgeous (at least, it wouldn't feel ashamed next to Bioshock graphics, and, seriously, does anyone need Crysis level graphics in a game that spends most of its time in concrete halls and near strange shiny green liquids?
Yes, if you pay close attention to level design, you'll see just how low poly all of them are. But then look around you next time you're in some underground parking lot. Are those shapes complex? You don't notice any lack of fidelity, because most of the places Mr. Freeman visits aren't really palace party halls, those are functional, simple, and, until recently, were being used for practical things. Enough about graphics. Those are sufficient and do not get in the way of enjoying the game.
As some other reviewers mentioned here, this is one of the first cutscene-less games that manages to tell a story. No extra reading needed, you get to see (and hear) everything through the eyes of your character. Speaking of which, I often hear Bioshock Infinite criticized for not having the option for a female character. Black Mesa will not give one to you either. In case of the former it's the setting - there was no way someone would send a female detective (there weren't any) in Bioshock's time. In case of the latter, Half Life 1 had Gordon Freeman, and so shall Black Mesa. There simply can't be someone else in this game, male or female (or alien, for that matter).
It is a great game by all accounts, but it is not quite finished yet. So expect some quirks. It is also trying to be as close to the original as possible, so expect some more quirks that the original had. Ladders *cough cough. Those are actually worse than I remember. Textures here and there aren't fully uprezzed (or they need another pass). If you are the kind of player that gets disappointed by game glitches or other deficiencies, wait for release. If you can tolerate these, don't think twice, grab this. Whether to take a nostalgic tour in what gaming was at its finest, or to simply have a break from CoD-style drivel, you owe it to yourself to give this a try.

I hated the first Dark Souls. The camera was awful and the multiplayer was married to godawful Games for Windows Live. The monsters would use attacks that you had no way to anticipate. It was a chore and I didn't finish it.
Dark Souls II, however, was absolutely wonderful.
All issues from the previous game are fixed. Instead of trial and error, the game rewards smart and cooperative play.  This game then becomes the game that the first game promised to be, mainly a challenging Metroidvania style dungeon crawler with unforgiving (but fair) enemies. Exploration, backtracking and mental mapping the area are all rewarded.
Even the things you would think you would hate, mainly Invaders, actually end up being surprisingly fun. Taking out some slob with a giant sword with good positioning and manuevers is really quite satisfying and, even when they get you, it's not like it's the end of the world. You can easily restore your humanity via the co-op system and souls can be easily recovered if you play smart. And there's a covenent for those who crave the old ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t 'real gamers have no friends' system, so the neckbeards can hardly even complain.
Will you die? Sure. Will you swear at the screen? Yep. But it's never stupidly hard and you never are killed by something you couldn't have seen coming.
The story is also surprisingly compelling once you get in on it. The Emerald Herald is a fascinating character, while some of the little characters you meet like Lucatiel of Mirrah are genuinely moving personalities. It's less grim and morose than the first game, which is fine by me as the first game's tone was so heavy that I found it to be pretty inaccessible in terms of narrative.
Whatever the case, the game is highly compelling. Five stars. Will probably do New Game + later on.

If you are looking for an easy experience, a game you can run through with ease, then this game is not for you. You will die. A lot. And it feels like a fresh break from the more casual games that are coming out these days, and a throwback to the challenging old school games, like Ninja Gaiden, where you learned from death and victory wasn't assured.
Many people were worried that Dark Souls II would be a lot more casual than its predecessor, and I can assure you, it's not. It manages to be just as challenging, while still being more accessible for beginners. There are changes that make the game more convenient, such as bonfire teleportation from the beginning of game. Combat in the game is improved, and is as fun as ever. One thing I wasn't a fan of was the large enemy mob encounters. Encountering groups of large enemies is more irritating than challenging, causing the player to go out of their way to use tactics they normally wouldn't. The boss fights are unique, and are some of the coolest parts of the game.
Unlike the first, I played through the entire game with keyboard + mouse, definitely and accomplishment for a Souls game, the graphics are also massively improved.
The story is great, although it doesn't pop out at you, but that doesn't matter in a game that is based so strongly on gameplay. The story lies in the lore of the world. While it definitely isn't as good as in the original, the world connects in interesting and cool ways.
Covenants are expanded in such great ways and make the multiplayer a strong point of the game. PvP is very, very fun, although the hitboxes and connection keep it from being perfect. With the improvement of online play also comes the improvement of co-op (Sunbros rejoice!)
While better than and worse than the first game in certain aspects, it is a highly rewarding blast of a game that will challenge you, and give you hours of fun. 10/10 from me.

If you're looking for a sort of "zen" game that you can sink plenty of time into on a casual basis, then Slime Rancher is for you.
As the name implies, your goal is to catch and raise Slimes and make money off of them. There are plenty of different slime types although 4 are available to you right off (Pink, Rock, Tabby, and Phosphoro)  with more becoming available to you as you unlock different areas. Naturally you need to keep your slimes fed or otherwise they'll bounce out of their corrals in search of food.
Some advice for beginners.
First, don't be afraid to breed Tabby Slimes with Pink Slimes to make Pink Tabby Largos (Largos are big hybrid slimes), the Pink Slimes will eat any food given to them which will come in handy as breeding meat (i.e. Chickens) is a bit of a chore and growing fruits and veggies are much easier and more sustainable in the long run. The same can be applied to the other carnivorous slimes as breeding them with herbavores or the omnivorus pinks can allow you to focus your food growth efforts to strictly fruits and vegitables which can be more cost effective, especially once you unlock the area to the immediate east of your ranch which has chickens, carrots, and pogofruit growing naturally and keep you constantly supplied with all three basic foods for your slimes if tended too properly.
Second, try to upgrade your corralls to the max (you can safely exclude the music box and solar shields for most corrals though if you're penny pinching) especially the plort collector (Plorts get you currency and allow you to breed slimes into largos) and this makes it easier to collect the plorts without accidently sucking up your slimes and having to fire them back into the corral.
Third, NEVER put more than TWO types of slime in the corrals. If a largo eats a plort that's neither one of its base slimes (i.e. a pink rock largo eats a tabby plort) it WILL become a Tarr (an evil eat-all slime) and can quickly leave you having to run and collect new slimes to replace the ones you lost. Worst case scenario, you lose all your slimes, including the harder to get ones. Tarrs can be killed with water so buy the water tank upgrade for your gun early on and keep it filled with water when you can.
Fourth, don't bother trying to capture the super rare Lucky or Golden slimes. You can't, game says no.
Fifth, don't make your corrals too full of slimes. The Slimes will eventually get too hungry and bounce out in spite of the air net and higher wall upgrades.
Now, as this is Early Access, there is some room for improvement. Gameplay wise, I think most of the bugs have been fixed but there are some suggestions would be helpful so if the developers are reading this, I'd encourage you to read the following suggestions.
General options: An option to sell upgraded ranch equipment (i.e. corral upgrades) for partial refunds would be helpful in a pinch. Namely, the ability to sell the solar shield upgrade on a corral when the slimes inside do not need protection from sunlight would be a good option.
Farm Plots: Farming for food is a very useful feature but even the plots could use some improvement. Two optional upgrades would be beneficial. The first would be an autoharvester which would suction all of the food and store it for pick up so that the plot can get to work on the next harvest as well as keep the food from going bad. A sort of mini-silo if you will. Second, an upgrade that eliminates the need to constantly re-seed the plot. The plots, as they are right now, only last for a few yields before dying off and having to be replanted. This can be problematic if you're growing rair foods like Heartbeats, Phase Lemons, Mint Mangos, and Odd Onions as you might end up running completely out and having to go hunt for them. An upgrade that makes the plots grow continuously until you decide to change what's grown would not go amiss.
Chicken Coops: At the moment, these are arguably the most useless features short of the incinerator in the game at the moment that i can tell. It's hard to tell if the chickens are indeed breeding as I never see any eggs and only occasionally see a few chicks peeping around. The higher wall upgrade, by the way, for the coop is useless as a hungry slime can still bounce right into the coop and consume your stock of chickens. I would suggest some kind of a roof for the coop or something more effective at keeping the slimes away. One upgrade I would recommend would probably be a sort of cloning feature which regularly produces whichever chicken breed is put into it much like the farm plots do.
Pools: The only place you can keep Puddle Slimes should also use a few upgrades. Third upgrades come to mind. First is a plort collector since, every time I collect the puddle slime plorts, I end up collecting the slimes as well and having to put them back in the pool. Another upgrade would be a fountain which would keep the water level steady and give you a place to easily replenish your water tanks for combating Tarrs without draining the pools of their water. Finally a third upgrade for the pool would be something that will help the shy puddle slimes feel less shy while in the pool (they won't produce plorts when around too many other slimes, including other puddle slimes so roughly 4 puddle slimes per pool at the moment). This upgrade would allow you to put more puddle slimes into the pool at a time.
Corrals: only one upgrade that I can think of for the corrals would be handy and that would be a "hazard shield" of some kind. Boom, Rad, Rock, and Crystal slimes have a nasty tendancy to damage you if you get too close, and that can be intentional (in the case of Rock and Crystal slimes) or accidental (in the case of boom and rad slimes) so a hazard shield that prevents them from harming you or anything outside their corrals would be helpful. I would recommend these shields also make it harder for the Quantum slimes to teleport out but that's not as big of an issue if managed correctly. The rock and crystal slimes will attack and damage you regardless of their moods while Rad slimes irradiate you if you get too close for too long so the shields should make getting closer much easier.
Odd Onions: So basically if you plant an Odd Onion in a farm plot, you get carrots with maybe two or three onions per yield. More onions per harvest would be welcome.
Gold and Lucky Slimes: these slimes are presently unable to be caught. Making them catchable, albeit with a high difficulty in keeping corraled would be a good addition. For instance, give the Gold Slime a high bounce when agitated and hungry so it bounces right out of the corral and then disappears if not tended too properly. Or both could simply disappear if left unattended or uncared for for too long. A good rancher with fully upgraded corrals should be able to contain them provided they have enough food. Make them picky eaters so that they will only eat one specific and hard to find food like the Phase Lemon. Make breeding them with another slime (like the pink) automatically turn them into that slime (non largo) and kill off the benefit of producing their rare plorts.
Naturally more slimes and areas would be a good addition along with more expansions to the ranch itself. Also if a teleporter from the lab expansion to the newly released ruins area (blocked by a Quantum guado perhaps?) could be added, that would be good for quick travel.
I would also like to take the opportunity and pitch a sort of marine slime, not like the puddle slime, but one that swims in the ocean and requires a special water filled corral to be kept in.
Also, if business is good enough, I'd recommend selling plushies of the various slimes. That'd be a money maker.
Anyway, that's all that I can think of. I eagerly await the next update. I highly recommend this game though to anyone and everyone.

Black Mesa is a modern remake of Half-Life, which started out as an ambitious mod and has been released as a fully fledged, standalone game, Currently in Early Access the developers have committed to continued support and bringing the final Xen levels that were missing from the mod. As it is set before Half-Life 2, Black Mesa follows the events that occurred to bring the Combine to Earth in the second game. It is part horror and part full blown action.
Black Mesa, as a mod, always had a rough ride in getting over the final hurdle. Changes in engine, team members, and the sheer pace in which modern games have evolved makes it an accomplishment that the mod was released and for free. They have now released their game on Steam and with a deathmatch component which is hoping to bring new players a small slice of what Half-Life Deathmatch was like. The retail version is running on a hybrid of Source engines so contains changes that aren't backwards compatible with the mod version. Most of the changes are subtle improvements in lighting, more stability and bugfixes, but also integration with Steamworks. Already there are new DM maps and mods for Black Mesa in the Steam Workshop which add to the experience.
Black Mesa is pretty comparible to other retail games. It has a good level of polish overall but has a few odd blemishes along the way. I think it is safe to say the Black Mesa, as the title suggests, is about the facility. The level of detail and focus put on the actual environment is very impressive. The machinery and laboritories are the best elements of the game. There is some equipment which is expertly modeled. When you see it in motion with the sound effects it is quite a sight. Overall the sound design is good, voice acting is well done with improvements to the HECU (marines) but there are some voices that are out of place. In some places Black Mesa also feels deathly quiet or slightly muffled with only an air con unit humming or a distant thumping. In Half-Life, sound was used to announce danger, so the HECU would be overly loud on their radios or the Vortigaunts would be gargling away. Yes, in Half-Life it was over the top but it made the game feel punchy. In places Black Mesa has no impact and I think it is down to the sound.
The AI have been reworked since the mod, so no more HECU soldiers sniping you with aimbot machine guns, and the aliens attacks have a bit more delay to them. However the developers seemed to have dialed them down too much to the point where the soldiers are almost pacifistic at times. They seemed to be scripted to hold back or huddle up. Some encounters I've seen them run back and forth between a rock and concrete block whilst I stood doing nothing. It is jarring and some battles become a duck shoot. The AI needs more work as it has turned the alien grunts and HECU into slightly timid enemies when they should be threats. On the other hand the assassins in game are agile but cause too much damage. This is being addressed by the developers but the levels with those enemies are almost unplayable. Its a shame as the enemy AI overall ranges from good (houndeyes and bullsquids) to bad (Ichthyosaur and alien grunts).
The set pieces in the game are still enjoyable and some are better than Half-Life. Most of the unforgiving insta-death moments in Half-Life are gone, but Black Mesa is still a lethal trial and error game in places. The On a Rail chapter is no longer a winding maze of rails and the Questionable Ethics and Lambda Core levels are really well done. Its a bit strange that with these improvements levels such as Residual Processing is still a bore and riding conveyor belts around with steep falls is plainly not fun. Surface Tension is also cut down so there is no sense of retreat by the HECU.
Deathmatch is in its early stages but a fun, chaotic, game which is more closer to HL2:DM than HL:DM. Olders players are complaining of the reduced movement but for me it is a fun distraction for a hour or two. Weapons are all solid and meaty and using the experimental weapons is still a lot of fun. Its death match so takes a lot of practice before you feel any ounce of skill.
How you view the entire package falls down if you have followed the development or not. If you have followed the project for a long time and want to award the devs for releasing the mod for free, then buy it on Steam. If you have been following the project and just want to play Xen then for now stick to the free mod version and wait. If you have not followed the project then I would suggest trying the free version for now as this is still being worked on.
I would recommend it based on the quality of other released games, however it is not Half Life, and needs tweaking. Let it mature a bit. The developers are still working on upgrading textures, tweaking multi-player and eventually bringing out Xen. I think it will be a few more years but hopefully a small monetary incentive will help them.

After three playthroughs and half way into my fourth I'd say this is my game of the year. I had some problems with performance at first but when running at medium preset setting everything was fine. Now with the patches I can run everything on high without any problems. Love this game and the story line is equally as good if not better than the original. Playing The Knife of Dunwall & Brigmore Witches DLC for the first Dishonored really adds to the experience.

Finally running fine after the 1.2 patch. It's quite a good game but at the end of the day it doesn't really improve on the first in any respect other than the engine and the scope of some of the levels. There have been a lot of mid-to-high-budget sequels to critical darlings landing with a thud in 2016 (Mirror's Edge, Deus Ex, XCom, Dark Souls, Uncharted, Watch Dogs, this), and while some of them are a lot better than others (Titanfall), I'm not sure this elevates itself beyond the rest of the pack. Like the first (and most Bethesda games), it still feels occasionally like you're playing as a camera on a stick in a world full of dopamine levers; the AI is fun to manipulate, but the whole thing is so messy and quicksave-y. As a stealth game I don't think it's as interesting (or as well-written) as the new Hitman, and while the narrativity of the levels themselves is great, the overarching plot is a step down from first Dishonored.
It's nice that the art design is less derivative of Half-Life 2 this time though :)
You know when a game looks absolutely beautiful at Ultra Settings, but you can't play at Ultra settings because the PC port is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Yeah, I do.

A number of people have commented on the technical issues plaguing the game - I won't touch those because it has already been beaten to death. Suffice it to say that even on a completely overpowered computer, there were periods of frame stuttering and what felt like delayed inputs. Graphics are so so for a game in late 2016.
Moving on from that, this game just isn't good in my opinion. They had an established universe to pull from and got lazy. The story is a cliched joke and feels extremely rushed the entire game. The Outsider is irrelevant and basically serves as a hint mechanism in the levels as to alternate eliminations. There are nearly no "side quest" things to do of any importance. Taking my time and exploring levels, reloading a lot to perfect the stealth approach, etc and my total playtime is < 20 hours.
There is no character development. I had no idea who / what / where I was going most of the time outside of "go here and do this". I had no attachment to anything - no choices seemed to matter except for the returning low / high chaos system. The "main crew" in the game might as well be cardboard cutouts - by the end of the game I didn't know anything about them or their motives. There are a few things you can find if you look hard enough (some letters and diaries), but even that is paltry.
A lot of things just aren't explained at all. During reload screens in the last level I was still reading those misc hints and thinking "Holy crap, I can do X? Why didn't they tell me I could do X at ANY POINT IN THIS GAME?!" More of the rushed atmosphere I guess.
The ending (no spoilers) left me puzzled. At one point I was convinced the game had glitched but there was a non obvious thing that had to be done. The ending sequence is about 20s long and adds absolutely nothing but re-stating the choices you make in the game.
It's a shame, too. The world of Dishonored is very interesting, and the whole Outsider concept could be explored a lot. I was hopefully for a moment in one of the later quests when you start to learn a bit about him, but it's over extremely fast.
As it stands though, the game is just awkward. I'd generously give it a 7/10. It certainly has its moments, and when it works it is pretty cool. If you want to blink around and do cool combo kills or whatever - this game might be right up your alley. If you're looking for a good story and an immersive world, you should probably look elsewhere.

Alien Isolation > Aliens: Colonial Marines.
You would think that the first statement should be enough, but it's not. So many people bitter from the travesty that was Aliens: Colonial Marines are directing their hatred towards Alien Isolation.
As was obvious from the first 5 minutes of gameplay, Alien Isolation is a beautifully created labor of love. They took great care in keeping as close to the source material as possible. The sounds, the sights and the beautifully terrifying alien did their job to completely immerse the player into a world that is far from pleasant. Alien Isolation also treats the canon of Alien sacred which is shown with the Alien killing you in a single stroke. Why people complain about it being fast, one-hit-kill, is beyond me. Have you not seen the movie?
I'm not going to touch on every little thing but the fact is, Alien Isolation is the best game to come from this franchise to date. Is it perfect? Certainly not, but I love it and will continue to play it. Let's hope that this is only a glimpse of more amazing work to come.

If you are looking for an easy experience, a game you can run through with ease, then this game is not for you. You will die. A lot. And it feels like a fresh break from the more casual games that are coming out these days, and a throwback to the challenging old school games, like Ninja Gaiden, where you learned from death and victory wasn't assured.
Many people were worried that Dark Souls II would be a lot more casual than its predecessor, and I can assure you, it's not. It manages to be just as challenging, while still being more accessible for beginners. There are changes that make the game more convenient, such as bonfire teleportation from the beginning of game. Combat in the game is improved, and is as fun as ever. One thing I wasn't a fan of was the large enemy mob encounters. Encountering groups of large enemies is more irritating than challenging, causing the player to go out of their way to use tactics they normally wouldn't. The boss fights are unique, and are some of the coolest parts of the game.
Unlike the first, I played through the entire game with keyboard + mouse, definitely and accomplishment for a Souls game, the graphics are also massively improved.
The story is great, although it doesn't pop out at you, but that doesn't matter in a game that is based so strongly on gameplay. The story lies in the lore of the world. While it definitely isn't as good as in the original, the world connects in interesting and cool ways.
Covenants are expanded in such great ways and make the multiplayer a strong point of the game. PvP is very, very fun, although the hitboxes and connection keep it from being perfect. With the improvement of online play also comes the improvement of co-op (Sunbros rejoice!)
While better than and worse than the first game in certain aspects, it is a highly rewarding blast of a game that will challenge you, and give you hours of fun. 10/10 from me.

I can safely recommend this title. It took me roughly 43-45 hours to beat the main story on new game, medium melee build with high stamina, strength, and poise. Only used coop on some of the bosses (3-4) that presented difficulty, such as the smelter demon where I had little flame resistance.
This was my first souls experience. I have dark souls sitting on my hard drive, but I clearly enjoy dark souls 2 a bit more considering it is a much better port then dark souls. I played the entire way through the game with a keyboard and mouse, and so the port was altogether fine for me. I'm not gonna lie and say the kb+m is perfect, because it isn't. Hopefully from can work a bit more with bindings in the next game, but kb+m is doable.
The gameplay is a bit interesting, but with flaws, and the combat is enjoyable, something most fans really put emphasis on. Outside of some stupid hitboxes and the camera lock on being a bit funky in some areas, I would give the combat a solid 9/10.
Some mentioned bosses that were less memorable then others. While this is true, there were bosses I won't forget for a while. The Lost Sinner, Old Smeltie, and the Giant Lord in particular were some that were quite memorable. Final Boss was fairly easy assuming you go in there with the right loadout.
Lore was very good, and the references to the last game were all there. Something something praise the sun.
Music was memorable. Majula is a very memorable theme along with the final boss's theme.
Pro's:
-Solid Combat
-Much better port then souls, will probably be even better in future updates.
-PvP
-Memorable bosses and areas
-Interesting lore
-Beautiful art direction
-Music is great
-Challenging, the curse and limited number of effigies
Cons
- camera and lock on issues
- few and between hitbox issues (most notably, some bosses with high range swings, like vendrick). Rumor has it the optional boss Ancient Dragon which I never fought has some really bad ones.
- Some bonfires are too close, taking some challenge away.
Final Score:
I would give it a 9.1/10. Not perfect, but it is worth the purchase. I will without a doubt play new game+ and make new builds for new characters.
