I won't get much into technical details, because i can't consider myself an experienced MMO player. I've tried playing several MMO's in my life, though i couldn't really internalize these games. Speaking in terms of abstraction, i couldn't help but see floating green letters and numbers of Matrix in them. The universes seemed contructed, artificial. I know they are contructed; maybe even our real universe is :) But ours succeeds to make us overlook this fact. That is what ESO succeeded for me too when i logged into its universe. This game is an MMO which doesn't feel like one. When i was roaming in Skyrim (i mean as game), i was feeling i am really there. The ambience was so tense that i didn't want to come back at times to our own universe. ESO is pretty much the same for me.
As for the technical details, first of all you don't need to click and hold on the right mouse button to look around. I don't know why but this is an important detail for me :) All the crafting opportunities offered by Skyrim have been multiplied and multiplied in this game and i have never seen a skill customization that gives you so much variety options. Probably no two players have the same skill tree.
But yet again, what really struck me is the ambience of this game. The first moment i bought a mount, i started to ride it. That moment i saw a thunder sruck in the horizon and it started to rain thereafter. That was one of the moments in my life that i didn't want to log off back into the universe i am actually living. But it was almost dawn here and i had to :)
If what matters to me matters to you as well, i would of course recommend this game to you. At least it made me write my first review on Steam :) Have fun guys ;)

EDIT 2015-12-03
Let me start by saying that although a beautiful rendition of the original, Black Mesa, when it first came out wasn't something that I was too fond of. It felt unbalanced and overall pretty underwhelming.
However, the updated version is something I loved from start to finish. Take it with the grain of salt though, because there may be some bias here, as it's much easier to criticize a free mod than a game for which I've spent 20 bucks on.
That taken out of the way, Black Mesa in its current state is a good if not great re-imagining of the original game. What was the most enjoyable part about this was the gunplay - most of the weapons were revamped and feel much more solid now. They even managed to fix the crowbar. And, surprisingly, I find the MP5 to be much more enjoyable here than in the original, because I hate how ineffective it feels in the predecessor. Other weapons roster was balanced and tweeked very nicely and at times I felt like playing the original - fast switching weapons in certain situations really captured the spirit of Half-Life, though here it felt much more fast paced. Vortigaunts are still as annoying though. Soldiers AI is better than in HL1, but that's to be expected as HL2 had pretty solid one. Still a bit buggy at places, but it isn't as cheap as in the original. Also, good thing they shortened the On Rail segment. To me, it felt like it overstayed its welcome there.
Graphically speaking, the game is an eye candy. Considering how old the Source Engine is, this rendition is nothing short of spectacular. And with all the fancy upgrades, it still runs relatively well. Loading times may be longer to what we're used to in Source, but that is to be expected when the maps are this lush and detailed.
However, there are some negatives - some places of the game were changed for the worst, some parts outright ignored. Remember the part in the garage that goes between Soldier fight against Aliens and the escape from Gargantua? The cut Surface Tension area? It's not here. Hopefully, uncut material will be added later in the Workshop.
Some parts were simplified for the worst. And other parts are just plain bloody cheap. The assassins sections have to be the worst I've played so far. Here it was way worse than it was in the original Half-Life. Developers made assassins pretty much into Godesses, those ♥♥♥♥♥es could hit me with 100% accuracy while doing bloody acrobatics. Took my life of 100HP and 100P to plain zeroes in the matter of seconds. This absolutely needs fixing, because it wasn't challenging, it was excruciatingly cheap.
Also, platforming sections need a bit of fixing, as at some places jumping bugs out (havoc physics and jumping mechanics doesn't mix well). Water drowning effects are quite overwhelming, it's hard to orientate when the screen continues to fade strong blue.
TL;DR
In the end, take it as it is - it's not perfect, but it's pretty damn good. (Haven't tried the multiplayer though) Xen chapter still ain't here, so that's still a negative for this game, but all is forgiven, because the game is really solid so far.

If you're looking for a sort of "zen" game that you can sink plenty of time into on a casual basis, then Slime Rancher is for you.
As the name implies, your goal is to catch and raise Slimes and make money off of them. There are plenty of different slime types although 4 are available to you right off (Pink, Rock, Tabby, and Phosphoro)  with more becoming available to you as you unlock different areas. Naturally you need to keep your slimes fed or otherwise they'll bounce out of their corrals in search of food.
Some advice for beginners.
First, don't be afraid to breed Tabby Slimes with Pink Slimes to make Pink Tabby Largos (Largos are big hybrid slimes), the Pink Slimes will eat any food given to them which will come in handy as breeding meat (i.e. Chickens) is a bit of a chore and growing fruits and veggies are much easier and more sustainable in the long run. The same can be applied to the other carnivorous slimes as breeding them with herbavores or the omnivorus pinks can allow you to focus your food growth efforts to strictly fruits and vegitables which can be more cost effective, especially once you unlock the area to the immediate east of your ranch which has chickens, carrots, and pogofruit growing naturally and keep you constantly supplied with all three basic foods for your slimes if tended too properly.
Second, try to upgrade your corralls to the max (you can safely exclude the music box and solar shields for most corrals though if you're penny pinching) especially the plort collector (Plorts get you currency and allow you to breed slimes into largos) and this makes it easier to collect the plorts without accidently sucking up your slimes and having to fire them back into the corral.
Third, NEVER put more than TWO types of slime in the corrals. If a largo eats a plort that's neither one of its base slimes (i.e. a pink rock largo eats a tabby plort) it WILL become a Tarr (an evil eat-all slime) and can quickly leave you having to run and collect new slimes to replace the ones you lost. Worst case scenario, you lose all your slimes, including the harder to get ones. Tarrs can be killed with water so buy the water tank upgrade for your gun early on and keep it filled with water when you can.
Fourth, don't bother trying to capture the super rare Lucky or Golden slimes. You can't, game says no.
Fifth, don't make your corrals too full of slimes. The Slimes will eventually get too hungry and bounce out in spite of the air net and higher wall upgrades.
Now, as this is Early Access, there is some room for improvement. Gameplay wise, I think most of the bugs have been fixed but there are some suggestions would be helpful so if the developers are reading this, I'd encourage you to read the following suggestions.
General options: An option to sell upgraded ranch equipment (i.e. corral upgrades) for partial refunds would be helpful in a pinch. Namely, the ability to sell the solar shield upgrade on a corral when the slimes inside do not need protection from sunlight would be a good option.
Farm Plots: Farming for food is a very useful feature but even the plots could use some improvement. Two optional upgrades would be beneficial. The first would be an autoharvester which would suction all of the food and store it for pick up so that the plot can get to work on the next harvest as well as keep the food from going bad. A sort of mini-silo if you will. Second, an upgrade that eliminates the need to constantly re-seed the plot. The plots, as they are right now, only last for a few yields before dying off and having to be replanted. This can be problematic if you're growing rair foods like Heartbeats, Phase Lemons, Mint Mangos, and Odd Onions as you might end up running completely out and having to go hunt for them. An upgrade that makes the plots grow continuously until you decide to change what's grown would not go amiss.
Chicken Coops: At the moment, these are arguably the most useless features short of the incinerator in the game at the moment that i can tell. It's hard to tell if the chickens are indeed breeding as I never see any eggs and only occasionally see a few chicks peeping around. The higher wall upgrade, by the way, for the coop is useless as a hungry slime can still bounce right into the coop and consume your stock of chickens. I would suggest some kind of a roof for the coop or something more effective at keeping the slimes away. One upgrade I would recommend would probably be a sort of cloning feature which regularly produces whichever chicken breed is put into it much like the farm plots do.
Pools: The only place you can keep Puddle Slimes should also use a few upgrades. Third upgrades come to mind. First is a plort collector since, every time I collect the puddle slime plorts, I end up collecting the slimes as well and having to put them back in the pool. Another upgrade would be a fountain which would keep the water level steady and give you a place to easily replenish your water tanks for combating Tarrs without draining the pools of their water. Finally a third upgrade for the pool would be something that will help the shy puddle slimes feel less shy while in the pool (they won't produce plorts when around too many other slimes, including other puddle slimes so roughly 4 puddle slimes per pool at the moment). This upgrade would allow you to put more puddle slimes into the pool at a time.
Corrals: only one upgrade that I can think of for the corrals would be handy and that would be a "hazard shield" of some kind. Boom, Rad, Rock, and Crystal slimes have a nasty tendancy to damage you if you get too close, and that can be intentional (in the case of Rock and Crystal slimes) or accidental (in the case of boom and rad slimes) so a hazard shield that prevents them from harming you or anything outside their corrals would be helpful. I would recommend these shields also make it harder for the Quantum slimes to teleport out but that's not as big of an issue if managed correctly. The rock and crystal slimes will attack and damage you regardless of their moods while Rad slimes irradiate you if you get too close for too long so the shields should make getting closer much easier.
Odd Onions: So basically if you plant an Odd Onion in a farm plot, you get carrots with maybe two or three onions per yield. More onions per harvest would be welcome.
Gold and Lucky Slimes: these slimes are presently unable to be caught. Making them catchable, albeit with a high difficulty in keeping corraled would be a good addition. For instance, give the Gold Slime a high bounce when agitated and hungry so it bounces right out of the corral and then disappears if not tended too properly. Or both could simply disappear if left unattended or uncared for for too long. A good rancher with fully upgraded corrals should be able to contain them provided they have enough food. Make them picky eaters so that they will only eat one specific and hard to find food like the Phase Lemon. Make breeding them with another slime (like the pink) automatically turn them into that slime (non largo) and kill off the benefit of producing their rare plorts.
Naturally more slimes and areas would be a good addition along with more expansions to the ranch itself. Also if a teleporter from the lab expansion to the newly released ruins area (blocked by a Quantum guado perhaps?) could be added, that would be good for quick travel.
I would also like to take the opportunity and pitch a sort of marine slime, not like the puddle slime, but one that swims in the ocean and requires a special water filled corral to be kept in.
Also, if business is good enough, I'd recommend selling plushies of the various slimes. That'd be a money maker.
Anyway, that's all that I can think of. I eagerly await the next update. I highly recommend this game though to anyone and everyone.

I have never reviewed a game before, but I had to get this out there.
The PC port of Dishonored 2 is a huge disappointment. The first Dishonored had a pretty great port, and I was extremely excited to play Dishonored 2. The game itself feels like it would be a great successor to the first, if it actually ran the way it should. The game looks great, but not great enough to warrant the terrible performance issues. Most of the six hours I've "played" has been me tinkering with settings to try to get a solid 60 FPS, but I just can't seem to get above about 48 FPS on any settings at all. It really is a shame that the game launched so poorly optimized. They just released an official patch, which seems to have increased framerates in areas that didn't have trouble in the first place, but if there are open areas with a lot going on, the game still has issues keeping up. The patch they've released two weeks after launch now still isn't enough to make the game play like it should.
In closing, save your money. Even if you're a diehard fan, wait until they actually fix the game or wait until a big sale on the title. It really is a shame that we are still getting terrible ports of AAA games, when developers know that a large PC market is there. I really wanted this game to be great, but I just can't recommend it at this time.

Mini spoilers ahead
Gameplay
This is easily my game of the year. This game takes the puzzle mechanics of Amnesia: TDD, the constant threat of Slenderman, the hiding mechanics Outlast and blends them all magnificently. That isn't to say that they straight-up copied these mechanics, either. Everything felt fresh and intuitive.
Setting/Atmosphere
I have not played a game that nailed FPHS this well in since Amnesia: TDD. The atmosphere is lonely and foreboding while remaining remakrably loyal to the setting of the Alien universe.  Lighting, sound, level design all was top-notch. the game is also very immersive the the aforementioned reasons as well as interesting controls. I really liked using mouse buttons to represent Ripley grabbing things, movement keys for pulling things and especially loved navigating the terminals without a mouse (They didn't have mice, so it wouldn't have even made sense to use the mouse!)
Nitpicks
I wasn't a big fan of the human AI in the game. In my experience there were two types of humans, those who were unarmed and helpless and those who would tell you to go away and shoot you anyway (the jerks).
I also dislike the baby aliens because they were hard to hit (maybe I just need to get good) and were a one hit kill.
Overall
I love this game and feel ready to tackle the DLCs and challenge mods next! If you plan on playing this game, do yourself a favor and play on HARD. It offers the most difficult and terrifying experience. It even says so in-game for the difficulties description: "The recommended way to experience the game. Challenging and terrifying."
If you took the time to read any or all of this, thank you for your time and I hope you enjoy AI!
If you are a fan of the original Alien movie and you enjoy jump scares, you will like this game.

As many remakes are flooding the "Next-Gen" market, this is one of the few I will love. Black Mesa is one of the funnest experiences I've had in gaming in a long time, and not because of "Nostalgia". Although I know the power of nostalgia, many reviews are just talking about the Nostalgia the game gave them, rather than reviewing the game for what it really is. So here is my simple review.
+ Great Level Design. Great levels are extended, and unnecessary levels are shortened.
+ Voice acting is now more believable and realistic, and overall well done (Some lines may need work).
+ Great graphics and well optimized, especially for the Source Engine.
+ The interactive parts in the beginning really set the mood.
+ Atmosphere is awesome, the beginning having the best mood of survival, the middle and end having action.
+ Weapons feel nice and polished. Weapons like the SMG feel real, and add to the already great atmosphere.
+ Great variety of enemies (All of them from Half-Life, but they feel more real thanks to Source)
+ Physics engine isn't used too much, but add a little 'zing' to the game.
+ Game is much longer than Half-Life (My Half-Life Completion time: 10 Hours | Black Mesa: 14 Hours)
+ Multiplayer with multiple game modes add to the great amount of content.
+ Exploration is encouraged and rewarded with extra ammo and health items.
+/- AI is better, but a bit clumsy. Marines sometimes run from my gun fire, sometimes they run into it.
+/- Small amount of bugs, but none of them game breaking (I can't be the only one with glitchy ties).
+/- A few frame drops here and there, but none of them too bad.
- The "On A Rail" feels way too short.
- The Xen chapters are missing. It feels awkward having the end game not there, sadly. (Anti-Climactic Ending, for now).
- Not many multiplayer servers, and hardly any people on those servers.
- Multiplayer lags sometimes, and can get you killed numerous times.
- Multiplayer has bad and unfair spawns sometimes (This is mostly in FFA).
- The helicopter fight is very unfair. I would tone down the damage.
- The ninja assassin guys should be nerfed, too. Tone down their damage or their numbers, and it would be alright.
A few other recommendations: It would be cool if you could see the corpse of your player when you died. Another cool thing would be if there were optional scientist rescue missions, where they lead you to a locked room full of supplies, but have to be protected from threats.
Overall, Black Mesa has only a few flaws, most of which are small, but the pros push out the cons, and this is just overall an amazing experience. One of the best purchases I've made on Steam in a long time. The subtle storytelling is kept, along with the great sense of dread and danger around every corner that will keep you on your toes. This is a must play, just like the original.
Score: 9/10

Unfortunately, writing this review I find myself torn. While I love the Souls series, and I still enjoy Dark souls II more than the majority of other titles I've played this year, I still find myself disappointed. The reuse of items from the first game were amusing for a little while, but eventually it started to get downright irritating. The locations are interesting, but don't have the same level of, artistry, that the first game had, and the bonfire warping changes the tone of the game greatly, removing any sense of gravity that existed with exploring any area, new or otherwise.
My largest complaint with Dark Souls II is the absolutely astonishing number of bonfires; with so many of them, and every single one available for quick-travel, any challenge which might have existed while traveling to the boss has become practically nonexistent comparitively speaking.
My next large issue is with the way that the story of NPCs is presented, in the fact that it is too overstated regarding locations in the game, and we get to see so very little of the people that they are besides talking exposition dumps.
On the positive side, gameplay was mostly improved upon in terms of mechanics, the addition of guardbreaks, increased difficulty of parrying and backstabs, as well as reduced invincibility frames on rolls were large improvements. PvP content I also found was improved upon, making connection easier overall, and adding more variety to the concept of multiplayer, both competitive and cooperative, though Soul Memory subtracts from the play life of an individual character.
In summary, I'd say that a veteran Souls player should probably still play Dark Souls II, but it will probably be best to do it after the price drops, because the game is made considerably easier, and less tense than the first. For those players who haven't played a Souls game yet, I think that this is quite possibly the one to start with, then move onto the others afterward. While I find it difficult to say the last bit, I feel that it may genuinely offer the best possible experience.
While I recommend the game with the selection on this post, I don't feel that it is as binary as all that, and that this title, while good on its own, just can't live up to the predecessors.

If you don't want to read this review, you can basically hear me read it out loud here, with a little bit of gameplay footage:
Aqua Fish (as opposed to what kind of fish?) is a casual Match 3 game where you swipe to make combos and complete basic tasks to progress through the 100 levels. Objectives include things such as getting a certain score, collecting special items by dropping them to the bottom, collecting a set number of different items, clearing blocks and other simple tasks. You build up combos and make special pieces by matching higher numbers of various assorted sea-side items, but there's nothing new or different in the gameplay to every other casual Match 3 game, a great deal of which are free to play.
For achieving these goals you are rewarded with dollars, which you can spend in the store on buying fish and decorating your aquarium. This is quite relaxing, but ultimately ends up being quite limited as there isn't that much to buy.
So, onto that last point... This game has 5 lives. If you fail a level, you need to wait 30 minutes for your life to regenerate. If you lose all 5 lives, you can no longer play the game. You can of course watch an in-game advert to regain a life instantly.
This is not a free to play game. This is a full price full-release buy in game at £1.99 that still time gates you and forces you to watch adverts in order to play the game you've paid for.
Even without in-game ads, this game is a clone of Playrix's mobile game "Fishdom". It brings nothing new to the table, but I could have given it an average recommendation for those who enjoy casual and relaxing gameplay. With the addition of freemium mobile elements in a buy to play game, it's getting a massive thumbs down from me, especially since this aspect is mentioned absolutely no where on the store page.

I've just about gotten through my second playthrough and the game has been pretty much 90% smooth sailing.
Hardware issues: The only issue I ran into running the game was on Ultra settings. My system is a few years old but was top of the line when I got it made, i7-4790k intel processor, 16gb ram, Nivida Titan Black GPU.
I tried running the game on Ultra first, and it ran on ultra fine for the first bit. Once I got outside though the game had some issues. I put it down to Very High and the game has ran without a hitch for me.
Gameplay is by far the strongest point of this game. you can play as Corvo or Emily and they both have a set of differing supernatural abilities that are fun to mess and mix with. Each mission is a self-contained sandbox where you can mess around to your hearts content.
Story: Unfortuantely the story is by far the worst part of this game, its by no means bad but its very much in your face and everything is basically told to you in the beginning except for one very minor twist near the end of the game. How you choose to play the missions does change the overall outcome by the end but there is no suprise on who your enemy is or suprise enemies that show up or twists that way. Overall, if you want to play your way and have fun playing as a powerful supernatural assassin in a clockwork deathmask this is the game for you!

ESO tries very hard to be Skyrim in terms of real time gameplay and interacting with quests that are for the hero/chosen one (you). Why the Elder Scrolls Online MMO is the Perfect Game for Those Who Hate MMOs:
I am a Tomb Raider explorer, Mass Effect galaxy vagabond, and Witcher monster hunter type gamer. I love stories. I love rememberable characters, both on and off the PC. I have tried several MMO's, and have enjoyed very few of them past 10 hours of gameplay and usually quit soon after from boredom. More so, I hate subscriptions. I hate the very concept. If I buy a game, I should own it.
So it was a great surprise to fall completely in love with Elder Scrolls Online (Tamreil Unlimited). Is it Skyrim Online? No, it is 10 x Skyrims. Maybe more? With nearly 50 hours under my belt, I have barely scratch the surface of the true shear enormity of the game. Each Alliance starts out at a different part of Tamriel (the game's world), with very different story quests, and unique characters. So even if you make a Nord and a Redguard, you will get a completely new experience with each character.
The controls are vastly different from Skyrim. Perhaps the consol  versions will be more similar to the previous games, but for the PC you map 5 powers on the number line and a "Nova" power with the Q key. Performing sneak, pickpocket, and lock picking are all still available in game. Characters are allowed to sell up to 50 items to a fence a day (upgrading the limit is available through the skill tree).
Unlike the previous Elder Scrolls, you choose a class at character creation. Each class is quite versatile and has access to all the armors, weapons, crafting, and magical staffs. Just because you choose a Templar, doesn't mean you have to play the group's main healer. You can be a Dragon Knight who sneaks around and snipes enemies from above, raining down a fiery destruction, or a Nightblade who charges headfirst into battle with heavy armor and a giant axe, invisible one moment and cleaving enemies in two the next. The choice is yours. Though some classes are obviously built better for certain styles of combat then others.
One of ESO's greatest strengths is the ever changing world. If you save a king, each time you go back to that city you hear NPCs call out to as that hero. If you remove the curse of a ghostly army, the army becomes peaceful and the gloom lifts. On the other hand, It can be a little strange if you have completed a quest that changed the area and some in your group hasn't. They may start attacking peaceful spirits or pouring potions on a seemingly dull rock. For the most part this doesn't diminish the atmosphere.
One of the biggest bonuses for me in ESO, is the ability to play it solo if I want. I have never had to join, or felt like I needed to, a group in order to beat a quest. In fact, the shear ability to do the whole thing solo makes helping random other players all the more purposeful. If all you want game with big groups however, ESO has the Alliance War function. The best part of this PvP  function is that you feel like you haven't left the rest of the game. If you are familiar with Oblivion, you might even see some familiar sites in the unbelievably massive map.
With very few bugs and next to no loading time between any area, its a little hard to pin down a poor function of this game. You can even add your own mods from Nexus to the MMO. There is a built in function for player add-ons!
The bottom line is: If you want a MMO, get Elder Scrolls Online. If you want an RPG, get Elder Scrolls Online. If you want a good game with memorable NPCs and amazing stories, get Elder Scrolls Online. Despite my effort, I don't enjoy many MMOs, but I love this game. No matter what kind of gamer you are, I'm betting you will too.

Specs: Intel i7 4790, 16 GB RAM, GeForce GTX 980 Ti
Based on the performance that I have experienced after the patch, I would now reccomend this game. Gameplay wise, if you liked Dishonored, then this is pretty much more of the same. Having two characters gives it some replay value, and while the game seems to reward stealth over combat, there's absolutely no reason why you can't charge through the game like a total psychopath if that's what you want to do.
Voice acting, story, setting, all top notch - as you'd expect following on from the strength Dishonored showed in these areas.
Performance wise - as I said above, the patch has improved performance considerably for me, framerates are now consistent, and the mouse feels much better. However, the Void Engine feels.. sort of sloppy. I'm not sure if it's the port, or the modded ID tech engine, but it doesn't feel as smooth and responsive as the old engine. It is very playable though, and when all the elements come together it's fantastic fun, but it is worth mentioning that the engine feels a little bit unfinished.
Bottom line, if you have a halfway decent system, updated drivers and a patched game, you should be able to run this ok, and if you liked Dishonored, you'll enjoy the gameplay. If the answer to all those is 'yes' then buy the game.

Edit: Updated with Crew Expendable and Last Survivor DLC thoughts. DLC at the very bottom.
Barring something amazing coming within the next 2 months, I have no hesitation in naming Alien: Isolation as my game of the year right now. It's an incredible experience that I will remember for a long time to come and it very much deserves to be included in the "Alien" canon. Every single survivor horror game will be compared to this until its bested. While I have a lot of love for the great games in the Resident Evil franchise and some other survival horror classics, this game is a totally different experience than all of them.
I want to preface this review by stating that before playing this game, you owe it to yourself and the creators of this wonderful game to watch the Ridley Scott directed 1979 classic, "Alien" that this game is inspired by and is essentially, a sequel to. I had seen the film multiple times, but watched it again 2 days before this game launched. I am glad that I did. There is a lot of fantastic detail that you will miss and may not even get if you don't have the film at least a little fresh in your mind. I can't understand why anyone would play this before watching it really. From minor things such as musical cues to much larger things that I won't mention. Watch the film, then play the game. You'll be glad you did and it will greatly enhance your experience.
To sum it up simply, Alien Isolation is in my view the greatest survival horror game of its ilk ever created. It's extremely challenging on low difficulties and it creates a feeling of tension that I have never experienced before in a game. Creative Assembly have created their magnum opus. You feel as Amanda Ripley feels. You feel the sense of dread and foreboding. That said, this is not a game that everyone will enjoy. Many people play games to have fun and don't take things too seriously. That's perfectly fine. The biggest standout of this game is how it takes the gamer to places they don't get to go too often in games. A very dark and scary place that tests your skill in every respect. It really is a "different kind" of fun.
Technologically, the game shines. The graphics are tip top with great use of particle effects and some of the best fire I've ever seen in a game. I have what I would consider to be a "mid-range" rig and I was able to Ultra everything and not once experienced any sort of dip in performance. Level design makes you feel that you're in this place that you have no idea how to get out of. Vents are terrifyingly claustrophobic at times. The sound is insane in respect to how much it adds to the game. "Thump, thump, thump". You will hear this. You will fear this. The attention to detail is borderline masochistic in how everything from a label to the Alien itself will have you shaking your head in awe. Even the music is composed and constructed in a way to help add to the tension.
If I have one tip for this game: SAVE IT EVERY TIME YOU SEE A SAVE POINT. Autosaves are only at the beginning of missions and missions tend to be long.
Here's a TL:DR Pros/cons list and some basic stats.
At the time of this review, I have logged 15.1 hours at about 40% on normal difficulty and 60% on easy. I have played and completed only the main story. I have played none of the DLC or challenge maps at all....yet.
Pros
+ This game is the "Alien" story's "Batman Begins". Great writing/storytelling and voice acting.
+ Exceptionally challenging. Easy difficulty is not easy. The game does not hold your hand at all.
+  The attention to detail at literally every single point in the game world is astonishing.  The art direction is Oscar-worthy.
+ This game has the best sound in video game history. The sound of the Alien hunting you is a sound you won't forget.
+ The score borrows aspects from the film and also has its own flavor. It works incredibly well. The musical cues that you recognize from the film fit perfectly.
+ A very nice length to the story mode. 15 hours for a game like this is not something that you see often these days.
+ Creates a feeling of tension and helplessness that I have never experienced playing a video game before.
+ The Alien's AI is unpredictable and constantly changes. Forces you to vary how you approach a situation. If he gets you once, be sure to change your tactic.
Cons
- As outstanding as it looks, facial animations rendered in-game are poor.
- There are some mechanics that are more frustrating than fun.
- Some cheap jump scares, mostly near the end of the game.
- A few immersion killing enemy placements  that will cause immediate deaths.
- Many false endings. You'll think you're done, but you're not.
- Story mode does not have a lot of replayability. There are 3 skill levels.  Its absolutely not the kind of game I want to jump back in and play again immediately though.
- The difficulty lets up a bit in the middle third of the game and while I was relieved a bit, I found the best parts to be when they were the most tension filled. Endgame (last 2-3 hours) are non-stop.
- The map is horrible. Probably by design. It encourages you to find the path without the map.
Needless to say, I am blown away by this game. It also has added to my appreciation of the film and I am extremely excited to play the "Crew Expendable" DLC soon, which is probably going to feel like a whole new game. I will review that and append this review once I have completed it.
Rating: 10/10 - No hyperbole. This game is pitch perfect and exactly the type of game I was hoping it would be.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREW EXPENDABLE & LAST SURVIVOR DLC
Both of these DLCs allow you to play two key scenes of the original film in a game form. As with Isolation, the attention to detail is tantamount to perfection. The digital re-creation of both the actors (+ they recorded new dialogue) as well as the Nostromo itself is astonishing and really the big star of the DLC. This is a bit unfortunate.
I was initially excited upon the announcement that we'd get to play this as the original film is a long-time favorite. However, rather than provide the gamer with a chance to "change" something from the original film (aside from a character selection in Crew Expendable), the gameplay depth is a bit shallow.  Basically both DLCs allow you to play through two key scenes from the film. Crew Expendable allows you to make a minor change in choosing between Ripley, Dallas or Parker, (Last Survivor is only Ripley) but the end is always the same. The objectives are always the same. My feeling on this DLC is that if the 1979 film was a game, these two slices would serve as perfect demos to the gameplay. However, knowing the story and film so well, they didnt do much for me as they're basically just scenes from the film with Isolation gameplay mechanics. I was also disappointed that "Last Survivor" felt unfinished, as the final showdown with the Alien on board the escape shuttle was not included yet the dramatic intent would lead someone whose not seen the film to think the end provided was the real ending. No Jonesy either.
Kudos to the designers and programmers for the stellar work. Kudos to the actors too. However, if this DLC is your main reason for buying the game, I cant suggest it at all. Isolation should be the reason.
Total gametime with 3 playthroughs of the DLC on normal difficulty (2 different characters on Crew Expendable + 1 play of Last Survivor) totaled around an hour or so. Its short, but definitely worth a look if you enjoy the film and an interesting way to re-live a film but no surprises.
Let me be clear as well, that my feelings on the DLCs gameplay depth have absolutely no bearing on my feelings towards Isolation.

Completely worth it. An amazing sequel to Dark Souls.  I have played like 250+ hours and still cannot pull myself away. A few minor changes to multiplayer and pvp matchmaking and the spawn system that introduced ascetics, but overall I have enjoyed this even more than Demon Souls or Dark Souls. The world is as dark and immersive as you could have hoped, the combat is exciting and challenging, and the jolly coop is fun and effortless. Also the console to keyboard port was done very well, and it only took me a few hours of play to accustom myself to the mouse + keyboard playstyle.

Dark Souls 2 is a good game, but it's disappointing in comparison to the first Dark Souls. This game had a different director than the previous Souls games and it really shows. Some comparisons:
- The writing in the first game was intriguing. The first game had you start at an asylum for the undead at the "end of the world," and next you're told to ring the bells of awakening. The writing for the second game isn't just bad in comparison, it's flat out bad. The second game starts with you being laughed at by old ladies, and then a NPC tells you to collect souls to break your curse. As souls are currency dropped by enemies, the plot amounts to "go kill things." The writing doesn't get much better. On a related note, there are no memorable NPCs this time around.
- Level design has also taken a step backwards. Levels are no longer interconnected like in the first game. It often feels as though the game has levels stitched end-to-end without regard for theme or geometry. This is probably why you can fast-travel from the start. Given this, it's not a surprise that floor plans have also been simplified. To its credit, the game is still loaded with secret areas to be found.
- Combat is probably a bit worse. Hitboxes are definitely worse, combos and ripostes are less satisfying, and enemies now spin and attack in ways that violate physical intuition. On the plus side, there are a lot of new weapons, more equipment slots, and a new type of magic.
- Leveling up now requires you to sit through two bonfire warps and some awful dialogue.
Dark Souls 2 is saved by the fact that the previous Souls games provided a very solid foundation. The combat system, combined with the bonfire system and tough enemies creates an engaging and addictive experience. And Dark Souls 2 does provide a lot of new, difficult content. Unfortunately, uninspired writing, subpar world design, and some questionable game mechanics make for a game that's almost entirely devoid of the "magic" the first game had.

Broforce was a game which I had watched people play on YouTube and thought it was just another fancy platformer shooter game with the added twist of action adventure movie heroes. While the game is exactly all of those things, it also has many other redeeming points.
The gameplay is overwhelmingly simple. There is nothing wrong with an easy game to play. I for one enjoy games where you can pick it up and play no matter what mood you are in. The fast paced action makes for a brilliant casual game to play when you have a few minutes to kill.
Storywise, there is none. From what I gather anyway. It's just a matter of shooting through hoards and hoards of bad guys and saving your chums who have been kept prisoner. The reward system is based on how many prisoners you actually rescure, and the rewards you get equate into new playable characters, or "Bros". You start off with being able to play Rambo and you work your way through to the likes of Conan the Barbarian, or Broman the Brobarian....
Completing the main game is very short, I managed to do it in roughly two hours of picking up and playing every now and again. There are still plenty of other game modes such as Arcade, coop, (online and local) as well as a level editor which will add hours of endless mindnumbing badguy killing frenzies.
I would highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys a shooting or action game. You cannot go wrong, and the devs are bound to add more features and levels in the future.

The Total War franchise by Creative Assembly is my all time favourite gaming series but to have thier latest game Rome 2 thrown at you a year to early and get told its done is surely a stain if not a insult to lifelong fans such as myself.In saying that this absoloute marvel of a videogame is something that all other RTS and TBS games should fear and here is why.
Pros:
-Massive scale battles in a big slice of the world from Briton to India, snowy mountains to barren desert flat lands, land and sea nothing is impossible to a battle location.
-Army size is huge being able to control 20 unit cards per army and than control a reinforcing army aswell to bring a total of 40 unit cards to a fight is something to awe over
-Navel battles allow you to bring the ancient worlds vessals to life with primative ways of dispatching enemy craft from ramming.shooting and boarding
-Co-op campaign is back and now after the latest patch it is still improving. but conquering the world together with a friend or against them is still fun even after the 20th try
-The AI has improved slightly fielding some more damaging units than when it was first released so on a harder difficulty they can be a bit of a challenge.
-scenery and graphics are fantastic (if your rig can handle it) I run 1980x1080 on the ultra graphic setting and it looks and sounds amazing
-You can be any number of factions from The Powerful Rome to the Majestic Egyptions. So much variety to let you pursue the new ruler of the world as your favourite ancient faction
-Historic portrayal of charecters units and settlements are gorgeous and terrificly done
Cons:
-AI even though slightly improved it's still useless i play every game on legendary difficulty and still rarely get beatin if at all. If the AI armies would use something rather than levy troops it may prove a challenge
-The game launch was a disaster so much was broken and game crashes were constant, Much has been fixed or is getting fixed and its still there in the back of everyones brain who bought this game when it first came out
-Co-op waiting time has been improved but we are still waiting minutes in between turns
-Some units are ridiculously OP if you verse someone online and they have one of these units (like pretorian gaurd) than you better shoot all you ammo into that unit or else they will wipe the floor with you
Conclusion:
Overall this game is brilliant at it's core minor cosmetic damge cannot stain a true work of art. If you are thinking about buying this game and are into TBS than this is a must have for any history nut or strategy game buff. I give Rome 2
9/10

I feel like I have to be a party-pooper, giving a negative review.
I don't feel the sense of accomplishment with this game that I would expect. The game works, and it presents a calm environment to enjoy doing what you normally wouldn't. I'd compare it to playing an idle game that you also can enjoy for its own reasons. So while the games mechanics as such are solid, there's a few issues with the game:
- The distances on the map are shortened massively, and as a consequence time itself is accelerated accordingly. While for the end result itself this might not be an issue, even bigger drives across Europe don't take too long. Crossing a country like France passes in a heartbeat. I would have liked the distances to be shorter on the map, but more "realistic" (still shrunk, but not to this degree). I'd feel happier if the base game contained the Benelux Countries and expanded from there.
- The detail of the road network is quite poor. Country-specific detail isn't there at all (e.g. highway exits), and the roads feel very gemeric. Also, the cities could be bigger, giving a bigger challenge navigating the truck (see the point above).
The only exciting thing I encountered was driving backwards with a trailer before concluding a mission. After a handful of drives, this factor wore off though, leaving me behind with no real motivation.
TL;DR: This game is good if you're looking for a relaxing game. If you need some purpose or challenge (like I do), look for something else. Microsoft Flight Simulator X might be something similar to consider then as it adds more challenge navigating and operating your "vehicle".

Slime Rancher is the sort of game that would happen if you fused Monster Rancher with Harvest Moon as an FPS with a Gravity Gun/Vacuum Cleaner. It is not a very photorealistic farming experience nor does the game excel in its several disciplines (plant growing, Farm Building, chicken tending, slime feeding, Resource & Time Management, Mining, Exploration, Researching Tech) very in-depth, but the charming design and the sum of its several parts fit well together to form a joyful, childfriendly farm game experience with a decent sense of wonder.
I found it quite hard to put this game down once i fired it up, it has its ways to get you invested into its economy quickly. The main attraction, the various cute slime creatures, do their part to hold your attention up. The desire to build up your little plot of land to a lush farm full of happy livestock is strong. The game currently lacks a decent sense of difficulty and needs some tweaking in its tech tree and economy, but i have a good feeling with the Dev team. They seem very engaged and competent.
Overall Rating 7/10. Good farm game if you have an itch for it. I recommend a purchase at around 15 Euros. Value will likely rise over time before release.

- The Game.
Just Cause 3 is an openworld sandbox game set in the beautiful mediterranean environment of the fictional nation of Medici. You play as Rico Rodriguez, a former mercernary for the Agency returning to his homeland after many years to discover it has been completely taken over by an evil dictator hellbent on terrorizing the people and ruling the world! Rico meets his childhood friend Mario, who explains to him that a local rebellion is fighting back and needs his assistance.
Thus, Rico and his newfound friends within the local rebel militia must liberate towns and destroy military bases to free the people from the grip of this evil dictatorship!
Just Cause 3 adds new mechanics and physics to the Just Cause series such as the ability to tear specific pieces off vehicles and the ability to destroy scenery in your own way. You can now tether your grapple to anything and reel it in to rip down just about anything piece by piece without firing a shot. Want to demolish half a bridge but leave the rest of it standing? Want to rip off a car door with your grappling hook? You can do that. In addition to this new content, Just Cause 3 takes all the good points of Just Cause 2 and improves upon them while taking away all the bad things that drove us all mad (such as quicktime events) to create a wonderful game experience.
With access to unlimited explosives, new gadgets, a huge arsenal of weaponary and vehicles on an absolutely massive map, Just Cause 3 takes the openworld genre to the next level. While the story itself isn't particuarly long nor very good, the dialogue, humour and the insanity of the missions you take on just make you want to keep playing them.
The graphics and sound design is stunning - the game looks and sounds absolutely beautiful. The characters and dialogue are humorous and entertaining and the driving/flying mechanics have had a huge overhaul from Just Cause 2. No longer will you have extreme difficulty trying to get anywhere in a car. Whether you choose to take a vehicle or simply your wingsuit, grapple or parachute, the game feels wonderful to get around. The controls are responsive and fluid and make sense unlike Just Cause 2's awkward controls.
Explosions, a huge part of the Just Cause series, feel extremely satisfying and a massive improvement over the last two games. The combat is complete insanity with a seemingly endless supply of bad guys coming at you at a given time, I even ran out of ammo a few times because there were simply too many bad guys coming at me. Luckily when the situation turns bad you can always make a quick getaway with your grappling hook.
As of writing this, I am ten hours in and so far I've only liberated one section of the map and am having a blast doing so. There are three main islands in total (excluding the secret island I haven't got to yet), one of which is at-least four times as large as the island I've currently liberated, meaning there's at-least 50 hours of content to this game. And you'll want to keep playing it once you're finished.
The game isn't free from bugs though, sometimes you'll find government forces still stationed outside of a liberated military base, you'll sometimes grapple to thin air (this seems to mainly occur under bridges) or your heat level will become locked and the only way to fix it is to restart the game.
So what are the downsides? The game is always online DRM, I freaking
always online DRM, if you don't have a stable internet connection (or say you're downloading something in the background and the game connection keeps dropping) the game will constantly try to connect to the Square Enix servers EVERYTIME you open the commlink or pause the game. This is extremely frustrating when you have selected offline mode and simply want to view the map.
The game runs perfectly fine on high settings on my system (1080p, GTX 770 4GB, 8GB RAM, i7 4770K) without dipping on framerate no matter how much insanity is going on, however a lot of users have said it runs poorly for them so this seems to be system specific. Many users have also reported crashing a lot, however this has not been an issue for me as in ten hours of gameplay I've only crashed once (excluding the times the game has frozen when I've quit out of it). New patches are being rolled out every week or so however they seem to be hit and miss with some users reporting that the patch has made the game stability worse while others saying it's been made better.
I can completely overlook these issues due to how much fun this game actually is, however if you're crashing every five minutes, have an AMD card or are only getting twenty frames per second, I totally understand where you're coming from. I wouldn't want to play it if this was happening either.
To summarize,
Visually gorgeous
Great sound design
Silly but entertaining humour
Driving/flying feels much better than JC2
No more quicktime events
Fun to get around
Massive map
Hours of content
Controls that actually make sense
Insane missions that keep you entertained through the story
Unlimited possibilites to create chaos
Hours of your life lost to this game
Poorly optimized on some systems
Always online DRM
It's buggy in places
Story is short
Overall, this is the funnest game I've played since Just Cause 2, I highly recommend it to anyone who loves openword sandbox action games or for anyone who just wants to screw around and have fun in a massive, beautiful world.

Dark Souls 2 is a good game, but it's disappointing in comparison to the first Dark Souls. This game had a different director than the previous Souls games and it really shows. Some comparisons:
- The writing in the first game was intriguing. The first game had you start at an asylum for the undead at the "end of the world," and next you're told to ring the bells of awakening. The writing for the second game isn't just bad in comparison, it's flat out bad. The second game starts with you being laughed at by old ladies, and then a NPC tells you to collect souls to break your curse. As souls are currency dropped by enemies, the plot amounts to "go kill things." The writing doesn't get much better. On a related note, there are no memorable NPCs this time around.
- Level design has also taken a step backwards. Levels are no longer interconnected like in the first game. It often feels as though the game has levels stitched end-to-end without regard for theme or geometry. This is probably why you can fast-travel from the start. Given this, it's not a surprise that floor plans have also been simplified. To its credit, the game is still loaded with secret areas to be found.
- Combat is probably a bit worse. Hitboxes are definitely worse, combos and ripostes are less satisfying, and enemies now spin and attack in ways that violate physical intuition. On the plus side, there are a lot of new weapons, more equipment slots, and a new type of magic.
- Leveling up now requires you to sit through two bonfire warps and some awful dialogue.
Dark Souls 2 is saved by the fact that the previous Souls games provided a very solid foundation. The combat system, combined with the bonfire system and tough enemies creates an engaging and addictive experience. And Dark Souls 2 does provide a lot of new, difficult content. Unfortunately, uninspired writing, subpar world design, and some questionable game mechanics make for a game that's almost entirely devoid of the "magic" the first game had.

Black Mesa is a great game, I played through the mod many times and I bought this version mainly for the multiplayer, which did not disappoint.
The multiplayer currently only has the deathmatch and team deathmatch gamemodes, but they're both a lot of fun. Deathmatch is just chaotic killing and I'm sure team deathmatch is a lot better with friends than it is on your own. The maps are full of detail, being big enough to survive and find a weapon, but not too big that you're isolated from the action. It's a shame there are only two gamemodes, but I feel the quality and quantity of the maps make up for that, and I'm looking forward to when they do add different gamemodes in the future.
The singleplayer is better than it was in the mod, there are several significant changes; the new sounds and models are great, the general look is better with various subtle changes, and some major ones too. Even though the game is unfinished, it still has a lot of replay value to it. I've played the mod excessively, yet I'm sure I'll play this newer version many times until the game is completed. So far, there haven't been any game-breaking bugs, the game crashed several times when I first started and there have been a few dodgy textures floating around but they are not frequent enough to be annoying.
Overall, I would recommend this game. It is reasonably priced by today's standards, and there is a lot to do in both the single and the multiplayer, even being unfinished.

Slime Rancher is the sort of game that would happen if you fused Monster Rancher with Harvest Moon as an FPS with a Gravity Gun/Vacuum Cleaner. It is not a very photorealistic farming experience nor does the game excel in its several disciplines (plant growing, Farm Building, chicken tending, slime feeding, Resource & Time Management, Mining, Exploration, Researching Tech) very in-depth, but the charming design and the sum of its several parts fit well together to form a joyful, childfriendly farm game experience with a decent sense of wonder.
I found it quite hard to put this game down once i fired it up, it has its ways to get you invested into its economy quickly. The main attraction, the various cute slime creatures, do their part to hold your attention up. The desire to build up your little plot of land to a lush farm full of happy livestock is strong. The game currently lacks a decent sense of difficulty and needs some tweaking in its tech tree and economy, but i have a good feeling with the Dev team. They seem very engaged and competent.
Overall Rating 7/10. Good farm game if you have an itch for it. I recommend a purchase at around 15 Euros. Value will likely rise over time before release.

- The Game.
Just Cause 3 is an openworld sandbox game set in the beautiful mediterranean environment of the fictional nation of Medici. You play as Rico Rodriguez, a former mercernary for the Agency returning to his homeland after many years to discover it has been completely taken over by an evil dictator hellbent on terrorizing the people and ruling the world! Rico meets his childhood friend Mario, who explains to him that a local rebellion is fighting back and needs his assistance.
Thus, Rico and his newfound friends within the local rebel militia must liberate towns and destroy military bases to free the people from the grip of this evil dictatorship!
Just Cause 3 adds new mechanics and physics to the Just Cause series such as the ability to tear specific pieces off vehicles and the ability to destroy scenery in your own way. You can now tether your grapple to anything and reel it in to rip down just about anything piece by piece without firing a shot. Want to demolish half a bridge but leave the rest of it standing? Want to rip off a car door with your grappling hook? You can do that. In addition to this new content, Just Cause 3 takes all the good points of Just Cause 2 and improves upon them while taking away all the bad things that drove us all mad (such as quicktime events) to create a wonderful game experience.
With access to unlimited explosives, new gadgets, a huge arsenal of weaponary and vehicles on an absolutely massive map, Just Cause 3 takes the openworld genre to the next level. While the story itself isn't particuarly long nor very good, the dialogue, humour and the insanity of the missions you take on just make you want to keep playing them.
The graphics and sound design is stunning - the game looks and sounds absolutely beautiful. The characters and dialogue are humorous and entertaining and the driving/flying mechanics have had a huge overhaul from Just Cause 2. No longer will you have extreme difficulty trying to get anywhere in a car. Whether you choose to take a vehicle or simply your wingsuit, grapple or parachute, the game feels wonderful to get around. The controls are responsive and fluid and make sense unlike Just Cause 2's awkward controls.
Explosions, a huge part of the Just Cause series, feel extremely satisfying and a massive improvement over the last two games. The combat is complete insanity with a seemingly endless supply of bad guys coming at you at a given time, I even ran out of ammo a few times because there were simply too many bad guys coming at me. Luckily when the situation turns bad you can always make a quick getaway with your grappling hook.
As of writing this, I am ten hours in and so far I've only liberated one section of the map and am having a blast doing so. There are three main islands in total (excluding the secret island I haven't got to yet), one of which is at-least four times as large as the island I've currently liberated, meaning there's at-least 50 hours of content to this game. And you'll want to keep playing it once you're finished.
The game isn't free from bugs though, sometimes you'll find government forces still stationed outside of a liberated military base, you'll sometimes grapple to thin air (this seems to mainly occur under bridges) or your heat level will become locked and the only way to fix it is to restart the game.
So what are the downsides? The game is always online DRM, I freaking
always online DRM, if you don't have a stable internet connection (or say you're downloading something in the background and the game connection keeps dropping) the game will constantly try to connect to the Square Enix servers EVERYTIME you open the commlink or pause the game. This is extremely frustrating when you have selected offline mode and simply want to view the map.
The game runs perfectly fine on high settings on my system (1080p, GTX 770 4GB, 8GB RAM, i7 4770K) without dipping on framerate no matter how much insanity is going on, however a lot of users have said it runs poorly for them so this seems to be system specific. Many users have also reported crashing a lot, however this has not been an issue for me as in ten hours of gameplay I've only crashed once (excluding the times the game has frozen when I've quit out of it). New patches are being rolled out every week or so however they seem to be hit and miss with some users reporting that the patch has made the game stability worse while others saying it's been made better.
I can completely overlook these issues due to how much fun this game actually is, however if you're crashing every five minutes, have an AMD card or are only getting twenty frames per second, I totally understand where you're coming from. I wouldn't want to play it if this was happening either.
To summarize,
Visually gorgeous
Great sound design
Silly but entertaining humour
Driving/flying feels much better than JC2
No more quicktime events
Fun to get around
Massive map
Hours of content
Controls that actually make sense
Insane missions that keep you entertained through the story
Unlimited possibilites to create chaos
Hours of your life lost to this game
Poorly optimized on some systems
Always online DRM
It's buggy in places
Story is short
Overall, this is the funnest game I've played since Just Cause 2, I highly recommend it to anyone who loves openword sandbox action games or for anyone who just wants to screw around and have fun in a massive, beautiful world.

Is this an Early Access game?
I’ve been playing Just Cause 3 since launch, and it really does not seem like a game that should have been released. Day 1 was riddled with bugs, many of which were game breaking. I know it is now common place for developers to release unpolished games, get the fans to pay full price for Beta testing then release enough updates to fix major issues, before moving on to making DLC in 3 months, completely ignoring the minor bugs and issues.
In addition to the bugs, it seems several mechanics are underdeveloped and I am concerned they will not be addressed. Civilian land vehicles for the most part drive atrociously, they are clunky and feel like vehicle controls of early 2000s sandbox games. I understand the game pushes you to use flight as your main method of traversal, because the wingsuit, parachute and air vehicle controls are really well done. But it seems strange to neglect a cars, particularly when the upcoming Season Pass content boasts additional land vehicles.
Just Cause 2 had challenges, which were optional and did not affect your experience. In this game unnecessary RPG elements are added which make these mini-games fairly essential as they unlock upgrades for Rico and his arsenal. Most of these minigames are exactly the same, and get repetitive. What makes this worse, is that many of these challenges can not be beaten with a maximum 5 cog rating, without completing other challenges or liberating specific bases  to unlock upgrades and better vehicles. So you essentially play a minigame, to unlock an upgrade to beat another minigame, to unlock and upgrade to get the max score on the first minigame. Fairly repetitive to even describe.
Once you put aside all these issues, the game is quite enjoyable. Beautiful landscape, huge map you can explore in many different ways and a lot of great fun blowing things up. This fun however, is only had when you can actually play the game. For some reason, there is an online scoreboard for challenges which requires you to always be connected to Square Enix servers. This connection is very unstable, and you frequently get disconnected, and the game locks you out whilst reconnecting, a process which takes about a minute. After the first failed attempt to connect, you are given an option to play offline. However, every time you complete a minigame, beat your highscore on a challenge or sometimes open the map, even when in offline mode, it tries to reconnect you.
Square Enix have made a fairly good game, but it should not have been released as a finished product. Ideally buy in a few months once the devs have ironed out the major issues.
EDIT
With all the patches and updates, the game runs fairly well and continues to look phenomenal.

If you seek or want some retro C64/easy simple puzzler goodness, a cut above in wonderful simplicity, I recommend.

Thoroughly hyped by SEGA via an advertising campaign that turned out to be of questionable morality, Rome II was a disaster upon release and hasn't gotten much better nine months later.
SEGA did a masterful job of marketing this game. Videos, press releases, and screenshots galore presented a title of great visual appeal and depth of play, and viewers were treated to numerous interviews with the developers, wherein those individuals shared the great new features and improvements that would be present in the game. In the event, said marketing campaign turned out to be utterly lacking in integrity. Those screenshots and videos? Doctored. Even on tip-top settings, the game doesn't look anywhere near as good as the game's marketing made it appear. All those new features? Many of them don't exist in the game, and numerous others are pointedly shallow. That talk about investing a large percentage of money into the AI, that aspect which has been such an area of disappointment throughout the series? Absolutely untrue, as Rome II's AI, in both campaign and battle, is, if anything, one of the worst in the series. Of particular concern is the siege AI, which was initially incapable of such commonplace feats as utilizing siege equipment and crossing bridges, not to mention perpetually engaging in tactics that can only be described as suicidal.
Of all the marketing elements, that with the most irony featured Mike Simpson---Creative Assembly's longtime creative director---and saw him gush about how unlike many other games, Rome II would come out of the proverbial box perfectly ready to play (of note is that this video was released soon before the game). Needless to say, this was a bald-faced lie, as the game was even more disastrous than the notoriously awful Empire: Total War was upon its own release. Mr. Simpson turned up soon after release to address the uproar amongst customers via a disingenuous apology that he probably wrote before release, having---assuming he has a brain---anticipated the reaction that this thoroughly incomplete product would generate.
Aside from the game's myriad bugs upon release---which are too numerous for me to contemplate listing here; fortunately, YouTube has rants and hilarious videos aplenty on the issue---came a host of incomplete or haphazardly-implemented features, and, in general, a title that, even had it been bug-free, would have been unremarkable at best. Gone was the depth of character native to all of the previous titles in the series; this one was shallow and bland.
Nine months later, after a great deal of patching, the game is still rife with bugs and flaws. Though this is less the case than it was at  release, the game nonetheless continues to be very mediocre; and because Creative Assembly's focus has, obnoxiously, long since turned to the development of DLC whilst the base game continues to suffer, Rome II's quality is unlikely to improve. I have been a fan of this series since 2002 and have played every game in it, and while I did not particularly enjoy Empire or Shogun II (as my reviews on those titles make evident), they are masterpieces in comparison to this product.

Dishonored 2 is a bittersweet extension of the original, and while I'm not on board with all the changes, I can recommend it as a worthy successor.
The game mechanics are a straight upgrade of those in Dishonored; I can say without reservation that everything that was excellent in the original made it into the sequel, and everything else feels like an organic improvement or extension. The game is simply a joy to play.
The story is serviceable, but far less engaging than the original. Depending on how you played it, the original could have been a story about revenge, about justice, about paternal love, about discovery, about building relationships. This one feels more restricted. Most characters are largely throwaway; the only ones that persist from mission to mission are cardboard villains, a cagey and emotionally walled-off ally, and an older and less interesting frienemy from the original.
The biggest complaint I have is the lack of mystery. The original implied many things without stating them. The sequel leaves little to discover. Part of this is the expanded role of the Heart. It's much more aware of what it is, and what its relationship is to you. It largely tells you what you want to know, rather than its poetically dreamy, half-mad ramblings. This allows the writers to violate the maxim of "show, don't tell." The lack of the unknown and unknowable make this otherwise amazing land of Serkonos feel more videogamey than Dunwall.
Don't get me wrong, though; I'm thoroughly enjoying the game, and I'd buy it again in a heartbeat.

I have played all of the Soul games, and Dark Souls II is by far my favorite. The reason for this is mostly what I would consider superior mechanics and a more fluid feel to the combat overall. Rolling in this game feels heavier than the previous two games, and it is slightly less forgiving in terms of invincibility frames and how far you roll, although that depends to some extent on your adaptability stat and your current equip load as well. At the same time, the attack you can perform directly after a roll happens much more quickly compared to Dark Souls I, which makes PvP seem slightly more dynamic, especially for Ultra Greatsword users. Not only that, but when using heavy weapons such as Ultra Greatswords or Greathammers, you can aim the attack even when locked on, allowing you to follow a player with your attack after you have pressed the attack button. This makes weapons that only do a downward swing attack at least somewhat viable for PvP.
Not only would I say this game is an improvement over the previous two games in terms of combat mechanics, it is also a very good jumping in point for people who are new to the series. It has a fairly extensive tutorial at the beginning of the game, and a lot of the mechanics have been simplified in certain ways. For example, attacks (even ranged attacks) will tend towards the closest enemy even if you are not locked on, allowing you to more easily move around a group of enemies by  not having to stay locked on to one enemy. Not only that, but this game adds the Small White Soapstone which you can get very early in the game. This item is just like the White Soapstone except you can fulfill your duty much quicker than with the White Soapstone. This is helpful because the White Soapstones allow you to regain your humanity when you fulfill your duty, allowing you to regain the health that you lose every time you die and become hollow. Dark Souls II also has a more refined and easy to use interface, especially if you use the mouse to navigate it, and it is also a lot easier and quicker to write and rate messages.
I'm not a big fan of the story of the Souls games, but I would say that I enjoyed what story there was in this game more than the story in Dark Souls I. However, many would agree with me that there are aspects of the story that are worse than they were in Dark Souls I, particularly the fact that there is only one ending as opposed to the two endings that were in Dark Souls I. However, the story in Dark Souls II I found was a lot easier to follow; meaning I actually somewhat understood what the back story was, if not what I was doing or why. Like I said though, the story of these games doesn't really matter to me so I can't speak definitively on the quality of this game's story any more than I can of the stories of the other Souls games.
Although this is my favorite of the Souls games, it still has some problems that I would like to discuss. First of all, the boss designs in this game are somewhat less inspired, at least in the early game. Most of the early bosses are simply big guys with big swords, and they tend to be really easy to just get behind and slaughter without any real danger of getting killed. Then there is the addition of a new stat called adaptability which increases your agility as well as your resistances to magic and status effects. The reason I think this is a somewhat negative change is because agility, the main reason to level adaptability, is somewhat mysterious in that it is not quite clear what exactly it affects. Supposedly, agility affects your character in ways such as decreasing the time it takes to drink an Estus flask, or increasing the invincibility frames in your roll, or decreasing the time it takes to raise or lower your shield after an attack. However, it seems that the only effect that agility has been proven to have is allowing you to drink Estus quicker, but it would certainly not make sense if this were the only effect that agility had. It is simply not known what effects that agility has or doesn’t have, which makes investing levels into this stat feel somewhat unsure. Another change that was made is that enemies despawn after you kill them 15 times, which seems to have garnered a lot of hate from other players. You can, however, burn a Bonfire Ascetic which will respawn enemies at New Game + difficulty. I have not personally had a problem with this because I have not once had an enemy despawn on me, but it is something to consider.
Overall, this game feels better to me than the previous Souls games in terms of the mechanics, but in terms of story, boss design, and mysterious additions like the adaptability stat, there are definitely aspects that could be improved upon.

A fun, albeit fundamentally flawed romp through a Japanese take on european high fantasy.  I have been a big fan of the 'Souls' series since first playing Demons' Souls on my ps3 so my thoughts may be slightly skewed in that direction.
One of the main reasons I enjoy the Souls series is the fact that 9 times out of 10 when I die, it's my fault, I messed up in some way.  Unfortunatley, in the majority of my deaths in DS2 this simply wasn't the case.  With enemies defying the rules imposed on the main character in order to get a kill.  For example, my sword pings off a wall, while an enemies weapon swings through it for a hit, being hit full force from behind a shield with 100% defence, being hit when clearly a few feet away from the enemy swing.  Artificial difficulty is also a major problem here too, as the combat engine and lock-on feature are geared towards 1-on-1 combat, and on far too many occasions you are beset by more than one or two enemies.
Speaking of enemies, The Ai seems a little off most times, with foes plummeting to their deaths on more than a few occasions, also, just standing there, spinning on the spot as I take pot-shots at them with a bow and the hawk ring.  Not to mention being able to essentially cheese the Dragonrider boss in Heides Tower of flame area.  After taking a few enemies out around the area, I decided to look at the place you fight him.  Standing on the platform just after the third knight, firing arrows at him, only to find when I start the fight, my arrows actually hurt him, and I 1-shotted him with 1 swipe of a dagger.  They also need to re-jig a few enemies in my opinion too.  as later in the game I came across a few enemies with what seemed to be no stamina bar.  BASH BASH BASH BASH BASH (all this while spinning on the spot with the attrocius tracking), dude, take a breather damnit!  Time to range-cheese this fecker...
The graphics seem to be a bone of contention among many people too, with what seems to be an ever growing munber of people citing that FromSoft blatantly lied about the game being built 'from the ground up' for the PC.  From what I can see here, this wasn't the case.  Yes, the game has many options for tweaking the PC graphics, but doesn't look anything like the demo we were shown in 2013, It seems to have been downgraded for last-gen consoles, and for me, that doesn't fly for a PC title.
The world itself is a mixed bag of pretty places and downright ugly texture-dumps with no cohesive geography unlike the connected world of DS1.  Here, I found myself feeling a little confused upon going way down in a elevator from sea level, and appearing at a different place that was still at sea level...
After looking at a few full map comparisons, I can safely say that continuity wise, the world of DS1 could exist, where the world of DS2 cannot, with areas overlapping each other a lot.  For me, this made the world feel more like seperately designed levels as opposed to a cohesive world.
The sound design seems ok, with the usual bangs and clanks of weapons and armour, but the soundtrack is ultimatley forgettable, with nothing memorable like Sif, Ornstein and Smough, and Gwyns themes all still recognisable to me.  Nothing had the same impact in DS2.
Enemy design is lackluster, with far too many bosses being large humanoids with a slam attack, swipe attack and gap-closer along with one 'unique' attack.  Again, as with the sound there was nothing memorable here.
I wont go into the much vaunted pvp too much, suffice it to say that it's broken all to heck, with the same problems as above, lag-stabs from 20 feet away, wonky hitboxes etc etc...
I'm still on-and-off enjoying my time in DS2, but the shortcomings are making me want to play less and less.
Make of the above what you will, they are only my opinions and experiences within the game.  Hopefully with a few patches, a few of the above problems will be fixed, but until then, I wouldn't recommend DS2, and it hurts me to say so.
