Alien: Isolation is the kind of game that you just can't afford to miss. Buy it. Play it. Experience it. Even those who aren't familiar with the Alien franchise will enjoy this game. It's tense,  interesting, and very, very scary. However, the best thing about Alien: Isolation is how masterfully the Sevastopol was created. It's incredibly immersive, and fans of the original Alien are going to feel right at home. Yes, the game is (very) long. This is good. Horror games are usually too short and can sometimes be finished in one sitting. Alien: Isolation uses its time wisely, allowing the anxiety and fear to build. There's a rich story to unfold, not just a quick scare.
Something to note is that this game has many, sometimes long, periods where not much happens. These are not boring. They give the player a chance to explore and the game a chance to build tension/suspense. The times that you do face the Alien are heart-stopping. This game doesn't just throw a jump scare at you and consider its job done. You will sometimes have to contend with the Alien for long, drawn out periods of time as it stalks and searches for you. I could feel myself sweating every second. Alien: Isolation is what the Alien franchise has desperately needed, game-wise, for a long time. 9/10.
P.S. It's also very refreshing to play a female protagonist, which is sadly still a rare feat in gaming. Amanda is a strong, defiant, well-rounded and independent heroine who's more than capable of fending for herself. She's a survivor. Well done, CA. I applaud you.

Let me preface this by saying I expected to like this game. I came in anticipating that it would be good. Maybe even great.
... It's bloody fantastic! Even as an unfinished project. Even in it's [at the time of writing 0.5.0b early access status. Not -perfect-, and I'll get to that. But it might someday be, if Monomi Park continues to invest the time, the love and the passion they've already demonstrated.
Visual/Animation - The good; It's vibrant, and colorful, and cheerful. The slime models are adorable, and the whole world succeeded in giving me a feeling of child-like delight, not just laying things out for me to go look at, but actively drawing me in, making me -want- to find out what is around the next corner, behind the next door, or underneath the next big slime.
The bad;  The slimes, while perfectly, delightfully adorable, colorful, bouncy, and cute, wouldn't be harmed by a little more differentiation in form. And I'm only saying this to be incredibly nit-picky, because I don't want to give any developer the satisfaction of knowing they absolutely have my number [Even if they actually might, Monomi Park...]
Audio/Sound Effects - The good; Okay, the slimes sound adorable. I mean really adorable.  The sounds of the vacuum gun [Your primary tool] are not disruptive to the overall experience. The music is bright, cheerful, well-implemented and not obtrusively used.
The bad; You use the primary tool constantly, so you'll be hearing the sound of it all the time. This is not the worst thing in the world as the sound isn't obtrusive, but it is something to acknowledge. The music could benefit from further diversity, but honestly, this is 0.5.0b, and I rather expect Monomi Park has other irons in the fire, and likely already plans to add further music to the game.
UI/Instructionals - The good; There is a well organized, well written index accessible in game by pressing the F1 key, this guide covers a lot of ground from basic tutorials to world-building lore and information about tools and resources at your disposal. Contents unlock as you first encounter these resources, preventing the data overload of having an encyclopedia given to you before you've figured out basic movement and interaction. The user interface is unobtrusive, and gives you every bit of data you could possibly need at hand.
The bad; Nothing to say here. The design and implimentation of the UI and information is, frankly, beautiful.
Gameplay - The good; A lot of places to go wander around. A ton of hidden secrets, and a good deal of diversity in the kinds of areas I visited, thematically. The controls are solid and the tools and devices are adequate to truly explore the world. As of 0.5.0b you are not limited by arbitrary invisible walls, there are many secrets, high and low. The ranch itself is fun, and central to the theme and gameplay without requiring an immense investment of time and effort to maintain, leaving it completely possible to spend all day exploring, instead of feeding the hens... cats... er... slimes. Feeding the cat slimes hens.
The bad; again, I note that this is 0.5.0b, but Monomi Park could definitely get away with adding in puzzles, platforming challenges, new tools, and just generally diversifying the kinds of activities we're getting up to here. [This is where the game hits "not quite perfect" status. The pieces are all here to make this a one-of-a-kind, to make Slime Rancher the kind of game other games imitate for the next ten years. All Monomi Park has to do is swing for the fences, and I believe, fervently, that they are capable of it. They've already shown me they are. ] The general gameplay hits a semi-repetitive lull about the time you're ready to start on some of the more advanced tools and mechanics, and there are only so many combinations you can make with two slimes.
Bottom line; Fun, friendly, cheerful and an absolute delight to play. I strongly believe it is worth the $20 USD entry price even in its unfinished form. Not only do I recommend this game, I recommend it as one of the best games I've played in years.
Monomi Park is on to something here, and if they pull it off, I might just throw a party.
---- Edited to add the following -----
Monomi Park nailed it. They've created something that is fun, fresh, and beautiful. Their design and world is a joy to play in, and I am profoundly grateful for having had the chance to experience it.
I have nominated Slime Rancher for the "Soul of Vitruvious" award on 11/24/2017. I could cite a number of things, from the adorable tabby slimes to the hens they feed on. Of all the games I've played this year, Slime Rancher stands out singularly for beautiful, elegant and lovingly crafted art.

My take on the PVE...
Once you understand how this game works, the mystery evaporates in a puff of smoke and you're left wondering why you are still playing.    Gearing up is as simple as identifying which set(s) you wish to have.  Many sets are drops, many are crafted.    If you want mother's sorrow, spend an afternoon running Dolmen's in Deshaan.  Each zone drops certain sets.  They can drop green, blue or purple.  In which case all you have to do is improve them at a crafting bench. If you don't get lucky or don't have time or patience just buy the stuff in guild stores. If you want to accentuate that with Juliano's or Seducer's find a master craftsman (if you aren't already yourself) and have it made.  BOOM.  You are geared.  At this point nothing that drops in a vet dungeon will improve your character (other than the xp).    You can go for the Maelstrom or Master gear of course but then you're done for sure.    Rare spawns?  No.  Just world bosses that spawn like clockwork and drop nothing but crap (occasionaly purple jewelry set piece based on what zone you are in).   Opening locked chests, even teh masters set rarely give anythig of much value or use.  Looting the leather bags that litter the landscape will net you a bag full of voidsteel (or shadowhide) gauntlets which have no gold OR deconstruction value what-so-ever.
There are aspects of the game that are well done.  The world is beautiful on my gtx 1070 in triple screen.  Lots of people mock the combat itself... enjoyed it.
I couldn't get my bow wielding night blade to amount to anything dps wise so I turned her into a speed freak gatherer (which was fun for a bit and lucrative).
But less than two weeks after coming back from a 2 year hiatus, I'm bored out of my mind again.
The dungeons, the world bosses, the chests, the dolmens, the bags, the bottles, the urns.  Just tedius nonsense for nothing but crap.

Broforce was a game which I had watched people play on YouTube and thought it was just another fancy platformer shooter game with the added twist of action adventure movie heroes. While the game is exactly all of those things, it also has many other redeeming points.
The gameplay is overwhelmingly simple. There is nothing wrong with an easy game to play. I for one enjoy games where you can pick it up and play no matter what mood you are in. The fast paced action makes for a brilliant casual game to play when you have a few minutes to kill.
Storywise, there is none. From what I gather anyway. It's just a matter of shooting through hoards and hoards of bad guys and saving your chums who have been kept prisoner. The reward system is based on how many prisoners you actually rescure, and the rewards you get equate into new playable characters, or "Bros". You start off with being able to play Rambo and you work your way through to the likes of Conan the Barbarian, or Broman the Brobarian....
Completing the main game is very short, I managed to do it in roughly two hours of picking up and playing every now and again. There are still plenty of other game modes such as Arcade, coop, (online and local) as well as a level editor which will add hours of endless mindnumbing badguy killing frenzies.
I would highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys a shooting or action game. You cannot go wrong, and the devs are bound to add more features and levels in the future.

This is a very hectic, scrolling shooter. I was expecting more freeform nagivation, but it's just swarms of different ships with different types of firepower coming from the right as you progress from the left. I should've noticed the "shoot-em-up arcade" part in the description.
You can pick up power-ups that will change your cannons to use fireballs, mines, and so forth. Your ship, as well as the enemies, fires in different directions and at different distances. Since it's continuously scrolling, it's very important to dodge and fire as fast as you can. If you're lucky, you'll pick up repair items and extra lives.
It's quite a straightforward arcade shooter, except it's boats instead of spaceships or airplanes. This isn't my usual type of game, but if you like shooters where you are constantly moving forward, you only can move Up/Down/Left/Right within your current frame, and you just shoot like crazy with unlimited ammo while avoiding getting blitzed by an abnormal number of enemy ships... then this might be for you. It's only $0.99, so why not?

After owning the game for almost 6 months, I finally almost forced myself to play it properly (After all I paid for it).
And with mods it CAN be an enjoyable experience, but it almost seems the developers were trying to ruin any fun you might have in a deluded quest to provide challenge for the players (and put it in the worst places possible):
- The province system basically forces you to conquer lands you might not want to and attack factions you might not want to.
- The food/public order is really annoying. Even at normal difficulty whenever you research new buildings (and therefore units), actually constructing the building becomes a whole another challenge (buzz-killing one). Almost every building in the higher tier requires food and causes significant unhapiness, while all the food-producing buildings also produce serious unhapiness. It just seems you are hindered at every step.
- No of armies(no. of generals/admirals) limits that are plain stupid and often insufficient to defend/help keep order.
- units can ONLY be/exist with a general, so no more creating units at one side of empire and then moving those units to the other side (where the current conflict might be). You have to create a general for that and if you have reached the limit and all others are occupied, tough luck!
- You think you made enough money to invest in either army or infrastracture and will reap the fruits of your labor? Think again, a minor nation can destroy entire towns with their agents. There is very little defence against that and repairing buildings is VERY costly and takes a long time - of course if you don't destroy the faction, there is no point in repairing as you will just waste all your money repairing again... in the meantime you will of course lose all bonuses/production/income of those building, most likely making you people quite miffed and your previously overflowing coffers dwindle.
- Faction destroying is ridiculous. Example: minor faction, one town. You take it in a single battle. Couple of remaining units, sometime just one (general always included) retreat to foreign provinces  or sea. On land you have to trespass (worsen relations with neutrals), on sea - well you have to create and keep ships just for that. If you don't their agents will continue to bother you.
- family trees, traits, marriages removed - never got attached in any way to ANY of the characters. It just doesn't suck you in anymore. (for me since Medieval 2).
- worrying trend towards Sims3-like DLC extortion (charging for things that should have been part of the 60Euro game in the first place or that should be free as they don't have much substance)
Most of these are just unecessarily limiting and annoying instead of providing any real challenge. Seriously, I do not remember any other game when I felt sort of "co*kblocked" so many times - frustrating. Sad to say, sometimes I cheat just to enjoy the game.
To be fair, I do not encounter any bugs or erros now and many issues/inbalances are fixed. Battlefield AI is much better and battles are fun to watch - if you have time to really watch as you have to constantly control the units in order to win. But you can watch replays I guess if you want to really enjoy the show. Siege AI is still a mess (so long after release).
Many issues are fixable to some extent with mods, and you will surely find some right up your rally.
But paying  55 euros for a game that is really unenjoyable and just feels broken even without CTDs until you mod it is not a good investment.
Pick it up on sale, don't have high expectations and mod heavily - that's what I did and I can recommend that!
At the current price and what you get for it (mods free of course), it's a clear NO for me.

Black Mesa. The game from way back that was reborn in the new day and age.   At first glance, people will remember how this came out a few years back as a massive overhaul, and was hyped because people were happy to see a old game like Black Mesa, be touched and enhanced in so many ways.   Few years after that, the present, we see that the game has been officially brought to Steam like promised, except this is where some people will hate it and others will be understanding.  My saying in this, is that some do not understand how a originally free mod (although technically its a game that is based off an older game thus not being a mod per se, but whatever) that redid an old game and is now being charged to play, but the thing is, is that this overhaul, is oversweeping, and while the free version of this is still enjoyable, it needed some changes, big time, and from someone who has played the older version, fully, and am still plugging away at this current version, I can compare the two in how they are.
Anyway, on to the review.   Oh, and one more thing.   This part of the review will be over just this version of the game and will be compared to the original game itself, rather than the free mod version.  That part will be later.

If you enjoy Half Life style gameplay, then you will enjoy this.  The game has been revamped in that the maps are much larger, weapons are balanced, enemies are improved, everything.   There are many chances where you will need to think ahead like, "How can I get up there, if I can not touch these surfaces", or "what do I do with this valve I found, and where should it go?".    So in short, it has the same type of 'puzzle solving' gamemechanic like how Half Life series does.   Also, there are various parts of the game where you can interact with random items.  They can be varied from things like the microwaves and pop machines, to hand dryers and experiment machines.  Personally, I enjoy those little interactive things because, I don't know, I just do.
Talk about overhaul, here is another massive and encompassing change that is very apparent.  The audio quality of the voice-lines, is night and day different.  While most of the dialogue itself is kept, the crystal clearness of the voices, is just beautiful and it makes it easier to understand what is being said.   Outside of voices, the sounds of the weapons were improved but many of them use default source sounds with minor tweaks.   The ambient sounds and noises have been enhanced as well, and they sound great.  Music is new and it just has that feel of a half life game.  Mix of rock, mechanical at times, etc.
This is probably the most visual difference that everyone can see, without a doubt.  The visuals were overhauled MASSIVELY.  Everything was redone and improved to a way that is just, beautiful.  Is it ultra 4k FXAA8+, better-than-enb- type of graphics, heck no, but half life has never been about being the best of graphics, but rather the best of gameplay.   However, the looks ARE good, and for someone with a weak computer, they can still run this, and tweak the settings for whatever they desire.   When maxed out, the game is just gorgious, and personally, I enjoy it too because of the smooth 60+fps, which is like liquid smooth.   Outside of the basic visuals, the animation quality has been improved for the people, enemies, and for the weapons.    The weapons, are just more, natural feeling to them and every now and then, a rare weapon-switch animation will occur, which are fun to watch for.  The animations for reloads, firing, switching, running while weapon is drawn, afk animation, etc. are very well done.
As for the UI,its good, especially when Gordon gets his suit for the first time, and the UI in the game is nice, but when paused, it becomes an issue due to transparency making it hard to read certain things.
This is an amazing game that I highly recommend to anyone who enjoyed the half life games, and wants to play another game like it.   This is not fully complete mind you, but the final chapter, will be added in the near future.  Now, I did not mention the Multi-player aspect, only because I have not yet played it.  Many have said it is good but needs tweaking, but I do not know.
And finally, how does this version, compare to the free version.  Well there are a few things, and if you did not see the discussion board topic that explains it, I'll explain the differences between the two.   The reasons may vary from big to small, but I will not list them in any particular order.
So, is this game, good enough to be charged for money?  Yes, yes it is.  The idea of this being a paid mod, is understandable but flawed.   From my view, a mod would mean that you have to play a game and then add this to it, to modify it, hence it being called a Mod.  For Black Mesa, you don't play the old game and then add this to it to modify it, you actually play this  and only this thing to play the game, so with that said, I don't think of this as a mod, but a new game that is based entirely off of an older game.
But, what about this version being paid for, versus the version that came out a few years back?   Well, that up to you.  Do you want to play a game that has a lot of minor things improved, not just visually, but mechanically, or do you want to stick with your rather unbalanced and also incomplete game?   This game itself, will be finished, while the other version, may possibly get finished, but has a much smaller chance, than this game.  The choice is yours, but don't be a party pooper for those who want to buy it and want to play it.

Let me preface this by saying I expected to like this game. I came in anticipating that it would be good. Maybe even great.
... It's bloody fantastic! Even as an unfinished project. Even in it's [at the time of writing 0.5.0b early access status. Not -perfect-, and I'll get to that. But it might someday be, if Monomi Park continues to invest the time, the love and the passion they've already demonstrated.
Visual/Animation - The good; It's vibrant, and colorful, and cheerful. The slime models are adorable, and the whole world succeeded in giving me a feeling of child-like delight, not just laying things out for me to go look at, but actively drawing me in, making me -want- to find out what is around the next corner, behind the next door, or underneath the next big slime.
The bad;  The slimes, while perfectly, delightfully adorable, colorful, bouncy, and cute, wouldn't be harmed by a little more differentiation in form. And I'm only saying this to be incredibly nit-picky, because I don't want to give any developer the satisfaction of knowing they absolutely have my number [Even if they actually might, Monomi Park...]
Audio/Sound Effects - The good; Okay, the slimes sound adorable. I mean really adorable.  The sounds of the vacuum gun [Your primary tool] are not disruptive to the overall experience. The music is bright, cheerful, well-implemented and not obtrusively used.
The bad; You use the primary tool constantly, so you'll be hearing the sound of it all the time. This is not the worst thing in the world as the sound isn't obtrusive, but it is something to acknowledge. The music could benefit from further diversity, but honestly, this is 0.5.0b, and I rather expect Monomi Park has other irons in the fire, and likely already plans to add further music to the game.
UI/Instructionals - The good; There is a well organized, well written index accessible in game by pressing the F1 key, this guide covers a lot of ground from basic tutorials to world-building lore and information about tools and resources at your disposal. Contents unlock as you first encounter these resources, preventing the data overload of having an encyclopedia given to you before you've figured out basic movement and interaction. The user interface is unobtrusive, and gives you every bit of data you could possibly need at hand.
The bad; Nothing to say here. The design and implimentation of the UI and information is, frankly, beautiful.
Gameplay - The good; A lot of places to go wander around. A ton of hidden secrets, and a good deal of diversity in the kinds of areas I visited, thematically. The controls are solid and the tools and devices are adequate to truly explore the world. As of 0.5.0b you are not limited by arbitrary invisible walls, there are many secrets, high and low. The ranch itself is fun, and central to the theme and gameplay without requiring an immense investment of time and effort to maintain, leaving it completely possible to spend all day exploring, instead of feeding the hens... cats... er... slimes. Feeding the cat slimes hens.
The bad; again, I note that this is 0.5.0b, but Monomi Park could definitely get away with adding in puzzles, platforming challenges, new tools, and just generally diversifying the kinds of activities we're getting up to here. [This is where the game hits "not quite perfect" status. The pieces are all here to make this a one-of-a-kind, to make Slime Rancher the kind of game other games imitate for the next ten years. All Monomi Park has to do is swing for the fences, and I believe, fervently, that they are capable of it. They've already shown me they are. ] The general gameplay hits a semi-repetitive lull about the time you're ready to start on some of the more advanced tools and mechanics, and there are only so many combinations you can make with two slimes.
Bottom line; Fun, friendly, cheerful and an absolute delight to play. I strongly believe it is worth the $20 USD entry price even in its unfinished form. Not only do I recommend this game, I recommend it as one of the best games I've played in years.
Monomi Park is on to something here, and if they pull it off, I might just throw a party.
---- Edited to add the following -----
Monomi Park nailed it. They've created something that is fun, fresh, and beautiful. Their design and world is a joy to play in, and I am profoundly grateful for having had the chance to experience it.
I have nominated Slime Rancher for the "Soul of Vitruvious" award on 11/24/2017. I could cite a number of things, from the adorable tabby slimes to the hens they feed on. Of all the games I've played this year, Slime Rancher stands out singularly for beautiful, elegant and lovingly crafted art.

A fun, albeit fundamentally flawed romp through a Japanese take on european high fantasy.  I have been a big fan of the 'Souls' series since first playing Demons' Souls on my ps3 so my thoughts may be slightly skewed in that direction.
One of the main reasons I enjoy the Souls series is the fact that 9 times out of 10 when I die, it's my fault, I messed up in some way.  Unfortunatley, in the majority of my deaths in DS2 this simply wasn't the case.  With enemies defying the rules imposed on the main character in order to get a kill.  For example, my sword pings off a wall, while an enemies weapon swings through it for a hit, being hit full force from behind a shield with 100% defence, being hit when clearly a few feet away from the enemy swing.  Artificial difficulty is also a major problem here too, as the combat engine and lock-on feature are geared towards 1-on-1 combat, and on far too many occasions you are beset by more than one or two enemies.
Speaking of enemies, The Ai seems a little off most times, with foes plummeting to their deaths on more than a few occasions, also, just standing there, spinning on the spot as I take pot-shots at them with a bow and the hawk ring.  Not to mention being able to essentially cheese the Dragonrider boss in Heides Tower of flame area.  After taking a few enemies out around the area, I decided to look at the place you fight him.  Standing on the platform just after the third knight, firing arrows at him, only to find when I start the fight, my arrows actually hurt him, and I 1-shotted him with 1 swipe of a dagger.  They also need to re-jig a few enemies in my opinion too.  as later in the game I came across a few enemies with what seemed to be no stamina bar.  BASH BASH BASH BASH BASH (all this while spinning on the spot with the attrocius tracking), dude, take a breather damnit!  Time to range-cheese this fecker...
The graphics seem to be a bone of contention among many people too, with what seems to be an ever growing munber of people citing that FromSoft blatantly lied about the game being built 'from the ground up' for the PC.  From what I can see here, this wasn't the case.  Yes, the game has many options for tweaking the PC graphics, but doesn't look anything like the demo we were shown in 2013, It seems to have been downgraded for last-gen consoles, and for me, that doesn't fly for a PC title.
The world itself is a mixed bag of pretty places and downright ugly texture-dumps with no cohesive geography unlike the connected world of DS1.  Here, I found myself feeling a little confused upon going way down in a elevator from sea level, and appearing at a different place that was still at sea level...
After looking at a few full map comparisons, I can safely say that continuity wise, the world of DS1 could exist, where the world of DS2 cannot, with areas overlapping each other a lot.  For me, this made the world feel more like seperately designed levels as opposed to a cohesive world.
The sound design seems ok, with the usual bangs and clanks of weapons and armour, but the soundtrack is ultimatley forgettable, with nothing memorable like Sif, Ornstein and Smough, and Gwyns themes all still recognisable to me.  Nothing had the same impact in DS2.
Enemy design is lackluster, with far too many bosses being large humanoids with a slam attack, swipe attack and gap-closer along with one 'unique' attack.  Again, as with the sound there was nothing memorable here.
I wont go into the much vaunted pvp too much, suffice it to say that it's broken all to heck, with the same problems as above, lag-stabs from 20 feet away, wonky hitboxes etc etc...
I'm still on-and-off enjoying my time in DS2, but the shortcomings are making me want to play less and less.
Make of the above what you will, they are only my opinions and experiences within the game.  Hopefully with a few patches, a few of the above problems will be fixed, but until then, I wouldn't recommend DS2, and it hurts me to say so.

I really liked this Call of Duty, I haven't liked one this much since Call of Duty 4. I'll try and do a Singleplayer and a Multiplayer review. And for the record: 6.7 hours is campaign, I have a good 20+ hours in Multiplayer.
Singleplayer: (Warning: Will have spoilers although I will try and make it not so obvious)
Story did a big come back after Ghosts, I know they're made by different people, but Ghosts set the bar pretty dang low. It did seem like they took parts out of different games though, the biggest example is the first level, going into the drop pod. It reminded me exactly of Halo: ODST, crashing into the building and everything. Anyway, Advanced Warfare didn't have the single "hunt for this really bad guy" as it always had, I guess this did too, but they executed differently and better, in my opinion. You hunt for this guy named Hades, and well as you can expect, you do get him and he winds up dying, then the game throws a pretty darn good plot twist, that I personally was already half expecting because well, it's hard to be completely original in shooters anymore and too be fair, there's only so much you can do with them unless you go on a different shooter type game like Metro 2033/Last Light. Campaign has amazing graphics though, a story that'll make you say "not bad" and when you upgrade your exo suit passive abilities, you get supply drops which goes into your multiplayer profile so that's kind of neat too, rewarding you for playing campaign because everyone plays Call of Duty for multiplayer... I don't know why people thought the campaign is &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, maybe it's because they're expecting too much? Or maybe they don't understand if you're going to have a war game based shooter there is only so much you can do?
Multiplayer:
Before there were a bit of connection issues, they said they'd make dedicated servers, I don't know if they did now or not, but my connection does seem better now. Anyway, Multiplayer is.. Decent I guess, enough for me to recommend it, only problem is, different versions of the guns. Now, it's a really good idea I'll give you that, it kind of reminded me of Team Fortress 2 in that aspect, a rare version of the gun (even though in TF2 it doesn't have to do with rarity) has boosts and drawbacks, but the problem with that, is new people are kind of screwed, it took me a while to get a good gun, but I still have the problem of everyone having literally no recoil and killing me from long range with an assault rifle and in 3 bullets while my 3 round burst gun with increased damage and range takes two bursts to kill someone long range. I can oddly look passed that though since I usually seem to catch a lot of people off guard, and speaking of off guard, the spawns kind of suck, I kill someone, and before I know it, 2 people spawn directly behind me, but that's classic Call of Duty spawning for you. All in all though, this game is so much more fun when you're playing with friends than by yourself, it takes a bit to get used to the different guns and spawns, but once you do, it'll be much more fun. The only major complaint I have about this multiplayer, the maps are too small, and there is too much in these small maps. Now, I like options and stuff on where to go to travel to the other side, but there is so many openings in different houses sometimes it is hard to find people and when you do, it's because this guy has been on your butt the last 4 hall ways then rabbit punches you.
Quick Edit: This game is pretty damn good optimized, I'm running dual 6770's and can run this game on High (above that is Extra, which makes it looks 5 times nicer) BUT, in order for it to work properly, you NEED only one GPU, so you HAVE to disable sli/crossfire or else it won't work properly.

Broforce features simplistic 2D graphics and is a cooperative multi-player side scrolling shooter/ platformer - it could easily have been a late 80's arcade game - one of the deluxe cabinets with 4 sets of controls - the kind of Gauntlet-style set up that had coin money written all over it. Get some friends and a steady supply of coins and you'd get multi-player gaming action unparalleled at the time.
Given that this is 2014, that Broforce could be perceived as a 1980's game could be considered as a knock, but Broforce so boldly embraces the old school, so lovingly evokes the spirit of 80's and 90's action games and movies, that it feels brilliantly refreshing.
Everything is pared down to focus on out and out, balls to the wall action. With little in the way of presentation or story you begin the game as a randomly selected Bro, an often charming parody of a popular 80's/90's action hero with parodies of Robocop, Rambo,Terminator and Ellen Ripley included to name just a few, each with a custom weapon load out and a distinct play style.
The aim of the game is to battle your way through the end of each tightly constructed and enemy laden level, take out the oddly weak and passive demon suited guys that wait at the end and leap onto a helicopter ladder to escape to glory. On the way you'll find other captured Bros in cages; free them and you take on their persona, your prior Bro being saved as a 'life', a well implemented system that ensures you're encouraged to try all the different gameplay styles each Bro offers, rather than just sticking with a well-worn favourite.
The side scrolling 2D gameplay is beautifully measured, with each tiny but perfectly formed Bro sprite capable of running and jumping with a Super Mario Bros like precision, whilst wielding an awesome array of weapons with slick gun play akin to Metal Slug, Contra, and Gunstar Heroes.
Broforce is already a potent mix with those attributes but it ramps up the ante by having almost fully destructible environments with some of the best explosions seen in any game, or in any medium for that matter. They've fully captured the excessively destructive spirit from their beloved influences. Many of Broforce's explosions are simply put, epic.
One hastily thrown grenade could just as likely lead to a chain reaction and blow yourself up as it could take out an enemy, so this explosive element quickly becomes integral to the gameplay, leading to some surprisingly tactical play options depending on what Bro you may be playing at that time.
The armed enemy forces are simple but varied fodder, that can regardless still handily punish any careless Bro, with a selection of well realised and balanced bosses featured at the end of selected levels. The varying play styles of each Bro offer different ways to tackle each enemy - one Bro might simply blow up the platform the enemy stands on - one might jump and shoot from long range - one might attack from close range with melee - there really are a lot of ways to approach each scenario.
But the true mayhem ensues when playing the drop-in, drop-out online multiplayer. Up to 4 players can co-op and it is in this mode that some of the best fun is to be had. Much of the time you'll be unwittingly exploding the hell out of one another, as screen filling explosions erupt and Bros fall to their doom, often with hilarious (or infuriating) results.
Though it's just as likely to get a cohesive team and it soon becomes evident what a great co-op game this can be, each Bro can complement the other, and with 4 at once from a huge range of Bros, it's rare you'll encounter the same combo twice offering a great deal of variety.
Still an early access game, Broforce offers many other modes at varying stages of completion and even offers a custom level design utility, with hundreds of custom maps ready to play and many more appearing on the horizon.
Even at this early stage, Broforce offers a lot for the asking price and is definitely one of the most promising early access games yet released.
Unfinished it may be but it offers almost instant gameplay gratification - no fuss, no filler, just good old school explosive arcade action.

My take on the PVE...
Once you understand how this game works, the mystery evaporates in a puff of smoke and you're left wondering why you are still playing.    Gearing up is as simple as identifying which set(s) you wish to have.  Many sets are drops, many are crafted.    If you want mother's sorrow, spend an afternoon running Dolmen's in Deshaan.  Each zone drops certain sets.  They can drop green, blue or purple.  In which case all you have to do is improve them at a crafting bench. If you don't get lucky or don't have time or patience just buy the stuff in guild stores. If you want to accentuate that with Juliano's or Seducer's find a master craftsman (if you aren't already yourself) and have it made.  BOOM.  You are geared.  At this point nothing that drops in a vet dungeon will improve your character (other than the xp).    You can go for the Maelstrom or Master gear of course but then you're done for sure.    Rare spawns?  No.  Just world bosses that spawn like clockwork and drop nothing but crap (occasionaly purple jewelry set piece based on what zone you are in).   Opening locked chests, even teh masters set rarely give anythig of much value or use.  Looting the leather bags that litter the landscape will net you a bag full of voidsteel (or shadowhide) gauntlets which have no gold OR deconstruction value what-so-ever.
There are aspects of the game that are well done.  The world is beautiful on my gtx 1070 in triple screen.  Lots of people mock the combat itself... enjoyed it.
I couldn't get my bow wielding night blade to amount to anything dps wise so I turned her into a speed freak gatherer (which was fun for a bit and lucrative).
But less than two weeks after coming back from a 2 year hiatus, I'm bored out of my mind again.
The dungeons, the world bosses, the chests, the dolmens, the bags, the bottles, the urns.  Just tedius nonsense for nothing but crap.

This game is hated on by many people.  I admit the release was a little rough, but the devs have definitely made many improvements to gameplay and balance.  As a fan of the Total War series, I find Rome 2 to be a great addition.  Dont listen to all the nay sayers, give it a chance!

While I know that quite a lot has been said (mostly on the negative end of the spectrum) about how the game's launch was hobbled terribly and that it was really only half a game.  The immersive and expansive feel to the game dwarfs most all of its successors.  Only Empire had as large or larger of a game screen/map... and it's launch went poorly, too.  That is, if I am remembering correcty...
Gameplay is fairly standard for a Total War series.  Fortunately, they have added a little flair in giving the units more individuality.  They aren't all marching lock-in-step.  Some of them trip, fall, get trampled, others react to it.  For what this game is... it does it well.
And, for as many hours as I have sunk into it... both in Single and Multiplayer... it must really have some replayability.  (Is that even a word?)
For my money's worth... good game to have.  A great iteration in the Total War series...
A cautionary note... This game is very, very, VERY DLC intensive.  In other words, the base game is fairly robust.  But, if you would like more of the bells and whistles... and continue to see Creative Assembly extend the life of the product - DLC is really the only way to go.  So, minor complaint... but the price tag you see is only for the base game.  Expect to shell out another $30 to pick up the add-ons.

I'm a self confessed Total War fan'boi'.
I would not recommend this game. I feel dirtied for having purchased it. I didn't get it at release because of the current state of main stream releases; bring it out with a plethora of bugs and fix them as they're reported. I managed to dodge the mess that was this launch where the game was fundamentally unplayable.
But it wasn't worth the wait. The game that is here now is a sad lament for what Total War games used to be. I've genuinely reinstalled Medieval 2 TW with 'The Third Age' mod to try and forget that this is where the series ended up.
The game isn't very pretty. By modern standards it's actually quite clunky, in particular the campaign map which is quite simply ugly to a modern market. But who cares about the graphics; The gameplay is where the game really lets you down. The battles are tedious, easy, and feel less like fights between individual soldiers (a hallmark of the series) and more like you throwing elaborate rocks at scissors and avoiding the papers. The intergration between naval battles and land battles is embarassingly clunky, and offer hundreds of immersion breaking exploits such as landing a crew of peasants in the middle of a major city and taking it whilst the AI twiddles thumbs on the walls. There are mods that can salvage this, but it isn't fair to review the game on a modded version.
The campaign management just isn't fun. You can tweak it with the mods again to rectify that, avoiding some of the now infamous 'agent spam' from the AI or also infamous 'pointless politics' which always culminate in scripted events whether you manage the country wonderfully or mash you face on the keyboard each turn. Building an invasion force becomes laughably easy on lower difficulty and pointlessly difficult on higher difficulty, tweaking the numbers rather than the ability of the computers.
All in all, this had the framework of a masterpiece. I enjoyed my time on it and if you're an absolute die hard fan of the series like me, then come on , we both know you have to buy it. But I know that if you are like me, you may also shed a tear when you see the list of DLCs, including playing as some content they originally made for vanilla but are locked until you cough up  a tenner. I'm not sure if the worst part of this game is that I can't play as Athens if I don't pay money equivalent to a whole new game, or if I also have to pay more money if I want to put the graphic settings on gory.

Black Mesa is an (almost) complete remake of the original Half-Life, created entirely by some community members. This mod is just fantastic, with very little bugs and no shortage of fun.
The mod is currently missing the Xen chapters from the original Half-Life, but those are to be released very soon. There's also a remake of Half-Life's Deathmatch mode, which, at the moment, isn't as fun as the core game, but I can definitely see it has some potential.
Black Mesa goes for $20 USD, which seems a little pricey. But hey, these awesome community members deserve the money, so you should definitely consider buying this just to support the developers. Can't afford it? Don't worry, there's a free version online somewhere. All you'd be missing out on are the new visuals, sounds and animations from Black Mesa's Steam release (Instead being replaced by older visuals/sounds/animations from BM's original release).
I can't recommend this game more. It is definitely a fantastic remake of Half-Life and is worth every single cent.

If you loved the original Half-Life like I did, or you're a newcomer who wants to play the experience that started it all (TF2, CS:GO, DOD, etc.) then this is the definitive experience. I can honestly say Black Mesa is worthy of the game it's based on.
If you're one of those people who says "I'm not paying for a MOD", then well, honestly, stop being cheap. The people who made Black Mesa put a lot of work into doing the original Half-Life justice, and it shows.
Buy it.

However it recently came to steam to expand its numbers and many many players have joined (or tried to) recently. The joining with steam has created a huge number of bugs that Hi-Rez thankfully is fixing, and the fledgling community has been beaten upon by the veterans who have become frustrated at the new number of players. Oh my! Where do I begin? I am an old D&D fan. I've played all the Neverwinter series of games from way back. I cut my teeth on MMORPG's with vanilla WoW. I played Neverwinter MMORPG. I came to hate MMO's after Blizzard released Panderia. I loathed and despised FTP/Pay to Win MMO's like Neverwinter. I swore I'd never play another MMO. Then I played ESO... Let me be clear I still hate MMO's, but ESO so far in my gaming does not really feel like an MMO overall. I came late to Elder Scrolls. I was too busy with Warcraft, Neverwinter Nights and other games. I'm sorry I missed it. Elder Scrolls is so rich and deep into fantasy D&D type gaming that playing any of the versions of it feels like computerized D&D to me. I tried Morrowwind but the graphics are too dated and bug me, but I did play Oblivion and Skyrim. I played Skyrim til there was nothing left to do then modded it and play some more. I'm hooked. I bought ESO because Skyrim left me wanting more and ESO has delivered in a huge way. I cannot say enough about my experience. BUY THIS GAME!
That said there are still little annoyances that go with online MMO's. You still get your irritating players spewing nonsense in zone chat and ESO seeems to have issues with latency. Depending upon your ISP connection speed and your 'puter you may experience many frustrating load screens when moving about the world of Nirn/Tamriel. I get this most when inside a city/hub. That would be my greatest peeve. I live with it though because ESO keeps me hungry to explore and quest and see what's around the bend. I could go on, but I won't. Buy the game and see for yourself!

TL;DR at the bottom!
Singleplayer: Kevin Spacey pretty much carries the singleplayer, it's super cool to see him both in-game and in pre-rendered cutscenes, and there's much fun to be had throughout the campaign. I want to keep this brief, so I'll just say that the story is nothing completely unique, just another Call of Duty, heroes take down the bad guys, but the gadgets and sometimes unique missions they have can be pretty fun. There's even a jet section, although it's very clunky and arcady, not taking advantage of your mouse capabilities to control, but only to click, firing rockets and whatnot. It also tolerates blatently running into the ground and scraping it for a few seconds, to give you an idea of how arcady it is. The game tries to throw emotional scenes at you, all though it's safe to say they all miss the target by a country mile, although, without spoiling anything, there are some genuinely disturbing moments. Overall, the singleplayer is worth a playthrough, in my opinion.
Multiplayer: The biggest, darkest black mark on this year's CoD is the lack of dedicated servers. The whole host-based games works terribly, as someone who lives in the Middle East, finding games is difficult. Once you do find a game, perhaps hosted by someone in Southern Europe, it's still pretty laggy, giving me MAX 3/4 bars (another note, please stop using arbitrary bars, we're not idiots who don't understand numerical ping), that being the highest I've ever seen. Then when that host decides to leave, there's a pretty large chance that the host to which the game is migrated to, lives farther away, resulting in 1 or 2 less bars than before, to the extent that it becomes unplayable and I'm forced to quit and find another game (which I might add, takes forever considering where I live). I don't understand why, with another CoD coming out every year, they have yet to figure out that dedicated servers on PC is the way to go. I applaud Treyarch for having figured it out, but it seriously boggles my mind that Sledgehammer and Infinity Ward refuse to do it. Not only would they fix the problem of having unstable games, with the host being migrated all the time, but as an owner of a dedicated server, you would have the ability to make rules and ban perpetrators, which leads me onto my next gripe with the multiplayer. Lasers are so so frustrating to play against. They have no ammo, so if you're not a 0/10, terrible player, and have the ability to manage the overheating mechanic of them (which is a non-factor if you're any good), you will never lose an extended fight. Secondly, firing from the hip with a laser gun is just as good as aiming down sights, since the cross hair is unbelievably narrow, leaving little room for scatter no matter how much you're jumping around. This allows you to fire from the hip and hit easily in a dogfight, because the other player (who we're assuming is using a regular bullet weapon) has to aim down sights to achieve the same level of accuracy. This is a problem because when you're jumping around constantly and your opponent is too, it's really easy to lose track of them, especially when you're aiming down sights and your FOV is seriouly restricted. The player with the laser doesn't have this problem cause he's happy just firing from the hip, making him even more likely to win the fight. To return to an earlier point, IF THIS GAME HAD DEDICATED SERVERS, AND YOU HATED LASER WEAPONS JUST AS MUCH AS ME, YOU COULD JOIN A  SERVER WHERE THE RULES BAN THE USE OF LASER WEAPONS. That's the biggest thing about dedicated servers, and the biggest reason why Sledgehammer are seriously mistaken for continuing the moronic trend of no dedicated servers. Anyway, so far we've talked about the lack of dedicated servers and the imbalance of laser weapons, which are pretty much the main two gripes I have with the multiplayer. To focus on the positive aspects, the addition of boost jump is super cool, adding an amazing amount of verticality to the game, as being on the ground one second and on the top of a roof the next second is fantastic. The boost pack also allows for some pretty cool dog fights, which greatly increases the skill ceiling of the game, effectively fixing the issue of past CoDs where you couldn't easily seperate the absolute best players, because the truly better player didn't have sufficient mediums through which he could prove his superior skills. The customization is fantastic in this game too, with guns having lots of attachments and with the player even having the ability to customize score streaks, adding additional affects to them. Unfortunately they lock all your gun attachments and you have to do a whole bunch of achievements to unlock the one you want, which I feel like a grind because it forces me to use attachments that I do not find fun, making it feel like a grind for what I truly want. Overall, the multiplayer is a potentially incredible experience, rivaling perhaps even the likes of CoD 4, but the lack of dedicated servers and thus no escape from the frustrating laser guns, anchor it down very tightly, making it a regrettably very infuriating experence in the end. Imagine no dedicated servers in CoD 4, so everyone uses the martyrdom perk. Yeah, it'd be something like this.

- Lack of dedicated servers. Really, Sledgehammer. Shot yourself in the foot there.

I'm a self confessed Total War fan'boi'.
I would not recommend this game. I feel dirtied for having purchased it. I didn't get it at release because of the current state of main stream releases; bring it out with a plethora of bugs and fix them as they're reported. I managed to dodge the mess that was this launch where the game was fundamentally unplayable.
But it wasn't worth the wait. The game that is here now is a sad lament for what Total War games used to be. I've genuinely reinstalled Medieval 2 TW with 'The Third Age' mod to try and forget that this is where the series ended up.
The game isn't very pretty. By modern standards it's actually quite clunky, in particular the campaign map which is quite simply ugly to a modern market. But who cares about the graphics; The gameplay is where the game really lets you down. The battles are tedious, easy, and feel less like fights between individual soldiers (a hallmark of the series) and more like you throwing elaborate rocks at scissors and avoiding the papers. The intergration between naval battles and land battles is embarassingly clunky, and offer hundreds of immersion breaking exploits such as landing a crew of peasants in the middle of a major city and taking it whilst the AI twiddles thumbs on the walls. There are mods that can salvage this, but it isn't fair to review the game on a modded version.
The campaign management just isn't fun. You can tweak it with the mods again to rectify that, avoiding some of the now infamous 'agent spam' from the AI or also infamous 'pointless politics' which always culminate in scripted events whether you manage the country wonderfully or mash you face on the keyboard each turn. Building an invasion force becomes laughably easy on lower difficulty and pointlessly difficult on higher difficulty, tweaking the numbers rather than the ability of the computers.
All in all, this had the framework of a masterpiece. I enjoyed my time on it and if you're an absolute die hard fan of the series like me, then come on , we both know you have to buy it. But I know that if you are like me, you may also shed a tear when you see the list of DLCs, including playing as some content they originally made for vanilla but are locked until you cough up  a tenner. I'm not sure if the worst part of this game is that I can't play as Athens if I don't pay money equivalent to a whole new game, or if I also have to pay more money if I want to put the graphic settings on gory.

I recommend you buy this game at half price at the very most. I do recommned the game, it's fun, has a very large and extensive campaign with many factions to play as. However, the game has been stripped of some features previous in older Total War games such as the family tree. The game in general moves far too fast to get attached to your commanders, like in previous games, and they die a lot without any real notice.
The buildings and campaign planning is now at an absolute minimum, with a new provincial system that works well when you are  a large nation, but suffers from a lack of depth when you are a small nation. The politcs screen does nothing, and can be ignored completely, providing nothing in terms of gameplay to the world.
Seasons have been re-introduced because the community cried out for it, however the game moves at one turn per year, so seasons don't fit the timescale and don't play much effect.
The graphics are top notch. Both on campaign and on battles, however my PC is very capable at running on Ultra, but only around an average of 30fps. Optimization is extremly poor for entry level PCs and the graphical fidelity falls extremely quick when you lower the settings.
Battles are fun to play, they look impressive and work well in general. It's taken 12 major updates to get to the stage where I am comfortable at recommending this to someone, but as with most TotalWar games, the AI is terrible. On the campaign it's fairly smart, however diplomacy is almost non existant. You can't trade money effectivley, you can't gift regions or demand them you cannot bribe armies or settlements, you cannot co-ordinate with any certainty your nation and another to attack a particualr spot or nation.
On land, battles work pretty well. The AI behaves appropriately and in some cases smartly. This is where the game is best. Open terrain battles with large armies clashing in the fields. In large towns, it's more cumbersome as the enemy try to navigate streets quite poorly. In full on walled cities, the game falls flat on it's face. The AI pathfinding is terrible and they will pretty much throw armies at one spot until they break through, which they never will.
The multiplayer scene is dead. For a game that's sold over 1m copies, you'd be lucky to find 20 active games.
Co-op campaigns are brilliant. This is because AI isn't an issue and you can play against someone for the entire game. You just need someone willing to play with you for a full campaign.
That's all. Like I said, half price at best. The game's DLC packs offer nothing great, more factions and more of the same. this is probably the worst Total War game to date. But it's still a Total War game, if you need to play battles where 1000's of troops clash together, this is your game. If you need good strategy, in depth campaigns or history, I'd look to Civilization V, Crusader Kings II, Total War: Shogun II or Europa Universalis IV
If you're a hardcore Total War fan who wants to boycott the series, no point, they've sold 1m+ games. It's by far their most successful game to date. Just don't pre-order the next one.

I absolutely adore Dishonored, and I feel that Dishonored 2 capitalizes upon both the first ones positives, and fixes its negatives. I found very few graphical issues, and those that I found were not nearly as game breaking as I had heard about them being. There was one very bad section for the graphical stuttering, which I encountered early on in Chapter 8 of the game, just entering in. It caused the game to run at a near stand-still, but once I had passed this section, It ran beautifully.
The few negatives moments I encountered while playing the game all centered around the Auto-Save system. It is set base to autosave whenever you open your Journal, as well as being spread out through sections of the map, some obvious, such as transitioning sections. Others I've still not figured out what triggered them, or why they were triggered, as they seemed to be in very odd locations, such as landing near a side of the map with a transition door, rather than the transition itself. Or getting, simply, near an objective, rather than using or interacting with the Objective.
Pros:
-Very much a continuation of Dishonored, both in heart and in thought, staying true to the characters, while developing new ones and allowing for a more diverse, growing universe.
-Skills are reworked and built upon in a way that they feel true to past, but are refreshing and vitalizing at their core, such as Blink getting a perk later on which allows you to stop time should you stop moving. Such as jumping into the air and releasing the forward key/stick and looking around for a spot to warp, allowing you to get to some of the far harder places to reach. Or Rat Swarm getting 2 swarms, and even larger swarms, or even having the swarms following you around!
-Fantastic Voice acting, with quite indepth backgrounds, even for the 'faceless' NPCs, those you would encounter who aren't truly important to have a name, but are there none the less.
-Character developement dependant upon choices made throughout the game. The loadscreen hints at this, but It is truly a MASSIVE difference, even from Chapter 1 to Chapter 2. There is also quite a bit of personal character developement for the main characters throughout the game.
-Challenging, delightfully unforgiving when attempting Unseen and Merciful gameplay (Never be detected + No Kills.)
-DIFFICULTIES MATTER. Hard is actually quite hard. Like, extremely hard. Outsider knows how hard Very Hard will be when I get to it.
Cons:
-Performance has some issues in places. Granted, I do not have the patch finished yet, so will ammend at a later date should this patch assuage the issues.
-Auto-Save system needs alot of rework. (In one instance, I accidentally killed a Guard, not aware I had shot a regular  both and not a Sleep Dart, dropped down to loot and not only had it saved shortly after the kill (within seconds) It also saved thirty or so seconds later when I got to the corpse. There is only 2 Auto-Save slots. There is no Chapter/Level restart, compounding the issue (As there are situations I had  been in where I would have prefered to restart the entire level, rather than simply  loading back an auto-save a few moments before hand.)
-NPCs and Guards are either comically evil, or simply misguided, the differences between them are utterly jarring. One guard could be a bloodthristy ex-con, while the one standing directly to his right could be Altruistic and Caring towards his fellow citizens.

WARNING: Long wall of text, but it is worth your time to read it.
I've waited most of a decade for Black Mesa, so i was very happy to finally see it on steam, and i bought and downloaded it on release over a week ago. No, i did not play the free mod. Since i knew BM was coming to steam, i decided to wait until then to play it.
Before i get into my review/opinion of BM, i just want to briefly share a special moment i had with BM after downloading it. You see, i was introduced to Half Life in 1999 when my father got it for his birthday, i was there with him when he first fired it up. It was such an important moment in my life that i had my father sit there with me when i first fired up Black Mesa. We were both in awe just at the train ride, and i played all the way up through a little bit of Unforseen Consequences with him.
So now, my opinion of Black Mesa.
It is absolutely extraordinary. I have played through BM 2 times so far, and i have thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it.
What i love in particular is that it is not just an HD remake of Half Life 1, it is a genuine unique remake. Alot of the areas and levels are essentially the same in terms of the layout, but they are often expanded and changed somewhat to add whole new things to do and alternatives. One of my favorite moments is actually handing the scientist the toilet paper. I also love all the new dialogue with the scientists and guards before the resonance cascade (listen for an Office Space reference in Anomalous Materials).
Some levels are changed, which is great. The first puzzle in Unforseen Consequences i was stuck on for a little bit, as that was not in the original Half Life (the one with the two red valves). I loved that my memorization of Half Life 1 (see my name) did not allow me to just instantly know what to do at every challenge. Some of the chapters are shortened, chiefly On A Rail and Surface Tension. I'm not sure how i feel about that, but it is still fun regardless. There are changes in some orders of events, you get the crowbar a little later than in Half Life 1, and can get the .357 magnum in Office Complex as opposed to Blast Pit.
My favorite newly designed level is actually the supply depot for the entry into Xen (the place where you get the long jump module), as i genuinely got a sort of NASA/Space station feel of it, like i was genuinely going to an alien world.
Very, very few of the models are direct copy-paste from Half Life 2. The ones that are just copied over are really expected and totally acceptable: Headcrab, Barnacle, G-man are virtually unchanged from HL2. Vortigaunt is probably 95-99% the same. 96-99% of all other models are original, or acceptably re-skinned. I love the de-aging of Eli Vance and Issac Kleiner. SFX and graphics are exceptional, with some error here and there which can be fixed (this is early access after all).
I love the weapons, my favorite has to be the MP-5/M-203, i was elated with the new model of it as well as it's change to 30 round magazine from 50 round magazine. The overall reduction in maximum ammo is a great addition.
The soldiers and their vehicles are great too, although i kind of miss hearing the troops though radio chatter.
The security guards are actually quite improved over Half Life 1, they are not stuck with the Glock, as some have the .357 and some have the Shotgun. Their AI is much better too, and they can be helpful.
I also love the changes to the events of the AI friendlies, They now fit into the enviornment and story more. Ill give an example of what i mean. The first guard you can work with in Unforseen Consequences. If he doesnt die by the time you get to the lobby, he will say that he is going to try to call for help on the comms system, and tells you to get up to the admin offices (Office Complex). In Half Life 1, if you kept the guard alive that long, he would just stand there as you leave him behind when you go beyond the point where he can follow you. It's the things like this that really make BM shine.
Other than those of the Headcrab, Vortigaunt and Barnacle, it seems to me that just about all of the sounds are original, which is a great plus for me personally: One part of me had a small fear that BM would be so fun and good that i would not play Half Life 1 again. The total changes in sounds prevent this, as i will always hold the atmosphere and sounds of Half Life 1 sacred.
One great moment for me was in Surface tension, i enter a dark area and hear some light sounds. I think "is that a puppy?" I am not kidding i genuinely thought there was going to be a puppy in a small cage. Nope, it was the bloody snarks!!!!
I wont comment much on the music for a special reason: the thing is, for reasons that i am not clear on, my dad and i always played Half Life without the music. I don't know if it was a bug or something, but i just know Half Life 1 without music. So with Black Mesa, i had the music on in the first run, but then turned it off. Nothing against the composer, i just prefer to play Half Life 1 and now Black Mesa w/o music.
I have not played BM Multiplayer, and i never played HL deathmatch, so i wont comment on that at all.
There are some problems though, most of which i wont say here as they are bugs that are most probably to be fixed.
One technical problem i have seen: the targeting map for the mortars at the end of Surface tension needs alot of work, it's clunky to use.
But in terms of design choices, there is one problem that i must insist upon a change:

All of the dark areas are fine for atmosphere and such, but the flashlight needs to be stronger. On my first playthough i was straining my vision at some points.
Thats about all i can say on the negative at this point.
I had no problem paying $20 for Black Mesa. These guys deserve our money, they poured their heart and soul into this, and the result is top of the line.
Should i buy Black Mesa? Hell yes!
Will Black Mesa replace Half Life 1?
Hell no, that game is still the classic that we all remember, and Black Mesa should be a welcome companion to that 1998 classic.
Other than the issue of the under-powered flashlight, i have nothing negative to say about Black Mesa, it is simply a masterpiece. If Valve had today's technology and resources when they made Half Life, it would probably look just like Black Mesa.

Alien: Isolation is a brilliant game. It merges action, horror, steatlh, and complete cinematic immersion into one full package. It's very likely that this particular package turned out to be one of the best Alien games of all time!
You play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of the famous Ellen Ripley. Throughout this journey that could take you up to 25 hours, firmly cementing the value of this game, you'll experience so much. Androids, scavenging humans, and the viscious alien! Even if there are only 3 of these enemy types, the game makes ample use of variety and pacing, so you'll often be faced with varying situations. The game, however, can drag and turn into a "walking simulator", but even these moments are made better by the stunning graphics or audio. Some of these moments are quite breathtaking, and only serve to aid the brilliant pacing of this game. It NEVER overwhelms you with too much action, but it continues to bombard you with tension and even fear.
To aid you in this crazy long journey, you must use your engineer skills to craft items from scavenged parts which are quite fun to loot. It feels quite similiar to Bioshock, in fact. You can create a wide variety of items, including things such as flashbangs or smokebombs. Sadly, I found that the game was too generous with certain components, especially for items that didn't get much use from me at all. The latter two items I just mentioned barely saw any use out of me, but as I progressed I did find some use out of some items. Even when crafting these tools of survival, the tension haunts you, as it takes precious seconds to create them!
Another thing the game is littered with are "light" quick time events and minigames. However, none of it felt tedious or forced. In fact, pulling levers, using the wrench, hacking terminals with the hack tool, and using the blowtorch is quite fun! Now that might come off as odd sounding to you, but hear me out. Since this is the PC version, it asks you to hold down LMB and RMB, then push one of the movement keys to use the wrench or pull a lever. Somehow it feels way more fun and interactive than simply using the use key. The game will give you moments where you have to do many of these in a row, but it's so damn satisfying that I almost didn't care! These moments also had such high tension and drama that I felt hurried, making those precious seconds really count!
When you use all your tools at your disposal, you'll stumble upon a few secret areas, in which you'll find fun collectable dogtags and the main event of collectables: The Nostromo Audio Logs! I haven't found all of these, and you might have to do a lot of backtracking in order to do so, because the game seems to let you travel wherever you want at certain points. This does give the game a "Metroidvania" feel to it, and I'd call this game "semi open world", but I have yet to test if it will let me travel to other parts of the space station whenever I want!
Now, that was a mouthful. But please, the game is very much worth so many words! Alien: Isolation is fantastic, breathing life into the horror genre again and into AAA gaming!

This game will stick on your mind after you've completed it. I haven't played such a nightmarish experience in a long time. And that's a good thing. When you think the nightmare is over you are thrown into another one. It took me 22 hours to get through the campaign on hard. The difficulty is perfectly balanced. As long as you take your time and proceed carefully you should be fine most of the time.
The gameplay mostly consists of you sneaking, staying quiet, hacking, crafting items to distract enemies or impair them. The further you proceed on your different missions you will find upgrades for your tools that will allow you to access areas you earlier couldn't. You will also get your hands on upgrades for your make shift weapons. Lethal weapons will eventually become part of your inventory but it's recommended to avoid using them but the further you get in the game the more lethal situations will become and they will come in handy. You can backtrack if you want to, or explore areas that are not part of the current mission. If you do you might find secret audio logs, items and easter eggs. So the game never feels very linear but instead quite free which I haven't seen since early days of Resident Evil. Of course there's always imminent danger that waits for you to make a mistake. It's even more similar in the way that you have to save your game at save stations, but don't worry, you don't need an ink ribbon. However, the game doesn't pause when you save and it takes a while for the station to load up. Nor does the game pause when you bring up your inventory and crafting system, which is reminiscent of Dead Space.
The story is good and quite straight forward, and it does contain twists and turns that did make me jump with excitement and surprise. However I wish that the conclusion would have been more satisfying. The voice acting is solid but the lipsyncing is quite poor. Especially when it's in-game and not a cut-scene.
The game itself is very well built. At no time did I experience any performance loss, crashes or game glitches that interfered with the gameplay. During my long playthrough I only noticed one or two oddity not even worth mentioning. I played the game on ultra settings and the visuals are very impressive when it comes to lights and shadows. There so many details in the environment in this game that it's amazing. At a closer inspection though, some low-res textures can be found but overall an incredible looking game.
The sound design is perfect, it re-creates and expand upon all the sounds and music from the movie Alien that it makes you feel like you really are in that universe.
The physics are great with your body reacting to everything around you in the environment, you might for example accidentally kick something on the floor and cause a loud noise or tip over furniture etc.
The option menu is well fleshed out with many different visual settings, including FOV.
The different mechanics like crafting, hacking, using tools and weapons is very intuitive. For example when entering a passcode you use your numpad, or when re-loading a weapon you must hold R to reload a full magazine, if you just press R once it will only load one bullet for example. Computer interfaces requires you to use your keyboard to navigate, like if there are no mouses which add to the push button feel of the 70s.
I was worried that the alien's "AI" would fail and break the game, but I'm glad to have been proven wrong. Not at any time did I see the alien glitch out or do something stupid. It really is a ruthless killer that requires your respect. The same goes for the humans and the androids. The humans work together as teams and if they are hostile you better avoid them or distract them to get to where you need to go. The androids are lethal if they catch you, they can't run but they do walk steadily towards you like a terminator.
Conclusion: While it does borrow a lot from other games in the terms of gameplay mechanics, this survival horror game combines old school gameplay with an extremely impressive, dynamic enemy, incredible visual and sound design and a thrilling story in full blown Alien spirit. It's a truly unique experience. If you are a fan, don't miss out on Amanda Ripley's struggle for survival and quest to find the truth..

I absolutely adore Dishonored, and I feel that Dishonored 2 capitalizes upon both the first ones positives, and fixes its negatives. I found very few graphical issues, and those that I found were not nearly as game breaking as I had heard about them being. There was one very bad section for the graphical stuttering, which I encountered early on in Chapter 8 of the game, just entering in. It caused the game to run at a near stand-still, but once I had passed this section, It ran beautifully.
The few negatives moments I encountered while playing the game all centered around the Auto-Save system. It is set base to autosave whenever you open your Journal, as well as being spread out through sections of the map, some obvious, such as transitioning sections. Others I've still not figured out what triggered them, or why they were triggered, as they seemed to be in very odd locations, such as landing near a side of the map with a transition door, rather than the transition itself. Or getting, simply, near an objective, rather than using or interacting with the Objective.
Pros:
-Very much a continuation of Dishonored, both in heart and in thought, staying true to the characters, while developing new ones and allowing for a more diverse, growing universe.
-Skills are reworked and built upon in a way that they feel true to past, but are refreshing and vitalizing at their core, such as Blink getting a perk later on which allows you to stop time should you stop moving. Such as jumping into the air and releasing the forward key/stick and looking around for a spot to warp, allowing you to get to some of the far harder places to reach. Or Rat Swarm getting 2 swarms, and even larger swarms, or even having the swarms following you around!
-Fantastic Voice acting, with quite indepth backgrounds, even for the 'faceless' NPCs, those you would encounter who aren't truly important to have a name, but are there none the less.
-Character developement dependant upon choices made throughout the game. The loadscreen hints at this, but It is truly a MASSIVE difference, even from Chapter 1 to Chapter 2. There is also quite a bit of personal character developement for the main characters throughout the game.
-Challenging, delightfully unforgiving when attempting Unseen and Merciful gameplay (Never be detected + No Kills.)
-DIFFICULTIES MATTER. Hard is actually quite hard. Like, extremely hard. Outsider knows how hard Very Hard will be when I get to it.
Cons:
-Performance has some issues in places. Granted, I do not have the patch finished yet, so will ammend at a later date should this patch assuage the issues.
-Auto-Save system needs alot of rework. (In one instance, I accidentally killed a Guard, not aware I had shot a regular  both and not a Sleep Dart, dropped down to loot and not only had it saved shortly after the kill (within seconds) It also saved thirty or so seconds later when I got to the corpse. There is only 2 Auto-Save slots. There is no Chapter/Level restart, compounding the issue (As there are situations I had  been in where I would have prefered to restart the entire level, rather than simply  loading back an auto-save a few moments before hand.)
-NPCs and Guards are either comically evil, or simply misguided, the differences between them are utterly jarring. One guard could be a bloodthristy ex-con, while the one standing directly to his right could be Altruistic and Caring towards his fellow citizens.
