This is a short but intricate and gritty stat-based survival simulation; playthroughs are exceptionally short but you'll never be able to stop at just one. With so many overlong romance based visual novels around, TBOTW is refreshing brief and focused on survival following a nuclear attack, with a further level of intriguing Carollian hints that all is not as it seems. There is optional romance, you'll die more frequently than Long Live the Queen, and working through multiple plotlines to reach the true plotline is an intriguing problem. Descriptions of a world gone mad are efficient and heartfelt, some of the deaths are incredibly dire. The ending has prompted a lot of complaints, but fans of short non-romantic and challenging visual novels should love this.

From Red Nettle Studios comes the visual novel, The Bottom of the Well. Released in 2016, this game has been rated very positively by Steam users all over the globe. In this game, you play as Alice. You remember, Alice in Wonderland, right? Except this is a whole new kind of wonderland. This is a post apocalyptic dream that you have to guide Alice through, hoping she survives your choices.
For a post apocalyptic game, I wasn't expecting much from this. I've played so many different kinds of games in the post apocalyptic genre, I didn't think this would have anything decent to it.
Oh boy, was I in for a shock.
This was creepy. This was so life like, not in it's drawings or characters, or it's soundtrack, but in its descriptions of a post apocalyptic world that we all dread happening one day. The descriptions of what happens in Alice's dream are scarily accurate to what we imagine what will happen. I had goosebumps playing through this game all the times I did and was genuinely creeped out when I finished it.
This game is brilliant. Red Nettle Studios have really grasped not only what a visual novel should be, but what a post apocalyptic game should be also. They have mastered this, and there is no way that any post apocalyptic game could beat this one.
The only downside I had was how long it took to load new games and to go back to the title screen after each play through. Most of my 53 minute play time was just waiting for everything to load up. The game itself runs incredibly smoothly, but oh man the waiting times. I had to knock half a star off for this.
Other than that, I would highly recommend this game to those who love visual novels and/or post apocalyptic games. The Bottom of the Well captures the essence perfectly. Just give it a try.

A truly solid game, with a really well-written narrative and compelling choices that matter. The characters are presented very well, with a high attention to details that bring the story to life. The puzzles you are presented with are solid, with hints sprinkled through the story if you pay attention. There are some flaws; the main objective of the game is slightly obtuse, and you will have to write things down as they appear (which I personally feel is slightly annoying). Some choices are also shut down in a harsh way, depending on the circumstances that brought you to that point. However, this is part of the replayability, and it being free is actually slightly baffling. Truly worthy of your time.
As a final little PSA: You are required to play this game several times; unless you use a walkthrough to get certain information you can't get the "right" ending. This is not a problem of the game, but rather a feature/function, as it is focused around exploration (which is rather enjoyable). However, people who want to simply "play through once and then be done" might want to reconsider.

WARNING: Long wall of text, but it is worth your time to read it.
I've waited most of a decade for Black Mesa, so i was very happy to finally see it on steam, and i bought and downloaded it on release over a week ago. No, i did not play the free mod. Since i knew BM was coming to steam, i decided to wait until then to play it.
Before i get into my review/opinion of BM, i just want to briefly share a special moment i had with BM after downloading it. You see, i was introduced to Half Life in 1999 when my father got it for his birthday, i was there with him when he first fired it up. It was such an important moment in my life that i had my father sit there with me when i first fired up Black Mesa. We were both in awe just at the train ride, and i played all the way up through a little bit of Unforseen Consequences with him.
So now, my opinion of Black Mesa.
It is absolutely extraordinary. I have played through BM 2 times so far, and i have thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it.
What i love in particular is that it is not just an HD remake of Half Life 1, it is a genuine unique remake. Alot of the areas and levels are essentially the same in terms of the layout, but they are often expanded and changed somewhat to add whole new things to do and alternatives. One of my favorite moments is actually handing the scientist the toilet paper. I also love all the new dialogue with the scientists and guards before the resonance cascade (listen for an Office Space reference in Anomalous Materials).
Some levels are changed, which is great. The first puzzle in Unforseen Consequences i was stuck on for a little bit, as that was not in the original Half Life (the one with the two red valves). I loved that my memorization of Half Life 1 (see my name) did not allow me to just instantly know what to do at every challenge. Some of the chapters are shortened, chiefly On A Rail and Surface Tension. I'm not sure how i feel about that, but it is still fun regardless. There are changes in some orders of events, you get the crowbar a little later than in Half Life 1, and can get the .357 magnum in Office Complex as opposed to Blast Pit.
My favorite newly designed level is actually the supply depot for the entry into Xen (the place where you get the long jump module), as i genuinely got a sort of NASA/Space station feel of it, like i was genuinely going to an alien world.
Very, very few of the models are direct copy-paste from Half Life 2. The ones that are just copied over are really expected and totally acceptable: Headcrab, Barnacle, G-man are virtually unchanged from HL2. Vortigaunt is probably 95-99% the same. 96-99% of all other models are original, or acceptably re-skinned. I love the de-aging of Eli Vance and Issac Kleiner. SFX and graphics are exceptional, with some error here and there which can be fixed (this is early access after all).
I love the weapons, my favorite has to be the MP-5/M-203, i was elated with the new model of it as well as it's change to 30 round magazine from 50 round magazine. The overall reduction in maximum ammo is a great addition.
The soldiers and their vehicles are great too, although i kind of miss hearing the troops though radio chatter.
The security guards are actually quite improved over Half Life 1, they are not stuck with the Glock, as some have the .357 and some have the Shotgun. Their AI is much better too, and they can be helpful.
I also love the changes to the events of the AI friendlies, They now fit into the enviornment and story more. Ill give an example of what i mean. The first guard you can work with in Unforseen Consequences. If he doesnt die by the time you get to the lobby, he will say that he is going to try to call for help on the comms system, and tells you to get up to the admin offices (Office Complex). In Half Life 1, if you kept the guard alive that long, he would just stand there as you leave him behind when you go beyond the point where he can follow you. It's the things like this that really make BM shine.
Other than those of the Headcrab, Vortigaunt and Barnacle, it seems to me that just about all of the sounds are original, which is a great plus for me personally: One part of me had a small fear that BM would be so fun and good that i would not play Half Life 1 again. The total changes in sounds prevent this, as i will always hold the atmosphere and sounds of Half Life 1 sacred.
One great moment for me was in Surface tension, i enter a dark area and hear some light sounds. I think "is that a puppy?" I am not kidding i genuinely thought there was going to be a puppy in a small cage. Nope, it was the bloody snarks!!!!
I wont comment much on the music for a special reason: the thing is, for reasons that i am not clear on, my dad and i always played Half Life without the music. I don't know if it was a bug or something, but i just know Half Life 1 without music. So with Black Mesa, i had the music on in the first run, but then turned it off. Nothing against the composer, i just prefer to play Half Life 1 and now Black Mesa w/o music.
I have not played BM Multiplayer, and i never played HL deathmatch, so i wont comment on that at all.
There are some problems though, most of which i wont say here as they are bugs that are most probably to be fixed.
One technical problem i have seen: the targeting map for the mortars at the end of Surface tension needs alot of work, it's clunky to use.
But in terms of design choices, there is one problem that i must insist upon a change:

All of the dark areas are fine for atmosphere and such, but the flashlight needs to be stronger. On my first playthough i was straining my vision at some points.
Thats about all i can say on the negative at this point.
I had no problem paying $20 for Black Mesa. These guys deserve our money, they poured their heart and soul into this, and the result is top of the line.
Should i buy Black Mesa? Hell yes!
Will Black Mesa replace Half Life 1?
Hell no, that game is still the classic that we all remember, and Black Mesa should be a welcome companion to that 1998 classic.
Other than the issue of the under-powered flashlight, i have nothing negative to say about Black Mesa, it is simply a masterpiece. If Valve had today's technology and resources when they made Half Life, it would probably look just like Black Mesa.

I did the big mistake of preordering this game. So I really tried and wanted to like it, being a huge TW fan anyway.
But I have to say R2 was and is a deeply flawed, partially completed, hastily assembled, sub-par product. It has no redeeming qualities compared to other games of the franchise. Yes they fixed some bugs and improved some features since the original release, but even now R1 back from 2004 still has the better gameplay experience in my opinion. Especially considering the abundancy of great mods for it. No, R1 wasn't perfect, it has it's flaws that's for sure. And modders work alot on R2 now too.
So one might ask why compare a vanilla R2 with a modded R1? I can only say Why not? Did time flow at a different speed in CA HQ? Is it unfair to compare the work of paid professionals to that of unpaid amateurs? The year is the same for everyone involved. R2 has to be judged in context and that contains all the modding advances since R1. Ideally CA would have incorporated all that, both in terms of essence and polish. And they should have dealt with issues like pathfinding that have plagued the franchise since the very beginning. They certainly had the time to.
All that being said, it is still only a game. It is playable. It does not CTD on launch. Has a menu. Options...
Why not get on with it? Well what ticks me off is CA showed some really poor business practices.
They just ploughed on into release of the game despite clear awareness of all the major inconsistencies in design. They heavily marketed and pushed the game despite knowledge of the inherent, dyed-in-the-wool problems. Simply put scamming customers by deceiving and misleading them.
And instead of taking responsibility and to apologise afterwards when people found out, they tried to cover up ("only 2%", "it's a feature") and shift blame on customers for their "unreasonable expectations". That I can not excuse.

When it comes to reviewing free games, the question of course turns from 'Do you get your value for money?' to 'Is this game worth your time?' and I am happy to say 'The Bottom of the Well' is very much worth your time. Though that time may range from a mere thirty minutes or so with various walkthroughs to several hours, trying every possible combination, this is a visual novel not to be missed. And speaking of visuals, the art in this game is beautiful, most of the time, some of it is going to wow you and make you wish you had it (the free DLC lets you have it) and some works well for the situation, providing simple black and white or red and white art, not breathtaking but letting your imagination still run free and really envision the various situations you'll find yourself in.
The premise provides an interesting idea, our protagonist, Alice, is having ultra realistic feeling dreams of a nuclear "apocalypse", you replay it repeatedly and the story supports a sort of groundhog day feel, getting a little bit more right each time. While the entire thing can be completed in less than fifteen mintues, it's main value resides in it's replayability, choosing different options and customizing Alice's various skills which unlock new options and ways to progress. Although certain skills are certainly more useful than others, you will likely max out each one in a subsequent playthrough with a custom Alice to try something new.
The gameplay itself is simple.  The game's narrative is told through a dialogue between two friends, in which you make choices as you tell the story, the choices you make determine the outcome of the story based on various factors such as the aforementioned skills and an inventory towards the beginning of the game. It's also saved everyone from having to read the same diaglogue again and again by including a welcome skip button although I believe it interferes with the "true" ending of the game from my experience. Without delving into spoilers I am going to say the "true" ending is rather confusing and once you finally get it, there is little incentive other than achievements keep playing.
The achievements themselves are rather fun with their various references; "Metro 2016" for example, referencing either the books by Dmity Glukhovsky, starting with Metro 2033, or the games adapted from the books. "I live, I die, I live again" and "Furiosa" are obviously references to Mad Mad: Fury Road and one of the branches of the story directly brings up the film franchise to my pure fangirling delight. And there are also lots of Alice (Adventures) in Wonderland, from the name of our protagonist, to her friend with which you converse and tell the story and the boyfriend Alice has in her dream. These references aren't a game changer but I did find them to be rather enjoyable as a fan of all things Alice. I should also note that despite these references, it doens't feel cheap or fan fiction like, it still tells a solid standalone story but the flair is greatly appreaciated.
While the game can feel frustrating at times, especially if you try to do something different but have the same results or don't try custom Alice because the game doesn't tell you what a big difference it makes (the moment you finish your first playthrough, do custom, sticking with default is ultra limiting), the fact is, it's good, very good actually, I found myself thinking it and contemplating it even when I wasn't playing, and when something this good is avaliable for free, there's no reason not to own it and play it.

The game does a great job of being free-to-play as there are no in-game purchases but it should also be noted that the game is no Nazi Zombies, not in terms of quality however, in terms of pacing. NMRiH is an excruciatingly slow paced zombie survival game that takes some time getting used to the methodical processes involved, but as slow as it is, the game can still make your heart race when there are giant hordes of zombies cornering you into a room near an objective that is about to be completed and you only have a bullet to spare. Scavenging for ammo and weapons feels rewarding and saving the ammunition for that last push through a wall of zombies or perhaps one that just snuck up on you makes the game feel that much more strategic. With the variety of weapons to find across games as well as the amount of maps that are included, the game also manages to keep itself interesting and diverse every match played, unless of course you are stuck in a looping session with the same map; but even so the map has at the very least three different approaches to the objectives whether that be to blast through a wall or to traverse in the infected sewage waters, the choice however is up to the game :/(i.e. it chooses the objective randomly). The only problems I have with the game is again how slow it can feel, with a walk that looks like your character is in desperate need of a porter-potty and can only move so fast (especially when walking backwards) with the pressure of his/her brain being eaten, or infected for that matter, so the game somewhat stumbles on the "realistic" approach in that area. The game also decided to put this hidden stamina meter than can be referenced by listening to how hard the character is breathing and after running a fatiguing 10 meters or so the game can slow down once more since your character is unable to melee and shove any zombies out if it's way; which is bit oxymoronic in a sense since melee can and will be the only source of protection in the game but that's arguably where the strategy kicks in again. I tend to overlook these flaws because of the gunplay, which is also slow, but fun nonetheless. Shooting the guns and gaining a succesful headshot is quite satisfying even if it doesnt really make a difference to the zombie count, it is just plain fun. In short, If you are into the rewarding sensation of spending some time scavenging for detailed modeled weapons and short supplies of ammo to use as a mean of methodically getting towards the objective rather than using them on zombies as an objective, then this is definitely the game for you. 8/10

Dark Souls 2 is not a bad game but despite that I can't help but feel extremely disappointed every time I play it. As a huge huge fan of the previous game this was easily one of my most anticipated games in years. The end result has left me feeling let down.
Let’s start with the most obvious flaw, the difficulty. Dark Souls 2 is easy. Even if this is your first Souls game, I can't see anyone having too much trouble beating this game. Sure you'll die a few times here and there but it doesn't matter because bonfires are like hobos in London in this game. There's one on every street corner. The game throws bonfires at you like they're going out of style. Remember that feeling from the first game? You're beat to hell, your weapon is about to break, you have no Estus left and you're miles from the last bonfire then suddenly you round the corner and there it is. That feeling is nowhere to be found in Dark Souls 2. The worst offender by far is Earthen Peak, where there are THREE bonfires mere minutes from each other.
The enemies offer little challenge as they are dumb as hell. They will make a beeline straight for you and their attacks are all massively telegraphed. This problem is made even greater when you realise that Dark Souls 2's idea of upping the difficulty is simply to throw more enemies at you at once. Enemies bunch together in one big cluster♥♥♥♥ and try to Zerg rush you. You will walk round every corner thinking to yourself "Gee. I wonder how many enemies are going to jump out at me this time?” I can see the planning sessions now.
"Hey hey guys listen. Remember that one part in Dark Souls where we made them fight 2 bosses at once? Well this time, you're gonna love this, this time we'll make them fight... 3 BOSSES AT ONCE!"
"♥♥♥♥ING GENIUS!"
The environments are not much better. I honestly cannot even remember half the names of the areas in this game let alone the layout of them. It's pretty frustrating considering the original had extremely memorable environments. I know everyone loves to hate it but you will never forget the first time you went through Blighttown. My favourite level from Dark Souls 1 is the Painted World. So far, there hasn't been even a single level that has even come close to those two in terms of design and the bosses are even worse. Not only are they just as forgettable as the environments but they're also♥♥♥♥♥♥easy. I beat most of the bosses on my first attempt without even really trying. The only boss I really enjoyed was the Pursuer mainly because it's one of the few I can actually remember.
Do you like using specific types of weapons? Well tough ♥♥♥♥♥♥s because the weapon distribution in this game is heavily biased. I like using dex weapons. Dex was my preferred build in the original Dark Souls so naturally I went with that for my first run through of Dark Souls 2. 20 hours in and I found ludicrous amounts of strength weapons and about 3 dex weapons.
One thing that particularly annoyed me was that the pre-release footage they showed of the game was a blatant lie because the game looks NOTHING like that, even on PC. Granted, the graphics are a step up from Dark Souls 1 but compared to the pre-release footage, it still looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥
All in all if you've never played Souls before and you're interested in this game then by all means give it a go. If you liked it then play Dark Souls 1. If you liked that then play Demon's Souls but if you're like me and you played the original Dark Souls to death then I really can't recommend this game to you. It'll just leave you feeling disappointed.
EDIT: So after almost a month of on and off playing, I finally managed to drag myself through the game in the hopes that I would eventually have something nice to say about it. Unfortunately I now feel like I straight up dislike the game rather than just being disappointed by it. Remember when I said Dark Souls 2 was easy? Well that's not entirely true. There are some parts that are difficult and that's great right? Well no not really. The great thing about Dark Souls 1 was that it did a great job of balancing difficulty with fun. If you were smart, didn't play like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and took a step back to think things through, you would generally make it out ok. Dark Souls 2 on the other hand is incredibly cheap. Enemy placement is all kinds of ♥♥♥♥ed up. Remember how I mentioned the designer's 'more = better' design philosophy? Well it gets taken to ridiculous extremes later on. Huge enemies with massive health bars are just copy pasted around every single god damned level and you will, more often than not, have to fight more than one of them at once. This is bad because it encourages players to be as cheesy as possible when trying to take them out. Melee characters will have a considerably tougher time trawling through the hordes of giant enemies on account of Dark Souls 2's completely unnecessary change to rolling.
Resistance has now been replaced by the Adaptability stat. This stat affects how many invincibility frames your roll has so now instead of investing points into something that's actually useful, you can now pour points into a stat that makes a basic combat mechanic work properly. If you're not willing to do that well then (thanks to the ludicrously oversized hitboxes) I hope you enjoy being vacuumed into grabs and being hit by things that are not even touching a single pixel of your character's geometry.
If that weren't bad enough they also changed parrying. I understand this was probably so that DS veterans couldn't waltz through the game parrying everything in sight. I was somewhat proficient at parrying in the first Dark Souls but to me it just doesn't seem viable in DS2. The window appears to be so small that it just doesn't seem worth it making it more about guesswork than fast reactions. Or maybe I just need to git gud.
So with rolling gimped and parrying nerfed, the obvious conclusion we can draw from this is that you're supposed to play this game as a ranged character? Maybe? I don't know.
I'm not going to bother talking about soul memory because everything I wanted to say has already been said in a million other reviews. All I'll say is that it sucks and I don't like it.
It really pains me to say this but I did not enjoy my time with Dark Souls 2. The hordes of enemies and completely bland level design made playing this game feel like a chore rather than a form of entertainment but I trawled through it regardless because I’m a masochist. I compared this to my first time playing Dark Souls 1, which pulled me in almost immediately. The first time I played that game it took me almost 4 hours to beat Undead Burg and I freaking loved every second of it. Now imagine if that was a Dark Souls 2 level. Replace all the hollows with those giant skeleton dogs from Tomb of the Giants, multiply them by 5 and stick them all over the place and instead of the rolling barrel trap, just make the floor spontaneously explode when you walk over it. Oh and place a bonfire where the Black Knight should be.
So in conclusion I still can’t recommend Dark Souls 2 despite having finished it. Having been extremely excited to play this game ever since it was announced, I gave it so many chances to impress me in the vain hope that it would eventually click and I would start having a blast just like I did my first time through Dark Souls 1, but in the end it never did.

Fundamentally the game is great, and I would recommend any hardcore action RPG fan (with a controller) out there to play it.
But once you start peeling off the layers, you can quickly see how the second installment is shallow compared to the first one.
What really drove me in with the first game was the level design where everything was interconnected and shortcuts were essential to move around quickly. Interconnected areas have been replaced with occasional branches through a generally linear world, and shortcuts have been replaced with bonfires. There are SO many bonfires in this game, removing the tension of exploring the world, having only that one final Estus Flask left before you desperately need a bonfire - tension which made the first game so great. It also doesn't help that the locations you can see in the distance don't make sense like they did in DS1 and is simply windowdressing because it wants to feel bigger than it really is (namely in Majula, the starting area).
The AI is incredibly dumb and is easy to exploit - and exploiting you will be REQUIRED to do, since Dark Souls 2's idea of difficulty differs a lot from the first game's.
The big problem with DS2's difficulty is that it's simply put not fair. Well, not as fair as the first game. The game ABUSES its own shortcommings in its design by throwing a bunch of stupid enemies at you rather than a single clever one when the combat system is designed for 1v1, it puts 1 meter high obstacles in your way, forcing you to make a huge detour even though a human being should be able to easily climb it, and the hitdetection is way off for a lot of enemies.
It's almost as if the developers want you to succeed by glitching your way through the game, because that is honestly the most practical way of doing it.
The port is NOT good, but it is servicable. It is clear that PC was never the target platform, even though From Software said so. The game runs at a locked 60FPS (which sucks for us 120/144Hz players), the online infrastructure didn't work for the first 2 weeks for many previously VAC banned players, and the overall graphical fidelity is only slightly better than DS1 with mods. Forget about playing with keyboard and mouse, it seems like they mapped the mouse movement directly to gamepad movement, which makes no sense (though I hear there's a mod for that).
The game will turn down your system volume when you're in a multiplayer session for some reason. This is really annoying for people listening to music, podcasts etc. while playing. One can assume this is to make voice communication easier, but it's only annoying and there's no way to turn it off.
This game is still better than most games out there today because of DS1's and Demon's Souls' fundamentally good combat design and innovative multiplayer component. But I would still recommend DS1 over DS2 looking at the base game design and ignoring the PC specific issues.

I bought the game pre-Tamriel Unlimited, but only played during the first 30 days before I had to pay to continue playing. And to be honest, it wasn't a game that was worth the subscription. Now that it's free to play after purchase, it's definitely a great MMO. I have to agree with what others have said about this game: you have to remember that it is primarily an MMO, and and Elder Scrolls game secondarily.
There's a lot of diversity between the classes and play styles. You can be pretty much any type of character you want, using whatever class you end up choosing. Don't get too caught up in the fact that it's an elder scrolls game with a class system (and only 4 classes at that). The game rewards you pretty early on with plenty of skills to choose from (including unique active and passive skills for werewolves and vampires) and skill points to spend, and you continue to reap those rewards as you get higher in level.
The game is pretty unique compared to other MMOs I've played. It's refreshing to see an MMO that doesn't have a cooldown for class abilities. It's also nice in that you're actively acomplishing tasks/earning achivements as you train your character, so you don't grind as much in the game, even at lower levels.
Some styles of combat can get a little glitchy. Spamming the attack button while using the bow or some staves can cause enemies to stand still and stop acting (because you dropped their health to 0) but are still targetable to attack until they drop to the ground dead. It doesn't happen all the time but it happens often enough that I really wish Zenimax works on fixing that.
Overall, it's a great MMO. It's best played when you're on a mic and partying with a friend (like all MMOs), but it's absolutely a fun game even on your own.

I really enjoyed this game when it came out, and enjoy it even more now that most of the rough spots have been patched out and the modding community has had time to sink their teeth in.
Positives:
- The battles are almost always enjoyable, if not a little more arcadey than previous Total War games.
- The graphics are amazing, this is one of the most beautiful strategy games you'll ever play.
- Like in Shogun 2, the art style (unit cards, etc.) reflects the time period
- Factions feel really diverse, playing as Rome, Sparta, barbarians, or nomads all feel distinct
- City management is really satisfying. It's nice to see your cities change and grow as you improve them.
- There are tons of mods allowing you to tweak the game to how you like it.
- Modding tools have been released making it easier to tweak the game yourself.
Negatives:
- The AI will continue to make questionable decisions at times.
- Without mods, diplomacy can be somewhat limited.
- I much prefered the family tree in previous games to the internal politics system Rome 2 uses.

It's a fantastic stealth game that has hardly aged at all, but oh man, the STORY! It's the usual cold war propaganda tripe one expects from a Tom Clancy novel: you're an American super-spy who gets carte blanche to blow up buildings, assassinate politicians, and commit other acts of terrorism, which the game justifies because the bad guys are "dirty commies" who "threaten our nice democracy". It's Tom Lehrer's song "Send the Marines" played out as an unironic video game.
That said, the only redeeming quality is the gameplay itself, which is worthy of a recommendation, because I believe that the level designers and programmers shouldn't be lumped in with the morron who created the story. It's a classic of the stealth genre, and for many (including myself) it was also their first introduction to stealth games. Like many of them (Deus Ex and Chronicles of Riddick come to mind), you generally have two options to approach any mission: go in loudly or quietly. The game would rather you go in quietly.
There are side-objectives, and numerous ways to complete main objectives (think Hitman).
The mechanics are surprisingly smooth, with a really nice interface (a lot of games nowadays like to get rid of interfaces entirely, while a lot of older games overload the UI to the point of insanity). I encountered a couple of glitches here and there, for when you play like an idiot and try to do the opposite of what the game tells you to do. Makes for some great laughs!
Overall: a strong recommendation based on gameplay alone, two thumbs down when it comes to the storyline. If you like Tom Clancy's writing,  there are adult literacy classes offered at most community colleges, maybe there's still some hope left for you. (I've noticed a curious correlation between fans of Tom Clancy and semi-literate violent pro-war nimrods. Coincidence? I think not! If you combined Mickey Spillane, Joe McCarthy and the soldier who led the massacre of My Lai, you'd still end up with a more subtle demagogue than Tom Clancy. )
If you want to play the game but not suffer through a plot so bad and embarrassingly patriotic that it would have been parodied in Get Smart (had it existed back then), just turn down the game's audio, and play "America F*** Yeah!" on repeat to get the same gist.

I cannot off the top of my head remember a less sympathetic protagonist, with less sympathetic goals, in any other piece of media. Maybe Alex from A Clockwork Orange. But Anthony Burgess' writing manages to convince the audience to root for or sympathize with Alex, in some small way. This game's writing, even given the boost of the player inhabiting its protagonist, fails at that, assuming the player knows the  barest minimum about world politics, national politics, the NSA, the history of US military intervention, or what violence is.
I am still very early in the game itself, and maybe it will pleasantly surprise me. If so, I will revise this review. And I understand the narrative becomes more personal, and viewed as more important to the core experience, as the series continues. Because the mechanics are (so far) sound, and I am curious how it will develop, I will keep playing. But as far as I've seen, this game contains incredibly disturbing and geniuinely dangerous messaging (woven into the gameplay through the story), and I cannot in good faith recommend that anyone, for any reason, support this type of content with their money.

Splinter Cell is yet another game that I played for the first time 15 years after its original release. The protagonist, Sam Fisher, is a veteran government agent tasked with infiltrating a variety of installations to extract information, eliminate bad guys, or some combination of both.
Most missions revolve around stealth, but combat is also required from time to time.  Some objectives can be accomplished in multiple ways, but generally speaking, the missions are quite linear. The game does not have difficulty settings, and things can get tough at times. Although I did resort to seeking help online to overcome a handful of obstacles (and one bug), I was able to get through my playthrough primarily on my own, with the occasional trial and error through reloading saves. For its age, the game holds up well, and while I would not call it revolutionary, much of the gameplay systems that I saw in Splinter Cell have popped up in other games since then, although I am not sure if this game was their direct inspiration. For example,
builds on a similar array of abilities, gadgets, and level design.
There is no customization or configuration of the protagonist, Sam Fisher. Since Fisher is a veteran operative, the lack of character growth makes more sense than if he were a rookie on his first assignment. Fisher has a dry sense of humor and is superbly voiced by Michael Ironside.
The story involves the rogue leader of Georgia (the country not the state) waging war on the United States. The missions that Fisher embarks on take him to Georgia and a few other exotic locales. While the mission locales are not particularly memorable in representing Georgia or other countries, the mission level design is fairly diverse, even within a single locale. As the game goes on, new challenges are introduced that put Fisher's arsenal of skills and gadgets to test. Much of the atmosphere of intrigue is delivered through the twists and turns in the story and the dialogue between Fisher, his handlers, and the hostiles he encounters. In between missions, we are also treated to snippets from a fictional cable news network that tell, at a high level, what's going on in the world.
For a game from 2002, the graphics and sound are excellent. Some of the dialogue, particularly by the guards and other extras, is somewhat corny, but those are offset by Fisher's lines.  Given that listening for noise is an integral part of the gameplay, music is primarily limited to combat sequences, but when it does surface, it contributes to the game's tense atmosphere. Aside from one bug that required some trial and error to get by, I did not encounter other technical issues. Prior to playing, I did apply some of the screen resolution changes suggested in the Steam community guides.
No replay value.

This game is flawed, but I still can't get enough of the damn thing.
Let's start with the graphics. They look good, not the best I've seen, but they look good and avoid uncanny valley. The animation is done well and the frame rate stays at a decent level, on my end anyway. I will say that for a few minutes when I first start it up, it does lag though. I'll be driving my car and all of a sudden be another block down the road, or in a pile of wreckage I don't remember being in half a second ago.
The social aspect is great. Most of the other players I've come across are courteous and personable, but still offer a challenge on missions. While there are occaisional hackers, they can be taken out, contrary to popular belief. It's not by any means easy, but it is possible. I will say that the armas marketplace is flawed. That and auctions. The armas forces you to have paid currency, which I cannot afford. While there might be a way to earn that for free, I don't know what that way is.
The driving is done really well. It splits the difference between arcade style and realistic into a challenging and fun way to quickly get around. I really like how the different types of cars have different handling, speed, etc. I do wish the cars were more affordable though. The one I want is $400000 in the in-game currency. I do like the customization you can do with cars, though. I have a couple anime-looking cars and a fun police car(yes, it has fun police symbols on it. It's amazing).
The character customization is one of the most in depth things I've seen in a game, next to maybe Skyforge and Skyrim. Ignoring Spore, as that's less customization and more straight up creation. But the character customizer in this game is so in depth, that I haven't seen two characters in the game that look exactly alike(If two players wanted to play as twins though, that would be really cool to see). The story is also loose enough that you can think of your own backstory to your character, if you like.
Now, for my big issues with the game.
There is a button to hide the HUD, which I've used a lot, but there doesn't seem to be a free cam mode, which is unfortunate. I'd be using that for screenshots pretty much all the time.
When I actually get into the game, it doesn't show on Steam, I don't know if anyone else is having this problem, but I've put 20+ hours into the game and it shows as <30 minutes on my profile. That also means I can't access the Steam Community within the game, and I can't take screenshots in which I can share with the community. I post my stuff I've used Ctrl+Prt Sc with on social media, but I can't do anything other than that. The anti-cheat should be quite a bit better, so legit players like me don't get screwed over by a team of hackers(Because that really is impossible to stop by players). Either prices in the marketplaces should be reduced or in-game money should be more abundant. It's annoying to have to play for hours on end to get a couple measely items. There should be facial presets, for people who have trouble with the character customizer and want a good look for their character's face.
But, if you like open-world MMO's and MOBA style shooters, I reccomend this game, as it's like a combination of the two.

This is in my opinion the Alien game we've been waiting for and as of now my Game of the Year.
Even without the Aliens unscripted AI this game would be brilliant with its well realised world that basically sits you in Ridley's idea for this universe buts its the Alien that sets this game apart from games like Outlast or Amnesia.
The issue most horror games have is predictable AI with set paths, while its still scary you can easily learn the enemies path and get into this repetition of waiting around a corner and then moving out when they've gone past, now while this does happen from time to time in Isolation with the other enemies (Androids and Humans), when you're dealing with the Alien there is no scripted path.

This is also another area games like Outlast and Amnesia have a problem with, giving you no way to defend yourself. Now while that may seem to be a good thing and be more scary, allowing you to have a fighting chance prevents the game from becoming boring and monotonous.
If you've been waiting for a proper Alien game this is as close as you're gonna get, great campaign length (took me 21 hours on Hard) and wonderful atmosphere make for one of the best survival horror games.

If you're a fan of the Alien series, this is the game you've been waiting for.
First of all, the graphics in this game are oustanding.  The quality of the textures and effects is some of the best I've ever seen, and the overall crispness and fidelity is mindblowing.  Not only is it beautiful, but it is also one of the best optimized games I've ever seen.  My system is not top of the line, and with all settings on ultra the game was running absolutely flawlessly.  This game is a technical marvel.
The atmosphere and sound design is amazing, everything in the game has been so painstakingly created while keeping faith to its source material.  Everywhere you look there is immense detail, so much work and passion went into this product and it shows.
It took me about 18 hours to beat the game, which is a really respectful length for a survival-horror game like this.  Some complain it is too long but for me, a fan who has waited a long time to play it, the length felt perfect; I even could have gone for a little more.  You actually get to fully explore the station you're on through the story, unlike games like Dead Space 2 where you only see a tiny fraction of the space of the structure.
The gameplay is stealth-focused, you're given some tools for deterring your many enemies but mainly you will be sticking to the shadows and hiding in cupboards as you make your way through the game.  The alien, the prime antagonist of the game, is stunningly recreated and an absolute terror to deal with.  This isn't your average horror game enemy, this thing is relentless.  It is smart, it is fast, and it will punish the hell out of you for making a mistake.  The other enemies you face are more forgiving but still deadly and they all have interesting reactions with one another.
The game uses a manual saving system with save points spread throughout its levels.  For me this was a big plus as it cuts down on save scumming and gives you a real fear of failure, because if you die you may lose progress.
The story is solid and if you're a fan of the Alien series you will be delighted with all the extra lore this game provides to extend your favorite universe.
I honestly have no solid complaints about this game, some of the early segments can feel too hard but it's only because you don't yet understand what you're doing wrong.  This game doesn't hold your hand, and you'll quickly learn what is getting you killed.
I cannot say enough good things about this game.
Creative Assembly, thank you for returning the Alien franchise to glory, and please bring us more.

Dark Souls II is a Japanese RPG set in a western medieval world. Unlike your generic Final Fantasy adventure this game's focus is more on the atmosphere and the survival element rather then story etc. No this game is dark and brutal meaning it's very hard and you will die... lots ! What makes the game so hard is death and souls (hence the title). When you kill an enemy you earn souls the ingame currency and experience points, when you die you lose all of your souls ! but... you will revive and can go back to the spot where you died to recollect your lost souls. Die on your way there and they are gone ! I know what you are thinking... this isn't fun... Well, it's a learning experience. This game literally trains you to get good. After passing through a hard area or defeating a boss you will get this amazing feeling of achievement and by the end of the game you can take on anything  this game throws at you. During your adventure you will either be leveling up your character or upgrading your equipment, this game doesn't punish you for experimenting, so pick a playstyle you feel comfortable with. This game also has a multiplayer feature, depending on with what covenant you are you can either be summoned (co-op) or invade/be invaded (pvp). co-op is just what it is, helping another player. Getting invaded however means another player has come into your world to kill and steal your souls, you can invade other players to if you join a certain "evil covenant", but remember killing npc's or other players will add "sin" to your character. If your sin is very high you can get invaded by players from a certain "good covenant" to avenge the fallen. And finally this game has a ng+ mode, all your gear and character stats will be carried over and in ng+ all the enemies and bosses are tougher but give more souls and better equipment. There is no connection between Dark souls 1 and Dark souls 2, it's a spiritual successor like dark souls 1 was for the Ps3 exclusive Demon's souls. You can find references and lore in the game toward either of the 3 games, if you look carefully enough. whatever you do hang on to your humanity, we hate to see you go hollow...

Well to no one's surprise ESO's subscription model was a massive flop but they managed to turn off the greed gene and turn on the ole brain and release the BTP (buy to play) version before the game turned out to be a memory in most peoples minds.
I was one of the masses that refused to buy this game and then pay per month even though I knew it woudl be an epic adventure.  Thanks to all those like me who were the direct reason ESO went BTP.
The game itself is brilliant and has delivered a true adventure for those who enjoy RPGs and MMOs which this is marketed as.  Graphics are good but not great, though the environment is truely beautfiful and at some points you will stop and just gaze at the sunset or the beautiful view from the top of a mountian etc, its the layout and design more than the graphics that gives you such great moments.
Audio is very well done and I love the vioce overs instead of reading text all the time.  Music is also very well done and it helps to immerse you in the game.
The weaknesses are almost all to do with MMO bugs and protocols which experienced MMO game producers already know and have tweaked to perfection in their own MMO games.  As this is a first crack at the genre for an ESO game the final result is a bit below par when trying to quest as a group with your friends, especially if they are not 100% synced up to your mission progress and other little problems that become apparant when you try and play it as a traditional MMO.
The best thing I can say after 100+ hours in game is that ESO will immerse you completely if you let it - Don't run through in a mad rush to get cheevos or other novelties, take your time and live each and every story to truely receive the benefits this game can give you.  If you are a bit of a solo MMO player and don't run with guilds all the time then this will really favor you.
Massive maps, very nice combat that skilled players can take advantage of even when out leveled, mounts, pets and varied quests give the gameplay a very high rating and a lot of re playability in my view.
Sooooo glad it went BTP so that all of us can enjoy the adventure in waiting.

Splinter Cell is a stealth title that was created as a "Metal Gear Solid 2 killer"; a MGS2 killer it is not.
A good game it is.
Rather than the MGS formula of using enemy line of sight as the danger, Splinter Cell uses light as the catalyst to all stealth play. At the bottom right you have a small bar that shows how visible you are; light sources shoot this bar all the way up and any enemy looking in your general direction will be alerted to your prescence. Sound also plays a role in this, as you can adjust Sam's move speed by 6 or so degrees. Different floors (wooden, grates, concrete) make different sounds, but the general idea is that in addition to staying out of sight, you must also stay out of sound.
In theory this is more realistic than MGS's stealth mechanics that almost look 'arcadey' by comparison (line of sight displayed on a minimap)-in practice it's actually rather unrealistic. If no light sources are hitting you, you are virtually invisible. An enemy can be right in front of you, and in some cases you are still clearly visible, but you're treated as a ghost. Other times you will be pretty far from an enemy, but somehow they have a sixth sense and will immediately know you are nearby based on nothing other than your light bar shooting sky high. For all purposes, what you see doesn't matter as much as how much light the bar says is shining on you. As for sound; it creates interesting scenarios whereby you use sound as a distraction, but the downside is that you are walking slowly most of the time and take longer to complete anything. It just slows things down; I'd prefer MGS's move speed.
I'd hate to continously compare this title to MGS; just as most FPS titles are no longer compared to Doom, we do a disservice to the developers of a title by not recognizing the game as its own product and see it instead as an offshoot or rip off. But the entire purpose of this game was to be designed as a rival to the MGS series, down to its thematic theme of political intrigue. Still, this does not mean Splinter Cell doesn't succeed in some areas, chief of which is map design.
It's a subtlety, but Splinter Cell features open maps that don't clearly dictate where you have to go. Rather, you are plopped in random areas of the map, are given objectives, and must proceed. This will lead to scenarios where you might feel lost or wonder where you have to go next. Fortunately it isn't an exercise in arithmetic, which means that I always had a sense of satisfaction when traversing the land. The game wasn't a linear map carefully guiding me a la the first few MGS titles, meaning that levels feel bigger than they actually are and you have a sense of solitude achieved only when the map designer makes you feel like you really are in the middle of the city. You may be in a square box, but you truly feel like you're by the cliffside of a palace or the alleys of China if the devs purposefully make you feel lost. It's subtleties like this that add so much but are only noticed by watchful eyes.
The plot is a treat for fans of political....anything. The plot deals with a Georgian (the nation not the American state, imbecile) leader that ultimately goes Rouge and launches underground, web-based attacks against US targets, becoming a terrorist. There's the threat of World War III with China which...well, I won't spoil it. Let's just say that if you loved the beginning parts of Metal Gear Solid 1 and *appreciated* how realistic the story was (at least, initially) then you'll appreciate Splinter Cell for the very same reason. The only thing is SC is less character and conversation driven, and those that don't appreciate political intrigue will probably tune out on the plot.
And realism is ultimately the goal here. Your aiming reticle isn't perfect, you can't move and shoot simultaneously and expect to hit anything, and there are no boss fights. There are also no facility wide alarm bells anytime you're spotted. Which is fine, but this means that any 'alarms' raised are only with the people immediately in the room you're in and nowhere else. You also only have two projectile based weapons in the game, since you're expected to stealth everything. My only complaint is that I would often stealth kill enemies, place them in hidden areas, yet 20 or so minutes later after I'm deeper into the level the bodies were somehow discovered. Which I guess is fine, but since the game penalizes disruption and noise by having a limited set of 'alarms' that can be raised, this can inadvertently give you game overs long after you've left rooms with deceased enemies. Which is ironically unrealistic, but otherwise I can appreciate what this game attempted to do differently and feel that with some tweaking it can really be perfected and allowed to shine. Just as an example: visual indicators for range of sound on bullets so that each room doesn't feel like its soundproof and only those within it will hear any noise.
I wouldn't call it a classic, but I would call it an important game in the stealth genre that has something to throw into the collective pot of stealth titles that others can learn from. Take that for what you will, but I ultimately enjoyed the game. Will certainly queue up the other titles in the series for future playthroughs.

Clock Simulator is simple and laborious. I suppose it has some interest to certain people but really you don’t need to pay 79p on it. Well I guess I’ll go over this game piece by piece.
-Gameplay
The game play is essentially the same for each gamemode. Make sure you can tap the spacebar or mouse every second on the second. There are 12 gamemodes:
Learn to Play
A game of shadows
Dungeons and the Aliens
The fragility of time
It’s QWOP
The spirits of time
Follow the Rhythm
From dawn till dusk
Pig got the Rhythm
A minute of perfection
Test your skill
Time to go digital
The first gamemode teaches you what a second is and how to tap every second. The second is the basic gamemode; like the first but there isn’t any help. In the third gamemode you press A and D to kill Aliens and Spaceships. The fourth gamemode is a harder version of the basic gamemode; where if you mess up a chunk of the clock hand is destroyed. The fifth gamemode you press Q,W,O and P to pass the corresponding barriers. The sixth gamemode is the first with spooky sounds overlaid. The seventh gamemode has a visual representation of a second, which you have to keep up with. In the eighth gamemode, when you mess up it gets darker. The ninth gamemode is jump rope with a clock hand; you have to jump every second. The tenth gamemode gives you points for every perfect tap you make. The eleventh gamemode gives you 5 points for every perfect tap and minus 1 for every wrong tap. Then finally the twelfth gamemode is the basic one but with a digital clock.
There isn’t anything else to comment on with this game. It’s tedious and very simple. If you can pick it up for free do so, to get the trading cards. Otherwise there’s no real worth to this game.

For a few cents and less than an hour of your time, it will be worth it. This is something at the level of a phone app.

If you're a fan of the Alien series, this is the game you've been waiting for.
First of all, the graphics in this game are oustanding.  The quality of the textures and effects is some of the best I've ever seen, and the overall crispness and fidelity is mindblowing.  Not only is it beautiful, but it is also one of the best optimized games I've ever seen.  My system is not top of the line, and with all settings on ultra the game was running absolutely flawlessly.  This game is a technical marvel.
The atmosphere and sound design is amazing, everything in the game has been so painstakingly created while keeping faith to its source material.  Everywhere you look there is immense detail, so much work and passion went into this product and it shows.
It took me about 18 hours to beat the game, which is a really respectful length for a survival-horror game like this.  Some complain it is too long but for me, a fan who has waited a long time to play it, the length felt perfect; I even could have gone for a little more.  You actually get to fully explore the station you're on through the story, unlike games like Dead Space 2 where you only see a tiny fraction of the space of the structure.
The gameplay is stealth-focused, you're given some tools for deterring your many enemies but mainly you will be sticking to the shadows and hiding in cupboards as you make your way through the game.  The alien, the prime antagonist of the game, is stunningly recreated and an absolute terror to deal with.  This isn't your average horror game enemy, this thing is relentless.  It is smart, it is fast, and it will punish the hell out of you for making a mistake.  The other enemies you face are more forgiving but still deadly and they all have interesting reactions with one another.
The game uses a manual saving system with save points spread throughout its levels.  For me this was a big plus as it cuts down on save scumming and gives you a real fear of failure, because if you die you may lose progress.
The story is solid and if you're a fan of the Alien series you will be delighted with all the extra lore this game provides to extend your favorite universe.
I honestly have no solid complaints about this game, some of the early segments can feel too hard but it's only because you don't yet understand what you're doing wrong.  This game doesn't hold your hand, and you'll quickly learn what is getting you killed.
I cannot say enough good things about this game.
Creative Assembly, thank you for returning the Alien franchise to glory, and please bring us more.

You will die often, and often times it's by a one-hit-kill that you can't do anything about. There's a run button, but running will get you one-hit-killed. If you're not careful you will also walk somewhere you shouldn't have and also get one-hit-killed.
There's hardly any down time either, the alien is in your face almost non-stop. The fantastic environments and the novelty of the enoucounters wear off and all you're left is repetition, replaying the same sections of the game over and over because you keep getting killed and sent back to some save point way back when.
---
Addendum: I finished the game. Most of the frustration I felt was during the scimed section of the game. It's the one part that drags down the rest of the otherwise phenomenal game.
There are still some parts that still feel horribly unfair, however, like getting killed in the middle of a cutscene/unskippable animation. But for the most part this game is actually not bad.

Amazing piece of survival horror game! I personally love the genre myself and I am also a huge fan of the Alien movie. Although the game is not flawless, it introduces a lot of game design choices that makes it somewhat a challenging experience (at least on Hard, which is the intended difficulty), but also makes the feeling of thrill, horror and stress much more present whenever you play.
For instance, save points are the only place to save your progress, which means if you die you have to start from the spot you last saved at (at least 98% of the time). Another feature is that you don't just walk through corridors to progress, you have to backtrack and explore, since you don't have a map on screen or indicator of what to do other than a bleep on the motion tracker.  Some might feel it belongs to old games, but i welcome it, as i through that experience the environment and visuals more.
If you feel you are not that much into hardcore experiences, I believe it could still be enjoyed on Easy. If you are someone who wants cutscenes and easy progression, this is probably not it. Story comes once in a while thorugh cutscenes, but mostly through gameplay and log files on computers you will need to find.
If you're into Alien, this is a MUST play. The level of detail and feel from the original Alien movie is captured very, very well and throughout the game you really feel the dread of being face to face with the Alien.
This is the best game i've played in 2014 since Mario Kart 8 and i strongly recommend giving it a go.

Company of Heroes is one of the best WW2 RTS games I have ever played. Of course, like all games, it is not without faults. However, the vast majority of gameplay concepts and mechanisms have been perfected to such a level that you will not regret your purchase.
I am a big fan of WW2 history and I have always wanted a real-time strategy game that would allow me to master combined arms tactics which were developed during WW2. The game has a wide variety of units including but not limited to infantry, tanks, mobile artillery, mortar and light armored vehicles. In order to defeat your enemy, you will have to use a combined arms approach that integrates all of these units. You won't be able to steam roll through the enemy lines with a single Tiger tank as it would get torn to shreds by Bazooka-wielding infantry units.
Overall, I must say Relic has created a true gem for all WW2 game fans. I wholeheartedly recommend buying this game!

Let me start by saying I played in the beta. For ... roughly five minutes, before going back to my beloved Skyrim. It simply did not hold my attention at the time.
I'm pleased to report that this has changed.
The world is expansive and interesting. Sure, it's a theme park MMO - but it's a good one.
Let's start with the quests. I've run into very few 'twenty bear asses' quests, and even those that are like that have lore and tie into larger quests, for the most part. Questing is really the best way to level, in my opinion - you can get more skill points that way, and run into more sky shards, lore books, and anchors - more on those later. Plus, it's just interesting. The stories aren't repetitive, and it's obvious the writers had some fun doing what they did.
If you don't like questing, there are alternatives, however: primarily, stabbing things in the face. Repeatedly.
So let's talk about combat.
It feels like Smite, a bit. Every attack is a skillshot, borrowing from MOBA terminology - you have to aim manually, rather than just tab targetting. You pick five abilities, a quickbar item, and an ultimate - and that's really all you can effectively use in combat. Surprisingly, that's enough. You pick your abilities intelligently, and you can do just about anything. Case in point: my level 13 vampire. The vampire quest requires you to kill level 38 enemies. Do the math. If I'd had the right abilities from the outset, I could have been a vampire at ten or less.
Which brings me to my next point - the customer service.
See, I'd been a little too trusting when I was hunting out an ... alternative life state, let's say. I was offered a chance at being horrifically mauled by a werewolf, and I accepted, eagerly. The guy who specifically offered me a bite, however, demanded five thousand gold up front, something I could barely afford. Still, I was being trusting, and I gave it to him. He then developed a mysterious case of werewolf ED, and couldn't complete the process. In troubleshooting, he suggested I log off, and so I did - whereupon he left group and ran off.
This sad tale got me a pity-bite from a vampire player, instead, which was lovely - but didn't get me back my gold.
So I reported the fellow who scammed me, thinking it wouldn't do much but vent my frustration.
Imagine my surprise when, the next morning, my gold was returned to me with an apology for the negative experience I encountered. The customer support representative did warn me that the market was very much 'buyer beware' and that they couldn't repeat this kindness - but really, getting 'bitten' once should be enough.
So that was nice.
Other things of note:
- My kleptomania is reaching critical mass. I'm making a decent profit by stealing literally everything I can get my grubby little Bosmer paws on. I'm curious if every faction has this many people trying to take anything that isn't nailed down, or if the Dominion - with Bosmer and Khajiit as two of the three member races - just has it particularly bad.
- The guards are OP, in other unrelated news.
- The game is not pay to win, so I bought a couple of things off the cash shop - cosmetic outfits and non-combat pets. I also acquired the 'any race, any faction' upgrade. It's nice, but not necessary - racial perks are just big enough to affect playstyle, without being game-breaking.
- The download feels like forever, even on a fast connection - I don't want to contemplate what it would be like on, say, my 1mbps friend's internet. It's a big download, because it's a big game.
- Explore everything. You might find something awesome.
- I can't honestly comment on PvP - I haven't tried it yet.
- I don't have to pay a subscription to maintain access to Tamriel.
- I disagree with a previous commenter - with the sheer volume of weapon, armor, and skill point choices, each of my characters feels and plays differently. I feel unique without being useless, as I try on a nightblade (rogue) tank, healer, and DPS - all separate characters. There's optimal - and then there's playable. Optimal is a small, niche market - you can play anything you want, effectively.
So far, there are small things that bother me - Molag Bal doesn't encompass all of the portfolios he's given in this game, you know - but overall I thoroughly enjoy this title, and feel it's well worth the money I spent.

While the game is not a bad game it is flawed in many ways. Allow me to explain why.
1 - Being hard
Now, i say that its hard, but I'm not complaining about it being hard in the traditional sense. I'm not asking for an easier game either since in my opinion that'd be 20 kinds of dumb.
I'm complaining about this because, while i enjoy a good challenging game, this game is hard just for the sake of being hard.
Allow me to exemplify. There is an optional area in the game where the boss consists of 4 minions and the boss itself. The boss is untargetable until you attack one of the 4 minions, meaning you can't weaken him before commencing the fight. As for the minions, the second you attack one of them the remaining 3 immediately become agressive and attack you giving you around 5 seconds or so to dispatch them before the boss drops into the area and begins attacking you as well. This would be fine if the minions didn't inflict a status effect that deals a large ammount of damage over time with a mere 2 hits. This means you have to deal with the 4 minions, as quickly as possible, without getting hit twice and possibly have to deal with the boss itself should you fail to dispatch the critters in time.
This is not what i'd call challenging, but as a gigantic pain the the neck instead. This isn't the only fight where this happens, but i'd rather not delve too much into it.
2 - Combat
While combat itself is pretty okay, i have some problems with it. Call it nitpicking if you will but there are just some things that don't really feel right.
The hitboxes feel off sometimes, there's no other way to describe it, while playing i'll sometimes  see the effect caused by a weapon clearly hitting my opponent without it actually happening, and it makes me wonder if something is actually wrong with either my game or my computer.
Another interesting little thing is that enemies never grow tired. The game itself has a stamina mechanic that forces you to think before you act, but enemies can dish out a flurry of attacks even though (from the story's/game perspective), they're in the same pseudo-zombified state as the player, the same can be said for their attack tracking ability, by this i mean there are certain enemies that will literally turn 180 degrees while in the middle of an attack just so they can attempt to hit you (in fact this was so bad in one specific enemy, that the developers actually had to reduce the tracking capabilities on said enemy's projectiles).
This feels a bit off, and dare I say, makes the game harder, just for the sake of being harder.
3 - Covenants.
This'll be a short one. You have no idea what you're getting yourself into. That's it. when you interact with someone or something that allows you to join a covenant, you get no information about what you're getting yourself into. In fact this occurred to a good friend of mine. While he was playing he found an object that allowed him to join a covenant, simply asking him if he's ready to face a bigger challenge. He then found out that by entering this covenant his damage was reduced and that he was unable to summon any NPCs or players into his world for help.
I may be mistaken, but there are several several possible outcomes when one decides do say that something will result in a bigger challenge. Usually people who decide to face a bigger challenge know what sort of mess they're getting themselves into.
This isn't the case.
4 - NPCs
Interaction with NPCs isn't really anything to write home about in most games, but some things in Dark Souls 2 annoy me.
Allow me to exemplify. In this game you are only allowed to level up by speaking with one specific NPC. Now instead of opening the menu and letting said NPC talk while you're navigating through the menu you are forced to skip 4 dialogue segments before you are finally allowed to level up.
Now, in this game you'll be interacting with this NPC quite a few times, seeing as this is the NPC that allows you to increase the number of innate healing items you possess in your inventory along with allowing you to level up. The result is that these "interactions" become extremely annoying extremely early in the game. Truth be told this is not something that should happen when you're dealing with an "important" NPC, or any other NPC for that matter.
5 - PvP
Last but not least, we have PvP. An addition to the game that should be fun filled, challenging and overall allow the player to enjoy him/herself even more.
If it was actually balanced that is.
Now in PvP (or Invasions) your goal is to either defeat the invader or the invaded (depending on whether you're invading or being invaded), but lets talk about accessing PvP first. there are 3 main PvP covenants within the game. One of them grants you a ring that automatically summons you into one of two areas in the game where you must face off against the player that set foot within that area. As a reward for this you get titanite chunks, which are relatively hard to come by and allow you to reinforce your weapons and armor.
The remaining two covenants make mostly use of cracked eye orbs (although one of these covenants gives you a ring that allows you to aid players from another covenant while said players are being invaded). The thing is, in your first playthrough, you are only given access to a limited number of orbs, making invasions during your first (and possibly even last) playthrough limited as well. Please note that these covenants require an immense ammount of invasions for the player to rank up (requiring a total of 500 victories for the player to achieve the third and final rank).
As for a way of replenishing eye orbs the player is given two options. Duel against players from the same covenant or buy them for a ridiculous ammount of souls in New Game +. Dueling on its own is a pain because you have to consume a different token for each covenant (these are obtained by either using eye orbs and defeating an invaded player, or by aiding another player as a phantom).
As a result, invasions during a player's first playthrough are extremely rare should you decide not to venture into the area protected by the 1st mentioned PvP covenant.
That aside there is also the case of extreme unbalance. The game features spells that can easily instantly kill a player for a measly soul cost or buff already hard hitting weapons along with weapons with a ridiculous attack speed or maybe even phantom reach (meaning that their reach is longer than it actually appears to be).
My main issue with this is that some of the builds that focus on using these spells/weapons, are relatively easy to make, and as a result my PvP experience went downhill at an astonishing speed.
Weaponry aside, invaders are unable to recover HP without resorting to spells. Making it so that even if the invading is actually fighting well, and in a fair way, nothing is stopping the invaded player from running away/hiding so that he/she may recover HP and then rush back into the fight without almost any form of punishment whatsoever. This just helps make PvP even more unbalanced (not to mention the fact that a player may summon 2 other players to their aid, turning the fight into a 3 vs 1 where the opposing trio has the ability to regenerate health).
6 - Conclusion
Please note that these are my opinions and that people are free to disagree with me, its also likely that its just me who's just bad at the game in which case i've been trying to git gud for a very long time, but the game as a whole has several blatant design flaws once you take a very good look at it, and while it is good on its own, it could have been a much better game in the end. So while i do recommend this game, i'd wait for a discount.

The first thing that's apparent about the Dark Souls series is how little the game teaches you about itself. But once you get over that steep hurdle, you'll find a beautiful, intricate, and truly challenging game beneath it.

Yes. Do it. You'll hate yourself, you'll hate the game, you'll hate that-was-obviously-the-controller-slipped. You'll hate everything until you're nothing but a hallow husk of desperation and loathing. And then, in a moment of absolution and exhausted elation, you'll win.
If you're a fan of the Souls games, this is a Souls game. If you're new to the Souls series (Demon's / Dark 1 & 2) then this will be a glorious rage inducing how-could-anyone-like-this-omg-why-did-I-buy-this thing that you will probably give up on in the first hour or two. The trick is to come back in a week, or a month, or a year, sit down, and convince yourself you're finally going to figure out what the hell everyone's been raving about.
tl;dr Dark Souls 2, get it and git gud.

This is a weird one.
First the good i guess.
- Great Multiplayer mechanics, feels like you actually need skill in order to get kills and its not the classis "Oh fuc**** hit markers" Situation, if you dont kill someone, its generaly because you got a sh** aim.
- Solid Upgrade system that doesnt feel like its overpowered the more you level up. It actually turns out that most people use the opening weapons quite a bit.
- The Map design really makes you think about where people are gonna pop out from, it can sometimes be too chaotic though which i shall explain shortly
Overall, the fresh new mechanics and the gun balancing and such really does make this the best Call of Duty since Modern Warfare. Still not better than it though, but i doubt anyone will ever match it
Now for the Cons:
- Fu**ing system hack. Oh my god. Is this annoying. Not only does your exo make a crackling sound audible to the opponents, but the bloody thing is so obtrusive it makes it almost impossible to get a kill, it also takes inbetween 30 and 60 seconds to "reboot" which means your KD goes t*ts up because of all the effects it has. Its not even that difficult to get points wise. Admitedly there is a perk that makes you immune to the effects, but you still cant call in killstreaks to defend your team-mates, in my opinion its a little OP in the scorestreak department, especially considering it costs so little.
- NO DEDICATED SERVERS! Come on guys, its 2014, no dedicated servers?? Are you serious, thats the one thing that made Ghosts so sh** besides all of the glitches, the terrible optimisation and such. The hacking is unbearable, and the occassionaly lag spike cause someone thinks its funny to make a lag switch. Maaaan, that sucks. Im pretty sure when the were advertising it aswell, they mentioned there would be servers, but hey, couldnt expect too much now could we.
- The Story is crap..... Not being frank, but besides the "pretty faces" and the voice acting, there really isnt anything good about the story, it introduces you to some neat abilities like the grappling hook and exo glide etc, but the story line is horrific and predictable. Modern Warfare is literally the best example of how to do a story. Loads of missions, a training ground, add a bit of competition to the timed run and then add in some likable characters. instead we have just the same as the previous versions. or maybe its just me having high expectations from a AAA game.
- Sometimes, having to check on so many axis for enemies can actually give you a headache, with people flying overhead, snipers at key points on the map and people dashing all over the place, sometimes, i find myself wishing that people would just stand still for a little but, and then, bam. Overall im going to give the game a thumbs up but its an iffy one. There arent many maps on release which makes the multiplayer get a little "boring" after a while i guess. The Campaign is naff, but the overall pace and skill required to play the game actually makes it enjoyable. I dont think its worth £40 but if you can pick it up for £20-£30 then id say go for it. It will kill your boredom for a while, just dont expect to get alot from the story besides some intel hunting.

username: Thief 2 is the best stealth game
text:
The Splinter Cell series is my second favorite stealth franchises right behind the Thief series. Ironically, I like Splinter Cell so much because it is very similiar to the Thief series. Both games have you sneaking through shadows, using your light gem/meter, and trying to keep the body count to a low and will probably be killing a lot of lights in your journey.
The levels in this game are varied enough and constantly get more tense and difficult. You go from sneaking into a police station to infiltrating the CIA HQ! The levels are a bit linear and offer a couple alternate routes contrast to Thief's open ended missions. You can go through most levels not killing a single guard. In fact, some missions FORCE you to go non lethal in them. Even when the game forces you to knock out or even kill a guard, it makes sense in the story and you can do it quietly unlike the Metal Gear series which forces combat and boss battles. I really appreciated this as I could still feel like I didn't waste my time carefully sneaking into an area only to be forced to fight a dude and have all my careful ghosting go to waste.
Speaking of story, Splinter Cell's story isn't the most upfront or engaging. Again, unlike the Thief series storytelling which had beautiful cutscenes and immersive world and characters. But still, this game does the story good enough to just barely engage me into what's going on. There are computer emails and guards to interrogate to get more of the story, so there's that.
Overall, this game marks the beginning of a great stealth series (minus Conviction) that heavily inspires from Thief and puts others like it to shame. Buy this game.
