I've played roughly 4 or so hours of this game so far, and the majority of what I've played is excellent. The universe it creates is spot on to the movies, the whole 70s-version-of-the-future is definately there, and it looks great; the graphics are fantasic. The gameplay is smooth and responsive, and the game itself is tense as all hell, I'm on the edge of my seat even when I know I'm safe from the Alien as I know it may be anywhere. There is some combat, mainly against androids, but you'll have to use your feet and weapons for distracting to get past the Xenomorph.
The only bad thing I have to say is actually something many other may like, and that's the saving mechanic. I hate it. I have a very good PC but sometimes the game has been unresponsive meaning I have to re-load my game, but so many times it takes me 10 or 15 minutes from where I left off. It's not awful, but when you have a game that is often slow paced and has little action, and you die, and have to do it ALL over again, it get's really annoiyng really quickly.
Other than that, the game is great. It's suspensful, true to the films, beautiful and overall a great experience so far. I've yet to complete it but I'll be sure to update my review to suit the entire game. My early review is postive. If you want any game this Autumn, this is the game to buy.

This was a good idea poorly implemented.  The mechanics in this game are all extremely shallow and basic.
-You can't design your own slime enclosures or customize them beyond upgrades you can buy.  All you can do is build prefab slime cages (and other structures) on plots of land picked by the game.
-Way too much unused space in your ranch.  Lots of walking between areas.
-Can't breed slimes.
-The game descriptions is misleading.  It says: "You wake at the crack of dawn and get to watering the crops at the ranch. Some slimes are vegetarian, after all. Then it’s time to gather up the plumpest hens from the chicken coop."
Crops require no watering, no fertilizer, and they replant themselves on their own.  You also do not need to watch after your chickens at all.  They take care of themselves.  You don't even need a chicken coop because chickens will spawn on your farm faster than they can reproduce in the coop to begin with.  There is 0 management involved.  There is hardly anything you need to actually do.
-Everything the game requires you to do is repetitive and unchallenging.  You vacuum up slimes.  You don't have to trap them or outsmart them or anything like that.  You can't even fight the ones that are aggressive, aside from hitting them with water.
-You interact with everything in the world with your vacuum, which is annoying.  Vacuuming up crops is slow and tedious.  You can't place a stack of ingredients in a container, you have to slowly vacuum them out/in.
-Gameplay is just plain annoying.  Slimes and other objects you don't want constantly get sucked into your vacuum.  Hunting slimes is annoying because slimes will transform into hybrids (which cannot be vacuumed up) almost immediately when you enter a new area, so you have to constantly run back and forth between the maps to get slimes right when they spawn.  It doesn't feel immersive at all.  It feels like I'm forced to adapt my playstyle to a crappy game mechanic.
The exploration aspect of the game is slightly better than the farming, but the maps aren't that big and only have a few points of interest, and after 7 hours of playing I've seen and done everything there is to do.  Considering there is no way to further improve my farm - all I can do is continue to feed the slimes and collect their poop - this game does not have much longevity.
I understand that this is an early access game, but I doubt any of those features I listed will ever be implemented.  According to the wiki all of the upcoming changes are additional areas and slimes.  I don't think the devs plan to expand the farming aspects of the game, and since this is a farming sim.... I just can't recommend it at this time.

Let me start by saying I played in the beta. For ... roughly five minutes, before going back to my beloved Skyrim. It simply did not hold my attention at the time.
I'm pleased to report that this has changed.
The world is expansive and interesting. Sure, it's a theme park MMO - but it's a good one.
Let's start with the quests. I've run into very few 'twenty bear asses' quests, and even those that are like that have lore and tie into larger quests, for the most part. Questing is really the best way to level, in my opinion - you can get more skill points that way, and run into more sky shards, lore books, and anchors - more on those later. Plus, it's just interesting. The stories aren't repetitive, and it's obvious the writers had some fun doing what they did.
If you don't like questing, there are alternatives, however: primarily, stabbing things in the face. Repeatedly.
So let's talk about combat.
It feels like Smite, a bit. Every attack is a skillshot, borrowing from MOBA terminology - you have to aim manually, rather than just tab targetting. You pick five abilities, a quickbar item, and an ultimate - and that's really all you can effectively use in combat. Surprisingly, that's enough. You pick your abilities intelligently, and you can do just about anything. Case in point: my level 13 vampire. The vampire quest requires you to kill level 38 enemies. Do the math. If I'd had the right abilities from the outset, I could have been a vampire at ten or less.
Which brings me to my next point - the customer service.
See, I'd been a little too trusting when I was hunting out an ... alternative life state, let's say. I was offered a chance at being horrifically mauled by a werewolf, and I accepted, eagerly. The guy who specifically offered me a bite, however, demanded five thousand gold up front, something I could barely afford. Still, I was being trusting, and I gave it to him. He then developed a mysterious case of werewolf ED, and couldn't complete the process. In troubleshooting, he suggested I log off, and so I did - whereupon he left group and ran off.
This sad tale got me a pity-bite from a vampire player, instead, which was lovely - but didn't get me back my gold.
So I reported the fellow who scammed me, thinking it wouldn't do much but vent my frustration.
Imagine my surprise when, the next morning, my gold was returned to me with an apology for the negative experience I encountered. The customer support representative did warn me that the market was very much 'buyer beware' and that they couldn't repeat this kindness - but really, getting 'bitten' once should be enough.
So that was nice.
Other things of note:
- My kleptomania is reaching critical mass. I'm making a decent profit by stealing literally everything I can get my grubby little Bosmer paws on. I'm curious if every faction has this many people trying to take anything that isn't nailed down, or if the Dominion - with Bosmer and Khajiit as two of the three member races - just has it particularly bad.
- The guards are OP, in other unrelated news.
- The game is not pay to win, so I bought a couple of things off the cash shop - cosmetic outfits and non-combat pets. I also acquired the 'any race, any faction' upgrade. It's nice, but not necessary - racial perks are just big enough to affect playstyle, without being game-breaking.
- The download feels like forever, even on a fast connection - I don't want to contemplate what it would be like on, say, my 1mbps friend's internet. It's a big download, because it's a big game.
- Explore everything. You might find something awesome.
- I can't honestly comment on PvP - I haven't tried it yet.
- I don't have to pay a subscription to maintain access to Tamriel.
- I disagree with a previous commenter - with the sheer volume of weapon, armor, and skill point choices, each of my characters feels and plays differently. I feel unique without being useless, as I try on a nightblade (rogue) tank, healer, and DPS - all separate characters. There's optimal - and then there's playable. Optimal is a small, niche market - you can play anything you want, effectively.
So far, there are small things that bother me - Molag Bal doesn't encompass all of the portfolios he's given in this game, you know - but overall I thoroughly enjoy this title, and feel it's well worth the money I spent.

-Like all stealth games patience and timing is key.

-Each mission introduces a new nice mechanic.

After numerous patches and hotfixes, Rome 2 is finally playable and enjoyable - though, it doesn't stand as nearly as polished as Shogun 2.
While not as polished and tight as its predecessor, CA's latest title is the largest in scope. Indeed, the narrative of 'empire' rings true if only based on the sheer *size* of the campaign map and by the end of a campaign, the 'imperial frontier' feels as such.
With that said, expanding is simplistic. Beyond any initial challenges associated with faction-based starting locations or penalities, few enemies stand as powerful as the Roman Legions. In fact, by the end of the campaign, I found myself entering the usual 'Total War' steamrolling strategy. The min-maxing dynamic between public order and food provisions doesn't allow for the intense construction-chain decisions akin to Shogun 2 and the building chains don't seem to rely on long-term investment strategies for good payoff and reward. Building simplicity plays into Agents as well - with skill trees enabling agent characters as taking the place of rock, paper, or scissor against others. The building and agent chains seem devolved from Shogun 2's system. It's fair to say that if it wasn't for this game's theme, I would find it boring.
Understandably, increasing difficulties and trying out new factions add to replayability, but these are the usual 'Total War' suspects for providing as such.
The political meta-game has still not been implemented to a state that deems it worthy to include. In other words, CA's attempt at political 'intrigue' and faction infighting was poorly executed for a title that was supposedly meant to feature it. "Dilemmas" have little consequence, aside from hits to the treasury or poor retinue characters. I never felt attached to my characters in the way that I expected to do so. Like the previous Rome Total War, my generals were mere place-holders for legions and added little to the overall experience of war and empire.
In any case, what was a rushed title has now turned into an enjoyably thematic strategy game and although some elements stand loosely against others, Rome 2 still holds its own in the Creative Assembly lineup - though only just.
A must if you have a super good computer!

This review is coming significantly after the admitedly disasterous launch. I believe CA has done a good job in addressing the main problems that plagued this title at and after the games release. Battle AI is adequete (as good as most TW games) and altough i never personally suffered from many of the technical difficultes some people experienced, I believe that the 10 + patches have alleviated this problem as well.
Unfourtunatly what was usually overshadowed by the citicisms of the game was some really excellent refinments in the TW experience. First the campaign view is much better and I don't need to spend nearly as much time micromanaging my settlements. However, I dont believe any auto-manage function exists in the game so I could see how that would disappoint some players. The visuals are fine, honestly not a huge improvment over shogun imo. The diversity of factions was a breath of fresh air after the monotonous choices in Shogun. Also, I really feel like for one of the first times in a total war game all agents can play an important role.
The first problem i have with the game is that despite patching i still feel like some features aren't implemented fully or simply far underutilized. Besides the forementioned auto settlement managment, the faction screen is hardly inspired. I enjoyed seeing my family tree grow and wither in other TW games. Now family and oppostion members seemingly pop out of the ground. Most of my other gripes are fairly minor. There are some problems with diplomacy, user friendliness (tooltips/icons are vague and often the games systems are poorly described) and AI behavior but as a TW vet I can usually see past these failings.
Overall I like this game. I've sunk 150 + hours into it. If you are a fan of TW I recommend it. If you are new to the series I would point you to Shogun II.

Now before you write this off as a fanboy review, hear me out. Don't listen to the negitive reviews, this game is a ton of fun.
It plays a lot like GTA Online but in a free to play format. That sounds like a nightmare, i know, but it really isn't. It's kind of grindy, but that is to expect from a F2P game. Don't expect to have to play 100+ hours for a single item.
There is an endless amount of character and vehicle customization, this is half the fun for me. A really interesting thing they did with vehicles is how the radio works. You can import your songs and play them through the car, like the "personal" radio channel in GTA. But wait, it gets better. Everyone in and around the vehicle can hear what you are playing, so the farther away the car is the less you can hear it. AND if you have the doors open(ie. when you are parked), the music is clear, and when the doors are closed, it's muffled. That's a very small thing to mention, but i like the attention to detail for this kind of stuff. I play this game myself and have made a few friends through this game, and it's a lot more fun if you have a friend to play with. Now, one of my favorite parts is that the chat is uncensored. It's hilarious.

This game is immersive, frightening, and very atmospheric. I've been playing for ten hours now and I can faithfully say that the game is not just about the 'scares' (jump scares, creepy moments, etc.) The game builds everything up. It makes you truly feel like you are essentially alone in your struggle with the monstrous creature hunting you.
For any fan of the Alien series, this is a fantastic game. For any fan of the first Alien movie, this is a masterpiece. Every door you open, every vent you enter, and every table or closet you pass could provide a temporary safe haven to hide and catch your breath, or it could spell your doom at the claws of the creature.
The Alien cannot be predicted nor can it be killed. It has one of the most, if not the most, advanced and clever AIs I have ever seen. It has no predictable patterns, it has no patrol cycles, it has no definite movements. It is truly an animal. There is only one Alien and, as such, it cannot be killed in gameplay. It can barely be repelled, though repelling it will only result in it being peeved off.
Avoiding it isn't easy either. I myself walked slowly out of a room, motion tracker in hand, and noticed a blip right on top of me. I couldn't see the creature anywhere so I assumed that it was on another level, until I saw a slow trail of slime dribbling from an overhead vent.
Moments such as that are particularly frightening when you consider that I was already hiding from another, much more human, enemy. I didn't think I even needed to be worried about the Alien at that point, having played many games in my lifetime. Typically, when one enemy in this type of game has made itself a major problem, there is no need to worry about the others at the moment. With Alien: Isolation, this is not the case.
Even when you are surrounded by a group of friendly survivors, you are not safe forever. You are constantly being hunted. You never know when the creature could drop from an overhead vent and rip apart every last person in the room. If you let your guard down for even one second, you could easily find a spike through your abdomen.
Overall, I'd give this game a 9.5/10 based purely off of what I've seen so far. This is the Alien game we've been waiting 35 years to see. It's scary, creative, and it really knows how to suck you in. If you haven't purchased this game yet, I highly recommend you do so. It is well worth the price.

Overall (played through once on Hard)
I found Alien: Isolation to be exceptional. It isn't the best game I've played this year but it's easily worth the time and money. I wouldn't say that it has any immediate replayability; you're not gonna finish your first playthrough and start another one right away, but I can see running through it again in a few months. I found the story and duration of the game to be quite good despite a couple of the reviews I've read. The great graphics, amazing and tense music, and terrific ambient sound all comes together to make an immersive and emotional experience.
Oh, the horror!
I don't play horror and shock games too often so I expected to have to wear adult diapers most of the time. The fright aspect wore often after a while and, strangely, I found myself far more jolted by the androids than the alien. But the sense of fear wearing off wasn't synonymous with boredom, not at all. I was actually a bit relieved, especially since I like to play games before I go to sleep (and I always carry that stuff into my dreams). But the horror was replaced with a tension that I really appreciated for the duration of the game. There were little respites from the tension where I was able to run freely, and run I did because it was an opportunity that didn't exist in the rest of the game without risking getting the top of my skull ripped off from the darkness of an overhanging vent shaft or hearing the slippery thud as the alien dropped down in the next room over before screeching and tearing after me.
Was the game too long?
Let's be real, I put in 24.1 hours for one playthrough on Hard. Absolutely nothing about that is too long. But did it FEEL too long? Not at all. Alien: Isolation does not stick to a common, dull story arc that has a predictable climax and ending. But this seemed to actually be a bad thing to some people, as though they wanted a completely predictable narrative. I've read reviews with complaints about how the game was tedious, repetitive, and just ran on too long. Descriptions go like, "You just find a thing to open a door so you can find a thing to open a door, over and over." These sorts of complaints sound like all those people who don't understand why anyone plays games at all; "So, like, you just click the mouse over and over all day? Why don't you just leave the house and do something real?" We all know it's a ton more complex than this ridiculously mundane view, and the same goes for Alien: Isolation. In addition to having an interesting story arc that will keep you guessing even when you think you're done, there are, in short, qualities of constantly managing a ton of things throughout the duration of the game in order to strike the right balance that allows you to progress while minimizing risk and being able to adapt to danger as it appears.
The best test I have for a game is time travel. Having played through it and knowing what I know, would I go back in time and buy it and play through it again? Yeah, I totally would.

Amazing Half-Life remake, the developers did an extraordinary job and deserve to have their work appreciated.  It really shows how big of a fan the developers are of the Half-Life series. I have never seen a group of people put so much effort into a free mod that is being turned into a work of art and something that will be recognized world wide as a master piece.  With all that said, the multiplayer needs a ton of work:
1) The game crashes often
2) Very poor performance (studdering, low framerate, ladders are very laggy and netcode needs optimization)
3) The bunny bhop doesn't work well
4) The crossbow zoom isn't instant, can't quick zoom
5) Crossbow bolts aren't hitscan like HL1DM or Adrenaline gamer
6) The gauss charges slower than HL/AG
7) The gauss no longer does splash damage on corner wall shots
8) The gauss doesn't penetrate walls effectively and do splash damage behind
9) Suit chargers are not 30 points anymore (75 now) and charge way too quickly for competitive play
10) Spawning takes up to 7 seconds or more and the camera follows the fragger.  HL/AG is instant respawn and HL2DM is 4 seconds.  This isn't ideal for competitive play especially when playing 2v2's and 3v3's.
I really hope the developers keep these things in mind and implement them as the game gets developed.  As of right now, the game is no where near ready for competitive play (weapon and gameplay wise).  Alot of old HL1DM and Adrenaline gamer players that quit in late 2005 would only come back if these major unique gameplay features are implemented.  The days of fast paced arena deathmatch games of the late 90's and early 00's are long gone but I hope this game gives that genre one last breath.

This game does several things right.  The music is great and very atmospheric, and the presentation is also strong: the game takes the form of a conversation that the protagonist has with a friend after having a very ludic dream, and you alter the events of the dream as you're telling him about it.  Conceptually, it's strong.  You play through different scenarios with various options and approaches, and you can customize your protagonist to make her better suited to tackle some of the challenges.
There are also several problems that I have with this game.  The game expects too much of you with too little payout.  By  this, I mean that there's a "true ending" that you're always working towards, which requires numerous playthroughs and specific endings to get the code for.  I ended up looking online for where to get the code because I had already gotten a ton of endings and didn't realize that I needed a certain item to even find the code at all.  Without looking online, I'm sure it would have taken hours of additional replays just to find the information I needed to reach the true ending.  Then the real problem was with the true ending itself.  I won't spoil anything; I'll just say that it was a serious let down.  Nothing was explained.  If I actually had taken the time to find the code myself, I'd be even more irritated because I would have wasted a ton of time.  The true ending doesn't bring some new understanding of the events or reach some shocking conclusion or, well, anything really.  I even looked online to see if I had gotten the wrong ending, if there was something else I had missed, and I watched the end of a youtube playthrough where the player reached the end and was just as disappointed as I was.
I know I've ranted a lot, so it might seem weird that I still recommended the game.  Altogether, I did enjoy playing it.  The story was interesting, and the atmosphere was great.  It had its flaws, but as long as you're aware of them, and as long as you're the kind of person that really enjoys atmospheric visual novels, there's still enjoyment to be had in this game.  Maybe there'll be a sequel!

The Bottom of the Well is a visual novel telling the story of Alice C. who has experienced a lucid dream about nuclear bombing. Throughout the game, the player will make several choices which greatly affect the outcome of the game.
The story is told through the protagonist's dialogue with Mad H. (rings a bell?). At the start, the player gets to customise Alice by allocating up to nine points into six skills (Survival, Fitness, Social Life, Supplies, Career, Dating) and later by choosing a few items, depending on the skillset and the number of playthroughs. One can also choose one of the preset characters.
The game's art style is outstanding. Monochromatic drawings combined with haunting, sparse music create a melancholic vibe which corresponds well with the story. Even though there are a few typos here and there, they do not detract much from the experience. One could also say that this game is a bit short (half an hour at most per playthrough, unless one has to rely on using the dictionary a lot) but it makes perfect sense – one of the selling points is that the choices actually matter and influence how the story evolves. That should warrant multiple playthroughs. There also are achievements for those who like to hunt them.
To conclude, The Bottom of the Well is an astounding title
(this joke never gets old... or does it?). I highly recommend everyone give it a try. Maybe you will be as pleasantly surprised as I was.
P.S. There is a place, like no place on the Interwebz. A land full of walls of text, biased opinions, and devoid of silly memes and politcal correctness. Some say, to survive it, you need merely basic reading comprehension skills.

User interface: This game has a rather clean and helpful UI. Without any of the windows opened, there are about 6 or so widgets on-screen. Also, every button or stat has a tooltip explaining what it does or its significance. Also, certain parts of the UI are locked for low players, which I would like say is a good move as it help to gradually introduce complexity instead of just perplexing new players with an assortment of mechanics and features that only becomes relevant at higher levels.
Quests: All quests involve simple cutscenes of some sort where the NPC or NPCs converse with you or with each other. This is certainly a step above most F2P MMOs that usually only offer a one-sided conversation with the player character.
Combat: The combat is standard action bar MMO-fare. Select a target and spam your rotation. However, there a few bugs with the combat I've experienced. Primarily, the game doesn't seem to take into account line-of-sight. That means that one can stand about-face from a mob, spam bullets, and have those bullets go backwards through your character and hit the mob.
Leveling: The leveling seems fairly balanced. As long as one is doing quests, one shouldn't have to grind mobs to get to the next level and, at the same time, one never gets the feel that one might be leveling too fast.
I have no opinion on any late game content nor any group content. I will update this review once I've played more of this game.

This game is immersive, frightening, and very atmospheric. I've been playing for ten hours now and I can faithfully say that the game is not just about the 'scares' (jump scares, creepy moments, etc.) The game builds everything up. It makes you truly feel like you are essentially alone in your struggle with the monstrous creature hunting you.
For any fan of the Alien series, this is a fantastic game. For any fan of the first Alien movie, this is a masterpiece. Every door you open, every vent you enter, and every table or closet you pass could provide a temporary safe haven to hide and catch your breath, or it could spell your doom at the claws of the creature.
The Alien cannot be predicted nor can it be killed. It has one of the most, if not the most, advanced and clever AIs I have ever seen. It has no predictable patterns, it has no patrol cycles, it has no definite movements. It is truly an animal. There is only one Alien and, as such, it cannot be killed in gameplay. It can barely be repelled, though repelling it will only result in it being peeved off.
Avoiding it isn't easy either. I myself walked slowly out of a room, motion tracker in hand, and noticed a blip right on top of me. I couldn't see the creature anywhere so I assumed that it was on another level, until I saw a slow trail of slime dribbling from an overhead vent.
Moments such as that are particularly frightening when you consider that I was already hiding from another, much more human, enemy. I didn't think I even needed to be worried about the Alien at that point, having played many games in my lifetime. Typically, when one enemy in this type of game has made itself a major problem, there is no need to worry about the others at the moment. With Alien: Isolation, this is not the case.
Even when you are surrounded by a group of friendly survivors, you are not safe forever. You are constantly being hunted. You never know when the creature could drop from an overhead vent and rip apart every last person in the room. If you let your guard down for even one second, you could easily find a spike through your abdomen.
Overall, I'd give this game a 9.5/10 based purely off of what I've seen so far. This is the Alien game we've been waiting 35 years to see. It's scary, creative, and it really knows how to suck you in. If you haven't purchased this game yet, I highly recommend you do so. It is well worth the price.

Overall (played through once on Hard)
I found Alien: Isolation to be exceptional. It isn't the best game I've played this year but it's easily worth the time and money. I wouldn't say that it has any immediate replayability; you're not gonna finish your first playthrough and start another one right away, but I can see running through it again in a few months. I found the story and duration of the game to be quite good despite a couple of the reviews I've read. The great graphics, amazing and tense music, and terrific ambient sound all comes together to make an immersive and emotional experience.
Oh, the horror!
I don't play horror and shock games too often so I expected to have to wear adult diapers most of the time. The fright aspect wore often after a while and, strangely, I found myself far more jolted by the androids than the alien. But the sense of fear wearing off wasn't synonymous with boredom, not at all. I was actually a bit relieved, especially since I like to play games before I go to sleep (and I always carry that stuff into my dreams). But the horror was replaced with a tension that I really appreciated for the duration of the game. There were little respites from the tension where I was able to run freely, and run I did because it was an opportunity that didn't exist in the rest of the game without risking getting the top of my skull ripped off from the darkness of an overhanging vent shaft or hearing the slippery thud as the alien dropped down in the next room over before screeching and tearing after me.
Was the game too long?
Let's be real, I put in 24.1 hours for one playthrough on Hard. Absolutely nothing about that is too long. But did it FEEL too long? Not at all. Alien: Isolation does not stick to a common, dull story arc that has a predictable climax and ending. But this seemed to actually be a bad thing to some people, as though they wanted a completely predictable narrative. I've read reviews with complaints about how the game was tedious, repetitive, and just ran on too long. Descriptions go like, "You just find a thing to open a door so you can find a thing to open a door, over and over." These sorts of complaints sound like all those people who don't understand why anyone plays games at all; "So, like, you just click the mouse over and over all day? Why don't you just leave the house and do something real?" We all know it's a ton more complex than this ridiculously mundane view, and the same goes for Alien: Isolation. In addition to having an interesting story arc that will keep you guessing even when you think you're done, there are, in short, qualities of constantly managing a ton of things throughout the duration of the game in order to strike the right balance that allows you to progress while minimizing risk and being able to adapt to danger as it appears.
The best test I have for a game is time travel. Having played through it and knowing what I know, would I go back in time and buy it and play through it again? Yeah, I totally would.

Just Cause 3 was so much better than I expected. I loved Just Cause 2 and had always gone back to playing it to goof around in and I'll definitely do it in this. I played Just Cause 2 right before playing Just Cause 3 to get a good comparison and the gameplay still feels simular but with so much more. I don't every preorder games anymore, but took the risk on this game and it was definitely worth it. But between Just Cause 2 and Just Cause 3, Rico and Tom Sheldon are the only reoccuring characters. The story and dialogue is better than Just Cause 2, but it isn't greatly story driven. Also when it comes to boss's and commanders, Just Cause 2's are tougher, though Just Cause 3 has tougher enemies. Another thing I noticed is that when it came to weapon choice, I prefered Using twin pistols in Just Cause 2 so that I could get a bunch of headshots in, but in Just Cause 3 I almost purely used a burst assault rifle.
There's a lot you can do in Just Cause 3, especially being able to have multiple grapples, being able to pull them together, having explosives that can upgrade to have jet propulsion, and much more. I abused the grapple so much for destroying things along with goofing around. It's a lot of fun grappling random vehicles and pulling them together and seeing what can happen along with occasional glitches that absolutely launch them. The wingsuit is a bit difficult to get used to, but is really awesome once you do (Watch out for trees though). When it comes to graphics, the game is absolutely gorgeous. The models and textures are absolutely amazing, and I personally think it looks as good, if not better than GTA 5 at max settings. I heard some people complain about the explosions not looking too great, but going from Just Cause 2 to Just Cause 3, it was a huge WHOA in difference. The only disappointing explosion I had the entire game was a story mission of dropping a "huge" bomb into the water.
Some changes that I would prefer is to be allowed to zoom in and aim right away instead of unlocking it along with being able to do some sort of multiplayer besides having a ghost doing challenges. I also wish that it got a bit more ridiculous like Just Cause 2, such as the story mission where you have to take down the 3 bosses atop the Three Kings Hotel. It would also be nice for shotguns to get more ammo. I used to use the shotgun a lot in Just Cause 2, and I'd run out pretty quickly. The dual wielding shotguns are awesome, but you run out really quickly and there's no other ammo lying around anywhere.
Overall, Just Cause 3 is definitely one of my favorite games of all time. Just Cause 2 was one of my all time favorites, but this sequel greatly improves upon everything it needed.

is the popular mod which aims to recreate (or re-imagine) the original
on the Source engine, providing much better graphics, mechanics and gameplay. The Crowbar Collective definitely achieved their goal,
is nothing short of Phenomenal. Over the years it has won various awards, and even with a year or so of inactivity on their ModDB profile at the time,
was still nominated to the top 10 mods of the year almost every time, and for a very good reason.
is very true to the original
in terms of level design, gameplay and difficulty, but at the same time it feels familar yet different, it is not a direct carbon copy. The chapter Questionable Ethics and Lambda Core are good examples of this. Some maps and areas are diferent or cut somewhat shorter such as On a Rail and Surface Tension which are both missing some sections found in the original game, this is the only real drawback, but it delivers in almost ever other aspect. All of the weapons you use in the original game make a return too, and while they now have a more limited aummunition capacity, they look excellent and are fun to use.
On top of the graphical overhaul,
delivers in terms of depth too, some excellent voiceacting and dialog really help add to the imersive atmosphere and explaining the story and situation further, not to mention the excellent quality of the maps making the game more atmospheric than it has ever been before.
Now that
is available on Steam to purchase as a standalone game, I couldn't recommend it more. The gameplay is solid and the game itself is flawlessly beautiful. The addition of achievements, the Steam Workshop and automatic updates add much more to make
even better and reliable. Valve themselves couldn't have done a better job on this, definitely worth the asking price.

is still under development, hence "Early Access", so the Xen portion of the game currently doesn't exist.

Honestly, as much as I want to beat the crap out of this mod for charging $20 when I ratted on Aperture Tag for costing $7, I can't. By comparison, this is actually worth your money. Where Aperture Tag was a literal mod that required a base game and only provided a whopping 3 hours of gameplay with an innovative but forgettable gameplay design, this comes with roughly double to triple that in single player gameplay (with more being added later), multiplayer, and it's entirely standalone.
The devs of this have worked their rear ends off to get this to where it is, with 8 years of work or so now. I have to praise every moment of it too, as while a lot of it is due to it simply being Half Life, this is also infinetly more enjoyable as Half Life has started to age a bit. The music and sound design is absolutely superb, the graphics are some of the best the source engine has to offer, and the atmosphere and gameplay have been massively improved, not taken away from, by this mod. This is not a simple graphical upgrade, but rather a full redesign of the entire game from the ground up. That means redesigned levels, movement, AI, etc. with all of it being extremely well made. It helps to make the entire game far more immersive, and it ends making me wish there was more - I know Xen is on the way, but that's not enough. The design of this mod is so great, it makes me want more of EVERYTHING. WHERE IS HALF LIFE 3, GABEN?
As it stands, I haven't touched the multiplayer yet, but I have run through the single player. I felt scared, alone, excited, surprised, and overall felt immersed far more into this than I ever could into the 1998 Half Life. Multiplayer is effectivelly a rehash of the original deathmatch, but now with workshop support and various other improvements. I imagine it would add many, MANY hours onto an already fantastic game, easily doubling or tripling what you can already get.
It's honestly hard to stop gushing and face facts, but there are some. This game has its' issues. I've encountered issues with enemies spawning in as blank, unanimated corpses that do nothing, issues with the AI getting permanently stuck on something, issues with clipping my view through stuff, and issues with sound effects overlapping each other to the point of my headset giving up and just delivering a blank rather than actual sound. And, admittedly, a lot of the gush is made possible simply because this is based on the fantastic Half Life. Were it not for that, I cannot say if it would be as good as it is.
However, I would indeed say buy this. You will not only get your money's worth, but you will be supporting devs who have been caring for this project for MANY years now, as well as simple convinience of things like auto-updating and such when new content and fixes come out. I recommend this easily.

NMRiH is an excellent mod. The fact that it is free just sweetens the deal. But im not here to tell you what is good about it.
Now don't get me wrong, I DO recommend this game, but I am writing this as a review to things you will probably find wrong with it.

So here we go:
-Its hard to find a server that is the default gametype. Yes you can type Classic into the filter but even then a lot of servers you will join will have changes made to them.
-Like most Source games, you cannot just create a session for you and a friend to hop onto. Which means you have to join a server or create one. So don't expect to just play with a friend or two without randoms joining.
-With that being said, randoms cause a lot of lag. This already difficult game, (if playing on "Classic") now becomes 100x harder with lag due to zombies killing you in 3 - 8 hits as you are depending on your melee weapon. (Tip: Melee then Shove, Melee then Shove)
-Maps do seem to bug out somtimes, doors will not open, getting stuck inside objects, etc. It doesn't happen often, but it's general Source bugs.
-Small learning curve. Expect to die a lot the first few times you play. But it does become extremely addictive.
-It could just be me, because im not a big fan of Survival/Wave type games. But the Survival Maps quickly become boring and seem a bit too easy compared to Objective/Linear maps.
- Only 3 types of zombies that arent all that different in terms of combat. Slow walkers, Runner and Children. (Children being just a smaller and weaker Runner) This isn't really a problem, due to the fact none of the zombies are that hard to kill. Its more a numbers game.
Anyways, like I said I DO recommend this game because it is fun, it is addicting, it is hard. But these problems were the largest that popped out at me. My friends had the same gripes aswell.
Add in easy session creation so you can just play with friends on the fly without joining/creating a server and I would pay $30+ for this game.

Like a deadbeat hooker doped on morphine, I grew ever so excited upon hearing that the sequel for Dark Souls was announced. Days went on as I watched videos and pleasured myself to the one aspect that I had waited for since the release of the first Dark Souls: to play a ported game that actually works properly.
Well, From Software didn't disappoint in the "playability" factor.
However, something about Dark Souls 2 doesn't settle in my stomach very well. It's like when you eat an entire pizza that's not from your usual pizzeria after not having a meal in a week. It's amazing; you enjoy every texture, the smell and feel are familiar but somewhat new, and you're willing to scarf it down without complaints.
But after a while, once you let it settle in your stomach, you kind of regret a few things. First, you just ate an entire pizza pie, you slob. Second, you were so into the pie once you got it, you didn't notice or chose to ignore the mold on the crust and tell yourself, "That's just extra parsley baked into the dough." And finally, the bathroom trip afterwards is no fun. You'll sit there for hours, constipated and upset by this pizza, trying your best to tell yourself, "It was a good pizza," over and over again.
That's not to say Dark Souls 2 is bad. Quite the opposite. It was rather good. The game looks beautiful, the fighting mechanics are solid, and the fact that multiplayer works properly now is phenomenal. My problem is that I started Dark Souls 2 expecting nothing to have changed. I was expecting the fluid, fast paced fighting from the original Dark Souls, being on my toes at all time, expecting enemy ambushes around every corner.
But Dark Souls 2 failed to pull that off. Instead, I got a couple enemies that faked being corpses and the occasional ridiculously hard boss battle out of no where before I was supposed to officially fight him. IT seems that the game was dumbed down for newer players. I get it: you want everyone to be able to play, From Software. That's cool. What's not cool is holding my hand throughout the game like I'm a child after the experiences I've had with the first Dark Souls. That's downright insulting.
And the lore. Dark Souls had a wonderful story and background to it. Not much info was forced down my throat throughout the game, From Software felt that there was no need to force a story into their original game. And to be honest, I think that was the best way to do it. To figure out the lore on my own while playing the first Dark Souls was amazing. It felt like I was actually a part of it, something a lot of RPGs fail to pull off nowadays. But Dark Souls 2 fell short on this aspect. I get that you wanted to center the story on me; that's cool. But don't water-down the characters around me.
Aside from that, the game itself was great. The PvP works flawlessly, so I finally enjoy being ganked and backstabbed like the casual scrub I am. Though the new fighting mechanics take a little getting used to and don't feel as nice as the original, they do work out well.
Anyone new to Dark Souls will thoroughly enjoy this game. Hell, even some people who played the previous Dark Souls might enjoy it. But as a diehard fan of Dark Souls, I have to say this game came up short and just barely passes my approval..

The entire Company of Heroes collection is a great RTS, especially for those who traditionally don't like to play this genre of game due to the punishing difficulty on new players (seen in the big name ones, like StarCraft). The fact that this is a World War 2 setting will also draw out some people to try the game out.
CoH doesn't have you building your base and gathering resources, rather it has you capturing points on the maps which provide you with increased resources and army capacity. This lets you worry more about managing position on the battlefield, rather than managing how many drones you have collecting resources. As you play more, you will see little nuances of the game that make the game deeper and more complex, like cover behind walls, flanking, and all the sorts of things you may expect from playing an in-depth, turn-based, strategy game.
Overall, the CoH collection of games have a great single player campaign experience, and a thriving multiplayer community. If you like real-world settings for war, this RTS is probably for you.
Tales of Valor has a much weaker single-player experience than the previous entries. It's really just more of the same, but with a bit taken out. Regardless, it is still worthwhile to have if you are a CoH fan.

Second, the game is very very linear, not only when it comes to level design but also when it comes to gadgets and weapons. You basically get a silenced pistol (which is as reliable as a slingshot), and everything else in your inventory is limited to specific situations. Each time you come across an obstacle, it's less about figuring out what's the best way of overcoming it, and more about figuring out what you're able to do, since you rarely have more than one option. This only makes the gameplay even more boring, as it doesn't take too long to realize it's mostly trial and error, over and over.
I'm very dissapointed in this game, but I might still give a chance to Chaos Theory some day, since I hear it's so great.

I wish I could just give this game a neutral rating instead of positive or negative only.
Don’t get me wrong I think this game is great and stood the test of time, it got good story and very fun gameplay.
I really enjoyed the game when I first played when it was released and I even enjoy it now,  but this version got some serious technical problem and some missing content.
So, I'll start with the positives:
Splinter Cell is a well-made entry-level stealth game for anyone to try and enjoy like I did.
You play as Sam Fisher, a recruited operative by the NSA to a newly formed division called the 3rd Echelon.
In this game, you will be dispatched to many different locations to do spying, date gathering and assassinations from time to time while using the many different tools that you will be handed and find on your missions.
The missions are very liner and you will sometime, though few and between, you will get occasions where you can get into a location in more than one way (that’s is the reason why I said entry level, If you want more challenge then play it on hard).
The stealth mechanic is based on line of sight, noise you make while moving on different terrains and the amount of light you are exposed to (which is displayed on a meter in your HUD).
The tutorial level is very good at explaining the basics and is masqueraded as a fitness checkup on an obstacle course and is done without insulting the player intelligence.
The voice acting is excellent and the dialogs you will hear sometime can be extremely funny (evidence of a good writing).
Even though the game was released in 2003, it still holds up, the graphics are serviceable and can improve by applying a fan made HD textures patch that are ripped from the remaster that the consoles got in the 2011 Splinter Cell HD Trilogy.
There is also a fan-made widescreen patch which includes the fix to the broken shadows problem (due to relying on now-obsolete functionality in NVIDIA GPUs, the default "buffer" shadows are broken on modern hardware).
So, what are the negatives? The short answer is that the steam release is not very good.
This release missing 3 official bonus missions that were released on the PC and yet not included in the steam version, so you will need to find and install them yourself, even though after all those year I would expect the steam version to be updated with them in already.
Another problem I have is Ubisoft practice, the first trilogy of the splinter cell games got a remaster with better graphics and widescreen support and no issues with the shadows.
I would expect them at least to do the same for the PC, to release the remasters or at the very least to patch the games so those problem will not be in it.
Another problem in this game is the aiming: for a vetern soldier, Sam Fisher can't shoot where the cursor is pointing to even at close range sometime and if you try to zoom in then you will see that the aim is moving all over the place it's like a drunk trying to hit the broad side of a barn.
I would also like to mention that the sequel Pandora Tomorrow, which had a release on windows, is now impossible to get (unless you pirate it) because of the same shadow problem that this game has (which a fan made patch can fix it or Ubisoft can just release the remastered trilogy on steam/GOG).

The first Splinter Cell is immense for being so old. Loads of detail and I've only just played the tutorial.
Different floor materials affect how loud you are when stepping on them.
The sound you make and the enemy's view of you are two things you always need to be aware of in this game.
Gun kills are a last resort in the first Splinter Cell. This is a huge difference in game design from a lot of stealth third-person-shooter games today.
Expect to interrogate and force guards to do things to progress, rather than just killing everyone in the room.
Shoot lights and weak cameras, or just navigate in the shadows to stay unseen by the enemy. Hide guards' bodies in dark places or you will be compromised.
I don't know if Splinter Cell is better than the Hitman franchise, but this game is beautifully fluid even on my non-gaming $300 laptop.
Above all, expect less hand-holding than nearly every other modern AAA game. I don't say this to be condescending; taking away ease-of-use and accessibility can hinder the modern player's enjoyment of a game. But in a true stealth game, there should be no hand-holding IMO. Struggle and use any tools at your disposal to survive. This is Splinter Cell.

At times, Tom Clancy’s Splinter Cell can feel like a product of 2002 in the worse ways possible. But clever design and compelling gameplay carry it forward into the bright, shining light of 2017.
Developed as Ubisoft Montreal's Hail Mary effort to not be seen as a studio that makes licensed kids games, Splinter Cell is a stealth action game that was designed to take on Metal Gear Solid, while also leveraging the Tom Clancy brand for credibility. The use of the Clancy branding is significant, because up until this point Red Storm Entertainment was the only studio that used it, due to Clancy himself serving as founder of the studio.
Splinter Cell was renowned for its clever use of light and shadow and it still look great in 2017. The game also goes to great lengths to establish the settings of your missions as real places, without the artifice of most games, and it mostly succeeds. Its greatest strength lies in its protagonist, Sam Fisher, a tired ex-SEAL and ex-CIA operative played in a delightfully deadpan and tired manner by veteran method actor Michael Ironside.
Sam isn't the only interesting character in the game. Your support staff also contain some interesting characters such as Lambert, your commanding officer. His is the voice you will hear most often, giving you orders and mission objectives. Lambert, along with supporting characters Grimsgottir and Wilkes, have a strong chemistry with Sam, and their dialogue reflects a real history between the team.
The storyline itself is compelling enough to drive the game, but it is also very standard issue Clancy. The president of Georgia is assassinated and after a bloodless coup d’etat, Kombayn Nikoladze, a Georgian billionaire and business mogul, seizes power. Fisher is sent to Georgia to investigate the disappearance of two CIA operatives, only to discover they stumbled onto something that could trigger a war. From there, you go all over the world following leads and lurking in the shadows trying to prevent things from getting worse. There are suitcase nukes, secret wars, information warfare, it’s all elements most of us have seen before in all kinds of media, but it does work in the game’s favor.
The game feels great to play. Sam is extremely nimble and his movements really sell the fact that he has been doing this for a long time. A novel concept is that the mouse wheel on PC controls the speed of your movement. For example, if you want to be as quiet and slow as possible, you move the mouse wheel down until Sam is moving so slow that you do not even disturb glass as you walk over it. It is a great idea that was never copied by games outside of the SC series, at least to my knowledge.
Where the game falls apart though is that Sam can sometimes feel clunky to control, especially when doing stance changes or jumping/mantling. Those actions feel extremely mechanical and when the game demands you do some of the more complex moves, such as split jumping, can prove to be extremely frustrating on mouse and keyboard. The times where the game puts you into combat scenarios also do not feel great, with the accuracy of your weapons being seemingly random at times, even when your crosshairs are completely locked in. Sam also isn’t superhuman and can only take a few bullets before dying, which is a problem when your enemies have automatic or burst firing weapons. There are also times where the AI can feel a little too aware of you, and is able to spot you in complete darkness, but these are rare.
Overall, though, the game is still a great time and really makes you feel like you are the master of espionage. To play the game, I used ThirteenAG’s widescreen fix to run at native 1920x1200 with proper aspect ratio, though it does break full screen video playback. Without the fix, the game is locked to 4:3 resolutions. The fix also comes with dgVoodoo2, which fixes the shadow rendering on modern GPU’s. Anti-aliasing and antistrophic filtering can also be safely forced through your GPU’s control panel to their highest possible settings for the best image quality. I also used the PS3 HD Texture pack to add in the re-mastered textures that were made for the PS3 re-release of the first three games of the series. Finally, I used a guide on Steam that was written by ThatDarnOwl
to add in the bonus missions that were downloadable on Xbox Live and published on PC in Europe only or with the Chaos Theory CE. However, to be honest, the missions are not anything to write home about, other than the final Sub mission.

This game is a (terrifying) love letter to any person who prefers the original Alien movie to its also fantastic sequel. Even players who don't usually like horror games will feel compelled to go on and explore the picture-perfect recreation of the dark, low-high-tech sci-fi vision of the 1979's movie, filled with CRT screens, mechanical computers and steam vents.
This is not a shooter, so be prepared to hide, crouch through vents, and peer in horror at your motion detector as the beeping green blip comes closer and closer to you while you try to hold your breath and not make a noise.
The game is difficult, occasionally unfair, and has a checkpoint save system that reminds me of Dark Souls' bonfires. It all works great to build an incredible level of tension and fear, but it will also be frustrating to players who don't want to try something different to modern straightforward shooters with quicksave systems.
Technically, the game is a wonder. Graphics are the best I've ever seen, and they feel very well optimized for PC. Sound is even better. Every mechanical noise will bring you back to the original movie, and the music feels dynamic and opressive, including some cues from the original movie soundtrack. The surround audio is also brilliant, and it's just as useful as your motion detector when trying to guess where the creature is.
I can't recommend this game highly enough for fans of the first Alien movie, OR fans of horror games. For everyone else, it will probably not be their cup of tea.

This game is a mixed bag. I'm not sure whether to recommend it or not. It's got fantastic graphics and the sound is top notch. You get to explore a dark, derelict futuristic environment while the creaks and groans of the space station build a creepy atmosphere. The art is very classy and really captures the feel of the 80's dystopian future of the Alien movies. It's got nice puzzle mechanics and a good story. The intro is very long and sets the scene nicely, giving the player a slow burning feeling of paranoia.
However for some reason it decides to occasionally go down the old tired unrealistic route of making the player hide and sneak past randomly patrolling enemies, exactly the way you've done before in 100 other games. However in this game, all you can really do is avoid enemies so you just have to wait ages for them to randomly wander away from you, or accidentally trigger a scripted event that makes them go do something else. If they spot you, enemies kill you almost instantly so you have to do it all again, trial and error style. The Alien is well designed and well animated, but we've seen it so many times before that it loses some of its magic.
It's a shame they decided to spoil the overall atmosphere with these annoying sneak-em-up sequences since it doesn't really add anything but length to the game. I'd really like to recommend Alien: Isolation but it falls kind of short of deserving full price. Maybe wait for a sale?

Visual novels are not my usual style of game to play, but the "Alice" theme combined with Atomic Apocalypse was just too intriguing to pass by.
So as Alice you try to survive a nuclear attack and the aftermath. There are plenty of choices to make, an important inventory, and plenty of different situations your choices will lead to or negate - this was an aspect I liked as it increases the interactive components, and makes for great replayability as well.
The music was calming, the artwork was appealing, and the gameplay was fun. Dialogue in this game is text-based, but I greatly enjoyed the characterization and quirky elements to this - also the references to movies/gaming/litereature, and the humour. It is worth noting that the dialogue is aimed towards an adultish market, and that it includes wording and references that Parents may wish to be aware of before letting Jnr into this one. That's subjective, but best to know in advance.
To complete the achievements, one could spend millenia and fill a filing-cabinet with notes - or one could check the community guides that have been dedicatedly (a real word?) created.
I recommend taking care if using the "SKIP" feature to whiz through text, as it tends to select choice-options if you go to far, but after getting the hang of that I found it useful in my replays.
I was disappointed the "Alice" theme wasn't really explored enough, in the context that was one of the main reasons I was interested in the game, but it is there...
Considering the art-style and humour put into this, I would love to see some Profile Backgrounds or Emoticons for this, however it is a freebie so that is not a big disappointment.
I would recommend this game for players who enjoy Visual Novels, and also to players who are looking for a game as an "Entryway" into Visual Novels (like myself). I got about 6 hours to complete the achievements (with Guide assists) out of it, I will probably play it more in future too.
Oh - and I did not think it was Overpriced :)
Well done to the Devs and Community for making this, overall, an entertaining experience

A good game, but not nearly as good as the first two Souls games, and suffers from a few critical flaws.
Soul Memory: Possibly the stupidest idea FROM has ever had. It makes it so that you are paired up with other players based on how many souls you have gotten in total on your character. This mechanic punishes you for playing the game alot by leaving you isolated from other players.
Level Design: dissapointing compared to the Dark Souls 1 game, which was intricate and connected. Dark Souls 2 is a bunch of isolated, linear paths. Being able to teleport between bonfires from the very beginning of the game is testament to the poor level design.
PvP: They added dedicated servers which is great, but it is ruined by Soul Memory, worthless covenants, and poorly balanced mechanics, such as backstabs and ripostes one shotting people (its ironic because FROM said they would adress how over powered backstabbing was in Dark Souls 1 and said they would nerf it and its even more broken than before).
Bosses: Some neat ones, but most of them are really boring and can be killed by just strafing around them and waiting for an opening. Theres also no way of punishing people for doing co op anymore, especially in newgame, and its dissapointing to see so many noobs giving themselves an unnessisary crutch against bosses with no penalty.
Despite alot of flaws and being a disspointment compared to the first two souls games, its still good game. It does alot of cool things such as extra challenges in NG+, bonfire aestetics, gimmicky weapons, and the upgrade paths.

(Note: I have not played this game in many years).
So, this can be a fun game.. The community sucks, but it can be fun at times. I'm just going to put an up-vote on it simply for the good times I had on it (while at the same time trying not to think of the bad times). I could make a really serious, thoughtful review, like usual. I even typed one up and erased it.
You know what, I'll make a somewhat decent review. That sounds nice.
So:
Lag:
There is a lot of it. Everyone on the server lags, Heck, the server itself lags. Try out the two closest servers to you. I used to play on one server that I thought would be the best for me, but it turned out that the next closest one was better. The difference was barely noticable while playing, but it made all of the difference.
Hackers:
Are there any? For the most part, not really. At least when I used to play, there were not.There were a few rare cases, but it was not often. What I noticed when changing from one server to the other is that I lagged just half a second less than other people, letting my hits register like they were supposed to and everything worked normally. Different connections to the server can make a big difference.
Pay to win:
This game is really big on paying for weapons with real cash. There are a few guns that simply can't (in my opinion) be beaten that are hard to buy ingame with ingame money. One of these is a sniper rifle that makes it really easy to jump into the air and shoot someone with extreme accuracy. No other gun in the game has this ability. There are ways to get it without paying a dime, however it is difficult to do, and the weapons will probably expire after a while.
(Note: while pay-to-win weapons do give people an advantage, skill plays a lot into it. If you take the standard, default rifle, if my memory is correct I believe it was named the STAR, you can usually hold your own. It is reliable close up and at a medium to long distance.)
Note: I have way more hours than steam shows, and I have never put a single penny into this game. It isn't/wasn't necessary.
Creativity/customization:
There are tons of different ways to be creative and customize your character. You can make your own symbols, put said symbols on cars, clothes, etc. You can also change the looks/parts of the cars after unlocking the parts. You can even make music/theme songs. If you are a premium player, you are able to do more with the symbol creator, and able to own more things, but you can get by without it.
Matchmaking:
From what I remember it kinda sucked. They changed it a few months before I quit playing and tried to match people by rank. Being a higher rank, I found it really difficult to get into a match. There were times when I repeatedly faced the same four or five people over and over. Not sure if they ever fixed this.
Frustration: Expect it.
What else.. what else.. hmmm....
Friends! Yes, definantly play with friends. It makes the game more bearable. Playing by yourself will probably cause you to get burnt out quickly.
Oh, one last thing. It used to be fun to just hang out with friends and horse around. Running eachother over, stunning/shooting eachother, etc., but they added an auto kick feature that kicks you for a bit after a certain number of team kills/stuns or damage. That ruined quite a bit of the fun.
Well, I guess that does it for the Serious-ish review!
So, now to what I really wanted to say:
So, you may already know that police (enforcers) get stun guns, like tazers and bean-bag rifles, to stun and arrest criminals. I got pretty good with those. They are extremely frustrating to the criminals, but that was not why I used them. They were hard to use, risky, and caused me a lot of deaths. People don't stay down forever you know. But eventually I unlocked the crowning jewel of the Non-Leathal weaponry. The Non-Leathal Grenade Launcher. Oh boy, those were the days. Me and a bright orange grenade launcher stunning and arresting anyone and everyone that I could find. Good times. And yes, I was *that* guy, lol.
Recommended :)

Ah, Sam Fisher's debut. How could I not be nostalgic about this? This game was, to me, proof that real spies wear neoprene suits and night vision goggles, carry a small (SMALL!) selection of useful gizmos and rely on cunning, timing, and... turning off lights. I mean, darkness. Real spies don't drink Martinis and drive fast cars, is what I'm saying.
I wrote about the first Hitman game and while it wasn't a far cry from what the series would eventually become, it still had traces of training wheels. This game is much, much closer to what it's successors would be and it is also a very solid entry.
First, the good:
This game looks amazingly good for such an old title. Lighting in these games is crucial and it still holds up today. Sadly, no native widescreen support, but with a few visual tweaks (curtesy of the Steam community), it gets there. Again, I don't mind putting 2 minutes into editing a text file to get what I need, but it might not be your point of view; you've been warned. That aside, have I mentioned it looks great considering it's age?
Voice acting is pretty good and the game runs smoothly.
The gameplay is stealth action at its finest; not as refined as Chaos Theory, but what it does, it does well. This game manages to strike that fine line between difficulty and handholding in the sense that you're never spoonfed solutions, but are also never stuck wandering around aimlessly and scratching your head in confusion about what to do next. The AI in Splinter Cell games has always been a bit debateable. Sometimes they are unbelieveably stupid, yet other times annoyingly alert, but again: this is all in the interest of dynamic and fun gameplay. You are given the means to achieve your goal, and how you go about it is your business.
The combat is good enough, but it's not like this game encourages it. There are a few instances where you're forced to fight, and while in Hitman these were annoying and chore-like, here it's over pretty quickly and the shooting is actually not that bad.
Speaking of bad:
there's not much to say, really. It's a pretty basic game compared to the follow-up Splinter Cell titles and there are some missions that leave something to be desired in terms of level design and objectives, but all in all, it's still decent to great. The story is a bit forgettable though - was Thief really the only stealth game to have a good story (I never played MGS so I might be at fault here)?! The humor and tone are pretty good too, again, Chaos Theory and Pandora Tomorrow got this great mix of serious and tongue-in-cheek down to a tee, but the basis is present here already.
The AI, as mentioned, is sometimes a bit arbitrary in that they respond to what's going on in a way that makes little sense. Luckily, this game doesn't punish you for killing people (mostly, except when your boss explicitly tells you not to), so if someone's acting up, you can usually just silence them.
Like I said, there's no native widescreen support but it can be fixed.
In conclusion, I'd say this is definitely a game stealth enthusiasts would enjoy and stealth newcomers would also find a good starting point in. Future releases would expand on this idea of a goggle-toting, acrobatics performing old codger sneaking past unsuspecting guards and chefs like it's nobody's business. The groundwork was lain here, and lain it was well indeed.

Well, my first 'not recommended' review of a game. Hmh. And it's on a game I still have to play.
. I'd just like to point out that the game is good, it's just not a good MMORPG and one that I'd recommend you stay clear of if you're looking for something to pour thousands of hours into.
I'll start with the good things, as to keep things chronological.
First, are the classes. Every class is fun to play as, and not to mention that you have seperated stat trees you can invest in every class, which can sometimes change how the class plays alltogether, and frankly, doing the number crunching, stat investing, and sometimes even doing the awesome things in the game is pretty cool (for ex. one boss spawns a near-insta-kill barrier every now and then, however if you leveled your Gunslinger high enough you can roll through it and take no damage). This game also includes something it calls Common Abilities (which I mentioned above). Every class has two common abilities that are unlocked at a specific level, and once you get these abilities, any class can use it.
The game looks visually unique, even though it sometimes looks mediocre, and frankly, the one thing that keeps this game together, at least for me, is the storytelling. This game has some really good and funny writing, and is one of the few MMOs I didn't skip out of on dialogues. Astral Adventures ties into this, giving you a Telltale-like ability to chose the outcome on certain stories, and that is genuinely fun.
However, now come my gripes with the game.
The animations are choppy, and cutscenes show this off in full detail. Also, some sounds and animations are reused for wildly different abilities.  The classes are confusing, it actually♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off that I went as Gunslinger, a rapid-DOT class, and was outdamaged by my girlfriend going as the Paladin, a tank class. Bosses are bullet sponges while being able to kill you easily if you haven't built health or defense, or aren't a tanky class.
If you want the better gear in the game, you have to spend time farming for items by putting your character at a Harvesting spot and just waiting. Ocassionally you may get a QTE for some of the better crafting items, but that's about it. Newer, stronger Senshis (essentially companions/pets) are locked behind a paywall, which I guess I should've seen coming. But so is furniture and some not-so-good gear, as then you either have to grind for it in the following way:
Some enemies have a small chance of dropping a rare item. You take this rare item and turn it in and fight a boss. You kill the boss and get 3-7 (depending on if you used a Bounty Token) items, of which you need 100+, to make the item. Or you can just pay for it right away.
The game's dungeons are always pretty challenging, and I'd honestly say they're fun...up until the last two. They spike up in difficulty suddenly, and to the point that it's punishing. If you went pure ATK or Crit build, you will get♥♥♥♥♥♥on, a lot. Your only options then are to either stick with your guts and beat it somehow or switch to a tanky class, farm for the EXP (if you haven't already) and then go beat it.
So, to sum it up:
Pros & Cons:
+Classes are fun to use
+The idea of Common Abilities is a good one
+The writing in the game is pretty damn good
+Astral Adventures are fun
+Active, helpful community
+Your weapons automatically switch to fit your class (so if you had say, Demonic Gunblades, and you go Dragon Knight, it'll become a Demonic Lance instantly)
=Fun with friends (but then again, what co-op/MMORPG game isn't?)
=Stiff animations and movement
=Slow start
-The Waterpark. ♥♥♥♥ everything about the Waterpark
-Unbalanced/confusing class roles
-Ridiculous grind for some items
-Boring professions that are almost shoe-horned into the game
-Bullet-sponging, nuke bosses
-The difficulty goes
too high up in the last eight of the game
-Quests are too repetitive
-Lootbox elements (granted, I'm guilty of using them)
The only reason why I'll be finishing this game is to put a final period on the story, which managed to get me hooked. Whoever was their writer, I salute you.

The performance of the game is surprisingly lack luster.  I had an R9 280 and I pretty much had to run this on low everything to get a decent frame rate.  I ended up deciding to do that overdue upgrade and picked up a GTX 1060 6gb and there were times when this game STILL ran as low as 10 fps in complex environments, though with settings maxed out completely.  For the most part it cruised along at about 30 fps.  Meanwhile, COD Advanced Warfare was well over 60 fps, consistently, Mirror's Edge Catalyst is well over 60 FPS, consistently... Clearly bethesda and arkane did not do even a decent job of optimizing this for the PC market. and that sort of sheer negligence speaks about the companies which throttle a game's success.   However, being a big fan of the first game, I decided to be a big boy and get over it.  Once you can get past the performance problems (if you are capable) then the game itself is quite good.
The overall story isn't bad, it's fine.  Once you clear the intro to the game, you can pretty much figure out the final outcome.  There are some great concepts they flesh out during the game, and a few points where they give the player a surprising amount of control over the immediate plot if the player thinks ever so slightly out of the box and off the game's "rails" (the dust district mission, and the stilton house... that's all I'm going to say).
The amount of thought put into the different elements of the environment is impressive.  The amount of detail in every aspect of the game is great, and there's huge amounts of lore to track down and enjoy.  The clockwork mansion had elements that were surprisingly well thought out for an FPS as well.
The gameplay was great.  If you're a stealth game nut like me, you're going to love this.  Arkane did a great job of making you feel like an assassin lurking along rooftops, rafters while stalking your target and avoiding detection.  If you're not a stealth nut, then the combat is still pretty fun.  I played through the game twice, once good and once evil, and both paths are equally fun.  The exploration potential in the game is huge as well.  I got bored with exploring considering how much time I spent at it, and upon my second play through I still found areas I handn't seen yet.
Sound and music were well done, no complaints there.
The endings were a bit short and felt a little lack luster.  Like, you could more or less predict what was going to happen once you had made decisions, and even then I was surprised that some of the decisions I had made had no bearing whatsoever on the ending.  It felt like this was another area where things felt like they didn't get enough attention, but it could also be that the creators didn't want to broaden the potential endings so dramatically that a third potential game would have to ignore many of the outcomes and stick to a very specific cannon outcome.  Whatever the case, I was actually a bit disappointed in the endings I was able to explore.
Overall, I do recomend this game, though I strongly caution players to research their GPU's ability with the game, and do NOT expect the same performance you get from other games with similar visuals.  The R9 280 chugged pretty hard on this one, and ultimately this was the catalyst to go for a significant upgrade, and even then the game had moments of surprisingly low performance.  Do your homework, check your gpu to see what it can do especially in the complex environments and decide what you're willing to accept.  If you can do that and you find yourself at peace with your expectations, then get this game because it's really well made.

Synopsis - Performance was a joke. Much better now. Recommended if you're a fan of the series; if not, buy Dishonored 1 for backstory and to wait for a sale.
I'm playing on an ancient rig that suffered HEAVILY pre-patch, yet I sucked it up and played quite a bit anyway. It was rough. But I waited it out and now that the beta patch, which unbounds mouse sensitivity from your framerate, has been released the game is very playable and enjoyable... even on my dinosaur hardware the game runs well at Medium settings.
There are still some small hitches, but nothing out of the ordinary. So, how is the game itself?
Gameplay is an absolute blast no matter how you play (stealth, balls to the wall, lethal, non-lethal.) AI is significantly improved from the first game and the difficulty levels actually reflect the game's difficulty (unlike Dishonored 1.) They made it less of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play non-lethally (thankfully.) Karnaca is a welcome change from dreary Dunwall. Tons of crossover lore from the first game and its DLC packs; you'll have tons of "AHA!" moments. Story feels well-paced and impactful on the feels, making you actually want to murder people who suck and spare people who don't suck as much. Tons of atmosphere and flavor via lore books, audiographs, notes, characters, dynamic events and the like.
Overall, the game had a rough launch and was rightfully criticized for its short-comings; AAA games should be held to a higher standard than this. Luckily, they seem to actually care about what people are saying and are attempting to resolve things. Though they still have some work to do on optimization, the game is really very well crafted in almost every way. I totally recommend this to fans of the series (even at retail cost.) If you are unfamiliar with Dishonored then don't buy this; go buy the first game and its DLCs so you have some context coming into Dishonored 2 and can maybe catch it on sale.
