Rejoyice fellow Alien & Predatorian fans because this is the game we've all been waiting for!
With that out of the way time to review!
Alien Isolation is a game developed by Creative Assembly & Published by Sega (who publish all Alien & Predator related games.)
Alien Isolation focus on a story line more than any of the other Alien or Predator games that i've played to this day & that's not a great deal, but it's enough to know that where others have failed this one stands tall above all of them.
Alien Isolation focuses on a solid storyline and Survival Horror gameplay designed to keep you on edge and worried about everything that is lurking around the corner & every little blip on your portable Motion Tracker.
Although i have not 100% completed the Main Story of this game yet i am at Chapter 14 which is near enough to give a good review. Will update after i complete.
The story starts out as you Amanda Ripley daughter of Ellen Ripley from the Alien franchise movies, are told that your Mothers last known location has been discovered and that you've got a 1 way ticket to discovering the truth about her.
Of course you accept this and shortly after are on your way to the Space Station "Sevastipol" which is owned by Weylan Yutani's competator company Seegson Corporation which have not been doing very well compaired to Weylan Yutani and were in the process of decomissioning their station.
Before you arrive the♥♥♥♥♥♥has already hit the fan and guess what, you're stuck in the middle of it. An "Unknown Life Form" has been brought upon the station and has been wreaking havok on the unsuspecting crew and so you're in a race to survive as well as find out the truth behind your mothers disappearance.
Along the way you learn more and more about Seegson Coporation & what happened to Sevastipol but i'll leave this here and allow you to learn more if you decide to play.
The Gamplay of Alien Isolation is that of any Survival Horror game, ammo and provisions are very limited and scarce, you need to scavange for scrap and parts in order to create your tools which you use to Survive.
The first 2 hours or so of the game you're unarmed and rely soley on using the tools you create in order to distract or incapasitate the enemies you encounter, you only encounter Human foes in the first part of the game & because they are human they're smart and can easily detect you.
Later on about 1 and a half hours into the game you have your very first encounter with the "Unknown Life Form" and from this point onward things become a lot harder and require you to do a lot more Stealthing until you get your first weapon & even then this Alien is very difficult to outsmart.
During the course of your playthrough you find blueprints which you use to upgrade all the different tools you can create which make them deal larger radious damage or increase the effects of which they output of course parts are very scarce and hard to come by to keep creating these tools, but they're also more common than ammo.
After you find your first weapon you're encouraged to keep using the tools you create to distract rather than kill, but of course it is up to you at this point whether or not you feel you have enough ammo to take down the foes put in front of you.
After about 2 and a half hours of gameplay you're given the most vital tool you will find in the game "The Motion Tracker" but beware just because it's very useful doesn't mean it is 100% accurate or 100% fool proof because enemies in close proximity will hear the beeps & FOV is limited to about 90 degress infront of you & while your vision is focused on the Tracker it becomes increasingly hard to pay attention to your surroundings.
A new section for this review is going to go over the Enemies because they're a bit different than the average "Survival Horror" game.
Enemies in this game can be killed except for 1 of them but it can still be dispatched for a short time giving you time to hide or escape the area.
It can be very hard to determine who is a "Friend" & who is an "Enemy" in this game because there's really no differentiation in models or dialogue for the enemies except for when they detect you.
Standard survivors just like you or me just trying to get by, they're smart & generally won't attack you on sight but if you're complacent or don't listen to them will attack you. These enemies can be killed if you want to and only take a few bullets.
The Synthetic Humanoids in this game work as you would expect, very anomatronic and follow set paths but will stray off from said path if you're caught & are very hard to dispatch but are not impossible just tricky, they also become very annoying as they will chase you down unless you manage to hide.
The Alien is the only enemy which cannot be killed, it can be scared off by using Fire but it won't remain hidden for long, the Alien is smart and it learns from it's mistakes, it is very hard to track down but the Motion Tracker is the best and safest way to find out where it's coming from but plan your next move quickly because it's fast and hard to outsmart sometimes the Alien is even clever enough to hide and wait for someone to walk into it's trap.
Alien Isolation is the game that a large portion of the franchise lovers have been waiting for, it's true to the Alien series name & it brings the feeling that the movies did, alone & against an undefeatable & smart enemy that learns from its mistakes.
While a lot of the beginning of the game was very slow and took a while to get into & a bit later into the game after the Alien is "removed" from the picture for a while things become a bit easier you don't feel quite as on edge because there's nothing hunting you. However you still need to be careful because you can't just run & gun like in Colonial Marines, you need to be smart and save your resources as best you can.
I have been playing on Hard difficulty since i started & everything is a threat to you so there's no room for mistakes & the scarcity of save points makes all the mistakes you make mean something if you die there's no room for error and if you screw up then you'd better get ready to run or to redo the things you didn't get a chance to save.
The Graphics for this game are very VERY nice and it's atmosphere feels and looks like Alien should, there's a few minor things that i notices that could have been improved and thought about, Self Shadows for your character & a First Person body would have helped immersion, but i'm not going to fail it on that because i'm not a graphics freak.
Creative Assembly if you read my review please keep in mind for the future if you make any games, small even minor details like Self Shadows or First Person Bodies go a long way for immersion.
From me Alien isolation receives a solid 9/10 because it's so true to the franchise & it's everything i expected from a game centered around this wounderful series.
The game is very hard and it punishes you for making mistakes, it also requires you to be careful with resources & keeps you on edge (especially around the Alien).
The game makes me feel for the characters as well which makes me want to ensure that Amanda and the others survive rather than somebody who i have no connection with like faceless and nameless characters would.
Before i close i just want to say a few things:
I came into this game expecting the worst, so this review is very unbiased because of Colonial Marines.
I'd also like to thank Creative Assembly for finally removing that bad taste from my mouth and releasing a true Survival Horror experience that this franchise required!

I don't care what anyone says...this game is scary! When you first come into contract with the Xenomorph all you can say is aww sh*t. Do you enjoy quick time events for every encounter? Do you enjoy mini-games for every locked door and some objects? Do you love a feeling of boredom that makes you get angry because you are so bored? If you answered yes to any of these then Alien: Isolation is for you!
While graphicaly impressive that is the only positive thing it has for it, it is a bore fest of running down the same hallways to collect keycards to open doors, running back across the station to use a computer, or just running down empty areas with no enemies. Isolation is filled with things that should not exist such as, making you play areas while locking you into walk only mode across 10 - 20 minutes of nothing that should of been a cutscene, walking across a room after a loading screen to get another loading screen.
Did I mention you can craft? Well let's start there. Isolation is filled with items to collect to craft items, some of them are Medkits, Noise Makers, EMP Mine, and Smoke Bombs. Seems like quite the selection, yet you need some deadly enemies to use these and are the enemies deadly? No, in fact all the human enemies you encounter act as if it's against the rules of the game to engage you. Some Synthetic enemies can not be harmed by anything except all of your ammunition, and the Alien can not be harmed at all.
Now, what about that revolutionary Alien A.I.? Well it's anything but revolutionary, it is the most basic seeking A.I. there is. Once you observe it you will be able to know where it is going to go and what it is going to do and the best part, is you don't even need to hide in lockers from it, you can just crouch down and move behind objects. What about the human enemies? What can I say, it's the same as the Aliens.
Now the synthetic androids, you will encounter these more then humans and aliens combined! These guys are ruthless in a hunt and will follow you across entire levels, they take stupid amounts of ammunition to kill one and you can not hide from them, good thing about them is that they can only walk but that will not stop them in their hunt for you. Hm, maybe this should of been called "Android Invasion."
Now for the story. What story? You just read it in the store page description, and that's exactly what it is 12 pain staking hours to hear a brief recording and another 3 hours to get off the ship. Yes, Isolation is a mental strain across 15 - 20 hours of nothing but, collecting items to craft and evading enemies, and the reward you get? The worst ending in a video game. Maybe the DLC will be better and shorter, much much shorter.
It's not Colonial Marines.

I have mixed feelings towards this game.
On the one hand, it's a good game. As far as turn-based strategy games go, it is a good game. There are a lot of cool aspects to this game if you're a first timer. The conversations the soldiers have between themselves is a nice touch (although forced in my opinion). And the battle sequences are entertaining (to start off with).
However quite quickly you get over the the pointless frills of the game and you get into the grit of it. As a huge fan of this game since Rome: Total War I am absolutely livid with the progress. The Grand Campaign makes no sense to me. So many buildings have negative effects on your campaign (i guess to promote balance). Generals will fight two or three battles before they die of natural causes so you will never really develop a general into a scary♥♥♥♥♥mutha f***** (which used to be one of my favourite aspects of the game). There is no family tree (which is also one of the most annoying aspects of the game). And the inner faction conflicts make absolutely zero sense and have zero visible effects on the game. Medieval 2/Rome was still the best game Total War game to date, simply because everything was awesome in it and I never stopped dropping my jaw.
Anyway, because there is no neutral button I would have to say No, do not purchase this game.

Total Playtime: 60 Hours (Including control struggles, covenant farming, armour collection etc)
Score: 6 / 10
Recommended purchasing price: $15.99 or less
Dark Souls II: Prepare to Meh Edition
The third in From Software's series, Dark Souls II is unfortunately a turn for the worst from the previous Dark Souls. Despite an additional month to work on what they claimed was a game being designed for PC, there is hardly any major graphical differences and keyboard + mouse controls are an atrocity. Guard Breaking and Jump Attacks are nearly impossible to do, combined with the new "double click" half second delay on attacks this can end up leaving your character standing there instead of attacking, blocking or performing the correct attack. As you might imagine, this is completely unacceptable in a game whose core combat mechanics are designed around timing.
The world of Dark Souls II looks fantastic still. Locations are large and definitely lovely to look at. Unfortunately the weapons, armour sets, bosses and basic enemies are lackluster missing the creativity of those in it's predecessor. No longer is there the feeling of awe and enormity over bosses. Many follow the same attack patterns with only elemental damage being the real difference. No longer does the overpowering size, speed, design or lore leave an impression on the player.
Difficulty is less a manner of finding out timed patterns as overcoming mobs. In my opinion, it's a cheap way to try and bump up difficulty. Nevermind the fact there is a limit on enemy respawns now! That's right. Struggling through a boss? Let us remove the enemies for you and hold your hand walking up to the boss! Fifteen is the magic number for enemy respawns. I can only assume this was done to prevent soul farming but it's not like FromSoftware couldn't have kept the enemies in and dropped the soul drops to maintain difficulty.
PvP is something I havn't engaged in much personally. It's usually a 2 - 3 on one gangbang and generally not in your favour, especially in the Bellfreys. Servers are still up and down making connections and latency an issue still.
All in all, Dark Souls II has lost the luster that made the series great. It's still more Dark Souls, but not in a way you might have hoped for. Best to get it on sale.

In a world where death is an impermanent obstacle, what is the meaning of life? Dark Souls 2 does not pretend to answer these questions. Instead, it takes a much more nihilistic view. You would think that never being able to die would be amazing, but to the undead, it is not so. Pain, death, amnesia, and a loss of sanity plague these pseudo-immortal souls. Thus, many set out to find a cure to the curse of the undead. So, where does an undead seeking death go? Drangleic.
From the moment you set foot on this strange and forlorn land, you understand just how weak the flesh truly is. Your body is rotting away, clothed only in tattered rags. You are surrounded by kobolds, strange dog-like creatures, who seem to be eyeing you as their dinner, or perhaps breakfast? Looking to the sky, you see that this sect of the world seems to be caught in an endless embrace of twilight. Don't linger, too long; however, as the kobolds are nipping at your ankles.
Obviously, this is only the first minute or two of the game, but it quickly sets the tone of your adventure-to-be. Dark Souls 2 is not an RPG where everything goes your way. You will die over, and over, and over, and over again, hollowing you to the bone. But, each time you die, you learn to live a little longer. You press forward, learning the secrets of this ancient land through items and dialogue from travelers as hopeless as yourself. Some friend, some foe.
The combat is where Dark Souls 2 truly shines. It is not flashy, and it is not fast. It is slow, methodical, and oh-so satisfying. Defeating a worthy challenger is like climbing a mountain, and it leaves you seeking out more success.
You can talk about Dark Souls 2 for hours, but I'll wrap up my fantastical ramblings now. Dark Souls 2 is a satisfying and deep experience rivaled only by its predecessors. 10/10.

Back in 2012 when the mod came out the developers would not accept my money. Now they've made a standalone version, and the question is, do I still want to give them my money? Hell yes. Is this version worth it over the free mod version? Hell yes. The mod was worth my money, and this version even moreso. The amount of polish is on the level of Valve products. Even compared to the mod, this feels like an entirely new game. Recommended.

If Black Mesa still was a usual mod, I'd give it as many positive screams as possible, and would be running with it around screaming on every corner how awesome it is. Basically, at the time I more or less did it, when original mod came out. But this is not a mod. This is a game that's sold for a price. This is a PRODUCT. Even more so, this is now just another HD remake, like Homeworld Remastered, Majesty Gold HD or Silent Hill 2 HD. And I am evaluating it exactly this way.
Half Life - the original game - was nearly flawless in terms of level design. Environments were expressive, but never restrictive, all levels differed from one another, and the game was overall one whole innovation. But this is not 1998, it is 2015. How does this remake hold up?
Let's start with some positives. Environments are stunningly great. Details on all models and in all location are epic - you can see there was a lot of attention put into the game. Same goes to new models, like bullsquids, military guys, alien grunts, black ops, helicopters and so on. All areas look more or less realistic. Huge machinery is simply breathtakingly awesome.
All weapons are back as well, and they all are quite pleasant to use.
Story wise nothing has changed - it is the same old Half-Life with some lore-friendly elements added from Half-Life 2, like Dr. Vance and Dr, Kleiner.
Most of the levels follow the original with added level of details like additional doors to mimic open environments. Some areas changed though - especially Surface Tension level, which got a lot bigger, and On The Rail, getting MUCH smaller.
Music came out to be great and atmospheric, an actual improvement over original soundtrack, I must admit.
But what's bad? Level design and atmosphere - this is where problems start to pop up. For starters, some later levels were showing alien infestation spreading in the area - weird fungus, strange surfaces, odd looking formations; in this game there are THREE areas which at least resemble alien infested zones that were in the original, and they both seem soooo much out of place because the rest is absent.
In Half-Life there were areas where you needed to get help from guards and scientists - now there is only one area where you REQUIRE them. Also there is zero tension between Freeman and military now. Famous "Forget about Freeman!" line is now absolutely out of place - mostly thanks to super-cut On the Rail level, whic actually was built around the idea of marines hating Freeman even more then the aliens.
But the worst part is combat itself. It swings around from ridiculously easy (like vortigaunts fire, which can be avoided like there is none) to absurdly hard, as in case of helicopter fight on the cliff (made better in 0.2 patch, still annoying though). This comes from reworked enemy patterns, which were crafted with great care in the original, and seem pretty much random in Black Mesa.
Uber-detalisation I mentioned before, while improving visuals, harms level awareness, making some areas too obscure and hard to orient, which never was the case in Half-Life, and obviously will not be fixed at release.
Some things can be credited to Early Access state - like possibility to see into nothingness in some areas, camera often clipping through models, and even untriggered ladder in final area (before leaping to Xen).
As a mod, it would be a great experience for nostalgic players. But as a standalone game? It feels too amateur to be taken seriously, and I highly doubt it will get better a release point.
I can advise this to extreme fans who wish to experience nostalgia only; all the rest - grab original Half-Life, it's a much better option.
P.S. AI and animation bugs, as I hope, will be fixed in release version, so I don't put emphasis on it.

A truly amazing remake of Half-Life, which goes way beyond a simple graphical update. It is a completely new experience.
Old Half-Life players should play this because they get to explore Black Mesa again, except now the complex seems alive and the laboratories actually feel like laboratories. Instead of empty corridors, you have offices and NPCs.
This remake is also great to introduce new players to the Half-Life universe, because let's face it the original game is getting dated now. Nostalgia is enough for us, but I doubt younger players would get past the first guard's face.
Now we just have to wait for the Xen release. I just can't wait to try it.

+++PROS+++
The basic idea is wonderful. It's an open world city with customized characters pitting cops vs robbers for strategic operations and car chases.
This game is known for its vast customization. The Player Characters' bodies are customizable, tattoo-able, clothing customizable, cars customizable, theme songs, equipment, weapons.
The style of the non-player content is very attractive, a motion graphic setting a metropolis plagued by stylish punks; even the corporate executives are stylish.
If you're bored of killing, you can spend hours customizing or you can scrape some money up robbing places, catching robbers, stealing and returning cars. There are other things to do than missions.
It is not a pay to win game. Paying players will have some advantage, but it's really not a problem.
I'm going to go ahead and put the game's city in the Pros section. The cities do feel half alive. When I'm in the game, I feel like I'm in a city, not a backdrop of buildings, as I felt in Borderlands. There are plenty of stores, shops, apartments, places cities would need, and civilians walking around. The civilians are walking talking dolls that interact minimally, but it is just barely enough to make the city feel alive as I'm cruising in my car, looking at these "civilians." I do, however, wish the player contacts would interact with players more; they truly are cardboard cutouts, even with some of their dialogue.
---CONS---
The game runs horribly. I'm no tech wizard, and I do have an old laptop, but for a game of this age with this level of texture and model quality, it's odd that I'm lucky if I can get any steady 10-15 frame rate at all.
This game is not especially well designed for the strategic action that was intended.
The levels are not perfectly balanced. There are only two city districts to play missions in, the main content of the game. The mission objectives are often in siege points of cqc mazes, surrounded by vast open areas; the enemy can see you coming from any direction, especially if they know the game's spawn points and routes well, and even if you manage to close the distance, they'll be waiting for you with cqc weapons ready. There aren't a lot of ways to flush enemies out of a siege position, other than being high leveled and affording grenade launchers.
The game's action is fast; characters are pretty zippy, compared to real life anyway. So, like Counter-Strike, this game gives strong favor to physical skills, reflexes and aim. Strategy and brainpower can help greatly, but a player can more easily brute force their way and kill enemies from disadvantaged terrain than they could in Ghost Recon Phantoms or even TF2.
Cover is used in this game minimally, you're obviously better off behind cover than in the open, the game does not really encourage strong use of cover. Cover is generally only provided in those cluttered maze like cqc areas. On the street, there is no cover except for exploding cars that do not protect your feet. In cqc areas, cover is less used because the fights are dances between two players with fully exposed hitboxes. There are short time limits on the missions, so players cannot wait around too long, especially if a fast moving enemy is patrolling the area. Once you get into cover to face an enemy at range, there's not a lot you can do to leave cover, as there is not a web of cover to leapfrog to and you don't have a lot of grenades and you don't have time for the coordination required for suppressive fire.
Teamwork is needed, but not really emphasized. Because of the low team sizes, teams are better off splitting up to attack from multiple angles. Being so far away from each other, players tend to act on their own; the only way to coordinate a team adequately is with a microphone; there is nothing to rally players together. Players do not need each other as all players have just about the same abilities; this is not TF2, where classes have strengths and weaknesses and are rallied by a medic.
The matchmaking is horrid. The game sets up some pretty unfair matches. Part of this is due to the low population, which is no doubt thanks to the game's problems and lack of aid to new players. And as you climb the ladder in skill, you will eventually find yourself constantly losing against the players at the top of the ladder, who never lose; they are lethal at all distances with an assault rifle and have the money to spam missiles and grenade launchers if they want to.
You win some you lose some, but all these things add up for too many moments where you'll have to learn the humility to surrender, knowing there was nothing you could do. Or if you do finally kill the guy who has been killing you over and over again, it was because of the luck of the aim rather than you being smarter. You just keep throwing yourself like water at a stone.
The community is horrid.
There are a lot of cheaters.
The game is an MMO. MMO's must constantly release new content until they eventually die out. This game is in its old age and it's handled by a small team that cannot release new content as often as needed. Even if they did, it wouldn't fix the base problems of the game.

Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell is a game where you give people phobia of sweaty old men hiding in dark places.
You play as Sam Fisher, a formerly retired special operative of NSA's Third Echelon, a covert organization who's operatives can enact the “Fifth freedom” which basically means they can screw with people in other countries and get away with it.
The game starts in the DISTANT FUTURE OF 2004! The Georgian president is assassinated and billionaire Kombayn Nikoladze  takes power in a bloodless coup. And yes I did have to look up how to spell that name. But something fishy is going on and Third Echelon sends Michael Ironside's voice to find out what!
Splinter Cell is one of those stealth games that came out when stealth games were expected to be stealth games and not action games where you sneak every now and then. You have to keep track on three factors, darkness, sound, and space. If you move too fast or aren't in suitable shadows, then nearby guards will pick up that something is screwey.
Back in the day, Splinter Cell was being pushed against Metal Gear Solid for king of the genre, and by pushed I think Game Pro wouldn't shut up about it for months before getting bored and going on to...I don't know, Warcraft III, I guess. It's kind of an unfair comparison, though, since both series go about their core gameplay completely differently.
Since Splinter Cell is from 2002, it obviously has some of that old clunky game feel that game journalists seem to not be able to overcome. Like if a game doesn't play itself then it “didn't age well.”
This is why you shouldn't listen to game journalists, they are smelly idiots and I am cooler than them.
Splinter Cell expects a certain amount of competency from it's players. It shows you how to use everything you need in the tutorial level and then eases you into it with a pretty basic first level. Unlike later games in the series, Splinter Cell is rather straight forward and linear, making each room more like a stealth challenge than a stop on the way to your actual objective.
Going back and playing the original game now kind of makes it feel like a prototype to the next two games, all of the features are there but not as fine tuned as it would come to be in Pandora Tomorrow, or Chaos Theory. Everything works, don't get the wrong idea, it's still a solid experience, but it doesn't hold up to it's successors.
Still, Splinter Cell is a very charming game, you can tell a lot of love and attention to detail went into it when it was in development. Hey, check out this super neat lighting system on Unreal 2.0! Can you believe we're pulling this off on the PS2 as well? And look at our movable fabrics and objects, isn't that insane!
The characters in Splinter Cell were also something not common for the genre or even other Tom Clancy games at the time or in the future. They were all professional characters, but the banter and discussions between Sam and the others was something endearing and really sold you on them as human beings instead of just polygons and coding.
Sam, played by Michael Ironside, has this very distinct gravel to his voice, but instead of being a gruff, grr, “Whiskey Tango Foxtrot” kind of military guy, he's instead a wisecracking, charismatic older man with a sense of humor and a moral code. The banter between him and Irving Lambert, played by Don Jordan, are the highlights of the Splinter Cell story, even more so in later games.
So looking at the more recent games, it kind of hurts a little that they
but also completely cut out the fun and humorous segments between Sam and his crew in favor of being “Darker” and “Grittier”.
To be more specific it's lame and whoever thought those changes for later games is also lame.
EDIT: Oh yeah, I forgot to mention that you can control your movement speed with the mouse wheel. I mean, how cool is that? Why don't more games do that? That's ingenious.
It's still holds up, it's nowhere near as good as Pandora Tomorrow or the masterpiece that is Chaos Theory, but you can see all of the framing and build up in this game that eventually made those two pillars of the genre they are today. If you like the series but somehow haven't played the original, you should probably give it a shot.
Also, there's a glitch in the second level I found that makes it unbeatable unless you restart or cheat. It was nothing that soured me to the experience, I just thought I should let you know.

The class system is somewhat like in Dream of Mirror Online (DOMO) where you can play and level every class on one and the same character, even unlocking some skills to be usable with any class, which is great.

This game is truly challenging commended for mmorpg players :)

Although only 4.6 hours clocked I did play this during the closed beta, and found it alright at the time.
Back then it was on a bad PC that didnt run games very well, but even so it ran alright, and now with my new PC it runs great most of the time. Ive seen people talk about frame drops and even on ultra everything I dont get that problem, but then again I do have a lot of money in this rig.
So where to begin... I love the art style, did from the start and still do. It's just pleasant to look at all in all. Also the game is quite large. You have an overworld of sorts, and then you have the areas in that overworld which all have a good size to them. Also there's lots to do, from side quests to hidden quests to main quests. Lots of quests really, oh and dungeons, but you never really need to stop and grind as doing these keeps you up with the level and gear standard of that point in the game. The classes are all seen and heard of before your tank your healer etc etc, however you can switch between all of the classes you've unlocked at any time meaning you can find a play style that suits you (and it's the only time you really need to grind as unlocking new classes means levelling them up from 1 again). Also you get a terracottage, which is literally a big turtle house that walks around the overworld for faster travel.
Combat itself is, not gonna lie, pretty dull. It's your standard press buttons that aren't on cooldown, however there isnt NO strategy as skills interact with each other like "casting this within 3 seconds of that casts Z as well". Also while we're on the negative train, the overworld isnt all that exciting unless you're into the whole professions thing. You can fish, forage, alchemise? There are little stories to do in the overworld but often dont reward much except for either lore or comedic pieces that are hit and miss.
There is an in game micro transaction store that you can use but it is cosmetic stuff and mounts all your standard stuff. You can grind up loyalty points instead for use in the loyalty shop. Everything in said shop just costs way more LP than your regular special currency but it is free so if you want that mount or whatever you can get it.
All in all during the beta I enjoyed it and I still enjoy it now. Still am yet to make it to the end game content so ill be happy to update this and see how the game holds out later on, but for now im recommending.
TLDR
+Great art style, big world, deep(ish) lore, good customizability for how/what you want to play, Terracottage.
- Dull at times (mostly combat), tries to be funny and sometimes fails, nothing much that hasnt been seen before.

Before I get started: Dishonored 2 is a direct continuation of #1. If you didn't play Dishonored 1, I'd say you're missing out on one of gaming's greatest experiences and you should go play that before starting this one. Assuming you have played #1....
Dishonored 2 is a beautiful, multilayered stealth / action game with multiple paths to every mission and a fairly comprehensive story and cast of characters to back it up. It's kind of what you'd get if you took Thief 2 and aged it up to more modern sensibilities. Where Thief 2 was slow and methodical, Dishonored excels at fast-paced stealth and subterfuge. The magical abilities each character unlocks help broaden the already wide net of possible ways to approach missions and individual encounters.
The art is fantastic -- everything is stylized and beautiful, with most textures feeling hand-painted rather than photogrammetry-driven. The characters are interesting and... my god, the amount of incidental dialogue you can encounter by sneaking or using items is truly jaw-dropping. There are so many pieces of written plot, snippets of overheard conversation and background information you can pick up that the world feels much, much more well-defined than most games that are much more RPG-ish. The action is great, the world is coherent and the game feels more like a comprehensive world than any I can remember in recent times.
That being said, the game's performance is bad. It's absolutely bad. It's not GAME DESTROYING bad, despite what other Steam reviews might lead you to think, but it's not great. Especially considering that idTech 5 is designed to hit 60fps at all times -- it's quite bizarre that this game runs so poorly. I remain convinced that it's going to get fixed, but it's a shame that it doesn't run well right now. And it's totally unknown as to when it will be fixed.
Basically I think this review comes down to one thing: Do you want to support story-driven, complex stealth / action games that are clearly made with love and devotion but run poorly, or do you want to support Call of Battlefield 9 that runs fantastically but is crapped out every year on some aging engine by committee? Because that's what purchasing this game is about. The game is awesome -- it really, really is. It runs badly. That's true too. You can decide how much those matter to you.

This game is really great, I put my hours into it and it was all worth it. I met many new friends because of this game.
At first, the game is terribly difficult to play but once you put couple of hours and learning game mechanics, you'll be doing pretty well in this game. The amount of zombies/walkers/runners/zombie kids/crawlers are huge but they can be outplayed by you easily once you get the feel of the game. There are moderate amounts of weapons and almost all of them are unique, with their own charging time (melee weapons), reload time, damage, rate of fire, weight, etc. Some of the weapons also have special abilities. For example, if you stand still while aiming a pistol for a few seconds, you can get damage boost. There is also stamina in the game, which adds a little bit of realistic touch.
The drawbacks of this game, which can be a little frustating are that hit registration is not well polished, sometimes you hit a zombie and see it flinched but then you realized you did no damage at all. Bugs and glitches may happen every once in a while. However, since the game is made an indie dev team, I forgive them.
So, for players who want some hardcore F2P zombie game, this is a solid selection.

If Black Mesa still was a usual mod, I'd give it as many positive screams as possible, and would be running with it around screaming on every corner how awesome it is. Basically, at the time I more or less did it, when original mod came out. But this is not a mod. This is a game that's sold for a price. This is a PRODUCT. Even more so, this is now just another HD remake, like Homeworld Remastered, Majesty Gold HD or Silent Hill 2 HD. And I am evaluating it exactly this way.
Half Life - the original game - was nearly flawless in terms of level design. Environments were expressive, but never restrictive, all levels differed from one another, and the game was overall one whole innovation. But this is not 1998, it is 2015. How does this remake hold up?
Let's start with some positives. Environments are stunningly great. Details on all models and in all location are epic - you can see there was a lot of attention put into the game. Same goes to new models, like bullsquids, military guys, alien grunts, black ops, helicopters and so on. All areas look more or less realistic. Huge machinery is simply breathtakingly awesome.
All weapons are back as well, and they all are quite pleasant to use.
Story wise nothing has changed - it is the same old Half-Life with some lore-friendly elements added from Half-Life 2, like Dr. Vance and Dr, Kleiner.
Most of the levels follow the original with added level of details like additional doors to mimic open environments. Some areas changed though - especially Surface Tension level, which got a lot bigger, and On The Rail, getting MUCH smaller.
Music came out to be great and atmospheric, an actual improvement over original soundtrack, I must admit.
But what's bad? Level design and atmosphere - this is where problems start to pop up. For starters, some later levels were showing alien infestation spreading in the area - weird fungus, strange surfaces, odd looking formations; in this game there are THREE areas which at least resemble alien infested zones that were in the original, and they both seem soooo much out of place because the rest is absent.
In Half-Life there were areas where you needed to get help from guards and scientists - now there is only one area where you REQUIRE them. Also there is zero tension between Freeman and military now. Famous "Forget about Freeman!" line is now absolutely out of place - mostly thanks to super-cut On the Rail level, whic actually was built around the idea of marines hating Freeman even more then the aliens.
But the worst part is combat itself. It swings around from ridiculously easy (like vortigaunts fire, which can be avoided like there is none) to absurdly hard, as in case of helicopter fight on the cliff (made better in 0.2 patch, still annoying though). This comes from reworked enemy patterns, which were crafted with great care in the original, and seem pretty much random in Black Mesa.
Uber-detalisation I mentioned before, while improving visuals, harms level awareness, making some areas too obscure and hard to orient, which never was the case in Half-Life, and obviously will not be fixed at release.
Some things can be credited to Early Access state - like possibility to see into nothingness in some areas, camera often clipping through models, and even untriggered ladder in final area (before leaping to Xen).
As a mod, it would be a great experience for nostalgic players. But as a standalone game? It feels too amateur to be taken seriously, and I highly doubt it will get better a release point.
I can advise this to extreme fans who wish to experience nostalgia only; all the rest - grab original Half-Life, it's a much better option.
P.S. AI and animation bugs, as I hope, will be fixed in release version, so I don't put emphasis on it.

Grab its attention, bypass and be home free. I shoot, I hide in a locker. The alien climbs out of the vent closest to me (by the way the animations are so god damn nice its borderline life like) and I stay there for 10 minutes crying because I can't hear it anymore but I know its close. So I decide to get out where I fumble with the reload, start putting the rounds into the cylinder of the pistol when I hear this huge thud behind me and its hiss, not even a meter away from me. I stay still for like 10 seconds when I slowly turn around and then it pounced. Creating this truly terrifying animation where I had to pause the game and revert save as it was too much. This is the first game to have ever made me feel this scared in all of my life and has truly set the bar for new horror games.
CA have made a beautiful organism which it truly deserved, as said before, it could have just pounced and got it over with. But instead, it knew it had me, so it was basically just toying with its food. That's what really scared me. The fact that in the 10 seconds I was just praying for it to get it over with, it didn't. It just decided for me to either run or to turn to look at it. CA have made this creature have a fantastic AI which is fantastic
The game just oozes atmosphere. You don't even see the Alien for 2 levels. Its only till the end of the 2nd mid 3rd you actually see it. But I was still jumping at every hissing pipe, vent noises. Anything which could have been the alien.
Bottom line is. This game is truly a great example of what gaming can make you feel. CA have done a brilliant job and this is what should have been made first. Not Aliens: CM

A failed uptopia, from its citizens to its infrastructure.
I love this game, and I may sometimes hop on, but I cannot in good conscience honestly recommend it.
+++PROS+++
The basic idea is wonderful. It's an open world city with customized characters pitting cops vs robbers for strategic operations and car chases.
This game is known for its vast customization. The Player Characters' bodies are customizable, tattoo-able, clothing customizable, cars customizable, theme songs, equipment, weapons.
The style of the non-player content is very attractive, a motion graphic setting a metropolis plagued by stylish punks; even the corporate executives are stylish.
If you're bored of killing, you can spend hours customizing or you can scrape some money up robbing places, catching robbers, stealing and returning cars. There are other things to do than missions.
It is not a pay to win game. Paying players will have some advantage, but it's really not a problem.
I'm going to go ahead and put the game's city in the Pros section. The cities do feel half alive. When I'm in the game, I feel like I'm in a city, not a backdrop of buildings, as I felt in Borderlands. There are plenty of stores, shops, apartments, places cities would need, and civilians walking around. The civilians are walking talking dolls that interact minimally, but it is just barely enough to make the city feel alive as I'm cruising in my car, looking at these "civilians." I do, however, wish the player contacts would interact with players more; they truly are cardboard cutouts, even with some of their dialogue.
---CONS---
The game runs horribly. I'm no tech wizard, and I do have an old laptop, but for a game of this age with this level of texture and model quality, it's odd that I'm lucky if I can get any steady 10-15 frame rate at all.
This game is not especially well designed for the strategic action that was intended.
The levels are not perfectly balanced. There are only two city districts to play missions in, the main content of the game. The mission objectives are often in siege points of cqc mazes, surrounded by vast open areas; the enemy can see you coming from any direction, especially if they know the game's spawn points and routes well, and even if you manage to close the distance, they'll be waiting for you with cqc weapons ready. There aren't a lot of ways to flush enemies out of a siege position, other than being high leveled and affording grenade launchers.
The game's action is fast; characters are pretty zippy, compared to real life anyway. So, like Counter-Strike, this game gives strong favor to physical skills, reflexes and aim. Strategy and brainpower can help greatly, but a player can more easily brute force their way and kill enemies from disadvantaged terrain than they could in Ghost Recon Phantoms or even TF2.
Cover is used in this game minimally, you're obviously better off behind cover than in the open, the game does not really encourage strong use of cover. Cover is generally only provided in those cluttered maze like cqc areas. On the street, there is no cover except for exploding cars that do not protect your feet. In cqc areas, cover is less used because the fights are dances between two players with fully exposed hitboxes. There are short time limits on the missions, so players cannot wait around too long, especially if a fast moving enemy is patrolling the area. Once you get into cover to face an enemy at range, there's not a lot you can do to leave cover, as there is not a web of cover to leapfrog to and you don't have a lot of grenades and you don't have time for the coordination required for suppressive fire.
Teamwork is needed, but not really emphasized. Because of the low team sizes, teams are better off splitting up to attack from multiple angles. Being so far away from each other, players tend to act on their own; the only way to coordinate a team adequately is with a microphone; there is nothing to rally players together. Players do not need each other as all players have just about the same abilities; this is not TF2, where classes have strengths and weaknesses and are rallied by a medic.
The matchmaking is horrid. The game sets up some pretty unfair matches. Part of this is due to the low population, which is no doubt thanks to the game's problems and lack of aid to new players. And as you climb the ladder in skill, you will eventually find yourself constantly losing against the players at the top of the ladder, who never lose; they are lethal at all distances with an assault rifle and have the money to spam missiles and grenade launchers if they want to.
You win some you lose some, but all these things add up for too many moments where you'll have to learn the humility to surrender, knowing there was nothing you could do. Or if you do finally kill the guy who has been killing you over and over again, it was because of the luck of the aim rather than you being smarter. How about the weapons then?, you ask.
Well, yes these weapons deal more damage. But that's at the cost of firerate, weapon magazines or the most important one: accuracy. See, in APB reloaded it's more important that you are accurate than that you deal a lot of damage.
You can have a weapon with OVA NEIN TAUSAAHND damage, if you can't hit a thing it's worthless.
Also i have to make a note of the grat costomization. It's awesome. You can spray your own cars and design your own clothes. The bad thing is that a lot of this awesome customization is locked behind their "premium" subscription.

A mix of different mini games.  Most focused around clicking each second and trying to have perfect timing.  The two games that are slightly different are:
- A pig jumping over a circling second hand, different in the sense that you get the visual clues as to when to jump not just knowing how long the second is.
- A pig being chased by giant cogs with a letter marked on them Q,W,O,P and having to push the right letter to turn the cog and not hit the pig.
I actually enjoyed the two pig-themed games the best, and I hope the developer can add some more like those.
In regards to the second-timing games - I would like them a lot more if there was some sort of indication whether you had clicked a bit too slow or a bit too fast.  The essence of games is learning from your mistakes and getting better, but it's hard to learn when you aren't sure what your mistake was (too fast or too slow).  So rather than just flashing red when it's not close enough I would like to suggest it flashes red for too fast, and orange for too slow.

So, having been a veteran player of the souls series, both Demon Souls and the original Dark Souls I have to say I'm pleasantly surprised overall with Dark Souls II, and here is my brief summary for people interested in potentially buying:
Pros:
- Continued familiar and varied iconic Souls series locations, equipment, combat and lore
- Many returning pieces of gear from the original Dark Souls game
- Quite a large amount of consumable content, at least on par with the previous two if not a tad more
- End game has been fleshed out a lot more for those seeking to extract as much long term play out of it as possible. Items like Bonfire Ascetic make the game so much more challenging (An item that you use on bonfires to increase the difficulty of the location).
- Fluid combat much more reminiscent of Demon Souls (This is good or bad depending on your outlook!)
Cons:
- PvP is a pile of excrement: They've done away with SL, and replaced it with something called "Soul Memory", this in theory was a great idea as it stops low level griefing. Unfortunately at top end playing it is completely ruined. I shalln't go into the finer details of why, but if you want to read more there are plenty of discussions about it on various forums, suffice to say that people who want to cap their level and play with skill are no longer equally matched due to the fact that everytime they kill someone in pvp the souls they receive increase their soul memory, this in part forces them to level up if they want to remain competitive, this unquestionably ruins pvp since you get people, eventually, with maxed out skill points who just WTFpwn your face with little to no chance of you even being able to get a scratch on them. Anyway, stay away from PvP until they patch it (If they patch it). /rant
- The game is still quite glitchy in places, not horrific, but a pain nonetheless.
- No Solaire of Astoria (Booo!), at least they still have the "Praise the Sun" gesture though!
Overall, this game is still amazing and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good challenge and some amazing boss encounters and story lore.

Game isn't bad, but isn't good. There are many downsides to counter the upsides, so unless if you really want to kill some time on a game that doesn't have all too many people online at any given moment (maybe 500-700 at very most across the 7 servers), then this is a game for you
I'm not bashing it, I just feel this game wouldn't go too well with somebody who considers themselves a pro gamer, and it wouldn't go well with a casual, just somewhere between where you have time to kill on games, but you aren't a pro, but you don't just play it off and on.
A major issue I have is that unless if you have a friend before joining the game, it's really awkward to make any in-game simply because of the low playerbase at any given time, that even if you find that rare encounter with another player in the vass overworld or zones where the quests take place in, the two of you are too shy to talk to each other, one is ignoring chat and doesn't notice that you're trying to talk to them, the other person is too shy to accept your party invite so they just put it off to the side until it times out naturally, or the biggest issue with making friends, the level difference. Sometimes it's something small like level 39 and level 46, but because that level 46 person is 7 levels ahead, they're farther into the main storyline quests than the level 39. This follows another issue I have with this game, the exp. Unless if you do quests, it's nearly impossible to level up with only mobs. While with no exp bonuses, a normal player at around level 20+ gains ~0.2% or less exp per kill. that means that if you want to level up once, you have to kill mobs 5000 times to level up. Now maybe other games are this bad and people still grind it, but this game does a bad favor by giving too much exp in the quests, and having the exp to level up rise expedentially so mob exp can't keep up. If you try to level up 2 jobs at the same time, you end up having both fall behind and you start to notice a difference between your character level and your job levels. This isn't too much of an issue, but simply because of how the exp system rises like such, and how mob exp doesn't do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥for your character, once you run out of quests to do, it's simply doing daily quests and running dungeons that give you 7% exp at most for 10-25 minutes of button mashing.

Choose your own adventure games are usually fun because you get to explore the author's mind.  You find out what makes sense to the author between decisions and consequences as well as how the author likes to describe the setting to suggest that certain decisions are feasible.  You also find out what sorts of traps the author likes to set in order to entice you to veer off track.
This game doesn't really work like that.  A lot of the dialogue is very simple and bland.  There isn't much to describe, and some of the decisions you make are disregarded.  For example,
.
I'm guessing the Furiosa achievement's broken as well.
The plot is kind of ordinary as well.  While it's nice to see how it takes place in a dream and is dynamically communicated between yourself and a friend, there really isn't anything more typical than a
.
Furthermore, the game doesn't have clear indicators on when or how to use items in your bag.  In fact, you might not even have an inclination to use them at all since it's a text-based game.  You'd expect the game to either automatically use them, or to unlock options from items carried along, but it doesn't work like that.
On top of that, the game mostly boils down to trial and error experimentation.  You design a character with attribute points, and figure out how much you need to overcome obstacles.  There's no real predictable rhyme or reason to figuring out how much you need in advance.
The game's free, but honestly, it's best to play this as an example of how programming software can be used to make a game.  You shouldn't spend your time playing this as a form of entertainment.

A brilliant reimagining of a timeless classic. If you've never played the half life series before but are turned off by the dated-ness this is a great way to get the same experience with a more modern feeling. It stays true to the original but it's also not a carbon copy.
For those of you who are familiar, this is not just a fresh coat of paint or some HD textures. It's the entire game redesigned and remastered. The levels and puzzles will be familiar, but the entire thing feels different; it's a totally new experience and  absolutely worth playing.
Now for the thing on everyone's mind: is it worth $20? As a standalone product, absolutely. It delivers enough content with the quality to justify that price tag.
The point of contention here is that the game was released earlier as a free mod. I haven't played much of the mod, but the money and valve's support here seems to have been used to take the mod a bit beyond what it could achieve as a mod alone - full use of the latest source engine, a multiplayer mode with steam workshop integration for maps, graphics and sound improved even further, gameplay stability improved greatly (I haven't encountered a single bug or glitch on my playthrough).
Certainly, this is an improved experience from the mod and not just the same thing with a price tag slapped on. I'm given to understand the devs have kept the mod release (now legacy version) available for free so it's up to you to decide whether $20 is a worthy asking price.

Is it some kind of rule that stealth games never get it right on the first try? Hitman and Splinter Cell are both venerable classics of the genre and their first entries both frustrate me to no end. While I eventually concluded that I just don't like the Assassin's Creed franchise at all, most people will agree it didn't really hit its stride until Ezio showed up. And as much as I want to love Thief: The Dark Project as much as I love The Metal Age, its controls needed some polish and the level design was frankly way below its sequel's quality.
In Splinter Cell's case, it was a few mild but persistent irritations that eventually killed any interest I had in playing through it just for completeness' sake. The controls are clunky and simple tasks like disengaging from a ladder are somehow more complicated than Tomb Raider's tank controls. The levels are totally linear and feel less like locations and more like obstacle courses, and it can be almost impossible to differentiate between a scripted incident and a tactical failure at first glance. And Sam Fisher is the worst marksman I have ever seen in a videogame, taking a dozen shots to hit targets most people could make with a sufficiently vigorous loogie.
I'm going to hold out hope that Chaos Theory is a substantial improvement, as the common sentiment seems to rank it among the best stealth games of all time, but this first try I'm done with.

Alien: Isolation has the virtue of following Aliens: Colonial Marines - so in one sense, expectations are pretty low to begin with, however the preview footage and articles suggest a finer experience which has done much to give fans of the franchise good reasons to have cause for hope.
And in many ways, it is a vastly superior effort.  The attention to art design and sound is second to none.  The Sevastopol - the arena in which the narrative plays out - provides multiple opportunities for the player to discover expositional background which fleshes out the events prior to the player's arrival.
Unfortunately, and yes, I'm afraid this is the rub - the experience is ruined by what is some truly excruciatingly poor game design and some truly dire AI.
The problem is the way in which Creative Assembly has decided the alien isn't just a formidable killing machine - it's also psychic and tracks the player throughout a vast complex with the single-minded dedication of the shark from Jaws 4: The Revenge.
This has the net effect of turning what could be a tense game of cat and mouse into a frustrating, annoying wait for the alien killing machine to go away.  Which it never does.  Ever.
This - on its own - is a gameplay killer, but the developer's insistence on disempowering the player to the point of lunacy completely removes any incentive to progress.
Let's count up the ways in which the alien has the advantage over the player:
1)  Fast - much faster than the player when they're running.
2)  Any attempt to run gives the Alien a lock on your location.  See point 1 - "Fast"
3)  Invincible - the Alien cannot be killed or injured
4)  Alien rubber bands inside a 40 foot radius from the player - it never leaves unless scripted to do so.
5)  Hyper senses mean it can spot you when humans and androids cannot
6)  Traverses through vents in the ceilings which the player cannot
7)  Any attempt by the player to use vents results in broadcasting a ping to the Alien which then investigates the vents.

Oh, and the best bit.
8)  Line of sight killer - if it sees you, you're dead.
The player's advantages:
A) Motion tracker with an extremely limited range.
B) You can hide in floor vents which the alien doesn't appear to have worked out.
Alien: Isolation is a victim of exceptionally lazy game design.  Creative Assembly were so focused on terrifying the player, that they forgot to give the player the means to survive effectively.  Far too much of the player's progress is dependent upon luck or sheer dogged persistence in the face of highly random events.  The player spends far too much time listening to the motion tracker and has no opportunity whatsoever to engage with the world.  It's a tragic mis-step which completely undermines all the creative effort which has gone into the rest of the game.
The worst part is that this game has such potential.  It serves as an object lesson in the absolute necessity for someone who understands game design to participate in the process.
Gameplay is a cascade of feedback loops.  The primary loops are:
1)  Moment to moment gameplay.  This is the primary loop which comprises the player action/feedback cycle which powers most of the game.  In Alien: Isolation this is limited to watching/listening to the motion tracker and diving under tables or into lockers.  It absolutely CRIPPLES the gameplay experience.
2)  Short term strategising - Typically this is scenario-based planning which allows the player to size up a situation and construct a strategy to deal with the scenario.  The reward feedback is a more effective and easier execution of the primary loop in response to their planning.
Alien: Isolation allows none of this.  No strategising is available because the only game loop is the "run and hide" cycle.
3)  Medium term resource planning - This is where players make medium-term decisions in regard to the allocation of resources.  Typically it's choosing abilities, powers or artifacts which allow the player more options to influence the world.  Strategy involves delaying expenditure to "save up" for more powerful abilities or artefacts.
Alien: Isolation makes a vague attempt at doing this with the ability to construct artefacts but the strategic imperatives for each artefact hark back the run and hide cycle and do little to enable the player's strategic choices.
Ultimately, this is a wonderfully realised world with incredibly disappointing gameplay which cripples the experience.
Not recommended.

Greetings everyone who decides to read this Review of APB.
I'm an EX-player of APB:R after an insane amount of time and felt it was a duty to help give some advice on this game.
**NOTE: I'VE HAD AN APB ACCOUNT PREVIOUS TO THE CREATION OF MY STEAM ACCOUNT.**
The world of APB:R is immense in the sense of how whacky and fun it can be. You'll encounter strange occurances with objects (cars in this instance) interacting stupidly with other objects and it's all a joy. I've sincerely have had a lot of fun with this game. Oh! One more thing, the entire concept of APB:R being "Pay to Win" is a complex haox from everything I've encountered in my 4 year run with APB.
How is it not Pay to Win?
Simple. All "ARMAS" weapons you'll see in the game are typically re-skins or variations of the same weapon you can achieve with normal gameplay and progression.
Example: Joker CR Rifle is the exact same as the N-TEC and VARS-SWORD.
Many of these guns just are bought for their advantages due to their pre-set modifications which even then an ordinary player can obtain after playing for a bit of time.
The Customization is ABSOLUTELY FANTASTIC, I've never had such a creative outlet in my life previous to APB:R. Making a fresh and beautiful designed IO: GROWL, or FireHawk Vegas or whatever car of your pleasing is one of the best things you can do in APB:R. Show it off to your fellow faction-mates and even those on the opposing side! Make your own death-theme for your victims to listen so that they know it was YOU who ended their misery. Customize your clothing, get creative with tattoos! Enjoy an environment that's not restricted to just PRE-SET PRE-DESIGNED decals like most games would have.
Wait! This review is NOT recommending this game why?
Over the last couple of weeks, something has been happening. Something that has been triggering/messing with player-base. The ANTI-CHEAT SYSTEM: FAIRFIGHT, in addition to the formerly used PUNKBUSTER, has been flagging players, both cheaters and non-cheaters, and respectfully banning the player in question.
Isn't that a good thing?
Well, I'd suppose it would be a good thing that the anti-cheat system is actually banning people and actively detecting the use of horrid third-party programs and the lot, but, what about those who were non-cheaters?
I'm one of those players.
I'm formerly known as the criminal: xShadowscythe.
A few days ago, I logged into the game I've loved for so long, entered a match, and as I was driving to my next destination BANNED.
Oh? Banned? You could just open a ticket to GamersFirst, maybe they'll help you out?
NOT AT ALL.
Although the game is fantastic and such, the company that hosts the game is unwilling to clarify/justify/assist any of it's players with any information regarding to why they were banned.
Upon sending an email to the support staff, I've been handed an automated letter and have not been given any insight onto why I was banned from the game other than "Someone has been conducting suspicious activity that violates our Terms of Service." Upon a request for clarification or for a reason I was promptly sent away and denied with yet another automated message.
For those who have read this review and thinking of still playing APB:R
I sincerely hope you give the game a shot and help in it's resurrection, but please be aware of the corruption and malfunctioning system in place as of OCTOBER 31ST, 2016.
I sincerely hope you all have a good time in the game and will leave this review with one final piece of advice.
Please DO NOT spend any money on the game for a good amount of time.
Please take time to talk to other players, preferably veterans, about the status of the game, the recent banning issues and how GamersFirst communicates with it's players.
Love,
xShadowscythe.

I've tried DOTA, and it wasn't the MOBA for me. The constant overhead view and indirect control over your main unit just never felt truly inclusive or a fun experience. Literally, the reason I love Smite is simply the third person view. Given this viewpoint you have complete control over every single step or attack your god makes, and literally the only possible thing that can be blamed for a mistake is yourself. Sure the overhead MOBA can say the same thing, but for me the very fact that you cannot see the perspectiveof the battlefield from your character's POV (or as close to it as possible with 3rd person POV) makes that argument so much more lacking. I feel that the overhead MOBA is more about clicking than actual gameplay. What's the difference? I've felt that timing, the short and long games, and particularly variations in play style are all better executed through Smite than other MOBAs. DOTA and League are much closer to the RTS genre in gameplay style, which is a genre that I actually like, but I feel the mesh of a MOBA with RTS isn't well executed. Smite offers that extra immersion from just changing the camera angle and direct controlling how and when your character moves and attacks in a way better executed than the simple clicking on a screen. Smite is extremely well designed, love the idea of incorporating gods and goddeses into a free-for-all combat game (adding even more to the game's likability compared to randomly created characters that are cool but don't really have a backstory), and is honestly very immersive for the short bouts of gameplay that exist in a MOBA.

A brilliant reimagining of a timeless classic. If you've never played the half life series before but are turned off by the dated-ness this is a great way to get the same experience with a more modern feeling. It stays true to the original but it's also not a carbon copy.
For those of you who are familiar, this is not just a fresh coat of paint or some HD textures. It's the entire game redesigned and remastered. The levels and puzzles will be familiar, but the entire thing feels different; it's a totally new experience and  absolutely worth playing.
Now for the thing on everyone's mind: is it worth $20? As a standalone product, absolutely. It delivers enough content with the quality to justify that price tag.
The point of contention here is that the game was released earlier as a free mod. I haven't played much of the mod, but the money and valve's support here seems to have been used to take the mod a bit beyond what it could achieve as a mod alone - full use of the latest source engine, a multiplayer mode with steam workshop integration for maps, graphics and sound improved even further, gameplay stability improved greatly (I haven't encountered a single bug or glitch on my playthrough).
Certainly, this is an improved experience from the mod and not just the same thing with a price tag slapped on. I'm given to understand the devs have kept the mod release (now legacy version) available for free so it's up to you to decide whether $20 is a worthy asking price.

Twin Saga gets a thumbs down from me due to one element. The translator. This is a fantasy anime game designed for kids & Teens and yet the translator goes out of their way to either insert terminology that not even a tenured professor would use in a conversation without good reason or saturate the story with enough jokes and puns to make Disney balk. Here are some examples:
"Croaking crocs wasn't exactly what you saw yourself doing this afternoon, but saving a few innocent lives might snag you some much needed Karma for future feats of peril. You nod your head with zealous affirmation--time to see ya later some alligators!" (*cringe* So not punny)
"Maybe you really ARE  destined to be this 'chosen one' she's talking about. Who knows! But you'll certainly regret throwing in the towel and not giving it the ol' college try." (The ol' college try... This. From a woodland's elf mixing roots and eating berries in the woods. *cringe*)
"With the answers to your many questions finally in front of you, questions begin spewing from your mouth like feculence from a sewage pipe." (Feculence... term is so rarely, if ever, used, steam is trying to auto-correct it because it doesn't believe it's a real word.
"Congratulations! It's a girl! And to think you hadn't even been showing. What sort of pre-pubescent legerdemain IS this?!" (Legerdemain... had to google this one. I didn't even know this was a word. Seems It's a overly pretentious way to simply say cunning. Dat thesaurus yo.)
"Time to send these ghoulish gadabouts back into the darkness from whence they came..." (gadabouts... sweet heavens. more rare thesaurus speak. Ghoulish must've really been lonely.)
"You make your way to see what all the kerfuffle is about." (Kerfuffle... Rings with a slight familiarity. I think I heard some old grannies use this term once when I was about seven.)
"I'll need you to sacrifice your body to take out as many of these splenetic specters as humanly possible." (Splenetic... another holier-than-thou term for ticked off. But it chimes in nicely with specters so confusion & pretentiousness be damned.)
Sekhmet's love corner
"The glimmer of trepidation in Sekhmet's glossy pupils metamorphoses into a glimmer of hope." (Glossy pupils? Sorry, not a bl fan. And ya know, could've just used 'turned into' in place of the pretentious metamorphoses.)
"Sekhmet's pileous brows curl and uncurl in thought." (Good to know? Wait, why do I need to know that they're 'pileous'? Another rare term that steam doesn't think exist.)
"Sekhmet turns to each of you in turn, so swiftly, at times, that his rapidly flailing scarlet thatch could simultaneously generate enough electricity to power a small light bulb as well as put out the flames of a burning building." (Right Right, Sekh has nice hair. Gotcha. But remember this is a anime fantasy story, not your sleazy romance paperback. So kindly change ya undies and get back to or rather start translating the story.)
"Sekhmet lets out an equally as cacophonous squawk of his own, thrusting his sword into the wraith's soft body with a forceful lunge." (*cough* *fans self* Lady, penthouse is dat way ->)

K nuff of dat. Point is translation is a pretentious word salad heavily drenched in unnecessary jokes, puns and in-depth descriptions of characters body language. This is not and I repeat NOT the fault of the developer. They did the right thing overall in not trying to translate it themselves and instead hiring a native English speaker, but they simply had the bad luck of hiring a pretentious wannabe comedian tard. The cinematics and untranslated dialogue give off a more serious tone to the story with light sprinkles of humor, which is why I tried to keep trudging forward in spite of the off the wall translation. Like the Elf mentioned earlier is the kind soft spoken caring archetype when speaking in the cinematic, in opposition of the backwater rancher the liberal translator portrays her as in the text. However, after needing an asprin to keep going, I gave up. Twin Saga in all other aspects is a great game tho.

Oh...Dark Souls 2. First, let me say I loved the first one. It was an amazing world, lovingly crafted with secrets around every corner. There were tons of things to discover, the first playthrough and even the next two were filled with discoveries, wonder and - of course - an ironhard difficulty. Bosses had to be practiced, even normal monsters were a huge challenge. I played through the game once on Steam and many more times on my PS3, and I had a blast every single time. Yes, that was Dark Souls to me. And now we got a successor and hell, I was excited! I was so excited to dive into a new world.
So damn excited. And then I fired up the game and played through it over the next two weeks.
This will most likely be a long and complicated review. You probably saw the big red thumbs down up there...but it is actually very hard for me to decide between recommending it or not recommending it. A very hard decision indeed, and I decided on the latter.
Why?
Because, simply said, there is something missing.
Something that made the Souls Series so awesome. Something that did lend it it's spark and made it live and breathe. It is...missing from this game. And describing this is the hardest thing I have ever attempted to write.
The beginning is somewhat similar to the first one. You start in a tutorial area that is not without dangers and can leave you dead a lot already. Yay, Difficulty, I thought. Just what I remembered. At some point then you get to Majula, the main hub. You will return here often through the ability to teleport to every bonfire you have visited, and level up at the lady.
Wait, at the lady? Yep, you can not level up at the bonfire anymore. I am really not sure about the reason for this, but it is there, as a mechanic. It is only mildly annoying as the loading times are pretty fast and the menus are too. But I wanted to mention it.
But while I am at the bonfires - this was one of the greatest disappointments for me.
There are TOO.DAMN.MANY.OF.THEM. How many you ask? Well, sometimes two minutes between one another, given that you do not die, and usually not more than 10 minutes even if you die. Most of the times you see a bonfire, then kill monsters and explore, maybe die once or twice and not even ten minutes later, you stand in front of the next bonfire. Some Areas have 4 or even 5 Bonfires despite not even being so big. WHY? This was one of the greatest things in the first Dark Souls - when I saw a bonfire there, I was relieved. So long since I have seen a bonfire, so long. I happily sat down and made myself ready to press on.
Whenever I saw a bonfire in this game, I shrugged and said "Again? Well...meh". Only once or twice there was a stretch between them and I really felt relieved to see one. ONCE. TWICE. Ugh.
The general difficulty level of this game...went so far down the drain. It is still a hard game, but it is not "Souls"-hard anymore. Yes, some bosses can still give you problems and I was happy, imagine that, I was genuinely happy whenever I died to a boss - because he was hard and then it took me some tries and the old Souls-Feeling of taking down a boss was back.
Oh excuse me, did I say boss? Because I had no idea when I was really facing a boss in DS 2.
There are  way too many bosses - as a result I have killed over HALF of them at my first try. OVER HALF. In DS 1 there was only one boss I have killed on my first try - because of a freaking exploit. There are so many and so many are so easy. Really. I was genuinely sad that this challenge was mostly gone.
The final boss too. A huge disappointment. Probably the second- or third-easiest boss in the game. I died once because of bad placement and that was it. I only rarely had to figure out a boss battle, apply tactics like in the first Dark Souls. (I have never played Demon Souls by the way - I have heard people saying that DS 2 has more similarities to Demon Souls than Dark Souls.)
See, I could go on so long - about the different healing  mechanics, the uncreative areas. But there was one time, one time, where I was just...wow. One time where I gazed upon the screen and it made all the easiness, all the gentle waves the game threw at me, better. It didn't completely remove the fact that I disliked that the game is so much easier, that I disliked some of the new mechanics,but...
Light Spoiler below.
But overall...I don't want to play through it again. I know there are a lot of things I haven't mentioned, but my major gripes - the easier difficulty, too many bonfires, too many easy "pseudo-bosses" that are only different from the normal monsters by having slightly more health and a health meter at the bottom of the screen - are reason enough for me to not recommend it.
But NOW. Do not get me wrong. It is by no means a bad game. I still had fun. The graphics are pretty great, the combat is still really solid and works exactly like in the first with only some minor changes, the covenants and multiplayer are great (and will probably keep me coming back), but...it may be a good game, but compared to the first one...it is a bad Souls Game.
You could say that it lost only a tiny spark of it's soul - and that is not what I wanted to play. You will probably have fun with it, but if you are an really avid fan of the first Dark Souls and/or Demon Souls - you might be very disappointed. You might be. I know I was, somehow, despite having fun.
As I said, a complicated matter. Take my thoughts for what you will.
/thoughts end
