The word "realism" in the context of a fantastical setting such as that of a zombie apocalypse may seem a little bit out-of-place, but No More Room in Hell is to Left 4 Dead as Insurgency is to Call of Duty.  The overall concept may be similar to other zombie apocalypse co-op adventure games, but the mechanics favor a level of real-life authenticity that others lack, and it's much stronger for it.
One of the biggest differences is how rare guns and ammunition are.  Finding an M-16 with a whole entire full magazine is a treasure to be coveted and a tool not to be wasted.  Much more common are six-shooters, 9mm handguns, lead pipes, fire axes, and more of their ilk.
Ammunition comes in different calibers that must be matched to the appropriate weapon.  5.56×45mm NATO cartridges used in the M-16 won't fit into a .357 revolver, and .22s useful for a Ruger rifle will be rather useless when you only have a double-barrel hunting shotgun instead.  It's paramount that the players share ammunition with each other to keep everyone armed, especially when someone finds ammo they can't use but know someone else can.
Melee weapons, which come in a wide variety in levels of effectiveness and inventory weight (more on this later), will be the real primary weapon for dealing with most zombies, especially when there are many players in a game (resulting in a much thinner distribution of ammo; unlike Left 4 Dead, more than four players can play together, depending on server settings).  While melee weapons do indeed follow the zombie apocalypse adage "swords don't need reloading", using them comes with a significant risk: not only can players not see their own health levels and take no insignificant amount of damage with hit, and not only will zombies sometimes grapple onto victims and stop them from moving, but players run the risk of being bitten and infected.
Infection cannot be cured; only temporarily staved off with pills.  Infected players can ultimately complete levels together with non-infected players, but without a steady supply of pills, they will eventually drop dead and their corpse reanimate as a fast zombie.  As infection worsens, the player's vision will gradually become more obscured, until they are eventually completely blind.  If friendly fire is enabled in the game, this would generally be a good time for another player to put the victim out of their misery before they have to deal with another zombie.
Players can also start bleeding out after being hit.  Their health levels will slowly deteriorate over time until a bandage is applied, adding another important tool to keep an eye out for.  When a player’s health becomes critically low, their vision will turn to black and white.  This is the player’s urgent warning: find a medkit, find a bandage, find something or you’re toast.
There are a multitude of tools and items to be found in No More Room in Hell.  Pills, medkits, grenades, guns, melee weapons, and gas cans all make an appearance in identical or similar roles to their Left 4 Dead 2 counterparts, but added are flashlights, radios (players can only hear each others' microphones if they are near each other unless they are carrying radios), welding torches, bandages, individual ammunition boxes/half-spent magazines, and more.  Every map is peppered with item spawns, but the sheer variety of them can make it difficult to find the specific one that's actually needed.
It's entirely reasonable to leave an item pickup where it is because it might not be worth carrying in your inventory at the moment.  Inventories are separated into two sections: guns/items, and ammunition.  Both work on the same system - the item's size and weight affects how much space it takes up in your inventory.  The closer your inventory is to being full, the slower the player will run.  Carrying around both a sniper rifle and a pump-action shotgun may be a powerful combination, but it will also leave very little room for other equipment.  It might be wiser to give one of the weapons and its accompanying ammo to a teammate, or even to simply leave one of them behind.
The zombies themselves come in the slow, shambling variety, many of whom will ignore the player if they don’t linger around for too long.  They can soak up many bullets to the chest, but will crumple quickly with one or two shots to the temple.  Occasionally, a fast runner - or even worse, a half-height running child - will appear and chase down the players; these enemies especially dangerous not just because they can attack the player faster, but also because they are harder to hit while being just as durable as a normal zombie.  This forces the players to make a split-second decision: risk infection by trying to hit it with a melee weapon, or burn through large amounts of precious ammunition to gun it down before it gets close.
Levels come in two modes: objective and survival.  Objective mode is analogous to Left 4 Dead's main adventure mode.  Players must work together to travel from point A to point B, scavenging for supplies and overcoming obstacles along the way.  Routes and obstacles, in a similar manner to Left 4 Dead’s system, vary randomly.  However, unlike in Left 4 Dead, the different routes can sometimes be dramatically different from the others, and some levels even can be played backwards.  This adds a great amount of replayability to the official levels, and there are many quality player-made maps floating about, as well.
Survival mode tasks the players with not only simply surviving successive waves of zombies, but also with defending certain zones on the map from zombies.  Players will receive a supply drop at a random spot between waves containing random weapons and items, which must be found and used in enough time to return to the holdout area before the next horde of shambling monsters arrives.  Both surviving every wave and protecting at least one of the zones will achieve victory, but failing in either will result in a defeat.  The quality in survival maps varies; some are significantly more fun to play than others, but there are, of course, many custom maps for this mode as well.  Simply put, it’s an interesting alternative to the Objective mode that some players might hate and some might prefer.
The game definitely has that distinct “Half-Life 2 mod” feel to it (which is to be expected given that that’s what it started as), so don’t expect any revolutionary graphics or animations.  The gameplay is the important aspect here, though; No More Room in Hell is an excellent example of the “graphics alone don’t make a good game” argument.  That said, the age of the Half-Life 2 engine does come with some limitations, namely in the netcode: a high ping to the server can make zombies significantly more difficult to hit, especially given how important headshots are.
tl;dr: No More Room in Hell is a unique take on the co-op zombie survival adventure game that puts a slower, more realistic spin on Left 4 Dead’s formula.  It demands that players work together and share resources if they hope to survive, but that makes the grand achievement of simply completing the level all the more rewarding.  Being a standalone version of what used to be a mod, the game is free (not free-to-play-with-strings-attached; just free), so you have nothing to lose by trying it out.

When the game works, it's great, but when it doesn't - it's a nightmare. I have played both previous "Souls" games (Demon's Souls on PS3, and Dark Souls on X360). And Dark Souls II regretably is the worst game of the 3. The game is by no means bad, but the problem is that too much was recycled from the previous (Dark Souls) game, that the game feels stale, even before you reach the end of your first playthrough. I'm not much for the Singleplayer experience, I've always played the Souls games for their unique multiplayer, which in theory should be brilliant, but it has too many flaws to even be considered good. I'll get back on that a little bit further.
Talking about the Singleplayer experience, the overall "map" of the game feels disjointed, and many areas feel out of place, and don't have the same feeling of fitting together like in the previous game. The locations seem huge, but ironically placed like Heide's Tower of Flame, a location that at first seems overwhelmingly huge, is actually really small, and has barely any exploration value, other than a branch that leads to a lackluster recycled boss battle. Many of the game's various locations feel like having the same problem. Remember exploring the Duke's Archives, New Londo Ruins, the Lost Izalith or even the Sen's Fortress in the previous games? Those locations were decently complicated and challenging enough to keep you entertained, and often made you feel like a mouse in a maze (especially the first time playing). This time around, everything got really linear, in terms of level design. Only 2 levels in my opinion have a more complex design, and that would be The Gutter and Lost Bastille. The bosses are either stupidly easy, or stupidly hard, but hard not because they have are difficult to evade, time your attacks or anything like that, but simply because their attacks are so erratic and damaging, that most of the time you get 1-2 shotted, but other times, bosses are so easy, you even question yourself why did they make some parts of the game feel trivial, and others overwhelmingly difficult. Souls series was always about being challenging, but also being fair at the same time. This time around, when you die, it feels like the game really took the cheap way out on trying to kill you, rather than trying to test your mettle. I can't say how many times I just didn't care about fighting those damn One-Eyed Ogres, or Mace Wielding Drakewatchers, and just used a bow with poison arrows to kill them. Their movesets just feel too damn imposing and unfair to tackle them 1on1 with melee attacks.
Now, onto the multiplayer aspect. Co-op as in every games works fine, it's a great way to gain assistance, if you're stuck in a particular area of the game, or you just want to have a good time with random people in general (socialites will have their fun). The game has a built in voice chat now, so it doesn't feel as eerie as it did in the previous games, which I think isn't bad, but no voice chat had it's charm (it still does, you can turn in off completely), when you had to communicate in gestures. Co-op works, and it's a part of Souls series since forever. There can be lag here and there, but it's hardly a problem, when you're not fighting other players.
Now is where things get slightly unpleasant if you like PvP. The lag is often so bad, that you get killed 10 seconds, after you run away from your opponent to heal yourself. Sometimes you will get hit quite a distance apart from your foe (know as phantom hits), because the game was lagging, but the hit was still registered by the game. Most of the time, the lag will be your biggest nemesis, not the other player you are facing. I will not delve into the other problems of PvP, since it's more of a community centered issue, and not everybody will understand why it's a problem. The lag  Like for example the players that use the most cheesiest possible builds in the Arena to just grab easy wins, simply because that tactic is so damn strong, and there's very little counter play to it (Santier's Spear, Katanas + Resonant Weapon etc.).
I hate that everytime From Software announced a new Souls game, they would go on, on how the game's online will improve significanly and fix the issues that persisted in the previous game. Those issues never get fixed (online lag for ex.)
I love the Souls series, I spent more than ~300hrs playing Demon's Souls, about ~700hrs playing Dark Souls (which about 500-600hrs was purely PvP/Invasions). But I feel that the lack of the series creator (Miyazaki) screwed the entire development team by taking away their direction. Also the false advertisement about the quality of graphics is also a very bad move by Namco, prior release. Check the footage on how the game looked BEFORE it was released. I don't doubt that those downgrades were made for the console market, and the PC only got the better framerate.
If I had to rate the game, I would give it 7/10. I know I didn't touch the better aspects of the game, but I think that knowing the game's weaknesses is better, because sometimes knowing the bad before you get to the good is better. I stay optimistic, because FromSoft is bound to release patches in the future that increase the quality of the online significanly, that happened with prevous games, so there's still hope to get a stable online experience. At the moment, I think that if you want to buy this game, you should refrain from doing so. Wait for a sale, or fixes.
P.S. - English is not my main language, sorry if it seems convoluted and difficult to understand.

After 15 hours into the game - on hard difficulty (as recommended by the game itself) - I am still immensly enjoying myself.
I had a look at the negative reviews and it seems for the most part those people didn't pay attention to which genre this game is. It's survival and horror. Yes, you hide for the biggest part of the game and sneak around, it has this stealthy component to it.
It's not an AvP or CM game where you are armed to the teeth and shoot everything you see. It took me 14 hours to get the second weapon (not gonna spoil), and the first one is only really helpful against humans. But your best weapon remains stealth. Cause shooting is pretty loud and noise attracts attention....
I love that there is lore scattered around everywhere. You can access computer terminals and read emails of the staff etc. It reminds me of the good old AvP2 game. I was sceptical about the crafting at first, but it ties in very nicely and it has a nice Alien-esque touch to it (remember how the motion sensor was assembled by Ash on the spot in the first movie).
The leveldesign is a real joy for Alien-fans. It looks as if you were in the movies down to the smallest details like the cereal-boxes we saw on the Nostromo. Not to mention all the familiar sounds.
After 15 hours it lost some of its horror though, to me at least. The "oh sh*t!" moments keep coming though.
I'm really satisfied with this game. After the past disappointments (you know what I'm talking about) this is really a great positive surprise and I can only recommend it to every Alien-fan out there, as well as to any stealth/survial fan who wants to try it.

At first  I thought this was a crap game; for the longest time I had never made any real progress. Then recently when a friend of mine bought the game and got me to play with him - my eyes were opened; what threw me with this game was not that it was a bad game - but rather that I had been in the dark to many of its secrets because of lack of understanding.
The Game Starts Slow - my time before my friends proves that. It's Definitely better played WITH someone than alone; and most of all you really have to be patient; Even so this is a gem - which sparkles only in the darkest night.
Gameplay is not really "survival" nor truly "base-building" instead I'd liken it to a construction kit for legos back in the day - you are given resources but no clear objectives and there's no "Wrong" Way to play. The game is currently devoid of storyline in any fashion, and what's more the tutorials are basic and not completely informative. When you look at the disassembled puzzle it doesn't make much sense - but when you apply a little creative thought a brick builds upon a brick and goals will suddenly become aware. It uses a rather simple interface and graphics art style - however the real value of any game is in it's mechanisms; which Astroneer has quite a few tucked away in the depths of gameplay. I won't spoil anything but I would caution anyone thinking about buying this game to consider that it takes either a friend to show you the way OR a person capable of indepentant thought and creativity to make anything "good" out of the game.
Do i recommend it? For the longest time I would've said "no". But Now that I can see clearly - I would recommend it with the conditions that a person understand it's caveats.

It is worth the $22 dollars - even without Xen (for now).
Black Mesa does something that Half-Life was unable to do to the fullest extent - show the true horrors and the absolute desperation caused by the Resonance Cascade. With Black Mesa, your experiences wandering through the halls and engaging in fire fights with either aliens from another world, or military officers that have been sent to kill you and all employees, has been amplified. The original story of Half-Life now touched upon, the voice cast have also improved their performances, giving us incredible and very immersive characters to meet and save.
The recoil mechanics provide an excellent balance to the sheer power your weapons possess. Various new models have been added to the game, along with previous models getting a touch up. Weapons now look much nicer, and the H.E.V Mark IV is now a nice blend between the original Mark IV model, and the Mark V from Half-Life 2.
Overall, Black Mesa is an incredible game. It serves as a nice way to bring those that are looking to enter the Half-Life series (game and lore wise) by bringing the game into modern times.

Also a quick note: The PC port was made with old Nvidia cards in mind, so on most modern hardware you'll be missing many of the special effects the original Xbox version had, as it falls back to a generic setting. The worth of the time you spend on this game is how willing you are to work towards either the 'True' ending or the Achievements and until Guides are made for the game, that's going to take a great deal of Trial and Error.
For a free game, this game has some interesting moments, and if you are looking for a visual novel that's gritty and depicts what things may well be like when The Bombs Hit, then Bottom of the Well is a good game for you. However, parts of the game can be frustratingly vague. For example, I had died at some point and unlocked a portable Crowbar, but as I ended up playing 'Dark Alice' just trying to find out what could and could not be traversed/overcome, there was no point where it was necessary and it felt awkward to put on.
A lot of times I end up getting very similar endings to previous runs, either something like 'So Close' or making one bad decision or waiting something out and then dying of Radiation Poisoning. Until a guide comes out depicting how each ending is achieved, you WILL see these endings a lot.
The game mentions a Save function, but I sure as hell can't find it. Also if you try starting a new game too fast, the game won't process it correctly and you'll be forced to restart the client (count to 4 after the main menu shows up, and you should be fine, might have something to do with how I put it on 'Fantastic' graphics which, honestly, I question where Graphics even come into play in the main game.) Group and Social Dynamics in the game are laughable, they seem more like a narrative crutch than an actual mechanic within the game itself.
Also Inventory can be... really stupid honestly. Dark Alice doesn't have the same issues that Default Alice does and while the game recommends you play Default Alice first, Dark Alice is much better to get a feel for the game and what you can/cannot accomplish.
I haven't spent long on this game... an hour, hour and a half? I mean it's a good game, and if you like trial and error to find the way to your ideal ending, then that's great! Until a guide is made for this game though (and so far there's just a paultry first playthrough where the player fails to reach adequete shelter in time) I cannot, in good faith, recommend this game to others as there is no clear path (and even Default Alice herself offers very little hint on how exactly to accomplish the True Ending, much less other endings)

In Splinter Cell you play as one of the best and agent Third Echelon has to offer, Sam Fisher (Michael Ironside).
He travels to several locations under command by Irving Lambert (Don Jordan) in the world to find out about Kombayn Nikoladze and his connection in several assassinations close before his rule.
Developed by Ubisoft Montreal, a modified Unreal Engine 2 was used to allow the light and dark stealth mechanic.
Using light and dark to your advantage, shadows, the game still holds up to this day.
I did looked up on the guide section to edit the graphic settings to enhance it a little bit.
Of course in the backgrounds you see the age of the game, but it did not bother me.
You can use the light and dark to get around. A nice meter in the down right corner tells you if you are a ninja or a Christmas tree.
The enemies can interact with the environment in numbers of ways. Like they search for you if they had seen you and might call others for help.
Stealth is the key in this game and you do not have enough firepower to shoot through the game (although possible but not recommend).
It took me about 6 hours to get to the end on normal difficulty with a few retries because failing some levels which never frustrated me.
Sound is important in this game and has descent ones. You recognise most of them instinctively to know what is going on in the world.
Sometimes you hear a nice background music to set the mood.
In combat you do get the same tune everytime which is slightly annoying.
The guns Sam carries are most silent and therefore there is nothing interesting for the sounds to note here. You do get some nice fireworks though.
Still got the looks.
Still plays as a unique game.
Story is easy and fast, most of the time told by news reports (cut scenes).
Nice unique variety of levels. Makes most use of the game mechanics. Especially the end game.

I wanted to love this game so badly. It has so much going for it — absurdly cute graphics, fun level design, great music. But the controls were a massive nightmare and the levels were repetitive. I hemmed and hawed a lot about whether to rec this or not and ultimately put it here because I did spend so much time frustrated, but it was also enjoyable, so…? IDK. If the issues that bothered me seem minor to you, you’ll probably enjoy it and should pick it up next time it’s on sale.
It’s hard to explain the problems with the controls. You can only jump a certain distance, and you can’t move while you’re in the air. This makes the precise jumping platforming requires impossible. On top of that, sometimes when you hit a wall you turn and face the other direction, and sometimes you don’t, and I couldn’t quite figure out when each happened. So you’d try to chain jump and just end up spinning and going back the way you came, usually dying. And even once I started to get used to the jump distance, I found it absurdly frustrating to have to line myself up just right (which sometimes was impossible) and then press A and cross my fingers. I also found that the controls were not sensitive enough to detect tiny movements back and forth, so a lot of time I’d try to line up a jump over and over and over only to discover that it was almost impossible to get to the exact spot I needed to be in. Worse still, the game was bad at indicating what was coming up — I often found myself getting into a rhythm only to be killed by a baddie just offscreen that there was no way I could have anticipated. This is the worst kind of difficultly in a platformer.
But even once I got used to that and got through the first set of levels, I was disappointed to find the other three locked level sets were just the same ones with fewer checkpoints and/or more baddies. So the game was actually only 25% as big as I thought it was, which was super disappointing.
Yet I kept playing it. There’s something oddly relaxing about it right up until it gets frustrating. I found myself playing in 10-minute spurts — I’d clear a level, hit a point I couldn’t get past for 5 minutes, quit in frustration, do something else for an hour, and then start over. The game had all the elements of something I liked, but just couldn’t follow through. And it’s so sad, because I want it to work so badly, but ultimately it just couldn’t get its♥♥♥♥♥♥together for long enough.

The word "realism" in the context of a fantastical setting such as that of a zombie apocalypse may seem a little bit out-of-place, but No More Room in Hell is to Left 4 Dead as Insurgency is to Call of Duty.  The overall concept may be similar to other zombie apocalypse co-op adventure games, but the mechanics favor a level of real-life authenticity that others lack, and it's much stronger for it.
One of the biggest differences is how rare guns and ammunition are.  Finding an M-16 with a whole entire full magazine is a treasure to be coveted and a tool not to be wasted.  Much more common are six-shooters, 9mm handguns, lead pipes, fire axes, and more of their ilk.
Ammunition comes in different calibers that must be matched to the appropriate weapon.  5.56×45mm NATO cartridges used in the M-16 won't fit into a .357 revolver, and .22s useful for a Ruger rifle will be rather useless when you only have a double-barrel hunting shotgun instead.  It's paramount that the players share ammunition with each other to keep everyone armed, especially when someone finds ammo they can't use but know someone else can.
Melee weapons, which come in a wide variety in levels of effectiveness and inventory weight (more on this later), will be the real primary weapon for dealing with most zombies, especially when there are many players in a game (resulting in a much thinner distribution of ammo; unlike Left 4 Dead, more than four players can play together, depending on server settings).  While melee weapons do indeed follow the zombie apocalypse adage "swords don't need reloading", using them comes with a significant risk: not only can players not see their own health levels and take no insignificant amount of damage with hit, and not only will zombies sometimes grapple onto victims and stop them from moving, but players run the risk of being bitten and infected.
Infection cannot be cured; only temporarily staved off with pills.  Infected players can ultimately complete levels together with non-infected players, but without a steady supply of pills, they will eventually drop dead and their corpse reanimate as a fast zombie.  As infection worsens, the player's vision will gradually become more obscured, until they are eventually completely blind.  If friendly fire is enabled in the game, this would generally be a good time for another player to put the victim out of their misery before they have to deal with another zombie.
Players can also start bleeding out after being hit.  Their health levels will slowly deteriorate over time until a bandage is applied, adding another important tool to keep an eye out for.  When a player’s health becomes critically low, their vision will turn to black and white.  This is the player’s urgent warning: find a medkit, find a bandage, find something or you’re toast.
There are a multitude of tools and items to be found in No More Room in Hell.  Pills, medkits, grenades, guns, melee weapons, and gas cans all make an appearance in identical or similar roles to their Left 4 Dead 2 counterparts, but added are flashlights, radios (players can only hear each others' microphones if they are near each other unless they are carrying radios), welding torches, bandages, individual ammunition boxes/half-spent magazines, and more.  Every map is peppered with item spawns, but the sheer variety of them can make it difficult to find the specific one that's actually needed.
It's entirely reasonable to leave an item pickup where it is because it might not be worth carrying in your inventory at the moment.  Inventories are separated into two sections: guns/items, and ammunition.  Both work on the same system - the item's size and weight affects how much space it takes up in your inventory.  The closer your inventory is to being full, the slower the player will run.  Carrying around both a sniper rifle and a pump-action shotgun may be a powerful combination, but it will also leave very little room for other equipment.  It might be wiser to give one of the weapons and its accompanying ammo to a teammate, or even to simply leave one of them behind.
The zombies themselves come in the slow, shambling variety, many of whom will ignore the player if they don’t linger around for too long.  They can soak up many bullets to the chest, but will crumple quickly with one or two shots to the temple.  Occasionally, a fast runner - or even worse, a half-height running child - will appear and chase down the players; these enemies especially dangerous not just because they can attack the player faster, but also because they are harder to hit while being just as durable as a normal zombie.  This forces the players to make a split-second decision: risk infection by trying to hit it with a melee weapon, or burn through large amounts of precious ammunition to gun it down before it gets close.
Levels come in two modes: objective and survival.  Objective mode is analogous to Left 4 Dead's main adventure mode.  Players must work together to travel from point A to point B, scavenging for supplies and overcoming obstacles along the way.  Routes and obstacles, in a similar manner to Left 4 Dead’s system, vary randomly.  However, unlike in Left 4 Dead, the different routes can sometimes be dramatically different from the others, and some levels even can be played backwards.  This adds a great amount of replayability to the official levels, and there are many quality player-made maps floating about, as well.
Survival mode tasks the players with not only simply surviving successive waves of zombies, but also with defending certain zones on the map from zombies.  Players will receive a supply drop at a random spot between waves containing random weapons and items, which must be found and used in enough time to return to the holdout area before the next horde of shambling monsters arrives.  Both surviving every wave and protecting at least one of the zones will achieve victory, but failing in either will result in a defeat.  The quality in survival maps varies; some are significantly more fun to play than others, but there are, of course, many custom maps for this mode as well.  Simply put, it’s an interesting alternative to the Objective mode that some players might hate and some might prefer.
The game definitely has that distinct “Half-Life 2 mod” feel to it (which is to be expected given that that’s what it started as), so don’t expect any revolutionary graphics or animations.  The gameplay is the important aspect here, though; No More Room in Hell is an excellent example of the “graphics alone don’t make a good game” argument.  That said, the age of the Half-Life 2 engine does come with some limitations, namely in the netcode: a high ping to the server can make zombies significantly more difficult to hit, especially given how important headshots are.
tl;dr: No More Room in Hell is a unique take on the co-op zombie survival adventure game that puts a slower, more realistic spin on Left 4 Dead’s formula.  It demands that players work together and share resources if they hope to survive, but that makes the grand achievement of simply completing the level all the more rewarding.  Being a standalone version of what used to be a mod, the game is free (not free-to-play-with-strings-attached; just free), so you have nothing to lose by trying it out.

I'm going to make several admissions before I start talking about this game. First is that I haven't completed it. I've only played up to the first serious encounter with the Alien and have only died a couple of times. The second admission is that I had my first experience with a Xenomorph when I was barely past toddler age. Because my parent introduced me so early to the genre and the experience of the movies, I've played pretty much every Alien game that came into being on console or PC.
This is also an experience I've been waiting just about my entire life to have.
From that first moment where you land in the airlock, things are tense. You can easily get drawn in by the artwork and the small tasks you are required to do in the early stages, and something as small as falling off a plank bridge (combined with the cutscene that entails) really pulls you into the experience. The story behind it is true to the lore and the even the Alien looks as badass as Ridley had envisioned 35 years ago.
I've read a few reviews where people have been complaining about the stressfulness and the near impossibility of getting aruond the senses of the Alien, and to them I say this. Harden up. This game is meant to make you feel despair, and accomplishment, and any number of other emotions. That thing is out there searching for you, and if you stay put, you're going to get found. I watched in amazement during my first try with the encounter. It was a stunning experience to watch for all of three minutes as it employed a search strategy I've seen in reality, but not before in videogames. After 3 minutes and 27 seconds, he found me hiding under the gurney (the one all the promo videos move the character under.)
For the first time I felt the imperative to move, and that I couldn't stay still. He's looking fo ryou and will find you eventually. Every time he employs another sense, or stops to listen beccause you brought the motion tracker up, or moved. On another encounter he even lured me into a trap. I was hiding in an air vent (not recommended) and I saw him run off in a direction, I moved towards the exit in the opposite direction, but saw him come out of a door at full pace. I backed off and made for the opposite end, only to be greeted by his extremely detailed and terrifying head cutting me off. It's quick when it knows where you are.
This is piece of lore I've been wanting my entire life while I watched developers butcher the series with crossovers and attempts at badassery that have ultimately failed time and again. This game makes you feel weak, helpless and ultimately expendible. This game makes you understand what it feels like to be hunted.
If you want a horror game that's going to hold your hand, you're looking in the wrong place. This is the Dark Souls of the horror genre. You want your victory? Come and get it.

This is the Aliens experience I have been waiting for! Played a lot of them over the years, most recently Aliens Colonial Marines. I know ACM got a lot of flak from players but I did enjoy it for what it did get right. The motion tracker for example was spot on. Isolations' motion tracker is a little off to me.
Back to topic: Isolation, that is what you will fell. I am five hours in and just starting to feel the real tenseness of the game. The atmosphere is brought out and begins to close in on you by lots of subtle little cues. The sound is exceptional at this. Passes Doom 3 for sheer creepyness. The graphics are surprisingly clear and smooth without being too dark all the time. When you do find yourself in a truly dark area it becomes suffocating in its' envelopment. I find myself creeping along walls with only the faintest light from my head gear to see the edge, afraid to turn on the flash light for fear of attracting attention and wasting battery life. This is not the usual way that I approach most games. Guns a blazing is the norm but not here. An instinct of self preservation is cultivated naturally by this game and I found that refreshing. A truely emmersive experience so far.

The best Alien orientated game I've played since Alien vs Predator 2 which came out at least 12 years ago. Aliens: Colonial Marines was such a let down that I now refuse to invest in any Gearbox game, but it's great to see that Sega backed Alien: Isolation following Gearbox's terrible addition to the franchise.
As I was playing it through, memories of Dead Space sprang to mind regularly. If you enjoyed the Dead Space series, you will love this! Sections of it are pretty tough, but once you have an idea of what you can get away with, it becomes slightly easier. I've had a  lot of fun playing this game. It isn't too difficult to get what you want, but requires you to go on an adventure. Lots of interesting twists and turns. One time I was trying to get Malachite in a deep mine, when a plant suddenly stabbed me in the back. I must have died 3 times to that one plant trying to get my stuff back again. If you ever got stuck in a storm far away from home, you will know this. This game has a lot of good parts, but also some bad parts. I think you should be able to scrap items. I have at least 8 generators just laying around ever since I switched to solar, and I could really use the compound. Maybe add a furnace or trash compactor. Also, you should be able to delete certain parts of your base. Overall, this game is very fun to play. If you like adventure, space, and industrialization I would definitely recommend it to you.
Edit: I think that a helpful addition to the game would be a sort of weed killer. Maybe a mod on the terrain shaper that kills plants like the spikers, acid pots, exploders, etc. This could be useful for mining, and would allow you to get rid of plants without making the path more difficult to travel. Also, maybe an unstuck button.

1. The art style is simple (Vector, like mentioned before)and not very resource intensive. While its simple its also very beautiful. The worlds are very intereresting and vary alot.

Black Mesa: Source or Black Mesa is a Half Life 2 Modification by very enthusiastic Half Life gamers. This modification is less of a modification and more of a total conversion overhaul. This game is a complete rehaul of the original Half Life with almost identical levels & gameplay, what makes this game so special that it's not like any of the other "Half Life" remakes or Half Life: Source? Read on and find out!
Black Mesa re-tells us an already very familiar story and amps up the anty by 10, with the solid plot line from the original Half Life with the glory of the Source Engine 2013 technology.
You are Gordon Freeman, a scientist hired to perform experiements in an underground research lab below Mexico desert. One day on your job you're tasked to insert a rare specimen from the planet "Xen" into a reactor machine which causes a resonance cascade that destroys the research facility, but the worst is yet to come. As you battle your way out of Black Mesa research facility through these strange alien creatures & a corrupt military task force hired to keep the Black Mesa incident a secret and stop anybody that is attempting to escape from the facility a strange man in a blue suit stalks Gordons every move, who is this strange man & why is he here? It's up to you to unravel the mystery of this strange man.
The gameplay is the same familiar gameplay you would expect from any Source Engine game, it works identical to that of Half Life 2, it's got solid gameplay, a beautifully & lovingly crafted modification that everyone expected "Half Life: Source" to be but were let down, this is what we wanted from Valve but in the end we got it from a very tallented modding team.
With a complete overhaul of Half Life you can expect things to be compaired to the original & with this total conversion you should expect to see a few significant changes to the original game, some new places to explore, some alternate paths to take and some new faces to encounter, although not identical to the original game it's very cannon to the original & nothing that is in the game feels out of place.
The gameplay is solid, the guns feel like the original game & most importantly the game has 100% it's own content, nothing is stock Half Life 2 assets, even the enemies are recreated with rather noteable modifications, they even went as far as to add their own voice actors to the game rather than using the voices from Half Life 2, however in the Steam release you will hear that a few of the characters are using the original voice actors from Half Life 1 & 2, this is nice to have the noteable voices back in a game that is trying to be the Half Life game it does so well to replicate.
Yes i certainly recommend this game, if you're still on the fence about paying for a modification then you can try the free version of this available here:

Anyone who knows me knows what I think about this game. It's an RTS that does a lot of things differently from the Starcraft/C&C crowd, with brilliant new ideas that make for excellent gameplay. It is, bar none, my favorite RTS of all time.
Resource income is based on control of territory sectors distributed all over the map. Your economy hinges on being proactive and willing to fight to push the front line forward. Turtling in your base is effectively forfeiting the match.
Combat is more nuanced -- less about reflexes and more about tactics. Reading the terrain and making use of environmental cover is a vital skill. Flanking, formations, suppression, combined-arms assaults... very few of these concepts matter in most RTS games of today, but they're all here and all important components of victory in CoH.
I don't know if this game is ever going on sale again, but if you have money to spend, get this game. You'll get a fresh, masterfully-crafted experience, and countless hours of fun in online matches alongside, or against, your friends.

A 2d platformer with a simple control scheme that makes for a surprisingly good challenge. The player moves forward by walking or jumping on a fixed arc ala Ghosts n Goblins on the classic "get hit twice and lost a life" bit from Mario and... Ghosts n Goblins... requiring the player to look ahead of them and plan their route rather than just run through everything. And with no other means of self-defense, it's like a pacifist run of Ghosts n Goblins, except all the hazards are in the same exact spot each time you try so there's no random luck; just patience and memorization. The graphics are extremely soothing and the in-game BGM sounds like it's straight from a SNES game by Jaleco. Really, it has that same scheme of beeps and boops and MIDI instruments that were unique to the SNES. Play "Battle Master" or one of the Sailor Moon SNES games after playing this. Fun fact! The Capcom Play System 1 aracade cabinets (Final Fight, Street Fighter II), Sharp x68K and Sega Genesis all had Yamaha-made sound chips but Nintendo made their own! ... oh right, reviewing this game. The music is cheerful and calming (bc SNES tunes) and goes great with the soothing sunset backdrop and mind-clearing game. A great game for relaxing at the end of a day of work, or to entertain the kids. Except for that giant fish with lots of teeth, or the skeleton-ghost-toucan when the player loses a life. 2 spooky!

I am a big ES fan and love this game.  I have no regrets in purchasing this game at all.
Here's my list of Pros and Cons.  These are based on my opinion.
PROS:
You move slowly enough through leveling (especially if you love to immerse yourself into the stories & not just speed through to your next quest objective) that it feels like the game could go on for forever, unlike some other MMO's I've played (not going to mention names).
I've played a few different races so far and the main quest lines are the same (mages guild, fighter's guild and main quest line) but all the other quests are totally different, so you don't get bored starting a new character as a different race.  I can really appreciate that since I love to play alts. Yes, every pact has their own starting area as well (there's three in total).
If you like crafting you can do all that this game has to offer, you are not limited to choosing what your MO will be.  Your crafting materials can hang in the bank (which is shared between all of your characters) so you don't have to lug that stuff around.
I do like the character creation, you can spend some time going through it all and perfecting your look, all very typical of ES games. You can even pick what voice you want your character to have, which is cool (and funny, if you imagine your character in the bathroom while you are picking your voice).
You can dye your armor, too (does not cost you a dime).
Your quest rewards are not bound to you, so if they do not fit your character build, you can deposit them into your bank and an alt can pull it out and use it.  In fact, a lot of items you can put on and use are not bound to you unless you dye them.
You can wear costumes to hide your armor as well, if you want a different appearance.
You can play a lot of the game content solo, which is a big plus IMO.  I hate nagging guild members, complete strangers for help, or waiting till someone can help you before moving on in your quests (GAH!).
There is no lag at all in battle sequences.  You hit your #3 button (as an example), your attack assigned to 3 executes as expected.  Some f2p games do not have a great battle response time (lag) but ESO does not.
The button assignments are very similar (almost mirror image) of PC Skyrim.  I really appreciate that.  That also means, battles play out the same, but ESO does have a bit of a 'guidance' system with ranged attacks - specifically bows.
The talk sequences are so cool (and so like other ES games), it really makes this game more immersive.
The graphics are awesome!
They will be adding more guilds (thieves guild, etc.) in the future.
CONS:
Sharing a bank with all your characters CAN be a negative.  You are limited on space, so sometimes you have to make tough decisions on what you want to hoard.  You can buy more bank space, it just gets pricey very quickly.
You are limited on how many guilds you can be in (some find that a negative), and all of your alts are in the same guilds your alts are in.  It is confusing.  Essentially, you are limited to being in 5 guilds, so guild chatter shows up in your feed from ALL the guilds you are in, they are just labeled g1, g2, g3, g4, g5 (you can color-code them, too).  At least you won't miss any juicy drama.  *shrugs*
I have not joined a guild yet, but I did attempt to start my own guild to see if I could use it as a bank (500 slots, mind you - that is a lot of hoarding), but it requires ten people to unlock and your alts do not count even though they are automatically in your guild.
You can only have 8 characters in total (some find this a negative, that's why I put this here).
You cannot change your facial/body appearance after you leave character creation.
Mounts are not cheap.
Buying additional bag and bank space is expensive (and yet, so necessary).
That's all I can really come up with!
Overall, I feel this game is well worth the money to purchase and play.  I will be playing this game for many years to come.  The negatives - for me - do not outweigh the positives.
The only recommendation I have for those of you considering buying/playing ESO: Unlimited: buy the Imperial Edition if you can throw an extra 20 bones towards it.  I didn't and regret it.  The ability to buy a mount for one gold shortly after you start playing your new character verses thousands of gold pieces and many levels later is a bummer.  Yes, you can still buy that package deal through the crown store (their in-game cash store), but it just makes more sense to buy the edition that already has that built-in, because it is cheaper.

Black Mesa is a full-on remake of the original Half-Life, which was one of my favorite games of all time. I've been following the mod for a few years, eagerly awaiting the full release of the game, and, well, Half-Life 3.
Well. now at least one of those are out, and in Early Access, at least. If you have played through the mod before and don't feel like dropping $20 on this game, there are some very noticeable differences and additions made to the Steam release that the mod doesn't have. New reload animations, graphical updates, map layout tweaks, workshop support, and even a Multiplayer Deathmatch mode that remastered some of the original Half-Life Deathmatch maps. However, the game still isn't done. Xen is not available at the time of this review (Hence, Early Access) and there are some bugs, so it definitely isn't finished.
However, the amount of content you get for only $20 is downright outstanding. I would've gladly dropped $60 on this game right now, even in its state of Early Access. The new Early Access Version of Black Mesa has seen major improvements and detail overhauls compared to the free version of BMS that came out a couple years ago from the time of this review writing. I've played every Half-Life game including the expansion packs for HL1, and while this game won't ever have the classic charm of the classic Half-Life, this HD port and it's creators exceeded my expectations for mod that seemed almost impossible to be true, I like HD overhauls of certain games, and the development team did very well with this, they deserve something for their hard work, and that's why I decided to buy this version, and needless to say, I wasn't expecting a more polished copy, so I was very happy and surprised from what I see in this version. I will describe below how this version is improved upon the original BMS to better help the reader decide if this is worth their buy or not.
-NOW HAS A WORKSHOP!!!!!! LET THE MODDING BEGIN!!!!
-
and scenarios are greatly improved from the original BMS, in general, I like them, and they provide a new experience for me and doesn't make me feel like I'm just playing Half-Life 1 in HD, it forces you to come up with new ideas and ways of approaching certain obstacles and enemies, while keeping level design feel more immersive and realistic, almost as if you could role-play, it's just great.
-
over BMS, many sounds have been refined a well as the adrenaline pumping soundtrack of this version, weapon sounds and NPC voices have also been slightly improved from what have seen so far, as well as level elements, and enemy idle sounds. A couple of examples would be the HEV suit with a new sound filter on the original voice making it feel more immersive and futuristic, fitting to the game very well, and other sound examples such as the guard post between the two doors leading to sector C, where the guard makes a comment on Gordon's ponytail removal, before his voice was heard as if he was next to you talking, and now he talks through a COM like filter while behind the window in the guard post, counting as a nice improved detail that even I missed to question in the original BMS.
-
while still keeping a balanced ammunition pool that's more realistic and adds more difficulty to the game. One example of a weapon overhaul would be the Glock-17 which now has a new model, scratched details to show wear and tear of being an old used gun, it's original functions from HL1 have returned, and normal fire shoots at the same speed as the original glock in Hl1, and has seen the return of it's famous Alt-Fire Rapid mode, and has very nice muzzle flash, and blowback animations, as well as new idle animations, and a cool sprint animation as you have it equipped.
-
balancing out the loss of certain hard nonsense obstacles with the new realistic level designs implemented. Enemies are more quick, accurate, can quickly kill you in groups at close range, and are a lot harder to kill as you turn up the difficulty. The bullsquid for example used to be an enemy you could kill quickly at any range, but it now has much higher health, more damaging attacks, and it's spit attack has splash damage that can still be fatal, if most or all of it hits you, and almost more than one magazine of a glock can kill one on Normal assuming all hits land, and their close range attacks are still dangerously damaging, I now hate seeing bullsquids ever so more. And houndeyes not only can destroy you in large groups if allowed to attack in time, their attacks can optionally (can be toggled in settings) Ring your hearing and normally can disorient your vision with their sonic attacks, making it hard to aim and hear, thus making them also more formidable than before.
-I LOVED the new HEV visual intro as you pick up the suit, not only was there a new voice, but when the HEV is checking systems and analyzing defensive weapon selections and vital monitoring, it will show the pieces of the HUD that it is referring to, and use the HUD bloom accordingly to show everything, and will even give a detailed visual interpretation of the suit and the wearer's physical attributes and weight. I also LOVED the loading screens having new fun looks, and gameplay hints showing a really refined experience, and even details like that are what make a game nice to have.
-Some level hazards from the original game that could still be implemented and not hurt the realistic design are missing, one example is when you go through to restore the power for the blast pit, before you could see a puddle or water, and later it would be electrified forcing you to find a method to get across, or perhaps a new route or vent would be nice to see, but that's only my personal prefence on some of these level hazards, they don't have to be there but it does make some areas easier than they should have been.
-The crobar hitting speed is way too fast, it should be nerfed a bit slower, perhaps the same as HL1's crowbar, I love how the model and animations for the crowbar were improved and more enthusiastic, but the hit speed seems unrealistic and a bit overpowered, and encourages spamming to kill headcrabs rather than accurate timing for their jump trajectory.
-I'm excited to see Xen and anticipate it very much, this is not a con that it's not out yet, I understand the detail you developers want to implement and I say, Take all the time you need, it will be worth the wait for all of us.
-This game is very fun and it's a whole new experience for Half-Life lovers, even if it's not an official valve game, that doesn't mean it wasn't carefully worked on and detailed, and by the time the full version releases, we will see a very polished and fun game to play with lots of features, some being new over the older HL1, and BMS. Help this developer finish this game and give them what they deserve for their years of hard work and dedication, and enjoy the refreshed experience that even valve liked to see!

This has been a game that we (even I) wanted forever, and especially after the disasterous Aliens: Colonial Marines.  This catches the time of the first movie with its 1979 Sci-fi look, and the music is always nailing it at all times.  The atmosphere is the most impressive I have ever seen in an Alien game, and is the best so far hands down.  I've played horror games before, and because of the predictable AI I felt that there was no challange even on the toughest difficulty.  Since the Xenomorph has a none scripted, unpredictable AI I felt like I have found my match, I hid under a desk, it went by, and once I got out, it had turned around and therefore I was in its sights and I got mauled.  Though you may still be a little unsure about this game because of IGN, Gamespot, or other reviewers who reviewed it very badly, just to let you know, this is a very, very good game.  The IGN reviewer as I remember said to have the game on it's easiest difficulty.  Well don't go by his word, as he probably thought that this was a CoD game, and I think that the reviewer on Gamespot got kind of confused and thought it was a straight on action game. (although it can be but there's a huge risk of getting nomed by the alien)  But I implore you all to do the game on the hardest difficulty, because this came from Gary Napper (lead designer) that the meat of the game is learning what the alien is capable of, and that is true.  The levels are extremely well made, and you (and even the alien, other people, and androids) have multiple routes to take.  I've never been so scared by a game like this in a long, long time, and if it can get my heart racing, then it is a great, true horror game.  So if you want the crap scared out of you, then Alien: Isolation is the best one you can get. And another thing, this is around 15 hours or more to complete, so you'll be scared longer than any other game which is great.  If this review has helped you decide to buy this game and you enjoyed it, then leave a thumbs up.  Thank you for reading, and stay safe from getting your skull chewed on by the alien, Peace.

Don't let my small amount of hours on steam playing this fool you- I've been playing this through the official Aeria launcher for daaaaays now, and easily have 8 something hours on it outside of steam. This is surprisingly good F2P MMO, and I've played a LOT of them (ESO, Allods Online, Runes of Magic, Aura Kingdom, Wildstar, RO2, Dragon's Prophet, Riders of Iccarus, etc) and this one is easily in my top 3, and here are my reasons why;
Graphics: This game is beautiful. The quaint, chibi styled art is adorable and endearing, not to mention colorful and uniform, creating a sense of immersion that I find many other F2P games surprisingly lacking. Shadows, water shaders, FX, DoF, and other high quality special FX really make this game look beautiful, but run surprisingly well.
Music: The music is super cute, well done, and very reminicient of many JRPG style games from SNES/DS eras of gamging, which gives the game a nastolgic feel, even though you may never have played it before.
VoiceActing: I can't speak for the english tracks, because *drum roll* it has the Japanese AND Chinese audio tracks included as optional use! To that end, the Japanese VA's are very well done, and are dripping with tons of typical anime tropes and voices, and I absolutely love it. I can't tell you how much I appreciate the fact that I can use the JP audio- it really makes it feel like I'm playing an interactive anime.
Questing/Story/Dungeons: While it CAN be a little boring doing the main quests, there are TONS of side quests that unlock, and if you do their maximum per day, will give you an XP bonus to everything you kill until the daily quests reset the next day. Not to mention, there are 'hidden' quests where, if you read the npc dialogue, they will give you clues of what to look for while you're out doing the main story quests. Doing these hidden quests will usually give you some really nice rewards, and are some of the only ways to obtain certain titles in the game, so if you collect those kinds of things, you'll enjoy that. Dungeons come in Solo and party variety, PERFECT for some casual, or friendly gameplay. Not enough time to party? That's ok, do the solo version 3 times in a row! Have time to party? Sweet! Pop a loot drop scroll (obtainable from quests, dalies, battleground events etc) and get 2-5 extra pieces of gear from the dungeon boss!
Events: There are events that rotate throughout the day, and they can reward a variety of items including costumes, loyalty points (one kind of currency used in the item mall), loot drop scrolls, exp vials, etc. They are fun, interactive events that bring players togather for fun, REGARDLESS of level, because some of them aren't fighting events! Players are put on teams and need to dodge, run, jump, etc through obstacles to gain points for their team, or find hidden items around an area.. all the events are a bit different, and surprisingly fun. The best part is that these event times are broadcasted via the system just before start, and there's a dedicated button on the mini-map to access them- no hunting around for a portal or teleport!
Houses: Players get ADORABLE mobile houses that they can decorate, craft in, place objects in, and have friends visit! Magical homes they can use for quicker transport across the 'Overworld' map, but can also access Tardis style by going inside. Each one has three floors- there are NO expansions, and NO crazy prices for upkeep like some other games (I'm looking at you RoM >: | ). Greenhouse to grow crops for crafting, Main Hall for a common area & Workshop for alchemy and armor crafting are all open the minute you unlock the house FOR FREE. The house is free via a required main quest, and remains free FOREVER. While you CAN buy furniture/patterns for these houses in the item mall, you can easily buy/make them in game with just a little bit of farming and effort, or a heafty amount of gold via the auction house. Again, unlike a lot of other games, the only 'limit' on the number of items you have placed in the home is based on the size of the homes warehouse, and you get about 45 slots for START. FIFTY. That's easily 30+ more slots than RoM, all for free, simply for completing the quest.
Class System: The class system is really cool. In a lot of ways, it reminds me of the old Job system from FF11 (which was my first MMO, and I hold it dear to my heart). You're able to switch your job at ANY time, and all jobs level up individually. When you hit a certain level of a job, or unlock a certain job (unlocks are available through QUESTS, you do NOT have to purchase them in the store!) you will gain access to certain skills from that job that can be used while you play OTHER jobs. So my Paladin can use some of my DragonKnight skills, and my Dragonknight can use a Cleric skill... this adds a lot of depth and gives you flexibility in how YOU want to play the game. Each job also has two 'specialization' trees where typically one is more offensive, and the other is more defensive; but you can mix an match the points you get via level up in these two trees however you want! Every class can also equip Starstones, which are basically like slotted boosts. These gems drop constantly- you get them from quests, killing monsters, dungeon bosses etc, and there are 3 tiers. As the tiers progress, the starstones' purpose gets more specific, and can really help you narrow down the focus of your class by boosting the damage of skills, threat generation, ability range, and stats of what you use the most.
Combat: Though the targeting is a little wonky when a pack of enemies decends on you, for the most part, it doesn't effect much, because your character will auto-target and turn towards the enemy when you use an attack. Many attacks for several classes are also AoE (or can be made to cause AoE damage with starstones), so in the end, it doesn't matter too much, cause everything is getting hit by spalsh damage. Some attacks will also effect one another, and using one after the other will result in a buff for you, or a debuff for your enemy. There are also special combat 'pets' called Senshi that you can recruit through quests.. these add a ton to the storyline, and all of them have slightly different specializations to help you in combat, no matter if you're a tank, dps, or healer. You can also have 3 of these slotted at a time, and 'call' one of them at any time, even during combat. Tank Senshi isn't doing enough damage? Pull out your mage Senshi and do some AoE badassery! Getting pummled by a boss? Pull back out Tank Senshi!
Overall, if you love anime and chibi style art, and you want a free game to play, I would recommend you give this a try! Worst that happens is you uninstall it cause you don't like it.

Let me start by saying that Dark Souls is probably one of my favorite games. The first is a complete masterpiece.
That's a tough act to follow, but Dark Souls II does a good job. The combat and base mechanics are essentially unchanged (which is good). The aesthetics and the lore are as great as ever, and the ever punishing difficulty is still present. Those worried that they might have made it too easy, fear not.
This really is a great game, and mechanically I feel like the online elements were all implemented much better than the first. From a technical standpoint, this is leaps and bounds above it's predecesor.
There is one thing I want to mention though... The world of the original Dark Souls, the labyrinth of zones that all twist and connect to each other, is a much better crafted world than that of Dark Souls II. Dark Souls did an amazing job at pushing you further and further, eroding you, until you didn't think you'd make it... only to have to find a door, ladder, etc at the last second that connected you back to safety. It's really amazing how well the first world is made. The world of Dark Souls II, although also well made, is more split into "zones" and loses the punishing labyrinth feel of the first. It's not bad, in fact the world is quite well made, but it just isn't as conhesive as that of the first game, and for that I think it suffers. They did add the ability to fast travel between bonfires, which is great, but I feel like this also takes away from the exploration that was so amazing in the first game.
But really, overall, Dark Souls II is still great. It's hard to be a sequel to one of the best games ever, and if my biggest complaint is "well it's not as good as the best game ever" then I think it's still pretty solid.
Play both, but if you're only going to play one, I think I'd play Dark Souls over the sequel.

Dishonored 2 is a masterpiece of modern game design, and a true sequel.
The first game showed us how artistic vision can overcome the idea of graphic resolution by presenting us with beautiful environments and an immersive dark atmosphere. The characters were memorable, and the story always seemed much larger than the game let on, as notes and other dialogue often hinted at places far away from Dunwall.
The sequel, which takes us to Karnaca - another small part of the world Arkane has built, while going for a more colorful atmosphere manages to maintain the Dishonored feel, and builds on the already amazingly simple yet deep and unpredictable gameplay. The game, while short adapts to the player’s preferred playstyle, allowing them to feel the consequences of their actions. The experience largely depends on the player placing certain limitations on themselves like not killing anyone, or doing things a certain way, for the sake of challenge or morality, which in turn allows for replayability further amplified by the choice between two different characters with different points of view on the story. Even though all actions eventually boil down to a binary chaos system, Dishonored manages to make a spectrum of small choices to feel significant and memorable.
This is the Dishonored we know, but better, with larger maps to explore and discover small bits of story, new powers to play around with, and more of this great world to immerse ourselves in.

I am a big ES fan and love this game.  I have no regrets in purchasing this game at all.
Here's my list of Pros and Cons.  These are based on my opinion.
PROS:
You move slowly enough through leveling (especially if you love to immerse yourself into the stories & not just speed through to your next quest objective) that it feels like the game could go on for forever, unlike some other MMO's I've played (not going to mention names).
I've played a few different races so far and the main quest lines are the same (mages guild, fighter's guild and main quest line) but all the other quests are totally different, so you don't get bored starting a new character as a different race.  I can really appreciate that since I love to play alts. Yes, every pact has their own starting area as well (there's three in total).
If you like crafting you can do all that this game has to offer, you are not limited to choosing what your MO will be.  Your crafting materials can hang in the bank (which is shared between all of your characters) so you don't have to lug that stuff around.
I do like the character creation, you can spend some time going through it all and perfecting your look, all very typical of ES games. You can even pick what voice you want your character to have, which is cool (and funny, if you imagine your character in the bathroom while you are picking your voice).
You can dye your armor, too (does not cost you a dime).
Your quest rewards are not bound to you, so if they do not fit your character build, you can deposit them into your bank and an alt can pull it out and use it.  In fact, a lot of items you can put on and use are not bound to you unless you dye them.
You can wear costumes to hide your armor as well, if you want a different appearance.
You can play a lot of the game content solo, which is a big plus IMO.  I hate nagging guild members, complete strangers for help, or waiting till someone can help you before moving on in your quests (GAH!).
There is no lag at all in battle sequences.  You hit your #3 button (as an example), your attack assigned to 3 executes as expected.  Some f2p games do not have a great battle response time (lag) but ESO does not.
The button assignments are very similar (almost mirror image) of PC Skyrim.  I really appreciate that.  That also means, battles play out the same, but ESO does have a bit of a 'guidance' system with ranged attacks - specifically bows.
The talk sequences are so cool (and so like other ES games), it really makes this game more immersive.
The graphics are awesome!
They will be adding more guilds (thieves guild, etc.) in the future.
CONS:
Sharing a bank with all your characters CAN be a negative.  You are limited on space, so sometimes you have to make tough decisions on what you want to hoard.  You can buy more bank space, it just gets pricey very quickly.
You are limited on how many guilds you can be in (some find that a negative), and all of your alts are in the same guilds your alts are in.  It is confusing.  Essentially, you are limited to being in 5 guilds, so guild chatter shows up in your feed from ALL the guilds you are in, they are just labeled g1, g2, g3, g4, g5 (you can color-code them, too).  At least you won't miss any juicy drama.  *shrugs*
I have not joined a guild yet, but I did attempt to start my own guild to see if I could use it as a bank (500 slots, mind you - that is a lot of hoarding), but it requires ten people to unlock and your alts do not count even though they are automatically in your guild.
You can only have 8 characters in total (some find this a negative, that's why I put this here).
You cannot change your facial/body appearance after you leave character creation.
Mounts are not cheap.
Buying additional bag and bank space is expensive (and yet, so necessary).
That's all I can really come up with!
Overall, I feel this game is well worth the money to purchase and play.  I will be playing this game for many years to come.  The negatives - for me - do not outweigh the positives.
The only recommendation I have for those of you considering buying/playing ESO: Unlimited: buy the Imperial Edition if you can throw an extra 20 bones towards it.  I didn't and regret it.  The ability to buy a mount for one gold shortly after you start playing your new character verses thousands of gold pieces and many levels later is a bummer.  Yes, you can still buy that package deal through the crown store (their in-game cash store), but it just makes more sense to buy the edition that already has that built-in, because it is cheaper.

I spent quite a few of my adolescent years playing Half Life 2 and its modifications. I started at Garry's Mod 9 and worked my way through the gauntlet of single player and multiplayer mods. Of course, this meant I spent hours on Friday and Saturday nights playing things like Zombie Master, and Zombie Panic: Source. By the time I was thirteen, I think I played just about every mod based around zambambos or infected under the sun. Little did I know, one of the best zombie-based mods was one which I wouldn't get to play for years.
In No More Room in Hell, (henceforth referred to as NMRIH,) the formula is simple: you and (up to) seven friends need to go from point A to point B without getting shot, bitten, bludgeoned, or succumbing to the horde. Very standard when it comes to zombo gameplay. Of course, there's a catch: ammunition and weapons can be scarce. And even when you happen to luck out and arm yourself to the teeth, you find that precious pharmaceuticals are nowhere to be seen. NMRIH is a zombie game that not only enforces the idea that you must be cautious, but rewards it This plays a vital role in your strategies to combat the infected.
Avoiding zombies is a fantastic way to keep yourself alive. Many zombie-based games and mods portray the horde as bullet catchers, nothing more and nothing less. However, with the scarcity of ammo in NMRIH, zombies are more of an obstacle and hinderance. Many maps have closed off corridors, sewers, or city streets with randomly spawning groups of ghoulies that force you to dip and dodge through crowds. This makes for a dynamic experience, as an alley that you found to be a much needed shortcut can become a bit of a problem in the event that you need to do a bit of backtracking, or in further playthroughs of said map. Strategies like this also create hilarious (see: not hilarious) situations where your friends are left in a crowd full of bloody biters. Fun!
While the gameplay in NMRIH is some of the best I've experienced from this sort of game, it also captures the atmosphere that many shambler-centric mods for Half Life 2 strived to attain yet fell short of. The moment you land at the menu of NMRIH, the music sets a precedent for what you're probably about to experience. Beyond that, the score for your entry into the map of your choice just feels dark and somber. In fact, everything in this mod has an air of dread to it. Even in situations where things are going right for your group, there's a sense of hopelessness lingering. You know damn well someone can be get reckless and find themselves keeling over to an infection minutes later, or come across a horde upon expending your last rounds. NMRIH sets out to create a harsh and melancholic environment, and, in my opinion, blows most other mods out of the water.
In a recent update, the developers added a special keybinding. One they claimed would "protect your friends from your advanced infected state." Punching your own ticket. A macabre subject, but one that comes up in nearly every bit of zombie media. If you're infected, you can only prolong the inevitable for so long. Just this feature adds so much to the game itself, as I found myself making damn sure that I kept one bullet in my pockets in case things were headed south. A bit dramatic, sure, but the needs of the many do indeed outweigh the needs of the one.
NMRIH is a dark, unsettling, and very tense experience that I'd gladly recommend to anyone looking for a challenge.
Tread carefully however, because when there's no more room in hell... well, you know.

This has been a game that we (even I) wanted forever, and especially after the disasterous Aliens: Colonial Marines.  This catches the time of the first movie with its 1979 Sci-fi look, and the music is always nailing it at all times.  The atmosphere is the most impressive I have ever seen in an Alien game, and is the best so far hands down.  I've played horror games before, and because of the predictable AI I felt that there was no challange even on the toughest difficulty.  Since the Xenomorph has a none scripted, unpredictable AI I felt like I have found my match, I hid under a desk, it went by, and once I got out, it had turned around and therefore I was in its sights and I got mauled.  Though you may still be a little unsure about this game because of IGN, Gamespot, or other reviewers who reviewed it very badly, just to let you know, this is a very, very good game.  The IGN reviewer as I remember said to have the game on it's easiest difficulty.  Well don't go by his word, as he probably thought that this was a CoD game, and I think that the reviewer on Gamespot got kind of confused and thought it was a straight on action game. (although it can be but there's a huge risk of getting nomed by the alien)  But I implore you all to do the game on the hardest difficulty, because this came from Gary Napper (lead designer) that the meat of the game is learning what the alien is capable of, and that is true.  The levels are extremely well made, and you (and even the alien, other people, and androids) have multiple routes to take.  I've never been so scared by a game like this in a long, long time, and if it can get my heart racing, then it is a great, true horror game.  So if you want the crap scared out of you, then Alien: Isolation is the best one you can get. And another thing, this is around 15 hours or more to complete, so you'll be scared longer than any other game which is great.  If this review has helped you decide to buy this game and you enjoyed it, then leave a thumbs up.  Thank you for reading, and stay safe from getting your skull chewed on by the alien, Peace.

Brutally terrifying with an excellently created atmosphere. You really feel like you're in the Alien universe and not just on a space ship with an alien. The cut scenes are fun to watch with beautiful graphics (I MEAN DAMN THOSE EYES ARE GORGEOUS!) and great theatrical angles. Then the writing really hits it out of the park with realistic reactions from different and interesting characters. This really is the game that gives the fans exactly what they've been waiting for with a few good treats for those of us who enjoy movies all together.

This is the Alien game we've been waiting for so long. The atmosphere and the whole world it creates is top notch, the gameplay is rock solid, Alien ai: terrifyingly clever. The game stands well on its own, and within Alien franchise for sure. With a 15-20 hour long campaign (apparently) you're definitely getting your money's worth.

A truly great Alien game, destined to be one of the few classic attempts at a video game set in this universe. A wonderfully slow build up and a pace that lets you drink in every moment of terror. Strange how intimate the relationship between you and this silent alien slithering about and trying to kill you in lonely corridors feels after a while. I even get a Stockholm Syndrome-like twinge of gratitude and even affection for it when it finally leaves me alone for a bit. The look of the levels perfectly evokes retro 70s sci fi and it is great to spend time in that world.
A visceral experience that is rare in gaming, Aliens: Isolation evokes the primal, heart-thumping fear of being hunted and powerless, which we remember from some dark forest of the past. If you like the Alien movie, and particularly if you appreciate the fact that evoking true dread requires a slow, creeping and relentless pace, this is the Alien game for you. There is plenty more to do in this world than flee from the creature, but lurking behind everything else is this cunning killer, returned finally to its rightful place at top of the monster food chain.
