Before Buy: I, like most people, absolutely hated this game without ever playing it. I got on the ESO hate-wagon and said I would never buy it blah blah. I believed the game would fail and that going free-to-play meant the end of it blah blah. But I also hate WoW so I think most my hate stemmed from the subscription cost, which has been gone for a week now :).
Why I Bought: It was spring break, had the cash, had no plans, why not spend $60 on a game just so I could make fun of?
After the Buy: My mind is blown at how good this game is. There are a few games that make me spend 60+ hours and counting on it. All the people hating on this game need to play it before they hate on it, and the people who still hate it after playing do have a right to state their opinion and MMO's just aren't for everyone.
Graphics: 10/10 when compared to other MMO's, but 7/10 compared to other games. This game actually looks like a game and not just a bunch of low-polygon, texturized, low-budged, 3D film characters running around. The game is also diverse enough that you don't feel like you are looking at the same building, tree, rock, etc. over and over again.
Lore: 9/10, ESO dives into the Elder Scrolls lore which is quite rich when you consider that the Elder Scrolls games start back in the 90's with the release of Arena. There is so much to read if you take the time to read it, but that is the downside as well. I would also dare to say that Elder Scrolls has a richer lore than WoW.
Action Bar: 8/10, the action bar is really frustrating with it only having 5 skills and 1 ultimate. But when you consider how devastating the skills can be if you arrange them correctly it does make sense. PvP would be at a permanent dead lock if a class had more than 5 skills equipped (my dragon knight would be an unstoppable tank if I could use all the defensive and offensive skills).
Combat: 8/10, it brings the Elder Scrolls feel in how you can use any weapon no matter what class you are. Though classes do favor some weapons over the other in how well the weapon meshes with the class skills. Also the collision detection is phenomenal, I have yet to get frustated by a phantom reach (cough cough DARK SOULS cough cough). There is a solidness to the combat as well, each hit resonates with a solid strike, blocking a strong attack offsets the enemy, attacking an offset enemy makes them crumble to the ground, it is a satisfying combat experience.
Player Base: 10/10, I have played games that were populated by ***hole players but so far I am always satisfied with interactions had. Players are willing to converse while out doing a dungeon together, are willing to help out quite readily, and there is very little rage quitting.
Justice System: 8/10, I enjoy this part of the game and how it gives you a break from the general mechanics of it. When I first started the game I went and stole myself a nice set of armor, a shiny sword, and then sold the rest of the loot to a fence. Also attacking NPC's can be hilarious, I broke into a house and the owner was being annoying, but beware that only a few NPC's are killable so sorry trolls and griefers.
Looting: 6/10, I will admit that gaining gold is really frustrating. Little gold is actually dropped and you get most of it from selling your loot. If you deconstruct your loot you can turn it into a lot more gold if you invest into crafting. In dungeons each player has their own instances of loot and there is no rolling for the best item at the end of it (I like this aspect a lot).
Leveling: 5/10, I am frustrated with the level system. Leveling is easy until you reach 30 because it seems after level 30 players stop doing dungeons and just go to Cyrodil (PvP); doing dungeons was the easiest way to level up. Also allocating your skill points is a pain with how strategic you have to be, but to be fair it is really fun to strategize on how to allocate points to optimize your build.

Picked this up to play on stream with a friend this week.  I highly recommend it, but with a few caveats.
First, the graphics.  I ran everything on the highest setting and the game looked fantastic.  I have a geforce 1060 6GB card and never experienced any real hiccups or rendering issues, which, to me, is crazy for a game currently in the 0.5 version.   Light effects are beautifully done and the movement of the light sources is handled so well.   Changing the terrain feels quite visceral as if you have a shop vac and the terrain is made of play-doh.   I always play the rather portly explorer and his movements are just fantastic.  When you hit a low grav area it's basically like you are playing Mario.
Second, the sound.  The soundtrack is fantastic and I highly recommend picking it up if you can.  That said, there were several glitches that happened with sound.   Being caught in the storm is very intense on your character and the game does a great job of making it feel that way and sound that way.  A few times I would not hear the storm coming and then would see the stones flying around me and the sky darkening.  Not that bad, but was a bit jarring at the time.   There's not a lot of sound effects to the organics you harvest, but the ships/modules moving around are great.
Third, the gameplay.  The game is heavy into farming and research; two things I love to do in games.   You take apart the world to expose materials that you use to build new components to both your vacuum and your buildings.   There is currently no method of upgrading things, you simply build the new module and add it.  By default, you pull up soil with the item you are farming which permanently changes the planet and this can later be a problem as you could theoretically completely strip mine a planet.   The amount of resources required for building is fairly nominal which is for the best considering the amount of effort you may have to go through to stay alive away from your base, as oxygen/power become issues.   You'll find ways to mitigate these issues in time, but it brings me to my largest caveat.
Lastly, my issues.   The scale of the game is a bit off at the moment.  If I were playing this as a single player, it would probably take me quite a few play sessions to build a proper compound and be ready for space exploration (or maybe I'm just bad at video games, who knows).   With a friend, we managed to research most of the tree and ended our 10+ hour day with a quick jaunt to two nearby planets.  Honestly, I was in awe of this and probably looking like a kid in a candy store on stream while we were landing on new places and just looking up to see how the sky was different.    I think I would have taken a much slower approach if it were just me farming up the materials we needed, but having a friend to go farm/grab research pieces while I kept the generators running really helped move things along.
Overall:  Loved it.   It's well worth the small price tag associated with it and the developers should be very happy with what they have created so far.   I will be in from time-to-time to check new updates and maybe grow my base a bit, but won't have as much to keep me in game every day at the moment (aside from a few more hours of exploration and base expansion).    I've logged about 14 hours at the time of this review which is a little over $1 an hour for what I paid.  That's a huge bang for your buck.  So just get it already.
p.s.
There are some issues with tethers creating lag issues after you've placed, like I had, hundreds of them ... so try to play a bit more conservative with them.   Build a rover, get some mini batteries/oxygen tanks, or something to avoid them in large quantities.

I've been playing this game since it became accessible on Steam. It started so simple, and has grown into a complex and adorable game. It's basically a first-person farming simulator, but without all the obnoxious wait times and "rushing".
Pros:
Graphically beautiful and adorable at the same time.
Literally the cutest and most laid-back game I've ever played. It's a great game to play when you're feeling sad.
Plenty of variety and things to do now that it's been developed more.
Lots of secrets to explore and find.
No need to wait for food to grow if you're impatient. You can sleep for the night and your crops will be done.
For me, lots of replay value. It's fun to challenge myself to see how much money I can make in the shortest amount of time, or how quickly I can find all the slimes.
Cons:
It starts really slow, but it ramps up quickly, then eventually you run out of things to do.
Even with the ranch expansions I feel like always run out of plots to build stuff.
Would LOVE a mini-map that you have to fill in with exploration or something.
So, I mean, for an early access game it's got a lot to do, and it's crazy fun, but you're probably only going to get around 6-8 hours of gameplay if you only play it once.

I'm a big fan of zombie survival rpgs and I must say this is the best one I've played. Granted the graphics are low res and the combat is pretty simple, but thats not what I'm tipically looing for in a game like this.
For me, I'm interested in the difficulty of surviving, which this game does perfectly with food, water, sleeping, stamina, blood loss, ect. even things like lung cancer from cigs, dehydration from alcohol, even insulin for diabetics, this game takes it to the next level!
The next thing I look for is community building. In games like state of decay, you can only build bases in certain locations and your community can only be so big. In survivalist, you can build as many bases as there are materials, wherever you like, you can even calim or destroy previously existing buildings, and you can potentially recruit every character in the game.
After that I look for social/political dynamic and this game nails it! There are a multitude of shanty towns, gangs, communities and so on and so forth and every single character in the game has a unique personality and story. Even the characters most people would just shoot, if you actually talk to them, you can learn that they have a story too. There are so many living communities that you can ally with or declare war against or recruit from/trade with and nothing is scripted. Theyre serviving just like you and one day their crops might die and they might come to you for food, or they might go to war with another faction and get wiped, or someone might burn down some of their fence right as a horde is approching and they dont all survive the invasion lol who knows? sky is the limit.
Another thing i look for is replayability, basically is the storyline made in a way in which I could play it differently over and over again, and my answer is yes. There is enough content to be explored to the point that I think the game could keep you content for at least 3 playthroughs. Roughly 150hrs of playtime.
Overall, not a perfect zombie survival game, but the best one I've seen so far. I hope they base any new ones off of the concept established in this game. 8.5/10

Let me start this review with the following:
1. I've encounted very few bugs and no performance issues at all bar 3 crashes to desktop with no event log errors. My rig allowed me to run the game max out @ 1440p @ roughly 100fps, as such, I can't really comment on the technical problems this game seems to have per multiple sources, though naturally,  the coming patch at the very least serves as acknowledgment from the devs. that there are issues and hopefuly those will be adressed quickly.
2. I very much value story driven games with non-linear levels and opportunities for exploration and different approaches to problem solving, as such, this review might be biased since Dishonored 2 falls neatly into the mold.
3. I did only one semi-stealthy completely non-lethal playthough for Corvo, and yet to play as Emily.
With all that said, I think one full playthrough of the game is enough for me to provide a brief review of this product.
In short: This is a must buy for any Dishonored or Thief fan, and even Bioshock / Systemshock fan. This is an extremely well-made story-driven single-player experience and I dare to say one of the best games that came out this year.
So, what do we have here is more Dishonored, bigger, better, smoother. The levels are very well made, with some extreme attention to detail put in certain places, and overall the artists and designers made sure that the game oozes with Atmospohere.  The story is fairy predictilbe, but in Dishonored, I would almost argue that it's the journey that matters, rather than the overarching plot - you listen in on conversations, quick-read notes and exerpts, listen to music and audio records, break into appartments and even do a few shop robberies if you fancy that sort of things, and it all clicks together. I never got the feeling that "this level is 110% artificially created", for the most part Karnaka feels very believable.
Gameplay-wise the controls are quick and responsive, on higher difficulties enemies do spot you rather quickly if you aren't careful enough, they react to sound, open doors, etc - it's your standard fair, but NPC's do their job fairly well. Naturally, you don't have to sneak, since Corvo is the very definition of cheese (as I am yet to play as Emily, I can only wonder if she also has the same insta-win combos) and won't lose to anyone in any fight ever as long as he has vertical blink, but sneaking in this game is genuinely fun and provides a completely different experience as oppose to rushing head on
Presentation-wise the game is stylized, to make it look similar to Dishonored 1, only with more attention to detail. The "Void Engine" is a modified Id Tech 5 (or at least it looks like it, and behaves like it), and as such it allows for some nice eye candy and lots of details when it comes to filling environments with clutter and making it look believable. If I had to make a comparison, I'd say it looks on par with Wolfenstein: New Order.
Sound - The voice acting was very solid, ambient sound adds to the atmosphere, weapons and firearms sound alright - overall it's decent, and there was not a single instance where I would shake in dissapointment.
Now, the most imporant part: Enjoyment.
Well, since enjoyment is a very subjective criteria that is hard to gauge I will say this: I loved every minute of my playthrough. I was looking for a single-player-only experience, with solid story, great atmosphere and well-made stealth gameplay and I got all of that tenfold.
If narrative-driven games with non-linear level design is your cup of tea then at the very least try this game when it's discounted. If you played and like Dishonored 1, whether you played it as a stealth game, or an action game or a mix in between - this is a very likely must by from you, because, well, it's more Dishonored.
If you played and liked Thief, Thief 2, Theif: Deadly Shadows or Thief "meh" edition (the 2014 game), or Bioshock / SystemShock series - give Dishonored a try, through I'd say play the original AND the DLC for the original Dishonored first and then jump into Dishonored 2.
If you only like CoD or DOTA and tried and did NOT like Dishonored 2 - this game will probably dissapoint you as well.
Thank you for your time reading this review. I hope it was at least a bit helpful.

It was excellent as a mod. It's excellent as a game. I feel the price could be a bit lower, $15 seems like a more ideal starting point for anything running on the Source Engine at this point especially in Early Access when we're still waiting on Xen, but regardless, what this is is a finely crafted masterpiece that stands up there with official Valve games in presentation and quality. It also stands as an example of how I believe modders should be able to make money from their work, by starting off with a free base and using that to craft something that is genuinely retail quality, and going through official channels like Greenlight to become an official product with all that entails instead of the vaguely defined rules and assurances and horrible implementation of that disastrous Workshop incident with Skyrim.
If nothing else, buy this game as a statement of how mods turning into retail products is supposed to work, following the legacy of the likes of Counterstrike and Team Fortress and Red Orchestra. But better yet, buy it because it's just an awesome game, squeezing the best graphics seen yet out of the Source Engine with superb gameplay that fills a gap in the Half Life universe many gamers hadn't experienced due to Half Life 1 being before their time.

Okay. It's time for a review to this. I'll base this review mostly on the state of the multiplayer of the game.
First the TL;DR: Nope, not going to recommend it right now. Too much things went wrong after release.
Now, what is different from previous CoDs? Well, you got a jetpack. So basically you can jump and dash around very quickly which increases the speed of the game even more than before. Something fresh! Some people may call it "ripping off from Titanfall", but really, Titanfall has jetpack jumping and wall-running while this has jetpack jumping and dashing. It's more like comparing "Matrix with jetpacks" vs "Quake with jetpacks".
Create-a-Class is very much similar to Black Ops 2, with a "pick-13" system. So if you know Black Ops 2's class-builder you'll know what this one is all about. Has some things changed, like adding Exo-abilities (activateable abilities to boost something, like movement-speed, health or make you harder to see for a short time) and removing Equipment (only one grenade-type can be carried now, no more combo of Frag/Flash or something). But other than that mostly the same.
Time to kill is between Black Ops 2 (TTK was rather long here) and Ghosts (TTK was basically melting in 3 bullets) so that's fairly fine, but some weapons need balancing.
PC-Port is also pretty well in the hardware-department. Runs pretty good (way better than Ghosts did), but is FPS-locked to just above 90 FPS. FOV can be set in-game. If you want more infos to al that, do go and check Youtube for TotalBiscuit's Port-Report to the game.
Now, sounds good so far, right? Well... The state of the game went down south now after release because of some things.
First: SHG suggested that they'd give the game dedicated servers for matchmaking (a system used in Black Ops 2). But nope, is the generally bad P2P-System. Means there's lags and - a point I'll get to in a bit - cheaters have it way easier with that.
Second: Cheating. According to some sources (most of them coming from the cheat-makers themselves) the game features a very poor version of VAC, one that basically doesn't function. Their reasoning with that is that VAC is 32-bit while the game runs 64-bit. According to SHG the game also uses a Demonware-Anticheat (some middleware), but I HONESTLY don't feel ANY effect of that. When you queue up to find a game you can be pretty sure that half your games you find has at least one cheater in them. It's pathetic, and there's been reports that you can just snatch a copy of the game for less than Counter-Strike GO costs right now if you know the right sources. So there's basically no end to the wave of cheaters coming in now. It will eventually get even more out of hand than Ghosts did, just before Infinity Ward actually turned around and said "damn, we must do something now...".
So yep. Mostly based on those two factors I'd say "nope" about recommending this right now. It may be that this changes in the future, but so far, SHG was very silent when it came to support for PC. Even so far as that the most recent update for the game only hit XBone and PS4 now. Usually they release updates parallel for all the "new-gen" platforms.

What a rollercoaster of a game this is.
I initially thought there would not be enough content for me to enjoy solo however it's been eighteen hours already and I haven't even started researching space craft or any of the associated technology.  It was a really fun experience getting lost and deciding to try to find my way back, and I really appreciate that the developers went to the trouble to include non-technology related mechanics that allowed me to find my way back to my base.
The terraforming is magnificent. The only thing I would change is I would improve the flattening tool such that it brings all ground around it level to the ground in the centre of the selector. As it stands I find it relatively confusing/useless.
The under ground experience, while initially fun becomes a tedious game of run-tether-run-tether. I experimented with driving a wagon train of two Small Rovers under ground with a bunch of small batteries and a generator but it was made arduous by power management, holes to lower caverns, and object clearing so I abandoned that effort. The above ground experience is much more enjoyable and I love the vehicle train mechanic.
Once you understand it the inventory mechanic in this game is great. I really enjoy the Medium Storage mechanics on large base structures.
I find the friction in this game a little off for my tastes: Ground vehicles behave as if the tires are clad in teflon and are extremely light weight, and walking down slops can be a little absurd at times.
And now I'm at the end of the review word limit!

Machine animations are wonderful, exploring caves and lanscapes for minerals is dangerous and exciting, managing inventory and storage space to balance cargo and power/oxygen is challenging, finding materials in wreckage sites is rewarding, expanding your base is hard-worked for, inclement weather is scary and thrilling, even the multiplayer is solid.

ASTRONEER opened my eyes to the reasoning behind the Space Core.
Now, let me explain. A friend and I, both having Steam accounts, occasionally buy games for eachother, and find games we can play together. For a very long while, the game we primarily played was Don't Starve Together. But then it got out-of-hand and crazy and we lost interest. So we were just kind of floating adrift, no games we really played that extensively or seriously. We downloaded some old games we both had, maybe played that for a bit. But for the most part, we never really played anything significant.
That's when we stumbled upon ASTRONEER.
I had watched an ASTRONEER playthrough on a YouTube channel, so finding it again lead me to believe it would be something fun to pick up. My friend LOVES space, and probably eventually be a future NASA employee, so I thought it'd be a nice gift for the both of us to play online.
I told him about it, we both bought the games ourselves. Ever since we bought it, the game has quickly replaced Don't Starve Together in every aspect. The graphics are absolutely FANTASTIC. This game looks beautiful, from every mineral to every landscape. Absolutely gorgeous game. Whoever is designing the graphics, bravo, bravo.  The gameplay is great as well. The game highly focuses on exploration, which is benefited by the limitless amounts of things you can find, and the graphics. The 3D aspect helps this as well. Your really just exploring with a friend the numerous cave systems, crashed spaceships, and etc. The game doesn't have a tutorial either. You have to figure everything out yourself. And as soon as you figure stuff out, it's an accomplishment. Everything you do in this game is an accomplishment. Researching a blob, mining some compound, building a tether system to a cave; all of it's truly great.
However, the game is not polished well. It lags on even good computers. It's buggy, and events in the game will bog the game down a sizeable amount, especially sandstorms. It's also really confusing to find how some things work. You WILL need Google by your side when you're trekking the planets. It's a little contentless, but hey, that will change.
I may have only 4 hours now, but my friend and I will have around hundreds. This game has replaced that special game for us, and rivals the likes of Don't Starve, besides the flaws.
I'd reccomend to wait a little bit more to buy this if you are thinking about it. Perhaps until the next big update. Perhaps until release. You never really know with Early Access games. But still, if you buy it now, you have a darn good game at your hands.

I'll say it once, and I'll say it again. This game is beyond repair. Incompetent developers, as well as publishers, have let this game slip into decadence. Updates to this game are very little; often just minor bug fixes and occasionally a new weapon which is typically only able to be unlocked by paying for it with real money. Developers have constantly teased the playerbase with an alleged engine update, which has been in the "works" for almost three years, which has had progress shown twice.
When players said that APB: Reloaded is pay to win, I often brushed them off and called them a crybaby. But now that I look back at this game, I see really how pay to win this game was. Having premium (boost to your XP and cash gain) halves the cooldowns of your abilities such as Field Resupply, taking the powerful ability from a two minute cooldown to a measly one minute cooldown. Not paying for premium also greatly hinders your customization capabilities, aswell as progression as a player. Getting to the higher ranks level gains slow to a crawl, and the grind demands extreme amounts of time.
Don't be fooled by the seasonal events, they've been in the game for years. The christmas event has been in the game for almost 4 years now, and has reappeared each time with nothing changing. The same thing applies to other events, nothing has changed. We haven't seen the release of a new map since the literal release of the game.
So, do I recommend this game? Hell no. Don't come near this god awful shipwreck of a game. It should have stayed dead when Realtime Worlds shut the game down in 2010. Instead, it was revived and used as a method of taking the money from every single weeaboo and furry to ever lay eyes upon this festering pile of refuse. As a person playing since 2011, please

Dishonored was wonderful, and Dishonored 2 is mostly more of the same, and that's a very good thing. The level design is still masterful, the powers are still tons of fun to play around with, and the writing and world-building are still among the best in the industry.
Where changes have been made, they are also welcome. Emily is a fun protagonist, and her powers are different enough from Corvo's to encourage different tactics. New enemies, like the clockwork soldiers, also make for a nice challenge (and a nice opportunity to vent your violent urges if you're doing a no-kill run).
On the negative side, it seems many people are still reporting performance issues, though I didn't encounter this. I did get some weird graphical glitching a few times that required restarting the game: it seemed to happen immediately after launching or not at all, so it wasn't a huge deal since it didn't interrupt me while I was in the middle of playing.
The biggest issue for me is that Dishonored 2 seems, overall, buggier than it's predecessor. There were two bugs  I noticed repeatedly: First, the clipping seemed a bit aggressive at times, which would prevent me from crawling through some small spaces unless I approached them jusssst right. Not a huge deal, but in a situation where you're trying to hide quickly before you're spotted it can be annoying. The other bug I encountered was that enemy AI would sometimes randomly decide to go into high-alert mode and go looking for me, shouting things like "where is she?": they would do this when I had not been spotted at all, ever (I did a ghost run), when they were full buildings or streets away from me, and on levels where I hadn't even killed or knocked out anybody yet, so there wasn't anything to trigger them. Kinda funny, really, but also a shame since it kind of disrupt's the game's otherwise excellent atmosphere & sense of "reality".
For me, at least, those bugs ended up being minor annoyances. If you're not affected by performance woes, then Dishonored is just as magnificent as its predecessor and well worth your time.

The first of the Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell series is, without a doubt, the definition of stealth that we had been looking for in video gaming for a long time. A bit rough around the edges and with a dubious production, this game beat all odds to launch one of gaming's most recognized stealth franchises to date. That being said, this game has not aged as well as Pandora Tomorrow or even arguably the greatest in the series, Chaos Theory.
The graphics for this game are still top notch for what was considered to be top of the line at the time of its release. It wasn't pushing the Xbox completely but came close. The areas are well defined, the shadows are masterfully used to set the scene and going without the night vision goggles on constantly guarantees some rather astounding sights, especially the oil rig and china levels. However, the game is quite dark and players learn to rely on their night vision goggles early, cancelling some of the amazement of the scenery as everything is viewed in dark-greenish/gray. Today, the graphics have not aged well. The models look very dated, as does the scenery in general compared to later games in the series.
Sound/music wise, this game still holds some edge. The opening song still puts people in the mood for some good stealth action, while the environmental noise/music in most of the stages helps set the tone for stealth. The detection music as well as the combat themes get the blood and adrenaline pumping as you find a way to escape conflict or end it through epic gunfighting. The other sounds from interacting with objects are down perfectly as well, which makes me wonder how Sam Fisher still hasn't been heard by the guards...
Which brings me to the actual AI. Admittedly, there are far better guards than these, or far worse guards. Either they have eagle vision if you're even slightly out of the light and will see any form of movement, or they will be so oblivious that even when you're right next to them in the darkness, they won't see you due to the way the game is designed around using shadows to hide rather than just cover. Being in total darkness means that as long as you don't bump into them, aren't directly in front of them, or don't make noise, they will never see you (which is somewhat, but not entirely, realistic). In combat, they are terrifyingly accurate if they can see you. If they can't, they will almost always miss, opening them up to a headshot to take them out. They also have a bad tendency to rush to a body left in the open for them to see, leaving them open to an untimely demise as well.
As for the actual physics of the game, they also tend to be quite rusty. The movement feels somewhat stitled, and particularly on the PC version, there are times where collision detection is extrmeely buggy, often making the player stick to the terrain or not be able to make several jumps. Lighting and vision is off as well in the PC version, allowing enemies to either see you or not see you depending on the circumstances. The lighting is also off on the PC version, due to the projection lights not showing, meaning spotlights are impossible to see. This can ruin gaming experiences, unfortunately, as one level in the game is very much impossible without being able to see where the spotlight is. (no spoilers here).
Combat in this game is also oddly done and generally, you are encouraged to avoid it. When you have to engage in it, aiming mechanics are simple but Fisher has a hard time hitting anything with just the normal crosshairs when it is too far away, making getting up closer and person with the enemy a necessity for consistent hits. With the SC-2000, however, that vanishes entirely. The alternate fire has endlessly useful tools at your disposal, and it has a scope, meaning that sniping comes into play during combat, which greatly changes the dynamic. Just be sure to to get used to holding your breath with the alt fire in scope mode if you don't want it to be waving all over the place.
The controls in this game are also where the PC port falls apart. On the console, they work fine. On the PC, they generally work okay as well, but they get around the issue of changing your walking speed by mapping it to the mouse wheel on the PC's mouse. You can generally map this to something else, though a good chunk of the other buttons are taken for something else. Jumping is not done with space-bar by default, but rather is the shift key, which is a pain to get used to for people who are used to PC platforming. The menu is on the "Ctrl" key which is fine, but also hard to get used to for people who might be used to the tab function being the key generally used for inventory mapping. On the console, everything felt streamlined and perfected. In this, the controls are flimsy and hard to get used to for those not adept to keyboard+mouse controls.
The last urksome thing that this game chose to do, that has been an on/off staple for the Splinter Cell series, is forced combat scenarios. There are scenes later in the game that you are automatically put into high alert and have to fight off people who are trying to kill you. The game's already clunky combat controls are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to work with already and being required to use them, when the rest of the game encourages pure stealth and remaining invisible and anonymous to bypass obstacles, was a terrible game design choice, one that was fortunately minimalized or foregone in later installments.
That being said, this is still a game that should not be missed. The lighting problem that I was talking about earlier can be solved by going through the ini file and changing the coding. It works beautifully. Courtesy to the forums at UbiSoft here:
The keyboard and mouse controls are clunky but with enough time, offer an arguably high amount of playability, particularly with the aiming mechanics using the mouse rather than a control stick. And with enough knowledge of the physics, several bugs can be avoided. And if all else fails, console commands are your friend with the PC version, as is quick saving (a function that was added in the HD version, but not available in the original console version). If you're comfortable handling some more clunkiness in order to play an old classic, then definitely try this game. It may not hold up to the standards of its successors but it was the game that launched this phenomenal series and turned it into the gaming giant it was today. Oh, and the story is worth seeing through as well. Please, give this game a try. Give it some love, as it still definitely deserves it.

BroForce is easily one of the best early access games I've played. If you'd like to see a playthrough of the campaign from the newest update see below. If that doesn't convince you of it's awesomeness, keep reading.
BroForce is basically about a group of thinly-veiled parodies of various action movie stars/characters with Bro substituted somewhere in their name fight masked terrorists (?) called Mooks in Vietnam because 'Merica. While there is basically no story, it doesn't really matter because the gameplay is quite fun.
It's a shooter in the vein of Metal Slug and similar games where you're running left to right and shooting/blowing up various things, from Mooks to giant armored tanks. There are a few different game modes and this is the general idea throuhout. While you can only shoot left or right (apart from one Bro who shoots down) the enemies do the same so you're not at a huge disadvantage. On hit will kill you but if you save a Bro in a cage you switch Bros and gain a life (this is also how different Bros are unlocked, each with a certain number of rescues to the next unlock). One thing this has going for it however is that nearly all terrain is destructable. You can literally flank a Mook by shooting a tunnel underneath him and emerging behind him. It's also not unheard of to accidently (or not so accidently) set off massive chain reactions of explosions as parts of the ground get obliterated and send exploding bits of things onto other things that would very much like to also explode, seeing as how all their friends are doing it.
Each Bro also has a unique special move that has a limited number of uses. They range from grenades, slowing time to even Broniversal Soldier's ability to ressurect dead Mook and Bros to help him. These are almost always helpful to get out of tight spots of get rid of particularly troublesome Mooks.
I also have to mention the campaign map. You fly a helicopter to different areas and unlock more by beating an area. The best part? You can hit the seagulls with the helicopter. Good times. At least for us (the seagulls not so much).
All that being said there are some issues:
-The white area of text (shown in their videos) on the campaign map that list the area and say LIBERATE! is a lightish black, making it hard to read. I don't know if it's every version or just Mac specific.
-Not all Bros are suited to every suitation and the only way to switch is by dying/saving another Bro. Saving a Bro is random which one you'll get, except when doing so results in an unlock.
-This isn't so much an issue as something to be aware of but it is possible to destroy enough scenery to make advancing impossible without dying to reset the level. Devs, maybe put undestroyable scenery at the bottom everywhere EXCEPT where you want bottomless pits?
-Expendabros is PC only (I need more BroForce awesomeness!)
The issues are pretty minor and there's enough content here it could be released now and still be one of the best Steam games but Free Lives is taking their time to make this a finely-polished explosion extravaganza. With a lot of early acces games it's hard to reccomend getting it until it's finished but BroForce has enough polish, content and (most importantly) fun packed in it that I can easily reccomend anyone toget it.

I'm not exactly sure how I feel about this Kinetic Novel. It's short, I've played just a little over an hour and that is with time afk to deal with other things. The characters aren't very well developed and mostly seem like caricatures, the most interesting, to me, was the last one we meet, the wanna-be-hero, and even then it kind of fell flat on its face.
The premise of it and the part we play, don't feel to mesh too well. One day in the 'real world' to interact with 'real people' in an attempt to alter the decision? I cannot believe for a second that any AI as..advanced..as she is suppose to be, would bother with something so inconsequential. She points this out, a few times, and it seems impossible to me that such useless things would somehow alter the decision she had come to all 9 times.
Which make the 'choice' at the end even more baffling. Only one answer works, the one that she has come up with 9 times so far. The other answer feels extremely forced and doesn't seem remotely plausible in the context of the story. To make it worse, the 'eplilogue' of the BS route is nonsensicle, almost entirely because of one thing: 'I'm a real girl now'.
And yet....I feel like this really had potential, that if more work and effort had gone into it, and the characters were made to be...well, characters instead of a caricature, and maybe, just maybe, Kyuu had been given a year, or hell, even 6 months, the options at the end might make more sense.
There was something here, but it fell short and landed on its face. And I find that really disappointing.

Here comes an honest review from someone who really digs this series.

:
Stacking boxes is much harder than it was in the original, thanks to the voxels, which make certain box ordering combinations from the first game impossible to pull off in this new one. Forklifts feel quite a bit different from the first game. They seem to get stuck on things more often, and seem to struggle picking up boxes at certain angles that were possible (and encouraged) in the first game. I haven't dug too far into the maps, but i'm fairly certain that a lot of these are just copies from the first game. The lack of new content in that department is quite dissappointing. Menus are not controller friendly at all (I have a wired xbox 360 controller for those interested). You cannot choose any on-screen options with the controller and must instead use a mouse. You can 'pause' the game with a controller, but that's as far as you can interact with the menu system if you're using a controller.
Speaking of the menu system, Storage Inc. 2 has one of the worst ones I have ever used. Menus are annoying (why can i choose a map from a button on the main game screen and not by pressing 'esc' at any given point?) or straight up confusing (1] getting into the 'choose a map' screen reveals a bunch of maps that you can choose from and add strange icons to with mouse clicks? 2]  when I 'finish a map' i don't feel like I actually did. The only time the game lets you think that you beat a level is when your deliveries have been done flawlessly and you have been greeted by a string of text that says 'perfect' at the top of a menu that pops up. If you don't have a flawless game (not missing one delivery, adding every + box that pops up, never letting a delivered box blow up thanks to a new one being delivered behind it) the game presents you with a 'try again' screen for committing just one infraction. This is weirdly discouraging).
:
The voxels look pretty nice, especially when you deliver a package and it explodes into little bits. Multiplayer is as fun as ever, and I love how anyone can play this at any skill level. The game's action is just as hectic as ever, and it is still very satisfying to create an ordered warehouse and pull off shipments quickly. I like the added + box to keep things extra tense and interesting while you sort boxes.
:
This is a step back for the series in many ways, but it's still one of the best games in the genre. For 10.99$(CAD) this isn't worth it, especially when the 360 version of the first game retails for 2.99$(CAD) and is better in every way that counts. If the price were less, or if the game were at least as good as its predecessor i'd recommend it, but until either one of these things happen I cannot recommend it.

Let me start off by saying that I have read most of the reviews for this game, both the good and bad ones. And after playing the game for about 7 hours, I definitely see where both parties come from.
You all know what this game is about so I won't go over that. Gameplay wise, it's great. The controls are as smooth as silk. Once you obtain the majority of your weapons and gadgets, you'd think switching between them would be awkward, but thankfully that is not the case. Your radar is assigned to the right bumper (did I mention I'm playing with an Xbox One controller?) and you hold it down for however long you want to hold it. Weapons are assigned to a radial dial on the B button. You can alsom craft items here as well. Y controls the flashlight, and everything else is standard FPS controls.
Now, about dat Alien. Is the Alien scary? YES. The developers weren't lying when they said the Alien was unpredictable and no two playthroughs would be the same. The first time the Alien stalked me, it came out of a vent and walked down a hallway. About a minute later, it came roaring down another hallway, saw me hiding under a desk, ran behind the desk and pulled me out and killed me. The second time, it ran down the hall and investigated others rooms, leaving me mere seconds to plan a route to another hiding spot. This game is tense.
Is the game difficult? Yes. Too difficult? That depends on your play style. Each area has taken me quite a bit of time because of trying to avoid the Alien at all costs. Some people may be a little more hardcore and try and simply get past it quickly. But because of how smart this thing is, the latter method doesn't work too often (though I was able to sneak past it a couple of times).
But because of the difficulty, the game does tend to drag. There was a point where I waited in a locker for a good 3-4 minutes as the Alien kept roaming up and down the hallway near the room i was in. On paper that may not seem like a lot of time, but when you're in the locker, constantly looking at your radar and waiting for those beeps to become less sporadic, it does feel like forever.
But I love it so far. It's tense, atmospheric, beautifully detailed, and scary.

Sadly PVP is a mess. This is Player vs Player. PVP is what many of the long time souls fans crave when the game has been out for months and and PVE as become redundant. PVP is sloppy with terrible slow controls. Terrible design choices like allowing to heal in Arenas. While some covenants are pointless or a grind fest to rank up. This game just isn't what the hardcaore soul fan desires once they step into the PVP half of the game. Much of the pvp involves people abusing the Avelyn crossbow for cheesy victories. This game is supposd to have dedicated servers altho lag can rear it's ugly head. It always seems to come out when magic is hurled your way or someone back stabs you from 15 feet away even though you were facing them. The hit boxes feel like they have extended too far off your body. You often get hit even though the weapon never touched you on your screen. Dark Magic is way too over powered. A lot of try hards with go the dark magic route for easy wins. The mechanics of this game ruin the classic 40 / 40 builds as they can never dish it out like a hybrid mage or faith/ warrior build can. The soul memory mechanic is terrible as level 400's have invaded my 145 slv character on NG+.  Poise is in rough shape as it doesn't work like it used and seems to be almost pointless. PVP just feels like a after thought and it shows. The Arenas are not that fun to particpate in.

DISCLAIMER:                 I know this has already been stated by everyone and their cousin's uncle's grandmother's friend's son's adopted child's cousin's neighbor's roomate, but this game is LACKING. Dark Souls One, or as I like to call it; "See how long you can survive hanging from a noose of your own entrails" provided the player with a challenge to rise up to the occasion of, including; death, monsters, weaponry you must train to use, death, monsters, DARK SPIRIT xXWutRUCasulXx HAS INVADED, and death. It was up to the player to formulate and strategize the world around them and overcome the obstacles. The controls were nice and all that too yadda, yadda, yadda.
Now onto Dark Souls II or as I like to call it; "A little gnome has allowed you to use him as a stepping stool to relieve the pressure of the noose we called Dark Souls."
SECTION 1:      This game tries to ride the rails of "The Hype Train" by giving you the nice cinematic at the beginning and then- SCREW THAT AREA, NEW PLACE! It feels like Dark Souls II is a little kid coming home from Summer Camp, showing off everything it did in one sitting. "And then I- I- I- Ooh! I made a castle!" I was utterly baffled when I went from SPOILERS: A venomous tower to a seemingly geographically impossible CASTLE OF FIRE AND LAVA. It feels like Dark Souls II WANTS to give you the adrenaline of challenge after challenge, but it does it in such a spontaneous manner it turns you off. The story is, well... Not there. The game literally tells you what you will do at the beginning and that YOU won't even know why. MORE SPOILERS: You know that wife (so wait, lesbians exist in the Dark Souls universe since you can be a female and somehow had a child? FromSoft, you cheeky dogs. :P) and child you had in the intro? POINTLESS, Dark Souls II wants you to see these nice new character models and mechanics! It then gives you the option of Route A, B, C, or D in terms of soul acquisition since you get ANOTHER FOUR SOULS TO EMBRACE? DANDY. Dark Souls II, you made that exact same popsicle stick house LAST time we sent you to Summer Camp... Anywho, the game continues on and you'll soon notice a relative theme here: Knightly beings and big suits of armor, oh, and those NOT knightly beings or big suits of armor here and there. And I know this is supposed to be a Fantasy Genre game but at least make the anatomy LOGICAL. You expect the Giants from Dark Souls 1 right? Nope, "Big Bubba"s with holes for faces that turn into trees when they die. And some weapons and armor from the first game appear. And you know how all items had some lore to them? Now it's all: "It's old! Why is it here? Did this event happen?"
And on to controls: Ugh. The controls feel so useless especially since now your character lurches forward before taking a step, like an old car slowly dying or an animal unsure of what to do which can lead to a misstep and falling to your death. And you slip and slide to where you feel like someone waxed all those decrepit caves and castles just recently.
Now for everyone's favorite: PVP! The PVP is still as refre- excuse me for a moment I had a stroke and almost said refreshing. What I meant to say was: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The PVP has little to no worth anymore like it did in the first game where upon trading in the lives of countless foes and allies, you'd be showered in the spoils of war. In Dark Souls II: "Hey I killed 30 people, what do I get?" "A chance to kill MORE people." "Ohh...*Groan*" And the ARBITER SPIRITS. Don't get me wrong, I've always enjoyed using those blue eye orbs in Dark Souls II to ruin some guy's day but when they're halfway through the game and in a locked to me area on the same Soul Level and I'm still at Heide's Tower, it feels kind of broken compared to how in the first game you had to be in the same area. Then there's the abilities this time around: Magic, Pyromancy, and the newest of them: HEXES. People hate Hex builds with good reason: The caster is so afraid to do anything they invest skills into spells that basically beat down kids on the playground for lunch money while the player can only suffer the beating while the caster stands behind the bully, arms crossed and full of pride and self-respect falsely given. Nice thing though is the addition of Voice Communication which is SELDOM USED. You'd think the community would want every possible corner cut in terms of winning this game, but instead they put cotton swabs in their ears while their 2 summoned chums are yelling for you to attack it in the middle of it's charging attack. And on the other side of this double edged sword, hatemail was removed which was also fun for PVP, but I'm not too scathed on the matter. And yes, ganks still exist with every covenant, get used to it.
****And now comes the momentary intermission in this review for you to go use the bathroom or fetch a snacky cake or what have you.****
Bosses: Everyone loved the Dark Souls 1 bosses, but this time around they are ALL THE SAME. Either a big monsterous cretin, a weapon wielding freak of nature, or a SUIT. OF. ARMOR. They all have their own attacks though that range from Puddle of hazardous material to stream of hazardous etc. etc. etc. And WE GET IT. YOU CAN STOP CAPITALIZING IT AS The Dark. Just call it Darkness after a certain point instead of popping up like a PC reminder saying: "Your computer needs to update The Dark. Update The Dark by clicking this bubble to activate The Dark's updating wizard."
Enemy types: Dark Souls II does offer a lot more in terms of enemies but at the same time does not. Old enemies, new paint essentially. You can see a decrepit soldier still reliving a battle long passed and then later on see that same enemy in an unrelated location only for the sake of difficulty maneuvering around its attacks in the limited area. And here's all the enemy types: Zombie, Armor, Freak of nature/science, person, giant, nature, OR dragon. No ghosts or goblins this time around. And the enemies DESPAWN which is like training wheels on a bike, give me back the challenge, not reward me for hitting this enemy for the umpteenth time by taking it away, limiting my experience.
Final point of this review, honest: The game has some interesting additions which I will NOT spoil for New Game Plus and so on, but some of them feel like they should have been there in the first place and that your first run through the game is a warm-up lap leaving you desperate for more to the point of by the time you get it, all you do is sigh and resume your completed already adventure. I'd love to reccomend this game, I really would, but it's kind of a downgrade.
Final Standing: Play at your own risk.

The first summarized feeling that I can express is that it seems to be bigger and a bit longer than original; but to my suprise Steam's statistic shown nearly exact same number of 66 and 62 hours for sequel and first installment respectively.
Before we go further I must warn you, that this comes from PVE-carebear who finished this game once and has no intention to do all those crazy NG+ stuff like many hard-core fans seemingly would. I died… well I can't really say a lot, but that's mostly because I summoned two phantoms for every boss and high-faith-lightning-spears-throwing build seems to be incredibly overpowered for beating AI. And I switched to it immediately after things got a bit tough.
Before that I approached the same leveling as I did in first game: lots of strength and relying on heavy two-handed weapon (I bouth Pursuer's Ultra Greatsword). That was halfway through the game if you're wondering. I already killed Old Iron King, did both Belfrys, and made it through the Warf, Forest and Bastille. I even finished Grave of Saints. Anyway, it was a pure-melee character. And I encountered those flaming lizards, you know them, if you finished the game. It doesn't matter if you know them, if you didn't. They were hard for me. Like really hard. I did little to none damage to them, but a few tries and that rolling around did the trick: I killed the first one, and then the second one. Third one stomped me. The narrow passage, the death-bringing fire spits, the horros, the wrong time to drink Estus. You know how this happens. The whole way back from the bonfire I hoped that they are treated like mini-bosses, and don't respawn. They did. I realized that either I can spend another hour trying to beat what seems like the hardest challenge I met in the game or I can visit them later. Some poison-arrows, some ranged stuff, which I was lucking. And that's where things got interesting. Rather than finishing later there is third option in sequel, one which original lacked. You can just redistribute your spents souls. And my inventory was crawling with all kind of stuff suitable for caster. And in a thirty minutes I was newly-born battle-cleric.
That sweet feeling of smartly overcoming the problem is good enough for me. It may be not as challenging in terms of perfect reaction, precise directional control and ability to automate sequences of same movements, but it doesn't matter for me. What I like in metroidvanias is that little hidden secrets left by developers. And in that sense Dark Souls is a proud member of the genre. Hidden walls, locked doors, smart usage of enemy attacks for opening new passageway, vulnerabilities of certain enemys — and most of those things not only present you with another glimpse of actually rich lore but make you more powerful or capable with dealing with some problem. And that's it, you just have to think and look for clues.
Second game's world became a bit more widespread, more star-shaped like with a central hub, that's it. It feels slightly more sensible or easier to decipher, but and in a many ways sequel actually is. Ability to change character build was already mentioned. And then there's less-restrictive weapon upgrading, and special rings that increase your chance to be summoned by your friend rather than stranger. It never goes as far as forcing you to navigate through complete dark area with deadly cliffs all around. That was what first game did. And while I admire this non-compomising approach of the developers, it was not fun. Yes, you could actually find a source of light before heading there, but that was so obscure, that I didn't. And I seriously doubt anyone on first playthrough without a guide would. So Dark Souls II changed a lot of stuff, that wasn't fun. It still sometimes isn't, but at least it doesn't irritate, and that's good.
It's steal hard to the limit, that I felt satisfaction beating it. It required time, dedication and work of thought. And it was worth it. It still is in a lot of ways beautiful. With that oblique beaty, that you won't find on the first look. This style develops with progressing in the game, rather than trying to blaze all guns at you at the first second. Of course it's technically crappy, and some locations look even horrible, but the overall design atones it all. It comes a long way from minimalism to grotesque staying true to itself and game atmosphere. And despite all transformations it never looks like an eclectic mess.
This post-apocalyptic fantasy world is still deep, depressing and has a lot of history it doesn't really want to share. Or at least it won't if you won't work for it. But that's okay. That's how metroidvanias work.

I was about 8 when I learned Black Mesa existed.
I hadn't played Half-Life 1 yet, but damn was I excited to see what it was all about.
I was 16 by the time of writing this review, and it made me tear up and almost cry.
Because I realized I had spent an entire half-life waiting for this game's release.

An excellent re-imagining of the original half-life!
If you liked half-life 1 then you'll definitely enjoy Black Mesa.

If you're a fan of Half-Life at all, chances are you'll probably also thoroughly enjoy Black Mesa. It combines the best of both Half-Life and Half-Life², into one very solid game, with the technology of the Source engine. If you played the mod version that was released about 3 years ago, you will be very surprised to see that the standalone version is almost an entirely different game, attributed to the amount of upgrades and polishing that has been done to the single-player campaign. Most of the weapons have new models, and all of them have completely new animations. The MP5, Hand Grenades and explosive Satchel Charges have received some gameplay improvements, with the MP5 now being full auto, rather than 3-round-burst. Hand Grenades and Satchel Charges can now be thrown much farther than in the previous version, and you can now cook grenades to have them detonate sooner after being thrown. Voice acting in this version is top-notch, with a lot of lines being re-done to do a better job at making the characters seem more like real people.
The new multiplayer mode of the game is really really fun, and it is very similar to the multiplayer component of the original Half-Life, although it currently seems to almost lack the ability to bunny-hop. Weapon balance seems to be pretty good, although in my opinion, the Tau Cannon's secondary fire should need to be charged for a longer period of time to be a one-shot kill.
Now for the big question... is the game currently worth it? That's a decision that I can't make for you. If you're a huge fan of Half-Life and you really think you'll enjoy what the game currently has to offer, then, by all means purchase the game. I see the $20 price tag as more of a donation to the developers than an actual price for the game itself. The Crowbar Collective has been working on Black Mesa for about 10 years at this point, and now is the best time for the community to show even more appreciation for their work. Black Mesa is outstanding, and it's only going to get better from here on out.
Bring back so much memories! Highly recommend!!!

This is a very short, but funny and well written Visual Novel (or a kinetic novel really, as the only choice it offers comes at the very end, while main part of the story is completely linear).
Apart from delivering decent humour and consistently good dialogues,
does surprisingly good job at presenting and giving resolution to its main premise. Kyuu is really amusing as the logical, cold machine with a bit of sarcastic humour added into the mix, while the situations and moral questions she encounters have a bit more meaning and depth to them then I would expect from such a small VN. But, above all, they’re all fun and interesting to read through (which also applies to the endings, rather predictable, but still very much enjoyable).
A funny short visual novel. Highly recommended to casual gamers and achievement hunters alike.

I will get to the meat of the situation here for those who are distrusting of this game as Ripley is to a Synthetic. The Alien, IS terrifying. We've seen it a hundred times in games, comics & movies but its never gripped me with fear and dread the way Creative Assembly have designed their monster here. This is an 8-foot creature of some kind with acid for blood, and it arrived on the Sevastepol. It kills on sight, and is ...generally unpleasant. It will stalk, hide, skulk and creep through every inch of this Space Station in order to make your life total sh*t. If you so much as breathe the wrong way in its general direction it will bend you over the nearest object ...and have you. Make no mistake, if you do not treat this creature as a 'true' intelligent threat, you will be playing sections of this game over and over and over again. The lack of a checkpoint system present in this game is brutally wonderful, instead it is replaced by a manual save system consistent to that of Resident Evil's type writer so if thats where you last saved and you're clumsy and you bite the big one... or the big one bites you... then thats where you'll end up loading back to when your hands have untensed from around the controller. or mouse and keyboard, but don't fret these save stations are in abundance (at least 10 hours in they are.) Its a gameplay mechanic that has been locked away in hypersleep for far too long and makes a welcome return back into the realms of this survival horror.
If you're a fan of the franchise and specifically the first movie, knowing every line, every scene, every set-prop, you my friend are going to have the most authentic Alien experience that life can offer you right now. You will assume the role of Amanda Ripley and own that little piece of the Universe all for yourself. The attention to detail in this game is absaloutly on a 1:1 scale with the original 1979 movie. You will breathe the dank atmosphere, you will live its claustrophobic environments and you will survive the terror that awaits you beyond that airlock, There is no greater homage to the Alien franchise than this.
Creative Assembly, you F'ing owned this.

I am unimpressed with this game.   Obviously this  is a port from a console... X-Box or something, and it sure shows.  But that isn't the real problem.
This game lacks depth.  It's basically a base builder/resource gather type game.  But it was too easy, so the developers threw in the twist that one of your starter colonists has diabetes, and you scramble like mad the first part of the game trying to buy/cheat/and steal your way to keep her in insulin so she doesn't die.  They try and make it moral dilemma, by throwing in marginally easier options to obtain the insulin early on, by stealing and causing trouble between two rival factions.
The combats are mostly harmless once you aquire a couple shot guns.  Those that aren't are easy to steer clear of until you're ready.   One of the biggest problems with the game is the limited camara field of view.  There's no scroll out, and your primary character can see about 10 feet for some reason.  Zombies hurl themselves at you from off screen as you explore new areas, and this is what passes for a fun combat system for most of the game.
The base building aspect is actually pretty well done, with a good balance between resources needed to construct new buildings.  Beyond that, there's not that much innovative with the game.  Simple graphics, a sound track that could have been ripped from some Euro-Electric rave, make the entire title feel like a PC one man indie title.
Don't get me wrong, I'm all for indie games, but if you want a much funner and more engaging challange, try Rimworld or Judgement Apocalypes for PC.  Both titles have the depth and fun game play you'd expect for PC games.

TL; DR: No Man’s Sky has billions of star systems to explore, and yet I was somehow captivated by scooping colourful poop FAR more that should be allowed.
One of the rare early access games that caught my eye via Jim Sterling, and as soon as it was on sale I decided to buy it. Even though it’s still in development the updates come regularly, there still tons of promised things that will be implemented, and I have NO reason to not believe they will come through with everything, because everything they said will be implemented was implemented! The version of the game I’m currently playing (at the time of writing this) is 0.4.3c and even in this state it gave me tens of hours of fun!
It has a certain cartoonish feel and since you’re scooping poop for a living, there is nothing to complain about here. Other than that, the Unity engine it uses does it’s work and really shows what Unity is possible if your idea doesn’t involve blocks and zombies (Google UnitZ Jim Sterling) and you’re capable of transferring your idea on paper onto a 3D medium. And the developers of Slime Rancher have done just that. The graphics presented here are JUST right, from the lighting to the physics everything works as one would expect!
The world is BIG, I mean it’s not Skyrim big, but believe me I was happy once I got my 3rd teleporter, because it’s big enough to be an inconvenience when you need to go to a part far away! Loading on my PC is instantaneous, so I can’t really say if it’s good or bad, but MY personal experience is excellent!
There isn’t much to say about the sound. The soundtrack playing in the background kind of blends with what you’re doing. Other than that, all I can say is that everything has a sound and everything works as intended.
The gameplay becomes slightly repetitive, but the game always gives you more tools and things to do within the game world. In this version of the game it took me about 18 hours to create a full self-sustainable ranch and get all the achievements. And I still haven’t found all the treasures and I haven’t even gotten all the upgrades, AND I haven’t even seen the secret Slime that you need for one achievement, so there is still loads to DO! And the world still has so much secrets I need to explore.
There are (JUST) a few things that do bug me and I hope that the developers read this:
: 9/10 (I'm 110% sure this will change to 10/10 once they release version 1.0.0)

Campaign: I did not finish the entirety of the campaign, however from what I did play, I felt that the mechanics of the story (newly introduced things such as walking up walls) were introduced, used for a few minutes, and then not really revisited much, if at all. It is a decent story, but pretty similar to what we have seen before and not really long enough to validate the game's price at this moment. Throughout the entire campaign, I was able to run it at 60+ FPS on Ultra graphics, with more or less all other settings at maximum.
Multiplayer: This is the part of the game that I have played a lot more of. I have about 6 hours of gameplay in the multiplayer aspect, and it has been pretty dissapointing. The construction of the maps have anice feel to them, and their layout was definitely built with exosuit parkour in mind.
The class creation system is very similar to that of Black Ops 2, in which you have up to 10 "points" that can be spent on any form of equiptment, as well as wildcards. I have personally found this system difficult because it feels as though there are enough slots for an adequite primary and secondary weapon, with perks and even one wildcard. Regardless, you have enough space to make a fairly decent class.
Also something new to Advanced Warfare is the loot drop system. Every X amount of minutes, certain actions (dying, calling in a scorestreak, getting a kill, objective, etc) trigger the drop. Inside there are generally three objects, and the contents can range from different "flavors" of weapons, clothing, and reinforcement items. As far as weapons, through leveling you unlock the vanilla weapon, standard color and no attachments by default. Weapon variants you unlock can have different rarities, forced attachments (regardless of what you have unlocked), and special patterns. Clothing is just different with every piece you unlock, and really introduces a new form of customization we have not seen before. Reinforcement drops consist of timed scorestreak drops, and also the chance to find 45 minutes of double XP, a pretty nice perk.
Scorestreaks are pretty much the same as they were in Black Ops 2. They are not only unlocked through killing players, but also through gaining points from playing the objective.
What I found most dissapointing about the multiplayer part of the game is the actual performance of it. As I mentioned earlier, single player performed very well at Max settings, however multiplayer is quite the opposite. For this part, it is important that I mention my internet connection is around ~30Mbps down and ~10Mbps up, while my ping is generally very low. The multiplayer aspect as a whole is verry laggy and horribly optimized. Some maps, when the game starts drops the game to single digits frame rate, both on max and minimum settings, which is unacceptable, especially on such a high end graphics card. Aside from that, during most multiplayer maps, (all matches tested were TDM, with occasional domination) had frame rate fluctuate A LOT, with mine (on LOW) ranging from 12 FPS to 94 FPS, and this was merely wandering the map looking for enemies, not with things exploding everywhere.
Overall, this game is certainly a step-up from the abomination that was Call of Duty: Ghosts, but it still has a way to go before this game is anywhere near worth purchasing for the PC. The single player campaign runs very well, and is interesting, although fairly short and in my mind does not justify the price. Multiplayer, while keen on introducing new mechanics to the series, runs absolutely terribly, almost to points where multiplayer matches can be unplayable. While the new loot system and exosuit is neat, there is no justification in how bad the multiplayer runs. Unless you have money burning a hole in your pocket, and you can get this game on a good sale, it is absolutely NOT worth buying right now, unless you really like the CoD campaigns.

At the heart of Call of Duty Advanced Warfare is a really fun game, probably the best CoD in the series since CoD4. However the game suffers from the CoD syndrome in which a predictable story and lack of engrossing singleplayer affects how good the game can really be. Also I’m kidding about pressing F, there are no QTE’s here.
Much like most other recent Call of Duty’s, Advanced Warfare is a military shooter where the player gets access to many different weapons and gadgets to use all throughout the campaign only to never be used again. One of my biggest complaints in regards to that style of gameplay in the single player is the gadgets are just gimmicky and removes any feeling of choice of gameplay style in the campaign. The big improvement in this game is the player’s exo suit that allows for many different abilities including boosting your damage, having a shield that pops out and being able to use boosters to give you essentially a double jump. I feel like this adds the most to the game in that it makes the gameplay in both single player and multiplayer a lot faster and a whole lot more fun. You can get to ledges you wouldn’t have been able to otherwise and also dodge midair if you need to. This brought an aspect to the multiplayer that was missing in subsequent Call of Duty’s, a speed much like that of the original Quake’s. The multiplayer is a lot more fun that it has been in the past and with the added difficulty of getting kill streak rewards, it now relies a lot more on skill than it used to. The game still suffers in MP with campers in corners like other CoD games but with the advent of the quick boosters it is a lot easier to avoid those players. It also seems like a lot of people haven’t gotten the hang of the boosters yet, even some of the higher level players. While playing myself I noticed a lot of players that just weren’t using the boosters and couldn’t get the hang of it while a select few in the server were absolutely dominating while using them. It seems that it added a bigger learning curve than a lot of former CoD players are willing to learn. That isn’t necessarily a bad thing however.
The campaign of CoD:AW starts out following a couple of marines including your character (Private Mitchell voiced by Troy Baker again) that are getting ready to disembark some ship in order to fight back the advancement of North Korea into Seoul. All during this mission you get the basic tutorial of how to use the exo suit along with learning about the current events of the world. When you finally get to your objective, some artillery bot, your best buddy gets killed and you lose your arm. During his funeral you end up meeting Kevin Spacey’s character, Jonathan Irons, who happened to be your best bud’s father and is also the CEO of ATLUS, a private military contractor. Irons offers Mitchell a second chance including giving him a prosthetic arm and a place in a Special Forces squad. Now this might be spoilers however it should be obvious seeing how Kevin Spacey usually always plays as a bad guy, but eventually Mitchell discovers a plan by Irons to take over the world. Mitchell’s first missions included going after a Terrorist organization called the KVA in which a man by the name of Hades plans to remove the technology of the world. During this pursuit, the KVA successfully destroy a lot of nuclear power plants that displace a large number of population in NATO countries and their allies.
This allows for ATLUS to provide security to the world while they hunt down the KVA. After Mitchell kills Hades he discovers that Irons has a plan to take over and control the world with a biological weapon in his hands. There was a humorous point in which Irons goes in front of the UN to tell them that he has this weapon and will use it unless they obey his control. I will say that Sledgehammer did bring back that which I personally loved in CoD4 and that was stealth “sniper” missions. Those were a nice change of pace to the high action of the campaign and brought a lot more story and character development to the game than a fast pace action “Ramirez do this, Ramirez do that” type of game play with endless soldiers spawning. However the campaign still has those kind of missions and in some instances the pacing is all over the place. You skip around from location to location with no real in between explanation other than an unskippable cut scene. At one point you are fighting North Korea, another you are doing a simulation and walking around a base, then followed up with a few action missions, stealth and action again. The game is short too, only 6 hours, so it never really takes the time to create an engrossing story but instead just gives lots of explosions instead. On top of that at a lot of instances it is nothing but Quick Time Events which doesn’t add much to gameplay other than the game saying “hey you haven’t done anything for a bit, click this button.”
Now the graphics in this game are impressive and are the best in the series but it comes with a technical bug/limitation. As I wrote a week ago or so, the graphics textures are tied to the amount of VRAM a video card has. If you run out of VRAM based on settings being on or off then the game automatically decreases the texture resolution regardless of how much better the memory core clock might be.  The 2nd screenshot above was the texture resolution set to low thanks to me not realizing this earlier in the game. The main card in my current computer is a 780ti and despite it having only 3gigs of VRAM it can use that VRAM much faster and more efficiently than say a 670 that has 4gigs of VRAM. But despite all that the game still set the texture resolution to low unless I set my supersampling to 2x instead of the 8x it was original set to. You can see the comparison shots between a 670 with 4gigs of VRAM and 780ti with 3gigs here:
. Despite this I can say that this is one of the better looking games out there and it feels like they improved on what they had previously unlike what they claimed Ghosts could do. The game also runs well and when I had supersampling down to 2x, with ultra textures and everything up on max, I was able to easily get 80-90 fps.
Now the sound is quite good especially from the two main voice actors Troy Baker and Kevin Spacey. Troy has done his usual great job with his character but Kevin Spacey was so well done that I must give him a lot of credit for bringing his mannerisms and likeness of his past characters to this game. All I could think about all during the game is how much he played very much like his character in Usual Suspects. Calm and collected while all the time creating a façade to his real persona. The sound effects and music aren’t bad however they weren’t anything spectacular either.
Overall this game is a great addition to the Call of Duty franchise and is the most fun I’ve had with a CoD since CoD4. The campaign may be pretty mediocre and predictable but the gameplay itself and how much fun multiplayer is more than makes up for that shortcoming. Despite a few bugs and a lack of dedicated servers this is in my opinion a must play for those that like high action multiplayer

The game that started the entire series. If you enjoy stealth, then this is the right game for you! Starring Sam Fisher voiced by the famous Micheal Ironside.  Warning ahead of time; the controls and movement is a little clunky. In tight situations, the controls will fail to help you at most times...time your movements correctly.
The story is amazing, characters are easily enjoyable, even though some of the script is a little cheesy, but still hilarious at most times.  The equipment that you recieve is easy to use. The further that you go through the missions, the more gadgets you get, which is a plus.
The missions get harder, as you progress. Changing the from lethal to non-lethal, alarms to no alarms.  The security expands and the cameras are harder to avoid.  The game really tests your patience and strategy.
There are some glitches that can help you in a few missions, when its really not going your way...which reminds me, save frequently.  You're going to run into difficult situations, and saving is your backup.
A good idea if you don't want to get spotted is to shoot out lights, hide bodies in dark areas, and throw objects for distractions.  Stick to the shadows (obviously), thick darkness is your best bet.  Save your ammunition, don't rely too much on your gadgets.
Overall, this game is amazing.  Patience is the key...if you don't have then go watch CenterStrain's videos on youtube for a wonderful stealth-through
