Dark Souls returns in an unforgiving 3rd-person RPG rogue-like. You will beat your head against difficulty until you experience the glorious realization that you were doing it wrong. I would say DS2 is more newbie friendly by design (not the enemy), but that doesn't mean much: there is no guidance, NPCs & Pathways you need to progress are still hidden or obscured, and you will die... a lot.
Keep in mind I played solo without any help most of the time and I am writing generally from a solo perspective. Playing solo does make Dark Souls harder but also far more interesting.
The bosses are generally imitations of the boss from DS, this is good and bad. This means you don't have strange/interesting boss like sif ( a dog with a sword) or cool/horrific demons (gaping demon), but then you don't have any/many stupidly annoying boss (Snorlax&Pikachu).
DS2 is the opposite of DS in some ways: the game is very open at the start with the pathways to game completion becoming linear latter on. But in most ways DS2 is more of the same DS which I suppose is a good thing.
Online play has been improved significantly with no widespread online hackers, invasions being more optional than insistent, more people can join, and the various purposes of the convenants are more meaningful. So now you really want to stay human rather than staying hollow and do a covenant when online. Online play does make DS2 more interesting.
This is not an awful port like DS1, having said that you can tell DS2 wasn't designed for PC (eg. VOIP is default disabled and no push-to-talk). No Modding support, in fact you risk a VAC ban if you try. Using a dual-thumbstick gamepad is a very strongly recommended even though the keyboard support is functional this time.

Fortunately I've not encountered the technical issues a lot of users are experiencing. The game runs well on my PC @ medium/high settings (nVidia 980 GTX). The DRM is an abomination and angers me as a consumer. That said, let's get to the game itself.
As is to be expected, it follows in Dishonored's footsteps, but provides a much smoother and varied experience.
+ I love having a choice between Emily and Corvo. Both feel quite distinct.
+ Powers have been refined; they're a lot of fun to use.
+ Gear is much more varied. New types of crossbow bolts and mines have been added for additional tactical choices.
+ Combat feels very fluid and 'visceral'. Really well done.
+ Significantly more options than before for solving missions. Full combat, full stealth, mix, speedrun -- everything is possible and viable.
+ No more magic guard respawns. You can actually clear areas.
- In general I find sneaking much harder than in the first game, guards seem to have eagle eyes. And those bloody civilians ratting me out to guards tempt me to go on a murderous rampage. This is compounded by the following issue:
- AI is wonky. Sometimes guards will get stuck in place or do some really weird stuff, requiring a reload if you're unlucky and want to complete a full ghost run.
- No "New Game+", though we might possibly get that patched in in the coming weeks.
+ Level design is detailed and interesting. Treasure seekers and explorers will love this world -- there's little stuff going on EVERYWHERE, be it unique conversations, treasures, or little 'side-quests' (that don't show up in the journal) that include, amongst others, saving people, breaking into shops, or making public speeches.
+ The reactivity of the game world to your playstyle is mindbogglingly well done. It's true, you have to play it at least twice to notice all the differences. So many choices to be made!
+ NPCs are significantly more varied, as are the areas: basically, no district / level feels the same, it's a significant improvement over Dishonored 1.
+ I like the more nuanced Chaos system, now not every kill counts the same. Killing baddies will be okay-ish most of the time, but kill an angel and take the chaos hit. (I could nitpick a bit but that's spoilerish and too detailed for a review.)
+ Investigating thoroughly opens up frequent unique remarks/oneliners of the protagonists that help give them personality. I especially loved evil Emily's quips.
+ The lore has evolved from Dishonored 1; it's a joy to learn more about the new world and its people as well as about characters / regions that you've already seen in Dishonored 1 -- if you want to, of course.
- Main antagonist is recycled, including the end-game flavour. Bit of a dampener.
+ The voiceacting in general is great. Emily's is fantastic; Corvo's not so much... (though I may be a bit partial here.)
+ The art style is consistent with Dishonored 1, which was already unique, but more detailed and significantly more varied.
+ I love the music; especially the title track is very catchy.
+ Some manage to feel downright creepy. Music, diaries / voicerecordings and graphics can make going through these a rather unsettling affair.
- Subtract 1 from the score if you put a large emphasis on viewing distance and close-quarters texture quality. I personally do not find the deficiencies in these areas significant enough to justify a point loss, but others may not share this opinion.
Dishonored 2 is a fantastic game if you are lucky enough not to run into technical issues. If you liked Dishonored 1, you'll love this as it's a much more refined experience. The game could use some bugfixes to the AI and a "New Game+" mode, however.
For me, Dishonored 2 is the best and most fun game I've played since The Witcher 3.

I've bought this game a long time ago, it was a solid base game with good fun, and potential with new content begin released. However its most recent update completely changed the gameplay, the game is now very buggy. And even though there is plenty of content it is very hard to get to see any of it. With the new update, i have started 10 games, out of which 1 only got to be semi-fun. The lack of resources, and unlocked research as you start the game, make it very hard to progress. And generally a grind to play.
The game used to be about exploring the planet, discovering fun things, and building your base. Now you build your initial 2 buildings and are left to wonder.. what now. You don't start with tethers anymore, so you can't go mining for research. And the 1 single run out of 10 happened to have 2 trees with some research pods on it, not the research you need to actually progress ofcourse. If a 10% chance of maybe having fun is enough reason for you to spend money on this game, then by all means do. But in it's pricing bracket and genre, there are tons of other games that will guarantee you a good time. Take a look at those instead, or wait and see what the dev team for this game does with this new direction.
As for bugs, the ingame options menu is not interactive in windowed mode, you have to go fullscreen to change options. Making changes to volume settings, put a weird echo on my ingame actions. And turning down all audio options to 0 did nothing.  The only way to "mute" the game is through windows audio control panel. Dropping or dragging interactable objects/research through structures and letting go will get them stuck in whatever you dragged them against. They sort of clip into each other and become none-responsive. Mind you, i've noticed these bugs in merely 30-45 minutes total of gameplay. Who knows how many more bugs there are.

I will get to the meat of the situation here for those who are distrusting of this game as Ripley is to a Synthetic. The Alien, IS terrifying. We've seen it a hundred times in games, comics & movies but its never gripped me with fear and dread the way Creative Assembly have designed their monster here. This is an 8-foot creature of some kind with acid for blood, and it arrived on the Sevastepol. It kills on sight, and is ...generally unpleasant. It will stalk, hide, skulk and creep through every inch of this Space Station in order to make your life total sh*t. If you so much as breathe the wrong way in its general direction it will bend you over the nearest object ...and have you. Make no mistake, if you do not treat this creature as a 'true' intelligent threat, you will be playing sections of this game over and over and over again. The lack of a checkpoint system present in this game is brutally wonderful, instead it is replaced by a manual save system consistent to that of Resident Evil's type writer so if thats where you last saved and you're clumsy and you bite the big one... or the big one bites you... then thats where you'll end up loading back to when your hands have untensed from around the controller. or mouse and keyboard, but don't fret these save stations are in abundance (at least 10 hours in they are.) Its a gameplay mechanic that has been locked away in hypersleep for far too long and makes a welcome return back into the realms of this survival horror.
If you're a fan of the franchise and specifically the first movie, knowing every line, every scene, every set-prop, you my friend are going to have the most authentic Alien experience that life can offer you right now. You will assume the role of Amanda Ripley and own that little piece of the Universe all for yourself. The attention to detail in this game is absaloutly on a 1:1 scale with the original 1979 movie. You will breathe the dank atmosphere, you will live its claustrophobic environments and you will survive the terror that awaits you beyond that airlock, There is no greater homage to the Alien franchise than this.
Creative Assembly, you F'ing owned this.

Close to two years ago, to the disdain of many, one of the greatest accomplishments in modding history became a full-fledged game with an asking price. While some decried this move, saying that the full release didn't have enough new content to justify the price/buying it instead of just playing the mod, others took the move as an opportunity to finally reward the team for their work. This ended up placing the game into a kind of early access morality limbo, that still sparks heated arguments on video game discussion boards to this day.
Well, I can gladly say to those who're still holding out that the amount of content that's now on offer is definitely worth the asking price. While some segments still lack polish, the game as a whole works well as an accessible alternative to the somewhat dated original Half Life. Additionally, anyone who really just wanted a visual upgrade to that game can have it their way with the installation of a few workshop mods. Just about anyone can find their ideal Half Life experience through this title!
As a side note: Xen's remake is honestly one of my most anticipated releases of the next year. If the Crowbar Collective deliver on their promises, this should finally be the definitive version of HL1 they promised all those years ago.

TL; DR: No Man’s Sky has billions of star systems to explore, and yet I was somehow captivated by scooping colourful poop FAR more that should be allowed.
One of the rare early access games that caught my eye via Jim Sterling, and as soon as it was on sale I decided to buy it. Even though it’s still in development the updates come regularly, there still tons of promised things that will be implemented, and I have NO reason to not believe they will come through with everything, because everything they said will be implemented was implemented! The version of the game I’m currently playing (at the time of writing this) is 0.4.3c and even in this state it gave me tens of hours of fun!
It has a certain cartoonish feel and since you’re scooping poop for a living, there is nothing to complain about here. Other than that, the Unity engine it uses does it’s work and really shows what Unity is possible if your idea doesn’t involve blocks and zombies (Google UnitZ Jim Sterling) and you’re capable of transferring your idea on paper onto a 3D medium. And the developers of Slime Rancher have done just that. The graphics presented here are JUST right, from the lighting to the physics everything works as one would expect!
The world is BIG, I mean it’s not Skyrim big, but believe me I was happy once I got my 3rd teleporter, because it’s big enough to be an inconvenience when you need to go to a part far away! Loading on my PC is instantaneous, so I can’t really say if it’s good or bad, but MY personal experience is excellent!
There isn’t much to say about the sound. The soundtrack playing in the background kind of blends with what you’re doing. Other than that, all I can say is that everything has a sound and everything works as intended.
The gameplay becomes slightly repetitive, but the game always gives you more tools and things to do within the game world. In this version of the game it took me about 18 hours to create a full self-sustainable ranch and get all the achievements. And I still haven’t found all the treasures and I haven’t even gotten all the upgrades, AND I haven’t even seen the secret Slime that you need for one achievement, so there is still loads to DO! And the world still has so much secrets I need to explore.
There are (JUST) a few things that do bug me and I hope that the developers read this:
: 9/10 (I'm 110% sure this will change to 10/10 once they release version 1.0.0)

I am neither a COD fanboy nor a hater. I am just an average gamer who games a few hours a day.
First, I am really surprised to see a fresh new COD rather than a mediocre shooter.
Then, let's just start the review.
There are many pros in this game.
1. Graphics. It is a giant leap for COD series. This game is a true next-gen game. New technologies like Bokeh DoF, SSS shader, Deferred rendering, Tessellation, and more are used in this game to make it look epic.
2. Sound. The sound effect team did an awesome job to increase the immersion. Especially, the weapons sound like real weapons not like toy guns in previous COD games.
3. Voice acting. Voice actors played well. It helps shape the characteristics of people.
4. Gameplay. The core function is about the same, but there are various approaches to win. And in single player campaign, every level is giving you fresh air.
5. Great story. It's somehow predictable but it is logical and reasonable. The story goes smoothly. I like how they made sarcasm about U.S.
However, I still have some complaints about it.
1. My keyboard doesn't work. I tried to plug it into every usb port, I tried to restart windows, and I tried to restart the game. But no use at all. So I played it with a Xbox 360 controller. It is fine for me to play the campaign, however, when it comes to multiplayer, OMG, it is unplayable. There is a aim assist option, I leave it as checked but I don't think it will work. In one match, I was killed 10 times before I killed one guy...
2. Cutscenes are laggy, don't know if it is because of my low frequency CPU. I just found that it was too laggy that when I opened the game, the COD title screen stopped but music went on. I didn't the title intro before main menu came out.
3. Multiplayer. I have no problem with no dedicated server if they make multiplayer consistent. I cannot find online games. It will take 10 times to try before I successfully join a game. And most of the time, it gives me "server not available" error...
4. Music. Please hire a hollywood movie composer like Hans Zimmer to make an epic theme music. Hans Zimmer did an excellent job making MW2 theme, and 5 years later, the COD AW theme still cannot catch that level. The theme is forgettable and not epic either.
But overall, this a great game. A great new start for COD.

This is a great game, yes it has its flaws and its dev team can be very untrustworthy for what they say. But all in all this game is awesome. The biggest cry you will see out there is "P2W" and "Hackers".
This game is far from P2W, one of the most powerful weapons in the game is the Starter gun known as the STAR-556 with its big brother the N-Tec, both f2p weapons that can beat ANY gun at ANY range with the proper amount of skill. In fact around 90% of the games Premium Weapons are Re-skinned versions of the f2p varient with a different look and sound (N-Tec=CR-5[AK->M16]) granted there are a few weapons that are unique in the premium (ARMAS) store but they are far from P2W, requireing a situational or unique playstle to use/master, the problem comes down to price with permanant premium guns costing $20-$60 each.
The next cry comes from hackusations. Where as i found hackers are really far and few in between depending on your server (EU servers and Asian Servers have time and time again proven to have more hackers 10 fold) and when you do encounter a hacker they can be outplayed just like any other player. Wallhacks wont help you here, aimbots only aim they dont account for recoil or dispersion.
This game is great even at its current state, where most of its negitive reviews come from F2P warriors that cant even afford a summer sale game or a runescape membership and people that just cant cope with its learning curve (which is very steep). But once you learn the game and are able to stick with it, you will LOVE it. with endless customization and tons of laughs to be had ive found myself playing this game over Triple A games.
Give it a shot and dont give up too soon.

This game is excellent, it's a great concept, great design, great art, and has great balancing (mostly). The thing it lacks is player count. The average player knowledge of the game is... lacking. This is true even in the highest levels of ranked play as it's entirely possible for very new players to be placed in games with the best players in the world (or at least the region). This is entirely because the game benefits players who go on small win streaks in their quialifing matches with too much elo and then places them in matches where, in order to cut down on match queue length, the game places people together with widely varying elo ranges.
If all you're really looking for is casual play with some variation on the MOBA style, this is a great game. If you're looking for a game with a very competitive ranked play mode, you're going to be somewhat disapointed. There's tons of casual modes to choose from, Arena, Joust, Siege, and Assault are all outside the realm of the 3 lane MOBA map with slight tweaks to the mentality of the game. These modes all have strengths and weaknesses, and are one of Smite's biggest faults. These modes are all fairly imbalanced as a result of the game being balanced around Conquest, however the game presents Arena as the premiere game mode, leaving Conquest and its meta a mystery to the newer player. This is because the meta changes often in the premiere game mode as a result of balancing changes to buff timers and camp spawns, something that's changed multiple times over various Conquest map incarnations.
I'd say pick up Smite, have fun with it, and enter ranked play if you really want to try hard, but don't expect people to know what they're doing or what gods or items do until you get really, really high in ranking, because the player base just isn't there, and what is there is mentally challenged on multiple levels more often than not.

takes place in the not-too-distant future. For decades, scientists have been constructing more and more powerful supercomputers hoping that one will give an answer on how to save Earth from the problems of environmental degradation and other issues. However, the answer is always the same. Either mankind must go extinct or be enslaved. People lose hope, but one scientist, now elderly, constructs the latest supercomputer/android. He builds it to resemble a regular teenage girl and calls her Kyuu. It is Kyuu's mission to spend one day among human society and learn about mankind through direct interaction before casting final judgment on whether or not humanity must perish.
This game is a visual novel, a type of game that is entirely story-driven. It can be played through as fast as the player can read it. I would guess that one play-through should take only around an hour. Unlike other visual novels, this one is mostly linear with only one choice late in the game. There are two different endings to achieve.
The art in the game is pretty good with detailed-enough backgrounds and well-drawn CGs. The sprites in the game are necessarily limited with only some different facial expressions. The music is quite good as well and forms a good background to the main story.
Of course, the main thing here is the story. What this game manages to be is a pleasant combination between comedy and philosophical musing. The comedic aspects mostly come from Kyuu's character and the situations she finds herself in. Being an android, she only tends to think and speak in the most robotic and logical ways which constantly clash with the irrationality of the people she encounters. The more philosophical part comes into play when Kyuu is wondering if humanity is really worth saving. She finds many faults with the people she encounters, but these faults just might be what makes humans good, if not always perfect.
I think my only real criticism of the game is that, especially in the first half, there are a few too many dirty jokes/toilet humor. I will admit that I certainly do not mind some of these types of jokes, but considering the short length of the game, it felt excessive.
Overall, this is a great free visual novel that contains good art, an interesting story, and humor. If you like visual novels and are looking for a short story, I would recommend checking this game out.

This 4th visual novel and 2nd free to play visual novel by Zetsubou feature an android with a schoolgirl appearance Kyuu and her creator, an unnamed professor who has spent many decades working on the best supercomputers money can buy to calculate and predict whether humanity will survive and can be saved with the impending destruction of the planet. After having been disappointed time and again with the same prediction that humanity must perish entirely or be enslaved despite numerous hardware and software upgrades, the professor decides to make one last wish out of Kyuu, to spend one day among the human populace and report to him on whether she would still hold true to her existing belief that humanity must be wiped out entirely.
The story and plot is written like a science fiction comedy with appropriate background music and optional pop-up windows that can be opened to describe more on various scientific and computer technical terms. Soundtracks, CGs and overall game presentation are good. Recommended as a free to play visual novel for those who like a short visual novel with science fiction and humour in the story or for those who like a short game to finish and get all achievements in less than 10 hours.

Utilizing technological advancements and the dependency humans have towards it, supercomputers called 'companions' virtually seize control of the job market and serve as a reducer of the human reproduction rate. You play as the most powerful one named Kyuu, and after assessing a day in the life of the typical person, it's her responsibility to judge whether eliminating mankind will save the planet or if cooperation between androids and humans can benefit the planet. Humanity Must Perish is a kinetic novel. Well, almost a kinetic novel as you will have to make a choice in the end. But given the price, as it's free, you should really try it.
Kyuu is an android whose purpose is to find how to save Earth. The only answer is either destroy mankind or enslave it. Before the final decision, its creator gives a last directive: spend time outside in order to gather data and decide if humanity will survive or not.
Kyuu will see the worst but also the best that humanity can offer but what will be the choice in the end?
That choice, it's yours. And the only one in the game that you can make: either save humanity and propose solutions or wipe it out. Given the fact that you have both achievements, you bet that you'll do both. However, what's making that kinetic novel interesting, apart the title, is the fact that you'll have terms which will be explained. Some may be obvious for anyone having knowledge in computers but it's still a great idea to present Linus Torvald or to explain what's an OS or Android or even... what's cosplay.
That fact alone is why I've downloaded that free game. While I understand the message behind (make something to preserve the planet and to respect it), I think that people will be more appealed by the facts stated than it (or they will be attracted by the possility of ending mankind).
The drawings are also good, even bordering on fanservice. I really liked the dialogues too: between the young girl and the otaku girl, without forgetting the young man in the end or even the pervert with the dog, it's really funny: imagine a robot being mistaken for a real girl, that can't even understand the word "pee". Yeah, it's great.
The soundtrack didn't really stuck in my head but it was fitting to the game.
Anyway, you have comedy, philosophy and interesting information in a short game, with achievements, multiplatform and for no bucks. What are you waiting?

is a free and short, almost kinetic visual novel with a philoso-scifistic theme: ís humanity worth its trouble?
It begins as a supercomputer in the shape of a teenager girl is sent to spend a day among the mere mortals in the not so distant future of Earth.
Their mission? To learn and realize an answer to the question: to destroy all the humans... or not?
The android Kyuu approaches everything matter-of-factly and strictly logically. Naturally, this results in all kinds of peculiar and silly situations.
Frankly, I felt the humor was often forced and mediocre, though otherwise I enjoyed the writing and the fatalistic theme. The side characters are executed well, even if rather stereotypically, and the length of the piece (about 2 hours) is adequate for a free novel.
Visually, the artstyle is anime-like, though everything is depicted by still-pictures. All characters have several facial expressions, which brings them alive.
Music is pleasant and futuristic but ultimately forgettable.
One should note that while the writing was alright, it contains lots of technical terms from computing. However, the terms are adequately explained with in-game info boxes. This slows down the reading a bit but at least one is not left in the dark in case of unfamiliar terms.
Curiously, the game allows one to skip the (as self-proclaimed by the game as technically challenging) introduction.
The alternative skips the other main character, the professor, almost altogether and replaces his story by a bland onslaught of insults from Kyuu.
Kyuu comes off as entirely different personality because of this: hostile instead of skeptical, condescending instead of merely clueless.
Needless to say, I urge you to check the full introduction regardless. It's cool, ominous, and way better than the alternative.
The whole thing is less than 2 hours read (or you can skip through in 5 min and miss out...). Being free and decent, it's an intriguing way of spending those couple of hours.

Edit: This review is based on multiplayer experience. Single player runs significantly better although still not at 60 fps all the time especially once you expand your base alot. Also single player is pretty much bug-free and the rovers work better. All the glitches I experienced were apparently multiplayer related.
The game is a terribly optimized (especially when you are hosting multiplayer), buggy mess with major oversights that render it much more unpleasant than it could be.
There is some fun to be had for sure and I enjoyed my time on the first planet for the most part but once you expand to the other planets, you realize that nobody had a second thought about how the mechanics that work just fine on the first planet incorporate into the other ones.
You see, the rovers or trucks, which are absolutely crucial to do pretty much anything at any reasonable level of efficiency can only handle straight surface. Drive over a bump and in the better case scenario, you will get stuck or do a 180 and end up on the roof. In the worse case scenario, your rover will glitch out and fly into orbit (yes that happened to me personally) or fall through the floor and get stuck 10 miles underground (that also happened to me).
Now none of this occurs very frequently on the first planet, which has a relatively smooth surface. But on the other planets, where the terrain is much more complex, the rovers are just straight up impossible to use which to me, is incredibly infuriating.
In spite of all this, I would still recommend it. There is a quite a lot to do even just on the first planet and the game does a lot of things right. Like inventory management, in most games I hate it but something about how it is done in Astroneer actually makes it fun. The way you move stacks of resources from your backpack to the rovers and haul it back to base is just incredibly satisfying.
So even if this is a "positive" review, beware. This game is early access and it's definitely not one of those "early access but pretty much finished". NO. This game needs a lot of work and polishing. Like I said, it is very buggy and unoptimized but the 20 hours I spent in it were mostly enjoyable. I might even come back to it once I shake down the frustration induced by the Exotic planet.

I followed the Elder Scrolls Online for a long time through it's development, mid-2012 at the very latest. I watched countless hours of interviews, Shoddycast Elder Scrolls Online Weekly and Elder Scrolls lore videos, read the newsletters and "Ask Us Anything" articles on the ESO website. I built up my own hype for this game, engaging in lengthy conversations and even arguments with my friends and high school classmates about this game. I think the pinnacle of my hype came in late 2013 while watching the stream for the E3 convention. The trailer featured the voiceover of Michael Gambon, the actor who played the late Dumbledore in the Harry Potter franchise, whom I instantly recognized and which triggered me to send several texts to my friends, and a tweet or two on top of that. Following that, the coverage of Elder Scrolls Online, and my overall opinion of the game, began to slowly plummet. I was part of two weekends of beta testings, much of which I encountered bugs and glitches which did not surprise me or dissuade me in the slightest- a large MMO such as this was bound to have a good number of them. Coverage of these bugs was fairly brutal, however. But the thing that did deter me was, of course, payment. I have never, nor most likely will I ever, pay a monthly fee for access a game. $15 a month was just too much to ask for, even though I was making $11.25/hr sorting packages for FedEx. Beyond that was the announcement of the imperial edition. I was very enthralled in learning about the preorder package, coming with a sculpture of Molag Bal himself, and a nice lore-oriented  artwork book. But I was not keen on learning that the imperials became an entire race available only to those who got the imperial edition, as well as the any-race any-alliance malarkey. I had one friend who went and bought the $100 box set, recieved the plastic Molag Bal statue, the book, and the digital content, and then proceeded to pay $15 a month of his parents' money up until now. I did not buy the game at all. There came a point where I sat down and looked at my collection of Elder Scrolls games and basically gave up hope for ESO. I wasn't going to buy the game at all. Not even the game going on sale on Steam could assuage me. ESO fell from my high aspirations as a game that me and my friends could play together and enjoy to a very sat state indeed. Zenimax, as painted and portayed by the gaming media, became greedy and did not listen to the cry of the consumer. This sad affair lasted until my one friend who had bought and subscribed to ESO told me and a few other people that Elder Scrolls Online was going buy to play. My interest was rekindled in the game, and I found myself watching the cinematic trailers once again. I bought ESO a couple days before it officially went B2P for $60, the first time I had spent $60 on a single game since Skyrim. It took me two agonizing days for the download to complete, which aligned itself with my spring break. It took me four hours to come up with a name and design my new character and join the game, comparable to my past Elder Scrolls character creations. Joining the game, I soon realized that ESO has changed a fair bit since I last experienced it, it has relatively become a word I use very selectively- polished.  In this past week, I have spent 32 hours on ESO. That's a lot for me, to the point that I should be recalculating my life. But do I regret it? Not in the slightest. Elder Scrolls Online is an enjoyable experience, and feels the way an MMORPG should feel. The UI is not the main focus of the game, thankfully. I don't feel rediculous when I use hotkeys. The various quest lines do not feel linear in any way. Exploration is something I want to do. Crafting doesn't make me suicidal. PvP isn't as big of a cluster ♥♥♥♥ as it could have been. This game feels like it belongs in the Elder Scrolls universe to me, and can be enjoyed with friends and other people. Though, I still firmly believe that Zenimax has a ways to go with this game, I can recommend playing Elder Scrolls Online to people who are as I was- fenced between the overall bad public image of the game and the incredible potential of this game. I just hope and pray that Zenimax knows what they're doing with the introduction of the crown store.

Classic Splinter Cell at its best.
This game is quite good for fans of the Splinter Cell series as well as anyone wanting a good stealth adventure. Beware, you will need to use important tactics like sticking to a wall as an enemy passes by you or hiding bodies in the shadows so that other guards will not find them and alert the other troops. You must make sure that as you are moving nearby enemies that you have scrolled your mouse wheel all the way down so that you are really sneaking so slow they will not hear you. Sometimes though, even the slowest speed will alert them, so this is also a game of patience. It may feel at times however that you will not know where to go (these were the days before flashing arrows to point you in the right direction all the time).
Graphics may not hold up to today's standards but this game is around a decade old, so I wouldn't hold that against it. The challenge comes in when you have to maneuver your way through different areas of a level in a manner so that the enemy does not see you. Of course, you could take the other route and kill everyone you come across in order to move to the next stage, but you're going to want to kill them one by one and make sure that you hide the bodies in very dark corners so that guards will not come across them and raise the alarm.
The plot is good old Tom Clancy: terrorist activities are threatening the safety of American people and war looms on the horizon. It is up to Sam Fischer, a special ops commando trained in the ways of stealth and military combat, and Third Echelon to infiltrate enemy bases and find inteligence, save hostages, eliminate targets, etc.
Overall, 8/10. Great stealth game, but the AI can be pretty annoying to deal with as you may find yourself scratching your head and saying "how the heck did he see me from there?"

Smite. Hands down my favorite MOBA out. Don't be fooled by my low Steam playtime, I've been playing it through their launcher since Beta. I really enjoy the 3rd person view and how everything is skillshot based. Some other MOBAs allow one to right click for auto attacking, Smite does not. I also like how they allow a "all gods" pack for one price, you get all current and future Gods after that purchase. It has mulitple modes, Arena (5v5 with no towers), Assault (Random God, Towers, 1 lane), Conquest (5v5, 3 lanes, towers), Joust 3v3 or 1v1 and a random game mode. Overall, awesome and great MOBA!

Smite is a great MOBA still very early in its lifetime, and already doing things so much better than veterans of the game style like LOL. I love the view perspective I love being able to move WASD instead of clicking. 10/10 for me in terms of MOBA's.

There are very few games as addicting as Smite. Before it came to Steam, I have logged 777h as of this post (funny coincidence) and I will continue to play it into the future.
Why is Smite so addicting? It gives the great parts of a MOBA, without the RTS style of gameplay. I'm not good at RTS's, hence why I don't like others. This has the easy to use 3rd person feel, and it is one of the most complex games at the competitive level. Great deal for 30$ getting all the gods, and the game is in a great state of balance (mostly).
And if you don't want to spend 30$? That's okay! You can get all the gods ingame either by renting for a match or a day, or buying the gods for permanent use, all using the ingame currency of favor. And guess what? You can get a decent amount of skins for the gods using favor as well.
I truly love this game, and considering that its almost the only game I've played over the last 2 years, I think it is definitely worth checking out. Still would recommend this over any other free game.

I'll start off by saying this game is gorgeous and some of the various mechanics are extraordinary. But I'll have to do the same and start off by saying it is having some performance problems for more than a handful of people.
Initially, I was part of that "more than a handful." I just barely met minimum system requirements, with the EVGA GTX 760 ACX 2GB being the primary culprit. I was running the game with Low settings across the board and experiencing low frame rates and extreme frame rate fluctuations during gameplay. But it's an old card, I needed an upgrade anyway, and I had just bought the Collector's Edition, so I upgraded to the Recommended System Requirements with the ASUS GTX 1060 OC 6GB. I now run the game with several settings set to Ultra, and most at Very High, with frames ranging from 60-100fps (with V-Sync enabled to lock at 60). Please note my purchase was not exclusively for this game (although even that is worth it so far), but rather a much needed computer upgrade.
Once you finally get past the horrendous optimization, this game is incredible. The visuals, although using a different art style that have made other reviewers question why it's so system intensive, are phenomenal. They are a considerable step up from Dishonored, and transition beautifully from luxurious interiors and well-maintained patrolled streets, to dingy and infested interiors and dilapidated back-alleys more appropriate for vermin. Gameplay mechanics are so well polished and refined from Dishonored that it nearly plays like an entirely new game. You can perform non-lethal take downs from above and during combat engagements, unlike DIshonored, making it far easier and realistic to complete a non-lethal playthrough. You can now craft and upgrade all Bone Charms and Runes, deeply increasing the customization of different play styles. Combat is far more fluid and dynamic, with an increase in difficulty and timing that feels more rewarding. Powers have more than a simple two-tier system, and can further tailor to different playstyles. Just about any way the first game could have been improved has been done with this, and it truly is a worthy sequel.
Pros:
- Beautiful environments ranging from lavish apartments to infested cesspits
- Wide range of customizable mechanics such as abilities, Bone Charm crafting, and stealth
- Sophisticated level design compatible with non-lethal stealth, savage butchery, or even a combination of both
- Well populated areas complete with unique NPC dialogue
- Multi-leveled maps that let you slip by like a cat, or keep a bird's eye view from above
Cons:
- Poor optimization for a very wide range of builds; ranging anywhere from Minimum to Recommended Requirements, people are having terrible frame rate issues across the board
- Minor audio glitches will rarely pop up, such as dialogue being cut off mid-sentence when other sounds are initiated
- Samuel the Boatman died :'(
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game. However, that comes with a grain of salt, because the game is having terrible optimization for a great deal of systems. When you're able to run it properly, it is incredible, but people with GTX 9 & 10 Series cards should not be experiencing issues to the degree that is being reported.

Splinter Cell, a Stealth Action game very much like Metal Gear Solid, except not nearly as over-the-top ridiculous awesome (although this game is pretty awesome). You play as Sam Fisher, America's resident badass to prevent major world conflict (particularly war) and save the lives of many many people. Sam is a no-nonsense guy who is VERY good at his job.
Story: 9/10
The story is pretty good, a little cheesy at times but good nonetheless. You are basically traveling across the world infiltrating places (EVEN THE CIA) in order to find out more information about your enemies. Sam is an NSA agent, part of Third Echelon, which is supposed to be super top-secret, the kind that if you are caught, it will cause an international crisis because you are probably breaking a few treaties.
Sound: 10/10
Sound is a MAJOR element of the game. The effects are pretty good and whatnot, and "Name of the Game" by Crystal Method is a kickass song. I'm giving this a 10 because the game relies on you being STEALTHY, which means sneaking and timing and making minimal errors, prepare to save often!
Graphics: 10/10
Considering the game was released in 2003, the graphics are way ahead of its time! You use the element of surprise and hide in the shadows in order to achieve your objectives. This combined with the sound factor from above basically make you a modern day ninja with night vision and death at your fingertips.
Gameplay: 10/10
A little complicated at times, things aren't always so obvious, and that is a really good thing. The game is really easy if you know what to expect, so on your first playthrough be prepared to have a lot of "WTF" moments. With everything flowing together so well, you really find yourself immersed and FEELING like Sam Fisher. When you have to run, your heart will race. When you have to be quiet, you will find yourself holding your breath. This game is truly magnificent for its time.
Overall: 9/10
Naturally, I would give this a 10/10, but I have one major gripe. The xbox version came with FREE DLC, which were 3 additional levels after the end of the game. We don't get those on PC. Apparently there is a way to grab them, I think it was supposed to come with a 1.3 patch if you also have Chaos Theory (Splinter Cell 3) installed, I didn't try though. The game isn't any less good because of it, just a little depressing.
I should also like to note, if you are looking at the sequels, Steam doesn't have Splinter Cell 2, Pandora Tomorrow. There is apparently a PC version you can go buy or something, so I'm not sure why it isn't on Steam, it is depressing, so until we get it, enjoy playing Chaos Theory and so on.

As you get a few levels into the game, you unlock grenades and other interesting devices, but they are really hard to aim, partially due to the controls, and partially just not coded that well. For example, you see some enemies about to cross a bridge and plan to blow them up on the bridge. First, switch to the grenades (Q to cycle through weapons) then prepare to launch (E) which will give you a dashed line trajectory, but it's really hard to aim that, or hold a trajectory you like until the right moment. Panning the camera to be able to see the enemies approaching also uses the mouse so you have to watch then blindly toss the grenade where you think they will be.
It can be difficult to gauge jumping over a hole because you can't clearly tell where the ground actually ends. I suspect this would get better with frequent play, but sometimes you hit a weird glitch where your character multiplies and the two of them spasm in place when you were trying to jump.
Overall, it's a great effort, and I see a sequel has been made which I am looking forward to trying, in the hopes that improvements were made, but this game I cannot recommend,

I like the game, has a lot of ups, but has a few serious downs.
The player's range to hit with melee weapons is often displaced from the view of the player, mainly with the one handed weapons (example: Breaking down a barrier to a door is easy when using a Fire Axe or FUBAR weapons, but when I have faced a barrier when using a Lead Pipe or Machete, the barrier should break (a noise will play that sounds like wood splintering), but I'll end up hitting two or three inches under the barrier, which I notice there is now a hit decal where I supposedly hit (along with a noise that indicates you hit concrete or something unbreakable), I'm guessing that it'd be pretty hard to miss a massive wooden plank from 2 inches away from the player's weapon, but somehow you managed to hit below or above the area that you think you have hit.
The zombies that will grab the player can put themselves in unhittable positions. Normally when grabbed a player can swing or shoot their weapon at the grabbing infected to break free, or press the "V" key to shove them away. Sometimes a zombie will grab you from behind or to the side (outside of the player's field of view), and when you turn to attempt to break free, the zombie will appear to have grabbed onto nothing and can clip into objects and scenery (I've had several occasions where a zombie has grabbed me from the side, and due to the "grabbing nothing" position, they have clipped into buildings, behind shelves, among other things where shooting, swinging, and shoving does nothing as they have now moved into or behind an object that cannot be damaged by weapons or moved (cars, buildings, and other scenery), forcing you to lose your progress and any supplies you have gathered because you are going to eaten and beaten by the rest around you as you can not break free. You can earn respawn tickets by killing zombies which can be useful in situations like these knowing that you don't have to restart the entire level or sit out for the round (if you are on a server with others), but still annoying.
Some of the objective levels (starting with the prefix "nmo_") have issues with completion. Some critical items will not spawn or some objectives are broken. Examples:
1. nmo_brooklyn has an objective where a lock needs to be broken, which you are to use a Welder to break open, in most cases, the welder will not spawn anywhere, and when you do have the chance of getting it to spawn (by console commands in a solo server or if you're lucky on a public server), the lock has about a 10% chance of actually being welded off (You can right-click to attempt to weld everywhere on the lock and surrounding the lock, but you'll only do a secondary melee attack with the welder)
2. nmo_cabin, once you have successfully called for help if you are given the objective to go underground, will play the little cutscene that rescue is coming, and you have to get to it. Only issue is, the rescue area is on the other side of the cabin behind two unaccessable gates and a  unopenable door inside the cabin. If you are lucky enough to get to waste time attempting to find ways around the gate or otherwise, that is. Most times you will call for help, and within five seconds the message "The Survivors Have Been Overrun!" will appear and you'll be back at square one.
Besides the few flaws that can get really annoying and some might say break the game or make it not fun, the game is great overall. Tons of fun, when playing on a public surver or with friends on a private server, it forces you to act as a team (it's considerably harder to solo, but it's possible). The game looks nice and runs smoothly, and will provide hours of fun and can be replayed a lot as when you fail an objective map and restart or if you are lucky enough to load it up, there are different paths that can be taken to complete the levels that will be chosen by the game (Cabin has two possible options that I remember "Weld through the kitchen door, connect phone line and call for help" or "Go underground, find car battery, call for help.")
Overall I recommend this game to anyone who wants to have fun and has a high tolerance level for when things might go bad.

SMITE really surprised me coming in, which is getting pretty rare anymore.
Somehow SMITE stays true to the moba standards set by League of Legends and DotA while having a general control scheme more akin to a classic mmorpg. Being a League player primarilly, I still found the game and characters to feel similar enough to LoL to make an quick transition from 'wtf does this do' to 'next I need (item/ability here)'.
The game is more casual, than LoL or DotA have been in my experience, but that may just be because I'm not at ranked matches yet. This works to a general benefit in less people raging, but there also seems to be no deterent from afking/leaving a game when you feel like it since there seems to be a general afk rate of 1/4 games.
The free to play option seems to be well done. 'Influence" is your free-to-play currency and is gained at a rate that will feel pretty familliar to present day League of Legends players, but HiRez also has log-in bonuses that give you small amounds of 'Gems', the premium currency, for getting on 7days consecutively. It's a great draw to keep you coming back for more and the development seems to be coming along smoothly for character releases.
If it's not clear from the above "general control scheme more akin to a classic mmorpg", this is not a mouse-click movement oriented game. You use your classic WASD controls and number keys to move and select abilities, with your mouse aiming your general direction and being the trigger to activate your selected abilities.

The game is absolutely incredible. I've read a lot of negative reviews, but I believe most of them aren't justified. People call the game "unfair" to new players. But seriously, the game is no different than any MMORPG out there, you can't start a character on level 1 and expect to kill level 100 players. The difference is a lot smaller though, I've made 17 kills in a mission versus top-level opponents as soon as I started playing the game, with only starter weapons. Other complains are that it's "pay to win", which is also untrue. Basically premium only helps you speed up the process and get money faster to buy weapons, also unlocks more customization options. Actually the community is slowly starting to grow back. It gained 16% more players just this month, so the game isn't really dying at all. Some districts are so crowded that it gets even annoying. Another complain is that the community sucks and people are teamkilling eachother. Basically it's no different than CS:GO. I still don't know what's the problem, but even with lag I can't help it, but enjoy the game. It's just awesome. Tons of customizations, tons of fun, cars, weapons .. everything. This game is one of those games that looks like a cheap goodie, but it is really just cheap.
Here's a breakdown of my gripes with it:
-Shooting System: For those who have not played the game, the shooting mechanics are the longer you focus on a target, the better chance one has in hitting their target. My gripe with it is that it takes too long to aim, but some players of the game say that it gets better as you level up, which leads to my next gripe.
-Leveling System: If you are going to make a terrible shooting system that gets better as you progress into the game, at least have it awarding more experience when you go into combat. I am not also going to spend time with each of my individual squad members grinding my way up just to make shooting managable. It gets boring and makes the game lame.
-Inventory Management: I have no problem with list inventories and a weight system. I view it gives more depth, but please add a search function to them when I go to my bunker to get something. It would be helpful.
-Community Micromanagement: I do not want to scroll through each of my individual cast to get to the one I care about. I know I can quickly switch between multiple people using F1's community menu, but it gets harder to manage when you have more and more members. At least make it managable by letting us chose who to cycle through.
-Combat and Vision: The combat is alright when I am facing zombie enemies, but when multiple looters come and attack this is when the issues arise. There is no vision cone wich matches the viewing angle of the charater, so when doing medium range combat with the assult rifle. I had died multiple times to looters because I know that they are there, but the game would not render them because "They were out of my sight." I would not have a problem with this if the vision cone was longer from the eyes of the charater.
I had alright hopes for this game, so I was not afraid to be disapointed. But if you want to feel boredem and small fustrations, this is the game I would recomend.

To any RTS lover this is a wonderful WWII rendition.

Company of Heroes has been a hugely successful RTS series that has set a new standard for games of this type.
This Real Time Strategy (RTS) focuses upon the key events of WWII and the Allied and Axis forces. Commanding units, ranging from artillery, tanks, infantry and aircraft, is rewarding with cover use and destructible environments.
The Good:
- Destructible environments. Waging war in a changing environment gives added depth and realism.
- Balanced forces. While each force has its' strength and weaknesses, the remain reasonably well balanced for multiplayer matches
- Graphics. Not of the highest detail close-in, but quite good, given the game's age.
- Cover use. Multiple levels of cover type, destructibility, and protection.
- Units. Authentic of the era, great audio to match and very diverse.
The Bad:
Multiplayer is hosted "peer-to-peer", relying on other people's PC's. Can sometimes lead to lag issues, however, this is not very common.

I am not quite sure why I have never reviewed this game before. Perhaps it's because I don't play ETS2 quite as much as I used to - but not because I'm tired of it - rather, I don't have as much free time as I used to.
I bought my copy years ago, back when ETS2 wasn't available on Steam. When updates were still distributed via bit torrent, so as not to overload SCS' servers. Before we had all the goodies we have now, such us all the major brands, amazingly detailed expansions and all the improvements that have become simply too vast to enumerate.
Even without all these things we now take for granted (and believe me - ETS2 has come an incredible way since its release), I managed to clock hundreds of hours just driving around the main map. No mods, no add-ons, just the basics. That is how good this game was. And it only got better. And it's getting better and better still. Despite all the vitriol being poured out every time a new bit of DLC is announced or a long awaited update slips - we still waste hours upon hours driving through picturesque landscapes, even though we know some (if not most) of the roads by heart. If that doesn't make it worth the pittance this game costs every time it goes on sale, I don't know what ever possibly will.
If you're on the fence about getting it, while feeling like you might enjoy it - just get it. I can't imagine you could possibly regret it. This is quite literally one of the most enjoyable mellow games out there - it scratched an itch I never knew I had, and, hopefully, it'll be around for many years to come. I'll start off by saying this game is gorgeous and some of the various mechanics are extraordinary. But I'll have to do the same and start off by saying it is having some performance problems for more than a handful of people.
Initially, I was part of that "more than a handful." I just barely met minimum system requirements, with the EVGA GTX 760 ACX 2GB being the primary culprit. I was running the game with Low settings across the board and experiencing low frame rates and extreme frame rate fluctuations during gameplay. But it's an old card, I needed an upgrade anyway, and I had just bought the Collector's Edition, so I upgraded to the Recommended System Requirements with the ASUS GTX 1060 OC 6GB. I now run the game with several settings set to Ultra, and most at Very High, with frames ranging from 60-100fps (with V-Sync enabled to lock at 60). Please note my purchase was not exclusively for this game (although even that is worth it so far), but rather a much needed computer upgrade.
Once you finally get past the horrendous optimization, this game is incredible. The visuals, although using a different art style that have made other reviewers question why it's so system intensive, are phenomenal. They are a considerable step up from Dishonored, and transition beautifully from luxurious interiors and well-maintained patrolled streets, to dingy and infested interiors and dilapidated back-alleys more appropriate for vermin. Gameplay mechanics are so well polished and refined from Dishonored that it nearly plays like an entirely new game. You can perform non-lethal take downs from above and during combat engagements, unlike DIshonored, making it far easier and realistic to complete a non-lethal playthrough. You can now craft and upgrade all Bone Charms and Runes, deeply increasing the customization of different play styles. Combat is far more fluid and dynamic, with an increase in difficulty and timing that feels more rewarding. Powers have more than a simple two-tier system, and can further tailor to different playstyles. Just about any way the first game could have been improved has been done with this, and it truly is a worthy sequel.
Pros:
- Beautiful environments ranging from lavish apartments to infested cesspits
- Wide range of customizable mechanics such as abilities, Bone Charm crafting, and stealth
- Sophisticated level design compatible with non-lethal stealth, savage butchery, or even a combination of both
- Well populated areas complete with unique NPC dialogue
- Multi-leveled maps that let you slip by like a cat, or keep a bird's eye view from above
Cons:
- Poor optimization for a very wide range of builds; ranging anywhere from Minimum to Recommended Requirements, people are having terrible frame rate issues across the board
- Minor audio glitches will rarely pop up, such as dialogue being cut off mid-sentence when other sounds are initiated
- Samuel the Boatman died :'(
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game. However, that comes with a grain of salt, because the game is having terrible optimization for a great deal of systems. When you're able to run it properly, it is incredible, but people with GTX 9 & 10 Series cards should not be experiencing issues to the degree that is being reported.

I've played the game through once, as Emily, and I've enjoyed it quite a lot. It's a worthy successor to the original Dishonored, which is one of my favorite games of all time. The new powers are interesting and make for some varied gameplay. As always, there are multiple ways to complete the missions.
I think the game is a bit harder than the original. Playing on the normal setting, I found it more difficult to do a low chaos run. And more difficult to maintain complete stealth. But that might just be down to me learning the new areas.
The story is interesting, although I think not quite as compelling as the original. It's a bit harder to empathize with Emily now that she's the Empress, I suppose. And Corvo isn't the outlaw anymore. In fact, the named Dishonored doesn't fit so well with this story. But it's still a good story, and the environments have a lot to them.
The graphics are upgraded nicely, everything looks really good. The AI is a little better too, with your enemies acting a little more intelligently.
I'm on my second play-through now, doing it as Corvo this time, and working harder on getting a low chaos result.
I highly recommend this game. It's a keeper.

The only thing that is missing is selecting what monitor you want the game to display on, but you can get passed this by making the monitor you want to play on the default monitor on Windows.
People complain about no dedicated servers and I can see why. However I don't have much lag issues and 95% of bullets do register. Speaking of lag, this game is kinda heavy on your CPU and GPU, but I can get by with 60+ FPS on High settings with a Core 2 Quad @ 2.5 Ghz and a 750ti SC.
Of course, there are cons to this game, just like most games. The Exo is wierd in the sense that people will be jumping around, and you will find yourself flicking your mouse a lot to try to kill a guy that was just in front of you but he boosted a lot. Honestly it's the only Con I have right now. The weapons could be adjusted and patched a little to balance the game, but it's not really a con to me, since there's counters for everything.
Controller support: Stellar. Best controller support I've seen in a CoD Port since BO2, and there's aim assist included.
Overall, I give the game a solid 8.5/10. Go buy it on♥♥♥♥♥for a better value if you don't wanna pay full price for it.

SMITE really surprised me coming in, which is getting pretty rare anymore.
Somehow SMITE stays true to the moba standards set by League of Legends and DotA while having a general control scheme more akin to a classic mmorpg. Being a League player primarilly, I still found the game and characters to feel similar enough to LoL to make an quick transition from 'wtf does this do' to 'next I need (item/ability here)'.
The game is more casual, than LoL or DotA have been in my experience, but that may just be because I'm not at ranked matches yet. This works to a general benefit in less people raging, but there also seems to be no deterent from afking/leaving a game when you feel like it since there seems to be a general afk rate of 1/4 games.
The free to play option seems to be well done. 'Influence" is your free-to-play currency and is gained at a rate that will feel pretty familliar to present day League of Legends players, but HiRez also has log-in bonuses that give you small amounds of 'Gems', the premium currency, for getting on 7days consecutively. It's a great draw to keep you coming back for more and the development seems to be coming along smoothly for character releases.
If it's not clear from the above "general control scheme more akin to a classic mmorpg", this is not a mouse-click movement oriented game. You use your classic WASD controls and number keys to move and select abilities, with your mouse aiming your general direction and being the trigger to activate your selected abilities.

APB: Reloaded is controversial, and rightfully so.
Let me throw this out there: I love the game, hence the positive review, but I'm not going to sugarcoat it and pretend like it has no problems.
The game is a third-person (sort of open-world) shooter. The bulk of the game is the missions, which are comparable to modern FPS' with gamemodes like capture the flag, defending points, and deathmatches that transition smoothly through the course of a mission.
Customization: Unlike any game I've ever seen. There's so much customization you can do and thanks to decals you can fully customize tatoos, cars, and clothes with your own custom decals. There are also weapon skins, which are meh, but you can attatch things to weapons (like scopes, etc.)
Gameplay: Once you get past the steep learning curve (which I'll explain in a minute), the gameplay is solid and for the most part fun. There are very few hackres and in all of my 150 hours of playing the game I have not encountered a single one.
Map: The maps are reasonably sized, allowing players to tackle a mission however they want- whether sniping or running in guns blazing. The maps are well-made and look convincing.
Graphics: The game's graphics are good, but not great. They are comparable to GTA 4's.
The BAD:
Community: The community is extremely toxic and unwelcoming. Just a fair warning.
ARMAS market place: The game sells weapons that make the game, quite simply, easier on the marketplace, which you need to pay real money for. Once you get good at the game, though, the difference is really unnoticeable (i play against ARMAS weapons all the time and do well anyways). It's more of a problem for the newer players.
SUPPORT!!!!!: GamersFirst inherited the game and created the ARMAS marketplace, making the game a whole lot worse. Additionally, they don't listen to community feedback and mostly just update the game to add more ARMAS weapons. Recently, they've expanded to consoles, but that's about it.
Conclusion:
APB Reloaded is a good game, but in order to have fun playing it, you have to get past the steep learning curve.
Tip: For new players, don't let the game automatically put you into a district. Instead, click the 'advanced' button on the district selection, and play the district you want with the bronze rank or green rank. The game goes like this: Players who are new play on the green server (bronze and green threat level). Players who have a silver threat level play on bronze. Players who have a gold threat level play on silver (for the most part), and nobody plays on gold. Select your district accordingly.

Although more stubborn players might not enjoy how easy it is to get carried in this game as opposed to the original, the challenge is still there, and any true fan who wishes to venture through Drangleic on his own will definitely get the same sense of satisfaction after defeating a hard enemy or invading phantom as they did in the original. The game's challenge increase is much more noticeable than its predecessor, and some interesting surprises await you, especially in later new games.
In conclusion Dark Souls 2 is a great game, and I would recommend it to anyone who played the original and is a fan of the series. 10/10

Developers are always trying to innovate genres in order to keep things fresh, for themselves and the consumer. A-Men is a side scrolling action-adventure puzzle game which requires you to scan the levels and plan out your actions before you begin. You could compare it to something like Lemmings except a lot more hardcore.
A-Men has all the bells and whistles of an action puzzle game except it has several hardcore features such as, you lose points when saving at a checkpoint, everything is an insta-kill, very low vision and only 1 shot at most puzzles. Now usually I’m into these hardcore style games, Dark Souls and Path of Exile are right up my alley. Now what differentiates those games to A-Men (besides genre) is the fact that A-Men feels very clunky, unresponsive and has one of the weirdest control schemes I’ve ever seen.
To its credit the levels are usually quite varied and have a decent number of backdrops which should keep you from getting eye strain. There’s a large variety of characters who all play differently and you need to switch between these characters in order to progress through most of the levels, it feels the hardcore niche it was aiming for while still having a variety of options.
The PC port isn’t terrible; you have the options of mouse and keyboard or gamepad, which are interchangeable in the options menu. Both are equally janky so don’t threat if you don’t have a gamepad. The UI shows all the keys you can press which actually helps a bunch if you decide to switch control schemes half way. It’ll show you the buttons you need to press to switch weapon, use an item or how to start a level. The options are lacking though but due to its simple design it shouldn’t really be an issue.
A-Men boast great replay value with each level containing a best time and high score tracker plus 4 sub-objectives. You’ll need to replay the levels at least twice in order to best all the sub-objectives. There’s tonnes of cosmetic changes you can make to your characters which just adds a bit of spice to the game and is a pseudo progression system. It also has a large variety of medals, which sadly don’t link to any Steam achievements which is a wasted opportunity. A lot of people pick up these small indie games just for the sake of getting more achievements, personally I couldn’t care less but that’s a large player base you miss out on for very little effort for implementation.
A-Men is a game that had me puzzled when I first saw it on Steam and after playing it for several hours I’m still puzzled. I’m trying to debate whether the puzzles were challenging and innovative, or they just seemed that way due to clunky movements and a janky control scheme creating a pseudo hardcore experience. It’s quite a shame really, there aren’t many hardcore action puzzle solving games, but maybe there’s a good reason for that.

I have to make full disclosure here, A-Men and I got off to a bad start. Once again another game that can’t seem to support two monitors in portrait mode. I had to switch over to landscape, tilt my head, tweak settings, and tweak again, and again, until I finally got the game working in windowed mode. And if I ever go back to the options the game crashes, probably when trying to detect available resolutions. *sigh* Just kinda sick of such poor quality control. A-Men bills itself as a platform puzzle game “inspired by classic, well-known titles, such as Lemmings and Lost Vikings.” and that they decided to “go for clever and addictive entertainment for hardcore players.” Sadly I’m not sure if I could describe this game as being clever or addictive.
The goal of the game is to destroy a certain number of A-droids, androids that look like Napoleonic toy soldiers, all equipped with… muskets. Really not the most terror inspiring foe, and all that I’ve come across just wander around aimlessly and stab you if you get too close. I can’t help but thinking the entire time a single soldier with an assault rifle and plenty of ammunition would have no trouble cleaning up the mess. But sadly no, you just have a hapless soldier with almost no ammo and has to rely on various methods in the environment to deal with the disappointing death droids.
There’s a decent variety of ways to deal with the droids but I’d describe the game as unintuitive rather than difficult. The first few times I played I had few clues as to what I should do. Once I had finally figured out the thought process involved in the level design the game was no longer difficult, it was just tedious. Basically you look over a level, find kill spots, slowly and methodically get your guys to the right spots to interact with things, and kill off enough droids for the chopper to land and take you off to the next zone. It felt like I was taking care of mechanical janitorial work, not some fun, thrilling, life or death struggle.
The game is definitely not helped by the cast of characters and the cheesy cut scenes between each mission. Sadly they’re not cheesy in a funny, campy sort of way. More cheesy in a five year old playing with toys while copying what his dad screams into his headset ‘pwning newbs’ in the latest Call of Duty multiplayer game. I wouldn’t be surprised if the game resorts to toilet humor at some point but I just couldn’t keep enough interest to play past the first few tedious levels.
The game just wasn’t hard or mind boggling as advertised, nor did it feel like I had to use much creativity to find ways to kill the required number of droids. Just tedious, dull, and bleh. It’s not that the game is terrible it’s just… not as challenging or interesting as I was expecting. I’d give this game a definite pass if I were you. Oh and PS: Having a snarky Engineer that breaks the fourth wall by constantly criticizing your game, probably not a good idea. Players might start to agree with him.

Had a rough day? Don't feel like playing a game that requires you to focus? Feeling like you just want to sit down and relax? If you answered yes to those questions then I really recommend giving this a try.
While ETS2 doesn't really look that appealing or exciting to most people, it's still a damn brilliant game. Years ago I bought this kind of as a joke but after couple of hours in-game I actually realised how relaxing it can be. I mean come on, what's not to love about driving around and enjoying the scenery that passes you by.
Plus you can make the game even better with the workshop which provides you with wide variety of mods. May it be graphical mods or performance or something else, pick your poison and have fun. And the kind people of the internet has provided ETS2 players a multiplayer mod too, for those times when you are bored with the silly AI crashing into you and/or the load you are delivering from point A to B, causing damage and cutting your profit, which makes you wanna step out the truck and have a small amount of the well known road rage. But then again... It's multiplayer so..
Also with the few map expansion DLC's that are available, you get even more road to travel and more sights and scenery to admire, highly recommend getting all of them if you like the base game itself. Map itself in the base game is already pretty big but with the downloadable content, boy you are in for a surprise.
After spending a mere 200 hours on the game I simply can't recommend this game more for people who want to sit behind the wheel, tune in their favourite radio station and drive towards the horizon.

I've played the game through once, as Emily, and I've enjoyed it quite a lot. It's a worthy successor to the original Dishonored, which is one of my favorite games of all time. The new powers are interesting and make for some varied gameplay. As always, there are multiple ways to complete the missions.
I think the game is a bit harder than the original. Playing on the normal setting, I found it more difficult to do a low chaos run. And more difficult to maintain complete stealth. But that might just be down to me learning the new areas.
The story is interesting, although I think not quite as compelling as the original. It's a bit harder to empathize with Emily now that she's the Empress, I suppose. And Corvo isn't the outlaw anymore. In fact, the named Dishonored doesn't fit so well with this story. But it's still a good story, and the environments have a lot to them.
The graphics are upgraded nicely, everything looks really good. The AI is a little better too, with your enemies acting a little more intelligently.
I'm on my second play-through now, doing it as Corvo this time, and working harder on getting a low chaos result.
I highly recommend this game. It's a keeper.

I am a huge fan of The Elder Scrolls serial, every sequel offered months (noth hours) of fun and every next release offered something new but still very dedicated to original lore and basic game principles. After release of latest "The Elder Scrolls Online" i knew something is different. First of all, it became an MMO with consistent and ever changing world even more alive than before. That's a good thing but they also introduced the monthly subscription. You could not buy the game and enjoy it for ages, you had to pay for every month being in Tamriel (yes, the whole Tamriel, huge continent with all regions from the previous titles). Many players were complaining and i was refusing to even try it. After little more than a year my lost hope and lost love is back again. Zenimax and Bethesda presented Elder Scrolls Online - Unlimited edition with all that amazing stuff available withouth monthly subscription, until now they released 6 major updates that improves almost every aspect of the game. Trust me guys the price of 55eur is nothing compared what this game can offer.
As a sidenote, all races are split in 3 different factions and each faction have it's own starting area and different story main quest. Crafting looks complicated in begining but you will understand it really fast if you give it a try. There is Enchanting, Blacksmithing, Woodworking, Clothing, Alchemy and Provisioning. Every type of crafting have it's own skill line so you should level up only what you really need if you don't wanna miss combat skills. Every weapon and armour, beside enchantment, can have an extra trait that will buff your character so with all of that crafting becomes really important part of the game.
I could spend few hours writing about every aspect of the game so if you have some extra cash and a lot of free time to spare, buy it and try it. You won't be sorry for sure.

I like the game, but it is far too crowded.  I've done research and I don't think it's the whole FTP ordeal but the game in general.  The fact they made it only one server has not exactly helped it any, in my opinion.  People have been complaining about the overpopulation for a while now and they have yet to fix the issue.  They either need to fix the population issue or allow us to switch their so-called "world instances" because there are too many players either wiping out every monster, camping every boss or over populated the area to where every NPC spawns too fast and you can't enjoy reading the notes or books scattered about to take in the lore without getting attacked every three seconds.  If you want to try, people have said the EU server is dead, but I have not tried it out since you have to redownload and repatch the game to play specifically on either server.  You can't simply change over like every other MMO.
I also hate the fact they advertise all of Tamerial is open, but it's not.  No, you cannot go back to your Morrowind days and explore Vvardenfell.  You cannot explore Cyrodil as a questline, only as a battlefield.  And you cannot revisit Skyrim, except for Windhelm and Riften.  Also, Blackmarsh is closed, Summerset Isles is closed, Elyswer is closed, and many more are closed.  I do believe that since this is an MMO they will have them open as a DLC, but they are not right now, which they said it would be open.
I will be returning and if I see the population issue is resolved, I will recommend it, but for now, no.  I also have zero hope it will be fixed given Bethesda's history and the history of all MMOs when they go Megaserver (with the acception of EVE and Star Trek Online).
