As of 5/11/14 I bring you small pro's and con's. Opinionated obviously for those who think otherwise.
Pros:
- Excels in "almost" everyway (Combat wise) to Dark Souls 1.
- Interesting landscapes and armors.
- Secrets galore.
- Creatures are a lot harder.
- Covenants work differently than before and actually work in most cases (I.E Grave Lords)
- I think the game is balanced, I haven't been killed unfairly. Mostly everything has a counter from Dark Magic to The Havel faith Great Sword wielders. (This only accounts for SL 150 and below and about 3m Soul Memory below). Anything higher and you'll run into people with maxed stats and using every magic or weapon.
Cons:
- Soul memory is the worse form of balance for determining invasions and PVP.
- The mouse Cursor is constantly in the middle of your screen with no apparent fix within the game itself.
- The issue with Lag stabs and hit detection (Based on Peer 2 peer, or just problems server side should it even exist) still appear through out the game.
- Because of optional bosses the game feels shorter, however for the first playthrough it should prove long enough for the veteran player who did not spoil him/herself using a walkthrough.
Final judgement 9/10. I'm a fan boy of the series from #1. I would have given it a 7/10 out of fairness for the horrible PVP reasons but the PVE is almost flawless and because of my Fanboy-ism I have given it a 9/10. Enjoy and don't go hollow out there :).

APB: Reloaded is controversial, and rightfully so.
Let me throw this out there: I love the game, hence the positive review, but I'm not going to sugarcoat it and pretend like it has no problems.
The game is a third-person (sort of open-world) shooter. The bulk of the game is the missions, which are comparable to modern FPS' with gamemodes like capture the flag, defending points, and deathmatches that transition smoothly through the course of a mission.
Customization: Unlike any game I've ever seen. There's so much customization you can do and thanks to decals you can fully customize tatoos, cars, and clothes with your own custom decals. There are also weapon skins, which are meh, but you can attatch things to weapons (like scopes, etc.)
Gameplay: Once you get past the steep learning curve (which I'll explain in a minute), the gameplay is solid and for the most part fun. There are very few hackres and in all of my 150 hours of playing the game I have not encountered a single one.
Map: The maps are reasonably sized, allowing players to tackle a mission however they want- whether sniping or running in guns blazing. The maps are well-made and look convincing.
Graphics: The game's graphics are good, but not great. They are comparable to GTA 4's.
The BAD:
Community: The community is extremely toxic and unwelcoming. Just a fair warning.
ARMAS market place: The game sells weapons that make the game, quite simply, easier on the marketplace, which you need to pay real money for. Once you get good at the game, though, the difference is really unnoticeable (i play against ARMAS weapons all the time and do well anyways). It's more of a problem for the newer players.
SUPPORT!!!!!: GamersFirst inherited the game and created the ARMAS marketplace, making the game a whole lot worse. Additionally, they don't listen to community feedback and mostly just update the game to add more ARMAS weapons. Recently, they've expanded to consoles, but that's about it.
Conclusion:
APB Reloaded is a good game, but in order to have fun playing it, you have to get past the steep learning curve.
Tip: For new players, don't let the game automatically put you into a district. Instead, click the 'advanced' button on the district selection, and play the district you want with the bronze rank or green rank. The game goes like this: Players who are new play on the green server (bronze and green threat level). Players who have a silver threat level play on bronze. Players who have a gold threat level play on silver (for the most part), and nobody plays on gold. Select your district accordingly.

Well, it sucks to "be there." :P
I am a fan of the Alien franchise, and so far I probably quite underrated the first movie, as a slow one compared to the others. Also, I found most of the Aliens and AvP games not to grow up to the movies (although Monolith's AvP2 was very enjoyable.) And now, Alien: Isolation managed to do justice to the first movie, and also prove that you can make an Alien game that is so good that I don't wanna play it any longer. And that is a huge praise. ;)
What I took away from the first few minutes of the game (up to an hour or so, taking it very slowly), is that it is very atmospheric, uses lights and shadows very well, and does not have too many cheap jump scares, luckily. The story plays out in a crumbling, mostly abandoned space station, that looks very very much like the Nostromo from Alien. You are all on your own, and in the first hour or so, not much happened. The game looks great, they could have made humans a bit more realistic, but it's not disturbing, but these will not matter in five minutes because of the situation that you are in. ;)
After one hour, during which I explored about 2 corridors and a room, crawling my way through the shadows just in case, I felt that I have to stop. I realized that sitting in a dark room, I am very badly scared. The game does its job so well, that with minimal exposition of the story so far, just the ominous setting gave me a surprisingly strong feeling of dread. I was seriously concerned how much worse this would turn if the monster showed up. ;) (I might update this review if I find it. :)) )
In my opinion, this game really does the Alien universe justice. It brings you there, where the crew of the Nostromo was, and teaches you a lesson on your own skin on how much it sucked to be them, something that probably no movie could do. Extremely well done, although I might have to take it in small portions, in a well-lit room... :P I very highly recommend this to anyone who likes the atmosphere of the Alien stories, and is not (medically) faint of heart. ;) (Actually this may not be a joke... :P)

Without mods, we wouldn't have so many games we love nowadays. But they have to deserve it, because those are the exceptions that make it to greatness (do "Contagion" and "The Stanley Parable" sound familiar?).
And that's why this game deserves to be that, a game, a release, and have a pricetag of its own.
After playing the multiplayer experience for a while (and in the company of some of the game's developers!) I finally realized that the game I waited for since 2004 finally came to be. An enjoyable experience in both single and multiplayer.
This release improves upon the (still free) mod released in 2012, adding new voiceovers, maps, textures, built on the newest Source engine, new models, and a lot of rework for certain mechanics.
If you loved Half-Life: Deathmatch, love tearing limbs apart with rayguns and explosions, and loved the original Half-Life single player experience, you should get this.
Because this is the reason why selling mods is only allowed in some exceptional cases. This is the reason why only a few great players get into the major leagues.

This game has many faces and it is what you make of it which mirrors the expression what it wants to be. It can be a buy2play MMO (if you'd want to spend some dough on it), it can be a great fantasy MMO with RPG elements set in the world of the elder scrolls along with their lore (look, we all did wish Skyrim went multiplayer).
TBH, i only got hooked on the world of TES recently (again), which is Skyrim and I really loved Skyrim-the mechanics of Skyrim itself (along eith the original play, DLC and let's not forget about those community mods in total) was never suited to be a multiplayer (maybe it could but only support up to 2 people max-which would be a total bummer).
So, in response to the crave for a multiplayer, it did dawn on the developers that they would try to at least please the crowd. Yes, there are cases where MMO have made some good turnaround (take Marvel Heroes for example-now they seem to have a decent enough community going, and rathe rhave learned their lesson from their past actions) and i do hope very much that The Elder Scrolls: Tamriel Unlimited would take such an example in their (further?) development plan.
My judgement lays in the playstyle itself. Yes, trying to fit as much of Skyrim & Oblivion playstyle inside sounds good but that's not how you'd want your MMO to be if it does effect the performance of the gameplay. The clunkiness of the GUI, the first person not being too aware of the environment (because of limited visuals) and many others could be taken badly but it really does depend on the player.
I myself had started with a MMO RPG I'd still very hold dear which is called The Secret World and it left an impression on any other MMOs I've tried to play with. So, yes, I may be not fit to judge this game. But, so far, the servers may need some boosting (lags are the worst) and there should be more focus on the player's interaction (whether  it be with the enemies or other players).
To the Developers: Take a page or two from Funcom, make the playstyle more dynamic (capture your audience)- make the players want to interact and not feel annoyed with other players barging in to make the kill. Create a better reason for the players to want to PvP (giving them enough to even rather sit throug rather than give up with it totally). And don't let this become another cash-grab, future contents are alright but the community always comes forst (because they are the support group of the developers).
And to the players, I do encourage a shot at this. It may be stiff at times (it's not Skyrim), but other times it does compensiate. Don't get too judgemental about this one as they're still trying, but if you don't like this particular game- go play other then- there are many other MMOs out there that may or may not suit your playstyle. And remember, people really did work hard/at least had a smidge of effort in the production of this game.
Stay safe, folks :)
Holly OUT.

I would first like to start off my review by saying this PLEASE REMEMBER THIS IS AN MMO, IF YOU COME IN EXPECTING SKYRIM ONLINE YOU WILL BE EXTREMELY DISAPPOINTED.
With that being said, on to the review!
Elder Scrolls Online is the first MMO i've ever REALLY got into besides LOTRO, now don't worry about my hours as since I launch ESO.exe and not the launcher steam doesn't track my hours because overlay isn't on, I have played this game every night till 5 am for the past week and it's still fun, let's take a look at some pros and cons!
PROS:
+Great Enviroment
+Beautiful Graphics
+Fun Combat (Not your usual tab targeting system)
+Fun Quests (quests are also a con but I'll get to that)
+Unique Classes, now I say this because with there being a skill tree for each weapon type it makes class abilties kinda like helpers, you can play a Nightblade(rogue class) and be a healer so you don't have to do what say the class focus is, which reminds me of skyrim as you can play anyone and be anything
+Neat Story
+Great PVP
+Fun Dungeons
+Easy and Rewarding Crafting
Cons:
-Quests, now I listed the quests as a pro because the quests are great but as with any MMO sometimes you get the repetitive vibe and with a lot of the Daggerfall Ccovenant Quests I got that vibe hard, does that mean the game is bad? No! Not at all, but be expecting some repitition when questing.
-Crafting, again I listed as a pro but it has its faults, sometimes gathering materials can be tedious and annoying, hides don't drop everytime, you don't get markers on map or compass for gather mats like Jute, but this is easily fixed by UI Addons but i still have to list it as a con because it should already be in the game
-Latency, the Mega Server technology is still new so the latency a lot of times (especially peak hours) can severely hurt the gameplay, a lot of people don't have issues a lot do, me i get 50ms in every other online game except this one, so at times fighting mobs can be a pain and PVP is just not fun
-PVP, you get the option to PVP at LVL 10, now even though theres others who are Veteran Rank 14 you scale up to that rank, so if you're LVL 10 your stats scale up to VR14, simple right? Unfortunately that isn't enough as you are still level 10 so you dont have access to skills a VR1-14 would have, so you can't perform well in combat so it's IMO pointless to PVP at 10, until you can have a full build you are comfortable with I would wait to PVP till 50-VR1
-Race System, one of the biggest faults is dividing things up into 3 factions to make the game more like an MMO, it sucks if your friends want to be in Ebonheart Pact but you like a race in Daggerfall Covenant, you can't group and so that is not fun, this is solved by getting the Adventure Pack in the Crown store it lets you play any race with any faction and that was a preorder bonus but its still a con because it gets annoying
-Guild System, the guild system is great you can join 5 guilds but guilds are alliance wide which is again great but like I mentioned you can't group with people in other alliances so why they made guilds alliance wide I'll never understand
All in all I rate this game a 8/10, go in with the mindset of skyrim online you'll hate this game, but if you love MMO's i would recommend this game, I played it during the closed beta and it sucked they have improved so much in the next year and its nice to see the developers actually making the game better, this game has a bright future ahead and I would recommend you hop in and join us.

Okay, this is just based on my own personal experience. I understand there have been a lot of major performance issues for a lot of people. I count myself fortunate that these issues have not happened for me for the most part.
The Good:  If you liked the first Dishonored you will like this game. The gameplay and mechanics are essentially the same (which is a positive as they were good in the first game)  except for the option to play as Corvo or Emily and a few new abilities that come with her character.  The gameplay and level design are the game's strongest aspects with multiple paths and options available to complete a mission in a variety of ways. The clockwork mansion and the crack in the slab level (where you travel between the past and present) are probably the best of these. As before I found the world design and lore very interesting and was alway eager to explore more. Combat is very smooth and the AI (I played on hard) seemed quite intelligent and challenging # most of the time. I didn't get any crashes or low FPS (but maybe I was just lucky) There was a small amount of stuttering a few times but it literally only lasted a few seconds and certainly wasn't game breaking for me.
The Okay: The graphics are okay but nothing that would impress you much. There are definate improvements over the first game but and lot most impressive in actual gameplay but oddly cut scenes seem to be of a lower quality for some reason and there is a very cartoony feel about the visuals which works some times and not others. Powers are pretty cool to use. You will probably want to decide how you want to play the game when upgrading (ie: stealth or assault) otherwise you'll end up with skills you'll never use. I would have like to have seen more options available in terms of abilities to create more customization but what is there works well enough to have an enjoyable expierience.
The Bad: There is not much inovation here. The story and narrative are essentially an rerun of the first game. The maps might be a little bigger but not in any way that you would notice greatly. There is no option to re-visit locations or collect items you did not get initally, and with the story about deciding who controls this vast empire, I would have liked to see more locations and a sense of scale and history of the place, not just Dunwall and Karnaca. As with the first game I would have liked more of an introduction to the world before you are an outlaw so we can see what things are like in good times before they turn bad. There is not a lot of characterization going on. Emily and Corvo are little more fleshed out than the first game but more still needed to be done before I get completely invested in them. The villains are effective in the levels they appear in but I would like to see some appear in more parts of the game and given more developement to seem more of a threat.
Overall: I enjoyed this game a lot though I was a little disappointed there more improvements from the first game were not made. I would give it a 7 ot of 10.
I hope the series continues because I would definately like to see more from this world and characters. In future I would like to see more locations, to show the true scale of this empire and a very different story.  I would also not want to see another internal power struggle, an external threat to the empire would make sense such as an invasion by another state.

The player is set in the boots of a captain living among islands and isles looking like somewhere in the Carribean. You can aquire and complete quests, battle and loot other ships, find buried treasures, buy and sell goods, and upgrade your ship to better models and equip it with looted items, and the match-three game exists only in the naval battle.
The first 2-3 hours were exciting and enjoyable. However, after that the game become old very quickly, since there are only a handful kinds of missions, the profits from trading becomes very neglectable, and the battle are also relatively repititive (the system itself is okay, but you have to do it again and again uncountable times, especially in late time where you have almost nothing else to do).
So in summary, this game feels like a simplified version of Sid Meire's Pirates. Only recommended when you think the current price of Loot Hunter is worth a two-hour-long game life.

I got this game in a bundle a while back as I was intrigued by the gameplay (part Sid Meier's Pirates, part match 3), and finally thought I would give it a try, thinking it would be fun to play for an hour or two.
7 hours later...
I am trolling the high seas wiping out pirates, dodging fleets, and finding buried treasure.
Is it flawed?  YES.  How so?  Well the match 3 doesn't work like it does in 99% of others, in that there are often threes and fours sitting there, but not used.  You have to move between two of the three or four to trigger it, and there is no collateral threes and fours that happen for chains... I assume it is because it is OP, but the documentation is almost nothing, so you can only guess.  Also, you are the only one doing match 3, so it takes turns but you can't really tell what the PC is going to do.
Is it fun though?  Yes.   It has cards, too.  Good for maybe 6-10 hours, and gets a bit grindy for achievements or level 15 (and the big ship).
Do I recommend it?  Yes.  In a bundle or deeply on sale.  Not as compelling at full price.  Sweet spot for me would be 75% off or better (< $2, but I am cheap).  At that price or in a bundle it is easily 8/10.   Don't pay the full price of $8.
A minimalistic game that will give you exactly what you expect for the price you are paying.

Let me first say that I have several hundred hours from the sandalone version, so I've played more than the 7.9 on my account. The game is fun, it's sort of like a knockoff GTA. You can be a bad guy, rob shops and get into turf wars, do fun violent things, etc. The games biggest benefit, though, is the fact that you can also be a cop. Any cop players who see the criminal players doing bad stuff or doing missions can immediately intervene and **** them up, which makes for some good fun, and fighting real players as cops is a lot more fun than the crappy AI in games like GTA.
However, this game suffers immensely from it's pay-to-win tactics, through which you will dominate all other players if you have $20 to blow. The devs tout your ability to customize your character, despite the fact that if you want to place more than a few decals on your car or make an intricate design on your clothes you again have to pay money. Want one of the good guns? Give us money. Want to use said guns for more than a few days? MORE money. Want to get a decent car? ALL THE MONEY. You want to KEEP that car? Oh baby you know that's only allowed if you want to spend money. "Wow our game is so cool and free-to-play."
Honestly if they scrapped all the pay-to-win stuff and just charged $10-$20 for the game, this would be a fantastic game. The core features and physics are strong, the gameplay is fun when you're not being bulldozed by people with expendable income, and the game has tons of variety. But all of these strengths are shadowed by the money-grubbing nature of this game. Until they update to a new engine as they've been promising for a long time, and at least cut back on the pay-to-win features, this game is NOT worth playing.
In my opinion, the devs should just design the game again from the ground up with a new engine and release it as a seperate game at a reasonable price. There's no excuse to not do that.

Let's talk about that chop first. It's jarring, especially for a precision-based stealth game. While it doesn't happen all that often and mostly outdoors, the uneven framerate has caused more than its fair share of deaths, which can be brutal given the stringent checkpoint system and quick save mechanic that doesn't let you lock in a save while you're in combat, or shortly after being spotted. I haven't had any crashes or egregious errors in both of my playthroughs, but this is a level of optimization that shouldn't have made it past the QA stage. That isn't including the often stilted voice acting and script issues, despite the compelling narrative.
With that said, the actual stealth playground is glorious. Both characters bring something unique to the table, and Emily and her subversive shadow powers alongside of Corvo and his more hands-on style of play make for two distinctly different runs. That's not including the light choices you can make (that mostly just play out in the short term), the ability to trigger hardcore mode at the start (no powers), or the chance to collect every rune and bonecharm in the game. At no point does a 15-hour playthrough feel like it contains bloat.
That breakthrough is what makes the technical problems that much tougher for me to cope with. Dishonored 2 tries to take on so much that it can't actually keep up with itself, even on PC. If Arkane can get a handle on the optimization and deliver a DLC campaign that's on par with the original's take on Daud, it'll be one of the easiest recommendations I've made all year.

Dark Souls II, Prepare to Die?
Or Prepare to Cry?
Dark Souls II is the direct successor of the critically
acclaimed game Dark Souls. A game that built it's
reputation upon making it's players suffer
death and disparity, the slightest little misstake in timing
was a cause of a punishing death.
Dark Souls II takes place 1000-2000 years after the
events of the first game, where the age of darkness
was brought upon the land of Lordran. This time we get
to visit the land of Drangleic, we play
as an unfortunate cursed undead, and you have to
find a cure of the undead curse which is ravaging the land.
As a huge fan I was both excited and nervous for this
upcoming sequel of my all time fave game Dark Souls.
Rumors was spreading that the game was made easier
and more casual, something we did not want.
There's just so much to Dark Souls II to write about,
so this is going to be a long review.
Let's start with the graphics.
Dark Souls II runs a Havok Physics based engine,
much the same as Dark Souls, but it's gotten some neat
upgrades and graphical enchantments so it looks updated.
When it comes to the graphics, this is far from as pretty
as Crysis 3, Battlefield 4, Metro: Last Light and other heavy titles
on the technical scale, but the game do have some incredible
design. The world looks marvelous, I had to stop some times
to just stare out on the scenery that stood infront of me.
The huge variety of armors and weapons looks great, the
different locations you visits are interesting and stands out
from each other, creating a fantastic amount of variety
to the world of Drangleic.
This proves that graphics technology isn't everything, you can still
create a really beautiful game on a lesser graphics engine.
The soundtracks in this game is also splendid and really
sets the mood for the different locations you visit.
Boss battles has dramatic soundtracks to amp up the intensity,
dark and dangerous areas has a low and subtle soundtrack
so you can listen for danger and enemies, and Majula the safe haven
has a calming soundtrack to it, making sure that you feel safe
in the only safe area of the game. Except from those 3 little
piglets near the manison, ♥♥♥♥ them.
The game do unfortunately suffer slightly on the sound effects
department. Most of the battle sounds are great. Heavy greatswords
really pack a hefty sound when hitting objects or walls, making it
a believable heavy weapon, weapons clashing against armors,
and the ratling of the different armors sounds good. But the footsteps,
some places, sounds horrible and just becomes annoying, especially
around grassy parts and wooden floor. But other than that, the sound
effects are mostly good.
In the gameplay department is where the game really shines, and the
combat is as intense as before, where quick thinking and good timing
is key to survival. The game mechanics are much like the previous game,
there's the familiar classes and weapon classes. They have also
indroduced new things into this game, new type of weapons,
new improved bow mechanics, a larger variety of weapon buffs,
new armors and finally proper Dualwielding class.
Much of the game elements is the same as the previous game,
only fine tuned and made more convenient. The game is still
as hard as before, and the slightest mistake might cause
your death. The game has been made more convenient,
such as now you have the ability to travel between bonfires
from the beginning of the game, weapons no longer require
a blacksmith to restore it's durability, resting on a bonfire
will restore your weapon and armor back to full durability, it's
only if your equipment breaks that you require the help of a blacksmith.
Some other areas that has gotten some changes and improvements
is the Multiplayer part and being hollow. Now if you stay hollow for too long
your healthbar will gradually reduce as you die in hollow form, this is
because you by each death in hollow form comes closer to
actually becoming a hollow (It'll stop at around 50-60% reduction
of your healthbar). You can now also be invaded even when
in hollow form, making the other players a constant treath,
but you still need to be Human to be able to summon NPC's
and other players to aid you in your journey.
Players can now be summoned almost everywhere, to help you
in a difficult part of the game or help you in a boss battle, making
it more fun and more co-op to play with your friends.
There's now more bosses, this game has 31 bosses, some
of them are optional.
PVP is still as fun as ever, the game features a PVP arena where
you can duel against another player, you can get invaded,
you can invade other players, covenants now have a more
important role towards the multiplayer part of the game.
Reading messages from other players has become more fun due
to the extended list of words and phrases you can type giving you
a hint or warning of what is around the corner, bloodstains that
shows you the last 10 seconds of some player's life before he dies
giving you a clue to what might kill you next, and seeing the shades
of other players slipping in and out of their dimension into yours
giving you a shimmer of hope and comfort during your lonely travels.
The story of this game is played out similar to the first Dark Souls.
The story is told through some cripted dialogue with NPC's,
item descriptions and locations of the world, it's not spoon fed
to you, and you're probably not going to learn everything and you'll
have some questions which you won't get answers to. The story
is vaguely told, and the rest is left to the community. Theorizing and
discussions in the community is needed to tell the full story of this game,
and I very much like that. It makes the game so much more, it involves
the entire community to peace together the lore and story of this game
and creates some interesting theories.
This game brings a huge value to it's 49.99€ price tag.
It took me 45 hours to complete it once, bringing down
all the 31 bosses. After completing the game once, you'll have
the option to start all over again on New Game+. You'll
start all over again, but you'll keep your weapons, Soul Level,
Souls, inventory, everything except for keys and story items.
On New Game+ there are more enemies, the enemies and
bosses deals much more damage and they have much more health.
Also some armor/weapons are only obtainable during and
after New Game+, and after NG+ you can go to NG++ (and so on).
Dark Souls II also has a lot to give you during End-Game, some optional
bosses, getting summoned to boss fights helping other players,
PVP, leveling up covenants and more.
Or you could start over again making a new character, which I have.
This game really gives many quality game hours for the price.

Dark Souls 2 is the third iteration of what is commonly known as the Dark Souls series that started with Demon's Souls which just happens to be the same abbreviation.
The basic idea is still the same, a dark, morbid fantasy world where you are bound to die rather sooner then later...a lot ...before you get to the end of your destiny encountering the most horrid and strange creatures you have ever seen in a DND style setting with a big japanese twist.
All this is achieved by the player without the most basic of tutorials which really don't help at all but make you feel even more helpless in the dark universe you have been mysteriously plunged in to.
Jut a tip from a veteran here...wiki is your big warm friend in times of dire need.
What i really like about this game is how much attention has been given to the different multiplayer factors without compromising the wonderfull gameplay elements that the franchise is now known for.
Thanks to not using GFWL anymore the multiplayer actually works well now....what a relief !
The immersive game and the almost seemless way multiplayer is fitted into the world makes this a wonderfully weird experience. An element which has been the main reason i started Demon's Souls at the time and to be honest...it never gets old.
Sure, it is hard to get to know and play... sure, nothing is really explained well ( except the basics of play ) but that is the whole charm of the game. If this game is not hard enough for you ( a much heard complaint at this point ) then i doubt you will find much games that are hard enough for you really.
Graphics take this sequel over the top and the fact that this time the power of the PC is really used is a great way FROM software makes up for the previous part which was really just a port.
The only real comment i would have for this game is the fact that the levels aren't intertwined as it was in Dark Souls. You can link the world together still but it's just not as genius as the leveldesign in DS was... but to be honest that doesn't take anything away from this masterpiece.

Cons:

I know it's early access, but I'm rating this game on the developers' apparent willingness to fix glaring, long-term issues with the game, instead of only producing new content and features.
At some point in the game, you are going to craft yourself a rover, or several of them, to travel around the game and expand your range of exploration and resource gathering.
Then you will exit the game, come back later, and your rover with be stuck in the ground and need digging out,
.  Chances are you're going to have some bad luck in the space of just a couple of days playing, and your rover will instead fall right through the ground and either end up in some cave you have to tunnel down to, fall all the way to the center of the planet, or just fly off into space.
Rovers have been in the game over a year, they have been doing the above for over a year.
For something that is such a major investment of time in game, and a major part of gameplay, to have such a serious issue for so long, paints a
poor picture of the developer's priorities, especially when the root cause - that vehicles are loaded into the game before the terrain for them to sit on is - shows a total failure to understand basic game design principles.
And despite that clear indicator of technical incompetence, some other very minor changes could go a long way towards either fixing or alleviating this problem, like having vehicles fall up when stuck in the ground (like player characters do, and many larger items of flora), or making the overhead icons on vehicles visible through terrain, so you at least know where they've gone to go and dig them up.

Let me first say that I have several hundred hours from the sandalone version, so I've played more than the 7.9 on my account. The game is fun, it's sort of like a knockoff GTA. You can be a bad guy, rob shops and get into turf wars, do fun violent things, etc. The games biggest benefit, though, is the fact that you can also be a cop. Any cop players who see the criminal players doing bad stuff or doing missions can immediately intervene and **** them up, which makes for some good fun, and fighting real players as cops is a lot more fun than the crappy AI in games like GTA.
However, this game suffers immensely from it's pay-to-win tactics, through which you will dominate all other players if you have $20 to blow. The devs tout your ability to customize your character, despite the fact that if you want to place more than a few decals on your car or make an intricate design on your clothes you again have to pay money. Want one of the good guns? Give us money. Want to use said guns for more than a few days? MORE money. Want to get a decent car? ALL THE MONEY. You want to KEEP that car? Oh baby you know that's only allowed if you want to spend money. "Wow our game is so cool and free-to-play."
Honestly if they scrapped all the pay-to-win stuff and just charged $10-$20 for the game, this would be a fantastic game. The core features and physics are strong, the gameplay is fun when you're not being bulldozed by people with expendable income, and the game has tons of variety. But all of these strengths are shadowed by the money-grubbing nature of this game. I already had the free version of Black Mesa mod and have been playing the Unforseen Consequences level back-to-back with this new Steam release of the same mod with added polish.
So how does the paid version of Black Mesa compare to the free mod?
It's a bit early to tell, but the overall scenes seem slicker with some nice atmospheric fog added to the larger rooms.
New weapon models/skins are added to the paid version.
More NPC voice scripting/nicer animations.
But one thing noticeable was, playing on normal, the enemies took less ammo to put down. In fact, just a few hits with the crowbar was all it took to level a zombie, whilst 2 rounds of the pistol took out a headcrab.
Another noticeable thing was crouch-jumping onto pipes, etc was a lot smoother.
So is it worth paying £14.99 when there's a free version out there? To a lot of people probably not. The free mod is such a joy to play in itself, it hardly seems justified to pay 15 quid for the newer version.
But here's why I did:
Having loved Half Life 1 for so long over the years, I want to experience the very best it can be, complete with atmospherics, weapon balancing and NPC dialogue/animations.
The original Black Mesa may have 'just been' a fan-made mod, but it turned out to be so well crafted. It has given me many hours of enjoyment that I feel I want to give something back to the devs in the way of paid support.
I trust the devs to deliver the Xen level which I'm really looking forward to. And the multiplayer support.
So in a nutshell. I'd say buy this game if you're a Half Life afficianado and want to support the devs, play multiplayer, but for others, I'd say stick with the free mod until there's enough difference between the two.

I was going to recommend this game initially, but one month after release and the developers seem to have gone silent on us, no more updates or messages on the steam community. I am going to split this review into two parts, single player and multi player and talk about the pros and cons. Here we go:
The Single-player campaign - Length: 6-7 hours - Difficulty: Average ( I played about 8 hours of it )
So we get another typical cod campaign, the story is great, altho not at the same level as Black Ops 2 was, your choices do not impact the ending, in fact the campaign is preety much all linear. Graphics are the best the franchise has ever seen, and so are the audio effects, also gameplay has been refined to be extremely fast paced and enjoyable. Kevin Spacey's performance is incredible, at some points the engine is struggling to keep up with his performance, making you wish Sledgehammer would have used live action cutscenes instead of CGI. The campaign is overall a great experience, if not a bit too short, they could have expanded on it and made it longer, it has some plot holes and rushed moments.
Pros:
+ Cool story
+ Fast paced gameplay
+ Great graphics and audio design
+ Kevin Spacey, Troy Baker give incredible performances
Cons:
- No decisions to take
- Completely linear
- Very short, you can finish it in a day or two
- Lots of plot holes
The Multi-player: ( I played about 15-20 hours of MP )
The core multiplayer experience is great, the freshest cod we got in years, the amount of guns is lower than in previous cods but they compensate by adding a lot of customization to your character and weapons, game uses the Pick 13 system from BO2 but improved, you get 13 points that you can use to create the kit that suites your playstyle most, even the killstreaks are customizable. The exosuit completely changes the gameplay, making it extremely fast paced and way more enjoyable than the past cods. At this point, you might ask, what's there to hate about it....and here comes the bad part. They done ♥♥♥♥ed it up again.... Devs promised dedicated servers prior to launch, went completely silent about it after launch, they also keep ignoring all the problems most of the playerbase is having, continuing to push updates that balance a few guns and fix a few prestige issues...really? At this point they seem to have completely forgotten about everyone who bought it, playerbase is dying by the day, already at 5k ppl online/day from the 30k+ on day one and they just don't care about it.
Pros:
+ Exo-suit completely changes the way multiplayer works
+ Great graphics and audio design
+ Preety cool future inspired weapons
+ Lots of customization
Cons:
- Terrible post-launch support from Sledgehammer Games
- No dedicated servers ( game uses p2p connection resulting in horrible host advantage that ruins the game )
- Connection issues on a lot of maps, most people can't ever join certain maps cause of sync issues
- Extremely fast progression, I got to level 50 in less than 10 hours ( not that much of a con, still...)
- Cutting off features to sell them as DLC later on ( also splitting the community )

The makers of CoD need to specifically balance the game on the computer instead of making a direct port, because the laser rifle irritates me to no end. Bullet shots should hinder someone's ability to shoot more, not just show a bloody screen with a little bit of hop of the player's view.  If i shoot someone in the leg, or foot, they should fall over; if i shoot someone in the arm, they shouldn't be able to knife/throw grenades, or even shoot their gun if i get their right arm.  All shots to the face should be one-shot kills, and a shot to the helmet should be like a concussion grenade from mw3, except last for MUCH longer.  I KNOW they where kevlar, but if i shot someone in the chest six times from ten feet away, that is at the very least going to collapse a lung, making it impossible for the person to move, and they die soon after.
I AM ALSO TIRED OF BEING SHOT 10 TIMES IN THE FOOT AND DIEING.  In real life you can empty clips of ammo into me feet without killing me, but if you just had dedicated servers these somewhat demanding bio-physical calculations wouldn't be a problem anyway.
In addition to this, if you are shooting at someone, these calculations will cause the person running at you unable to melee you.  Three shots to the chest will take all the power out of a left-hook.  I understand the exo-suit makes everyone a super-soldier but COME ON.  The physics don't make sense.  The acceleration of someone hitting the ground after using the "ground-pound" move while in air would be so high it would break their legs, it's simple physics.  It doesn't matter that the suit has leg braces, because the force has to go somewhere, and those braces are attached to the player.
Going off onto another point, what is with your perfect accuracy mechanics.  No matter how far away someone is, if my sights are perfectly on them, it will hit them.  there might be vertical kick, but the vertical kick should un-align the front and rear sights, because unless you are using a holographic style sight, or a scope (which i will get into later) you have to  line up your sights again.  It's like you player can keep the gun perfectly straight at all times, where the gun doesn't kick at all, it just remains perfectly aligned, and makes the player's view go up.  this is equivalent to bolting the gun onto a wall which is on a hinge attached to your spine, and there is NO LATERAL un-alignment of the sights either.
Going off the perfect accuracy point, there needs to be a few things: bullet drop, wind affects, and entity-based bullets.  It shouldn't be a ray that hits the player in one game cycle after being shot, it should spawn from the GUN (not the persons head) and wind and range should be calculated every couple frames.  THE BULLET SHOULD SLOW DOWN WHEN GOING THROUGH MATERIALS.  This way, it accurately goes through things, and air counts as a material, so the velocity is lower when it hits the player after going through air, making the damage calculations based on velocity which is lowered by air resistance (having the initial one be set by the gun resource) NOT a preset per-weapon damage-range curve.
Now onto the scopes in this game.  I feel they have GREATLY improved over BLOps2 and MW3, but this is ridiculous, it is like the character can have their head perfectly aligned with the scopes at all times, because if you have ever looked through a real scope, if you are just a few degrees off looking through it, you get a big black circle, and if you are too far away, or too close to the scope, the image gets smaller, and it has a big fat black ring around it.  while standing up, their "weapon sway" is not nearly enough either.
Onto the laser rifle, but more the only thing I want to change about it.  PLEASE make it so the player can't shoot it while hip-firing, because since there is no inaccuracy, or bullet spread, there is no point to ADS with it.  There are variants of this gun i have been victim too which can kill you with a .3 second (i timed it) swipe across your crotchal region.
Net code is another one of my complaints.  I HAVE FIBER OPTICS WITH A 16ms ping, and this is STILL how it happens: I die, the bullets come, the player turns the corner.  GET YOUR CRAP TOGETHER, because that is dumb, and I play PC, obviously, and i don't want a ping scale of 1-4 "bar"s.  I am not afraid of an ACTUAL ping number.  Also, when I first got this game, and this has happened with all of my friends who got it too, the second and or third day you play, you WILL NOT be able to join a game.  The game hangs or just gets stuck while "Synchronizing game settings" for no real reason.  The map doesn't matter.
There are really only two things that impressed me.  The DDOF (dynamic depth of field), which i am sad to say doesn't take into account optics and sights (i.e. BOTH what you are looking at and your optic/iron sign/scope crosshairs are in focus at the same time.).  The other thing is how the graphics look pretty nice without being very demanding, ( a 650Ti can run it on ultra @60fps).
Lastly, i would like to say, this game is not too kind with my computer.  I have played it a little under 30 hours, and it has blue screened me 3 times, made my computer completely hang 5 times (I've had to manually reboot) with looping audio, and has made my computer just shut off 3 or 4 times.

tl;dr version: good but not great, PvP sucks once you hit 1mil SM.
I had high hopes for this game.  I've happily spent 343 hours in Dark Souls across several characters, cleared NG+7 with a black knight cosplay build, enjoyed invasions and being invaded.  I was looking forward to spending just as much time with 2.  Unfortunately, I probably won't. Not to say that it's a *bad* game; it's just not as good as expected, and there are a number of decisions made that seem to imply that FROM looked at the wrong features of what made DS good.
You will die in DS2 many times, yes, but not always due to lack of skill; half the time it will be to bad hitboxes causing you to take damage from blows that did not appear to land on your character at all.  FROM apparently took only a superficial look at PvP in Dark Souls when looking at what to improve; they seem to have looked at the prevalence of dark magic users in DS and assumed "Oh, lots of people use dark magic, it must be popular, let's expand on it in DS2."  Dark magic was never common in DS because people liked it; it was common because it was overpowered to hell, and in DS2 it's no different.  Hex builds will frequently one-shot you at any level, and the PvP meta is full of them once you get into higher levels.
That brings me to my primary complaint: Soul Memory.  Soul Memory is a metric tracking all the souls (effectively EXP and money) you've ever collected with a given character, and is used as the determining factor in who you can summon, invade, or otherwise interact with.  This sounds fine in theory, but there's a critical problem; SM does not necessarily track the actual strength of your character.  A player who collects 100,000 souls and spends them all directly on leveling up and improving their favorite weapon, and a player who collects 100,000 souls but lost half of them with deaths, will have the same SM and will be in the same multiplayer bracket.  This means that every soul lost on a death (which there will be many of) is a permanent liability for the character.  This means that in a PvP situation, the player who's died less (and thus lost fewer souls) has an outright mechanical advantage over one who's struggling, effectively exaggerating the skill difference with  a level difference on top of it.  Couple this with the frankly unbalanced PvP meta in which three builds make up ~80% of players (duel mundane avelyns in harvel's, sunset staff and hexer's hood spellspam, resonant weapon katanas, and santer's spear, or "unstaggerable burst damage: The Build," "Let's play rocket tag," "twenty-foot hitboxes and swinging for half health," and "haha time for infinite stunlock" respectively) results in PvP being far more likely to result in a three-second fight won by whoever hits first than an enjoyable fight.
*note: Couple minor spoilers in this bit*
On the PvE side, the game is... average.  Most of the bosses were at least somewhat interesting, but none really stuck in my memory (which is not an entirely bad thing; there are no completely terrible Bed of Chaos-tier bosses this time around), and an awful lot of them fell in the same "giant dude with a sword" style that got a bit repetitive in feel.  There are four bosses in particular that I have a real problem with, made all the worse by the fact that they're all endgame.  The final boss is, frankly, underwhelming, although it had excellent music and fairly good visual design.  Vendrick is difficult not because of a diverse moveset (in fact he has a total of five attacks, two of which only used at distance) or requiring skill to fight (swing twice, circle right, repeat for half an hour, win) but because he has upwards of 10,000(!!) hitpoints and defenses that ranges from "manageable" if you've collected all the giant souls to "I have 40 strength and dexterity and my +10 zweihander is doing 22 damage a swing" if you don't.  The fight is an exercise in attrition and was very boring.  The Darklurker taxes you a human effigy (one humanity, in DS terms) every time you want to enter the area to ATTEMPT the fight, which is frankly insane.  And the Ancient Dragon is, quite frankly, a bad joke.  It replaces a diverse moveset with simply overwhelming damage and massive AoE, and lives at the end of an area populated with outright broken enemies.  That is not hyperbole: they're hard because of an obvious programing oversight.  Somebody forgot to put a cooldown on any of their actions and as a result they'll happly repeat the same two-swing combo at a steady, consistent pace for as long as you're in range (specifically, I'm talking about the greathammer wielding drakekeepers, which you can see at 1:06 in the first video trailor here.  It's just those two swings, over and over. You take their hits on your shield like the guy in the demo did and you're going to stay like that until your shield breaks).  As a result each attempt at the boss is punctuated by a half-hour slog through the area that will probably deplete most of your spells and estus, although the latter isn't particularly important since you're never going to survive a hit from the dragon anyway, so having full health doesn't actually help.
*EDIT*  Drakekeepers got patched and no longer chain forever, area is now much more tolerable.
Fortunately, the latter three bosses are completely optional, so you can choose not to bother fighting them, but fact that "you can just skip it" is a positive feature of a fight really only speaks to how poor the fight itself is.
All together, I don't regret purchasing Dark Souls 2.  I've spent 90 hours so far and I'll probably continue until I've cleared a NG or two.  What I regret is looking forwards to it.  Playing DS2 after Dark Souls is like a parent finding a solid mix of C's and B's on their kid's report card.  It's not bad, it's just not the AAA result I was hoping for.

Dark Souls 2 is the obvious sequel to Dark Souls, and has the same level of depth, but not of difficulty. I cleared DS2 in around 40 hours, and new game plus, in around 24 total. It's as engaging as the first, but lacks the challenge, not to mention the new invasion system, while refreshing, can be grating at times if you're just backtracking for loot you've missed. You can be invaded while hollow, and it takes the same system from Demon Souls in which everytime you die, it erodes your health slightly. This in tandem with the invasions while hollow, during busy times of the day can prove irritating, as you enter an area and immediately get invaded by "Seph1r0th", who kills you with Dark Magic, taunts and it leaves you with less hp.
For PvPers: Yes, the netcode is still atrocious. And Dark Magic definitely need some tweaks, as two shotting people loses it's novelty if everyone tries to do it.
For PvEers: Yes, there is a covenant to make the game harder. It awards you with a ring that lets you punch people.
Bosses: The boss battles for this game were interesting, most of the challenging bosses aren't actually necessary to finish the game, and some of the ones necessary to progress just felt repetitive and too easy to complete. Overall, if you liked the difficulty of the bosses in DS1, seek out the additional bosses, you won't be disappointed.
Weapons and Builds: Having tried a Strength, Dex and Magic based build, I can say if you want a more difficult DS2 Experience, go with a melee build. If you want an easy ride through to PvP level, then pick magic, as sorcery is hilariously easy.
Music: The music in boss battles is once again fantastic, though a little less memorable than the tracks in DS1. Notably, my favourite would have to be
It really adds to the atmosphere of the fight.
Overall, It's a great game, just outshined by the first. Is it worth £40? That's up for debate. I'd say the original was, but I certainly don't feel robbed for having paid it. Personally, I'd wait for a sale, it's a good game thought it doesn't have the spirit of the original.
Overall, I'd give it a 8/10.

Absolute gem of a game. It'd be a crime not to buy it for 2.50 on sale. It may seem like a basic zombie indie game, but trust me when I say that it runs much deeper than one can imagine.
It's one of the better zombie survival games out there. It's shocking how much content (game mechanics, map size, dialogue and quests) there is in such a small game. There is a huge map to explore, with areas separated by different strains of zombies that act as difficulty barriers. Plenty of loot and communities spread around, with some hidden areas as well. You can capture enemies alive and make them work for you in your community, or kill pretty much anyone except the main character, without the game ending. Almost everyone (except zombies and some generic looters) are named which is sweet. Characters have personality profiles and preferences. Zombie strains infect you via bite at different speeds (how many days / hours it takes to turn) and people who die to a zombie bite can turn into a named zombie, which will be marked on the map and stay there forever when killed (serves as a cool reminder of who you lose). Can build your own place anywhere on the map, plant crops, make wells, etc. but has a lack of crafting (can't craft weapons, ammo, clothes).
Combat is basic, aim at something and wait for the reticle to turn red before shooting for an accurate shot. Depends on your firearm skill and the weapon you're using, as well as if you're in a watchtower or not (elevation seems to confer bonus for you and debuff for enemy, vice versa). It's a bit fast paced, especially when fighting humans, but the mechanics are very solid. Get shot in the arm and have a debuff to your firearms, for example. Bleeding requires bandages or cloth. View distance and weapon range depends on weapons that you're using (sniper rifle having one of the longest ranges and view distance, as far as I know).
Dialogue is fairly simple for all characters, but have a lot of contextual meaning. You can always ask someone what's up (their interests), what's their opinion of you, for work, offer them gifts, offer to trade supplies, hold them up (as in rob them) or kill them. What's cool is that if someone is thirsty, hungry or is injured, they can ask nearby people for help (free or paid). Who you talk to (and how you talk to them) can affect your characters relationship with that person as well as their friends and enemies. Who you use to talk to the character also matters, so just because one person in your community knows the name of another and are good friends, doesn't mean that everyone in your community has the same relation with that person.
There are numerous quests scattered throughout, and aside from the main quests, some of the smaller ones involve fisticuffs or taking out a group of looters. There are some big main quests which have interesting stories.
Most buildings can be destroyed and you can occupy (and fortify) existing buildings rather than building your own (so technically you don't really need construction skills). Buildings have a weight limit to the amount of things it can carry which is cool.
Inventory management is a nightmare without a backpack and fitness skills.
Skill books in the game can be stacked for multiple skill level bonuses. Skills themselves are varied, in that whilst level 5 is the maximum, some characters can only attain 1~4 levels in a certain skill. So job dedication does sort of matter.
Eat, sleep, drink. Some people also have special conditions, like diabetes requiring insulin, or lung cancer, etc.
You can recruit a crap ton of people for your community. It's almost silly running around with a 10 man raid group.
Best of all, press G to fast forward the game. Saves so much time running to and from or when you are just idling cause people are asleep or carrying loot back home.

Love blowing stuff up? Love platforming goodness? Are you a total bro? Check out Broforce! Awesome by yourself, even better with friends. Check out my video review below!
Great Game! It's addictive, fun, and uses great wordplay. Play with your bros for some extra fun!

First off, I think that this game is incredible. I began playing late last year back before the game came on Steam, and I love all the advances and changes since then. Let's get down to the details of this review.
Gameplay: It's very simple- run, jump, and shoot your way to the end of the level. Every so often, you fight a boss. Like many have said before, there is a definite inspiration from the likes of Contra, Metal Slug, and Gunstar Heroes. But Broforce is far easier than any of those games. Broforce provides a challenge that seems somewhat difficult at first, especially to someone new to video games or side-scrollers. You die in one hit, the enemies are numerous, and the boss fights- just like in Metal Slug, can take hundreds of bullets to kill. But you have infinite continues, extra lives scattered about each stage, and most importantly- your weapons are far superior to that of the average mook.
The game's screen is very large, and your characters are rather small-meaning that most of the time you have a chance to see enemies and hazards before you get to them, ensuring that you can be prepared for what you have to face up against next. The enemy has to see you to shoot you, and they will become more alert to you if they have already caught sight of you. This adds a layer of stealth gameplay- insomuch as steath gameplay could mean "shooting everyone in the room before they can react."
In Contra, all of the characters were comparably large- meaning you often had a quarter of a second to react to an incoming bullet. Broforce is more acessible- not because it slows down the bullets or gives you a health bar- but it makes sure that you know that there's an enemy there, if he has seen you or not, and approximately what time he will open fire. It's a bit hard to explain, but there's a definate time period from when the mook sees you to when he opens fire. Before long, you can have this time period subconsiously memorized, letting you plow through levels at record times and destroy everything in your path. The game does have a learning curve, but it's fairly short- taking a couple of hours or so until you feel comfortable and confident with how Broforce handles. And the over-the-top explosions and antics are enough to hook you in until then.
(If you want a hardcore gaming experience, the game also has a hard mode enabled in the options. Sadly, all this does is speed up enemy reaction times, meaning you have to relearn them all over again. This also reveals a slight problem with weapon range in the game. Most mooks have weapons with a longer maximum range than your character, (with the exception of Snake Plissken. Yes, he is in the game. Yes, this is awesome.) meaning that many areas that felt just fine to play in normal mode leave you wide open to getting filled full of holes by the basic mooks. The normally-well planned level designs don't feel suited or balanced for hard mode. Instead of increasing reaction times, the devs could have just added more enemies so you could feel like a bigger badass.)
Sound: The updated voice acting for the mooks and the announcer are very nice. Roasting a bunch of mooks with a flamethrower produces a entertaining cacophony of high-pitched screaming, and the announcer sounds like a cross between David Hayter and Stone Cold Steve Austin. That is a good thing. The sound effects do their job without getting in the way too much, but they do add to a lot of the game's satisfaction- swinging a knife produces a clean slick sound, firing a grenade launcher produces a satisfying phump reminicent of the Demoman's from TF2. And the explosion sound effect never gets old- which is also a good thing. You'll be hearing it a lot.
Characters: The Brominator, Indiana Brones, Col. James Broddock, Rambro, Ellen Ripbro... Every character is an 80's or 90's action movie hero. There's already a lot of them, and every major update adds more. Each and every one of them plays differently. By that I mean that they each have guns that work differently, and completely different special attacks. Unlike most other games though, you can't decide your character at the start of the game- or even the start of each level. Your character randomly changes each time you rescue a hostage and get an extra life.
This does mean that you can be in a spot where one character would be better than the one you have currently, but the good level design and character balancing means that this usually isn't too noticable. In doing this, there are also several intresting side effects. Let's say that you like the character you are playing as, and don't want to change. You can keep playing as them, but you can't rescue any hostages or you'll change. Limiting yourself like this makes the game much harder because you can't get more extra lives, but you can just go for it. Also, there isn't any character stagnation like in fighting games or other such games with lots of characters- where people have one or two characters that they only play. This isn't possible in Broforce. Finish the game twice, and you will have played as every character. And this is a great thing because you have to get used to each character and become used to their little tricks. For instance, Indiana Brones used to seem really weak in the old versions of the game. His gun and whip did very little damage, and if you could have chosen your character, most people wouldn't have played as him at all. But you had to play as him, and his whip let you swing around the level and could stunlock large mooks. He was balanced, and the random character select helped show that.
Story: There's not much to it- and that's actually a genius idea. Not just as a homage to classic gaming and it's excuse plots, but also as a commentary on the unfortunate implications this might have. Regardless of the reason, the members of Broforce are literally murdering hundreds and hundreds of people to get to the helicopter. And when you do get to the chopper, the entire level explodes behind you-taking out anyone you missed, while "AREA LIBERATED" fills the entire top half of the screen. This ironic statement is a small one that doesn't really impede the fun murder-filled rest of the game, but it does manage to provide an opportunity to pause and think about what you've done-and the cultural values of both America and videogames that led you to do it.
Overall: If you like hardcore oldschool action shooters, this game is for you. If you always wanted to like oldschool action shooters but were put off by the difficulty (like me) then this game will probably be what you always wanted. If you only play games like Farmville and are wondering what this is- then watch the trailer. Still intrested? Then try the game out. This game may seem somewhat hard at first. There's no tutorial and no handholding, so you have to do everything yourself. But isn't that what videogames are supposed to be about? One or two people taking on the world- and Broforce encapusulates that idea along with a copious amount of awesome.
(Also, there's a 4-Pack for this game so you can play with your friends easily. Yes, it has online multiplayer. Yes, it has 4 players at the same time. Yes, you can all play on one computer or over LAN. Yes, the game is twice as awesome with a bro to play with you. Yes, this is all amazing.)
One final note- the price. This game is $15, which may seem like a bunch for an indie early acess game. Well, considering how I probably spent 50 hours playing this game before it got on steam and nearly 30 now that it's on steam, I'd say that I've gotten what I paid for. Or you could just let the game go on sale and get it then. Either way, playing this game is worth it. And it's not even finished yet. Normally, I would say that you are buying an incomplete game and you should be careful. But in this case, I feel that I can safely say that the best is yet to come.

Let's talk about that chop first. It's jarring, especially for a precision-based stealth game. While it doesn't happen all that often and mostly outdoors, the uneven framerate has caused more than its fair share of deaths, which can be brutal given the stringent checkpoint system and quick save mechanic that doesn't let you lock in a save while you're in combat, or shortly after being spotted. I haven't had any crashes or egregious errors in both of my playthroughs, but this is a level of optimization that shouldn't have made it past the QA stage. That isn't including the often stilted voice acting and script issues, despite the compelling narrative.
With that said, the actual stealth playground is glorious. Both characters bring something unique to the table, and Emily and her subversive shadow powers alongside of Corvo and his more hands-on style of play make for two distinctly different runs. That's not including the light choices you can make (that mostly just play out in the short term), the ability to trigger hardcore mode at the start (no powers), or the chance to collect every rune and bonecharm in the game. At no point does a 15-hour playthrough feel like it contains bloat.
That breakthrough is what makes the technical problems that much tougher for me to cope with. Dishonored 2 tries to take on so much that it can't actually keep up with itself, even on PC. If Arkane can get a handle on the optimization and deliver a DLC campaign that's on par with the original's take on Daud, it'll be one of the easiest recommendations I've made all year.

Ingredients
100g plain flour
2 eggs
300ml semi-skimmed milk
1 tbsp sunflower oil or vegetable, plus extra for frying
pinch salt
Method
Blending in the flour: Put the flour and a pinch of salt into a large mixing bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the middle, then pour in about 50ml milk and 1 tbsp oil. Start whisking from the centre, gradually drawing the flour into the eggs, milk and oil. Once all the flour is incorporated, beat until you have a smooth, thick paste. Add a little more milk if it is too stiff to beat.
Finishing the batter: Add a good splash of milk and whisk to loosen the thick batter. While still whisking, pour in a steady stream of the remaining milk. Continue pouring and whisking until you have a batter that is the consistency of slightly thick single cream. Traditionally, people would say to now leave the batter for 30 mins, to allow the starch in the flour to swell, but there’s no need.
Getting the right thickness: Heat the pan over a moderate heat, then wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Ladle some batter into the pan, tilting the pan to move the mixture around for a thin and even layer. Quickly pour any excess batter into a jug, return the pan to the heat, then leave to cook, undisturbed, for about 30 secs. Pour the excess batter from the jug back into the mixing bowl. If the pan is the right temperature, the pancake should turn golden underneath after about 30 secs and will be ready to turn.
Flipping pancakes: Hold the pan handle, ease a fish slice under the pancake, then quickly lift and flip it over. Make sure the pancake is lying flat against base of the pan with no folds, then cook for another 30 secs before turning out onto a warm plate. Continue with the rest of the batter, serving them as you cook or stack onto a plate. You can freeze the pancakes for 1 month, wrapped in cling film or make them up to a day ahead.

A rather  deep 4X game based in the 'Star Traders' universe created by the Trese Brothers.
Unlike other 4X games I've played, this one has 3 races of peoples trying to colonize planets deep in space, and they HATE each other.  Your role is the leader or overseer of them, and politics play a huge role in this game.  In addition to trying to build the colonies, research a huge tech tree for economic and weapons tech, build up a defense system and fleets of different ships, you have to worry about the different races spying, going to war, barring trade with each other.  All have negative effects on the overall economy.
There are several difficulty levels, tons of maps, and 9 different races to choose from.  Really good value and replayability from this alone.
Ship customizing is quite detailed, allowing you to build about 10 different ship types, and customize engines, shields, crew training and more (once you have researched the tech).
Ok, now add to this the ability to add one or more alien races to the game, all with different personalities and tendencies (more aggressive, etc...), and they are trying to kill off all of your planets.  Late in the game, you are tinkering with the economy, politics, research, building, moving ships, attacking the enemy, invading their planets, repairing your vessels, and more on EACH TURN.  Quite complex and fulfilling.  Fortunately, there are several Let's Play vids now available on youtube, and the Trese Brothers forum is active and full of helpful players to learn strategies, ship build designs, etc...
While the graphics are 2D and a bit on the simple side, I can whole-heartedly recommend this game.  Frequent updates are the norm with Trese Brothers, so UI improvements, new tech tree options, features, balancing, etc... happen on a regular basis.

8/10 - This game is quite undervalued. It seemed rather simplistic when I first started playing, like a typical ipad-game, and I didn't like it. However, it turned out to be rather deep once I got under its skin and it's got some entirely unique qualities that make this an excellent 4x.
Unique 1: Your viewpoint is from that of a military umbrella-government that rule 3 human empires under martial law. This because you're fleeing home due an alien invasion. The challenge in this game then comes as much from internal strife between the 3 empires under your control and their wish to end your martial rule sooner than later, or even dominate all humans in your sector, as from deadly xenos. If you don't succeed in keeping the power of the 3 in balance you'll see a slew of detrimental effects on the planets affected by their politics, which in turn can cripple your ability to fight off external enemies. Very appealing game mechanics.
Unique 2: You're calling the rest of the exodus fleet, letting them know you've settled. Your population growth doesen't come from new births but from immigration. As a result population growth is out of your control as long as you have a place to settle the newcomers. This result in a very different early game from other 4x games, where there is no value in expanding to new uninhabited worlds just to have more places to grow population. You total population growth is the same with one world per faction as with 10 worlds, as long as there is room to settle the newcomers. This make the early gameplay and expansion in general far more interesting than in other 4x.
Another interesting facet of this game stem from the abilities the 3 factions afford your united realm. You get a choise of different factions to pick your 3, and they can have abilities like skilled pilots from superior millitary traditions. But if you choose to base all your united millitary from out of that faction during the game (to get the strongest millitary possible) that would lead to the millitary faction declearing war on the other defenceless ones. This means you cannot simplify your choise of factions into "roles" based on their specialty, but must maintain a more complex view of the composition.
There are other less appealing game-mechanics that prevent this game from truly shining. There are some rather easy-to-find strategies that the AI simply can't handle. Some of the graphics is unappealing, not just low quality (I don't like the ship models). The fuel and logistic mechanics could be more inspired. But despite all this, Star Traders 4x remain a solid 8/10.

Well, since I followed the development of this one from the early days, I felt 20 Euros (fifteen pounds) was a small price for the workmanship present here.

The Deathmatch maps also look as I expected they would, without much deviation from the formula, which is nice, but there's no Datacore... yet.
If you're looking for a faithful remake of HL1 from the ground up, then you've found it.
If you're looking for something to whinge about, download the free version and be an entitled prick in the community section, either way, I enjoyed it, and I felt no shame in supporting the team for their decade of sweat and toil.

A good game but it doesn't best the first Dark Souls title sadly. After getting used to the mechanics and having a feel for the world you can easily measure it up alongside its predecessor and it just falls short. The intricacy of the dungeons, the enemy and trap placements all feel a bit off and uninspired. You can tell the team that worked on the game changed and it shows.
However the game itself is still worth playing, if you look past some of the design choices (that I personally disagree with) the game stands up on its own fairly well and still provides allure in its atmosphere and ambience. You'll recognise themes, music, items from the first one; but it'll feel a little cheapened because you get the feeling that this is a lesser game that is feeding off the success of the first Dark Souls.
That and the director has some weird affinity for boss fights with multiple targets, which highlights the fact that the combat has taken a blow with the introduction of tracking-based attacks. This and poorly designed items such as the shield-halberd defence combo and the heal-over-time ring make me feel like I've been given a little bit too much help overcoming obstacles.
Overall it's still worthy of being a Souls game IMO and is still a lot of fun once you get the hang of it, but it still could have been a more impressive sequel with better decisions having been made.

This is a typical Match-3 game with some additional contents. The match 3 game is the solution of the naval battles between the different ships of the different nationalities. You might find Treasures, you have to quest, and of course you won't all to soon develope sea legs.
In the pirate genre game this is a weak title, but with a twist... Superficially everything else is put on the Match-3 but if you dare to take a closer look you will find out that somehow in this game there is something amiss... Right, all stuff with 3 or more symbols isn't cleaned out automatically, you have to do this all by yourself - that is the strategic part of the game. If you just match 3 your foe might shoot back, you can stun him by matching four or more of one symbol or by matching several different symbols at once. The more you clean out in one go, the more you'll achive in damage, repair, action points, gold or cannons...
There are several aims to reach in this game, get a landowner, rich, or a famous sea-captain... Wage war with other nations, of course on a real abstract level.
Pro:
- Nice Music, really this game has some nice music to go with.
- Simple and easy to learn and to master gameplay, you'll having a lot of success as soon as you know how this game ticks.
- It has both cards and achievements, both are gathered real fast.
- Trading of loot and stuff included... And Bounties ahead!
Cons:
- The game is at times stupiditly easy... like, oh another pirate? *moans and yawns*
- You think at times you are playing Sid Meyers Pirates when you are on the Map, of course it isn't but there is always the feeling that you soon will have to duell the other captain... which gives an old timer like me a real weird feeling.
- I haven't found any practical use of the land grants... Damn, I want to build my own sugar cane farm... Rum To Go!
- Like any Match-3 it can wear the player off if played over a long period in one go, so you have to take care to play it as a casual game - try to get achievements, once you got them all it might be the time to move to greener pastures already.
- The value for money is a bit... low. It would probably a slightly better deal at two or three bucks lower.
This game is nice to play as a casual game and off course it's a game which might please anyone who is for this type of game. Furthermore it might be a game that interests people who like Match-3 Games, Pirate themed games or simple games with easy to reach achievements.  And then there is the value for money problem, there are a lot of Match-3 titles around, some like Bejeweld are well worth their money because of the different play styles, others which remain unmentioned aren't even worth a farthing - because of different reasons. This game is solid, make no mistake, but some more unique features - like the stuff with the land grants... would have been very nice addition indeed.
