Loot Hunter is a game of questing and looting. There's no story. You start out in a little ship and travel around the map uncovering new ports. At these ports you can buy and sell goods or accept and turn in quests. There are only a handful of quest types. There's bounty hunting, which is taking out a pirate in a marked place on the map and then returning. There are war missions, which call for you to acquire a number of flags from the sunken enemy ships. There are delivery missions which just have you taking x amount of goods from one port to another. And finally there are gathering missions which have a port asking for x number of a specific good, and you have to obtain it by fighting enemies or shopping at other ports to get enough.
You can get experience points and other random drops from the enemy ships you sink. Getting enough experience will level you up, giving you a choice between three things every time. You can get more land, which is simply to help increase your rank. You can choose to get more gold, to help you buy more things. Or you can choose to have peace with all unfriendly nations, which will become that way once you've attacked one of their ships. Being at war also bars you from visiting ports of that nation, though you can buy peace with them at any time. Plus you will get land as a reward for some quests and gold for rewards, for selling goods, and for defeating enemies. So everything is obtainable without the leveling, and leveling up does not make you any stronger.
To get stronger, you need to find or be rewarded upgrades. These come in the form of items you can equip to your ship. The perks of them range from being small trade-offs of good and bad to large buffs. Getting a good combination will help you strategize your fighting a bit. You can also buy new ships at one port, which will give you more cannons, hp, and equipment slots. There are also a few techniques you can learn and upgrade to help with your skirmishes, which can be purchased at a few different ports.
There are also treasure maps you can find, generally leading you to sums of gold. The other bit of strategy comes with buying and selling goods. If you are at a port and one of the goods for sale has a highlighted number, it means it's a good buying price. Likewise, if any goods in your inventory are highlighted, that means they are a good price to sell. This can be used to gain a small profit form port to port, though the stock of goods at ports changes after every fight, so be aware.
Now, let's get to the combat, the thing you'll be doing for most of the game. It revolves around a matching game. Swap the position of two tiles to line up a row or column of three or more of the same symbols. Getting more than three will give the effect a bonus as well as grant you an extra turn before the enemy can attack. Naturally, this give you the advantage in an otherwise fair fight. Matching cannon balls fires your cannons. Matching swords makes you do a melee attack. Matching treasure chests gets you more gold for winning. Matching steering wheels gives you more action points. The action points are used to perform special techniques that you purchased at the scattered ports. These can be very helpful for your strategies, along with the equipment and ships you've acquired. Varying levels of enemies can appear, sometimes leaving you outmatched even with the best ship. This is where smart playing, bonus turns, and luck are going to be needed. And these are arguably the most fun part of the game.
My issues with this game come into play when you consider how boring and tedious it becomes. The first one or two hours are fun. You explore new places, learn mechanics, get new gear, and everything is fresh. After you've uncovered the entire map, bought the best ship, have all the techniques, have a full stock of equipment, and max out your rank, it gets tedious. You repeat the same few types of quests over and over again. You go to the same ports, back and forth. Your gold becomes next to useless, as does your land. Finding treasure, flipping goods for profit, bonus gold in battles... it becomes rather pointless. And it will take you far longer to complete the land and treasure achievements than any others. Plus, with the battling getting so stale after so much time, the game has a lot of padding and no real end to be had outside of maxing out your rank and getting the achievements.
I thought perhaps this game would get more quests, upgrade paths for leveling, more story/goals, more items to loot, more places to explore, or just more things in general with future updated. It has been a while since the last update and even though I asked about such features or new things coming I got no response. This makes me assume not much will change. If it does, then you can disregard a lot of this review if you feel it's tainted by the times. As of right now, the game seems to be a finished product. I got this game for free. It has the start of a good game here. Lots of potential. I just sincerely hope the developers will work on it and make it into the great game it can be. At the asking price of 8 dollars, I can't recommend it. It's just not enough content to justify the price. Perhaps for 1 dollar, 2 at most it'd be fair. 5 would at least make more sense. But even so, it's a steep price for the yet shallow experience. Good for some fun, but not for the price on Steam. Get it on sale or wait for more content to come. Loot Hunter gets a 4 out of 10 for having the building blocks of a good game but not quite making it there yet.

It feels like this game could have been so much more with just a few adjustments. I really like the idea of buying and selling to make a profit, upgrading your ship, crossing swords with pirates and navies alike, and an intriguing match 3 system. Ultimately though it seems like everything comes up short.
The end result feels like a poorly made mobile port.
The game holds your hand on the trading portion of the game by telling you what is a good buy/sell instead of letting you figure it out on your own, or even tracking what you paid per unit. The result of which just leads to simple grinding to make gold.
Questing feels rather shallow with the standard fetch and deliver or bounty tasks. Some complexity or variety could definitely help in this regard.
Sailing in itself is a bit of a chore as well. The game could stand to gain from a mini-map (or even, in keeping with the theme, a map item in your inventory that would also serve to track quests), and landmasses seem a bit sticky especially with a lack of path-finding.
Accumulation of land also seems like a bit of wasted potential. Why not have it so you can use the land to set up some sort of sugar cane farm or distillery in order to produce your own goods?
The match 3 portion has a rather unique twist to it, and this was probably my favorite part of the game, though I feel like this should be tweaked a bit as well. I won't nitpick here though.
I respect this developer for his continued involvement and dedication towards improving his game. He seems to be very active in engaging the players and responding to feedback.
Can I recommend this as it stands?
It's an average time waster if you don't mind the grind, and some might find the match 3 portion rather fun. As for me, I really tried to like it, but is was mediocre at best and just couldn't hold my attention.

Slime rancher is one of the most disturbing games I've played. It features unique gameplay that is repetetive yet strategic. It's graphics are simply yet pleasing, and it relies on the player to "assume the story".
I hope I didn't assume wrong.
Initially, you are presented as Beatrix LeBeau, a slime rancher that attempts to gain profit. With it she is greeted by her neighbors through e-mail, and also requested to gift slimes to nearby researchers.
As the main character, you are told to round slimes, grow crops, and feed them to drop "plorts", which can be sold on what is essentially a stock market.
Eventually, when a player becomes skilled enough, they are presented with largos; a slime that has eaten a plort from another slime of a different kind.
Then comes the horrid part.
When a largo consumes another plort of a different kind than the original two, it gets consumed by greed and turns into a "tarr," a rainbow devil that immediately consumes slimes. The hunger transforms the slime into a monster, and you as the protagonist cannot save the devil inside it; you merely are given water to shoot at it, and it will disspate, leaving residue behind. Slimes that are not consumed by hunger are terrified as they see their aquantances' bodies become horribly tranformed; but they do not learn. They follow them, as a sheep will follow another, all towards an infinite doom of mutation.
You trap slimes and give them food, seperating them from the wild and family all for a needy desire for wealth. You are shown that you must selectively breed two slimes, in an attempt to gain more plorts, and more money. With this money, more land is bought, more power, and more upgrades; but these upgrades are not to help people, but rather help you gain more profit.
You are also presented with doors; man-made doors, sealing off slimes from the rest of the land, most likely in hopes to prevent them from suffering. But you, as the protagonist, are not allowed to stop there. Gordo slimes are large slimes that are one species, and too fat to move. You must force feed them, until the point they explode into regular slimes, and are given the key. It's similar to ripping a slime open for a key.
Unlocking the door expands new lands, new foods, and more subjects to torture.
Slime Rancher is a kid-friendly game with endless opportunity. It features unique gameplay and simple yet pleasing graphics.

On 5/25/17 Half-Life 3's story was revealed.
As I am constantly replaying the game or sections this  review has been updated as of: 2/24/17
Also I have all of the achievments for what that's worth:
In it's current state Black Mesa is impressive. The singleplayer game still requires a little more polish as things are still a little glitchy (Also the marines STILL sound awful even after getting a new voice actor to redo all the dialogue.) but it's coming along nicely and blast to play for the most part and I haven't seen so much love go into a similar 1:1 remake since Resident Evil 1. The weapons really need to be exactly like they were in Half-Life because strangely (And in regards to Half-Life 1 this isn't that nitpicky I swear.) the small changes made to how they work just make them not very fun to use. The combat is kinda dull. Before an update May 14th here is how I felt about two important enemy types you'll encounters remade incarnations: "What it really needs to do is fix the soldiers as they are not as intelligent or as fun to fight as their GoldSource counter parts...". While the HECU's AI in the 2007 release had a jaw dropping aimbot combined with an insane firing rate (which did get fixed in the retail version) before a recent update the soldiers still acted less like HECU (Flesh and blood humans) and more like reskinned Combine in terms of behavior. As of the update currently the HECU run away, group up and spread out a lot more than before AND even make meangful hand signals which is a big improvement even though they aren't as smart as their Gold Source and  flawed Half-Life: Source counterparts YET.
I've seen soldiers try and sometimes succeed in distracting me with supressing fire after gesturing a soldier to try to move up to my position which having check the console was done by  the AI and not thanks to a triggered scripted sequence. Effectivley they will sometimes try to sneak up on you. The Vortiguants now have similar timing for charging and aiming their lazers where as before in the 2012 version they completley missed the point of their Half-Life counterparts having a charge up times. The only problem now is that you can dodge their attacks without getting behind cover like in Half-Life and can simply strafe right or left. On another dour note the Source engine is really starting to show it's age as these remade visuals are ( a wee bit) inconsistant in terms of quality.
My favorite chapter "Surfave Tension" has terrible performance during the uncut sections because it's lacking a few more NODRAW textures and because it's pushing the engine past breaking point. It seems silly to say this after complaining about performance but I feel like some sort of Ultra option for textures and models should be added to uncompress the textures or use 2048x2048 resolution textures for the NPC's model and just have higher poly versions of the models in general. Some of the faces look great while others look more dated than the faces from Half-Life 2 which might I add have aged quite well even more so for 2004. Even with all of that said this is probably the best game on early access right now and this iteration improves greatly apon the 2012 mod version. In Early Access so far there haven't been many updates other than officially un-cutting Surface Tension and adding some more deathmatch maps but it's a shinier version of Half-Life that none the less faithfully recreates it. Not everyone will be able to enjoy a game thats aged as well gameplay wise as Half-Life or get immeresed thanks to the originals visuals like I was and still am which makes this a must play for newcomers intersted in the series or without any new enteries to look forward to.

This game is what Civ wishes it could be. When I saw that they ported it over to PC, I could not stop smiling. It's just got that spirit to it, you know, that a developer who loves what he does gives to his game. Now, that is not to say that it doesn't have its flaws, the mobile UI comes to mind, but, still, an excellent game.
Gameplay: The game starts slow, and there can be turns where you literally have nothing to do but hit "end turn", but the gameplay is generally fairly balanced and fun. The combat seems as if it uses a random number generator to determine whether or not you hit with any of your attacks, however, it still feels intuitive, and the satisfaction that devastating an entire Xenos fleet with four fighters through hit-and-run tactics is just amazing. The world management is quite fun, if you manage to learn how to do it properly, is very well done, if a touch shallow. Overall, the gameplay is quite good, though it's not the best.
UI: The mobile UI seems to have carried over, which is rather disapointing. Now, that being said, they do seem to be slowly improving it and adapting it to PC, however, it is taking time. The UI could be much worse than it currently is, but I'm looking forward to its continued improvement.
Graphics: Not too shabby, not too good. It isn't great, but it could definitely be significantly worse than it is.
Overall: This game is an excellent addition to the Star Traders sequel, and it's only getting better, as it is being constantly updated. However, it was poorly ported over to the PC, and everything "mobile" about it is obvious, and annoying. At its current stage in development, I'd give it a 6/10, simply due to the shoddy interface and obvious port over from mobile. Given continued updates, I could easily see this skyrocket up to a 9.

If you're tired of all those zombie games that use the whole "Oh you're immune and there's tons of ammo lying around 'Just because'" excuse, then this game is for you! You're not 'Immune', no one is. The zombies are actually a HUGE threat, if you don't have a weapon, your only bet is to run away. It takes only a few hits from a zombie to kill you, and no, not incapacitate, only for someone to come revive you, I mean DEAD. There's barely any medical supplies lying around, and every attack taken from a zombie has a chance of infecting you. Once the infection is in your system, it's staying there. You can take pills you find to extend the amount of time you have before it takes you, but a cure? Nope. You're stuck with the infection. And weapons and ammo are more scarce than a TF2 drop. If you get your hands on a gun and some ammo, you better aim like your life depends on it, because it does. And while melee weapons are ammo-less, they require you to get up close, so be careful. It's much better than most zombie games, simply due to how realistic it is. If a zombie apocalypse really DID come around (Which it won't), this game would be by far the closest thing to it.

We can't buy Richard Burns Rally anymore, but we can buy this instead. It's not exactly a simulation (even on "simulation" mode), but it is a ton of fun. The physics are based in reality, and you can use all of the standard techniques to induce oversteer. It's a bit easy to go sideways, especially in a FWD car, but not glaringly unrealistic. I am not a rally driver, but I checked the FWD performance against Live For Speed (an acknowledged "realistic" sim) on its rallycross tracks, and I was able to get a similar FWD car (the Mini clone) to oversteer using throttle liftoff and brake, just like I was doing in Xpand. One funny thing is that you seem to be able to do powerslides in FWD cars in Xpand, which is obviously unrealistic. But that's fine, I just imagine that the FWD cars are AWD. The bottom line is that the physics are authentic enough that you can use the instincts you have developed in sims and have fun doing it.
Apart from physics and realism, the game is just a lot of fun to play. I have played the first stage about a dozen times, just because it's really fun. If you do nothing but play that first race, it will be more than worth the price. The stage design is one of the best things about this game: the stages are all completely crazy, with lots of tight turns and elevation changes keeping you on your toes without being unrealistic. And unlike many newer games, you don't have to sit through cutscenes, tutorials, and boring intro missions to get to the gameplay. Thankfully, you just turn it on and go right to the good part (the sideways racing).
It is an old game, so you will have to edit a configuration file if you want full 1080p resolution and 144Hz refresh rate, but it's easy. The file you're looking for is called VideoSettings.scr, and it's located in the Xpand Rally\Data folder. The settings in the file are clearly labeled and self-explanatory. Have fun!
Edit: This game has a crazy difficulty curve. Don't try to drive insanely "at the limit," because some very strange things can happen with the physics at the limit. Instead, upgrade your car and drive carefully according to the pacenotes. Still a fun game and worth $5.

I started playing SMITE during their beta phase, I played both LoL and Smite for quite some time but ultimately sticking with League just because most of my friends didn't want to make the switch to SMITE at that time even though I did.
Let me put it that way:
From a pure gaming standpoint: Is it "better" than League? No. It's not as well thought through into the last detail, it's not quite as balanced and tactical decisions are not as deep and impactful as in other MOBAs.
From an aesthetic standpoint: Is it better than League? No. Riot has better artists than Hi-Rez. Hands down.
Is it more fun to play SMITE than any other MOBA? Absolutely.
Why? Well,
1) The community isn't quite as toxic as in League or other MOBAs I have played. Sure I have been wished to get cancer and been asked to deinstall the game, but the density of REALLY badly behaved players is lower than in other games of that genre.
2) Community support. Riot please! While it is sometimes hard to understand the decisions of other game companies and how they treat their communities, HiRez is doing a pretty good job giving the players what they want.
3) Diversity: While Riot announces "featured game modes" a month before they come out and then have them run for two weeks and make a whole fuzz about it, there is a new featured game mode every couple of days in SMITE, usually suggested by the community via Twitter. Remember when millions of players wanted the "ultra-rapid-fire mode" in League back and had to beg in every way shape and form for a whole year before Riot made it available again for 2 weeks? Yeah ... with HiRez you just tweet them...
Summary: If you are sick of the community and poor support in League of Legends, this game is for you.

Dark Souls II is a fantastic game, one that you'll find yourself spending countless hours playing through and then replaying on New Game+.
When comparing it to its predecessors, i'd say its a cross between both Dark Souls & Demon Souls. The layout of the world is in such a way that it isn't so finely compressed and weaved together like Dark Souls, but neither is it as spacious and large as Demon Souls. The game itself doesn't necessarily match the lore and story of Dark Souls, but there are many interesting things to learn through items and progression throughout the game. I've read alot of people complaining about boss fights, and although i will admit i didn't necessarily find them as memorable as those in Dark Souls I, they are nonetheless challenging and unique for the most part.
As a standalone game, it is easily a 9/10, if not 10/10. For such a high rating you'll be expecting to get alot from the game, and you do. Not only, as mentioned earlier is there a vast amount of replayability in the game but the simplicity of mulitplayer and the features it offers will also add to your game time; whether you want to invade worlds, duel other players or engage in 'jolly co-operation', you'll enjoy every minute of it.
For those people who are new to the Franchise, never fear! The tutorial at the start of the game is much more fleshed out than in Dark Souls, therefore you won't find yourself necessarily stuck at an early section of the game for too long, as long as you have a decent amount of common sense.
With regards difficulty, if you're a person who enjoys a good challenge, i'd say for the most part play alone, or at least try not to summon in Players for boss fights. I say this simply because for most bosses (Exceptions being Smelter Demon etc.) grouping with 2 players will make the game so much more easier, and while it's fun to do so it does take away a large portion of the challenge you're faced with. Then again, this isn't a flaw because it's up to you whether you do summon or not.
You'll also find yourself putting in alot of time into Dark Souls, and the RPG elements and character customization through armour, weapons and stats are nicely done. You can adapt your character to your playstyle, and this is a nice feature as it adds a unique feeling to each encounter with other players. Quite surprisingly you'll find that players really do vary in classes and armour when grouping up, and from what i've played so far no one character feels OP in every situation compared to another (Of course some classes are better suited to certain situations).
Graphically the game is good looking albeit nothing special. There are mods out there which improve lighting and other aspects, but the game is pretty enough to draw you into the many lands you'll find yourself exploring, but don't expect gorgeous scenery (which i will say there is) and the such. The graphics are meant to feel quite dark and monotone in parts, as this is a world full of undead and sorrow.
Overall Dark Souls II is worth a buy, whether you're new to the franchise or not. The gameplay, replayabiltiy and multiplayer segments of the game are a joy. So, what are you waiting for? I'll see you in-game!

4X Empires is exactly what I expected from developers like the Trese Brothers. Following the success from their previous titles Star Traders and Templar Assault, 4X Empires builds upon the lore of the Star Traders Universe by giving the player a completely new perspective on the deeply enriched story previously told.
This game is played in the perspective of the venerable Templars, protectorate of the bickering factions and guardians of the quadrant. As such, you are unable to directly control the factions and their politics, only what they build, what they research, and when. The politics system is a formidible beast, and truly gives the player the feeling that the Templars are not completely in control. It is this politics system that makes the game unique, and at times, infuriating. I have lost several games solely because the warring factions would rather fight amongst themselves than band together to fight the Xeno scourge.
Gameplay can be slow at times, but it is only because empire building takes time. Time that the player does not always have. The Xeno are always waiting just outside the field of vision, building their own empires to combat your own. The different types of Xeno make each of them unique in their own right. Some are slow to build up, but release extremely powerful ships into the quadrant, others expand at reckless paces, their factories spewing out hoardes of assault craft. Still others deal tremendous amounts of damage through radiation technology, which bypasses conventional armors to wreak havoc on your forces and systems. Still more exist in the quadrant, and each of them difficult in their own rights.
Fortunately for the player, a rich, complex, and infinitely customizable ship builder has been implemented, and hundreds if not thousads of ship configurations are possible, some more effective than others. System upgrades can provide valuable defensive structures that help a beseiged system hold their own until help arrives. The ship builder is honestly the crown jewel of this  game, as the designs made, the amount of ships created, and how you deploy them in the quadrant will MAKE or BREAK your game. But one can never lust for too much power, as the upkeep cost of the ships and every other system upgrade must be kept in balance with the amount of income your factions can create.
If you enjoy 4X games, dont mind a slower pace, but truly want a deeply satisfying gameplay that fully delivers on its promises, look no further than Star Traders: 4X Empires. Not only does the new and improved tutorial give you the basics of the game, the Trese Brothers have an amazing forum set up, and are 100% involved, answering any question you may have, here at
If anyone deserves your time and patronage, it is Trese Brothers Games, happy hunting!!

This game plays like many of the older TBS games, like Alpha Centauri, and its ilk. It has a vast tree of technology that progresses pretty intuitively, but the controls and gameplay itself is rather hard to master.
Once you figure out the basics and get an understanding of how the game progresses and works, It becomes easier to work through the game.
It essentially centers around colonizing planets that then become their own centers of production. Each planet has a "quality rating" that determines its potential for use. Lower quality planets will end up being burdens on your empire, while high quality planets will be the center for constructing your fleets and providing income.
Planets have a "resource" called population that is not so much usable, but must be managed to keep the empire from falling apart. Higher populations require more management to keep happy, but come in handy to protect planets from capture.
One you figure out that you can research higher levels of buildings for your colonies, the game becomes significantly easier to manage the lower quality planets, and to capitalize off of the higher quality planets.
The game generally culminates in a match to invade and bombard each others planets, with the option to completely destroy the planet (by reducing it's Quality rating), or by reducing the planet's population to zero. You have three invasion options: Bombard (which has a high chance of lowering quality), Invade {which has a low chance of lowering quality), and Scout {Which may not always lower population, but never reduces quality!). Systems recover 1 population per turn, so to actually capture a system, you have to really have a big fleet.
The game is clever and addictive, and overall I suggest it to any fans of the old Sid Meyer's stuff.
